signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: What is a heart murmur?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back: The sound of turbulent blood flow across the heart or great vessels. It may be innocent (flow) or pathological (structural valve/septal lesion). The clinical task is to distinguish the two and decide who needs an echo.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: List the features you assess when characterising a murmur.
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back:
• Timing (systolic/diastolic/continuous),
  • Site of maximal intensity + Radiation,
  • Character/pitch,
  • Intensity (Levine grade 1-6),
  • relation to Respiration and dynamic manoeuvres, and
  • Associated signs (pulse, apex, added sounds, features of heart failure/endocarditis).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: Which timings of murmur are ALWAYS pathological?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back: A PURELY DIASTOLIC murmur is always pathological — there is no such thing as an innocent one. A continuous murmur is nearly always pathological too, but there are TWO innocent exceptions: a venous hum in a child and a mammary souffle in late pregnancy or lactation. Systolic murmurs may be either.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: Define the Levine grading scale for murmur intensity.
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back:
• Grade 1 = very faint, only heard with effort;
  • 2 = soft but readily audible;
  • 3 = loud, no thrill;
  • 4 = loud WITH a palpable thrill;
  • 5 = very loud, audible with stethoscope edge on chest;
  • 6 = audible with stethoscope off the chest.
A thrill means grade ≥4.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: What is a thrill and what does it imply about grade?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back: A thrill is a palpable vibration over the precordium from a loud murmur. Its presence means the murmur is at least grade 4/6 and therefore always pathological.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: What are the classic features of an innocent (flow) murmur?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back:
• Soft (≤2/6),
  • systolic,
  • asymptomatic,
  • no radiation,
  • no thrill,
  • normal S1/S2,
  • varies with posture, and
  • no other cardiovascular abnormality.
Common in children, pregnancy, fever, anaemia and hyperthyroidism (high-output states).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: Which red flags around a murmur mandate an echo and cardiology referral?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back:
• Any diastolic murmur, or a continuous murmur you cannot abolish at the bedside;
  • a loud (≥3/6) or radiating murmur, or a thrill;
  • symptoms (syncope, exertional chest pain or dyspnoea);
  • an abnormal ECG or CXR;
  • and signs of heart failure or infective endocarditis.
In an adult, add age over 75, AF or an abnormal second heart sound.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: Describe the murmur of aortic stenosis.
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back: Ejection-systolic murmur, loudest at the right 2nd intercostal space, radiating to the carotids. Louder sitting forward in expiration. Associated: slow-rising (plateau) pulse, narrow pulse pressure, soft/absent S2, heaving apex.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: Which triad of symptoms indicates severe aortic stenosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back: Syncope, Angina and Dyspnoea (SAD) - exertional symptoms mark severe/critical AS and carry a poor prognosis if untreated.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: Describe the murmur of mitral regurgitation.
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back: Pansystolic murmur, loudest at the apex, radiating to the axilla. Louder on expiration (left-sided). Associated: soft S1, thrusting/displaced apex; may have a third heart sound.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: Describe the murmur of aortic regurgitation.
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back: Early-diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge, best heard with the patient sitting forward in held expiration. Associated: collapsing (water-hammer) pulse, wide pulse pressure, and eponymous signs (Corrigan's, de Musset's, Quincke's).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: Name three eponymous peripheral signs of aortic regurgitation.
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back:
• Corrigan's sign (visible carotid pulsation),
  • de Musset's sign (head bobbing with each beat),
  • Quincke's sign (nail-bed capillary pulsation).
All reflect the wide pulse pressure / collapsing pulse of AR.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: Describe the murmur of mitral stenosis.
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back: Mid-diastolic rumble with an opening snap, loudest at the apex, best heard in the left lateral position using the bell. Associated: loud S1, atrial fibrillation, and malar flush.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: Describe the murmur of tricuspid regurgitation.
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back: Pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge, louder on INSPIRATION (right-sided). Associated: giant V waves in the JVP and a pulsatile, enlarged liver.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: Describe the murmur of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM).
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back: Ejection-systolic murmur at the left sternal edge that gets LOUDER with Valsalva/standing (decreased preload) and SOFTER on squatting. Consider in a young person or athlete presenting with exertional syncope.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: Describe the murmur of a ventricular septal defect (VSD).
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back: A harsh pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge, often with a thrill; louder on handgrip. A smaller defect can paradoxically produce a louder murmur.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: Describe the murmur of a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA).
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back: A continuous 'machinery' murmur at the left upper sternal edge/infraclavicular area, running through S2, with a wide pulse pressure. It is pathological — and the key bedside step is to show it is NOT a venous hum, which would disappear on lying the child flat, turning the head, or compressing the jugular vein.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: What does the mnemonic RILE describe?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back:
Which manoeuvre accentuates which murmurs by laterality:
  • Right-sided murmurs are louder on Inspiration;
  • Left-sided murmurs are louder on Expiration.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: Why does inspiration accentuate right-sided murmurs?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back: Inspiration reduces intrathoracic pressure, increasing venous return to the right heart. This raises flow across right-sided (tricuspid/pulmonary) valves, making those murmurs louder (RILE).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: How do Valsalva and standing affect murmurs?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back: They reduce venous return (decreased preload). This INCREASES the murmur of HOCM (and mitral valve prolapse) and DECREASES most other murmurs, including aortic stenosis.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: How do squatting and handgrip affect murmurs — and why are they not the same test?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back:
They are often lumped together but differ.
  • SQUATTING raises both preload and afterload: it quietens HOCM and increases MR, AR, VSD and AS.
  • HANDGRIP is the pure afterload test: it increases MR, AR and VSD, quietens HOCM, and changes AS little — which is how you separate AS from MR at the bedside.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: What is the single key investigation for characterising a murmur/valve lesion?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back: Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) - it identifies the lesion, quantifies severity/grade, and assesses ventricular function. Transoesophageal echo (TOE) is used for poor windows, prosthetic valves or suspected endocarditis.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: What baseline investigations accompany the assessment of a pathological murmur?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back:
• ECG (LVH in AS/AR, P-mitrale and AF in MS, RVH),
  • CXR (valve calcification, cardiomegaly, pulmonary congestion), and
  • bloods including FBC and TFTs for high-output causes.
Echo is the definitive test.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: A patient has a NEW murmur and fever. What must you think of and do?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back: Infective endocarditis until proven otherwise. Take blood cultures BEFORE antibiotics and arrange echocardiography, then apply the Duke criteria. Three sets from separate sites over 24 hours if the picture is subacute — but if the patient is acutely septic, two sets within an hour and then start antibiotics; do not delay treatment to complete three.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: Which high-output states commonly cause innocent/flow murmurs?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back:
• Pregnancy,
  • fever,
  • anaemia and
  • hyperthyroidism (thyrotoxicosis).
Increased flow across a normal valve produces a soft systolic murmur; check FBC and TFTs.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: Describe Still's murmur in children.
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back: The commonest innocent murmur of childhood: a soft, systolic, musical/vibratory ('twangy') murmur at the left sternal edge that varies with posture. No radiation, thrill or symptoms - reassure, no echo needed if features are clearly innocent.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: Which paediatric murmur features are red flags mandating referral?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back:
• A diastolic murmur,
  • a pansystolic murmur,
  • a loud murmur or thrill,
  • associated symptoms, and
  • abnormal pulses (e.g. radiofemoral delay suggesting coarctation of the aorta).
These warrant paediatric cardiology assessment and echo.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: How does the pulse character help differentiate aortic valve lesions?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back:
• Aortic stenosis gives a slow-rising (plateau), low-volume pulse with a narrow pulse pressure;
  • aortic regurgitation gives a collapsing (water-hammer), high-volume pulse with a wide pulse pressure.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: Where do aortic stenosis and mitral regurgitation murmurs radiate?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back:
• Aortic stenosis radiates to the carotids;
  • mitral regurgitation radiates to the axilla.
Radiation is a useful clue that a systolic murmur is pathological.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: Summarise the decisive fork when a murmur is heard.
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back: Is it innocent (soft ≤2/6, systolic, asymptomatic, no radiation or thrill, normal S1/S2, varies with posture) or does it carry a red flag (diastolic, loud/thrill, radiating, symptomatic, abnormal ECG/CXR, heart failure or fever)? Innocent = reassure; anything else = echo and refer. Note 'innocent' is a much weaker category in adults than in children — a newly heard murmur in an older adult usually earns an echo.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: What ECG and imaging changes support mitral stenosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back:
• ECG shows P-mitrale (bifid P waves from left atrial enlargement) and often atrial fibrillation;
  • CXR shows left atrial enlargement (double right heart border, splayed carina).
Echo confirms the diagnosis and grades severity.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.front: Which murmur is louder in the left lateral position with the bell, and why?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.back: Mitral stenosis - the left lateral decubitus position brings the apex closer to the chest wall, and the bell best transmits the low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble. AR is instead best heard sitting forward in expiration.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: Where is the apex beat normally palpated?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back: 5th intercostal space, mid-clavicular line. It is the most inferolateral point at which the cardiac impulse is palpable.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: A laterally and inferiorly displaced (“down & out”) apex beat indicates what?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back:
LV dilatation — volume overload or failure:
  • aortic/mitral regurgitation,
  • dilated cardiomyopathy,
  • chronic heart failure.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: What does a heaving (sustained, forceful, NOT displaced) apex beat indicate?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back: LV pressure overload — aortic stenosis or hypertension (LV hypertrophy).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: What does a thrusting (diffuse, displaced, hyperdynamic) apex beat indicate?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back: LV volume overload — aortic regurgitation, mitral regurgitation.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: What is a tapping apex beat and what does it signify?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back: A palpable loud first heart sound — the classic sign of mitral stenosis.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: A double apical impulse suggests which diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back: A double apical impulse points to HOCM (LVOT obstruction, often with a palpable presystolic S4). A palpable S4 alone also doubles the impulse in any stiff, hypertrophied LV (LVH, aortic stenosis, hypertension) — distinguish HOCM by an ejection systolic murmur that gets louder on Valsalva.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: A dyskinetic apex beat after a myocardial infarction suggests?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back: Left-ventricular aneurysm (often with persistent ST elevation on ECG).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: List causes of an impalpable apex beat.
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back:
• Obesity,
  • COPD / lung hyperinflation,
  • pericardial effusion,
  • a thick chest wall, and
  • dextrocardia (apex impalpable on the left but palpable on the right).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: A displaced apex beat WITH a deviated trachea and acute breathlessness suggests what (non-cardiac)?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back: Mediastinal shift — tension pneumothorax or a large pleural effusion — an emergency, not a cardiac cause.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: What must you exclude before documenting an apex beat as ‘displaced’?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back: Dextrocardia — and confirm the tracheal position; the impulse may simply be shifted by lung/mediastinal pathology.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: What is the definitive investigation for any abnormal apex beat?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back: Echocardiography — chamber size, wall thickness, valve lesions, ejection fraction and regional wall motion.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: What ECG finding would you expect with a heaving apex beat?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back: Left ventricular hypertrophy (e.g. Sokolow–Lyon voltage criteria).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: What is a palpable thrill at the apex, and what does it imply?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back: A palpable murmur — a haemodynamically significant lesion. A systolic apical thrill suggests severe mitral regurgitation; a diastolic apical thrill suggests mitral stenosis.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: Which CXR sign corresponds to a displaced apex beat from LV dilatation?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back: Cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio >0.5).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: What is a left parasternal heave, and what does it signify?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back: A sustained lift felt with the heel of the hand at the left sternal edge → right ventricular pressure/volume overload (pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale, pulmonary stenosis, large ASD). It is distinct from the apex, which is the localised inferolateral impulse.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: How do you re-examine an apex beat that seems impalpable, and why?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back: Roll the patient into the left lateral decubitus position and palpate in held expiration. This recovers a difficult apex and accentuates the tapping apex and diastolic thrill of mitral stenosis.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: The apex and trachea are both shifted — how does the direction distinguish the cause?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back:
• Shifted away from a side = pushed (tension pneumothorax, large pleural effusion).
  • Shifted toward a side = pulled (lobar/lung collapse, fibrosis, pneumonectomy).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: What pulse and murmur accompany the heaving apex of aortic stenosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back:
• A slow-rising (plateau) pulse with a narrow pulse pressure,
  • an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids, and
  • a soft or absent A2.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: What peripheral signs accompany the thrusting, displaced apex of aortic regurgitation?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back:
• A collapsing (water-hammer) pulse and wide pulse pressure,
  • an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge (sat forward, expiration), and
  • eponymous signs (Corrigan's, de Musset's, Quincke's).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: What apex and murmur characterise chronic mitral regurgitation?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back: A displaced, thrusting (volume-loaded) apex with a pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, and a soft S1.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: Besides the tapping apex, what other signs point to mitral stenosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back:
• Malar flush,
  • a loud S1,
  • an opening snap,
  • a low-pitched rumbling mid-diastolic murmur (left lateral, bell, expiration),
  • atrial fibrillation and
  • signs of pulmonary hypertension.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: How does the HOCM murmur change with Valsalva, and why?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back: It gets louder — Valsalva reduces venous return (preload), shrinking the LV cavity and worsening dynamic LVOT obstruction. The murmur of fixed aortic stenosis softens instead.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: How do the murmurs of HOCM and aortic stenosis behave on squatting vs standing?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back:
• Squatting (↑preload/afterload): HOCM softer, AS louder.
  • Standing / Valsalva (↓preload): HOCM louder, AS softer.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: What does a palpable S4 (presystolic impulse) at the apex indicate?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back: Forceful atrial contraction against a stiff, non-compliant, hypertrophied LV — aortic stenosis, hypertension or ischaemia. It can produce a double apical impulse.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: What does a palpable S3 at the apex indicate?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back: Rapid ventricular filling into a dilated, volume-overloaded or failing LV — heart failure, dilated cardiomyopathy, or severe mitral/aortic regurgitation.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: What is Beck's triad, and which apex finding accompanies it?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back: Hypotension + raised JVP + muffled heart sounds = cardiac tamponade. The apex beat is impalpable.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: What is pulsus paradoxus, and in which apex-related emergency does it occur?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back: An exaggerated (>10 mmHg) fall in systolic BP on inspiration — a key sign of cardiac tamponade (also severe asthma).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: What is cor pulmonale, and which precordial sign suggests it?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back: Right heart strain/failure secondary to chronic lung disease (e.g. COPD). It produces a left parasternal (RV) heave, a loud P2 and a raised JVP.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: Which congenital lesion gives an RV heave with fixed splitting of the second heart sound?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back: An atrial septal defect — the left-to-right shunt causes RV volume overload and fixed splitting of S2.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: When is a forceful, hyperdynamic apex beat normal or non-cardiac?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back: When it is undisplaced and non-sustained — in a thin/young chest wall, or in high-output states (anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, pregnancy, fever, exercise).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: State the Sokolow–Lyon voltage criterion for LV hypertrophy.
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back: S wave in V1 + R wave in V5 or V6 > 35 mm (also R in aVL > 11 mm).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: What ECG hallmark accompanies the dyskinetic apex of a left ventricular aneurysm?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back: Persistent ST elevation weeks to months after a (usually anterior) MI, often with pathological Q waves.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: Which CXR silhouette suggests a pericardial effusion?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back: A globular, 'water-bottle' cardiac silhouette with clear lung fields.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.front: How is dextrocardia confirmed when the apex is felt on the right?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.back:
• Heart sounds are loudest on the right;
  • a standard ECG shows an inverted P/QRS in lead I with poor R-wave progression (corrected by right-sided chest leads);
  • CXR shows a right-sided cardiac apex.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: In what order should you assess the pulse you feel?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back:
• Rate and rhythm at the radial,
  • then character (waveform) and volume at a large central artery (carotid/brachial).
(Comparing pulses across sites is a separate, vascular examination.)

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: Why is character best assessed at the carotid or brachial rather than the radial?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: The peripheral pulse is delayed and damped by the arterial tree, so subtle waveforms (slow-rising, collapsing, bisferiens) are read more reliably at a large central artery.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: What does an irregularly irregular pulse indicate?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: Atrial fibrillation — no pattern and a beat-to-beat variation in volume; an apex–radial deficit supports it. (A regularly irregular pulse suggests ectopics or 2nd-degree heart block.)

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: What is the apex–radial (pulse) deficit and what does it suggest?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: The apical (auscultated) rate exceeds the radial rate because weak beats fail to open the aortic valve / reach the wrist — supports atrial fibrillation (also seen with frequent ventricular ectopics).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: Describe the slow-rising pulse and its cause.
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: A small-volume, late-peaking (plateau) pulse with a narrow pulse pressure → aortic stenosis (fixed outflow obstruction).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: Describe the collapsing (water-hammer) pulse and its causes.
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: A rapid rise and rapid fall with a wide pulse pressure, exaggerated on raising the arm → aortic regurgitation or a high-output state.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: Which peripheral eponymous signs accompany chronic aortic regurgitation?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back:
• Corrigan’s sign (visible vigorous carotid pulsation),
  • Quincke’s (nailbed capillary pulsation),
  • de Musset’s (head nodding),
  • Duroziez’s (femoral to-and-fro murmur)
  • and Traube’s (pistol-shot femorals).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: What is a bisferiens pulse and what causes it?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: A pulse with two systolic peaks → mixed aortic valve disease (AS + AR) or HOCM.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: What is a dicrotic pulse and how does it differ from a bisferiens pulse?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: A dicrotic pulse has two peaks with the second in diastole (after the dicrotic notch) — seen in low-output states (severe LV failure, sepsis, hypovolaemia) or post-AVR. A bisferiens pulse has both peaks in systole.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: What is a jerky pulse and what does it suggest?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: A sharp, rapid upstroke from early rapid ejection then mid-systolic obstruction → hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: What is pulsus alternans and what does it indicate?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: Regular rhythm with beats that alternate strong and weak → severe left-ventricular systolic dysfunction.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: What is pulsus bigeminus and its classic cause?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: Beats in coupled pairs — a sinus beat followed by a premature ectopic — giving a regularly irregular pulse of alternating strength. Classic cause: digoxin toxicity (also frequent ventricular ectopics).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: What is pulsus paradoxus and how is it defined?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: An exaggerated >10 mmHg fall in systolic BP on inspiration (the pulse weakens/vanishes) → cardiac tamponade, severe asthma or massive PE.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: What is the mechanism of pulsus paradoxus?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: On inspiration, increased RV filling bows the septum into a constrained LV (effusion/tamponade or hyperinflation), so LV stroke volume and systolic BP fall >10 mmHg.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: What causes a bounding / large-volume pulse?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: A high-output / hyperdynamic state — sepsis, thyrotoxicosis, anaemia, CO₂ retention, pregnancy, fever, or aortic regurgitation.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: What causes a thready / low-volume pulse?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: Hypovolaemia, cardiogenic or obstructive shock, or severe aortic stenosis (reduced stroke volume).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: A slow, regular pulse with cannon a waves and syncope suggests?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: Complete (third-degree) heart block — AV dissociation gives intermittent cannon a waves; also consider excess rate-limiting drugs (β-blocker, digoxin, verapamil).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: How does the pulse in aortic stenosis differ from aortic regurgitation?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back:
• AS — slow-rising, small volume, narrow pulse pressure.
  • AR — collapsing/water-hammer, large volume, wide pulse pressure.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: Why can severe aortic stenosis be missed on pulse examination in the elderly?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: Stiff, calcified arteries transmit the pressure wave faster, masking the slow-rising character — so a normal-feeling carotid pulse does not exclude severe AS in an older patient.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: What bedside manoeuvre exaggerates a collapsing pulse?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: Raising the patient’s arm above the head while palpating the radial — the water-hammer character of aortic regurgitation becomes more obvious.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: Why should you never palpate both carotid arteries simultaneously?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: It risks compromising cerebral perfusion and may trigger a vagal bradycardia/syncope via the carotid sinus.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: Which investigation confirms the cause of most abnormal pulse characters and murmurs?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: Echocardiography — valve gradients and pulse-pressure lesions (AS/AR), LV function (pulsus alternans), tamponade physiology (pulsus paradoxus) and HOCM.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: How do you investigate an irregular pulse that is intermittent?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: 12-lead ECG first; if paroxysmal, ambulatory (Holter) ECG or a prolonged monitor to capture the arrhythmia.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: What pulse and BP findings accompany cardiac tamponade?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: Pulsus paradoxus (inspiratory systolic BP fall >10 mmHg) and a narrow pulse pressure; the accompanying signs are Beck’s triad (see the Beck’s-triad card). Confirm with urgent echo.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: What is Beck's triad?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: Hypotension + raised JVP + muffled heart sounds → cardiac tamponade. (Pulsus paradoxus is a separate, associated sign.)

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: What does a narrow versus wide pulse pressure suggest?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back:
• Narrow → reduced stroke volume (aortic stenosis, hypovolaemia/shock, tamponade).
  • Wide → aortic regurgitation or a high-output state (and stiff arteries in the elderly).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: Which first-line bloods help explain a bounding, high-output pulse?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: TFTs (thyrotoxicosis) and FBC (anaemia); consider markers of sepsis. For a thready/shocked pulse send a VBG/lactate and group & save.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: What chest X-ray findings support cardiac causes of an abnormal pulse?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back:
• Globular heart → pericardial effusion;
  • cardiomegaly / pulmonary oedema → LV failure (pulsus alternans).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: How do you interpret the rate and rhythm of a pulse before its character?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back:
• Fast + regular → sinus tachycardia, SVT, atrial flutter or VT;
  • fast + irregular → atrial fibrillation (or flutter with variable block);
  • slow → bradycardia/heart block.
A phasic quickening on inspiration that is otherwise regular is benign sinus arrhythmia. Count a full 60 s if the pulse is irregular.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: How should you examine the peripheral pulses systematically?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back:
Palpate and compare:
  • both radials & brachials,
  • carotids (one at a time),
  • femorals,
  • then popliteal, posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis;
compare limb-to-limb, radial-to-femoral, and measure BP in both arms.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: How do you distinguish an expansile from a transmitted pulsatile abdominal mass?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back:
• A true aneurysm is expansile — it pushes your two hands apart.
  • A mass merely overlying the aorta is transmitted — it lifts both hands up together.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: How does the level of an absent pulse localise arterial disease?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back:
• Absent femorals → aortoiliac disease;
  • present femoral but absent popliteal → femoropopliteal;
  • absent foot pulses only → distal/tibial disease.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: What are the features of chronic peripheral arterial disease on examination?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back:
• Weak/absent foot pulses,
  • a cool, hairless, shiny foot,
  • delayed capillary refill,
  • arterial ulcers,
  • intermittent claudication
  • and ABPI <0.9.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: What are the ABPI cut-offs and their meaning?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back:
• >1.3 → calcified, non-compressible vessels (diabetes/CKD) — use the toe-brachial index or duplex instead;
  • 0.9–1.3 → normal;
  • 0.5–0.9 → claudication-range PAD;
  • <0.5 → critical limb ischaemia.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: What are the 6 Ps of acute limb ischaemia?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Perishing cold, Paraesthesia, Paralysis — a surgical emergency; revascularise within ~6 hours.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: What is the immediate management of acute limb ischaemia?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back:
• Immediate IV heparin,
  • urgent vascular referral,
  • and revascularisation (embolectomy or thrombolysis) within ~6 hours;
  • analgesia and treat the cause.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: How do you distinguish embolic from thrombotic acute limb ischaemia?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back:
• Embolic — sudden, no claudication history, a source (AF, post-MI), contralateral pulses present.
  • Thrombotic — on a background of PAD, prior claudication, diseased vessels bilaterally.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: What does radio-radial delay or an absent unilateral upper-limb pulse suggest?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back:
• Aortic dissection,
  • proximal subclavian artery stenosis,
  • or Takayasu arteritis.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: What inter-arm systolic BP difference is significant, and what does it suggest?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: A difference >20 mmHg → aortic dissection or subclavian stenosis (≥10 mmHg is also linked to PAD and raised cardiovascular risk).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: What is radio-femoral delay and what causes it?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: The femoral pulse lags behind the radial → coarctation of the aorta (with upper-limb hypertension, weak leg pulses, a murmur over the back and rib notching on CXR).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: What are the features of Takayasu arteritis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: A large-vessel vasculitis, typically a young woman, with absent/asymmetric upper-limb pulses ('pulseless disease'), an inter-arm BP difference, bruits, claudication and a raised ESR/CRP; confirmed on MR/CT angiography.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: What is subclavian steal syndrome?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: Proximal subclavian stenosis so that arm exercise reverses vertebral artery flow, causing arm claudication and posterior-circulation symptoms (dizziness, visual disturbance) with an inter-arm BP difference and a subclavian bruit.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: How does an abdominal aortic aneurysm present on examination, and when is it an emergency?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: A central, expansile pulsatile mass. Sudden abdominal/back pain, a tender mass and hypotension/collapse indicate a ruptured AAA — a surgical emergency.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: What is Buerger's test and what is a positive result?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: Elevate the leg — pallor at a low angle (Buerger’s angle <20°) indicates severe ischaemia; on dependency the foot becomes ruddy/dusky red (reactive hyperaemia). A positive test suggests critical peripheral arterial disease.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: How do you confirm and map peripheral arterial disease?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: Arterial duplex ultrasound first, then CT or MR angiography to map the disease before angioplasty or bypass; ABPI quantifies severity at the bedside.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: What is the confirmatory investigation for suspected aortic dissection?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: CT aortography (transoesophageal echo if unstable) — image before anticoagulation or thrombolysis.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: How is an abdominal aortic aneurysm investigated?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: Abdominal ultrasound for screening/surveillance (UK screens men at 65); CT angiography defines size and detects a leak before repair (elective repair usually at ≥5.5 cm).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: How do chronic and acute limb ischaemia differ in presentation?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back:
• Chronic — gradual claudication → rest pain → tissue loss, with time for collaterals.
  • Acute — sudden onset with the 6 Ps and a threatened limb needing emergency revascularisation.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: Why must you always check a radio-femoral delay in a young hypertensive?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: Coarctation of the aorta is an easily-missed, treatable secondary cause of hypertension — the radio-femoral delay is the key bedside clue.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: How do you distinguish neurogenic (spinal) from vascular claudication?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back:
• Neurogenic (spinal stenosis) — pain eases on leaning forward/sitting, variable walking distance, normal pulses and ABPI.
  • Vascular — pain eases on stopping (standing still), fixed claudication distance, weak pulses and ABPI <0.9.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: What is thoracic outlet syndrome and how does it affect the pulse?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back: Compression of the subclavian vessels/brachial plexus at the thoracic outlet (e.g. cervical rib). The upper-limb pulse may weaken or disappear with arm positioning (positional radio-radial asymmetry), with arm claudication and neurological symptoms.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.front: How does constrictive pericarditis differ from cardiac tamponade at the bedside?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.back:
• Constriction — Kussmaul’s sign (JVP rises on inspiration), a pericardial knock, and no pulsus paradoxus.
  • Tamponade — pulsus paradoxus, muffled heart sounds and a JVP that falls on inspiration (Kussmaul’s classically absent).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: What are palpitations?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back: An unpleasant awareness of the heartbeat — fast, slow, irregular or forceful. Most are benign, but the task is to exclude a dangerous arrhythmia.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: Which four questions sort most palpitations?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back:
• Fast or slow?
  • Regular or irregular?
  • Sudden or gradual onset/offset?
  • Any syncope or chest pain?

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: What is the single most useful investigation for palpitations?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back: An ECG captured during symptoms. If episodes are intermittent, an ambulatory monitor (Holter / event / loop recorder) bridges the gap.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: Which features of palpitations are red flags for a ventricular arrhythmia?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back:
• Associated syncope or chest pain
  • palpitations on exertion
  • a family history of sudden cardiac death <40
  • and known structural or ischaemic heart disease.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: A sudden-onset, fast, regular palpitation that stops abruptly (often with Valsalva) suggests?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back: Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (AVNRT or AVRT) — an ‘on/off switch’ regular tachycardia.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: A fast, irregularly irregular palpitation with a variable pulse suggests?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back: Atrial fibrillation (or atrial flutter with variable block). An irregular tachycardia in COPD with ≥3 P-wave morphologies is multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: A regular palpitation around 150 bpm with a sawtooth baseline suggests?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back: Atrial flutter with 2:1 AV conduction (atrial rate ~300, ventricular ~150).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: What is the typical description and significance of ectopic beats?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back: Isolated ‘skipped’ or ‘thumping’ beats, often worse at rest and settling on exertion — usually benign if the heart is structurally normal.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: What distinguishes sinus tachycardia as a cause of palpitations?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back: A gradual onset and offset of a fast, regular beat with an identifiable driver — exercise, fever, pain, anxiety, hypovolaemia, anaemia or thyrotoxicosis. Treat the cause, not the rate.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: Why is a broad-complex tachycardia treated as VT until proven otherwise?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back: Ventricular tachycardia is the commonest and most dangerous cause of a broad-complex tachycardia, especially with structural/ischaemic heart disease; misclassifying it as SVT with aberrancy and giving the wrong drug can be fatal.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: Which endocrine cause of palpitations should always be excluded, and how?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back: Thyrotoxicosis — look for tremor, heat intolerance, weight loss and a goitre; check TFTs (suppressed TSH, raised free T4/T3).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: How can anaemia cause palpitations?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back: Reduced oxygen-carrying capacity drives a compensatory (high-output) sinus tachycardia, with pallor, fatigue, exertional breathlessness and a flow murmur; check an FBC.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: What triad suggests phaeochromocytoma as a cause of palpitations?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back: Episodic palpitations + headache + sweating with paroxysmal hypertension; confirm with plasma/urinary metanephrines.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: When should palpitations be attributed to anxiety or panic?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back: Only as a diagnosis of exclusion — situational episodes with hyperventilation, peri-oral/limb paraesthesiae, carpopedal spasm and a sense of dread, after arrhythmia and thyrotoxicosis are excluded.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: What ECG features suggest Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW)?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back: A short PR interval and a delta wave (slurred QRS upstroke) from an accessory pathway — a substrate for AVRT and, in AF, dangerous rapid conduction.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: Which ECG findings indicate a substrate for ventricular arrhythmia?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back:
• Long QT
  • pathological Q waves (prior MI)
  • LVH
  • an epsilon wave (ARVC)
  • or a Brugada pattern.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: How should intermittent palpitations with a normal resting ECG be investigated?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back:
Ambulatory ECG monitoring matched to frequency:
  • 24 h–7 day Holter for frequent symptoms
  • a patient-activated event/loop recorder for less frequent
  • and an implantable loop recorder for infrequent high-risk episodes.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: When is echocardiography indicated in palpitations?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back:
• When there is a murmur
  • an abnormal ECG
  • exertional symptoms
  • syncope
  • or a family history of sudden cardiac death
— to look for structural disease (e.g. cardiomyopathy, valve disease).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: Which first-line blood tests are sent for palpitations?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back:
• FBC (anaemia)
  • TFTs (thyrotoxicosis)
  • U&E, magnesium and calcium (electrolyte triggers)
  • glucose
  • and troponin if ischaemia is suspected.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: How do vagal manoeuvres help in a regular narrow-complex tachycardia, and what if they fail?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back: Vagal manoeuvres (modified Valsalva; carotid sinus massage — avoid if a carotid bruit or in the elderly) can terminate AVNRT/AVRT or transiently slow the rate to unmask flutter waves. If they fail and the patient is stable, IV adenosine is first-line (avoid in asthma/COPD — risk of bronchospasm; use verapamil instead).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: What history features suggest palpitations are from a benign cause?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back:
• Brief
  • occurring at rest
  • a sensation of skipped beats that settle on exertion
  • no syncope or chest pain
  • and a structurally normal heart.
(The red-flag/sinister features are covered separately.)

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: What is the significance of palpitations that occur with exertion?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back: Exertional palpitations raise concern for exercise-induced ventricular arrhythmia, HOCM or ischaemia — investigate with an exercise ECG and echocardiography rather than reassuring.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: Which cardiomyopathy classically causes palpitations with exertional syncope and a family history of sudden death?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HOCM) — an ejection systolic murmur that gets louder on Valsalva; a leading cause of sudden cardiac death in the young.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: What drugs and stimulants commonly precipitate palpitations?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back:
• Caffeine, alcohol, nicotine, cocaine/amfetamines
  • β-agonists (salbutamol)
  • theophylline
  • thyroxine
  • and sympathomimetic decongestants.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: Why must a patient with WPW and atrial fibrillation avoid AV-nodal blocking drugs?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back: AV-nodal blockers (digoxin, verapamil, adenosine) can accelerate conduction down the accessory pathway, risking degeneration into ventricular fibrillation; use flecainide or DC cardioversion instead.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: What electrolyte disturbances can cause palpitations/arrhythmia?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back: Hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia (and hypocalcaemia) predispose to ectopy and arrhythmia — correct them, especially before/after cardioversion.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: What is the initial management of any tachyarrhythmia with adverse features?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back: Per Resuscitation Council algorithm: if shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia or heart failure — synchronised DC cardioversion.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: How does atrial flutter differ from atrial fibrillation on the pulse and ECG?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back:
• Flutter — often regular (~150, 2:1) with sawtooth F waves.
  • AF — irregularly irregular with no P waves and a fibrillating baseline.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: What long-term risk must be assessed in a patient found to have atrial fibrillation?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back: Thromboembolic (stroke) risk — score with CHA₂DS₂-VASc and weigh bleeding risk (ORBIT — NICE-preferred; HAS-BLED still widely used) before anticoagulation.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: A young patient has recurrent palpitations with a normal heart and normal ECG; what is the likely benign diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back: Benign ectopic beats or brief paroxysmal SVT — reassurance, trigger avoidance, and ambulatory monitoring to document the rhythm.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: What is the role of the exercise ECG in palpitations?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back:
• To reproduce exertional palpitations
  • unmask exercise-induced arrhythmia or ischaemia
  • and assess catecholaminergic triggers.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: Why should you ask the patient to tap out their palpitations?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back:
The tapped rhythm is a simple, useful discriminator —
  • fast & regular (SVT/flutter)
  • fast & irregular (AF)
  • or single skipped beats (ectopics).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.front: How can a bradyarrhythmia or heart block cause palpitations, and how is it investigated?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.back: Patients may feel slow, heavy or ‘thumping’ beats (post-pause escape beats), often with dizziness or syncope. Investigate with a 12-lead ECG (looking for AV block/sinus pauses) and an ambulatory monitor if intermittent; review rate-limiting drugs.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: Define atherosclerosis and its end consequences.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Endothelial injury → LDL entry and retention in the intima → chronic inflammation with macrophage foam cells (fatty streak) → fibrous plaque → arterial stiffening, stenosis and plaque rupture → MI, stroke, peripheral arterial disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: Walk through the cellular sequence of atherosclerosis from LDL entry to plaque development.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: LDL particles enter the intima → monocytes adhere via adhesion molecules and differentiate into macrophages → engulf LDL → form macrophage foam cells → chronic inflammation and plaque development.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What is the goal of primary prevention in atherosclerosis, and which tool/threshold is used?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: No prior CVD event — calculate risk and intervene before disease manifests. Tool: QRISK3 (10-year cardiovascular risk); ≥10% → offer atorvastatin 20 mg. A score <10% does not rule treatment out — offer it if the patient has an informed preference or the score may underestimate risk (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What is the goal of secondary prevention, and what is the regimen?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Post-CVD event — prevent recurrence. Atorvastatin 80 mg for all established CVD; the 4 A's (aspirin, 2nd antiplatelet, ACEi, β-blocker) apply after MI, whereas ischaemic stroke/TIA use clopidogrel-based therapy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: Why does the primary vs secondary fork matter so much in lipid management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: It drives everything: statin dose, antiplatelet choice, and beta-blocker use all differ between the two arms.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: List the non-modifiable risk factors for atherosclerosis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back:
• Age
  • male sex
  • family history of premature CVD

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: List the modifiable risk factors for atherosclerosis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back:
• Raised cholesterol
  • smoking
  • alcohol
  • poor diet
  • physical inactivity
  • obesity
  • poor sleep
  • stress

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: Which comorbidities increase atherosclerosis risk?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back:
• Diabetes
  • hypertension
  • CKD
  • inflammatory disease (RA, SLE)
  • atypical antipsychotics (increased metabolic risk)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: Is hyperlipidaemia usually symptomatic, and what do clinical signs indicate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Usually asymptomatic — picked up on routine bloods or screening. Signs indicate severe/longstanding disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What are tendon xanthomata, where are they found, and how specific are they?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Hard nodules of cholesterol deposition. Sites: knuckles (extensor tendons), Achilles tendon. The most specific sign — near-diagnostic of familial hypercholesterolaemia; treat as FH until proven otherwise. Not strictly pathognomonic (rare sterol storage disorders also cause them).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What is xanthelasma, and what is its association with lipids?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Yellowish plaques on the eyelids; associated with dyslipidaemia but may occur with normal lipids.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What is corneal arcus, and when does it suggest a lipid disorder versus being normal?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: A grey-white ring at the corneal periphery. Premature (<45 years) = lipid disorder; normal in the elderly.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: Which lipid abnormality can precipitate acute pancreatitis, and at what level?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Severe hypertriglyceridaemia (>10 mmol/L) can precipitate acute pancreatitis — a serious complication.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What are the dietary targets for lifestyle optimisation in lipid disorders?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back:
• Total fat <30% of caloric intake
  • saturated fat <7% of calories
  • reduce sugar and refined carbohydrates
  • 5-a-day fruit and vegetables
  • at least 2 portions of fish per week, one of which is oily
  • reduce salt (especially if hypertensive)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What exercise and habit changes are advised in lipid disorders?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back:
• 150 min moderate OR 75 min vigorous aerobic exercise/week, plus 2× strength/resistance training/week
  • smoking cessation (single most effective CVD intervention)
  • alcohol ≤14 units/week spread across ≥3 days
  • treat comorbidities (HTN, diabetes, obesity)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: Which single lifestyle change is the most effective CVD intervention?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Smoking cessation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: Outline the primary prevention pathway using QRISK3.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back:
• Calculate QRISK3 (10-year cardiovascular risk)
  • ≥10% risk → offer atorvastatin 20 mg OD after lifestyle discussion (a score <10% does not rule it out)
  • recheck a non-fasting lipid profile at 3 months — aim ≥40% reduction in non-HDL cholesterol

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: Which patients qualify for an automatic statin without needing a QRISK calculation — CKD criteria?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: CKD (eGFR <60 or ACR ≥3): atorvastatin 20 mg regardless of QRISK; CKD independently multiplies CVD risk.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What are the automatic statin criteria for Type 1 diabetes?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Atorvastatin 20 mg if >40 years, OR diabetes >10 years, OR nephropathy; no QRISK calculation needed.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: In the secondary prevention 4 A's, what does the first A (atorvastatin) involve?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Atorvastatin 80 mg — high-intensity statin (any time of day). Target in secondary prevention is absolute: LDL ≤2.0 mmol/L or non-HDL ≤2.6 mmol/L (NICE). The ≥40% non-HDL reduction target belongs to primary prevention, where the dose is 20 mg.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: In the 4 A's, what is the antiplatelet regimen?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back:
Territory-specific.
  • Post-MI: aspirin 75 mg OD indefinitely, plus DAPT (aspirin + ticagrelor/clopidogrel) for 12 months
  • Ischaemic stroke/TIA and PAD: clopidogrel 75 mg first-line, aspirin if not tolerated

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: In the 4 A's, why is a beta-blocker used, and which is preferred?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Bisoprolol preferred (atenolol less favoured) — rate control, reduced cardiac remodelling post-MI, and reduced sudden death risk.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: In the 4 A's, what is the role of the ACE inhibitor?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Ramipril/perindopril — BP control, cardioprotection, remodelling prevention post-MI.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: State the key contrast between primary and secondary prevention regimens.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Primary = atorvastatin 20 mg alone (if QRISK ≥10%); Secondary = atorvastatin 80 mg + antiplatelet + beta-blocker + ACEi.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What is the mechanism of statins, and why are they taken at night?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Inhibit HMG-CoA reductase → reduced hepatic cholesterol synthesis → upregulate LDL receptors → reduced LDL. Short-acting statins (simvastatin) are taken at night as synthesis peaks nocturnally; atorvastatin/rosuvastatin are long-acting and can be taken any time.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: In the cholesterol synthesis pathway, which enzyme do statins block and what conversion does this prevent?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, blocking conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate and reducing downstream cholesterol production.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What baseline bloods are checked before starting a statin?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back:
• Non-fasting full lipid profile (total cholesterol, HDL, non-HDL)
  • LFTs (transaminases)
  • renal function
  • TFTs and HbA1c
CK only if there is persistent unexplained muscle pain — it is not routine. These also screen for secondary causes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What is checked at 3 months on a statin, and what is the target/stopping rule?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Non-fasting full lipid profile + LFTs. Primary prevention: aim ≥40% reduction in non-HDL. Secondary prevention: aim LDL ≤2.0 or non-HDL ≤2.6 mmol/L. If ALT/AST >3× ULN → stop the statin.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What is monitored at 12 months on a statin, and what transaminase rise is acceptable?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: LFTs. A mild transaminase rise is acceptable; >3× ULN → stop.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: Describe the myopathy → rhabdomyolysis side effect of statins, including the emergency sign.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Muscle pain/weakness → check CK. CK >5× ULN → stop the statin and recheck. Rhabdomyolysis (CK >10× ULN) → dark urine (myoglobinuria) = emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What is the T2DM risk associated with statins, and how does it affect prescribing?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: A modest increase in diabetes risk — but the benefit vs CVD risk still strongly favours statins in most patients.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What stroke-related consideration applies to statins?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: A small increased risk of haemorrhagic stroke — a relevant consideration in patients with prior haemorrhagic stroke.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: Why should a statin be held during macrolide antibiotic use?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Macrolides (clarithromycin, erythromycin) cause CYP3A4 inhibition → increased statin levels → increased myopathy risk, so hold the statin while on them.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What is the mechanism of ezetimibe, and how is it used?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Blocks intestinal cholesterol absorption (NPC1L1 inhibitor); used as an add-on to a statin or in statin-intolerant patients; well tolerated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What are PCSK9 inhibitors, how are they given, and who are they for?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Evolocumab, alirocumab — monoclonal antibodies, subcut every 2–4 weeks. Prevent LDL receptor degradation → profound LDL reduction. For FH or refractory hypercholesterolaemia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What is the role of omega-3 / fibrates in lipid management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Fibrates (fenofibrate) — for severe hypertriglyceridaemia. Omega-3 fatty acids — adjunct for triglyceride lowering.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What are the key features of familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Autosomal dominant — LDL receptor mutation (or ApoB/PCSK9 variants); very high cholesterol from birth, dramatically accelerating atherosclerosis; untreated → MI in the 4th–5th decade.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What are the Simon Broome criteria for familial hypercholesterolaemia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back:
Threshold for both tiers: total cholesterol >7.5 mmol/L or LDL >4.9 mmol/L (adult).
  • Definite FH = threshold + tendon xanthomata in the patient or a 1st-/2nd-degree relative, OR a DNA mutation in LDL receptor/ApoB/PCSK9
  • Possible FH = threshold + family history of MI (<60 in a 1st-degree, <50 in a 2nd-degree relative) or of raised cholesterol in a relative
DLCN is the alternative UK criteria set (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: Outline the management of familial hypercholesterolaemia.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back:
• Urgent specialist referral (mandatory if total cholesterol >9.0 mmol/L or non-HDL >7.5 mmol/L, regardless of family history)
  • do not use QRISK — it underestimates risk in FH
  • genetic testing
  • high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80 mg) aiming for a ≥50% reduction in LDL-C from baseline (NICE)
  • add ezetimibe if that is not achieved
  • PCSK9 inhibitor for refractory cases
  • cascade screening of first-, second- and where possible third-degree relatives, testing for the known mutation where one has been identified

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: Which secondary causes of raised lipids should be excluded before starting long-term treatment?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back:
• Hypothyroidism — the classic; check TFTs in everyone
  • Uncontrolled diabetes and excess alcohol
  • Nephrotic syndrome and cholestatic liver disease
  • Drugs — corticosteroids, thiazides, antiretrovirals, ciclosporin
Treating the cause may normalise the lipids on its own, and NICE advises excluding these before considering a familial disorder.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: Why does undiagnosed hypothyroidism matter twice over in a patient with raised cholesterol?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back:
1. It causes the hypercholesterolaemia — correcting the thyroid may normalise the lipids and avoid lifelong treatment.
2. It increases the risk of statin muscle toxicity — so if you miss it and start a statin, you have both mistreated the cause and made the drug more dangerous.
Correct the thyroid first, then re-measure the lipids.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What is inclisiran, and what is distinctive about how it is given?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back:
A small interfering RNA (siRNA) that silences hepatic PCSK9 production, so LDL receptors are not degraded and LDL falls.
Given subcutaneously, repeated at 3 months and then every 6 months — a twice-yearly injection, which is a major adherence advantage over daily tablets.
A specialist option when targets are not met on other therapy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: Why is bempedoic acid particularly useful in statin intolerance?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back:
It is an ACL inhibitor acting on the same pathway as statins but upstream of HMG-CoA reductase.
Crucially it is a prodrug activated in the liver but not in muscle, so it carries little myopathy risk — the very problem that makes statins intolerable.
Usually combined with ezetimibe.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.front: Name the three tunics of an artery wall from inside out and their main components.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.back:
• Tunica intima (endothelium + subendothelial CT + internal elastic lamina),
  • tunica media (smooth muscle + elastic fibres, bounded by the external elastic lamina), and
  • tunica adventitia (connective tissue with vasa vasorum and nerves).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.front: What is the internal elastic lamina and where is it?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.back: A wavy sheet of elastic tissue at the outer edge of the tunica intima, most prominent in muscular arteries.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.front: What are the vasa vasorum?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.back: Small blood vessels within the adventitia (and outer media) that supply the wall of large arteries and veins.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.front: How do arteries differ from veins histologically?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.back:
• Arteries have a thicker media, a smaller round lumen and more elastic/muscle;
  • veins have thin walls, a large lumen and valves.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.front: What defines an elastic (conducting) artery and give examples.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.back: A media full of fenestrated elastic laminae (~40–70 lamellar units) between smooth muscle (IEL/EEL present but not distinguishable among them); e.g. the aorta, pulmonary trunk, brachiocephalic, common carotid, subclavian and common iliac arteries.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.front: What is the windkessel effect?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.back: Elastic arteries stretch in systole and recoil in diastole, converting pulsatile ejection into smooth continuous flow and maintaining diastolic blood pressure.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.front: What defines a muscular (distributing) artery and give examples.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.back: A media that is predominantly smooth muscle (up to ~40 layers) with a prominent internal and external elastic lamina; e.g. the femoral, radial and coronary arteries. They regulate regional blood distribution.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.front: What is the structure and function of an arteriole?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.back: The smallest arteries (<0.1 mm) with only 1–3 smooth-muscle layers; they are the main resistance vessels, controlling flow into capillaries and setting systemic vascular resistance. (~0.1–2 mm = a small artery.)

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.front: Why are arterioles the main controllers of blood pressure?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.back: Because resistance is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the radius, small changes in arteriolar calibre produce large changes in systemic vascular resistance and diastolic BP.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.front: How do you recognise an elastic artery on a slide?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.back: Numerous wavy elastic laminae throughout the media (black on an elastic stain), with a thick wall and large lumen.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.front: How do you recognise a muscular artery on a slide?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.back: A prominent single wavy internal elastic lamina just beneath the endothelium, with a thick, cellular smooth-muscle media.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.front: Which stain identifies an elastic artery and the elastic laminae?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.back: An elastic stain (Verhoeff–Van Gieson or orcein), which turns the elastic laminae black.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.front: Which artery layer is affected in atherosclerosis?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.back: The tunica intima — lipid plaque with foam cells and a fibrous cap, in elastic and muscular arteries.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.front: What arteriolar change occurs in hypertension and diabetes?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.back: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis (and, in malignant hypertension, hyperplastic 'onion-skin' arterioles); medial hypertrophy.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.front: Which artery layer weakens in an aneurysm, and in aortic dissection?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.back: The tunica media — elastic/medial weakening causes aneurysmal dilatation; in dissection an intimal tear lets blood track into the media, most often on a background of hypertension (in younger patients, cystic medial degeneration as in Marfan).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.front: What is giant cell (temporal) arteritis at the tissue level?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.back: Transmural granulomatous inflammation centred on the internal elastic lamina of temporal/large arteries, with giant cells and IEL fragmentation; reactive intimal thickening then occludes the lumen and causes ischaemia.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.front: Which tunic is thickest in an artery, and what does it contain?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.back: The tunica media — smooth muscle and elastic fibres — is thickest in arteries (thicker than in the accompanying vein).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.front: What is the endothelium and which tunic is it part of?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.back: A simple squamous epithelium lining the lumen of all vessels; it forms the innermost part of the tunica intima.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.front: What are arteriovenous anastomoses and glomus bodies?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.back: AV anastomoses shunt blood directly from arteriole to venule, bypassing the capillary bed; encapsulated glomus bodies (a thick-walled, coiled Sucquet–Hoyer canal) in fingertips, nail beds and ears are thermoregulatory shunts and the origin of the glomus tumour.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.front: What is a metarteriole and precapillary sphincter?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.back:
• A metarteriole is the terminal arteriole feeding a capillary bed;
  • the precapillary sphincter is a ring of smooth muscle controlling flow into the capillaries.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.front: How does arterial ageing (arteriosclerosis) change blood pressure?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.back: Aortic elastin fragments and collagen increases, stiffening the wall and reducing the windkessel effect → isolated systolic hypertension and a widened pulse pressure; elastic recoil is greatest centrally (aorta) and diminishes peripherally.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.front: What endothelial-derived mediators regulate arterial tone?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.back: Nitric oxide (vasodilator) and endothelin (vasoconstrictor), among others.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.front: Classify the vasculitides by vessel size, with an example of each.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.back:
• Large: Takayasu (young Asian women, 'pulseless disease') and giant cell arteritis (elderly).
  • Medium: polyarteritis nodosa (HBV, renal/mesenteric microaneurysms) and Kawasaki (children, coronary aneurysms).
  • Small: ANCA-associated (GPA, EGPA, MPA).
Buerger's (young smokers) affects distal small/medium vessels.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.front: Outline the response-to-injury sequence of atherosclerosis.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.back: Endothelial injury/dysfunction (LDL, smoking, HTN, diabetes) → LDL entry and oxidation → monocyte adhesion and migration → macrophage foam cells → fatty streak → fibrofatty plaque with a fibrous cap over a necrotic lipid core (in the intima); cap rupture triggers thrombosis.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.front: What is the carotid sinus and what makes it a baroreceptor?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.back: A dilation at the origin of the internal carotid artery with a thin media and a richly innervated adventitia that senses arterial stretch (blood pressure); the nearby carotid body is a chemoreceptor sensing O2, CO2 and pH.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.front: Give three active (non-lining) functions of vascular endothelium.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.back:
• It is antithrombotic (releases tPA and NO, expresses thrombomodulin);
  • it stores von Willebrand factor and P-selectin in Weibel–Palade bodies;
  • and it regulates tone via NO (vasodilator, eNOS→cGMP) and endothelin-1 (vasoconstrictor).
Pulmonary endothelium also carries ACE.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is tachycardia defined, and what is the first and most important ECG step?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: A heart rate >100 bpm. The first and most important ECG step is to measure the QRS duration.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What QRS duration defines a narrow-complex tachycardia, and what does it imply about origin?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: QRS <120 ms — a supraventricular origin, because the impulse uses the normal His-Purkinje system.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What QRS duration defines a broad-complex tachycardia, and what is the key rule?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: QRS ≥120 ms — treat as ventricular until proven otherwise.It is the QRS width, not the origin, that triggers this rule.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: List the causes of a REGULAR narrow-complex tachycardia.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Sinus tachycardia
  • AVNRT (re-entry within the AV node)
  • AVRT (re-entry via an accessory pathway)
  • atrial tachycardia
  • and atrial flutter with fixed block (e.g. 2:1)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: List the causes of an IRREGULAR narrow-complex tachycardia.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Atrial fibrillation
  • atrial flutter with variable block
  • and multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: List the causes of a REGULAR broad-complex tachycardia.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Ventricular tachycardia (VT — most likely)
  • SVT with aberrant conduction (BBB)
  • and SVT with pre-excitation (WPW)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: List the causes of an IRREGULAR broad-complex tachycardia.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Pre-excited AF (WPW + AF — dangerous)
  • torsades de pointes / polymorphic VT
  • and AF with BBB

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the key rule for any broad-complex tachycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Broad-complex tachycardia = VT until proven otherwise.Never assume SVT with aberrancy without senior review.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Why does a narrow QRS almost always indicate a supraventricular origin?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: A narrow QRS means the ventricles are being activated normally via the His-Purkinje system, so the rhythm almost always originates at or above the AV node (fascicular VT is the classic exception).Note that stability, not QRS width, decides urgency — a narrow-complex tachycardia can still be peri-arrest.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Why is pre-excited AF (WPW + AF) so dangerous, and what must be avoided?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: It can cause a broad, irregular tachycardia that mimics VF. Do NOT give AV nodal blockers — blocking the AV node forces conduction down the accessory pathway, which can precipitate VF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: In the ECG diagnostic framework, what makes Step 2 (QRS width) a 'hard fork'?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Broad-complex rhythms go directly to the VT feature checklist, not to P-wave analysis — the QRS width determines the entire management pathway.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: On a tachycardia ECG, what do a completely irregular rhythm vs an irregular-with-a-pattern rhythm suggest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Completely irregular (no pattern) → AF or multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT)
  • Irregular with a pattern (e.g. varying groups) → atrial flutter with variable block

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: In narrow-complex P-wave analysis, what does a normal P wave before each QRS indicate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Sinus tachycardia — treat the cause.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: In narrow-complex P-wave analysis, what do absent P waves with a chaotic baseline indicate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Atrial fibrillation (fibrillatory f-waves).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What ECG finding of a sawtooth baseline at ~300 bpm indicates, and where is it best seen?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Atrial flutter — best seen in leads II, III, aVF and V1.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: A buried P wave producing a pseudo-R' in V1 and pseudo-S in II/aVF on a narrow-complex tachycardia points to which diagnosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: AVNRT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: A P wave after the QRS with RP < PR on a narrow-complex tachycardia points to which diagnosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: AVRT (accessory pathway).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Abnormal P-wave morphology at a rate of 100–250 bpm on a narrow-complex tachycardia suggests what?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Atrial tachycardia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: When you identify a broad QRS, why must you NOT proceed to P-wave analysis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Broad QRS = VT until proven otherwise; instead of P-wave analysis you check for VT features.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is AV dissociation, and why is it diagnostic of VT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: P waves march through independently of the QRS complexes — the atria and ventricles are beating independently, which is diagnostic of VT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are capture beats and fusion beats, and what do they indicate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Capture beats = rare narrow QRS amid the broad complexes; fusion beats = hybrid morphology.Both are diagnostic of VT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What does 'concordance' mean on a broad-complex tachycardia ECG, and what does it favour?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: All the V (chest) leads deflect in the same direction — this favours VT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: List the features that favour VT in a broad-complex tachycardia.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• AV dissociation
  • capture beats
  • fusion beats
  • concordance (all V leads same direction)
  • atypical BBB morphology (doesn't match classic LBBB/RBBB)
  • and structural heart disease / prior MI

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: If uncertain whether a broad-complex tachycardia is VT or SVT, how should it be treated, and what must never be given?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Treat as VT. Never give verapamil to a broad-complex tachycardia.
