conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the stability override principle in tachycardia management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Regardless of the rhythm diagnosis, haemodynamic instability = immediate synchronised DC cardioversion (or defibrillation for pulseless VT/VF).Do not delay to identify the rhythm.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What features define an 'unstable' tachycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Hypotension (SBP <90)
  • reduced consciousness (confusion, syncope, GCS drop)
  • ischaemic chest pain (not palpitations alone)
  • and acute pulmonary oedema (severe breathlessness, crepitations)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Do palpitations, anxiety or mild breathlessness count as instability in tachycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: No — the threshold for instability is end-organ compromise or haemodynamic collapse, not symptoms like palpitations or mild breathlessness.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How does management differ between a stable and an unstable tachycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Stable → time to identify the rhythm, consider pharmacological options and vagal manoeuvres
  • Unstable → call for help, IV access, synchronised DC shock, sedation if conscious

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the central conceptual question for any stable tachycardia, and why does it matter?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: 'Is the AV node in the circuit?' — it determines whether AV nodal blocking agents (adenosine, beta-blockers, verapamil, diltiazem) will terminate, slow, or endanger the patient.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Which tachycardias have the AV node IN the re-entry circuit, and what do nodal blockers do?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: AVNRT and AVRT (orthodromic) — the node is part of the circuit, so nodal blockers TERMINATE the rhythm.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: For which rhythms do AV nodal blockers provide rate control only (not termination)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• AF (atria sustain it; the node is gatekeeper)
  • atrial flutter (macro re-entry in the atria only)
  • atrial tachycardia (ectopic atrial focus)
  • and sinus tachycardia (treat the cause)
The node conducts but doesn't sustain the circuit, so blockers slow the rate but don't terminate.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: In which rhythms is the AV node NOT in the circuit, making nodal blockers dangerous or useless?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• VT (may cause arrest)
  • pre-excited AF (WPW — blocking the AV node forces all conduction down the accessory pathway → VF)
  • and antidromic AVRT (use procainamide/flecainide instead)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Give the key mnemonic linking narrow/regular/no-pre-excitation tachycardia to adenosine safety.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Narrow + regular + no pre-excitation → AV-node-dependent → adenosine is safe and likely terminates.Any broad-complex tachycardia → treat as VT; never give verapamil to a broad-complex rhythm.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: In the Resus Council adult tachycardia algorithm, what are the life-threatening (unstable) features, and what is the treatment?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Shock
  • syncope
  • myocardial ischaemia
  • severe heart failure
  • and immediately post-ROSC (Resus Council UK)
Treatment: synchronised DC shock up to 3 attempts (sedation or anaesthesia if conscious); if unsuccessful, amiodarone 300 mg IV over 10–20 min, then repeat the shock, followed by 900 mg over 24 h.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: In the stable narrow-complex REGULAR pathway, what is the first manoeuvre, and what drug follows if ineffective?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Vagal manoeuvres first. If ineffective, give adenosine (6 mg rapid IV bolus → 12 mg → 18 mg if needed) with continuous ECG monitoring — reduce the initial dose to 3 mg with dipyridamole or carbamazepine, a transplanted (denervated) heart, or central-line administration (BNF); if still ineffective, verapamil or a beta-blocker — never both.IV verapamil must not be given to a patient who has received a beta-blocker (risk of severe hypotension, AV block and asystole), and is contraindicated in significant LV systolic dysfunction (BNF).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: In the stable narrow-complex IRREGULAR pathway (probable AF), how is rate controlled and when is anticoagulation considered?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Control rate with a beta-blocker; consider digoxin or amiodarone if there is evidence of heart failure. Cardiovert only if onset clearly <48h, otherwise anticoagulate/TOE first; long-term anticoagulation is decided by CHA₂DS₂-VASc, not duration.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: In the stable broad-complex REGULAR pathway, what drug is given if it is VT or uncertain rhythm?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Amiodarone 300 mg IV over 20–60 min (the 10–20 min infusion is the unstable, post-shock dose).If there is a previous certain diagnosis of SVT with BBB/aberrant conduction, treat as for a regular narrow-complex tachycardia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: In the stable broad-complex IRREGULAR pathway, what are the possibilities and how is polymorphic VT (torsades) treated?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Possibilities include AF with BBB (treat as for irregular narrow-complex) or polymorphic VT (e.g. torsades de pointes) → give magnesium 2 g over 10 min.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What should be assessed and done in the initial ABCDE approach to any tachycardia, per the Resus algorithm?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Give oxygen if SpO₂ <94%
  • obtain IV access
  • monitor ECG/BP/SpO₂ and record a 12-lead ECG
  • and identify/treat reversible causes (e.g. electrolyte abnormalities, hypovolaemia causing sinus tachycardia)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What three features do all irregular narrow-complex tachycardias share?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Narrow QRS (<120 ms)
  • an irregularly irregular rhythm
  • and no consistent P–QRS relationship
The AV node is a bystander, not part of the circuit.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are the defining ECG features of AF among the irregular narrow-complex tachycardias?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• No P waves
  • a chaotic fibrillatory baseline (f-waves, best seen in V1)
  • and completely irregular R-R intervals

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What ECG features distinguish variable-block atrial flutter?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Sawtooth flutter waves at ~300 bpm (best in II, III, aVF)
  • an irregular ventricular response (varying block ratio)
  • and no isoelectric baseline

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What ECG features define multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• ≥3 distinct P-wave morphologies in the same lead
  • varying PR intervals
  • and an irregular rhythm with a rate typically 100–150 bpm

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the underlying mechanism of atrial fibrillation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Disorganised atrial electrical activity driven by multiple chaotic micro re-entry wavelets — there is no single focus and no coordinated atrial contraction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are the three key consequences of atrial fibrillation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Haemodynamic (loss of atrial kick → cardiac output drops 10–20%, worse in diastolic dysfunction)
  • thromboembolic (stasis in the left atrial appendage → thrombus → stroke/TIA, risk ×5 vs general population)
  • and tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy if a sustained fast rate is untreated for months

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: By how much does AF increase stroke risk compared with the general population?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Approximately five-fold (×5).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Define paroxysmal and persistent AF.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Paroxysmal = self-terminating <7 days (usually <48h), with sinus rhythm restored spontaneously
  • Persistent = duration >7 days; requires cardioversion to restore sinus rhythm

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Define long-standing persistent and permanent AF.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Long-standing persistent = >12 months, with rhythm control still being attempted
  • Permanent = cardioversion abandoned; rate control and anticoagulation only

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What distinguishes valvular from non-valvular AF, and why does it matter for anticoagulation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Valvular AF = AF with moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical heart valve. It matters because valvular AF requires warfarin (a VKA) — DOACs are contraindicated. All other AF is non-valvular → DOACs preferred.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What does the SMITH mnemonic for the causes of AF stand for?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• S – Sepsis, Surgery (post-op AF, esp. cardiac), Sleep apnoea
  • M – Mitral valve disease (MS/MR dilate the LA)
  • I – IHD/MI, Inflammation (pericarditis, myocarditis), Idiopathic (lone AF)
  • T – Thyroid (hyperthyroidism — always check TFTs in new AF)
  • H – Hypertension (most common modifiable cause worldwide)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the most common modifiable cause of AF worldwide?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Hypertension.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is 'holiday heart syndrome'?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Binge drinking (alcohol) triggering paroxysmal AF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Name additional causes of AF beyond the SMITH mnemonic.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Alcohol (holiday heart syndrome)
  • PE
  • COPD/pneumonia
  • obesity
  • HF/cardiomyopathy
  • and caffeine/stimulants (minor risk)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the hallmark ECG feature of AF, and what is the atrial rate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: An irregularly irregular rhythm (no two R-R intervals are equal) is the hallmark. The atrial rate is 350–600 bpm, with absent P waves replaced by fibrillatory f-waves (best in V1 and lead II).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the typical untreated ventricular rate in AF, and why is it slower than the atrial rate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Typically 100–160 bpm untreated — the AV node filters the chaotic atrial impulses, so only some conduct to the ventricles.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is unstable (haemodynamically compromised) AF managed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion regardless of onset time — do not delay for anticoagulation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are the first-line rate-control agents in stable AF, and the key cautions?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: NICE offers either a standard beta-blocker (not sotalol) or a rate-limiting CCB (diltiazem or verapamil) as initial rate-control monotherapy (NICE) — they are co-first-line.Avoid beta-blockers in decompensated HF and CCBs in HFrEF, and never combine a beta-blocker with IV verapamil (BNF). Digoxin for sedentary patients or HF with AF (poor rate control on exertion).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are the heart rate targets for rate control in AF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• HR <110 bpm at rest (lenient strategy)
  • <80 bpm if symptomatic

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: When can a patient with AF be cardioverted safely without prolonged anticoagulation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: If onset is <48 hours (or they have been anticoagulated for ≥3 weeks) → cardiovert safely.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is AF of >48h or unknown onset managed before cardioversion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Either perform a TOE to exclude a left atrial appendage thrombus
  • OR anticoagulate for ≥3 weeks before and ≥4 weeks after cardioversion

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Which chemical cardioversion agents are used in AF, and when is each chosen?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Flecainide if there is no structural heart disease
  • amiodarone if there is structural heart disease or HF

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the energy for electrical cardioversion of AF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Synchronised DC shock. For AF, an initial shock at maximum defibrillator output is supported rather than escalating from 120–150 J (Resus Council UK).120–150 J remains the starting energy for broad-complex/VT, and 70–120 J for atrial flutter and regular narrow-complex SVT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: List the CHA₂DS₂-VASc factors and their point values.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• C – Congestive HF (or LVEF <40%) = 1
  • H – Hypertension = 1
  • A – Age ≥75 = 2
  • D – Diabetes = 1
  • S₂ – Stroke/TIA/thromboembolism = 2
  • V – Vascular disease (prior MI, PAD, aortic plaque) = 1
  • A – Age 65–74 = 1
  • Sc – Sex (female) = 1

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How do CHA₂DS₂-VASc scores translate into anticoagulation decisions?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
NICE uses the same threshold for both sexes — female sex still scores a point, but it does not change the threshold.
  • Score ≥2 → offer anticoagulation
  • Score 1 in men → consider anticoagulation
  • Score 0 in men, or 1 in women arising from sex alone → do not anticoagulate (NICE)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Which anticoagulant is preferred in non-valvular AF, and which is required in valvular AF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran) are preferred for non-valvular AF
  • Warfarin (VKA) is required for valvular AF (mechanical valve, moderate-to-severe MS)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the macro re-entry circuit responsible for typical atrial flutter, and what is the critical slow zone?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: A macro re-entry circuit circulating around the tricuspid annulus. The cavotricuspid isthmus (CTI) — tissue between the tricuspid valve and inferior vena cava — is the critical slow zone; ablating it breaks the circuit.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are the ECG features of atrial flutter, including the typical atrial rate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Atrial rate ~300 bpm (range 250–350)
  • sawtooth flutter waves (inverted in II, III, aVF; upright in V1)
  • and no isoelectric baseline between flutter waves

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How does AV block ratio affect the appearance of atrial flutter?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Variable AV block → irregular ventricular response
  • Fixed 2:1 block → ventricular rate ~150, regular (which then appears as a regular narrow-complex tachycardia)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How does anticoagulation and cardioversion in atrial flutter compare with AF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Same CHA₂DS₂-VASc thresholds — the stroke risk is equivalent. The same <48h / >48h anticoagulation rule applies. Flutter is often more cardioversion-responsive than AF, needing lower energy — 70–120 J biphasic for flutter, whereas for AF an initial shock at maximum defibrillator output is now supported rather than escalating from 120–150 J (Resus Council UK).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the curative treatment for typical atrial flutter, and how effective is it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: CTI (cavotricuspid isthmus) ablation — curative in ~95% of typical flutter; first-line for recurrent or persistent flutter.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Why is cardioversion ineffective in multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: MAT is caused by multiple ectopic atrial foci firing chaotically — it is NOT a single re-entry circuit, so there is no circuit to interrupt with a shock.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the cornerstone of MAT management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
Treat the underlying cause
  • oxygen for hypoxia
  • optimise COPD
  • and correct Mg²⁺ and K⁺

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the preferred rate-control agent in MAT, and what is avoided?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: A CCB (verapamil or diltiazem) is preferred; avoid beta-blockers in bronchospasm (MAT is often associated with COPD).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Does MAT require routine anticoagulation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: No — MAT does not carry the same stroke risk as AF/flutter; it is not a re-entry rhythm with atrial stasis in the same way.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What three features do all regular narrow-complex tachycardias share?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Narrow QRS (<120 ms)
  • regular R–R intervals
  • and a rate >100 bpm

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Into which three groups are the regular narrow-complex tachycardias divided by AV-node involvement?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Group A — re-entry with the AV node IN the circuit (AVNRT, orthodromic AVRT)
  • Group B — AV node a bystander (atrial tachycardia, atrial flutter with fixed 2:1)
  • Group C — normal pacemaker (sinus tachycardia)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the '150 bpm trap' in regular narrow-complex tachycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: A regular narrow tachycardia at exactly ~150 bpm should be assumed to be atrial flutter with fixed 2:1 block until proven otherwise.P (flutter) waves may be hidden in the T waves; give adenosine to unmask them.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the shared treatment principle for Group A (AV-node-dependent) tachycardias?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: The AV node is an essential part of the re-entry circuit, so blocking it (vagal manoeuvres or adenosine) terminates the arrhythmia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is AVNRT, how common is it, and who does it affect?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Atrioventricular Nodal Re-entrant Tachycardia — the most common paroxysmal SVT. It affects young adults, more commonly women, with abrupt onset and offset (an 'on-off switch').

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Describe the mechanism of AVNRT.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Two pathways within the AV node — slow (slower conduction, SHORTER refractory period) and fast (faster conduction, LONGER refractory period). A premature atrial beat finds the fast pathway still refractory, travels down the slow pathway, and re-enters retrogradely up the fast → a sustained loop.Atria and ventricles are activated nearly simultaneously (P buried in or just after the QRS).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the ECG signature of AVNRT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Rate 140–280 bpm, regular, narrow QRS
  • P waves are buried in the QRS or immediately after → pseudo-R' in V1 (most useful sign) or pseudo-S in II/III/aVF
  • Short RP interval (RP < PR)
  • Abrupt onset, often triggered by a PAC

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the most useful ECG sign of AVNRT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: A pseudo-R' in V1 (from the P wave buried just after the QRS).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the stepwise acute treatment of AVNRT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Step 1: vagal manoeuvres — the modified Valsalva with legs elevated terminates ~40%, standard Valsalva or carotid sinus massage ~20–25%
  • Step 2: adenosine IV (6 mg rapid bolus → 12 mg → 18 mg)
  • Step 3 if adenosine fails: verapamil 5–10 mg IV over ~2 min with ECG monitoring (never if broad complex/pre-excitation) or metoprolol IV — never both
IV verapamil must not be given to a patient who has received a beta-blocker (risk of severe hypotension, AV block and asystole), and is contraindicated in significant LV systolic dysfunction (BNF).Synchronised DC cardioversion if haemodynamically unstable.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How does adenosine work in AVNRT, and what must the patient be warned about?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: It transiently blocks the AV node → terminates the circuit. Warn the patient about flushing, chest tightness and brief asystole (seconds).It is contraindicated in asthma and high-degree AV block. Reduce the initial dose to 3 mg if the patient takes dipyridamole or carbamazepine, has a transplanted (denervated) heart, or the drug is given through a central line (BNF).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the long-term/recurrent management of AVNRT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Beta-blocker or a rate-limiting CCB (diltiazem/verapamil) first-line for prevention
  • flecainide second-line (structurally normal heart only)
  • slow-pathway catheter ablation is curative (>95% success, low risk of AV block)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is orthodromic AVRT, and what is the path of conduction?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Re-entry using an accessory pathway (e.g. Bundle of Kent in WPW). Orthodromic = conduction down the AV node and up the accessory pathway → narrow QRS (normal ventricular activation).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the ECG signature of orthodromic AVRT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Rate 150–250 bpm, regular, narrow QRS
  • P wave after the QRS → RP < PR (inverted P in II/III/aVF), but a longer RP than AVNRT (P clearly visible after the QRS, not buried)
  • In sinus rhythm, look for a short PR + delta wave (WPW)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How does the P-wave position differ between AVNRT and orthodromic AVRT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• In AVNRT the P is buried in/just after the QRS (very short RP)
  • In orthodromic AVRT the P is clearly visible after the QRS (longer RP, though still RP < PR)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are the ECG hallmarks of WPW in sinus rhythm?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: A short PR interval and a delta wave (δ) — the diagnostic hallmark of pre-excitation, caused by the accessory pathway pre-exciting the ventricle.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Why does orthodromic AVRT produce a narrow QRS while antidromic AVRT produces a broad QRS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Orthodromic (~90–95%): antegrade down the AV node → His-Purkinje → ventricles activated via normal wiring → narrow QRS
  • Antidromic (~5–10%): antegrade down the accessory pathway straight into ventricular muscle, bypassing His-Purkinje → abnormal sequential spread → broad QRS (mimics VT)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What do 'orthodromic' and 'antidromic' refer to in AVRT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• 'Ortho' = correct direction (antegrade down the AV node)
  • 'anti' = opposite direction (antegrade down the accessory pathway)
The pathway taken determines the QRS width.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the treatment of orthodromic AVRT, including the definitive option?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Same stepwise approach as AVNRT — vagal manoeuvres → adenosine → verapamil or a beta-blocker (never both — IV verapamil after a beta-blocker risks severe hypotension, AV block and asystole; BNF) → DC cardioversion if unstable. Definitive: accessory pathway ablation (curative).Long-term, avoid AV nodal blockers if WPW is present in sinus rhythm (risk of pre-excited AF).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Why must antidromic AVRT be managed differently from orthodromic AVRT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Antidromic AVRT (conduction down the accessory pathway, up the AV node) is a broad-complex tachycardia, so it is treated differently (as per the Regular Broad section), not with AV nodal blockers.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the shared principle for Group B (AV node a bystander) tachycardias?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: The AV node conducts the impulse to the ventricles but is not part of the sustaining circuit. Adenosine transiently blocks AV conduction → unmasks the underlying atrial activity (diagnostic) but does not terminate.Manage with rate control.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the mechanism and rate of atrial tachycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: An ectopic atrial focus firing faster than the sinus node (enhanced automaticity or micro re-entry), at a rate of 100–250 bpm, regular.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the 'warm-up' phenomenon in atrial tachycardia, and what does it distinguish it from?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: The rate gradually accelerates at the start ('warm-up'), which distinguishes it from AVNRT/AVRT, both of which have an abrupt onset.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are the ECG features of atrial tachycardia (P wave and PR interval)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Abnormal P-wave morphology (differs from the sinus P in the same lead; P axis depends on focus location)
  • and a normal or prolonged PR interval (because the AV node is not part of the circuit)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are the causes of atrial tachycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Structural heart disease
  • digoxin toxicity
  • alcohol
  • and hypoxia

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is atrial tachycardia treated?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Treat the underlying cause (especially digoxin toxicity — stop digoxin)
  • rate control with beta-blockers or CCBs
  • rhythm control if needed (flecainide, amiodarone)
  • and focal catheter ablation if recurrent and drug-refractory
Adenosine may transiently block the AV node and reveal atrial activity but rarely terminates.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the ECG signature of atrial flutter with fixed 2:1 block?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Atrial rate ~300 bpm with fixed 2:1 AV block → ventricular rate ~150 bpm, regular. Sawtooth flutter waves (inverted in II, III, aVF; upright in V1), with no isoelectric baseline.Flutter waves may be hidden in the T waves at 2:1 — look carefully.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the '150 bpm rule' for atrial flutter, and how can adenosine help?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Any regular narrow tachycardia at ~150 bpm → consider flutter first. Adenosine increases AV block transiently → the flutter waves become visible.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is fixed 2:1 atrial flutter managed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Rate control with beta-blockers, CCBs or digoxin (same as AF)
  • anticoagulation using the same CHA₂DS₂-VASc thresholds as AF
  • cardioversion (highly effective, often lower energy than AF — 70–120 J for flutter, whereas AF is now shocked at maximum defibrillator output; Resus Council UK)
  • CTI ablation (curative ~95%)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the key principle about sinus tachycardia (Group C)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Sinus tachycardia is always a response to something — it is physiologically appropriate. Never rate-block it without identifying and treating the cause, as slowing the rate without addressing the driver can be dangerous.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are the ECG features of sinus tachycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Rate 100–160 bpm (rarely >200 in adults)
  • a normal upright P wave before every QRS (identical morphology throughout)
  • a normal PR interval (0.12–0.20 s)
  • gradual onset and offset (not abrupt)
  • and rate that varies with respiration and activity

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What does the PIRATES mnemonic for the causes of sinus tachycardia stand for?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• P – Pain, PE, Pneumothorax
  • I – Infection/Sepsis, Inflammation
  • R – Respiratory failure (hypoxia)
  • A – Anaemia, Anxiety, Alcohol withdrawal
  • T – Thyrotoxicosis, Tamponade
  • E – Exercise, Electrolyte imbalance
  • S – Shock (hypovolaemic, cardiogenic, distributive), Stimulants

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is sinus tachycardia managed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Treat the underlying cause. Beta-blockers or CCBs may be used symptomatically in specific contexts (e.g. inappropriate sinus tachycardia, thyrotoxicosis) but only after the cause is established.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Summarise the three-way treatment split for regular narrow-complex tachycardias by the unifying question.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
The unifying question is 'Is the AV node part of the circuit?'
  • Yes → terminate (Group A: vagal/adenosine/ablation)
  • No, but conduction via it → rate control (Group B: beta-blockers or CCBs — never a beta-blocker and IV verapamil together (BNF) — or digoxin; adenosine is diagnostic only)
  • No, physiological → treat the cause (Group C: sinus tachycardia)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the 'Golden Rule' for any regular broad-complex tachycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Treat every regular broad-complex tachycardia as VT until proven otherwise. Misdiagnosing VT as SVT and giving a nodal blocker (verapamil, diltiazem) can be fatal; treating SVT as VT is almost always safe — the exception is an undiagnosed irregular broad-complex rhythm that turns out to be pre-excited AF, where amiodarone is not safe.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are the three causes of a regular broad-complex tachycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• 4A — Ventricular tachycardia (origin in ventricle; most common cause; default assumption)
  • 4B — SVT with aberrancy (SVT + bundle branch block; pre-existing or rate-related; looks broad but isn't VT)
  • 4C — SVT with pre-excitation (antidromic AVRT in WPW; conducts down the accessory pathway; rare but important)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is a broad QRS defined, and what three factors guide the diagnosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Broad QRS = ≥120 ms (3 small squares), rate >100 bpm, regular R–R intervals.History, ECG morphology, and haemodynamic context guide the diagnosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Why does VT produce a wide QRS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: The impulse originates below the His bundle in ventricular myocardium and spreads cell-to-cell (not via the His-Purkinje system) — this slow, abnormal depolarisation produces a wide QRS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the most common substrate for VT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Re-entry around scar tissue from a prior MI or ischaemic heart disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is monomorphic VT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: VT with the same QRS morphology throughout, arising from a stable re-entry circuit.(Polymorphic VT / torsades is covered under irregular broad tachycardias.)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Why is a history of ischaemic heart disease or prior MI critical when assessing a broad-complex tachycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: In any patient with known IHD or prior MI, a regular broad-complex tachycardia is VT until definitively proven otherwise — the scar provides the re-entry substrate, raising the pre-test probability of VT to >95%.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Does haemodynamic stability rule out VT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: No — patients can be in VT and remain haemodynamically stable.This is a common and dangerous trap.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: List the ECG features with HIGH specificity for VT.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• AV dissociation (P waves and QRS march independently — pathognomonic)
  • capture beats (occasional narrow QRS when a sinus impulse briefly captures the ventricles)
  • fusion beats (hybrid QRS when sinus and ventricular impulses collide)
  • and concordance (all precordial leads V1–V6 point the same direction)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are the supportive (less specific) features favouring VT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Very broad QRS (>140 ms — the wider, the more likely VT)
  • extreme axis deviation (north-west axis / 'no man's land', −90° to ±180°)
  • an RBBB-like pattern but with a dominant S in V6 (not a tall R)
  • and an LBBB-like pattern but with Q or R in V1 (not a pure negative deflection)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What defines 'unstable' VT requiring immediate cardioversion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
Any of:
  • hypotension
  • shock
  • syncope
  • pulmonary oedema
  • or ischaemic chest pain

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is UNSTABLE VT managed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion (sedate first if conscious — midazolam/propofol).If pulseless, treat as VF — unsynchronised defibrillation + CPR (arrest algorithm).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is STABLE VT managed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Amiodarone 300 mg IV over 20–60 min (first-line UK), then 900 mg over 24h maintenance. Correct electrolytes (K⁺, Mg²⁺).Procainamide or lidocaine are alternatives. Prepare for cardioversion if drug therapy fails.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the mechanism of SVT with aberrancy?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: A supraventricular rhythm (AVNRT, AVRT, atrial tachycardia) conducts normally to the AV node, but below the AV node conduction is blocked or delayed in one bundle branch. The ventricle depolarises via the opposite bundle — slow spread → broad QRS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the difference between pre-existing BBB and rate-related (phase 3) BBB?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Pre-existing BBB is present at baseline with the same morphology in sinus rhythm
  • Rate-related BBB appears only at faster rates, when the bundle's refractory period is exceeded

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What ECG features help distinguish SVT with aberrancy from VT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Classic RBBB or LBBB morphology (not atypical)
  • no AV dissociation (no capture or fusion beats)
  • P waves visible and 1:1 with QRS
  • identical morphology to a prior 12-lead (if pre-existing BBB)
  • a narrow QRS at a slower rate on a previous ECG (if rate-related)
  • and termination/slowing with vagal manoeuvres or adenosine

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the clinical bottom line for using adenosine in a suspected SVT with aberrancy?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Adenosine is useful diagnostically — but only if you are confident this is NOT VT (old 12-lead showing BBB, no structural heart disease, haemodynamically stable, classic SVT history).When in doubt, treat as VT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Describe the classic RBBB vs LBBB morphology used to identify aberrancy.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• RBBB: rSR' in V1 and qRs in V6
  • LBBB: rS in V1 and R in V6
SVT with aberrancy shows one of these classic patterns — atypical morphology favours VT instead.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is antidromic AVRT, and what is its conduction path?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: In WPW, the accessory pathway conducts both ways. Antidromic: the impulse travels antegrade DOWN the accessory pathway, then retrograde UP the His-AV node. The ventricle depolarises entirely via the AP → maximally pre-excited → very broad, slurred QRS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How common is antidromic AVRT, and what are its ECG/clinical features?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
Uncommon — ~5–10% of AVRT in WPW patients.
  • ECG: broad, maximally pre-excited QRS (may resemble LBBB or be atypical)
  • regular tachycardia ~150–250 bpm
  • NO AV dissociation (the AV node is part of the circuit retrogradely)
A history of WPW or a δ-wave on the baseline ECG is a diagnostic clue.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Why are AV nodal blockers dangerous in antidromic AVRT / pre-excited WPW?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Nodal blockers (adenosine, verapamil, beta-blockers) would terminate a pure antidromic AVRT, but are avoided: if the rhythm is (or degenerates into) pre-excited AF, blocking the AV node lets impulses conduct unopposed down the accessory pathway → very fast rates → VF.Use flecainide or procainamide instead (or DC cardioversion).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What happens if AF develops in a patient with WPW?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: It becomes pre-excited AF — a life-threatening irregular broad-complex tachycardia (covered under the irregular broad section).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Summarise the ECG/clinical features that favour VT in the VT-vs-SVT decision.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• AV dissociation (pathognomonic)
  • capture or fusion beats
  • concordance in precordial leads
  • QRS >140 ms
  • extreme/north-west axis
  • known IHD or prior MI
  • structural heart disease
  • and atypical BBB morphology

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Summarise the features that FAVOUR SVT with aberrancy in the VT-vs-SVT decision.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Classic RBBB or LBBB morphology
  • P waves clearly 1:1 with the QRS
  • no AV dissociation/capture/fusion
  • identical to a prior ECG with BBB
  • young patient with no structural heart disease
  • termination with adenosine
  • and a prior history of SVT with no syncope

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are the three safety rules summarising VT-vs-SVT management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• 1) Stability first — unstable → immediate synchronised DC cardioversion regardless of diagnosis
  • 2) Doubt = VT — if you cannot confidently exclude VT, treat as VT (amiodarone IV); never give verapamil/diltiazem blindly to a broad-complex tachycardia
  • 3) The unifying question — 'Could this be VT?' If yes, treat as VT; step down only with clear evidence and specialist input

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the danger instinct to instil for any irregular broad-complex tachycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Irregular + broad → think pre-excited AF or polymorphic VT until proven otherwise.Never reflexively give AV-nodal blockers — it can be fatal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are the three causes of an irregular broad-complex tachycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• 5A — Pre-excited AF (WPW + AF; very fast, varying width; the lethal trap)
  • 5B — Polymorphic VT / Torsades (twisting QRS morphology, long QT substrate, can degenerate to VF)
  • 5C — AF with BBB (ordinary AF + block, fixed BBB morphology, managed as AF)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is a broad QRS defined for the irregular broad tachycardias, and why does distinguishing them matter?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: ≥120 ms, rate >100 bpm, irregular R–R intervals.Distinguishing the three causes determines whether you give a nodal blocker or avoid it entirely.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the mechanism of pre-excited AF in WPW?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: In WPW the accessory pathway (AP) bypasses the AV node. When AF develops, the chaotic atrial impulses conduct directly down the AP — bypassing the AV node's protective rate-limiting gating — so the ventricles are bombarded at near-atrial rates (300–600 bpm atrial, often >200 bpm ventricular).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Why does the QRS width vary beat-to-beat in pre-excited AF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Each beat may conduct via the AP, the AV node, or both — producing fusion beats with varying QRS width from one beat to the next.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the ECG signature of pre-excited AF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Irregular R–R intervals (underlying AF)
  • broad QRS (conducted via AP)
  • very fast (ventricular rate often >200 bpm)
  • varying QRS width (beat-to-beat fusion)
  • no organised P waves
  • and — if seen prior — a short PR + delta wave on the baseline WPW ECG

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Why must AV-nodal blockers NEVER be given in pre-excited AF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blockers and digoxin block the AV node and force all conduction down the accessory pathway → extreme rate acceleration → VF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is UNSTABLE pre-excited AF managed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion (sedate first if conscious).If it has degenerated to VF → unsynchronised defibrillation + CPR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is STABLE pre-excited AF managed pharmacologically?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: In the UK the RCUK algorithm says: seek expert help and consider amiodarone. Flecainide IV (no structural heart disease) or procainamide IV are the ESC/AHA options where available. All work by slowing accessory-pathway conduction rather than blocking the AV node. Consider early cardioversion if the drug response is slow. The non-negotiable point is that AV-nodal blockers are never given.Note the divergence: ESC classes IV amiodarone as not recommended and potentially harmful in pre-excited AF, whereas the UK algorithm still lists it as a consider-with-expert-help option (Resus Council UK). For UK exams and UK practice, follow the UK position.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is polymorphic VT, and what defines torsades de pointes specifically?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Polymorphic VT is VT with continuously varying QRS morphology and axis — irregular, 'twisting around the baseline'
  • Torsades de pointes is polymorphic VT occurring on a background of a prolonged QT interval

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the mechanism linking a prolonged QT to torsades?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Prolonged QT → prolonged repolarisation → spontaneous depolarisation in some cells (early after-depolarisations) → triggered VT.It is typically self-terminating but can degenerate to VF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the ECG signature of torsades de pointes?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: An irregular broad-complex tachycardia where the QRS complexes twist around the isoelectric baseline — amplitude waxes and wanes over 5–20 beats. The preceding sinus rhythm shows a long QT (key diagnostic clue). Rate typically 160–250 bpm; may self-terminate, recur, or degenerate to VF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is the QT interval measured, and what QTc values count as prolonged?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: QT is measured from the start of the QRS to the end of the T wave. Corrected QT (QTc) >440 ms (men) or >460 ms (women) is prolonged.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Name the congenital causes of a prolonged QT interval.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Long QT syndrome (LQTS — a channelopathy)
  • Romano-Ward (autosomal dominant)
  • and Jervell and Lange-Nielsen (associated with deafness)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: List the high-yield drug causes of a prolonged QT.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Antiarrhythmics (sotalol, amiodarone)
  • antipsychotics (haloperidol, quetiapine)
  • antidepressants (citalopram, TCAs)
  • antibiotics (macrolides — erythromycin, clarithromycin)
  • antiemetics (ondansetron, domperidone)
  • and antimalarials (chloroquine, quinine)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Which electrolyte abnormalities cause a prolonged QT, and which is the most common?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Hypokalaemia (the most common electrolyte cause), hypomagnesaemia, and hypocalcaemia — all impair repolarisation and lengthen the QT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is unstable or pulseless torsades managed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Unsynchronised defibrillation (polymorphic morphology makes synchronisation unreliable).If pulseless → arrest algorithm.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the first-line treatment for stable torsades de pointes, and the key point about it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: IV magnesium sulphate 2 g over 10 min — first-line even if the serum Mg²⁺ is normal, because it stabilises cardiac membranes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Beyond magnesium, what are the management steps for stable torsades?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Correct electrolytes (K⁺ >4.5 mmol/L; Mg²⁺ >1 mmol/L; Ca²⁺)
  • stop all QT-prolonging drugs immediately
  • treat the underlying cause
  • consider temporary (overdrive) pacing — which shortens the QT
  • ICD if recurrent/congenital LQTS
  • and avoid amiodarone (it itself prolongs QT)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Why is the distinction between sotalol and other beta-blockers important in torsades?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Sotalol prolongs the QT and can cause torsades — do not confuse it with other beta-blockers, which are safe and actually used in congenital LQTS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the mechanism of AF with BBB, and why is it the 'less scary' irregular broad rhythm?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Ordinary AF (irregular atrial activity) plus a pre-existing or rate-related BBB. The AF provides the irregularity and the BBB provides the broad QRS. The AV node is intact and still rate-limiting (ventricular rate rarely >180 bpm) — it's just AF that looks broad.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How do you distinguish pre-excited AF from AF with BBB on rate, QRS width, history and treatment?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Pre-excited AF: rate >200 bpm, QRS width varies beat-to-beat, history of WPW/δ-wave, treat with flecainide/DC
  • AF with BBB: rate typically <180 bpm, fixed BBB morphology, known BBB/structural disease, treat with rate control + anticoagulation

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is AF with BBB managed once pre-excited AF is confidently excluded?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Manage as AF — rate control (beta-blocker / CCB / digoxin) and anticoagulate per CHA₂DS₂-VASc score.If in doubt, treat as pre-excited AF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Summarise the discriminating features of pre-excited AF, torsades, and AF+BBB.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• Pre-excited AF: very fast (>200 bpm), varying QRS width beat-to-beat, history of WPW/δ-wave, no clear BBB pattern
  • Torsades: twisting QRS, preceding long QT, drug/electrolyte history, self-terminating but recurrent
  • AF+BBB: slower rate (<180 bpm), fixed BBB morphology, classic RBBB/LBBB, known BBB or structural disease

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are the three safety rules for any irregular broad-complex tachycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
• 1) Stability first — unstable → synchronised DC cardioversion (unsynchronised defibrillation + CPR if it degenerates to VF)
  • 2) No AV-nodal blockers — never give adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blockers or digoxin until pre-excited AF is excluded
  • 3) Deterioration risk — both pre-excited AF and torsades can degenerate to VF, so have a defibrillator immediately available

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: A patient survives an episode of sustained monomorphic VT. Beyond terminating it, what does their management involve?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
Find the cause, then decide on a device.
  • Correct reversible causes — ischaemia, K⁺, Mg²⁺, proarrhythmic/QT-prolonging drugs
  • Assess the substrate — echo for LV function + ischaemia assessment / angiography
  • Beta-blocker; treat underlying heart failure
  • ICD for secondary prevention if no completely reversible cause
  • VT catheter ablation for recurrent VT or repeated ICD shocks
  • Amiodarone/sotalol reduce episodes but never replace an ICD

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: When is an ICD not indicated after an episode of sustained VT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: When the VT had a completely reversible cause. Classic examples: VT within 48 hours of an MI that has been revascularised, or VT driven by a corrected electrolyte abnormality or drug.By contrast, VT arising from established scar with no reversible trigger does warrant an ICD — this is the discriminator examiners test.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What must you check before performing carotid sinus massage, and when should you avoid it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back:
Listen for a carotid bruit first. CSM can dislodge atheroma and cause a stroke. Avoid if:
  • a bruit is present
  • known carotid stenosis
  • or TIA/stroke in the last 3 months
Never massage both sides at once.Perform with continuous ECG monitoring, IV access and resuscitation facilities available.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Which vagal manoeuvre is the safer first choice in stable SVT, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: The modified Valsalva (blow into a syringe, then lie flat with legs passively raised).It carries none of the stroke risk of carotid sinus massage, and it is the manoeuvre with the best evidence — it terminates far more episodes than the standard Valsalva.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: What is a cardiomyopathy?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: A primary disease of the heart muscle itself — a structural/functional myocardial abnormality NOT explained by coronary artery disease, valve disease, hypertension or congenital heart disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: Distinguish primary from secondary cardiomyopathy.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: Primary = disease confined to the myocardium (often genetic). Secondary = myocardial involvement as part of a systemic disorder (e.g. amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, haemochromatosis).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: Name the three classic morphological/functional patterns of cardiomyopathy.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: Dilated, hypertrophic, and restrictive.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: Name two high-yield named cardiomyopathies beyond the three classic patterns.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy and arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: Which cardiomyopathy causes systolic dysfunction (reduced EF)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: Dilated cardiomyopathy (HFrEF).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: Which cardiomyopathies cause diastolic dysfunction with a preserved ejection fraction?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: Hypertrophic and restrictive cardiomyopathy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: What is the commonest type of cardiomyopathy?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: What is the core problem in dilated cardiomyopathy?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: A dilated, thin, poorly-contracting ventricle → systolic failure (HFrEF), arrhythmia and thromboembolism.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: List the main causes of dilated cardiomyopathy (ABCDE).
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back:
• Alcohol/Autoimmune (viral myocarditis);
  • Beri-beri (thiamine);
  • Cocaine/Chemo (doxorubicin, trastuzumab);
  • Dilated genetic (some forms carry conduction disease and arrhythmia) + Duchenne;
  • Endocrine (thyroid), peripartum, haemochromatosis, tachycardia-induced.
~50% idiopathic.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: What are the key clinical features/signs of dilated cardiomyopathy?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back:
• Heart failure (dyspnoea, orthopnoea, oedema, fatigue),
  • displaced apex,
  • S3 gallop,
  • functional mitral regurgitation,
  • AF and ventricular arrhythmia,
  • and thromboembolism from mural thrombus.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: Why is anticoagulation important in dilated cardiomyopathy?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: The dilated, akinetic chamber predisposes to mural thrombus and systemic embolism — anticoagulate if AF or intracardiac thrombus.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: Outline the management of dilated cardiomyopathy.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back:
Standard HFrEF therapy:
  • ACEi/ARB (or ARNI),
  • beta-blocker,
  • MRA,
  • SGLT2i;
  • diuretics for congestion.
Anticoagulate if AF/thrombus. Where EF ≤35%, the choice between an ICD and CRT depends on QRS duration, LBBB and NYHA class — a specialist decision, not EF alone. Treat the cause; transplant if end-stage.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: What is peripartum cardiomyopathy?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: Heart failure from LV systolic dysfunction developing towards the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery, with no other cause found. EF is nearly always below 45%; the LV is usually — but not always — dilated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: Which reversible causes should be screened for in dilated cardiomyopathy?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back:
• Alcohol,
  • thyroid disease,
  • iron overload (haemochromatosis),
  • thiamine deficiency,
  • and persistent tachyarrhythmia (tachycardia-induced).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: What is the inheritance pattern and gene type in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: Autosomal dominant, mutations in sarcomere protein genes — most often MYBPC3 (myosin-binding protein C) and MYH7 (beta-myosin heavy chain). A substantial minority of patients have no identifiable variant, so a negative test does not exclude HCM.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: What is the commonest inherited cardiac disorder, and its prevalence?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, ~1 in 500.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: Describe the core lesion in HCM.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: Unexplained LV hypertrophy (classically asymmetric septal) → a stiff, non-compliant ventricle (diastolic dysfunction). In ~⅓, systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve causes dynamic LV outflow tract obstruction (HOCM).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: What is the commonest structural cause of sudden cardiac death in young people and athletes?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (ventricular arrhythmia). Note that in UK autopsy series the single commonest finding is a morphologically normal heart — sudden arrhythmic death syndrome — with arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy and HCM the leading structural diagnoses.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: What are the symptoms of HCM, and which is a red flag?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: Often asymptomatic; exertional dyspnoea, angina, palpitations, and syncope. Exertional syncope is a red flag for sudden-death risk.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: Describe the murmur of obstructive HCM and how it changes with manoeuvres.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: An ejection systolic murmur (LVOT). It gets LOUDER with Valsalva/standing (reduced preload) and softer with squatting — the opposite of aortic stenosis for Valsalva/squatting. (Handgrip softens both HCM and AS, so use Valsalva/squatting for the contrast.)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: What are the ECG features of HCM?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back:
• LVH,
  • deep T-wave inversion,
  • and 'dagger' septal Q waves.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: What are the echo features of HCM?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy (wall ≥15 mm — but ≥13 mm is diagnostic in a first-degree relative or a genotype-positive person), systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve, and an LVOT gradient — remembered as 'MR SAM ASH'.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: List the high-risk features used to guide ICD implantation in HCM.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back:
The validated 5-year risk score (ESC) is built from
  • age,
  • maximal LV wall thickness,
  • left atrial size,
  • LVOT gradient,
  • family history of sudden cardiac death,
  • non-sustained VT
  • and unexplained syncope.
An abnormal blood-pressure response to exercise is a supporting consideration, not part of the score.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: Which drugs should be AVOIDED in obstructive HCM, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: Nitrates, ACE inhibitors, diuretics and digoxin — they reduce preload/afterload or increase contractility and worsen dynamic outflow obstruction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: What is the first-line drug management of symptomatic obstructive HCM, and where does verapamil sit?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: A beta-blocker first-line; verapamil second-line if a beta-blocker is not tolerated. Both are negative inotropes and reduce the outflow gradient. Verapamil is cautioned or avoided in SEVERE LVOT obstruction with a high gradient and hypotension — it is also a vasodilator, so it drops afterload and can worsen the obstruction and precipitate collapse.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: What invasive options treat refractory LV outflow obstruction in HCM?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: Septal reduction, either surgically (myectomy) or by catheter (alcohol septal ablation) — considered when obstruction remains refractory after a beta-blocker or verapamil, with disopyramide or a cardiac myosin inhibitor (mavacamten) tried first (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: What lifestyle advice and screening are important in HCM?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: Avoid competitive/high-intensity sport until assessed (sudden-death risk); advice is then individualised at a specialist centre. Offer genetic testing and cascade family screening.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: What is the core problem in restrictive cardiomyopathy?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: Rigid, non-compliant ventricular walls with normal chamber size and preserved systolic function → diastolic dysfunction and predominantly right heart failure. It mimics constrictive pericarditis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: What is the commonest cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: Amyloidosis (AL and ATTR).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: List other causes of restrictive cardiomyopathy.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back:
• Sarcoidosis,
  • haemochromatosis,
  • endomyocardial fibrosis / Löffler endocarditis (hypereosinophilia),
  • radiation,
  • scleroderma,
  • storage diseases,
  • idiopathic.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: What are the echo and ECG features of restrictive cardiomyopathy?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back:
Echo: non-dilated ventricles with marked biatrial enlargement and preserved EF. Wall thickness is normal in idiopathic RCM but INCREASED in infiltrative causes such as amyloid.
ECG: low voltage with a pseudo-infarct pattern — thick walls with a low-voltage ECG is the amyloid giveaway.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: How is restrictive cardiomyopathy distinguished from constrictive pericarditis, and why does it matter?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: Both cause diastolic (right) heart failure; constriction shows pericardial thickening/calcification and marked respiratory variation, and is surgically treatable — potentially curable — by pericardiectomy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: What is the histological hallmark of cardiac amyloidosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: Apple-green birefringence under polarised light after Congo red staining.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: Outline the management of restrictive cardiomyopathy / cardiac amyloid.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back:
• Treat the cause (chemotherapy for AL amyloid, venesection for haemochromatosis; ATTR amyloid has specific drug therapy);
  • cautious diuresis (preload-dependent filling);
  • manage AF;
  • poor prognosis;
  • consider transplant.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: What is Takotsubo cardiomyopathy and its typical trigger?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: Transient LV apical ballooning ('octopus-pot' shape) from a catecholamine surge after emotional/physical stress — classically a post-menopausal woman.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: How does Takotsubo cardiomyopathy differ from an ACS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: It mimics ACS (chest pain, ST elevation, raised troponin) but coronary angiography is normal/unobstructed; there is apical ballooning with basal hyperkinesis, and LV function usually recovers over weeks — but the acute phase is not benign: cardiogenic shock, arrhythmia and death occur, and it can recur.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: What is the pathology and inheritance of ARVC?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: Autosomal-dominant desmosomal-protein mutations causing fibrofatty replacement of the right ventricular myocardium.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: What are the ECG features and main risk of ARVC?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: T-wave inversion in V1–V3 (in the absence of right bundle branch block) is the commoner finding; the epsilon wave is the most specific but is seen only in a minority. the main risk is ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death in young athletes (manage with beta-blockers/antiarrhythmics, ICD, exercise restriction).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: What is the first-line/key bedside investigation for a suspected cardiomyopathy?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: Echocardiography (with ECG, CXR and BNP) — it assesses chamber size, wall thickness, EF, diastolic function and gradients.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: What is the role of cardiac MRI in cardiomyopathy?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: Tissue characterisation (late gadolinium enhancement) for phenotyping and prognosis — increasingly the gold-standard imaging test.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: When is endomyocardial biopsy used in cardiomyopathy?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: In selected cases, particularly to confirm infiltrative disease such as amyloidosis or specific inflammatory causes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: Summarise the general management principles across the cardiomyopathies.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back:
• Treat heart failure appropriately to the type;
  • treat reversible causes;
  • manage arrhythmias and anticoagulate for AF/thrombus;
  • stratify sudden-death risk and implant an ICD where indicated;
  • family screening/genetic counselling;
  • transplant for end-stage disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: What is peripartum cardiomyopathy?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back: Heart failure with LV systolic dysfunction developing in late pregnancy or the first ~5 months postpartum, with no other cause found. It behaves like a dilated cardiomyopathy — but the drug treatment differs while the patient is still pregnant.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: How does heart-failure treatment differ in peripartum cardiomyopathy before delivery?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back:
Withheld antenatally: ACEi, ARB, ARNI, MRA and SGLT2i — ACE inhibitors and ARBs are teratogenic.
Used instead: hydralazine + a nitrate for afterload reduction, a beta-1 selective beta-blocker, and loop diuretics for congestion. After delivery the full HFrEF regimen can be introduced, adjusting the choice if breastfeeding.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.front: Why is anticoagulation important in peripartum cardiomyopathy, and what is the caveat with bromocriptine?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.back:
The thromboembolic risk is high — pregnancy is prothrombotic and the ventricle is dilated and poorly contracting.
Bromocriptine (used in some centres to suppress prolactin) must always be given with anticoagulation, because it further increases the risk of myocardial infarction and stroke.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: What are varicose veins?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back: Dilated, tortuous superficial leg veins (>3 mm) caused by incompetent venous valves and venous hypertension.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: What is chronic venous insufficiency (CVI)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back: The wider syndrome of sustained venous hypertension causing skin changes and ulceration.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: What three things does normal venous return depend on?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back:
• Competent valves (stop backflow),
  • the calf muscle pump,
  • and patent deep veins.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: Which superficial veins are involved in varicose veins, and where do they drain?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back: The great saphenous vein (GSV, medial) and small saphenous vein (SSV, posterior calf); they drain into the deep system at the saphenofemoral (SFJ) and saphenopopliteal (SPJ) junctions, plus perforators.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: Describe the vicious cycle underlying varicose veins.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back: Valve incompetence → reflux → venous hypertension → further dilatation → more valve failure; sustained pressure causes capillary leak, inflammation and skin changes/ulceration.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: What is the commonest type of varicose veins?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back: Primary (idiopathic valve/vein-wall weakness).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: List the risk factors for primary varicose veins.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back:
• Increasing age,
  • female sex,
  • family history,
  • pregnancy (multiparity),
  • obesity,
  • and prolonged standing (occupation).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: Name secondary causes of varicose veins.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back:
• Previous DVT (post-thrombotic syndrome, damaging deep valves),
  • pelvic mass/obstruction,
  • arteriovenous fistula,
  • and congenital (Klippel-Trénaunay).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: What are the typical symptoms of varicose veins?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back:
• Visible dilated tortuous veins;
  • aching, heaviness and throbbing worse on standing/at the end of the day and relieved by elevation;
  • itching, cramps, restless legs and ankle swelling.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: List the skin signs of chronic venous insufficiency.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back:
• Oedema,
  • haemosiderin pigmentation,
  • venous (varicose) eczema,
  • lipodermatosclerosis (the 'inverted champagne bottle' leg),
  • atrophie blanche,
  • and venous ulceration.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: What are the complications of varicose veins?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back:
• Superficial thrombophlebitis,
  • bleeding (can be brisk from a thin-walled varix),
  • venous ulceration,
  • and progression of skin changes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: What is a saphena varix and how does it behave?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back: A dilatation at the saphenofemoral junction that gives a cough impulse and disappears on lying — don't mistake it for a femoral hernia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: What is the investigation of choice for varicose veins?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back: Duplex ultrasound.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: What does duplex ultrasound show and exclude in varicose veins?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back:
• It confirms reflux,
  • localises the incompetence (SFJ/SPJ/perforators),
  • excludes deep venous obstruction/DVT,
  • and guides treatment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: What must be done before applying compression to a leg?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back: Measure the ABPI to exclude significant arterial disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: What is the conservative management of varicose veins?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back:
• Weight loss,
  • regular exercise,
  • leg elevation,
  • avoiding prolonged standing,
  • and compression stockings (for those unsuitable for or declining intervention, after excluding arterial disease).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: List the NICE criteria for referral of varicose veins to a vascular service.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back:
• Symptomatic primary or recurrent varicose veins;
  • skin changes attributable to CVI;
  • superficial vein thrombosis with suspected incompetence;
  • and a venous leg ulcer (active or healed).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: What is the first-line interventional treatment for varicose veins (NICE)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back: Endothermal ablation — radiofrequency ablation or endovenous laser ablation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: What is the second-line interventional option for varicose veins?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back: Ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy (if endothermal ablation is unsuitable).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: What is the third-line interventional option for varicose veins?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back: Surgery — ligation and stripping ± avulsions (if the above are unsuitable).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: What is the mainstay of venous leg ulcer management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back: Compression bandaging (after excluding arterial disease with ABPI) plus wound care, and treating the underlying venous incompetence to reduce recurrence.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: Describe the typical site and appearance of a venous ulcer.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back: Gaiter area (above the medial malleolus); large, shallow, irregular and exudative.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: Describe the typical site and appearance of an arterial ulcer.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back: Toes, heel, pressure points or lateral malleolus; small, deep, 'punched-out' and dry.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: How does the pain differ between venous and arterial ulcers?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back:
• Venous ulcers are less painful and better on elevation;
  • arterial ulcers are very painful, worse on elevation and better when the leg hangs down.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: What are the ABPI findings in venous vs arterial ulcers?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back:
• Venous ulcer: ABPI ≥0.8 (compression safe; normal 0.9–1.3).
  • Arterial ulcer: ABPI reduced (<0.8).
An ABPI >1.3 suggests incompressible/calcified vessels (e.g. diabetes/CKD) and is unreliable.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: Which vein and junction most commonly reflux in varicose veins?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back: The great saphenous vein at the saphenofemoral junction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: Why is compression harmful if arterial disease is not excluded first?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back: External compression further reduces the already-compromised arterial inflow to an ischaemic leg, risking tissue ischaemia, pressure necrosis and ulceration/limb loss — so ABPI is measured first to exclude significant arterial disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: How should you manage a varicose vein that is bleeding torrentially?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back: Lie the patient flat, elevate the leg above the level of the heart, and apply firm direct pressure with a pad — the bleeding is venous and pressure-driven, so elevation alone usually stops it. Then apply a compression bandage and refer to treat the underlying venous incompetence, because it will bleed again. The classic error is sitting the patient up, which raises venous pressure in the leg and the bleeding continues.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: Why is superficial vein thrombosis (SVT) in the leg not a trivial diagnosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back: Around one in five patients with SVT has a concurrent DVT, and thrombus in the great saphenous vein can propagate through the saphenofemoral junction into the deep system. It needs a duplex ultrasound, not reassurance.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: How is symptomatic superficial vein thrombosis of the leg managed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back:
• Duplex ultrasound to confirm it, measure its length and exclude a coexisting DVT.
  • If it is ≥5 cm long, give a prophylactic dose of fondaparinux (or LMWH) for 45 days.
  • Shorter distal segments are treated with NSAIDs, compression and analgesia.
  • Thrombus within a few centimetres of the saphenofemoral junction is treated as a proximal DVT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: Do antibiotics have a role in superficial vein thrombosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back: No. Despite the tender, hard, erythematous cord that can look like cellulitis, SVT is a thrombosis and not an infection. Treatment is anticoagulation (if ≥5 cm), NSAIDs and compression.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.front: What should prompt you to look for an underlying cause in superficial thrombophlebitis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.back: Migratory, recurrent or multi-site thrombophlebitis, particularly in a non-varicose vein — Trousseau's sign of malignancy, a paraneoplastic marker of occult cancer (pancreatic classically).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: Define aortic dissection.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: A tear in the aortic intima → blood forces its way between the intima and media → creates a false lumen that propagates along the aortic wall.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: Why is aortic dissection a time-critical emergency, and what determines management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Type A mortality rises ~1–2%/hour without surgery. Everything hinges on Stanford A vs B — this determines management.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: How is aortic dissection classified by time from symptom onset?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back:
• Acute = ≤14 days;
  • subacute = 15–90 days;
  • chronic = >90 days
(the first 24 hours is sometimes called hyperacute).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What complications arise from anterograde propagation of a dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Anterograde → iliac arteries → limb ischaemia, renal/mesenteric malperfusion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What complications arise from retrograde propagation of a dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Retrograde → aortic root → aortic regurgitation, coronary involvement, cardiac tamponade.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: How does aortic dissection link to AAA/TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: 'Dissecting aneurysm' is an outdated term for dissection itself — most dissections occur in a normal-calibre aorta, and a dissection is not a true aneurysm (which dilates all three layers). The same connective-tissue thread (Marfan, bicuspid AV) runs through all three aortic pathologies.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: Which classification matters clinically for aortic dissection, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: The Stanford classification — it directly determines surgical vs medical management.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: Define Stanford Type A dissection and its management.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Involves the ascending aorta (± arch/descending) — a surgical emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: Define Stanford Type B dissection and its management.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Does NOT involve the ascending aorta (arch and/or descending) — medical management if uncomplicated.Note "distal to the left subclavian" is the narrower DeBakey III definition.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What is the mnemonic for the Stanford classification?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back:
• A = Ascending = surgery (Aaargh, operate!);
  • B = Below/Beyond subclavian = medical (Best managed medically).
