conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: In the DeBakey classification, what is the extent of Type I and its Stanford equivalent?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Type I = ascending + arch + beyond = Stanford A.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: In the DeBakey classification, what is the extent of Type II and its Stanford equivalent?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Type II = ascending only = Stanford A.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: In the DeBakey classification, what is the extent of Type III and its Stanford equivalent?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Type III = descending only = Stanford B.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What is the most important modifiable risk factor for aortic dissection, and which transient surges are especially dangerous?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Hypertension. Transient surges are especially dangerous: cocaine use, heavy weightlifting.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: Which connective tissue diseases predispose to aortic dissection, and what is notable about thresholds?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back:
• Marfan syndrome (FBN1 — weak media),
  • Loeys-Dietz and
  • vascular Ehlers-Danlos (COL3A1).
Marfan and Loeys-Dietz are repaired at lower thresholds; vascular EDS is the exception — the wall is too friable for routine prophylactic surgery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: How does a bicuspid aortic valve predispose to dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Associated aortopathy — intrinsic media weakness independent of valve haemodynamics.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What demographic profile is typical for aortic dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Male sex, age 50–70, atherosclerosis — a shared risk profile with TAA.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What is the cardinal symptom of aortic dissection, and how does it differ from MI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Sudden-onset, severe 'tearing' or 'ripping' chest pain — maximal at onset(unlike MI, which builds).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: How does the pain location differ between Type A and Type B dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back:
• Type A → anterior chest pain (ascending aorta);
  • Type B → interscapular/back pain (descending aorta).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What causes a pulse deficit in aortic dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Absent or weak carotid/brachial/femoral pulse — the false lumen occluding a branch.Present in only about a third of cases, so a normal pulse examination does not exclude dissection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What does a >20 mmHg inter-arm BP difference indicate in dissection, and what is the teaching?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Subclavian involvement — the classic discriminating sign, so check both arms in every chest pain.But it is present in only a minority, and a >20 mmHg difference also occurs without dissection: it raises suspicion rather than confirming or excluding.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: Why might a new AR murmur appear in aortic dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Retrograde dissection to the aortic root → aortic regurgitation (an early diastolic murmur).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What does hypotension/tachycardia in a dissection signify, and what classification should be assumed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Blood loss, cardiac tamponade, or severe AR — haemodynamic instability = Type A until proven otherwise.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: List the end-organ malperfusion effects when the false lumen occludes branches.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back:
• Stroke (carotid/cerebral),
  • paraplegia (spinal artery occlusion),
  • limb ischaemia (iliac/femoral),
  • AKI (renal artery),
  • mesenteric ischaemia (gut ischaemia),
  • MI (coronary ostium involvement).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: How can aortic dissection mimic MI/ACS, and why is this critical?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Dissection can cause MI via coronary involvement — never thrombolyse or anticoagulate a suspected dissection.Getting this wrong is fatal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: How does PE differ from dissection in pain quality and signs?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: PE: acute chest pain + haemodynamic compromise, but pain is usually pleuritic with no inter-arm BP difference.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: How does pericarditis differ from dissection in pain character?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Pericarditis: sharp positional chest pain, pleuritic, relieved by leaning forward, with no tearing quality.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: How does MSK back pain differ from dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: MSK back/interscapular pain has gradual onset, is positional, with no haemodynamic instability.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: State the safety rule about excluding dissection before anticoagulation.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Exclude dissection before anticoagulating for suspected MI/PE — CT angiogram first if any dissection features present (tearing pain, inter-arm BP difference, pulse deficit).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What is the role of ECG in aortic dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Often normal or non-specific — used to exclude/identify MI. May show ischaemia if coronary involved.A normal ECG in severe chest pain raises dissection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What bloods are taken in suspected aortic dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back:
• FBC,
  • U&Es,
  • clotting,
  • troponin (coronary involvement),
  • crossmatch ≥4 units,
  • G&S.
A D-dimer is often sent, but a negative result does not exclude dissection in anyone you genuinely suspect — it is only a rule-out alongside a formally low clinical risk score, never on its own. If you suspect dissection, image it.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What is the gold-standard/first-line definitive investigation for aortic dissection, and what does it show?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: CT angiogram — shows the intimal flap, true/false lumen, extent, branch vessel involvement.Used for classification and surgical planning.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: When is TOE used in aortic dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: If the patient is too unstable for CT, or to assess aortic valve/root involvement.Sensitive for proximal dissection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What CXR findings occur in aortic dissection, and what is the key caveat?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back:
• Widened mediastinum (classic),
  • double/irregular aortic contour,
  • pleural effusion (haemothorax).
May be normal — does not exclude dissection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What immediate measures apply to all patients with aortic dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back:
• Oxygen titrated to target — SpO₂ 94–98% (88–92% if CO₂-retention risk), with high-flow reserved for the shocked or peri-arrest patient rather than given routinely;
  • large-bore IV access × 2;
  • analgesia (IV morphine);
  • catheterise (strict fluid balance);
  • crossmatch ≥4 units blood;
  • careful resuscitation (target cerebral perfusion, avoid over-filling);
  • immediate senior referral — cardiothoracic surgery for Type A, vascular / complex aortic team for Type B.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What is the target SBP in aortic dissection, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Target SBP 100–120 mmHg (with HR <60 bpm) — to reduce aortic shear stress (dP/dt) and limit propagation.Lower it immediately, within about 20 minutes: dissection is the exception to lowering BP slowly.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What is the first-line agent for BP & HR control in dissection, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: IV labetalol (a combined α/β-blocker) — lowers both BP and HR simultaneously; IV esmolol is an equally acceptable short-acting alternative.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What is used for BP/HR control if a beta-blocker is contraindicated in dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: IV calcium channel blocker (diltiazem/verapamil).Beta-blockade is avoided in asthma, bradycardia/heart block, and severe acute AR — where the tachycardia is compensatory and blocking it drops cardiac output.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: Why must vasodilators not be used alone in aortic dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Vasodilators alone (e.g. nitroprusside) increase HR → worsen shear stress — always cover with a beta-blocker first.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What is the surgical management of a Stanford A dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back:
• Emergency sternotomy + excision of the ascending aorta;
  • replacement with a synthetic Dacron graft ± arch reconstruction;
  • Bentall procedure if the aortic root is involved (aortic root replacement with a prosthetic valve).
Without surgery, mortality ~1–2%/hour in the acute phase.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: How is an uncomplicated Stanford B dissection managed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back:
• Bed rest + strict BP control;
  • IV beta-blocker first-line;
  • transition to oral antihypertensives;
  • interval surveillance imaging.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: When is TEVAR indicated in a Stanford B dissection, and what does it do?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back:
Complicated Type B —
  • malperfusion (limb/renal/gut),
  • rupture or impending rupture,
  • rapid aortic expansion, or
  • refractory pain or hypertension despite maximal medical therapy.
TEVAR = a covered stent seals the entry tear, re-expands the true lumen and thromboses the false lumen.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What are the long-term management measures after aortic dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back:
• Lifelong antihypertensives;
  • surveillance CT/MRI — frequent at first, then annually;
  • avoid isometric exercise/heavy lifting;
  • genetic counselling if CT disease (Marfan, Loeys-Dietz, vascular EDS).
MRA is the most accurate modality but is impractical acutely (access, scan time, monitoring), so its role is surveillance — particularly in younger patients needing repeated imaging.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What are the complications of a Type A (retrograde + proximal) dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back:
• Cardiac tamponade (pericardial haemorrhage),
  • acute aortic regurgitation,
  • MI (coronary ostium dissection),
  • stroke (carotid involvement),
  • death.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What are the complications of a Type B (anterograde + distal) dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back:
• Aneurysm formation (commonest long-term complication),
  • rupture,
  • malperfusion (renal AKI, mesenteric, limb),
  • paraplegia (spinal artery).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: A patient with a Type A aortic dissection develops cardiac tamponade. Why must pericardiocentesis be avoided?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back:
Because the tamponade is temporarily limiting the haemorrhage.
Blood is tracking retrogradely into the pericardium. Draining it drops the pericardial pressure, the blood pressure rises, and bleeding into the pericardium restarts — this can be fatal.Correct action: immediate transfer to theatre, where the pericardium is opened under controlled conditions and the aorta repaired at the same time.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What are the two exceptions to the rule that cardiac tamponade is treated with pericardiocentesis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back:
• 1. Type A aortic dissection — do not drain; the tamponade is limiting the bleeding. Straight to theatre for aortic repair.
  • 2. Traumatic tamponade / haemopericardium — needle drainage is only a bridge; definitive treatment is surgical (thoracotomy) to control the bleeding source.
In both, the pericardium is filling from an ongoing arterial bleed that a needle cannot control.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: A hypotensive patient has tamponade on echo. What single feature of the history would change your management away from pericardiocentesis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back:
A history suggesting aortic dissection —
  • sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back,
  • an inter-arm blood pressure difference >20 mmHg,
  • a pulse deficit, or
  • a new aortic regurgitation murmur.
In that setting the tamponade is from a Type A dissection, and draining it can precipitate fatal haemorrhage. Arrange urgent imaging and immediate surgical transfer instead.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: Why can an aortic dissection present as an inferior STEMI, and what is the trap?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: The dissection flap can extend into a coronary ostium, and it most often catches the RIGHT coronary artery - producing an inferior pattern with ST elevation in II, III and aVF. The trap is treating it as an ordinary STEMI: tearing interscapular pain with an inferior STEMI is dissection until proven otherwise, and the answer is a CT aortogram rather than the cath lab, because thrombolysis or anticoagulation can be fatal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: Aortic dissection does not always present with tearing chest pain. How else can it present?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back:
• As collapse or syncope,
  • as a stroke (arch or carotid involvement),
  • as an acutely cold pulseless leg,
  • as abdominal pain from mesenteric or renal malperfusion, or
  • as unexplained shock.
The thread tying them together is more than one organ system failing at once - that combination should put dissection back on the list even when nobody describes tearing pain.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: If the blood pressure differs between the arms in aortic dissection, which arm should you titrate treatment against?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: The one with the HIGHER reading.The lower arm is being fed through a vessel compromised by the dissection flap, so treating down to that number under-perfuses everything else.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: Which surgical team should a Type A and a Type B dissection be referred to?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back:
• Type A goes to cardiothoracic surgery as an immediate emergency.
  • Type B is managed medically unless complicated, and complicated Type B - malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain or uncontrolled hypertension - is a vascular / complex aortic team decision, usually for TEVAR.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Janeway Lesions.back: Painless, erythematous or haemorrhagic macules on the palms and soles, caused by septic microemboli (microabscesses) in infective endocarditis.Mnemonic: “Janeway = painless”.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Janeway Lesions.front: How do Janeway lesions differ from Osler’s nodes?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Janeway Lesions.back:
• Janeway — painless macules on the palms/soles, septic emboli, more acute (S. aureus).
  • Osler’s — tender nodules on the finger/toe pulps, immune-complex, more subacute.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Janeway Lesions.front: What is the pathophysiology of Janeway lesions?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Janeway Lesions.back: Septic microemboli from valvular vegetations lodging in the dermis of the palms/soles, forming microabscesses (hence painless, not immune-mediated).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Janeway Lesions.front: Which organism and tempo are classically associated with Janeway lesions?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Janeway Lesions.back: Acute infective endocarditis due to Staphylococcus aureus — aggressive, embolic disease.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Janeway Lesions.front: What systemic complications share the embolic mechanism of Janeway lesions?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Janeway Lesions.back:
Septic emboli causing
  • stroke,
  • splenic/renal infarcts,
  • mycotic aneurysms, and
  • (in right-sided IE) septic pulmonary emboli.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Janeway Lesions.front: Which peripheral signs of endocarditis are embolic vs immune-complex?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Janeway Lesions.back:
• Embolic — Janeway lesions, splinter haemorrhages, systemic emboli.
  • Immune-complex — Osler’s nodes, Roth spots, glomerulonephritis.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Janeway Lesions.front: What are the non-endocarditis causes of red macules on the palms and soles?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Janeway Lesions.back:
• Secondary syphilis (classic palmar/plantar rash),
  • hand-foot-and-mouth disease, and
  • erythema multiforme
— palm/sole differentials to distinguish from Janeway lesions.
Sterile fibrin-platelet vegetations classically associated with advanced malignancy (and cachexia), causing systemic emboli with negative blood cultures.
Non-infective (verrucous) endocarditis associated with SLE (and antiphospholipid syndrome) — sterile vegetations on both valve surfaces, with negative cultures.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Janeway Lesions.front: What does a new murmur with acute heart failure indicate in endocarditis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Janeway Lesions.back: Acute severe valve regurgitation— a leading indication for urgent valve surgery.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Janeway Lesions.front: What are the main indications for valve surgery in infective endocarditis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Janeway Lesions.back:
• Heart failure from severe regurgitation,
  • uncontrolled infection (abscess, persistent bacteraemia, resistant/fungal organisms), and
  • recurrent emboli / large mobile vegetations.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Janeway Lesions.front: Is anticoagulation used to prevent emboli in infective endocarditis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Janeway Lesions.back: No — routine anticoagulation is avoided because it risks haemorrhagic transformation of septic emboli and intracranial bleeding; manage the infection instead.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Janeway Lesions.front: What is the diagnostic approach that confirms infective endocarditis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Janeway Lesions.back: Blood cultures (≥3 sets before antibiotics, when stable) plus echocardiography (TTE then TOE), integrated via the modified Duke criteria.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Janeway Lesions.front: Why does right-sided (IVDU) endocarditis cause chest signs?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Janeway Lesions.back: Vegetations on the tricuspid valve shed septic pulmonary emboli, causing pleuritic pain, cough and cavitating lung lesions.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What is myocarditis, and what are its three main consequences?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Inflammation of the myocardium leading to myocyte damage, ventricular dysfunction, and arrhythmia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Describe the typical clinical course of myocarditis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: A viral prodrome (fever, fatigue, myalgia) → days to weeks later → cardiac symptoms (chest pain, dyspnoea, palpitations, heart failure).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What is the key clinical flag for myocarditis over ACS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: A young patient + chest pain + recent viral illness should raise myocarditis — but assess and exclude ACS first.The diagnosis is supported once troponin is raised with unobstructed coronaries.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What is the commonest cause of myocarditis in the UK, and overall?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Viral — Coxsackie B virus is the classic commonest (parvovirus B19/HHV-6 most often detected on modern PCR).Other viruses include adenovirus, CMV, EBV, HIV, influenza and SARS-CoV-2.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: How does HIV cause myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Through direct infection plus immunosuppression.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: List the bacterial, spirochaete and protozoal causes of myocarditis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back:
• Bacteria: diphtheria (toxin-mediated), rheumatic fever (streptococcal).
  • Spirochaete: Lyme disease (Borrelia).
  • Protozoa: Chagas’ disease (Trypanosoma cruzi), toxoplasmosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Which protozoal infection causes myocarditis, and where is it common?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Chagas’ disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) — common in South America.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Which drugs and toxins cause myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Doxorubicin (dose-dependent cardiotoxicity), immune checkpoint inhibitors (pembrolizumab, nivolumab — a high-yield emerging cause), and cocaine, alcohol, radiation, clozapine.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Why are immune checkpoint inhibitors an important emerging cause of myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Pembrolizumab and nivolumab can cause fulminant myocarditis; management is to stop the drug and give high-dose steroids urgently.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What are the autoimmune and infiltrative causes of myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back:
• SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, sarcoidosis;
  • giant cell myocarditis (rare, aggressive); and
  • eosinophilic myocarditis (drug hypersensitivity).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Why is giant cell myocarditis clinically important?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: It is rare but aggressive, with high mortality, and is a poor prognostic factor.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: The clinical features of myocarditis arise from which two overlapping processes?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: The inflammatory process itself, and secondary myocardial dysfunction (heart failure).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What are the inflammatory symptoms of myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back:
• A recent viral prodrome (fever, rash, GI upset, myalgia, arthralgia),
  • chest pain (sharp/stabbing, may be pleuritic), and
  • dizziness/syncope (arrhythmia).
It can overlap with pericarditis → myopericarditis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What are the heart failure / muscle dysfunction symptoms of myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back:
• Dyspnoea on exertion → orthopnoea,
  • fatigue, ankle oedema,
  • biventricular failure (an acute dilated picture), and
  • palpitations (VT/VF risk).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What is myopericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Myocarditis overlapping with pericarditis — both components (e.g. pericardial rub + troponin rise + ST changes) are present and both are treated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What are the examination signs of myocarditis related to ventricular dysfunction?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back:
• Tachycardia (often disproportionate),
  • soft/muffled heart sounds,
  • an S3 gallop (ventricular dysfunction), and
  • bibasal crackles (LHF).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What examination signs of right heart failure and systemic illness occur in myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back:
• Raised JVP and oedema (RHF),
  • hypotension (if fulminant),
  • fever and signs of viral illness, and
  • a pericardial rub (if myopericarditis).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What blood markers indicate myocyte damage and ventricular dysfunction in myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Raised high-sensitivity troponin (myocyte damage — mimics ACS) and raised BNP / NT-proBNP (ventricular dysfunction).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What additional blood tests are done in myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Raised ESR, CRP and WCC (inflammation), plus an autoimmune screen.Viral serology is not routine — it rarely alters management; send only if a specific treatable infection is suspected (ESC).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What are the key ECG findings in myocarditis, and how do they differ from STEMI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Diffuse non-specific ST/T changes — the key difference from STEMI (which is territory-based).Also sinus tachycardia, heart block, VT/AF; it can mimic STEMI with widespread ST elevation. Serial ECGs are important.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Why is the ST change distribution useful in distinguishing myocarditis from STEMI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Myocarditis causes diffuse (widespread) non-specific ST/T changes, whereas STEMI changes are territory-based (in a coronary distribution).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What does echocardiography show in myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back:
• Ventricular dilatation,
  • reduced ejection fraction,
  • wall motion abnormalities,
  • a pericardial effusion (if myopericarditis), and
  • it excludes structural/valve pathology.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What are the CXR findings in myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back:
• Cardiomegaly (significant LV dilatation),
  • pulmonary oedema / pleural effusions if in heart failure, and
  • it may be normal in early/mild disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Why is cardiac MRI the key modern test for myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back:
It is the non-invasive gold standard in clinical practice:
  • late gadolinium enhancement shows myocardial inflammation/fibrosis,
  • the updated Lake Louise criteria are used for diagnosis — at least one T2-based marker of oedema plus at least one T1-based marker of injury, and
  • it guides prognosis and risk stratification.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What does late gadolinium enhancement on cardiac MRI indicate in myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Myocardial inflammation/fibrosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Which criteria are used for the cardiac MRI diagnosis of myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: The updated Lake Louise criteria — at least one T2-based marker of oedema plus at least one T1-based marker of injury (native T1, ECV or late gadolinium enhancement).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What is the pathological gold standard for diagnosing myocarditis, and which criteria are used?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Endomyocardial biopsy — using the Dallas criteria (an inflammatory infiltrate, typically lymphocytic, + myocyte necrosis).Modern practice adds immunohistochemistry and viral PCR on the sample.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Why is endomyocardial biopsy rarely performed, and when is it reserved for use?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back:
It is used selectively because of the risk versus benefit — but it is a strong recommendation in acute heart failure or cardiogenic shock (ESC). It is reserved for
  • haemodynamic compromise,
  • suspected giant cell / eosinophilic myocarditis, or
  • an unclear diagnosis after non-invasive workup.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What does endomyocardial biopsy histology show, and what does it identify?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: An inflammatory infiltrate (typically lymphocytic) + myocyte necrosis (the Dallas criteria), identifying the aetiology (viral, giant cell, eosinophilic).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What is the mainstay of management for myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Supportive care — most cases are self-limiting.Treat the underlying cause where possible.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What supportive measures are used in myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back:
• Hospital admission + cardiac monitoring (arrhythmia risk),
  • bed rest,
  • treating heart failure (diuretics, ACEi/ARB, beta-blockers once stable),
  • anti-arrhythmics if needed with a defibrillator on standby, and
  • specialist mechanical circulatory support in fulminant/cardiogenic shock.
NSAIDs are symptom-guided and best avoided where there is heart failure or LV impairment; add colchicine if there is a pericarditic component (ESC).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Why is cardiac monitoring required for myocarditis inpatients?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Because of the arrhythmia risk (VT/VF).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: How is heart failure managed in myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Diuretics, ACEi/ARB, and beta-blockers (once stable).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: How are specific underlying causes of myocarditis treated?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back:
• Bacterial: IV antibiotics (Lyme: doxycycline/ceftriaxone).
  • Chagas’: benznidazole.
  • Drug-induced: stop the offending agent immediately.
  • Autoimmune: steroids/immunosuppression.
  • ICI-associated: high-dose steroids and permanently discontinue the checkpoint inhibitor.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Why must strenuous exercise be avoided in myocarditis, and for how long?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: It risks haemodynamic deterioration and life-threatening arrhythmia; myocarditis is an important — and often under-recognised — cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes. Avoid competitive and strenuous exercise for 3–6 months, with return guided by symptom resolution, normalised troponin and inflammatory markers, and a normal echo/CMR and Holter.Current guidance (ESC) restricts exercise until remission — a minimum of about 1 month — then individualises return on the basis of those same tests; 3–6 months remains the usual exam answer.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What is the prognosis of myocarditis in the majority of cases?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Good — most viral myocarditis resolves spontaneously, with full recovery of cardiac function over weeks–months; a viral cause with mild dysfunction has an excellent outlook.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: List the poor prognostic factors in myocarditis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back:
• Fulminant presentation / cardiogenic shock,
  • giant cell myocarditis (aggressive, high mortality),
  • progression to dilated cardiomyopathy,
  • sudden cardiac death (young athletes, arrhythmia), and
  • persistent LV dysfunction at 6 months → treat as dilated cardiomyopathy (optimal heart-failure therapy, ICD assessment if EF remains ≤35%; transplant only for end-stage refractory disease).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What happens if LV dysfunction persists at 6 months in myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: It is treated as dilated cardiomyopathy — continue optimal heart-failure therapy and assess for an ICD if EF remains ≤35% after ≥3 months of optimal treatment.Transplant only for end-stage, refractory disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Exam pearl: what are the commonest causes of myocarditis in the UK and in South America?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: UK: viral — Coxsackie B (enterovirus) is the classic exam answer, though parvovirus B19 and HHV-6 are most often detected on modern biopsy PCR.South America: Chagas’ disease (Trypanosoma cruzi).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Exam pearl: which is the key non-invasive diagnostic test and which is the pathological gold standard for myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Cardiac MRI is the key non-invasive diagnostic (late gadolinium enhancement); endomyocardial biopsy is the pathological gold standard (rarely done).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Exam pearl: how do you recognise and manage myopericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: An overlap with pericarditis: a pericardial rub + troponin rise + ST changes — treat both components.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Exam pearl: why is myocarditis important regarding cardiomyopathy and young people?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: It is an important cause of dilated cardiomyopathy and sudden cardiac death in young people — hence exercise restriction after myocarditis — 3–6 months traditionally; current guidance restricts until remission, a minimum of about 1 month, then individualises (ESC).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What is vaccine-associated myocarditis, and who typically gets it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back:
A rare complication of mRNA COVID-19 vaccination.
Typically young males, within days of the second dose, presenting with chest pain and a raised troponin.Short-term prognosis is favourable — most cases are mild and self-limiting.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: How is vaccine-associated myocarditis managed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back:
Follow the standard myocarditis pathway:
  • Rest and monitoring — most cases settle spontaneously
  • NSAIDs ± colchicine where there is a pericarditic (myopericarditis) component
  • Standard heart-failure therapy if LV dysfunction or arrhythmia
  • A short corticosteroid course selectively
  • Rare fulminant cases need mechanical circulatory support
Refer all suspected cases to cardiology.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Why is endomyocardial biopsy performed in suspected giant cell myocarditis, and what treatment follows?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back:
Because the histological diagnosis changes management — it is done specifically in order to start treatment.
Treatment: combined immunosuppression — corticosteroids + ciclosporin ± azathioprine.First exclude active viral infection on biopsy PCR before immunosuppressing, and refer urgently for mechanical support / transplant assessment given the high mortality.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.front: What is the function of a capillary and what does its wall consist of?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.back: Capillaries are the site of exchange of gases, nutrients and waste between blood and tissue; their wall is just a single layer of endothelium on a basement membrane (no media or adventitia).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.front: What are pericytes?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.back: Contractile support cells (Rouget cells) that wrap around capillaries within the basement membrane; they aid support, repair and angiogenesis and can differentiate.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.front: Trace the microcirculation from arteriole to venule.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.back: Arteriole → metarteriole → capillary bed (flow controlled by precapillary sphincters) → postcapillary venule.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.front: Describe a continuous capillary and where it is found.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.back: Unbroken endothelium with tight junctions and a complete basement membrane; the least permeable and commonest type; found in muscle, skin, lung, connective tissue and the CNS (where tight junctions form the blood–brain barrier).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.front: Describe a fenestrated capillary and where it is found.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.back: Endothelium with fenestrae (~60–80 nm pores, usually bridged by a thin diaphragm) and a complete basement membrane; more permeable to water and small solutes; found in gut mucosa, endocrine glands, choroid plexus and the renal glomerulus.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.front: What is special about the fenestrations of glomerular capillaries?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.back: They lack diaphragms, making them especially permeable — suited to their filtration role in the glomerulus.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.front: Describe a sinusoidal (discontinuous) capillary and where it is found.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.back: Wide irregular lumen with large gaps between endothelial cells and a discontinuous/absent basement membrane; the most permeable type, allowing whole cells and proteins through; found in the liver (fenestrae in sieve plates, space of Disse, Kupffer cells), spleen, bone marrow and adrenal cortex.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.front: Rank the three capillary types by permeability.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.back: Continuous < fenestrated < sinusoidal (permeability increases as the wall becomes leakier).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.front: What components form the blood–brain barrier?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.back:
• Continuous capillary endothelium with tight junctions
  • pericytes
  • astrocyte foot processes
  • and the basement membrane

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.front: What forms the glomerular filtration barrier?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.back: Fenestrated endothelium + the glomerular basement membrane + podocyte foot processes.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.front: How are the three capillary types distinguished histologically?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.back: Mainly by electron microscopy (to see fenestrae and inter-endothelial gaps); they are hard to type on routine H&E.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.front: Which immunohistochemical markers identify endothelial cells?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.back:
• CD31
  • CD34
  • and von Willebrand factor

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.front: What happens to capillaries in diabetic microangiopathy?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.back: Their basement membrane thickens, contributing to retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.front: What drives new capillary formation (angiogenesis), and why does it matter clinically?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.back: VEGF drives angiogenesis in wound healing and tumours; it is an important therapeutic (anti-angiogenic) target.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.front: Why are capillaries ideal for exchange despite slow flow?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.back:
• Their walls are extremely thin (one endothelial cell)
  • their total cross-sectional area is enormous
  • and slow flow maximises time for diffusion

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.front: What is transcytosis in a continuous capillary?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.back: Transport of material across the endothelial cell in pinocytotic vesicles — a route for exchange where tight junctions limit paracellular movement.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.front: What is special about pulmonary capillaries?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.back: Continuous capillaries whose basement membrane fuses with the alveolar epithelium to form a very thin blood–air barrier; the pulmonary endothelium also converts angiotensin I to II (ACE) and inactivates bradykinin.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.front: What lines hepatic sinusoids in addition to endothelium?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.back: Kupffer cells (resident macrophages), which phagocytose material from the portal blood.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.front: State the Starling principle of capillary fluid exchange.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.back: Fluid movement across the capillary wall depends on the balance of hydrostatic pressure (pushing fluid out) and plasma oncotic/colloid pressure from albumin (pulling it back). Filtration predominates at the arterial end and reabsorption at the venous end; the small net excess plus any leaked protein is drained by lymphatics.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.front: What is the space of Disse and which cells does it contain?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.back: The perisinusoidal space between the hepatic sinusoidal endothelium and hepatocytes; it contains hepatic stellate (Ito) cells, which store vitamin A and, when activated, drive the fibrosis of cirrhosis.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.front: List the four mechanisms of oedema.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.back:
• Raised capillary hydrostatic pressure (heart failure, venous obstruction, fluid overload)
  • reduced plasma oncotic pressure (hypoalbuminaemia — nephrotic syndrome, liver failure, malnutrition)
  • increased permeability (inflammation, sepsis, burns)
  • and lymphatic obstruction (filariasis, post-node-clearance)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: Define chronic heart failure.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: A clinical syndrome resulting from a structural or functional cardiac abnormality, leading to an inability to maintain adequate cardiac output at normal filling pressures.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What ejection fraction defines HFrEF, and what is the underlying problem?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: EF ≤40% — systolic dysfunction with impaired contraction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What ejection fraction range defines HFmrEF, and why is it clinically important?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: EF 41–49% (mildly reduced). It behaves more like HFrEF and responds to HFrEF drugs — NICE now recommends considering all four pillars in HFmrEF (NICE), as does ESC; increasingly examined at finals.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What ejection fraction defines HFpEF, and what is the underlying problem?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: EF ≥50% — diastolic dysfunction with impaired filling.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What is high-output heart failure, and name its causes.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back:
Normal or raised cardiac output that is unable to meet the body’s demands. Causes:
  • anaemia,
  • thyrotoxicosis,
  • Paget’s disease,
  • pregnancy,
  • thiamine deficiency (beriberi),
  • and a large AV fistula.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What is the most common cause of chronic heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Ischaemic heart disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: List the main aetiologies of chronic heart failure (excluding high-output causes).
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back:
• Ischaemic heart disease (most common),
  • hypertension (chronic pressure overload),
  • valvular disease (aortic stenosis common),
  • arrhythmias (AF common),
  • cardiomyopathy (dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive),
  • and myocarditis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: In the pathophysiology of heart failure, what is the role of neurohormonal activation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: RAAS activation causes Na/water retention (raising preload), and SNS activation causes tachycardia and vasoconstriction (raising afterload).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: Describe the sequence of ventricular remodelling in heart failure.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Hypertrophy → dilatation → worsening dysfunction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: Outline the broad pathophysiological cascade of heart failure from injury to fluid accumulation.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Cardiac injury (reduced stroke volume/cardiac output) → neurohormonal activation (RAAS + SNS) → ventricular remodelling → fluid accumulation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: How does fluid accumulation differ between left and right heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back:
• Left HF → pulmonary venous hypertension → pulmonary oedema.
  • Right HF → systemic venous hypertension → peripheral oedema.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What does NYHA Class I heart failure describe?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: No limitation — symptoms only on extreme exertion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What does NYHA Class II heart failure describe?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Mild limitation — comfortable at rest, symptoms on moderate exertion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What does NYHA Class III heart failure describe?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Marked limitation — symptoms on less than ordinary activity; comfortable at rest.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What does NYHA Class IV heart failure describe?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Symptoms at rest — unable to carry out any activity without symptoms.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: List the symptoms and signs of LEFT heart failure.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back:
• Dyspnoea on exertion,
  • orthopnoea (breathless lying flat — ask about pillows),
  • paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea (PND),
  • cough with frothy white/pink sputum,
  • displaced apex beat (lateral + downward),
  • S3 gallop (always pathological >40 yrs),
  • and bibasal crackles (pulmonary oedema).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: List the symptoms and signs of RIGHT heart failure.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back:
• Raised JVP,
  • peripheral pitting oedema (ankles → sacrum),
  • congestive hepatomegaly,
  • positive hepatojugular reflux,
  • ascites (when severe),
  • and fatigue.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: Why is an S3 gallop significant in suspected heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: It is always pathological in patients over 40 years and is part of the classic HF triad (S3 gallop + displaced apex + bibasal crackles).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What is orthopnoea, and how do you elicit it in the history?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Breathlessness when lying flat — ask the patient how many pillows they need to sleep.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: Why is NT-proBNP raised in heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Ventricular wall stretch triggers BNP release, which causes vasodilation and natriuresis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: How do NT-proBNP levels guide the timing of echocardiography?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back:
• <400 = HF unlikely;
  • 400–2000 = echo within 6 weeks;
  • >2000 = echo within 2 weeks.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: Is NT-proBNP sensitive or specific for heart failure, and what else raises it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Sensitive but NOT specific — it is also raised in PE, CKD, sepsis and AF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What is the gold-standard investigation for heart failure, and what does it provide?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Echocardiogram — it measures EF, wall motion and valves, classifies HF (HFrEF/HFmrEF/HFpEF), and guides treatment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What can a 12-lead ECG show in heart failure, and what does a normal ECG imply?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: It may show LVH, LBBB, AF or ischaemia, helping to guide aetiology. A normal ECG makes heart failure less likely.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What are the CXR features of heart failure (ABCDE)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back:
• Alveolar oedema,
  • Kerley B lines,
  • Cardiomegaly,
  • upper lobe Diversion,
  • and pleural Effusion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: Which blood tests are sent in heart failure, and why check U&E in particular?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back:
• U&E (renal function before starting drugs),
  • FBC,
  • iron studies (ferritin + transferrin saturation),
  • TFTs,
  • HbA1c,
  • LFTs and cholesterol.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What are the 'four pillars' of HFrEF management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back:
• ACEi/ARB,
  • beta-blocker,
  • MRA (mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist),
  • and SGLT2 inhibitor.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: How does modern practice approach starting the four pillars of HFrEF treatment?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Early initiation of all four pillars together (or in rapid sequence) rather than strict sequential step-up. NICE moved to this position in its 2025 update and now offers all four first-line — an ACE inhibitor, a beta-blocker, an MRA and an SGLT2 inhibitor — as does ESC (NICE).How fast you build depends on symptoms, frailty, BP and renal function.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What is the role of an ACEi/ARB in HFrEF, and what must be monitored?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: E.g. ramipril (ACEi) — inhibits ACE, so angiotensin II falls and bradykinin rises (vasodilation, but also the dry cough). Losartan (ARB) blocks the AT1 receptor directly without raising bradykinin (no cough). Both reduce RAAS-driven remodelling with a mortality benefit. Check renal function and electrolytes 1–2 weeks after starting, 1–2 weeks after each dose increase, then every 3–6 months at the maximum tolerated dose; act if creatinine rises >50% or K⁺ >5.5 mmol/L (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: Which beta-blockers are licensed for HFrEF, and which are NOT used?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Bisoprolol, carvedilol or nebivolol only (nebivolol is licensed for mild–moderate HF in patients ≥70 and is usually third-line) (BNF). NOT atenolol or metoprolol in the UK — metoprolol succinate is used elsewhere but is not marketed here.Start low and titrate slowly.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: How does a beta-blocker benefit HFrEF mechanistically?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: It blocks chronically activated SNS → reduces heart rate and produces anti-remodelling effects.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What is the mechanism and key risk of an MRA (e.g. spironolactone/eplerenone) in HFrEF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Blocks aldosterone → reduces fibrosis and potassium loss. Key risk is hyperkalaemia — check renal function and electrolytes 1–2 weeks after starting, 1–2 weeks after each dose increase, then every 3–6 months at the maximum tolerated dose; act if creatinine rises >50% or K⁺ >5.5 mmol/L (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What is the mechanism of SGLT2 inhibitors in heart failure, and what makes them unique?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Dapagliflozin/empagliflozin reduce glucose reabsorption → osmotic diuresis and cardioprotection. They were the first class with outcome evidence in HFpEF (reduce HF hospitalisation) and are now joined there by an MRA (NICE).Given regardless of diabetes status.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What is the role of loop diuretics in heart failure, and the crucial exam point about them?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Furosemide/bumetanide for congestion/fluid retention — they reduce preload and relieve oedema and dyspnoea. Key point: NO mortality benefit (purely symptomatic).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: When is sacubitril/valsartan (ARNI) used, and what is the critical safety rule?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Replaces the ACE inhibitor when the patient remains symptomatic on maximum tolerated doses of all four pillars (EF ≤35%, NYHA II–IV, specialist-initiated) (NICE). Also an option if the ACEi is not tolerated — but use an ARB instead if the intolerance was angioedema. It prevents breakdown of natriuretic peptides. A 36-hour washout from the ACEi is required to avoid angioedema risk if combined.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What are the criteria for adding ivabradine in HFrEF, and its mechanism?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Sinus rhythm ≥75 bpm + EF ≤35% + NYHA II–IV on a maximally tolerated beta-blocker — or when a beta-blocker is contraindicated or not tolerated; specialist-initiated after 4 weeks stabilisation (NICE). It blocks the If (funny) current in the SA node → reduces heart rate without affecting contractility or BP.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: When is digoxin used in heart failure, and what are its key cautions?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Chiefly HFrEF with coexisting AF (rate control); also worsening or severe HFrEF in sinus rhythm despite optimal therapy. A positive inotrope (Na/K-ATPase inhibitor) that improves symptoms and reduces hospitalisations but has NO mortality benefit. Narrow therapeutic index — toxic in CKD/hypokalaemia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: When is hydralazine + ISMN indicated in heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back:
Two separate indications:
  • patients of African or Caribbean family origin with moderate-to-severe HF (an add-on regardless of ACEi tolerance),
  • and any patient intolerant of an ACEi/ARB/ARNI.
It provides vasodilation via a different pathway.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What are the indications for an ICD in heart failure (primary and secondary prevention)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back:
• Secondary prevention: prior cardiac arrest / sustained VT / VF — regardless of EF.
  • Primary prevention: EF ≤35%, NYHA I–III, on optimal medical therapy (ESC specifies ≥3 months; NICE selects the device by QRS duration and LBBB, and at QRS <120 ms only if at high risk of sudden cardiac death) (NICE).
It continuously monitors rhythm and shocks VF/VT back to sinus.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What are the criteria for CRT in heart failure, and how does it work?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: EF ≤35% + broad QRS + NYHA II–IV. NICE bands the QRS at 120–149 ms and ≥150 ms, with LBBB and NYHA class deciding CRT-P vs CRT-D vs ICD — at 120–149 ms without LBBB the device is an ICD (NICE); ESC uses ≥130 ms with LBBB. A biventricular (triple-chamber) pacemaker with RA, RV and LV leads resynchronises ventricular contractions → increases cardiac output.CRT-D adds ICD function.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What vaccinations and surgical options are offered in heart failure beyond drugs and devices?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back:
• Annual influenza vaccine + a one-off pneumococcal vaccine,
  • and surgical correction of underlying valvular disease where indicated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What is the classic auscultation triad of heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: S3 gallop + displaced apex + bibasal crackles.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: Which heart failure drug classes do NOT confer a mortality benefit?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Loop diuretics (symptomatic relief only) and digoxin (improves symptoms/reduces admissions but no mortality benefit).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: Which iron studies should be checked in heart failure, and what defines iron deficiency in this setting?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Check ferritin and transferrin saturation in every HF patient. The threshold used in heart failure is higher than the usual one, because ferritin is an acute-phase protein and is falsely raised by the chronic inflammation of heart failure — so the ordinary cut-off would miss most cases. Iron deficiency here is treated irrespective of anaemia, and oral iron does not work in HF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: Does a heart failure patient need to be anaemic before iron deficiency is treated?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back:
No — treat irrespective of anaemia.
Iron is needed by skeletal and cardiac muscle independently of haemoglobin, so deficiency worsens fatigue and exercise tolerance even with a normal Hb.Iron deficiency affects roughly half of HFrEF patients.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: Why is iron given intravenously rather than orally in heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back:
Oral iron does not work in HF.
Chronic inflammation raises hepcidin, which blocks intestinal iron absorption and traps iron in macrophages.IV ferric carboxymaltose bypasses the gut entirely — it improves symptoms and quality of life and reduces HF hospitalisation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: A patient with heart failure has an ICD fitted for primary prevention. How long must they stop driving, and must the DVLA be told?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back:
1 month off driving (Group 1).
The DVLA must be notified — this is true for every ICD.Contrast with secondary prevention (implanted after VT/VF): 6 months.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What are the driving consequences of an ICD for a Group 2 (HGV / PSV) licence holder?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: An ICD is a permanent bar to a Group 2 licence.Compare the far milder rules for a pacemaker / CRT-P: Group 1 1 week, Group 2 6 weeks.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What self-monitoring should every heart failure patient be taught on discharge?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back:
Daily weights — same time each morning, after voiding, before breakfast.
A gain of 1.5–2 kg over 2 days signals fluid retention and should prompt a call to the heart-failure team (often a temporary diuretic increase).Catching congestion at this stage is what prevents an admission.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: When should palliative care be involved in chronic heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back:
Alongside active treatment, not after it. Trigger points are
  • persistent severe symptoms despite optimal therapy,
  • repeated hospital admissions,
  • cardiac cachexia,
  • or a declining functional state.
Advanced heart failure carries a prognosis worse than many cancers, yet is referred far less often than cancer is.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What must be covered in advance care planning for a patient with advanced heart failure, and why is timing important?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back:
• What matters to the patient,
  • ceilings of treatment,
  • preferred place of care,
  • a DNACPR discussion,
  • and - crucially - ICD deactivation.
The heart failure trajectory is gradual decline punctuated by acute crises, so the conversation is held early while the patient is well enough to have it, rather than at the final admission.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: Why must ICD deactivation be discussed explicitly in advanced heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Because a device that keeps delivering shocks to a dying patient causes distress that is entirely avoidable.Deactivation is a planned conversation, not something arranged in the last hours, and it is one of the most commonly missed parts of end-of-life care in heart failure.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.front: What is a leg ulcer, and after how long is it considered chronic?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.back: A break in the skin below the knee that fails to heal within ~2 weeks. It is generally regarded as chronic once present ≥4–6 weeks. (some sources use ≥6 weeks / 3 months).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.front: What are the main cause “buckets” of a leg ulcer, and which is commonest?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.back:
• Venous (~70%, by far commonest),
  • arterial,
  • neuropathic (diabetic),
  • mixed arterial-venous,
  • plus the atypical “don’t-miss” ulcers (malignant, pyoderma, vasculitic, infective).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.front: Describe the typical site and appearance of a VENOUS ulcer.
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.back:
• Gaiter region (above the medial malleolus).
  • Shallow, irregular, sloping edge, granulating base, heavy exudate.
  • Surrounding skin shows haemosiderin, lipodermatosclerosis, varicose eczema and oedema.
  • Relatively painless / aching, eased by elevation.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.front: Describe the typical site and appearance of an ARTERIAL ulcer.
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.back:
• Distal — toes, dorsum of foot, heel, lateral malleolus / pressure points.
  • Deep, “punched-out”, pale or necrotic base, little exudate.
  • Very painful (worse on elevation and at night, relieved by hanging the leg down).
  • Leg is cold, pale, hairless with absent pulses.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.front: Describe the typical site and appearance of a NEUROPATHIC (diabetic) ulcer.
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.back:
• Over weight-bearing / pressure points — plantar metatarsal heads, heel.
  • Painless (loss of protective sensation), ringed by callus.
  • The foot is warm and well-perfused with reduced sensation ± deformity (Charcot).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.front: What is the single most important bedside test before treating any leg ulcer, and why?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.back: The ankle-brachial pressure index (ABPI) — it distinguishes venous from arterial disease and, crucially, decides whether compression is safe. Always measure ABPI before applying compression.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.front: Give the key ABPI thresholds and their meaning.
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.back:
• >1.3 — calcified / incompressible (unreliable).
  • ~0.9–1.3 — normal.
  • 0.8–0.9 — mild arterial disease (compression usually still safe).
  • 0.5–0.8 — significant / mixed disease.
  • <0.5 — critical limb ischaemia.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.front: When is compression bandaging safe, and when is it contraindicated?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.back:
• Full compression is safe when ABPI 0.8–1.3.
  • Between 0.5 and 0.8 full compression is contraindicated — only reduced compression under specialist supervision.
  • Below 0.5, none at all.
  • An ABPI >1.3 is incompressible and uninterpretable — do not assume it is safe.
Compressing an ischaemic limb causes pressure necrosis and limb loss.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.front: What is the mainstay of VENOUS leg-ulcer treatment?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.back: Multilayer compression bandaging (once ABPI ≥0.8), plus leg elevation, emollients and treatment of the underlying venous incompetence (endovenous ablation / surgery). Most heal within ~6 months.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.front: What is the key management principle for an ARTERIAL ulcer?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.back: Restore blood flow — refer to vascular for revascularisation (angioplasty / bypass) — and modify cardiovascular risk factors. Do NOT apply compression. Critical limb ischaemia is an emergency.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.front: Outline management of a NEUROPATHIC / diabetic foot ulcer.
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.back:
• Pressure offloading (total-contact cast / special footwear),
  • debridement,
  • tight glycaemic control,
  • treat infection / osteomyelitis, and
  • refer to the multidisciplinary diabetic foot team.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.front: Why can the ABPI be falsely elevated (>1.3) in a diabetic patient?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.back: Medial arterial calcification (Mönckeberg sclerosis) makes the vessels incompressible, so the cuff cannot occlude them — the ABPI reads falsely high and is unreliable. Use toe pressures / toe-brachial index instead.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.front: What is a Marjolin’s ulcer, and what should prompt you to suspect it?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.back: A squamous cell carcinoma arising in a chronic wound, ulcer or scar. Suspect it in an ulcer that fails to heal or develops a rolled / everted edge or heaped-up granulation — biopsy it.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.front: What is pyoderma gangrenosum, and what is the critical management pitfall?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.back: A rapidly enlarging, exquisitely painful ulcer with a violaceous, undermined border, showing pathergy (worsens with trauma). Associated with IBD, RA and haematological disease. Treat with immunosuppression (steroids / ciclosporin) — avoid debridement / surgery, which makes it worse.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.front: What do haemosiderin staining and lipodermatosclerosis around an ulcer tell you?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.back: They are signs of chronic venous insufficiency (sustained venous hypertension) — brown haemosiderin pigmentation and firm, fibrotic “woody” skin giving the “inverted champagne-bottle” leg. They point firmly to a venous ulcer.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.front: Which investigations are used to work up a leg ulcer?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.back:
• ABPI (before compression),
  • venous duplex ultrasound (reflux/incompetence),
  • biopsy if atypical or non-healing (Marjolin’s),
  • HbA1c and foot X-ray ± MRI for osteomyelitis in diabetics.
  • Swab only if clinically infected (not for colonisation).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.front: What is a mixed arterial-venous ulcer and how does it change management?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.back: An ulcer with features of both, typically ABPI 0.5–0.8. Full compression is unsafe — use reduced (modified) compression under specialist supervision only, and assess the arterial disease.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.front: Name two atypical causes of a painful leg ulcer besides pyoderma gangrenosum.
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.back: Vasculitic ulcers (painful, with palpable purpura and systemic features; associated with vasculitis / RA / SLE) and sickle-cell ulcers (young patients, chronic ulcers over the malleoli). Both need treatment of the underlying disease.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: What are the three main functions of the lymphatic system?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back:
• Fluid balance (returning ~10% of capillary filtrate, ~3 L/day, to the blood),
  • immune surveillance (carrying antigens and cells to lymph nodes, recirculating lymphocytes), and
  • dietary fat absorption via intestinal lacteals.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: Trace the path of lymph from tissue to bloodstream.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back: Lymphatic capillary → collecting vessel (with valves and interposed lymph nodes) → lymphatic trunk → thoracic or right lymphatic duct → subclavian vein.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: Where does the thoracic duct drain and what territory does it cover?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back: It drains all of the body except the right upper quadrant, emptying into the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: What territory does the right lymphatic duct drain?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back: The right upper quadrant - right side of head/neck, right upper limb and right hemithorax - into the right subclavian/IJ junction.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: How do you distinguish a lymphatic capillary from a blood capillary on H&E?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back: The lymphatic has a wide, irregular, often collapsed thin-walled lumen that is empty or holds pale lymph with NO red blood cells; a blood capillary is narrow and packed with RBCs.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: Why do lymphatic capillaries lack a continuous basement membrane and pericytes?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back: To be highly permeable, allowing large proteins, cells and even pathogens to enter freely - unlike the selective blood capillary.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: What are anchoring filaments and what do they do?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back: Anchoring filaments (fibrillin-containing microfibrils) tethering the lymphatic endothelium to the surrounding extracellular matrix; when tissue swells they pull the overlapping endothelial flaps open, increasing lymph uptake exactly when interstitial pressure is high.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: How do the overlapping endothelial cells of a lymphatic capillary function?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back: They form loosely overlapping flaps that act as one-way (primary) valves - opening inward when interstitial pressure rises to admit fluid and cells, then closing to prevent backflow.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: What is a lymphangion?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back: The segment of a collecting lymphatic vessel between two consecutive valves - the functional contractile unit that squeezes lymph forward.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: Describe the wall of a large collecting lymphatic vessel.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back: A thin three-tunic wall (endothelium, a little smooth muscle, adventitia) with numerous closely spaced valves giving a beaded appearance.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: What propels lymph, given there is no central pump?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back: Intrinsic lymphangion contraction plus extrinsic forces - the skeletal-muscle pump, respiratory pump and arterial pulsation - all made unidirectional by valves.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: What is a lacteal and what does it absorb?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back: A blind-ended lymphatic capillary in the core of each intestinal villus that absorbs dietary long-chain fats packaged as chylomicrons, forming milky chyle.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: Which dietary fats bypass the lacteals, and why does it matter?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back: Short- and medium-chain fatty acids are water-soluble enough to enter the villus blood capillaries and drain via the portal vein directly (only long-chain fats form chylomicrons taken up by lacteals); this is the rationale for medium-chain-triglyceride (MCT) diets in chylothorax and fat malabsorption.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: What is chyle and where does it drain?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back: Fat-laden (milky) intestinal lymph; it drains via intestinal trunks into the cisterna chyli and then the thoracic duct.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: What is the consequence of thoracic duct injury?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back: Leakage of chyle producing a chylothorax (or chylous ascites) - a milky, triglyceride-rich effusion.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: Which immunohistochemical marker is the go-to for lymphatic endothelium?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back: D2-40 (podoplanin).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: Name additional lymphatic-specific markers besides D2-40.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back: LYVE-1, Prox1 (the master lymphatic transcription factor) and VEGFR-3.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: What are Virchow's node and Kaposi sarcoma?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back:
• Virchow's node = an enlarged left supraclavicular lymph node (Troisier sign) draining via the thoracic duct, classically from gastric/GI/pelvic carcinoma.
  • Kaposi sarcoma = an HHV-8-driven endothelial tumour with a lymphatic phenotype (D2-40/podoplanin, LYVE-1, Prox1 positive), forming slit-like vascular spaces, AIDS-associated.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: What is lymphoedema and how is it classified?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back: Protein-rich tissue swelling from impaired lymphatic drainage; primary (e.g. Milroy disease) or secondary (surgery/lymph-node clearance, radiotherapy, or filariasis).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: What is the worldwide leading cause of secondary lymphoedema, and its severe form?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back: Filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti) obstructing lymphatics; severe cases cause massive limb/scrotal swelling termed elephantiasis.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: Why are lymphatics central to carcinoma staging?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back: Lymphatic (lymphovascular) invasion is the principal route of carcinoma metastasis to regional lymph nodes - the basis of sentinel lymph node biopsy.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: What is lymphangitis?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back: Infection spreading along lymphatic vessels, seen clinically as tender red streaks tracking toward the draining lymph nodes.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: What is a cystic hygroma?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back: A benign lymphatic malformation (lymphangioma), classically a fluid-filled swelling in the neck of infants.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: What is Stewart-Treves syndrome?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back: A lymphangiosarcoma arising in a chronically lymphoedematous limb, classically after mastectomy with axillary clearance.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: Roughly how much fluid do lymphatics return to the circulation daily, and why?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back: About 3 litres/day - the fraction of capillary filtrate (~10%) not reabsorbed by the venules, along with the proteins that leaked out.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: Describe the course of the thoracic duct and the 'button vs zipper' junctions.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back:
• The thoracic duct begins as the cisterna chyli at ~L1-2, ascends, crosses to the left at ~T4-5 and empties at the left venous angle.
  • Initial lymphatics have discontinuous 'button' junctions (permitting fluid/cell entry); collecting lymphatics have continuous 'zipper' junctions.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: Where in the collecting system is lymph filtered before returning to blood?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back: At the lymph nodes interposed along the collecting lymphatic vessels.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: Give the two structural 'valve' systems of lymphatics.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back: Primary valves (the overlapping endothelial flaps of the initial capillary) and secondary valves (the paired semilunar intraluminal valves of collecting vessels).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: Which tissues lack lymphatic vessels?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back: CNS parenchyma (which uses the glymphatic/meningeal-lymphatic route instead), epidermis, cartilage, cornea, bone marrow and other avascular tissues.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.front: What is the cisterna chyli?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.back: A dilated sac at the lower end of the thoracic duct that receives the intestinal and lumbar lymphatic trunks.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: What is the first priority when assessing any patient with chest pain?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: Identify or exclude the immediately life-threatening causes before settling on a benign diagnosis — don’t anchor.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: Name the six “can’t-miss” life-threatening causes of chest pain.
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back:
• ACS
  • aortic dissection
  • pulmonary embolism
  • tension pneumothorax
  • oesophageal rupture (Boerhaave)
  • cardiac tamponade

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: Why must aortic dissection be considered before giving anticoagulation/antiplatelets for suspected ACS?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: If the pain is actually a dissection, anticoagulation or thrombolysis can cause catastrophic, fatal bleeding. Check BP in both arms first.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: Classic pain character of ACS?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: Central, heavy/tight/crushing pain radiating to the arm, jaw or neck, with sweating and nausea; exertional or at rest.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: Classic pain character of aortic dissection?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: Sudden, severe, tearing/ripping pain, maximal at onset, radiating to the back; may migrate.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: Two examination findings that point to aortic dissection?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back:
• Inter-arm systolic BP difference >20 mmHg (or a pulse deficit) and
  • a new early diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: Features suggesting pulmonary embolism as a cause of chest pain?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back:
• Pleuritic pain
  • breathlessness
  • tachycardia
  • hypoxia
  • haemoptysis
  • unilateral calf swelling
  • and VTE risk factors

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: How is a tension pneumothorax diagnosed and treated?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: It is a clinical diagnosis (sudden dyspnoea, hyper-resonance, absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation, shock) — immediate needle/finger decompression; do NOT wait for a CXR.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: What is Boerhaave syndrome?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: Spontaneous full-thickness oesophageal rupture caused by forceful vomiting/retching (classically after an alcohol binge). The oesophagus has no serosa, so contents leak into the mediastinum → mediastinitis and sepsis.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: What is Mackler's triad (oesophageal rupture)?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: Vomiting + chest pain + subcutaneous emphysema.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: What is Beck’s triad and what does it indicate?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: Hypotension, raised JVP and muffled heart sounds — cardiac tamponade.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: What is pulsus paradoxus and where is it seen?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: An exaggerated fall (>10 mmHg) in systolic BP on inspiration — seen in cardiac tamponade (also severe asthma/constrictive pericarditis).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: Sharp chest pain that is worse lying flat and relieved by sitting forward suggests?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: Pericarditis.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: ECG findings of pericarditis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: Widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation with PR depression.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: Classic (though insensitive) ECG sign of PE?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: S1Q3T3 — usually just sinus tachycardia is seen, ± signs of right-heart strain.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: A patient’s chest pain is reproducible on palpation — does this exclude a serious cause?
