signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: No. Reproducible chest-wall tenderness suggests a musculoskeletal cause but does not exclude ACS or other dangerous causes.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: Burning, postprandial chest pain, worse lying flat and relieved by antacids, suggests?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: Gastro-oesophageal reflux / peptic ulcer disease — but exclude ACS first.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: Within what timeframe should a 12-lead ECG be obtained in acute chest pain?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: Within 10 minutes of arrival.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: What does a single normal troponin tell you in suspected ACS?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: It does not exclude ACS — troponin must be repeated (serial testing) per the local pathway.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: Definitive investigation for suspected aortic dissection?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: CT angiogram of the aorta (TOE if too unstable to transfer).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: Definitive investigation for suspected PE (adequate renal function)?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA); use a V/Q scan in renal impairment or pregnancy.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: Investigation of choice for suspected cardiac tamponade?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: Echocardiography — shows a pericardial effusion with diastolic collapse of the right heart.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: A widened mediastinum on CXR with tearing chest pain suggests?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: Aortic dissection.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: Which chest-pain causes are typically pleuritic (worse on inspiration)?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back:
• PE
  • pneumonia
  • pneumothorax
  • pericarditis
  • and pleurisy / pleural effusion

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: ST elevation on the ECG in chest pain — diagnosis and immediate priority?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: STEMI — immediate reperfusion (primary PCI, or thrombolysis if PCI unavailable).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: Exertional chest pain relieved by rest or GTN suggests?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: Stable angina.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: Young patient, recent viral illness, chest pain with a raised troponin — likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: Myocarditis (confirm with cardiac MRI).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: Dermatomal burning chest pain preceding a vesicular rash suggests?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: Herpes zoster (shingles).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: What is the role of D-dimer in suspected PE?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: Used to rule OUT PE only when clinical probability (e.g. Wells score) is low; it is non-specific and cannot rule PE in.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: Severe aortic stenosis classically presents with which triad?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: Angina, syncope and exertional dyspnoea; look for an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: First-line bedside work-up for undifferentiated acute chest pain?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back:
• 12-lead ECG
  • full observations incl. SpO₂
  • BP in both arms
  • IV access
  • bloods (troponin, FBC, U&E)
  • CXR
  • ABG if hypoxic

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: Free air/pneumomediastinum on CXR with surgical emphysema after vomiting — diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: Oesophageal rupture (Boerhaave).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: Why can a myocardial infarction be missed in diabetics, the elderly and women?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: They often have an atypical or silent presentation — epigastric pain, breathlessness, nausea, fatigue, syncope or collapse rather than classic chest pain. A normal pain history does not exclude ACS.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: Which common, benign cause of chest pain is a diagnosis of exclusion?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: Anxiety / panic disorder — situational pain with palpitations, hyperventilation and paraesthesiae; diagnose only after excluding ACS, PE and other serious causes.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: Match the STEMI territory to the ECG leads and culprit artery.
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back:
• Inferior — II, III, aVF (RCA)
  • Anterior — V1–V4 (LAD)
  • Lateral — I, aVL, V5–V6 (circumflex)

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: An inferior STEMI (II, III, aVF) with hypotension — what should you suspect, and why does it matter?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: Right-ventricular infarction. The RV is preload-dependent, so nitrates can cause profound hypotension — give fluids and use nitrates with caution (confirm with right-sided lead V4R).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: ST depression with a tall R wave in V1–V3 — what diagnosis must you consider?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: Posterior STEMI — confirm with posterior leads V7–V9; easily mistaken for an NSTEMI.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: A patient has ongoing ischaemic chest pain and LBBB on the ECG. Does that go down the primary PCI pathway?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: Yes. It is the clinical picture that decides, not the LBBB: ongoing ischaemic symptoms with LBBB are managed as a STEMI equivalent, and a known LBBB does not stand you down. What is no longer true is that LBBB alone, without ischaemic symptoms, is an automatic criterion. The (Smith-modified) Sgarbossa criteria help rule an infarct in when the picture is equivocal — they are specific but insensitive, so a negative score does not rule one out and must not delay the decision in a patient with ongoing pain.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: Does relief of chest pain with GTN confirm a cardiac cause?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: No — oesophageal spasm also eases with GTN, so relief alone does not confirm angina.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: Young patient with chest pain, agitation, dilated pupils and tachycardia — what cause should you consider?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: Cocaine-induced coronary vasospasm (can cause true MI). Avoid beta-blockers acutely; treat with benzodiazepines ± nitrates.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.front: A patient with sickle-cell disease develops chest pain, fever, hypoxia and a new pulmonary infiltrate — diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.back: Acute chest syndrome — a medical emergency needing oxygen, analgesia, antibiotics and often exchange transfusion.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.front: What is xanthelasma?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.back: Soft yellow plaques of lipid deposited in the skin around the eyelids (periorbital). It may occur with hyperlipidaemia or with normal lipids, and still carries a modest independent cardiovascular risk.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.front: What is corneal arcus and when is it significant?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.back: A white / grey ring at the corneal margin. Under 45 (arcus juvenilis) it suggests pathological hyperlipidaemia; in older people (arcus senilis) it is a benign, age-related finding.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.front: What do tendon xanthomata indicate, and where are they found?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.back: Nodular lipid deposits in tendons — classically the Achilles and the knuckle (finger extensor) tendons — they are near-diagnostic of familial hypercholesterolaemia.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.front: What is the significance of eruptive xanthomata?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.back: Crops of small yellow papules (often on the buttocks / extensor surfaces) that signal severe hypertriglyceridaemia (often >10 mmol/L) and a risk of acute pancreatitis.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.front: What is familial hypercholesterolaemia?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.back: An inherited (usually autosomal dominant, LDL-receptor) disorder causing very high LDL cholesterol from birth, tendon xanthomata and premature coronary artery disease. Relatives need cascade screening.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.front: Why must you always look for a secondary cause of dyslipidaemia?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.back: Because several are treatable: hypothyroidism, cholestasis (e.g. primary biliary cholangitis), nephrotic syndrome, diabetes, alcohol and certain drugs all raise lipids.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.front: What do palmar crease (striae) xanthomata specifically indicate?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.back: Yellow lipid deposits in the palmar creases are characteristic of remnant (type III) hyperlipidaemia (dysbetalipoproteinaemia).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.front: What lipid pattern do xanthelasma, arcus and tendon xanthomata reflect versus eruptive xanthomata?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.back: Xanthelasma, arcus and tendon xanthomata reflect high cholesterol / LDL; eruptive xanthomata reflect high triglycerides.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.front: How is familial hypercholesterolaemia diagnosed clinically?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.back: Using criteria such as Simon Broome or the Dutch Lipid Clinic Network (DLCN) score, which combine LDL level, tendon xanthomata, personal / family history of premature CAD and genetic testing.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.front: What blood tests are used to work up lipid stigmata?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.back: A non-fasting lipid profile (total, LDL, HDL, triglycerides — fasting is only needed when triglycerides are the concern), plus a screen for secondary causes: TFTs, glucose / HbA1c, renal function and LFTs.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.front: Why is severe hypertriglyceridaemia dangerous beyond cardiovascular risk?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.back: It can precipitate acute pancreatitis — a key reason eruptive xanthomata (a marker of very high triglycerides) prompt urgent triglyceride-lowering.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.front: How is cardiovascular risk managed in familial hypercholesterolaemia?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.back: Do not use QRISK — FH patients are treated as high-risk by default with a high-intensity statin (atorvastatin), aiming for a ≥50% reduction in LDL / non-HDL cholesterol; add ezetimibe or a PCSK9 inhibitor if targets are not met.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.front: What is the first-line drug treatment for hypercholesterolaemia and cardiovascular risk reduction?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.back: A statin (HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor), alongside lifestyle change; ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitors are added in familial hypercholesterolaemia or when targets are not met.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.front: Which endocrine disorder is a classic secondary cause of hyperlipidaemia, and what else would you find?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.back: Hypothyroidism — look for fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance and bradycardia; treating it improves the lipid profile.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.front: Which cholesterol thresholds support a diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolaemia (Simon Broome)?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.back: In adults, a total cholesterol >7.5 mmol/L or LDL >4.9 mmol/L, together with tendon xanthomata (in the patient or a first/second-degree relative) or DNA evidence, or a family history of premature coronary disease.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.front: What is cascade screening in the context of familial hypercholesterolaemia?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.back: Systematic DNA-based testing of first- and second-degree relatives (and, where possible, third-degree) of an affected person for the same lipid disorder / mutation, so that gene carriers are identified and treated early to prevent premature coronary disease.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.front: How is predominant or severe hypertriglyceridaemia managed?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.back: Correct secondary factors (alcohol, poor glycaemic control, drugs) and treat with a fibrate (± high-dose omega-3); very high triglycerides need urgent lowering to prevent acute pancreatitis.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.front: Which lipid stigmata should trigger urgent (rather than routine) action, and why?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.back: Eruptive xanthomata (severe hypertriglyceridaemia → pancreatitis risk) and tendon xanthomata (familial hypercholesterolaemia → very high LDL, premature CAD, family screening).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.front: What are tuberous xanthomata and lipaemia retinalis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.back: Tuberous xanthomata are firm yellow nodules over the elbows and knees (remnant / type III and severe hypercholesterolaemia). Lipaemia retinalis is a creamy-white appearance of the retinal vessels in very severe hypertriglyceridaemia.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.front: What monitoring is required when starting a statin?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.back: Check baseline LFTs (repeat at ~3 and 12 months) and ask about muscle symptoms; measure creatine kinase if there is unexplained myalgia. Persistent transaminases >3× ULN or a marked CK rise prompt review.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.front: What is the first question to ask about a swollen leg?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.back:
One leg or both?
  • Unilateral swelling is a local problem (exclude a DVT first);
  • bilateral swelling is usually systemic (heart, kidney, liver, drugs, venous / lymphatic).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.front: What is the must-not-miss cause of an acutely swollen, tender unilateral leg?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.back: A DVT — it threatens a pulmonary embolism.Score the probability (Wells) and confirm with a D-dimer or compression Doppler ultrasound.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.front: How do you distinguish a DVT from cellulitis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.back:
Both give a hot, swollen, tender leg.
  • Cellulitis is redder, with a clear portal of entry (tinea, ulcer) and systemic upset / fever;
  • a DVT is less inflamed but carries VTE risk factors.
If unsure, score and scan.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.front: Which causes give PITTING vs NON-PITTING leg oedema?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.back:
• Pitting → venous, heart failure, hypoalbuminaemia, drugs.
  • Non-pitting → lymphoedema, myxoedema (hypothyroid) and lipoedema (fatty, spares the feet).
The inability to pinch / tent the skin at the base of the second toe — a positive sign indicates lymphoedema (thickened, fibrotic skin).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.front: What are the systemic causes of bilateral pitting oedema?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.back:
• Heart failure (raised venous pressure),
  • hypoalbuminaemia (nephrotic, liver failure, malnutrition),
  • drugs (calcium-channel blockers), and
  • chronic venous insufficiency.
Calcium-channel blockers (amlodipine — the commonest), also NSAIDs, pioglitazone, gabapentin / pregabalin, and steroids / fludrocortisone.CCBs cause it by precapillary arteriolar dilatation.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.front: What are the hypoalbuminaemic causes of oedema?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.back: Nephrotic syndrome (urinary protein loss), liver failure / cirrhosis (reduced synthesis), and malnutrition / protein-losing enteropathy — low oncotic pressure allows fluid into the tissues.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.front: What is the triad of nephrotic syndrome?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.back: Heavy proteinuria (>3.5 g/day), hypoalbuminaemia and oedema (classically periorbital and dependent), with frothy urine and hyperlipidaemia.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.front: What is a ruptured Baker's cyst and how does it present?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.back: Rupture of a popliteal (Baker’s) cyst — usually with known knee OA / RA — causing sudden calf pain and swelling that mimics a DVT (“pseudothrombophlebitis”), often with a crescent bruise around the ankle.
A massive iliofemoral DVT occluding venous outflow, giving a blue, tensely swollen, painful, threatened limb — a vascular emergency risking venous gangrene.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.front: What are the two types of lymphoedema?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.back:
• Primary (congenital / hereditary, e.g. Milroy’s) and
  • secondary (after nodal surgery / radiotherapy, malignancy, infection — filariasis worldwide).
Both are non-pitting with a positive Stemmer’s sign.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.front: What is lipoedema and how does it differ from lymphoedema?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.back: Symmetrical fatty enlargement of the legs in women that is tender and characteristically spares the feet (cut-off at the ankles) with a negative Stemmer’s sign — it is fat, not true oedema; lymphoedema involves the feet.
Compression of the left common iliac vein by the overlying right common iliac artery, causing left leg swelling and a predisposition to left iliofemoral DVT.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.front: What defines pre-eclampsia, and why does it matter in a swollen leg?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.back: New hypertension + proteinuria after 20 weeks of pregnancy (± rapid oedema).Leg / facial swelling in a pregnant woman must prompt a BP and urine dip — pre-eclampsia is dangerous to mother and fetus.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.front: How is a suspected unilateral DVT investigated?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.back:
A two-level Wells score:
  • ‘likely’ → compression Doppler ultrasound;
  • ‘unlikely’ → D-dimer (scan if positive).
Proximal / recurrent cases may need CT / MR venography.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.front: What blood and imaging tests work up bilateral (systemic) leg oedema?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.back: Albumin, U&E, LFTs, TFTs and BNP, a urine protein:creatinine ratio, plus an echocardiogram and CXR — to separate cardiac, renal, hepatic, thyroid and venous causes.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.front: What examination signs indicate chronic venous insufficiency?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.back: Haemosiderin staining, lipodermatosclerosis and varicose eczema in the gaiter area, with varicosities and swelling that is worse by evening and eased by elevation.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What is intermittent claudication?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: Cramping muscle pain brought on by walking a reproducible distance and relieved within minutes by resting / standing still, from peripheral arterial disease — muscle ischaemia when demand outstrips a fixed arterial supply.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What are the four causes of leg pain on walking?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back:
• Vascular (peripheral arterial disease),
  • neurogenic (lumbar spinal stenosis),
  • musculoskeletal (hip / knee osteoarthritis), and
  • the rarer venous claudication.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: How does the SITE of vascular claudication localise the disease?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back:
• Calf → femoropopliteal disease;
  • thigh / buttock → aortoiliac disease;
  • buttock claudication + erectile dysfunction + absent femoral pulses → aortoiliac occlusion (Leriche syndrome).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What is Leriche syndrome?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back:
Aortoiliac occlusive disease giving the triad of
  • buttock / thigh claudication,
  • erectile dysfunction, and
  • absent or weak femoral pulses.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: How does neurogenic claudication differ from vascular claudication?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: Neurogenic (spinal stenosis): a variable distance, relieved by flexion (sitting / leaning forward) rather than by simply stopping, worse on standing and walking downhill, better uphill / leaning on a trolley, with normal pulses and ABPI.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What is the shopping-trolley sign?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: Leaning forward on a trolley (lumbar flexion) relieves neurogenic claudication by widening the spinal canal — so patients manage further uphill (spine flexed) than downhill (spine extended).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What is venous claudication?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: Bursting leg pain on walking after prior DVT / iliofemoral outflow obstruction, with limb swelling, relieved slowly by elevation rather than by quick rest.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: How does hip / knee osteoarthritis differ from vascular claudication?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: OA pain begins in the first steps, is localised to the joint, worsens with activity and eases with rest, with crepitus and reduced range of movement and normal foot pulses.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What is the key bedside test for claudication, and its thresholds?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back:
The ABPI:
  • 0.9–1.3 normal;
  • 0.5–0.9 claudication-range PAD;
  • <0.5 critical limb ischaemia;
  • >1.3 calcified / incompressible (diabetes / CKD) → use toe pressures.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What features signal that claudication has become critical limb ischaemia?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: Rest / night pain relieved by hanging the leg out of bed, ulceration or gangrene, and a rapidly-shortening claudication distance — a limb-threatening emergency needing urgent vascular referral.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: Why does intermittent claudication matter beyond the leg?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: It is a marker of systemic atherosclerosis — these patients are at high risk of myocardial infarction and stroke. The biggest wins are smoking cessation, a statin and an antiplatelet, plus BP and glycaemic control.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What is the first-line management of intermittent claudication?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: A supervised exercise programme plus risk-factor modification (stop smoking, statin, antiplatelet, treat BP / diabetes). Revascularisation (angioplasty / bypass) is reserved for lifestyle-limiting or conservative-failed disease.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What is Buerger's disease (thromboangiitis obliterans)?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: A non-atherosclerotic inflammatory occlusion of small / medium vessels in young male smokers, causing distal limb and digital ischaemia with claudication. The essential treatment is complete smoking cessation.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What is popliteal artery entrapment?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: Calf claudication in a young, active patient from compression of the popliteal artery by the gastrocnemius — foot pulses are normal at rest but disappear on active plantarflexion.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What is chronic exertional compartment syndrome?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: Tight, aching pain in a specific muscle compartment during exercise in young athletes, resolving slowly with rest, with normal pulses; diagnosed by raised intracompartmental pressures.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: Which investigations confirm the cause of leg pain on walking?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back:
• Vascular: ABPI + arterial duplex → CT / MR angiography.
  • Neurogenic: MRI lumbar spine.
  • Osteoarthritis: weight-bearing X-ray.
  • Venous: venous duplex.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What is the Fontaine classification of chronic limb ischaemia?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back:
• I asymptomatic
  • II intermittent claudication (IIa >200 m, IIb <200 m)
  • III ischaemic rest pain
  • IV ulceration / gangrene.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: How can diabetic peripheral neuropathy mimic claudication, and how is it told apart?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: It causes burning / tingling pain that is present at rest and at night, not brought on by a fixed walking distance; pulses and ABPI are usually preserved, with glove-and-stocking sensory loss.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What is the must-not-miss cause of leg pain at rest or at night?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: Ischaemic rest pain — the end-stage of peripheral arterial disease (critical / chronic limb-threatening ischaemia). It threatens the limb and needs urgent revascularisation.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: Where is ischaemic rest pain felt, and what relieves it?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: In the forefoot and toes. It is worse lying flat (loss of gravity-assisted flow) and eased by hanging the foot out of bed or standing — dependency improves perfusion.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: How do you distinguish ischaemic rest pain from neuropathic night pain at the bedside?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: The foot. Ischaemic pain has a cold, pale, pulseless foot with dependent relief; neuropathic pain is positional-indifferent with a warm, well-perfused foot and intact pulses. Pulses and ABPI settle it.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What defines chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (critical limb ischaemia)?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: Rest pain for >2 weeks, and/or tissue loss (ulcer or gangrene), with an ankle pressure <50 mmHg or ABPI <0.5 — a time-critical vascular referral.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: Why can the ABPI be falsely high (>1.3) in diabetes or renal disease?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: Calcified, incompressible arteries cannot be occluded by the cuff, giving a falsely elevated ankle pressure. Use toe-brachial pressures (small digital vessels are spared) or duplex instead.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What are the features of diabetic / peripheral neuropathy causing night leg pain?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: Burning, tingling, numbness in a symmetrical glove-and-stocking pattern, worse at night, with reduced monofilament and vibration sense but intact pulses and a warm foot.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What are nocturnal leg cramps and how are they recognised?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: Sudden, painful involuntary muscle contractions (a palpable knot) in the calf or foot at night, relieved by stretching. Common in the elderly and with dehydration, diuretics or statins; benign.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What characterises restless legs syndrome?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: An irresistible urge to move the legs with an unpleasant crawling sensation, worse at rest / in the evening and relieved by movement. Associated with iron deficiency, pregnancy, renal failure and family history.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What investigation should you check in restless legs syndrome, and why?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: Ferritin / iron studies — iron deficiency is a common, treatable cause; replace iron if ferritin is low (roughly <75 µg/L). Also review dopamine-blocking drugs.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: How does Buerger’s disease differ from atherosclerotic peripheral arterial disease?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: Buerger’s affects young male smokers with distal small/medium vessels and migratory superficial thrombophlebitis, with normal proximal arteries and corkscrew collaterals on angiography; atherosclerotic PAD affects older patients with proximal large-vessel disease and cardiovascular risk factors.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: How do lumbar radiculopathy and spinal stenosis cause leg pain, and how do they differ from vascular rest pain?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back:
• Radiculopathy / sciatica (disc / root): shooting, dermatomal pain worse on sitting, forward flexion and coughing, eased by standing / lying.
  • Spinal stenosis (neurogenic claudication): leg pain on standing / walking / spinal extension, eased by sitting or leaning forward (the ‘shopping-trolley’ sign).
In both the foot pulses are normal.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What is dependent rubor and elevation pallor?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: Signs of severe arterial insufficiency: the foot goes pale on elevation (gravity overwhelms poor inflow) and turns dusky red when hung down (reactive hyperaemia / maximal vasodilatation). Buerger's test.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What is the first-line management of chronic limb-threatening ischaemia?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: Urgent vascular referral for revascularisation (angioplasty / stent or bypass), with imaging (duplex → CT / MR angiography), plus best medical therapy (antiplatelet, statin, smoking cessation) and analgesia. Amputation if unsalvageable.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: Why is ischaemic rest pain worse at night specifically?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: Lying flat removes the gravitational boost to arterial inflow, cardiac output falls in sleep, and skin warmth diverts blood — so a critically perfused foot tips into pain, forcing the patient to hang it out of bed.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: Which bloods and bedside tests work up leg pain at rest / night?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back:
• ABPI (± toe pressures) and pulse palpation for ischaemia;
  • 10 g monofilament, vibration and ankle reflexes for neuropathy;
  • and HbA1c / glucose, B12, U&E and ferritin to screen for neuropathy and restless-legs causes.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What is intermittent claudication, and how does it differ from rest pain?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: Claudication is calf / thigh pain on walking, relieved by rest within minutes (moderate PAD). Rest pain occurs without exertion and signals critical ischaemia — a far more advanced, limb-threatening stage.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: A warm, well-perfused foot with palpable pulses makes which broad group of diagnoses most likely?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: Non-ischaemic (mimic) causes — peripheral neuropathy, nocturnal cramps and restless legs syndrome. Intact pulses and a normal ABPI effectively exclude critical limb ischaemia as the cause of the pain.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What analgesic approach is used for neuropathic leg pain?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: Neuropathic agents — amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin — alongside tight glycaemic control in diabetes. Standard analgesics are usually ineffective for neuropathic pain.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What are the 6 Ps of acute limb ischaemia?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Perishing cold, Paraesthesia and Paralysis. The last two (paraesthesia and paralysis) are late and signal a threatened limb needing revascularisation within hours.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: Why is a cold, pale, pulseless leg a surgical emergency?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: It is acute limb ischaemia — there is roughly a 6-hour window before irreversible muscle and nerve damage. Delay risks amputation, and reperfusion after that risks limb-threatening / life-threatening complications.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: How does the history distinguish an embolic from a thrombotic acute limb ischaemia?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back:
• Embolic → sudden onset (minutes), no prior warning, often AF or recent MI and a normal contralateral leg.
  • Thrombotic → onset over hours to days on a background of claudication (pre-existing disease).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: Why do the contralateral leg pulses matter in acute limb ischaemia?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: They reveal the mechanism. Present pulses in the other leg (a healthy vascular tree) favour an embolus; absent / reduced pulses (bilateral disease) favour in-situ thrombosis on a diseased vessel.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: Why does embolic vs thrombotic ischaemia change the operation?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: An embolus lodged on a healthy vessel is retrieved by embolectomy (Fogarty catheter). A thrombosis on a diseased vessel usually needs angiography then angioplasty / thrombolysis / bypass — you must image the run-off first.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What are the commonest sources of an arterial embolus to the leg?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: The heart — atrial fibrillation (commonest), mural thrombus after MI, prosthetic / diseased valves and endocarditis. Also AAA / popliteal aneurysm mural thrombus and, rarely, paradoxical embolus.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: Which two of the 6 Ps indicate a threatened (not just ischaemic) limb?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: Paraesthesia and paralysis. Sensory loss beyond the toes and motor weakness mean the nerves and muscle are failing — an immediately threatened limb requiring revascularisation within hours.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What is the Rutherford classification of acute limb ischaemia used for?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back:
To grade limb viability and urgency:
  • I = viable (no sensory/motor loss, Doppler signals present),
  • IIa/IIb = threatened (sensory ± motor loss — salvageable if revascularised),
  • III = irreversible (profound deficit, fixed staining → amputation).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What signs mean an acutely ischaemic limb is irreversible?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: Fixed mottling that does not blanch, hard, tender, woody (paralysed) muscles, and profound sensory / motor loss. This is Rutherford III — the limb is non-salvageable and needs amputation; attempted reperfusion risks fatal reperfusion injury.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What is the immediate medical management of acute limb ischaemia?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: IV unfractionated heparin straight away (limit propagation), analgesia, oxygen and IV access, keep the limb dependent (avoid elevating or actively warming it), and make an urgent vascular surgery referral — give the heparin before imaging.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What is phlegmasia cerulea dolens and how does it mimic acute limb ischaemia?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: A massive iliofemoral DVT obstructing venous outflow → a blue, tensely swollen, painful leg. Unlike arterial ischaemia the leg is swollen and not pale; it is a venous emergency risking venous gangrene.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: How does compartment syndrome mimic acute limb ischaemia?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: Raised compartment pressure (after trauma, fracture or reperfusion) gives pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch and a tense, tender compartment. Distal pulses are often still present early — a normal pulse does not exclude it.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What is cholesterol / atheroembolism (trash foot)?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: Showers of cholesterol crystals from a proximal plaque or aneurysm (often after angiography, surgery or anticoagulation) lodging in the digits — blue toes and livedo reticularis with palpable pulses preserved.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: Which don't-miss diagnosis presents as a cold, pulseless leg with chest / back pain?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: Aortic dissection extending into the iliac vessels — suspect it with tearing chest / interscapular pain, an inter-arm blood-pressure difference or a widened mediastinum. Confirm with CT aortogram.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What is the first bedside test in a suspected acutely ischaemic leg?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: Palpate and hand-held Doppler both legs. An absent arterial (monophasic / silent) signal confirms ischaemia; comparing with the other leg localises the level and hints at the mechanism (normal other side → embolic).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: Which bedside findings stage acute limb ischaemia as viable, threatened or irreversible?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back:
• Sensation and power intact → viable.
  • Sensory loss beyond the toes ± weakness → threatened (revascularise within hours).
  • Fixed mottling, paralysis, woody muscles → irreversible.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What investigations confirm and plan treatment in acute limb ischaemia?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: For a threatened but viable limb, urgent CT angiography (or on-table angiography) maps the occlusion for revascularisation. Add an ECG (AF), echocardiogram and AAA screen for an embolic source, plus FBC, U&E, coagulation, group & save, CK and lactate.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.front: What is reperfusion injury and why does it matter after revascularising a limb?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.back: Restoring flow to ischaemic muscle releases potassium, myoglobin, acid and CK → risk of hyperkalaemia, arrhythmia, rhabdomyolysis / AKI and compartment syndrome. Monitor U&E, ECG and CK, and consider fasciotomy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is acute pericarditis, and where does it sit in the broader disease spectrum?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Inflammation of the pericardium.It is part of a spectrum: acute pericarditis → effusion → tamponade, and separately → constrictive pericarditis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the commonest infective cause of pericarditis, and which organisms?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Viral is commonest — Coxsackievirus B, enteroviruses, EBV, CMV.Bacterial causes include TB (suspect with any exudative effusion).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Distinguish the two post-MI causes of pericarditis by timing and mechanism.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back:
• Early (1–3 days): fibrinous pericarditis from direct irritation.
  • Late (typically 1–6 weeks, occasionally later): Dressler’s syndrome — an autoimmune process with fever + pleurisy.
It is now rare in the reperfusion era (well under 1%, from 3–5% historically).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is Dressler's syndrome?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: A late post-MI autoimmune pericarditis — typically 1–6 weeks, occasionally later — presenting with fever and pleurisy.Now rare in the reperfusion era.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: List the systemic/inflammatory causes of pericarditis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back:
• SLE, RA and other connective tissue diseases;
  • uraemia (pericardial rub in renal failure);
  • hypothyroidism; and
  • malignancy (lung, breast).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the single largest group of pericarditis cases by aetiology?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Idiopathic — the largest single group, presumed viral.Other ‘other’ causes include radiotherapy and trauma.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the defining symptom of acute pericarditis, and its character?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Chest pain — sharp, pleuritic, retrosternal, worsened by deep inspiration and movement.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: How does positioning affect the chest pain of pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Relieved by sitting/leaning forward (lifts the inflamed pericardium away from the diaphragm) and worse lying flat — the latter being a key feature distinguishing it from ACS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Where does pericarditic pain radiate, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Classically to the trapezius ridge (via the phrenic nerve) — a useful discriminator from ACS; may also radiate to the neck/left shoulder.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the cardinal clinical sign of acute pericarditis, and its character?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: A pericardial friction rub — scratchy/squeaking, high-pitched, heard at the left sternal edge.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: How is the pericardial friction rub best heard, and what is its classic timing pattern?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Best heard leaning forward, in end-expiration. It may be triphasic (atrial systole, ventricular systole, early diastole).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What happens to the pericardial friction rub if a large effusion develops?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: It is evanescent — it classically diminishes or disappears as a large effusion develops and the fluid separates the inflamed layers, though it can persist.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What systemic features may accompany acute pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Fever (especially viral/infective), malaise and myalgia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What are the four diagnostic criteria for acute pericarditis, and how many are needed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back:
• Chest pain (sharp, pleuritic, positional, relieved leaning forward),
  • friction rub,
  • ECG changes (widespread saddle ST elevation or PR depression), and
  • a new or worsening pericardial effusion on echo.
≥2 of the 4 = diagnosis.Newer ESC guidance adds raised CRP and MRI evidence of pericardial inflammation as supporting criteria — 2-of-4 remains the exam answer.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Why is TTE (echo) recommended in all suspected cases of acute pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: To exclude a pericardial effusion and assess for myocardial involvement.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Describe the ST elevation seen in acute pericarditis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Saddle-shaped (concave) ST elevation, widespread (most leads — I, II, aVL, aVF, V2–V6), with a concave upward ‘saddle/smiley’ morphology that returns to baseline as inflammation resolves, and no reciprocal ST depression except ST depression / PR elevation in aVR (± V1).Spodick’s sign — a downsloping TP segment, best seen in lead II and the lateral chest leads — also favours pericarditis over STEMI.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Why is PR depression important in acute pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: It is highly specific for pericarditis, reflecting atrial epicardial involvement in the inflammation.There is PR elevation in aVR (the mirror image), and PR depression may precede the ST changes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: In which lead is PR ELEVATION seen in pericarditis, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: aVR — it is the mirror image of the PR depression seen in the other leads.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What other (non-ST/PR) ECG findings occur in acute pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Sinus tachycardia is common, and low voltage if an effusion develops.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Compare the ST shape and distribution in pericarditis vs STEMI.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back:
• Pericarditis: concave (saddle/smiley), widespread (most leads).
  • STEMI: convex (tombstone/frowning), territorial (leads facing the infarct).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Compare reciprocal changes and the PR interval in pericarditis vs STEMI.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back:
• Pericarditis: no reciprocal ST depression except in aVR (± V1), where ST depression and PR elevation are expected; PR depression elsewhere is highly specific.
  • STEMI: reciprocal ST depression in the opposing territory, with a normal PR interval.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Compare Q waves and ECG evolution in pericarditis vs STEMI.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back:
• Pericarditis: no Q waves; diffuse ST → returns to baseline.
  • STEMI: pathological Q waves develop; hyperacute T → ST rise → T inversion → Q wave.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: How does troponin differ between pericarditis and STEMI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Troponin does not reliably separate them. In pericarditis it may be normal, mildly raised, or substantially raised where there is myocardial involvement (myopericarditis). In STEMI it is often normal at presentation and rises over hours — so a normal or mildly raised troponin never excludes STEMI, which is diagnosed on the ECG and the clinical picture, not on the troponin.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What are the two hallmark ECG changes of acute pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Saddle-shaped (concave) ST elevation and PR depression.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What blood tests are relevant in acute pericarditis, and what do they assess?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: FBC, CRP/ESR, U&E (uraemia), TFTs and troponin (myocardial involvement) in everyone.Send ANA/dsDNA, TB testing and tumour markers only when the history or the course suggests a secondary cause — a routine aetiological hunt is not needed in a first, uncomplicated episode (ESC).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What CXR findings may occur in acute pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: It may be normal; an enlarged cardiac silhouette (if effusion) or a pleural effusion (Dressler’s) may be seen.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: When are CT/MRI used in acute pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: If the diagnosis is uncertain, or to assess pericardial thickening.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the first-line drug treatment for acute pericarditis, including doses and duration?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back:
• NSAIDs (ibuprofen 600 mg TDS or aspirin 750–1000 mg TDS) at attack dose until symptom and CRP resolution (~1–2 weeks) then tapered, with a PPI for gastroprotection;
  • plus colchicine 0.5 mg BD (0.5 mg OD if <70 kg) added to reduce recurrence, continued for 3 months.
These doses follow ESC guidance — NICE has none — and colchicine is used off-label in the UK for pericarditis.Colchicine safety: narrow therapeutic index and no antidote. Check renal and hepatic function before prescribing and reduce or avoid the dose in impairment; avoid altogether in end-stage renal disease (ESC). It is cleared by CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, so clarithromycin and other dual inhibitors can cause fatal toxicity and are contraindicated alongside colchicine in renal or hepatic impairment; co-prescription with a statin raises the risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis. Warn the patient that diarrhoea is the commonest early signal to stop and seek advice (BNF).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What does colchicine add to NSAID therapy in pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: It reduces (roughly halves) the risk of recurrence; it is continued for 3 months.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: How are the NSAID and colchicine stopped at the end of treatment in pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back:
• The NSAID is held at attack dose until symptoms resolve and CRP normalises, then tapered in steps.
  • Colchicine does not require tapering (ESC), but it is the last drug to be stopped, once sustained remission is confirmed.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What lifestyle advice accompanies pericarditis treatment?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Rest; restrict activity to ordinary sedentary life until symptoms resolve and CRP normalises.Competitive athletes: no return to competitive sport for at least 3 months from onset, and only once symptoms, CRP, ECG and echo have all normalised (ESC).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: When are systemic corticosteroids used in pericarditis, and what is the caution?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Only for an autoimmune cause (SLE/RA), refractory disease, or where NSAIDs/colchicine are contraindicated — they increase the recurrence risk, so lowest effective dose with a slow taper.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Which anti-inflammatory is used for pericarditis early after an MI, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Non-aspirin NSAIDs impair infarct healing (rupture risk), so aspirin at anti-inflammatory doses is the agent of choice (including for Dressler’s syndrome).Aspirin is itself an NSAID.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the caution regarding anticoagulation in acute pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Use with caution due to the risk of haemopericardium.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: List the high-risk features that warrant admission in acute pericarditis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back:
• Fever >38°C,
  • large effusion or tamponade,
  • elevated troponin (myopericarditis),
  • immunosuppression or anticoagulation, and
  • subacute onset or failure to respond to NSAIDs.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What are the complications of acute pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back:
• Pericardial effusion (most common),
  • constrictive pericarditis (chronic, especially TB),
  • recurrent pericarditis (15–30% after a first episode without colchicine, up to 50% after a first recurrence, roughly halved by colchicine), and
  • myopericarditis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the headline exam pearl distinguishing pericarditis from STEMI on ECG?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back:
These features shift the probability, they do not settle it — if the ECG or the story leaves STEMI a real possibility, treat it as STEMI and escalate on the acute coronary syndrome pathway.
  • Pericarditis: concave ST, widespread, PR depression, no reciprocal changes.
  • STEMI: convex ST, territorial, reciprocal changes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What positional chest-pain pattern should be treated as pericarditis until proven otherwise?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Chest pain relieved by leaning forward and worse lying flat.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is a pericardial effusion, and where does it sit in the disease spectrum?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Accumulation of fluid in the pericardial sac. It can result from any cause of pericarditis and is the bridge between acute pericarditis and tamponade.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Why is a pericardial effusion often asymptomatic?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Especially if accumulation is slow — the pericardium stretches to accommodate the fluid gradually.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What examination findings suggest a pericardial effusion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back:
• An obscured apex beat (fluid insulates and displaces the heartbeat),
  • soft/muffled heart sounds, and
  • dullness to percussion at the left base (Ewart’s sign in large effusions — dullness below the left scapula).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is Ewart's sign?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Dullness to percussion below the left scapula, seen in large pericardial effusions due to compression of the left lung base.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What ECG findings occur in a pericardial effusion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back:
• Low-voltage QRS complexes,
  • electrical alternans (the QRS amplitude alternates beat-to-beat as the heart swings in the fluid — specific for a large effusion), and
  • sinus tachycardia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is electrical alternans, and what does it indicate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: The QRS amplitude alternates beat-to-beat as the heart swings within the fluid. It is specific for a large pericardial effusion (and tamponade until proven otherwise).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the classic CXR finding in a pericardial effusion, and the threshold?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: A globular (water-bottle) heart — a flask-shaped cardiac silhouette when the effusion is >250 mL.The lung fields are clear (unlike heart failure).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Why are clear lung fields on CXR a useful discriminator in pericardial effusion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: They distinguish a pericardial effusion (globular heart, clear lungs) from heart failure (where pulmonary congestion would be expected).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the gold-standard investigation for a pericardial effusion, and what does it show?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Echo — it shows an echo-free space surrounding the heart, quantifies the size, and guides pericardiocentesis.It must be done urgently if tamponade is suspected.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Why does the RATE of fluid accumulation determine the haemodynamic impact of an effusion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Slow accumulation lets the pericardium stretch to accommodate 1–2 L with little effect, whereas rapid accumulation of even 150–200 mL can cause tamponade.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the mainstay of managing a pericardial effusion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Treat the underlying cause — most effusions resolve with this alone.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: When is pericardiocentesis indicated for an effusion, and what is done with the fluid?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: If symptomatic or large: echo-guided pericardiocentesis (aspiration). Fluid is sent for culture, cytology/histology, and PCR (for TB) — highest yield with large effusions.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is a pericardial window, and when is it used?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Excision of a pericardial segment to allow ongoing drainage — used if an effusion recurs or the fluid is loculated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is cardiac tamponade, and why is it a medical emergency?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Pericardial fluid accumulates faster than the pericardium can stretch → rising intrapericardial pressure compresses all four chambers → impaired diastolic filling → reduced cardiac output → obstructive shock → cardiac arrest if untreated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is Beck's triad of cardiac tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back:
• Hypotension (reduced cardiac output → shock),
  • raised JVP (impaired venous return into the compressed heart), and
  • muffled heart sounds (fluid surrounding and insulating the heart).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is pulsus paradoxus, and what is the threshold in tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: An exaggerated inspiratory fall in systolic BP >10 mmHg.On inspiration, increased RV volume pushes the interventricular septum into the LV, impairing LV output.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the mechanism of pulsus paradoxus in tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: On inspiration, venous return to the RV increases; with a fixed total cardiac volume, the increased RV volume pushes the interventricular septum into the LV, impairing LV filling and output → a fall in systolic BP.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Besides Beck’s triad and pulsus paradoxus, what additional features occur in tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back:
• Compensatory tachycardia and dyspnoea,
  • cool peripheries (reduced cardiac output),
  • an absent JVP y descent (heart volume fixed; venous inflow cannot increase in diastole), and
  • absent Kussmaul’s sign.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Why is the JVP y descent ABSENT in tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: The heart volume is fixed by the surrounding fluid, so venous inflow cannot increase in early diastole — abolishing the y descent.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the significance of Kussmaul’s sign being absent in tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Its absence distinguishes tamponade from constrictive pericarditis (where Kussmaul’s sign is present).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the classic ECG triad of cardiac tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Electrical alternans + low voltage + sinus tachycardia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the most sensitive echo sign of tamponade, and what does echo also guide?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Right atrial collapse is the most sensitive sign; right ventricular diastolic collapse is the most specific.Echo also guides pericardiocentesis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the definitive treatment of cardiac tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Urgent echo-guided pericardiocentesis — needle aspiration of the pericardial fluid.Untreated tamponade is fatal — it progresses to cardiac arrest; immediate haemodynamic improvement is expected after even small volumes are drained.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: When is a surgical pericardial window used in tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: If the effusion recurs or the fluid is loculated (fluid analysis: culture, cytology/histology, PCR for TB).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is constrictive pericarditis, and the most important cause worldwide?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: A chronic consequence of recurrent or persistent pericarditis, where the pericardium becomes a rigid fibrotic cage preventing diastolic filling. TB is the most important cause worldwide.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Why does constrictive pericarditis produce a right-sided heart failure picture?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back:
The rigid pericardium traps raised venous pressure that cannot go forward, causing
  • raised JVP,
  • dependent oedema, hepatomegaly and ascites,
  • pleural effusions,
  • SOB/exercise intolerance, and
  • (late) AF from atrial dilatation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is Kussmaul’s sign, and why does it occur in constrictive pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: The JVP paradoxically RISES on inspiration, because the rigid pericardium cannot accommodate the increased venous return that inspiration would normally allow.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is a pericardial knock, and what causes it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: A loud early S3 heard in constrictive pericarditis, caused by the abrupt cessation of ventricular filling as the ventricle hits the rigid pericardium.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: How does the JVP waveform differ between constriction and tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back:
• Constriction: prominent x AND y descents.
  • Tamponade: y descent absent (x descent prominent) — the y descent is the key contrast.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Why is the apex beat normal/impalpable in constrictive pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: The rigid pericardium restricts outward movement of the heart, so the apex beat is not displaced or thrusting.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: How is constrictive pericarditis distinguished from restrictive cardiomyopathy?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: They share the same haemodynamic profile, so the clinical picture alone is rarely sufficient — though Kussmaul’s sign and a pericardial knock favour constriction. Doppler echo and cross-sectional imaging are needed to separate them, and the distinction matters because only constriction is curable by surgery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Compare the pathology and onset of tamponade vs constrictive pericarditis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back:
• Tamponade: fluid in the pericardial space, acute onset (minutes–hours).
  • Constriction: a rigid fibrotic pericardium, chronic onset (months–years).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Compare Kussmaul’s sign and pulsus paradoxus in tamponade vs constriction.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back:
• Tamponade: Kussmaul’s absent, pulsus paradoxus present (>10 mmHg).
  • Constriction: Kussmaul’s present, pulsus paradoxus usually absent.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Compare the heart sounds, CXR heart size and calcification in tamponade vs constriction.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back:
• Tamponade: muffled sounds, enlarged (globular) heart, no calcification.
  • Constriction: pericardial knock (loud early S3), normal heart size, calcification may be present.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Compare the definitive treatment of tamponade vs constrictive pericarditis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back:
• Tamponade: pericardiocentesis.
  • Constriction: pericardiectomy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What are the key CXR findings in constrictive pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: A normal heart size plus pericardial calcification (best seen on the lateral film — strongly supports the diagnosis).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the role of CT/MRI in constrictive pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: CT/MRI demonstrates pericardial thickening ± calcification and is the key test for surgical planning.Note that pericardium of normal thickness does not exclude constriction (around one in five surgically proven cases), so a normal scan does not settle it — the diagnosis is haemodynamic.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What echo findings are seen in constrictive pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back:
• Septal bounce,
  • a dilated IVC, and
  • preserved systolic function.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the ‘square root sign’ on cardiac catheterisation, and when is it used?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: A dip-plateau pattern in the ventricular pressure trace, seen in constrictive pericarditis — used when imaging is inconclusive.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the only definitive treatment for constrictive pericarditis, and its risk?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Pericardiectomy (surgical excision) — a high-risk operation, reserved for severe or progressive disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What are the medical/supportive measures in constrictive pericarditis alongside surgery?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back:
• Diuretics for symptomatic fluid overload (a bridge to surgery),
  • treat the underlying cause (e.g. full anti-tuberculous therapy ± corticosteroids for TB to reduce fibrosis), and
  • rate control for AF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Exam pearl: what does pericardial calcification on CXR/CT indicate, and what is the surgical caveat?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Constriction. Pericardiectomy cures constriction, but there is no surgical fix for restrictive cardiomyopathy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Exam pearl: why always check a TB screen in an exudative effusion of unknown cause?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: TB is the most important cause of constrictive pericarditis worldwide, so it must be excluded in any exudative effusion without a clear cause.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: While arranging urgent pericardiocentesis for cardiac tamponade, what supportive measures help — and what must you avoid?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back:
• Give: if the patient is hypotensive, a cautious IV fluid bolus to raise preload and maintain filling against the raised intrapericardial pressure; keep the patient flat. The benefit is confined to hypotensive patients — in a normotensive patient large volumes can raise pericardial pressure and make things worse.
  • Avoid: diuretics, nitrates and other vasodilators — they strip the preload the compressed heart depends on and can precipitate arrest.
  • Beware: intubation and positive-pressure ventilation — they further reduce venous return.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Why is giving a diuretic in cardiac tamponade dangerous?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back:
Because the picture mimics heart failure — hypotension with a raised JVP — so the reflex is to offload.
But in tamponade the raised JVP is not congestion; it is blood unable to enter a compressed heart. Reducing preload lowers filling further, cardiac output falls, and the patient can arrest.
The treatment is to drain the pericardium, not to diurese.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Why is intubating a patient with untreated cardiac tamponade hazardous?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back:
Induction agents vasodilate and positive-pressure ventilation raises intrathoracic pressure, both of which reduce venous return.
In a heart already unable to fill, this can cause peri-induction cardiac arrest.
Where possible, drain the pericardium first.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What does "recurrent" mean in pericarditis, and how long is colchicine continued?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back:
Recurrent means a fresh episode after a symptom-free interval of at least 4–6 weeks (ESC); symptoms that never remit beyond 4–6 weeks are incessant rather than recurrent.
  • 3 months after a first episode.
  • 6–12 months if the pericarditis is recurrent.
Colchicine is the last drug to be stopped once symptoms have settled and CRP has normalised.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: A patient has recurrent, colchicine-resistant pericarditis. What is the appropriate next step?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Refer to cardiology.Corticosteroids relieve symptoms quickly but are themselves associated with more recurrence, so they are reserved for an autoimmune cause, refractory disease, or where NSAIDs/colchicine are contraindicated — lowest effective dose, slow taper.Further second-line options are specialist decisions and are not licensed for pericarditis in the UK.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.front: Fall risk: threshold to withhold anticoagulation in AF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.back: Patient must fall ~295 times/year to offset stroke benefit — falls alone are NOT a contraindication

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.front: Rate versus rhythm control in AF — what does the evidence show?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.back: Similar mortality for rate and rhythm control. Rhythm control had more hospitalisations.Choose based on symptoms.
Curative for typical atrial flutter (>95% success)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.front: AF + HFrEF: rate control drug of choice?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.back: Beta-blocker (bisoprolol) — NOT diltiazem/verapamil (negatively inotropic)

Supraventricular tachycardia — any tachyarrhythmia (HR >100 bpm) originating above the bundle of His.Includes AVNRT, AVRT, atrial flutter, AF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.front: What is the most common form of paroxysmal SVT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.back: AVNRT (AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia) — accounts for ~60% of SVTs.Due to dual AV nodal pathways forming a re-entrant circuit.
AV re-entrant tachycardia — re-entrant circuit using AV node + accessory pathway (bypass tract).Divided into: orthodromic (narrow complex) and antidromic (wide complex).
Pre-excitation syndrome — congenital accessory pathway (Bundle of Kent) bypassing the AV node. ECG: short PR interval + delta wave + wide QRS.Risk of AF conducting rapidly via accessory pathway → VF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.front: What is the ECG appearance of AVNRT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.back: Narrow complex tachycardia (HR 150–250 bpm), regular rhythm, P waves buried in or just after QRS (retrograde — 'pseudo-r' in V1), abrupt onset/offset.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.front: What is the first-line treatment for acute SVT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.back: Vagal manoeuvres (Valsalva, carotid sinus massage) — first-line. Then IV adenosine (6 mg, 12 mg, 18 mg).If haemodynamically unstable: DC cardioversion.
Adenosine blocks AV node conduction temporarily — terminates re-entrant SVTs depending on the AV node.Causes transient asystole/bradycardia. Very short half-life (10 seconds).

• Asthma (bronchoconstriction)
  • WPW (may enhance accessory pathway conduction causing AF → VF)
  • sick sinus syndrome
  • second/third-degree AV block

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.front: What is the long-term treatment for recurrent SVT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.back: Catheter ablation (radiofrequency) — first-line for recurrent symptomatic SVT. Curative in >95% of AVNRT.Medical: beta-blocker or flecainide as second-line.
Patient-initiated flecainide or propafenone taken at onset of SVT — for infrequent, well-tolerated episodes.Avoids need for daily prophylaxis.

Regular atrial tachycardia at ~300 bpm with 2:1 (or variable) AV block → ventricular rate ~150 bpm. ECG: sawtooth flutter waves (negative in II, III, aVF). Re-entrant circuit in right atrium around tricuspid annulus.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.front: What is the ECG appearance of atrial flutter with 2:1 block?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.back: Regular narrow complex tachycardia at ~150 bpm with sawtooth flutter waves at 300 bpm — 'think atrial flutter when rate is exactly 150 bpm'.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.front: How is WPW treated acutely if AF develops?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.back: DC cardioversion or procainamide/flecainide (avoid adenosine, digoxin, verapamil — these block AV node and may increase accessory pathway conduction → VF).
Forced expiration against closed glottis — increases vagal tone → slows/blocks AV node → terminates AVNRT.Modified: strain then leg raise (more effective). First-line non-pharmacological treatment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.front: EXAM PEARL: What 3 findings on ECG suggest WPW?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.back: Short PR interval (<120 ms) + delta wave (slurred QRS upstroke) + wide QRS — the WPW triad.If AF occurs with WPW: irregular wide complex tachycardia (pre-excited AF) = emergency DC cardioversion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: What is acute rheumatic fever (ARF)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: A multisystem, immune-mediated inflammatory disease that develops 2–4 weeks after a group A β-haemolytic streptococcal (Streptococcus pyogenes) throat infection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: What is rheumatic heart disease (RHD)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: The chronic valvular sequela of ARF — recurrent or severe carditis scars the valves (classically causing mitral stenosis), presenting years to decades later.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: Which organism causes rheumatic fever?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: Group A β-haemolytic streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: Rheumatic fever follows streptococcal infection at which site?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: Classically the throat (pharyngitis) — unlike post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, which can follow either throat or skin infection. In high-burden settings there is growing evidence that strep skin infection can also trigger ARF, but pharyngitis remains the answer expected in UK exams.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: What is the typical age group affected by rheumatic fever?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: Children aged 5–15 years.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: What is the mechanism of tissue damage in rheumatic fever?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: Molecular mimicry (predominantly a type II antibody-mediated hypersensitivity, with a type IV T-cell component): antibodies and T cells against the streptococcal M protein cross-react with human antigens in the heart, joints, basal ganglia and skin.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: What is the pathognomonic histological finding of rheumatic carditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: Aschoff bodies (granulomatous nodules containing Anitschkow ‘caterpillar’ macrophages) in the myocardium.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: Which layers of the heart does rheumatic carditis affect?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: All three — it is a pancarditis: endocarditis (valvulitis, especially mitral), myocarditis and pericarditis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: What is required to diagnose rheumatic fever (Jones criteria)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back:
• First episode: evidence of a preceding group A strep infection PLUS either 2 major criteria, or 1 major + 2 minor.
  • Recurrent attack (previous ARF or established RHD): 3 minor criteria alone will also do.
Sydenham's chorea is the exception to the strep-evidence rule — it is diagnostic on its own and does not need serological evidence, because titres have usually normalised by the time chorea appears.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: List the five major Jones criteria (‘JONES’).
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back:
• Joints (migratory polyarthritis)
  • Carditis (clinical and/or echo-detected subclinical)
  • Nodules (subcutaneous)
  • Erythema marginatum
  • and Sydenham’s chorea.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: List the minor Jones criteria.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back:
In a low-risk population such as the UK:
  • fever ≥38.5°C
  • polyarthralgia
  • ESR ≥60 mm/h and/or CRP ≥30 mg/L
  • and a prolonged PR interval on ECG.
(A feature counted as a major cannot also be a minor — no polyarthralgia if polyarthritis is the major, no prolonged PR if carditis is the major. Moderate/high-risk populations use lower bars: fever ≥38°C, ESR ≥30 mm/h, monoarthralgia.)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: How is preceding streptococcal infection demonstrated in rheumatic fever?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: Positive throat culture or rapid antigen test, or raised/rising anti-streptococcal antibody titres (ASO titre and anti-DNase B).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: Why are anti-streptococcal antibody titres more useful than a throat swab in rheumatic fever?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: ARF presents weeks after the sore throat, so the swab is often already negative; rising ASO/anti-DNase B titres give the evidence of recent infection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: What did the 2015 revision of the Jones criteria introduce?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: Two things: echo-detected subclinical carditis became a major criterion, and the criteria were stratified by population risk. The UK is a low-risk population, so arthritis must be polyarthritis; in moderate/high-risk populations monoarthritis or polyarthralgia can count as major, with lower fever/ESR cut-offs.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: Describe the arthritis of rheumatic fever.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: A migratory (‘flitting’) polyarthritis of large joints (knees, ankles, elbows, wrists), hot and very tender, with a dramatic response to aspirin/NSAIDs and leaving no joint damage.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: Which manifestation of rheumatic fever causes long-term damage?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: Carditis (a pancarditis) — the only manifestation with lasting sequelae, leading to rheumatic heart disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: What is the commonest acute murmur in rheumatic carditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: Mitral regurgitation (± a Carey Coombs murmur).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: What is the Carey Coombs murmur?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: A soft mid-diastolic murmur of acute mitral valvulitis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: Describe Sydenham’s chorea.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: A late feature (1–6 months) of rapid, involuntary, purposeless movements with emotional lability; it may be the only manifestation and is commoner in girls (‘St Vitus’ dance’).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: Describe the subcutaneous nodules of rheumatic fever.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: Painless, firm nodules over extensor surfaces/bony prominences, associated with severe carditis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: Describe erythema marginatum.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: Pink rings with central clearing on the trunk and proximal limbs that spare the face.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: What ECG finding is a minor Jones criterion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: A prolonged PR interval (first-degree AV block).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: What is the role of echocardiography in suspected rheumatic fever?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: It is recommended in all suspected cases — detecting valvulitis/regurgitation (mitral ± aortic) and subclinical carditis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: How is the streptococcus eradicated in acute rheumatic fever?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: In the UK, 10 days of oral phenoxymethylpenicillin (penicillin V). A single dose of IM benzathine benzylpenicillin is the WHO/international standard, used where adherence is a concern. A macrolide if penicillin-allergic.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: What treats the arthritis and fever of rheumatic fever?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: High-dose aspirin or NSAIDs (with corticosteroids reserved for severe carditis/heart failure).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: Why is the use of aspirin in rheumatic fever notable?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: It is one of the few settings (along with Kawasaki disease) where aspirin is deliberately given to children despite the usual Reye’s syndrome caution.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: What is secondary prophylaxis in rheumatic fever?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: Long-term penicillin to prevent recurrence — IM benzathine penicillin every 3–4 weeks (or oral penicillin V twice daily).
