conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: How long is penicillin prophylaxis given for ARF with carditis and persistent valve disease?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: 10 years, or until age 40 (whichever is longer) — sometimes lifelong.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: Which valve is most commonly affected in rheumatic heart disease, and what is the classic lesion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: The mitral valve; classically mitral stenosis (mitral regurgitation also occurs).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: What are the major consequences of rheumatic heart disease?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back:
• Heart failure
  • atrial fibrillation with embolic stroke (from left atrial dilatation)
  • and an increased risk of infective endocarditis (though UK practice is not to give routine antibiotic prophylaxis).
AF in rheumatic mitral stenosis is anticoagulated with warfarin — DOACs are contraindicated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: What is the single most important differential to exclude in a child with fever and a hot, swollen joint after a sore throat?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: Septic arthritis. Acute rheumatic fever arthritis is polyarticular and migratory (it flits to a new joint within days), whereas a septic joint is monoarticular and stays put in a systemically unwell child who will not weight-bear. If in any doubt, aspirate the joint (Gram stain, culture, cell count) and take blood cultures before antibiotics.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: What is post-streptococcal reactive arthritis (PSRA), and how does it differ from acute rheumatic fever?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: An arthritis following streptococcal pharyngitis that does not meet the Jones criteria. Compared with ARF it has a short latency (≤10 days vs 2–4 weeks), is additive and non-migratory rather than flitting, persists for weeks to around 2 months rather than a few days, responds only sluggishly to aspirin/NSAIDs, and lacks carditis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: How is post-streptococcal reactive arthritis managed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back:
• Eradicate the streptococcus
  • NSAIDs first-line (steroids if refractory)
  • and echocardiography in every case.
Because a minority later declare valve disease, secondary penicillin prophylaxis is generally given for around 12 months and then reassessed — if valve disease appears, reclassify as ARF and continue prophylaxis on the usual durations.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: Why should NSAIDs be withheld until the diagnosis of rheumatic fever has been made?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: Aspirin or an NSAID started early abolishes the fever and the migratory pattern of the arthritis — the very features the Jones criteria depend on. Confirm the clinical picture and exclude a septic joint first, then treat.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: Does the absence of a history of rheumatic fever exclude rheumatic heart disease?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: No. A large proportion of people with established rheumatic heart disease have no recalled episode of acute rheumatic fever — the carditis was subclinical or was never labelled. Rheumatic mitral stenosis stays on the differential for a mid-diastolic murmur, new AF or a malar flush, particularly in someone who grew up outside the UK.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.front: How do erythema marginatum and erythema migrans differ?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.back: Erythema marginatum (rheumatic fever) is multiple migrating pink rings with central clearing on the trunk and proximal limbs, sparing the face. Erythema migrans (Lyme disease) is a single expanding bull's-eye lesion at the site of a tick bite. Both diseases can also cause AV block.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the cardiac cycle, and into what two parts is it divided?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: The sequence of mechanical + electrical events in one heartbeat, divided into systole (contraction/ejection) and diastole (relaxation/filling).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the organising principle of the cardiac cycle?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Blood flows down pressure gradients, and valves open/close passively when the pressure either side reverses — every event follows from 'which chamber now has the higher pressure'.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Why does the cardiac cycle matter clinically?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: It explains heart sounds (valve closure), murmurs (valve disease), the JVP waveform, pulse, and the pressure-volume basis of heart failure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Phase 1 — atrial systole: what happens, valve state and pressure logic?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Atria contract → final 'top-up' of filling (the atrial kick, ~20–30%).Valves: mitral open, aortic closed · Pressure logic: atrial P > ventricular P

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Phase 2 — isovolumetric contraction: what happens, valve state and pressure logic?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Ventricle contracts, all valves shut → pressure rises sharply, no volume change.Valves: all closed · Pressure logic: ventricular P rising, not yet > aortic

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Phase 3 — rapid + reduced ejection: what happens, valve state and pressure logic?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Ventricular P exceeds aortic → aortic valve opens → blood ejected.Valves: aortic open, mitral closed · Pressure logic: ventricular P > aortic P

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Phase 4 — isovolumetric relaxation: what happens, valve state and pressure logic?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Ventricle relaxes, all valves shut → pressure falls, no volume change.Valves: all closed · Pressure logic: ventricular P falling, not yet < atrial

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Phase 5 — rapid + reduced filling: what happens, valve state and pressure logic?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Ventricular P falls below atrial → mitral opens → passive filling (most filling).Valves: mitral open, aortic closed · Pressure logic: atrial P > ventricular P

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Which phases make up systole and diastole?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Systole = phases 2-3 (isovolumetric contraction + ejection); diastole = phases 4-5 + atrial systole (relaxation + filling).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Why are the two 'isovolumetric' phases the key concept of the cycle?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: All valves shut, so the ventricle changes pressure without changing volume, bracketing ejection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What causes S1 ('lub') and when does it occur?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Mitral + tricuspid (AV) valve closure; occurs at the start of systole.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What causes S2 ('dub') and when does it occur?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Aortic + pulmonary (semilunar) valve closure; occurs at the end of systole.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What causes S3 and what is its timing and significance?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Rapid ventricular filling hitting a compliant/volume-loaded ventricle; early diastole.Normal in young/athletes but pathological in heart failure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What causes S4 and what is its timing and significance?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle; late diastole.Always pathological (LVH, HTN).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the principle linking heart sounds to valve events and murmur timing?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Sounds = valves closing, not opening; S1 opens systole, S2 closes it — so murmurs are timed relative to S1/S2.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is physiological splitting of S2?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Aortic closes just before pulmonary; the gap widens on inspiration (physiological splitting).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the Wiggers diagram logic?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Atrial, ventricular, and aortic pressure curves overlaid with ventricular volume + the ECG + heart sounds — every valve event is where two pressure curves cross.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does one cardiac cycle appear as a pressure-volume (PV) loop?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Filling (mitral open) → isovolumetric contraction (vertical line up) → ejection (aortic open) → isovolumetric relaxation (vertical line down).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What does the width of the PV loop represent?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Stroke volume = width of the loop (end-diastolic volume − end-systolic volume).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What changes the shape of the PV loop?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Preload, afterload, contractility.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What does the JVP waveform reflect?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: The jugular venous pressure reflects right atrial pressure through the cycle.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What causes the a wave of the JVP, and how does it change in disease?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Atrial contraction; absent in AF, with giant 'cannon' waves in complete heart block.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What causes the c wave of the JVP?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Tricuspid bulging into the atrium during isovolumetric contraction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What causes the x descent of the JVP?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Atrial relaxation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What causes the v wave of the JVP?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Atrial filling against a closed tricuspid.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What causes the y descent of the JVP?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Tricuspid opens → atrial emptying.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What are the clinical links of the JVP waveform abnormalities?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back:
• Absent a waves = AF
  • Cannon a waves = complete heart block
  • Large v waves = tricuspid regurgitation

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How do the ECG waves link to mechanical events in the cycle?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: P wave → atrial systole; QRS → ventricular depolarisation → isovolumetric contraction begins (S1 follows); T wave → ventricular repolarisation → relaxation (S2 around here).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the timing relationship between electrical and mechanical events?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: The electrical event always slightly precedes the mechanical one it triggers.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Why can loss of the atrial kick in AF be clinically significant?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Atrial kick lost in AF → reduced filling → can precipitate failure in a stiff ventricle.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does the timing of a murmur within the cycle help localise valve lesions?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Heart sounds + murmurs: timing within the cycle localises valve lesions (systolic vs diastolic murmurs).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What are the two linked ideas in this topic?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: The conduction system (the wiring that spreads the signal in the right sequence) and the cardiac action potentials (the ionic events in individual cells that are that signal).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the decisive distinction between the two types of cardiac cell?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: There are two types of cardiac cell with two different action potentials — pacemaker cells (SA/AV node — spontaneously fire) and contractile myocytes (atrial/ventricular — fire when triggered).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Why does the conduction system & action potentials topic matter?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: It underpins the ECG, all arrhythmias, heart block, and the Vaughan-Williams antiarrhythmic classes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the role of the SA node?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: The pacemaker (in the right atrium) — fastest intrinsic rate (~100/min, slowed to a resting 60-100/min by vagal tone) → sets heart rate.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the role of the atrial myocardium in conduction?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Spread across the atria → atrial contraction (P wave).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the role of the AV node?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: The only normal electrical connection atria→ventricles; delays the signal (~0.1s) to let atria empty before ventricles contract (the PR interval).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What are the roles of the bundle of His and the left + right bundle branches?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Bundle of His: carries the signal into the interventricular septum. Left + right bundle branches: down either side of the septum.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the role of the Purkinje fibres?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Rapid spread through the ventricular myocardium → coordinated ventricular contraction (QRS).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the pacemaker hierarchy, and what happens if the SA node fails?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: SA node 60-100 > AV node 40-60 > ventricular/Purkinje 20-40 — the fastest sets the pace ('overdrive suppression').If the SA node fails, a slower escape pacemaker takes over — the basis of escape rhythms in heart block.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Why is the AV nodal delay the key functional point?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: It ensures the atria finish contracting before the ventricles start (preserves the atrial kick) and protects the ventricles from very fast atrial rates (AF/flutter).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: In the contractile myocyte (fast-response) AP, what happens in phase 0 and which ion is involved?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Phase 0 — depolarisation: rapid upstroke; Na⁺ IN (fast Na⁺ channels).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: In the contractile myocyte AP, what happens in phase 1 and which ion is involved?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Phase 1 — initial repolarisation: small dip; K⁺ out (transient).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: In the contractile myocyte AP, what happens in phase 2 and which ions are involved?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Phase 2 — plateau: sustained — prolongs the AP, prevents tetany; Ca²⁺ IN balances K⁺ out.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: In the contractile myocyte AP, what happens in phase 3 and which ion is involved?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Phase 3 — repolarisation: return to baseline; K⁺ OUT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: In the contractile myocyte AP, what characterises phase 4 and how is it maintained?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Phase 4 — resting: stable resting potential (~−90 mV); maintained by Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Why is the plateau (phase 2) the key feature of the contractile myocyte AP?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Ca²⁺ influx both sustains the AP and triggers contraction (excitation-contraction coupling); it makes the cardiac AP long (~300 ms) so the muscle can't be tetanised (a fibrillating pump is useless).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: In the pacemaker cell (slow-response) AP, what happens in phase 4 and which current is responsible?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Phase 4 — spontaneous depolarisation (pacemaker potential): slow drift up to threshold → automaticity; 'funny' current (If) = inward Na⁺ via HCN channels (Na⁺/K⁺).Ca²⁺ (T-/L-type) contributes to late phase 4, separate from If.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: In the pacemaker cell AP, what happens in phase 0 and which ion drives it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Phase 0 — depolarisation: upstroke (slower than myocytes); Ca²⁺ IN (not Na⁺ — the key difference).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: In the pacemaker cell AP, what happens in phase 3 and which ion is involved?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Phase 3 — repolarisation: return to baseline; K⁺ OUT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What are the defining features of the pacemaker cell AP?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: No phase 1, 2 or stable resting potential; the upstroke is Ca²⁺-driven, not Na⁺; the slow drift in phase 4 (funny current) creates automaticity.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What does the slope of phase 4 determine in pacemaker cells?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: The slope of phase 4 sets the heart rate — steeper → threshold sooner → faster rate (the target of autonomic control + drugs).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What are the effects and mechanism of sympathetic input (noradrenaline, β1) on the heart?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Effect: ↑rate (positive chronotropy) + ↑AV conduction + ↑contractility. Mechanism: steepens the phase 4 slope → threshold reached sooner.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What are the effects and mechanism of parasympathetic input (vagus, ACh, M2) on the heart?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Effect: ↓rate + slows AV conduction. Mechanism: flattens the phase 4 slope + hyperpolarises.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Why does the vagus dominate at rest, and what are the drug implications?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: At rest the vagus dominates (intrinsic SA rate ~100; vagal tone holds it ~70).Which is why atropine speeds the heart, β-blockers slow it (block sympathetic phase-4 steepening), and digoxin ↑vagal tone — slows AV conduction, useful in AF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Why does the long plateau give a long absolute refractory period, and what does this achieve?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: The long plateau → a long absolute refractory period: the cell can't be re-excited until repolarised → prevents tetany + summation, and limits how fast the ventricles can be driven.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the arrhythmic significance of the relative refractory period?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: The relative refractory period + abnormal automaticity/re-entry circuits are the substrate for arrhythmias.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does the conduction sequence map onto the ECG waves?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: SA node fires + atrial depolarisation → P wave; AV nodal delay → PR interval; ventricular depolarisation (His-Purkinje) → QRS; ventricular repolarisation → T wave.The conduction sequence and the ECG are the same events viewed differently.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does heart block relate to the conduction sequence and pacemaker hierarchy?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Heart block: AV nodal/His disease → PR prolongation (1st) → dropped beats (2nd) → AV dissociation + escape rhythm (3rd/complete) — directly explained by the conduction sequence + pacemaker hierarchy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How do the Vaughan-Williams antiarrhythmic classes map onto the AP phases?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back:
• I = Na⁺ channel (phase 0)
  • II = β-blockers (phase 4/sympathetic)
  • III = K⁺ channel (phase 3, prolong AP)
  • IV = Ca²⁺ channel (nodal phase 0)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the mechanism of ivabradine, and its advantage?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Ivabradine = funny-current (If) blocker → slows the SA node specifically (phase 4) → rate control without affecting BP/contractility.Traps: It works only in sinus rhythm — it has no effect on the AV node, so it is not an AF rate-control drug (NICE), and it slightly increases the risk of developing AF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does hyperkalaemia alter the action potential, and by what mechanisms?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Two findings, two mechanisms. Raised extracellular K⁺ increases K⁺ conductance, steepening phases 2–3 and accelerating repolarisation → tall tented T. Separately it raises (depolarises) the resting membrane potential in phase 4, inactivating fast Na⁺ channels and slowing the phase-0 upstroke → broad QRS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What does the ECG record, and what is it in relation to conduction?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: The ECG records the summed electrical activity of the heart from the body surface — it's the conduction sequence + action potentials viewed from outside.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the single organising principle of the ECG?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: A wave of depolarisation moving TOWARDS a recording electrode = upward (positive) deflection; moving away = downward.Every ECG feature follows from this plus the fixed conduction sequence.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Why does the ECG matter clinically?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: It is how conduction disease, arrhythmias, ischaemia, and electrolyte/drug effects are detected.This note is the physiological basis (how the trace is generated + what each part represents), not a full interpretation tutorial.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What does the ECG actually measure as waves sweep across the heart?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: The potential difference between electrodes as depolarisation/repolarisation waves sweep across the heart.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the towards/away rule for ECG deflections?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Depolarisation towards an electrode → positive deflection; away → negative; perpendicular → biphasic/flat.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Why can depolarisation and repolarisation both produce upright deflections?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Depolarisation spreads endocardium→epicardium, but repolarisation goes epicardium→endocardium (opposite direction and opposite charge) → the two cancel into same-direction deflections (why the QRS and T wave are both usually upright).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How do the ECG leads view the heart?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: The leads view the heart from different angles (limb leads = vertical/coronal plane; chest leads = horizontal plane) — each 'sees' the same electrical events from its own direction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What electrical event and conduction structure does the P wave represent?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Atrial depolarisation; SA node fires → atria.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What does the PR interval represent, and what does it include?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Start of atrial depolarisation → start of ventricular depolarisation; includes the AV nodal delay.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What electrical event and conduction structure does the QRS complex represent?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Ventricular depolarisation; His → bundle branches → Purkinje.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What does the ST segment represent electrically?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Ventricles fully depolarised (plateau, phase 2).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What electrical event and AP phase does the T wave represent?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Ventricular repolarisation; phase 3.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What does the QT interval represent?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Total ventricular depolarisation + repolarisation — the whole ventricular AP.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Where is atrial repolarisation on the ECG, and why isn't it seen?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Hidden within the QRS — too small to see, masked by the much larger ventricular depolarisation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Why does AV block show as PR changes, and why is the QRS large but the P wave small?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: The PR interval = the AV nodal delay made visible — which is why AV block shows as PR changes. The QRS is large (large ventricular mass); the P wave is small (less atrial muscle).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What are the standard ECG paper speed and calibration?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Standard speed 25 mm/s, calibration 10 mm/mV.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What time durations do the ECG grid squares represent?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back:
• Small square = 0.04 s (1 mm)
  • Large square = 0.2 s (5 mm)
  • 5 large squares = 1 s

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How is heart rate calculated from the ECG?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Rate: 300 ÷ (large squares between R waves) if regular; if irregular, count the QRS complexes on the full 10-second rhythm strip (the standard 12-lead trace) and × 6.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What are the normal ECG intervals (PR, QRS, QTc)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back:
• PR 0.12-0.20 s (3-5 small squares)
  • QRS <0.12 s (<3 small squares)
  • QTc up to ~0.44 s in men and ~0.46 s in women (Bazett)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the cardiac axis, and what is its normal range?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: The overall direction of the ventricular depolarisation wave (normally down-and-left, ~−30° to +90°, because the large LV dominates).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What causes left and right axis deviation, and how is axis detected?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Left axis deviation (LVH, conduction blocks) and right axis deviation (RVH, PE) shift it — detected by which leads are positive/negative (the towards/away rule applied across leads).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the physiological basis of PR prolongation / dropped beats?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: AV nodal/His conduction delay or block (heart block).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the physiological basis of a broad QRS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Slow/abnormal ventricular spread (bundle branch block, ventricular origin, hyperkalaemia).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the physiological basis of ST elevation/depression?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Injury current from ischaemia/infarction — depolarised vs injured myocardium differ in charge.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the physiological basis of T wave changes?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Repolarisation abnormalities — ischaemia, hyperkalaemia (tall tented T).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the physiological basis and risk of a long QT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Prolonged repolarisation → risk of torsades (drugs, electrolytes, congenital).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the physiological basis of absent P waves + an irregular rhythm?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Atrial fibrillation — no organised atrial depolarisation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the physiological basis of no P-QRS relationship?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Complete (3rd degree) heart block — AV dissociation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What are the ECG electrolyte links (hyperkalaemia, hypokalaemia)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Hyperkalaemia → tall tented T → broad QRS → sinusoidal; hypokalaemia → U waves.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What are the ECG electrolyte links for calcium (hypocalcaemia, hypercalcaemia)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Hypocalcaemia → long QT; hypercalcaemia → short QT (Ca²⁺ governs the plateau).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What four categories of information is the ECG the bedside readout of?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back:
• Rate + rhythm (arrhythmias)
  • Conduction (heart block, BBB)
  • Ischaemia (ST/T — ACS)
  • Electrolyte/drug effects (K⁺, Ca²⁺, QT-prolonging drugs)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the unifying idea for interpreting any abnormal ECG?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Every abnormal ECG is either an abnormal rhythm (where the impulse starts), an abnormal conduction (how it spreads), or an abnormal myocardium (ischaemia/electrolyte/structural changing the AP).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is Starling's law (the Frank-Starling mechanism)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: The more the ventricle is filled (stretched) in diastole, the more forcefully it contracts — so stroke volume rises as end-diastolic volume rises, within limits.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What are the three factors governing stroke volume, and which one does Starling's law specifically concern?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Stroke volume is governed by three factors: preload, afterload, and contractility. Starling's law is specifically about preload.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Why does Starling's law / stroke volume matter clinically?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: It is the physiological engine behind heart failure, shock, valve disease, and the response to fluids/inotropes/vasodilators.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the principle chain of the Frank-Starling mechanism?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ↑venous return → ↑end-diastolic volume (EDV) → ↑stretch of cardiac muscle fibres → more forceful contraction → ↑stroke volume.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the cellular basis of the Frank-Starling mechanism?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Stretching the sarcomere to its optimal length increases the overlap + sensitivity of actin-myosin filaments to calcium → stronger contraction (the length-tension relationship).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the functional purpose of the Frank-Starling mechanism?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: It matches output to input automatically — if more blood returns, the heart pumps more out beat-to-beat, without nervous control.It also balances the two ventricles: if the right pumps more, the left receives more and matches it.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is plotted on the Starling curve, and what is its overall shape?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Stroke volume (or cardiac output) vs preload (EDV / filling pressure) → a curve that rises, then plateaus, and eventually falls.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What do the rising portion and the plateau/descending portion of the Starling curve represent?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Rising portion: more filling → more output (the normal operating range). Plateau/descending portion: beyond optimal stretch the fibres are overstretched → contraction weakens — the decompensated heart failure zone.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What shifts the Starling curve up + left, and what does this mean?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ↑contractility (sympathetic, inotropes); meaning: more SV for the same preload.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What shifts the Starling curve down + right, and what does this mean?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ↓contractility (heart failure, ischaemia, β-blockers); meaning: less SV for the same preload — needs higher filling pressures for any given output.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Why is the failing heart 'preload-dependent' and prone to congestion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: It operates on a depressed curve, needing high filling pressures → which back up into the lungs (pulmonary oedema).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is preload — its definition, what increases it, and its effect on SV?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Definition: the stretch/filling at end-diastole (EDV) — the Starling factor. Increased by: ↑venous return (fluids, lying down, exercise), bradycardia. Effect: ↑SV (up the curve).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is afterload — its definition, what increases it, and its effect on SV?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Definition: the resistance the ventricle pumps against (arterial BP/SVR; aortic valve). Increased by: hypertension, aortic stenosis, vasoconstriction. Effect: ↓SV (harder to eject).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is contractility (inotropy) — its definition, what increases it, and its effect on SV?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Definition: the intrinsic force of contraction, independent of preload/afterload. Increased by: sympathetic/adrenaline, inotropes (digoxin, dobutamine), Ca²⁺. Effect: ↑SV (curve up-left).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What are the determinants of preload, and how is it estimated?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Venous return, blood volume, atrial kick, venous tone, posture; estimated by CVP / JVP / EDV.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the afterload key point regarding hypertrophy and heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ↑afterload → harder ejection → ventricle compensates with hypertrophy (LVH).A failing ventricle is very afterload-sensitive — why vasodilators/afterload reduction help heart failure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does contractility relate to the Starling curve, and what raises or lowers it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Contractility = the steepness of the Starling curve; raised by sympathetic/inotropes, lowered by ischaemia/failure/β-blockers.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What are the formulae linking stroke volume and cardiac output?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: SV = EDV − ESV; CO = SV × heart rate.So CO is governed by the three SV determinants plus heart rate.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is ejection fraction (EF), its normal range, and what do reduced/preserved EF signify?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: EF = SV / EDV (normally ~55-70%) — the clinical marker of contractility; reduced EF = systolic heart failure (HFrEF); preserved EF with poor filling = HFpEF (diastolic).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does Starling/SV physiology explain heart failure and its treatment?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Depressed/shifted-right curve → needs high filling pressure → congestion; treat by ↓preload (diuretics), ↓afterload (ACEi/vasodilators), ± inotropes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does fluid resuscitation in shock work in Starling terms, and when does it help?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: A bolus ↑preload → ↑SV (climbing the curve) — only if on the rising part ('fluid-responsive').

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does aortic stenosis fit the Starling/SV framework?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Fixed ↑afterload → LVH → eventually failure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How do inotropes (dobutamine, digoxin) act in Starling terms?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ↑contractility → shift the curve up-left.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How do ACEi/vasodilators help in heart failure in Starling terms?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ↓afterload → easier ejection → ↑SV in the afterload-sensitive failing heart.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does atrial fibrillation affect stroke volume / cardiac output in Starling terms?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Loss of the atrial kick → ↓preload → can drop CO in a stiff ventricle.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does Starling's law explain the progression from left-sided to right-sided heart strain?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Starling balances the ventricles: left-sided failure → blood backs up → right-sided strain.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is cardiac output (CO)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: The volume of blood the heart pumps per minute — the central measure of how well the heart meets the body's demands.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the master equation for cardiac output?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: CO = Stroke Volume × Heart Rate — everything that changes CO works through one of these two terms.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does cardiac output relate to blood pressure, and where does CO matter clinically?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: CO feeds into blood pressure (BP = CO × SVR). CO is what fails in heart failure and shock, and adapts in exercise, pregnancy, and sepsis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What are the typical resting values for SV, HR and CO?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: SV ≈ 70 mL, HR ≈ 70 bpm → CO ≈ 5 L/min (roughly the whole blood volume per minute).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the cardiac index, and why is it used?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Cardiac index = CO / body surface area — normalises for body size, the clinical measure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What governs the two levers of cardiac output, and where is each covered?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Stroke volume: governed by preload, afterload, contractility (Starling note). Heart rate: governed by autonomic tone (SA node phase-4 slope) (conduction/AP note).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Recap: how do preload, afterload and contractility affect stroke volume?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Preload (↑filling → ↑SV, Frank-Starling), afterload (↑resistance → ↓SV), contractility (↑intrinsic force → ↑SV).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is ejection fraction (EF), its normal range, and what does a reduced EF indicate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: EF = SV/EDV (~55-70%) = the clinical index of the SV side; reduced EF = systolic heart failure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What sets heart rate, and how is it modulated?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: HR is set by the SA node, modulated by autonomic tone (sympathetic ↑, vagus ↓ — the phase-4 slope).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the crucial nuance about the relationship between heart rate and cardiac output?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: HR and CO are not simply linear: ↑HR usually ↑CO, but at very high rates (fast AF, SVT) diastole shortens → less filling time → ↓EDV → ↓SV → CO can actually fall.There's an optimal heart rate; beyond it, lost filling time outweighs the rate increase — why very fast tachyarrhythmias drop CO and cause syncope/shock.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does the autonomic nervous system regulate cardiac output?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Sympathetic → ↑HR + ↑contractility + venoconstriction (↑venous return) → ↑CO; parasympathetic → ↓HR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does the Frank-Starling mechanism contribute to CO regulation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ↑venous return → ↑preload → ↑SV (auto-matching).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How do hormones regulate cardiac output?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Adrenaline (↑HR/contractility); RAAS (↑volume → ↑preload, longer-term).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Why is venous return the often-forgotten driver of cardiac output?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: CO cannot exceed what returns to the heart — venous return and CO are interdependent (the heart only pumps out what it receives; Starling ensures it matches).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does cardiac output change in exercise, and by what mechanism?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ↑↑ (~4-5× to 20-25 L/min untrained; up to 35-40 L/min, 7-8×, in a trained endurance athlete); ↑HR + ↑SV (↑contractility + ↑venous return via muscle pump); SVR falls (muscle vasodilation) so BP rises modestly.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does cardiac output change in pregnancy, and by what mechanism?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ↑ (~30-50%); ↑SV + ↑HR + ↑blood volume; SVR falls.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does cardiac output change in early sepsis, and by what mechanism?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ↑ (high-output); ↓SVR (vasodilation) → reflex ↑HR/CO ('warm shock').

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does cardiac output change on standing, and by what mechanism?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Transient ↓; gravity → ↓venous return → ↓preload → baroreflex compensates.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Why is exercise the key example of CO adaptation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: All levers together: ↑HR, ↑contractility, ↑venous return, with the muscle + respiratory pumps boosting preload.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the Fick principle for measuring cardiac output?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: CO = O₂ consumption / arteriovenous O₂ difference — the classic method.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does cardiac output explain heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Can't generate adequate CO for demand → fatigue, poor perfusion + congestion; low CO → RAAS activation → fluid retention.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does cardiac output define shock?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Inadequate CO and/or perfusion: ↓CO (cardiogenic — pump; hypovolaemic — ↓preload) or ↓SVR with maldistribution (septic/distributive).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How do bradyarrhythmias reduce cardiac output?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Very low HR → ↓CO despite ↑SV compensation → syncope.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How do inotropes (dobutamine) raise cardiac output in cardiogenic shock?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ↑contractility → ↑SV → ↑CO in cardiogenic shock.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What limits exercise tolerance in relation to cardiac output?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Exercise tolerance is limited by the heart's ability to ↑CO (cardiac reserve).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does cardiac output feed into blood pressure, and what do low CO/perfusion and inadequate CO signify?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: BP = CO × SVR; low CO/perfusion = shock; inadequate CO for demand = heart failure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Why is blood pressure tightly regulated, and by what two timescales of mechanism?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: BP must be high enough to perfuse organs but not so high it causes damage — so it's tightly regulated by short-term (seconds-minutes, neural) and long-term (hours-days, hormonal/renal) mechanisms.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the master equation for blood pressure, and what does it imply for regulation and drugs?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: BP = Cardiac Output × Systemic Vascular Resistance.Every regulatory mechanism — and every antihypertensive drug — works by adjusting one or both.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does the master equation expand, and what sets SVR?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: BP = CO × SVR, where CO = SV × HR and SVR is set mainly by arteriolar tone (the 'resistance vessels').

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What raises heart rate/contractility, and which drug class targets it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ↑ by sympathetic; targeted by β-blockers.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What raises vascular resistance (SVR), and which drug classes target it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ↑ by vasoconstriction (sympathetic, angiotensin II); targeted by CCBs, α-blockers, ACEi/ARB.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What raises blood volume (→ preload → CO), and which drug classes target it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ↑ by Na⁺/water retention (RAAS, aldosterone); targeted by diuretics, ACEi/ARB.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What are the sensors of the baroreceptor reflex, and where do they report?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Baroreceptors (stretch receptors) in the carotid sinus and aortic arch detect arterial stretch (= pressure), reporting to the medulla (vasomotor centre).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does the baroreceptor reflex respond to a rise in BP?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ↑BP → ↑baroreceptor firing → ↑parasympathetic + ↓sympathetic → ↓HR, ↓contractility, vasodilation → BP falls back.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does the baroreceptor reflex respond to a fall in BP (standing, haemorrhage)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ↓BP → ↓firing → ↑sympathetic + ↓parasympathetic → ↑HR, ↑contractility, vasoconstriction → BP restored.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What are the key features of the baroreceptor reflex, including its failure and the role of chemoreceptors?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Fast (seconds), buffers moment-to-moment changes — most importantly on standing (prevents the gravity BP drop; failure → orthostatic hypotension).Chemoreceptors (carotid/aortic bodies) also contribute, responding to ↓O₂/↑CO₂/↓pH with sympathetic activation — mainly in severe hypoxia/ischaemia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What does the RAAS control, over what timescale, and which organ is the long-term BP controller?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system controls BP over hours-days by adjusting blood volume + vascular tone — the kidney is the long-term BP controller.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What triggers renin release in the RAAS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ↓renal perfusion / ↓BP / ↓Na⁺ / ↑sympathetic → juxtaglomerular cells release renin.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What does renin do, and what does ACE do, in the RAAS cascade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Renin converts angiotensinogen (liver) → angiotensin I. ACE (lungs) converts angiotensin I → angiotensin II.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What does aldosterone (adrenal cortex) do in the RAAS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ↑Na⁺ + water reabsorption (distal nephron) → ↑blood volume.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What are the four ways angiotensin II raises BP?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back:
• Vasoconstriction (↑SVR)
  • ↑aldosterone → Na⁺/water retention → ↑volume
  • ↑ADH + thirst
  • Direct renal Na⁺ reabsorption + efferent arteriolar constriction — maintains GFR, the ACEi-creatinine link

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How do the main RAAS drugs act?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ACE inhibitors (block AT-I→AT-II), ARBs (block the AT-II receptor), aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the effect of ADH (vasopressin) on BP?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ↑water reabsorption (volume) + vasoconstriction at high levels.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What are ANP/BNP, when are they released, and what is their effect on BP?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Released when atria/ventricles are stretched (volume overload) → natriuresis + vasodilation → ↓BP (the counter-regulator; BNP = HF marker).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Why are ANP/BNP described as the natural opposite of RAAS, and what is the clinical application?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: They dump salt and water and vasodilate; BNP rises in heart failure (stretched ventricle) → the basis of the BNP blood test.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the effect of adrenaline on BP?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Sympathetic — ↑HR/contractility/vasoconstriction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is organ-level autoregulation, and when does it fail?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Individual organs (brain, kidney, heart) maintain constant blood flow despite changing BP by adjusting their own arteriolar tone (myogenic + metabolic) — protects vital organs across a range of pressures.overwhelmed at extremes — hypertensive emergency, severe hypotension.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How is hypertension explained in BP-regulation terms?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Chronically ↑CO and/or ↑SVR; most 'essential' HTN involves ↑SVR ± RAAS; drugs target each lever.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does antihypertensive choice map onto BP = CO × SVR?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ACEi/ARB (RAAS/volume + SVR), CCB (SVR), diuretic (volume), β-blocker (CO).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What causes orthostatic hypotension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Failed baroreceptor reflex on standing (elderly, autonomic neuropathy, drugs).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How is shock explained in BP-regulation terms?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ↓BP from ↓CO (cardiogenic/hypovolaemic) or ↓SVR (distributive/septic); compensatory sympathetic + RAAS → tachycardia + oliguria.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the physiological response to haemorrhage?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ↓BP → baroreceptor reflex (immediate tachycardia/vasoconstriction) + RAAS (volume retention).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does renal artery stenosis cause secondary hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ↓renal perfusion → inappropriate RAAS activation → secondary hypertension.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does BP regulation explain heart failure treatment?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Low CO → RAAS activation → fluid retention (worsens congestion) → why ACEi + diuretics are core treatment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the vascular system, and what determines how blood flows through it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: The circuit the heart pumps into — its properties (resistance, compliance, capacitance) determine how blood flows and where pressure is generated/lost.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the organising principle of blood flow, and the specialised job of each vessel?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Blood flow is governed by flow = pressure gradient ÷ resistance (the haemodynamic Ohm's law), and each vessel has a specialised job — arterioles set resistance, capillaries exchange, veins store volume.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Why does the vascular system matter (what does it explain)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: It explains the SVR term in BP = CO × SVR, plus oedema, atherosclerosis distribution, varicose veins, shock, and vasodilators/vasoconstrictors.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the role and key property of elastic arteries?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Role: conduct blood at high pressure; aortic elastic recoil sustains diastolic flow (Windkessel effect). Key property: high pressure, elastic.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the role and key property of arterioles?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Role: the resistance vessels — adjust radius to control flow + BP. Key property: set SVR; heavily smooth-muscle-walled.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the role and key property of capillaries?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Role: exchange of gases/nutrients/waste. Key property: thin (one cell), huge surface area, slow flow.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the role and key property of veins?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Role: return blood; the capacitance vessels — hold ~65–70% of blood volume. Key property: low pressure, distensible, valves.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Which two vessel types are functionally the most important, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Arterioles (resistance/BP — the biggest pressure drop) and veins (volume reservoir — venoconstriction shifts blood back → ↑preload).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the master haemodynamic equation relating flow, pressure and resistance?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Flow (Q) = ΔP / R (pressure gradient ÷ resistance).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What does Poiseuille's law say about resistance and radius?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Resistance depends overwhelmingly on radius: R ∝ 1 / r⁴. So halving the radius increases resistance 16-fold — tiny changes in arteriolar calibre produce huge changes in flow/BP.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Why do arterioles control everything, per the r⁴ relationship?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: A small amount of smooth-muscle constriction dramatically raises resistance — the physical basis of all vasoconstrictor/vasodilator effects (and why arterioles, not capillaries, are the control point).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What other factors raise resistance besides radius?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Resistance also rises with blood viscosity (e.g. polycythaemia) and vessel length (fixed).But radius dominates.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does pressure vary across the circulation (arteries, arterioles, capillaries/veins)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: High + pulsatile in arteries (systolic/diastolic); the steepest drop is across the arterioles (highest resistance) → this dampens the pulsatility; low + steady in capillaries (protects the fragile exchange vessels) and veins.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is mean arterial pressure (MAP), and how is it calculated?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: The average arterial pressure driving organ perfusion: MAP ≈ diastolic + ⅓(pulse pressure), or MAP = CO × SVR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is pulse pressure, and what widens or narrows it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Pulse pressure = systolic − diastolic; widened in stiff arteries (age, atherosclerosis, aortic regurgitation), narrowed in low-SV states (shock, aortic stenosis).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What governs fluid movement across the capillary wall?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: The balance of Starling forces.Note: different from the cardiac 'Starling'.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the direction and effect of capillary hydrostatic pressure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Pushes fluid OUT → filtration (dominant at the arteriolar end).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the direction and effect of plasma oncotic pressure (albumin)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Pulls fluid IN, opposing filtration.In the classic model this gives reabsorption at the venular end; the revised (glycocalyx) model shows slight filtration continues along the whole capillary, with the filtrate returned as lymph.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the net result of the Starling forces across the capillary?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Slight net filtration out → returned by the lymphatics.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Which oedema cause is due to ↑hydrostatic pressure, and what are its examples?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ↑hydrostatic pressure: heart failure (venous congestion), venous obstruction, fluid overload.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Which oedema cause is due to ↓oncotic pressure, and what are its examples?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ↓oncotic pressure: hypoalbuminaemia — nephrotic syndrome, liver failure, malnutrition.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Which oedema cause is due to ↑capillary permeability, and what are its examples?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ↑capillary permeability: inflammation, sepsis, burns.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Which oedema cause is due to lymphatic obstruction, and what are its examples?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Lymphatic obstruction: lymphoedema (filariasis, post-surgery/radiotherapy).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What do the veins hold, and what does venous return depend on?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Veins hold most of the blood volume (capacitance) at low pressure; venous return depends on the skeletal muscle pump, the respiratory pump, venous tone, and gravity/posture.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does the skeletal muscle pump aid venous return?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Leg muscle contraction squeezes veins; one-way valves ensure flow toward the heart.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does the respiratory pump aid venous return?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Inspiration drops intrathoracic pressure → sucks blood back.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How do venous tone and gravity/posture affect venous return?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Venous tone: sympathetic venoconstriction → ↑return → ↑preload. Gravity/posture: standing pools blood in the legs → ↓return.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What are the clinical links of venous physiology (valves, stasis, venoconstriction)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back:
• Valve failure → varicose veins
  • Immobility + venous stasis → DVT (Virchow's triad)
  • Venoconstriction defends preload in shock

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Which organs autoregulate, and by what mechanism?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Some organs autoregulate (constant flow despite changing BP) — brain, kidney, heart — via myogenic + metabolic control of arteriolar tone.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How is hypertension explained haemodynamically?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Chronically ↑SVR (arteriolar) — the r⁴ point; treated with vasodilators (CCB, ACEi/ARB, α-blockers).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How is oedema summarised haemodynamically?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Imbalance of capillary Starling forces (↑hydrostatic / ↓oncotic / ↑permeability / lymphatic block).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How is shock explained haemodynamically, and how is distributive/septic shock treated?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ↓MAP from ↓SVR (distributive/septic — vasodilation) or ↓CO; vasopressors (noradrenaline) ↑SVR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Why does atherosclerosis occur at particular sites?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: At sites of turbulent flow (bifurcations, bends) where endothelial shear stress is disturbed.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What causes a widened pulse pressure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Arterial stiffening (age, atherosclerosis), aortic regurgitation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How do vasodilators/vasoconstrictors exert their effect?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: They act on arteriolar radius (r⁴ → big effect on SVR/BP).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What does the coronary circulation supply, and why is it clinically important?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: It supplies the myocardium itself — and has unique features that make the heart especially vulnerable to ischaemia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What are the two defining peculiarities of the coronary circulation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: (1) The heart extracts most of the oxygen (~70–80%) from coronary blood at rest, so it meets increased demand mainly by increasing flow, not extraction; and (2) the LV is perfused during diastole, not systole (it squeezes its own vessels shut when it contracts).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Why does coronary circulation physiology matter?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: It is the direct physiological basis of angina, MI, and the anti-anginal drugs.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What does the left coronary → LAD supply, and what infarct territory does it correspond to?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Supplies the anterior LV + septum; infarct territory is anterior MI (V1-V4).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What does the left coronary → circumflex supply, and what infarct territory does it correspond to?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Supplies the lateral LV wall (the posterior wall is usually RCA/PDA in right-dominant hearts, ~80%); infarct territory is lateral MI (I, aVL, V5-V6).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What does the right coronary artery (RCA) supply, and what infarct territory does it correspond to?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Supplies the RV, inferior LV, and SA + AV nodes (in most people); infarct territory is inferior MI (II, III, aVF), plus bradycardia/heart block.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Why does an inferior (RCA) MI characteristically cause bradyarrhythmias/heart block?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: The RCA usually supplies the SA and AV nodes → an inferior (RCA) MI characteristically causes bradyarrhythmias/heart block.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Where does coronary filling happen, and what conditions can compromise it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Coronary filling happens at the aortic root → aortic regurgitation/stenosis can compromise coronary perfusion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How much oxygen does the myocardium extract at rest, and how does this compare to most tissues?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: The myocardium extracts ~70-80% of oxygen from coronary blood even at rest (most tissues ~25%).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Because there is little extraction reserve, how must the heart meet increased demand?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: With little extraction reserve, to meet increased demand the heart must increase coronary blood flow.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does the coronary circulation increase flow to meet oxygen demand?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: By metabolic vasodilation — local metabolites, especially adenosine, dilate coronary arterioles when O₂ demand rises (coronary autoregulation / metabolic hyperaemia).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the clinical payoff of high oxygen extraction when a coronary artery is stenosed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: If a coronary artery is stenosed, flow can't rise enough to meet increased demand → demand outstrips supply → angina (pain on exertion, relieved by rest).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Why is the LV perfused mainly during diastole rather than systole?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: During systole, the contracting LV compresses its own intramural vessels → LV coronary flow is squeezed off; so the LV is perfused mainly during diastole (muscle relaxes, vessels open).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Why is tachycardia dangerous in ischaemia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ↑HR shortens diastole disproportionately → less coronary filling time and ↑O₂ demand (a double hit — why β-blockers help angina).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the coronary perfusion pressure equation, and what does it imply?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Coronary perfusion pressure = aortic diastolic − LV end-diastolic pressure → adequate diastolic BP matters.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Which region of the myocardium is most vulnerable to ischaemia, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: The subendocardium (innermost LV) is most vulnerable to ischaemia (furthest from epicardial vessels, highest wall stress) — first to infarct.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the unifying framework for myocardial ischaemia, and how do anti-anginal drugs work?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Ischaemia = demand exceeding supply — every anti-anginal drug works by tipping this balance.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What are the determinants of myocardial oxygen supply, and how can supply be improved?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Determinants: coronary flow (patency, diastolic time, perfusion pressure), O₂ content. Improve it with: nitrates (vasodilate), revascularisation (PCI/CABG), treat anaemia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What are the determinants of myocardial oxygen demand, and which drugs reduce it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Determinants: heart rate, contractility, afterload (wall tension), preload. Reduce it with: β-blockers (↓HR/contractility), CCB (↓afterload/HR), nitrates (↓preload).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the anti-anginal logic of β-blockers, nitrates and CCBs?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: β-blockers ↓HR (↓demand + ↑diastolic filling); nitrates ↓preload + dilate coronaries (↓demand + ↑supply); CCBs ↓afterload/HR — all tip the supply-demand balance back.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the mechanism of stable angina?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Fixed stenosis → demand-led ischaemia (exertion) → reversible, relieved by rest/GTN.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the mechanism of acute coronary syndrome, and its two outcomes?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Plaque rupture → thrombus → acute supply failure → unstable angina/NSTEMI (partial) or STEMI (complete occlusion → transmural infarct).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is collateral circulation, and why is acute occlusion so damaging?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Gradual stenosis can stimulate collaterals (partial protection); sudden occlusion gives no time for this → why acute occlusion is so damaging.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Why do β-blockers help angina (coronary-physiology explanation)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: ↓HR → ↓demand and longer diastole → ↑coronary filling.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How does GTN work in angina (coronary-physiology explanation)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Venodilation ↓preload (↓demand) + coronary dilation (↑supply).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: How can aortic stenosis cause angina even without coronary disease?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: (Even without coronary disease) ↑LV demand (hypertrophy) + ↓coronary perfusion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the difference between stable angina and ACS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Stable angina (fixed stenosis, exertional) vs ACS (plaque rupture → acute occlusion).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: At a resting rate of about 75/min, how long do systole and diastole each last?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: The whole cycle takes about 0.8 s: systole about 0.3 s and diastole about 0.5 s.At rest the heart therefore spends more time filling than it does ejecting.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: When the heart rate rises, which part of the cardiac cycle is sacrificed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Diastole. Systole is relatively fixed, so as the rate climbs it is the filling time that shortens - and it shortens far more than systole does.This single asymmetry is why a very fast heart fills poorly and drops its output, and why tachycardia starves the heart of its own coronary supply (the left ventricle is perfused in diastole).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: The plateau (phase 2) lets calcium into the myocyte. How does that calcium actually produce a contraction?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: The calcium entering from outside the cell triggers the cell's internal calcium store to release a much larger amount - calcium-induced calcium release. That calcium binds troponin, which shifts tropomyosin off the actin binding sites, letting myosin heads bind and pull. The result is systole.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What is the key difference between excitation-contraction coupling in cardiac and skeletal muscle?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Cardiac muscle depends on calcium arriving from OUTSIDE the cell to trigger release from the internal store. Skeletal muscle does not - its internal store releases calcium in response to the electrical signal alone.This is why cardiac contraction is sensitive to drugs that block calcium entry.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Why are verapamil and diltiazem negatively inotropic while amlodipine is not?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Cardiac contraction depends on calcium entering the cell, so blocking those channels in the myocardium weakens contraction. Verapamil and diltiazem act on the heart; the dihydropyridines such as amlodipine act mainly on blood vessels, so they lower blood pressure without the same effect on contractility.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Why is relaxation of cardiac muscle an active process, and what follows clinically?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Calcium has to be pumped back into its store and out of the cell against its concentration gradient, which costs ATP. So relaxation requires energy just as contraction does.In an ischaemic, ATP-starved myocardium the heart therefore struggles to RELAX before it struggles to contract - which is why diastolic dysfunction appears early in ischaemia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: What determines the stress carried by each part of the ventricular wall?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: It rises with the pressure inside the chamber and with the radius of the chamber, and it falls as the wall gets thicker.So a small, thick-walled ventricle at low pressure has low wall stress; a big, thin-walled ventricle at high pressure has high wall stress.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Why does the ventricle respond to chronic pressure overload by hypertrophying?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Because thickening the wall shares the load: with more muscle, each fibre carries less stress at the same chamber pressure.Hypertrophy is therefore a sensible short-term answer to hypertension or aortic stenosis - although it eventually stiffens the ventricle and outgrows its own blood supply.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.front: Why is a dilated failing ventricle mechanically inefficient?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.back: Because wall stress rises with chamber radius. A large, dilated chamber has to generate more wall stress to produce the same blood pressure, so it works harder to achieve less - and the dilatation feeds back on itself.It also explains why reducing afterload helps twice over: it lowers the pressure the ventricle pushes against AND lets the chamber empty more completely, shrinking the radius.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Why does rhythm classification matter so much in cardiac arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Rhythm classification determines the entire management pathway: shocking a non-shockable rhythm wastes time, while delaying adrenaline in a non-shockable rhythm loses the only treatment that works.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What are the two SHOCKABLE arrest rhythms?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Ventricular fibrillation (VF) and pulseless VT (pVT).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What are the two NON-SHOCKABLE arrest rhythms?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Pulseless electrical activity (PEA) and asystole.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Describe ventricular fibrillation (VF) and its ECG appearance.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Chaotic, disorganised electrical activity — the ventricles quiver with no coordinated contraction. The ECG shows erratic fibrillatory waveforms with no discernible QRS complexes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is pulseless VT (pVT)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Organised ventricular tachycardia (wide QRS, rate >100) but with no palpable pulse — it is too fast for effective cardiac output.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Why does defibrillation work in VF/pVT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: A single high-energy shock simultaneously depolarises the entire myocardium → brief asystole → the intrinsic pacemakers can then restart a coordinated rhythm.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is pulseless electrical activity (PEA)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Organised electrical activity on the monitor (it looks like a rhythm) but with no palpable pulse — the electrical system is intact but mechanical function has failed. It is almost always caused by a reversible 4H/4T.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is the defining feature of PEA on the monitor?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: It can look like any organised rhythm — the defining feature is the absence of a palpable pulse.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is asystole, and what determines its outcome?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: A flat line — no electrical activity. It is terminal unless an underlying cause is identified and reversed rapidly.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Why is defibrillation ineffective in PEA and asystole?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: There is no disorganised electrical activity to 'reset.' Defibrillating PEA or asystole does not help and wastes critical time.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is the first intervention for a shockable rhythm vs a non-shockable rhythm?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Shockable: 1 shock → CPR for 2 minutes. Non-shockable: CPR for 2 minutes + adrenaline as soon as possible.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is the main outcome driver in shockable vs non-shockable arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Shockable: early defibrillation. Non-shockable: finding and fixing the reversible cause.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is the monitored arrest exception to the standard ALS sequence?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: If the arrest is witnessed in a monitored environment (CCU, cath lab, ICU, or immediately after cardiac surgery) and a defibrillator is immediately available, give up to three quick stacked shocks first, then begin the standard ALS cycle. Those count as the FIRST shock of the algorithm — so adrenaline and amiodarone are still given after the third shock, which is two further shocks after the stacked set, not immediately after it (Resus Council UK).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What are the initial steps of the ALS algorithm before assessing the rhythm?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Confirm unresponsive + not breathing normally → call the resuscitation team / ambulance → start CPR 30:2 and attach the defibrillator/monitor → assess the rhythm.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What compression-to-ventilation ratio is used in CPR before the airway is secured?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: 30:2.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: In the shockable arm, what is the shock energy and why must it NOT be synchronised?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: 1 shock, unsynchronised, at least 150 J biphasic (or the manufacturer’s recommended setting). It must not be synchronised because there is no R wave to lock onto in VF/pVT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: After delivering a shock in VF/pVT, what is done immediately?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Immediately resume CPR for 2 minutes — do NOT pause to check the pulse after the shock.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: In the shockable arm, when are adrenaline and amiodarone first given?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: After the 3rd shock: adrenaline 1 mg IV (once compressions are restarted) and amiodarone 300 mg IV bolus.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How often is adrenaline repeated in the shockable arm after the first dose?
