conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: 1 mg every 3–5 minutes (every alternate cycle).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: When is the second dose of amiodarone given in the shockable arm, and what dose?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: After the 5th shock: amiodarone 150 mg IV.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: In the non-shockable arm, what is done immediately after identifying PEA/asystole?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Immediately resume CPR for 2 minutes and give adrenaline 1 mg IV as soon as IV/IO access is obtained — do not delay.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How does the timing of the first adrenaline dose differ between shockable and non-shockable arrests?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Shockable: adrenaline after the 3rd shock. Non-shockable: adrenaline immediately, as soon as IV/IO access is obtained.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How often is adrenaline repeated in the non-shockable arm?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: 1 mg every 3–5 minutes (every other cycle).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What are the two things NOT done in the non-shockable arm, and what replaces them as the priority?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: No defibrillation and no amiodarone. The priority instead is to identify and treat the reversible causes (the 4Hs and 4Ts).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How often is the rhythm reassessed during an ALS cycle, regardless of arm?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Every 2 minutes — both arms loop back to the rhythm check every 2 minutes until ROSC or a decision to stop.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Summarise the adrenaline 1 mg timing in shockable vs non-shockable arrest.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Shockable (VF/pVT): after the 3rd shock, then every 3–5 min. Non-shockable (PEA/asystole): immediately, then every 3–5 min.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Summarise the amiodarone timing across shockable and non-shockable arrest.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Shockable: 300 mg after the 3rd shock and 150 mg after the 5th shock. Non-shockable: never given. Lidocaine 100 mg IV (then a further 50 mg after 5 shocks) is an accepted alternative if amiodarone is unavailable or local policy uses it (Resus Council UK).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: When should a thrombolytic be considered in cardiac arrest, and what does this change about CPR duration?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Consider a thrombolytic if PE is suspected — and if given, continue CPR for 60–90 minutes after administration.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What are the target depth and rate for high-quality chest compressions?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Depth 5–6 cm (not deeper — risks injury) and rate 100–120/min (faster reduces perfusion).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Why is full chest recoil between compressions important?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Allowing complete chest recoil lets the heart refill — incomplete recoil reduces venous return and perfusion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What are the key quality rules for chest compressions regarding interruptions and compressor fatigue?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back:
• Minimise interruptions (no pause >5 seconds),
  • rotate the compressor every 2 minutes (fatigue rapidly degrades quality),
  • and use a hard flat surface with hands in the centre of the sternum.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Why should the compressor be rotated every 2 minutes?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Fatigue rapidly degrades compression quality (depth and rate), so swapping every 2 minutes maintains effectiveness.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Describe Step 1 of airway progression in CPR.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Basic airway: head tilt–chin lift or jaw thrust, with a two-rescuer 30:2 compression-to-ventilation ratio.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Describe Step 2 of airway progression (supraglottic airway).
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Insert a supraglottic airway (LMA, iGel) without stopping CPR, then attempt ventilation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Once an endotracheal tube is secured, how does ventilation change?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Switch to continuous compressions (no pauses) and ventilate at 10 breaths/min (no ratio). Confirm tube placement immediately.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How is endotracheal tube placement confirmed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back:
• Waveform capnography (the gold standard),
  • 5-point auscultation,
  • and a CXR when the patient is stable.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is the first-line vascular access in CPR, and the key practical points?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: IV first-line: a large-bore peripheral cannula, antecubital fossa preferred, flushing drugs with a 20 mL bolus.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: When is intraosseous (IO) access used, and how does it compare to IV?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: IO is used if IV access fails (proximal humerus, proximal or distal tibia). It is equally effective for all ALS drugs and rapid to insert under CPR conditions.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How does waveform capnography confirm correct ETT placement?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: A CO₂ waveform being present confirms the tube is in the trachea.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What ETCO₂ value suggests adequate chest compressions, and how should the number be read?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: ETCO₂ >2.0 kPa suggests adequate compressions — but read it as a trend across the arrest rather than a pass/fail cut-off. A falling value means deteriorating compression quality; a sudden rise suggests ROSC.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How does waveform capnography flag the return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: A sudden rise in ETCO₂ during CPR suggests ROSC — but do not interrupt compressions; reassess at the next 2-minute rhythm check.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What capnography finding is a poor prognostic marker in cardiac arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: A persistently very low ETCO₂ (<1.3 kPa / ~10 mmHg after 20 minutes of ALS) is a marker of poor prognosis. — used only as one part of a multimodal assessment, never alone.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What can point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) identify during the pulse-check window in cardiac arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back:
• Pericardial effusion/tamponade,
  • cardiac motion (organised vs fine VF),
  • IVC filling,
  • and pneumothorax
— all without interrupting CPR for more than the pulse-check window.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Why are the reversible causes (4Hs & 4Ts) so central to managing a non-shockable arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Non-shockable rhythms are won by finding and fixing the reversible cause — drugs alone will not restart the heart. In shockable rhythms you also search simultaneously, as failure to find the cause leads to re-arrest after ROSC.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: List the 4 Hs and 4 Ts (reversible causes of cardiac arrest).
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back:
• 4 Hs: Hypoxia, Hypovolaemia, Hypo/Hyperkalaemia & metabolic, Hypo-/hyperthermia (temperature extremes).
  • 4 Ts: Thrombosis (coronary or pulmonary), Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade (cardiac), Toxins.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How is HYPOXIA recognised and treated in cardiac arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back:
• Recognise: low SpO₂, cyanosis, poor bag-mask seal, obstructed airway, inadequate ventilation.
  • Treat: ensure the airway is open and patent, high-flow O₂, confirm ETT position, suction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How is HYPOVOLAEMIA recognised and treated in cardiac arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back:
• Recognise: visible haemorrhage, trauma, flat neck veins, haematemesis, AAA.
  • Treat: rapid IV/IO fluids, blood products early, control the haemorrhage source (surgery/IR if needed).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How is hyperkalaemia recognised and treated during cardiac arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back:
• Recognise: known renal failure, peaked T waves / broad QRS / sine wave on ECG.
  • Treat: calcium chloride 10% 10 mL IV to stabilise the myocardium, then insulin–dextrose (10 units soluble insulin in 25 g glucose) to shift K⁺; dialysis for definitive removal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How are hypoglycaemia and hypomagnesaemia treated in the metabolic 'H' of cardiac arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back:
• Hypoglycaemia: 10% glucose IV.
  • Hypomagnesaemia: magnesium.
(Calcium chloride is for hyperkalaemia; sodium bicarbonate for severe acidosis or TCA overdose.)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How is HYPOTHERMIA recognised and treated in cardiac arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back:
• Recognise: cold patient, core temp <30°C, J-waves (Osborn waves) on ECG, drowning/exposure.
  • Treat: warm IV fluids, external warming (warm blankets, warmed humidified O₂), and ECMO for deep hypothermia.
Modified ALS: if core temp <30°C withhold adrenaline and give a maximum of 3 shocks until the temperature is above 30°C; at 30–35°C double the drug intervals (adrenaline every 6–10 min) (Resus Council UK).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What ECG finding is characteristic of hypothermia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: J-waves (Osborn waves).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How is coronary THROMBOSIS recognised and treated as a cause of arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back:
• Recognise: preceding chest pain, STEMI on ECG, known CAD.
  • Treat: high-quality CPR whilst arranging emergency coronary angiography ± PCI (usually post-ROSC).
Fibrinolysis during CPR is for suspected PE — it is not the treatment for coronary thrombosis in arrest.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How is pulmonary THROMBOSIS (PE) recognised and treated as a cause of arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back:
• Recognise: PE risk factors, RBBB pattern, no other cause found, sudden arrest.
  • Treat: thrombolysis (alteplase 50 mg IV) — and continue CPR for 60–90 minutes after; surgical embolectomy if available.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: If a thrombolytic is given for suspected PE in arrest, how long should CPR continue?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: For 60–90 minutes after administration, to allow the thrombolytic time to work.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How is TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX recognised and treated in cardiac arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back:
• Recognise: unequal/absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation (late), traumatic arrest, ventilated patient.
  • Treat: immediate chest decompression — finger (open) thoracostomy is preferred in the ventilated or arrested patient; needle decompression (4th/5th ICS, anterior axillary line) if that is all that is available → definitive chest drain (Resus Council UK).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How is cardiac TAMPONADE recognised and treated in cardiac arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back:
• Recognise: penetrating chest trauma, known pericardial disease, Beck's triad (raised JVP, hypotension, muffled heart sounds), POCUS showing a pericardial effusion.
  • Treat: US-guided pericardiocentesis, or emergency thoracotomy if it is a traumatic arrest.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is Beck's triad, and which reversible cause of arrest does it indicate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Raised JVP, hypotension, and muffled heart sounds — indicating cardiac tamponade.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How are TOXINS recognised as a cause of cardiac arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back:
• Known ingestion/exposure,
  • a brady- or tachyarrhythmia,
  • miosis/mydriasis,
  • and the history.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Match each specific antidote to its toxin in cardiac arrest: organophosphates, opioids, local anaesthetic toxicity, digoxin.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back:
• Organophosphates → atropine;
  • opioids → naloxone;
  • local anaesthetic toxicity → 20% lipid emulsion;
  • digoxin → digoxin-specific antibody fragments.
Activated charcoal has no role during the arrest itself — it is for the peri-arrest poisoned patient, and only if they are alert and within 1 hour of ingestion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: When is UNSYNCHRONISED defibrillation used, and why is no synchronisation possible?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: For VF / pulseless VT. There are no organised R waves to synchronise to, so the device delivers the shock immediately on the button press.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What energy is used for unsynchronised defibrillation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: At least 150 J biphasic for the first shock (or the manufacturer’s recommended setting), escalating for subsequent shocks up to the device maximum. If VF persists after three shocks (refractory VF), check the antero-lateral pads are correctly positioned and consider a vector change to antero-posterior placement; routine dual sequential defibrillation is not recommended in the UK (Resus Council UK).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Where are the defibrillator pads placed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Right infraclavicular + apical pad in the mid-axillary line level with V6, directly below the armpit — or an anterior-posterior configuration. Correct apical placement matters: poor pad position is a leading cause of failed defibrillation (Resus Council UK).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: When is SYNCHRONISED cardioversion used, and how does the device behave?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: For an organised tachyarrhythmia WITH a pulse. The device waits for the R wave, then shocks — avoiding delivery during the vulnerable T-wave period (R-on-T → VF).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Why must a synchronised shock avoid the T-wave?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Delivering a shock during the vulnerable T-wave period (R-on-T) can induce VF, so the device synchronises to the R wave.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What energies are used for synchronised cardioversion in AF vs flutter/SVT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: AF: 120–150 J biphasic. Flutter/SVT: 70–120 J biphasic.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is the defibrillation safety drill?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Continue chest compressions while the defibrillator charges, then: 'Stand clear · Oxygen away (≥1 m from patient) · All clear · Shock' — visually confirm all personnel are clear, then resume compressions immediately. Total interruption under 5 seconds (Resus Council UK).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What are the immediate (minutes) priorities of post-ROSC care?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back:
• ABCDE reassessment,
  • SpO₂ 94–98% (avoid hyperoxia),
  • aim for normocapnia (PaCO₂ 4.5–6.0 kPa),
  • IV fluid if hypotensive with vasopressors if needed,
  • and a 12-lead ECG (STEMI → emergency PCI).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is the oxygen saturation target post-ROSC, and why avoid hyperoxia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: SpO₂ 94–98%. Hyperoxia is harmful (oxidative injury), so 100% oxygen is weaned to this target range.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is the target PaCO₂ post-ROSC?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Normocapnia — PaCO₂ 4.5–6.0 kPa.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What does targeted temperature management involve post-ROSC?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Active temperature control — prevent fever (keep ≤37.5°C) for at least 72 hours in comatose survivors. Routine cooling to 33°C is no longer recommended (TTM2).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What ongoing (ICU) post-ROSC measures are undertaken beyond temperature management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back:
• Identify and treat the cause (4Hs/4Ts, CTPA, echo, coronary angiography),
  • neuroprotection with seizure monitoring and glucose control,
  • and prognostication.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: When should neurological prognostication be performed post-ROSC, and why the delay?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Not before 72 hours — hypothermia (and sedation) delays neurological assessment, so early prognostication is unreliable.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: In what situations should CPR NOT be started?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back:
• A valid DNACPR order in place,
  • injuries incompatible with life,
  • or rigor mortis / dependent lividity present.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What are the criteria for stopping CPR?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: ROSC achieved. Otherwise stopping is a team decision, not a stopwatch: consider stopping when there is no ROSC despite prolonged ALS (commonly beyond 20–30 min of asystole) AND all reversible causes have been excluded or treated, with team-leader consensus. Continue longer if hypothermia, thrombolysis given for PE (60–90 min), toxins, pregnancy, or an ECPR candidate (Resus Council UK).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is the hypothermic arrest exception to stopping CPR?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Continue CPR until the core temperature is >35°C or ECMO is available — 'not dead until warm and dead'.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is the 'adrenaline timing trap' and why is it the most-tested ALS fact?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Non-shockable → give adrenaline immediately. Shockable → give adrenaline only after the 3rd shock (not the 1st). The differing timing is the most commonly tested ALS point.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: In which arrest arm is amiodarone used, and where is it never used?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Amiodarone is ONLY for the shockable arm. Never give it in PEA or asystole — it has no role and no evidence there.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is magnesium 2 g IV specifically indicated for in arrest, and is it routine?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: It is the specific treatment for torsades de pointes (polymorphic VT / long QT). Magnesium is NOT routine in all cardiac arrests.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is the most time-critical post-arrest intervention if the post-ROSC 12-lead ECG shows a STEMI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Emergency PCI — a STEMI after ROSC mandates the most time-critical post-arrest intervention (emergency coronary intervention).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What dose, route and concentration of adrenaline is used in cardiac arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back:
• 1 mg IV or IO = 10 mL of 1:10,000 (the pre-filled syringe).
  • Follow with a 20 mL flush to move the drug centrally during compressions.
  • Repeat every 3–5 minutes (alternate cycles) — immediately in PEA/asystole, after the 3rd shock in VF/pVT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Contrast the adrenaline used in cardiac arrest with the adrenaline used in anaphylaxis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back:
• Cardiac arrest: 1 mg IV/IO, 1:10,000 (10 mL)
  • Anaphylaxis: 0.5 mg IM anterolateral thigh, 1:1000 (0.5 mL)
Same drug — different dose, different route and different concentration. This is the classic confusion pair.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Why must 1:1000 adrenaline never be given intravenously in anaphylaxis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back:
It is ten times more concentrated than the arrest preparation, so an IV bolus delivers a huge dose centrally.
Result: hypertensive crisis, tachyarrhythmia, myocardial ischaemia — a recognised and serious medication error.
IV adrenaline in anaphylaxis is only ever a titrated infusion given by specialists; the ward answer is always 0.5 mg IM.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How does defibrillation pad placement change in a patient with a pacemaker or ICD?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back:
Keep the pads at least 8 cm from the generator, or use an anterior-posterior configuration.
Never place a pad directly over the device box — the shock can be shunted and the device damaged.
Interrogate the device afterwards: a shock can alter programming or damage the leads.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: A patient in cardiac arrest has an ICD that is discharging. Is it safe to continue CPR?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back:
Yes. Continue compressions without interruption.
A rescuer in contact may feel a harmless tingle — the delivered energy is small and confined to the patient.
Never delay or withhold CPR because the device is firing.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Death (necrosis) of body tissue due to failure of blood supply, infection, or both. Classified into dry, wet, gas, and Fournier's types.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is dry gangrene and what causes it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back:
Ischaemic necrosis without infection — occlusion of arterial supply (atherosclerosis, embolism, diabetes). The tissue desiccates and mummifies. Features:
  • black/brown shrivelled tissue,
  • well-demarcated line,
  • minimal pain (nerves infarcted),
  • no systemic upset.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is wet gangrene and what causes it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back:
Ischaemic necrosis + secondary bacterial infection. Features:
  • swollen, blistered, malodorous, moist tissue;
  • poorly demarcated;
  • systemic sepsis (fever, tachycardia).
Diabetics and immunocompromised are at highest risk. Surgical emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: How does dry gangrene differ from wet gangrene clinically?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back:
• Dry: black/mummified, demarcated, no systemic upset.
  • Wet: swollen/malodorous, poorly demarcated, systemic sepsis.
Wet is the surgical emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What organism causes gas gangrene, and what is its key feature?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Clostridium perfringens (Gram-positive anaerobe). Key feature: gas in tissues → crepitus on palpation / gas bubbles on XR. Rapidly progressive, life-threatening.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is the mechanism of tissue destruction in gas gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: C. perfringens produces alpha-toxin (lecithinase) → destroys cell membranes → rapid tissue necrosis + gas production (CO₂ + H₂) → crepitus.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What are the clinical features of gas gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back:
• Rapid-onset severe pain out of proportion to appearance;
  • bronze/brown discolouration of skin;
  • crepitus (gas in tissues);
  • sweet/offensive odour;
  • systemic toxicity (high fever, tachycardia, hypotension, confusion).
Rapid progression to death within hours if untreated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: How is gas gangrene treated?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back:
Surgical emergency:
  • wide surgical debridement / amputation.
  • High-dose IV penicillin G (+ metronidazole).
  • Hyperbaric oxygen — adjunct (inhibits anaerobic growth).
No role for delayed surgery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is Fournier's gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Necrotising fasciitis of the perineum/scrotum/vulva. Polymicrobial and synergistic (aerobic + anaerobic). Affects diabetics, immunocompromised, obese men. Rapidly fatal if untreated. Emergency debridement + broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam + metronidazole).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is necrotising fasciitis and how does it relate to gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Deep infection of the fascia causing spreading necrosis of fascia, subcutaneous tissue, and overlying skin. Gangrene of the skin overlies the fasciitis. Classified as Type I (polymicrobial) or Type II (Group A Streptococcus / 'flesh-eating').

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is the hallmark clinical sign of necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back:
Pain out of proportion to appearance + 'dishwater' (grey/brown) fluid on incision. Also:
  • woody induration,
  • rapid spreading erythema,
  • skin necrosis,
  • and crepitus (if gas-forming).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is the LRINEC score?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotising Fasciitis — uses CRP, WCC, Hb, Na, creatinine and glucose to risk-stratify soft tissue infections. Score ≥6 = high risk. Used to prompt urgent surgical exploration, not to delay it.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is the commonest precipitant of limb gangrene in clinical practice?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Diabetic foot — peripheral neuropathy (unnoticed trauma) + peripheral arterial disease + impaired immunity → infection + ischaemia → wet gangrene or neuropathic ulcer leading to gangrene.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is the role of ABPI in the assessment of gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: ABPI (ankle-brachial pressure index) quantifies peripheral ischaemia. <0.5 = severe ischaemia; <0.3 = critical ischaemia (tissue loss/rest pain/gangrene). Guides revascularisation decisions.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is the definitive management of established limb gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back:
• Revascularisation (bypass/angioplasty) if viable tissue remains.
  • Amputation if revascularisation is not possible or has failed.
  • Wet/gas gangrene: debridement first + antibiotics, then revascularisation/amputation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: At what ABPI level is critical ischaemia and tissue loss expected?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back:
ABPI <0.3 — critical ischaemia. Features:
  • rest pain,
  • non-healing ulcers,
  • gangrene.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What blood test is an early marker of tissue ischaemia and necrosis in gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Raised serum lactate (anaerobic metabolism from ischaemia); also raised CRP, WCC (if infected), creatinine (AKI from sepsis), clotting (DIC risk in gas gangrene).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise the four types of gangrene.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back:
• Dry = ischaemia, no infection, mummified, demarcated.
  • Wet = ischaemia + infection, swollen, sepsis.
  • Gas = Clostridium, crepitus, fatal.
  • Fournier's = perineal necrotising fasciitis, polymicrobial.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the key distinguishing feature of gas gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Crepitus (gas in tissues) from Clostridium perfringens — surgical emergency. Wide debridement + IV penicillin + hyperbaric O₂.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: EXAM PEARL: Pain out of proportion to appearance — what must be excluded?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Necrotising fasciitis / gas gangrene — requires immediate surgical exploration. Do not be reassured by normal-looking overlying skin.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the diabetic foot triad that leads to gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Peripheral neuropathy (unnoticed injury) + peripheral arterial disease (impaired healing) + immunosuppression (infection) = diabetic foot gangrene.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What are the two main types of gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Dry gangrene (ischaemic — peripheral arterial disease) and wet gangrene (infected — bacteria, often in diabetics).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is gas gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Rapidly spreading myonecrosis caused by Clostridium perfringens — crepitus (gas in tissue), severe systemic toxicity, very high mortality. Surgical emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What organism causes gas gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Clostridium perfringens (anaerobe) — produces exotoxins (alpha toxin) causing rapid tissue destruction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Rapidly spreading infection along fascial planes — polymicrobial or Group A Streptococcus. 'Woody-hard' induration, disproportionate pain, skin necrosis. Mortality 20–40%.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What imaging is most useful in suspected necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: CT with contrast — shows gas along fascial planes, fascial thickening, fluid collections. Does NOT delay surgical exploration if clinical suspicion high.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is the definitive treatment for necrotising fasciitis/gas gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Emergency surgical debridement (source control) + broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam + clindamycin ± metronidazole). Reconstruction later.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is the role of hyperbaric oxygen in gas gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Adjunct treatment (not first-line) — hyperoxic environment inhibits anaerobe growth and promotes healing. Used after surgical debridement.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: Why is gangrene common in diabetics?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Peripheral vascular disease (macroangiopathy) + peripheral neuropathy (painless injury) + impaired immunity → infection progresses unnoticed.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is the classic appearance of dry gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Dry, black, shrunken, mummified tissue with sharp demarcation line — usually toes/foot. Cold, pulseless. Represents ischaemic infarction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is the classic appearance of wet gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Moist, oedematous, foul-smelling, rapidly spreading necrosis — blurred margins. Associated with systemic sepsis. Requires urgent debridement.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is the surgical treatment of dry gangrene of the toes?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Amputation — level depends on blood supply (digital → forefoot → below-knee → above-knee). Revascularisation first if possible.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What investigations are needed when gangrene is suspected?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back:
• Bloods: FBC, CRP, cultures;
  • Imaging: X-ray (gas in soft tissue), CT (extent);
  • Ankle-Brachial Index;
  • Doppler USS;
  • Arteriography for revascularisation planning.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: EXAM PEARL: What triad points to gas gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: (1) Rapid onset after trauma/surgery; (2) crepitus in tissue; (3) profound systemic toxicity — emergency debridement + IV penicillin.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: EXAM PEARL: What distinguishes necrotising fasciitis from cellulitis clinically?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: NF: disproportionate pain, woody-hard induration, systemic sepsis, skin necrosis, rapid progression — cellulitis does not have crepitus, necrosis or this severity.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the most common causative organism in Type 1 necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Polymicrobial (mixed aerobic + anaerobic — e.g. E. coli, Bacteroides, Streptococcus). Type 2 = monomicrobial (Group A Streptococcus — commonest monomicrobial).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What antibiotics are used for necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Broad-spectrum IV: piperacillin-tazobactam OR meropenem + clindamycin (inhibits toxin production) ± IV immunoglobulin for streptococcal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is the mortality of gas gangrene if untreated?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Near 100% untreated. Even with surgery + antibiotics, mortality is 20–30%. Speed of surgical debridement is the key prognostic factor.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.back: Likely DVT — go straight to compression duplex USS
Compression duplex USS — non-compressible vein = thrombus
Low probability Wells score — negative D-dimer excludes DVT. Useless if high probability.
DOAC — apixaban (10 mg BD ×7d then 5 mg BD) or rivaroxaban
LMWH throughout (DOACs and warfarin contraindicated)
Hypercoagulability + Endothelial damage + Venous stasis
3 months
Minimum 6 months — consider indefinite
Warfarin (DOACs inferior in APS — higher recurrence)
Factor V Leiden (APC resistance)
Chronic venous insufficiency after DVT — pain, swelling, skin changes, ulceration
LMWH or DOAC (edoxaban/rivaroxaban) — both NICE-recommended
No — elastic compression stockings do not prevent post-thrombotic syndrome. Use only for symptom relief.
After completing anticoagulation — warfarin/DOACs falsely affect levels
Left iliac vein compressed by right iliac artery → left-sided DVT in young women
Deep vein thrombosis — clot (thrombus) forming in a deep vein, most commonly the calf, popliteal, femoral, or iliac veins.

Three factors predisposing to thrombosis:
  • (1) venous stasis;
  • (2) hypercoagulability;
  • (3) endothelial injury.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.front: Name clinical risk factors for DVT using Virchow's triad.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.back:
• Stasis: immobility, long-haul travel, paralysis;
  • Hypercoagulability: thrombophilia, OCP, pregnancy, cancer, polycythaemia;
  • Endothelial injury: surgery, trauma, IV catheters.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.front: What is the classic clinical presentation of DVT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.back: Unilateral calf pain, swelling, warmth, erythema — often after immobility. Homan's sign (pain on dorsiflexion) is unreliable.

Clinical prediction rule (0–8 points): score ≤1 = low probability; score ≥2 = high probability. Variables include active cancer, paralysis, recent immobilisation, tenderness along vein, swelling, collateral veins, alternative diagnosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.front: What D-dimer result excludes DVT in low Wells score?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.back: Negative D-dimer (<500 ng/mL) + Wells ≤1 = DVT excluded — no imaging needed. D-dimer is sensitive but not specific.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.front: What is the first-line imaging for suspected DVT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.back: Compression duplex ultrasound (USS) — non-compressibility of the vein = thrombus.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.front: What does proximal DVT mean and why does it matter?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.back: Thrombus above the popliteal fossa (femoral, iliac veins) — higher risk of PE than distal DVT.
DOAC (direct oral anticoagulant) — rivaroxaban or apixaban (NICE preferred). Alternative: LMWH bridging to warfarin.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.front: How long is anticoagulation continued after a first provoked DVT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.back:
• 3 months for provoked (identifiable trigger);
  • 6+ months for unprovoked;
  • lifelong if recurrent or active cancer.
Long-term complication of DVT — venous hypertension causing chronic leg swelling, pain, skin changes, ulceration. Caused by valvular damage.
Severe DVT with massive venous occlusion — massive blue, painful, swollen leg with risk of venous gangrene. Emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.front: What is the difference between DVT and superficial thrombophlebitis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.back:
• DVT: deep vein, risk of PE;
  • Superficial thrombophlebitis: superficial vein, lower PE risk, treated conservatively with NSAIDs and compression.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.front: What is the role of thrombophilia screening in DVT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.back:
Not done acutely (anticoagulation affects results); consider if:
  • unprovoked DVT,
  • recurrent,
  • young patient,
  • family history,
  • unusual site.
Includes Factor V Leiden, prothrombin mutation, protein C/S/antithrombin deficiency, antiphospholipid syndrome.
Acquired hypercoagulable state with recurrent arterial/venous thrombosis and pregnancy loss — diagnosis: positive lupus anticoagulant / anticardiolipin antibodies on two occasions ≥12 weeks apart.
VTE prophylaxis: LMWH (enoxaparin) + TED stockings + early mobilisation + hydration. Risk-assessed on admission.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.front: What is the mechanism of action of rivaroxaban?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.back: Direct factor Xa inhibitor — no monitoring needed, fixed dosing, fewer interactions than warfarin.
LMWH throughout pregnancy (DOACs and warfarin are teratogenic/unsafe). Continue for ≥6 weeks postpartum.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.front: What is IVC filter used for in DVT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.back: Inferior vena cava filter — used when anticoagulation is contraindicated (e.g. active bleeding) to prevent PE. Temporary or permanent.
Reserved for massive proximal DVT with threatened limb viability (phlegmasia cerulea dolens) — high bleeding risk.
Tumours produce procoagulant substances (tissue factor); venous compression; immobility; chemotherapy — Trousseau's syndrome = migratory thrombophlebitis with occult malignancy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.front: What is the diagnostic algorithm for suspected DVT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.back:
Wells score →
  • if low + D-dimer negative: exclude;
  • if low + D-dimer positive OR high Wells: compression USS;
  • positive USS: treat.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the Wells DVT score threshold for imaging?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.back: Wells ≥2 = high probability → duplex USS directly (don't use D-dimer). Wells ≤1 + negative D-dimer = excluded.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the danger of untreated proximal DVT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.back: Pulmonary embolism — thrombus propagates to pulmonary arteries causing ventilation-perfusion mismatch, hypoxia, right heart strain, death.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the DOAC of choice for DVT in cancer?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.back: Apixaban, edoxaban or rivaroxaban (DOACs are now preferred over LMWH in cancer-associated thrombosis), each supported by randomised evidence against LMWH.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: Define an abdominal aortic aneurysm, including the size threshold and the normal diameter.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: A permanent localised dilatation of the abdominal aorta ≥3 cm (normal ~2 cm). Most are infrarenal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: How do most AAAs present?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: The vast majority are asymptomatic — found on screening or incidentally.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What are the two exam anchors for AAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Size thresholds (when to watch vs when to cut — pure recall) and ruptured AAA (the high-stakes emergency scenario).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: How does the aetiology of AAA compare with thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: TAA has a different aetiology (Marfan's, bicuspid AV, dissection) and is kept separate; AAA is predominantly degenerative/inflammatory.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What is the strongest modifiable risk factor for AAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Smoking.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: List the risk factors for AAA.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back:
• Smoking — strongest modifiable RF
  • Hypertension
  • Hyperlipidaemia
  • Male sex (4:1 male:female)
  • Age >65
  • Family history (first-degree relative)
  • Atherosclerosis
  • Connective tissue disease (Marfan's, Ehlers-Danlos)
  • Inflammatory (Takayasu's aortitis)
  • Infection (rare)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: Describe the pathological mechanism of AAA formation.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Chronic inflammation → MMP activation → MMPs degrade elastin + collagen in the aortic wall → progressive wall weakening → dilatation.Atherosclerosis is associated, not directly causative.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: Which major cardiovascular risk factor is protective against AAA, and why is this notable?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Diabetes is protective — the only major cardiovascular risk factor that reduces AAA risk.Counterintuitive → frequently examined.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What symptoms can occur when an unruptured AAA becomes symptomatic?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back:
• Non-specific abdominal/back/loin pain
  • Distal embolisation → limb ischaemia
  • Aortoenteric fistula → GI bleed

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What might be found on examination of a symptomatic unruptured AAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: A pulsatile, expansile mass above the umbilicus; rarely, signs of retroperitoneal haemorrhage.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What is the main mimic of a ruptured AAA, and what is the key teaching?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Renal colic — back pain + collapse in an older man = rupture until proven otherwise.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: List other differentials for a symptomatic AAA besides renal colic.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back:
• Diverticulitis
  • IBD
  • Appendicitis
  • GI haemorrhage
  • Ovarian torsion

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What is the differential for an epigastric mass?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back:
• AAA
  • Gastric CA
  • Pancreatic pseudocyst/tumour
  • Pyloric stenosis
  • Transverse colon CA

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What is the National AAA Screening Programme, and who is screened?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: A one-off abdominal ultrasound for all men in the year they turn 65.Women are not routinely screened (lower risk); consider ultrasound in women aged 70 and over who have risk factors. Men aged 66 and over who were never screened can self-refer (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: On AAA screening, what is the classification and action for an aorta <3 cm?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Normal — no further action.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: On AAA screening, what is the classification and surveillance for a 3.0–4.4 cm aorta?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Small AAA — yearly USS surveillance.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: On AAA screening, what is the classification and surveillance for a 4.5–5.4 cm aorta?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Medium AAA — 3-monthly USS surveillance.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: On AAA screening, what is the classification and action for an aorta ≥5.5 cm?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Large AAA — refer vascular surgery, consider repair.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What are the driving rules for AAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back:
• AAA ≥6 cm → inform DVLA
  • AAA ≥6.5 cm → disqualified from driving

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What is the first-line investigation for AAA, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Abdominal USS — first-line for diagnosis and surveillance.Cheap, no radiation, repeatable.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: When is CT angiogram used in AAA, and what does it provide?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Once at threshold (≥5.5 cm). Gives anatomy for EVAR suitability planning; also used in stable rupture.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: On ultrasound, how is the AAA distinguished from the IVC?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: The AAA is round, pulsatile and thick-walled (on the left); the IVC is ovoid, collapsible and thin-walled (on the right); the vertebral body shadow lies below.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What conservative management applies to all AAA patients, and which part of it actually slows the aneurysm?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Smoking cessation is the only measure shown to reduce growth rate and rupture risk.BP control (target <140/90), a statin and an antiplatelet, and weight loss and exercise are offered for the patient's overall cardiovascular risk as an older vasculopath. No drug is recommended to slow the aneurysm itself — the evidence does not support one (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What are the three indications for surgical repair of an AAA (any one of)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back:
• Diameter ≥5.5 cm
  • Growth >1 cm in one year in an aneurysm already larger than 4.0 cm
  • Symptomatic — pain or tenderness in an otherwise fit patient

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: When might surgical repair be delayed despite a diameter ≥5.5 cm?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: In unfit/high-risk patients repair may be deferred with continued surveillance, balancing rupture risk against elective operative mortality.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: Describe the open repair technique for AAA.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Midline laparotomy or transverse incision; clamp the aorta proximally + iliac arteries distally; remove the segment → prosthetic graft replacement.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What are the advantages and disadvantages of open AAA repair?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: More durable long-term, but a bigger operation with longer recovery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: Describe the EVAR (endovascular) repair technique.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: A graft is introduced via the femoral arteries; the stent is fixed across the aneurysm under fluoroscopy, excluding the aneurysm from circulation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What are the advantages and disadvantages of EVAR?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Lower 30-day mortality + shorter hospital stay, but a higher reintervention rate + endoleak risk + late rupture.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: State the examinable trade-off between EVAR and open repair.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: EVAR = better short-term (lower peri-op mortality); Open = better long-term durability.Both are technically valid, but the UK steer is not neutral: open repair is offered first-line for unruptured infrarenal AAA, with EVAR reserved for people in whom open repair is contraindicated — by a hostile abdomen or similar co-pathology, or by anaesthetic risk and comorbidity (NICE). Practice elsewhere favours EVAR as the default (ESVS), which is why the UK line surprises people.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What is the overall mortality of a ruptured AAA, and how do rupture sites differ in prognosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: 80% overall mortality.Most ruptures — roughly four in five — are retroperitoneal (posterior, may be temporarily contained); the rest rupture free into the peritoneal cavity (anterior — near-uniformly fatal).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What is the presentation of a ruptured AAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back:
• Severe abdominal/back/flank pain — sudden onset, may radiate to groin
  • Syncope/collapse — haemodynamic instability: tachycardia + hypotension
  • A pulsatile expansile mass above the umbilicus (present in ~50%)
  • Vomiting
  • Tenderness on palpation

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What is the classic triad of a ruptured AAA, and in what proportion is it present?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Flank/back pain + hypotension + pulsatile abdominal mass — present in only about a quarter to a half of cases.So its absence proves nothing.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: Why might high-flow O₂ be given in a ruptured AAA despite a normal-looking SpO₂?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: SpO₂ may be falsely normal (remaining Hb fully saturated) — still give O₂.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What is the initial resuscitation in a ruptured AAA regarding access and bloods?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back:
• 2× large-bore IV cannulae
  • Urgent bloods — FBC, U&Es, clotting
  • Activate the major haemorrhage protocol and crossmatch ≥6 units

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What is permissive hypotension in ruptured AAA, what is the target, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Restrictive fluid resuscitation — accept a low blood pressure rather than chasing a normal one, because raising it dislodges the tamponading clot and unleashes torrential haemorrhage.The practical endpoint is the conscious level and a palpable radial pulse rather than a fixed number; the figure usually quoted for teaching is a systolic under about 100 mmHg (NICE gives the principle, not a target).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: How is a ruptured AAA managed, and who actually bypasses the scanner?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Peri-arrest or in extremis: straight to theatre for open repair, no imaging — that is the exception, not the rule for anyone hypotensive.Everyone else, including the shocked patient: CT angiogram provided it does not delay repair, because it decides EVAR feasibility — EVAR if the anatomy allows, open if not.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: After transfer to a vascular unit, how is a ruptured AAA triaged?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: By haemodynamic stability.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What is an endoleak, and what is its mechanism and consequence?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Incomplete seal around the graft → blood leaks into the aneurysm sac around the graft → the sac re-expands → risk of rupture.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What are the key points about endoleaks following EVAR?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Usually asymptomatic; any post-EVAR sac expansion → investigate for endoleak.Classified by mechanism (Types 1–5) — beyond most finals requirements.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: A patient develops bloody diarrhoea and abdominal pain three days after open AAA repair. What is the diagnosis and why does it happen?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Colonic ischaemia (ischaemic colitis).The inferior mesenteric artery is sacrificed during open repair, so the left colon depends on collateral supply from the marginal artery. If collaterals are inadequate, the colon becomes ischaemic.Investigation: urgent flexible sigmoidoscopy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What follow-up does EVAR commit the patient to, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Lifelong imaging surveillance — CT or duplex.The stent graft can develop an endoleak or migrate at any point after the procedure, allowing the sac to re-expand and rupture. This commitment is the real trade-off against EVAR's lower peri-operative mortality — a patient who defaults from follow-up loses the protection the operation bought them.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: List the important complications of open AAA repair.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back:
• Colonic ischaemia — IMA sacrificed; bloody diarrhoea in the early post-operative days
  • Spinal cord ischaemia — rare; paraplegia
  • Graft infection and later aortoenteric fistula — fever or GI bleeding
  • Renal impairment (especially with suprarenal clamping)
  • Cardiac events and distal embolisation (“trash foot”)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: Should the relatives of a patient with an abdominal aortic aneurysm be screened?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Yes. A first-degree relative of someone with an AAA carries a materially higher risk than the general population.Offer ultrasound screening to siblings and children rather than waiting for the national programme, which only invites men in the year they turn 65.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What is infective endocarditis, and what is its pathological hallmark?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Infection of the endocardium and valves. The pathological hallmark is the vegetation — a mass of platelets, fibrin, organisms and inflammatory cells (neutrophil-rich). Contrast the sterile vegetations of marantic endocarditis, which are bland fibrin-platelet thrombi without inflammatory cells. It is avascular, which is why it is so hard to sterilise and needs prolonged IV antibiotics.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Contrast acute IE and subacute bacterial endocarditis (SBE) by tempo, valve and organism.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back:
• Acute IE: fulminant (hours–days), on normal or damaged valves, classically Staph aureus.
  • Subacute SBE: insidious (weeks–months), on damaged valves, classically Strep viridans.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What is the strongest risk factor for infective endocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Previous IE.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What is the in-hospital mortality of IE, and what proportion require surgery?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: In-hospital mortality is 20–30%, and surgery is required in roughly 50% of cases.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Which layer of the heart does infective endocarditis infect?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: The endocardium — the innermost lining of the heart (and the valves).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Which organism causes acute IE on a normal or damaged native valve, and IE in IVDU?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Staph aureus (the most common overall).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Which organism classically causes IE after poor dental hygiene or a dental procedure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Strep viridans. Note: routine antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures is not recommended in the UK (NICE); good oral hygiene is the emphasis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Which organism causes early prosthetic valve IE (within 2 months of surgery, perioperative)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Staph epidermidis (coagulase-negative staphylococcus).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Which organisms cause late prosthetic valve IE, more than 12 months after surgery?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Strep viridans and Staph aureus.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Which organism links IE to colorectal cancer, and what investigation does it mandate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Strep bovis, now reported as Streptococcus gallolyticus ('bovis = bowel') → send for colonoscopy to exclude colorectal carcinoma.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What are the causes of culture-negative IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back:
• HACEK organisms
  • Coxiella burnetii (Q fever)
  • Bartonella
  • Brucella
  • Tropheryma whipplei
  • and prior antibiotics.
HACEK are the classic group, though modern automated blood cultures usually grow them within about 5 days.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What causes non-infective / sterile vegetations?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: SLE → Libman-Sacks endocarditis; malignancy → marantic endocarditis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What are the valve and patient risk groups for IE, with approximate proportions?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back:
• Normal valves (~50%, often mitral)
  • rheumatic valve disease (a declining minority in the UK)
  • prosthetic valves
  • congenital heart disease
  • and IVDU (→ tricuspid / right-sided).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Which valve does IE affect in IV drug users, and why does this matter?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: The tricuspid valve (right-sided IE), because injected organisms reach the right heart first — leading to septic pulmonary emboli.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Outline the mechanism by which a vegetation forms in IE.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Endothelial damage → a platelet-fibrin thrombus forms → pathogens seed it during bacteraemia → a vegetation forms.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What are the three consequence streams that explain almost every sign of IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: 1. Local destruction, 2. Embolisation, and 3. Immune complex deposition.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What are the features of the LOCAL DESTRUCTION stream in IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back:
• Valve regurgitation → heart failure
  • annulus / aortic root abscess → AV block (an ECG red flag)
  • and fistula / leaflet perforation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Why is a new AV block on ECG in IE an important red flag?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: It signals an aortic root / annulus abscess from local destruction — a surgical emergency until proven otherwise.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What are the features of the EMBOLISATION stream in IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Left-sided emboli to brain, spleen, kidneys, coronary arteries; right-sided (IVDU) septic pulmonary emboli; and Janeway lesions (painless infarcts).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What are the features of the IMMUNE COMPLEX stream in IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Small-vessel vasculitis, Osler's nodes (painful nodules), Roth spots, splinter haemorrhages, and glomerulonephritis (with a raised rheumatoid factor).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What are the systemic infection features of IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back:
• Fever (the most consistent sign)
  • malaise
  • night sweats
  • weight loss
  • anaemia of chronic disease
  • and (late/subacute) splenomegaly and clubbing.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What is the most consistent clinical sign of IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Fever.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What are the cardiac (local destruction) clinical features of IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: A murmur in ~85% — but a genuinely new or changing murmur is much less common and far more specific. Plus signs of heart failure, and an aortic root abscess → AV block.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: List the embolic / vascular phenomena of IE.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back:
• Janeway lesions (painless, palms & soles)
  • stroke/TIA (left-sided)
  • splenic and renal infarcts
  • conjunctival haemorrhages
  • and septic pulmonary emboli (right-sided).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: List the immune / vasculitic phenomena of IE.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back:
• Osler's nodes (painful, finger/toe pulps)
  • Roth spots (retinal, pale centre)
  • splinter haemorrhages (subungual)
  • glomerulonephritis (haematuria, casts)
  • and a raised rheumatoid factor.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What is the classic exam discrimination between Janeway lesions and Osler's nodes?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Janeway = painless = embolic infarcts (palms & soles). Osler's = Ouch = painful = immune vasculitis (finger/toe pulps).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Why are blood cultures the cornerstone investigation in IE, and how are they taken?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: 3 sets from different venepuncture sites, ≥6 h apart, taken before antibiotics. Exception: in severe sepsis or septic shock take 2 sets from different sites within 1 hour and start antibiotics immediately — treatment is not delayed to complete the cultures. ≥2 sets positive with a typical organism is a major Duke criterion; persistent bacteraemia is characteristic.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What is the role of TTE vs TOE in IE, and which is more sensitive?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: TTE first (less sensitive). TOE if TTE is negative but suspicion is high, or for a prosthetic valve, poor window, or complications — and also when the TTE is positive, to exclude perivalvular abscess, fistula or dehiscence; the one exception is isolated right-sided native-valve IE with a good-quality, unequivocal TTE (ESC). A normal echo does NOT exclude IE — do TOE if clinical suspicion is strong.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Does a normal echocardiogram exclude infective endocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: No — a normal echo does not exclude IE. If clinical suspicion is strong, proceed to TOE.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What is the characteristic echo finding in IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: A vegetation — a mobile echogenic mass attached to a valve leaflet.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What ECG change is monitored for in IE, and what does it signify?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: A new AV block → an aortic root abscess (a surgical emergency); a prolonging PR interval is a red flag, so ECGs are serially monitored.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What blood and urine abnormalities are seen in IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back:
• Normocytic anaemia
  • raised ESR/CRP
  • leucocytosis
  • raised creatinine with haematuria and red cell casts
  • a raised rheumatoid factor and immunoglobulins
  • and serology for culture-negative organisms (Coxiella, Bartonella, Brucella).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: How is 'definite IE' established under the Modified Duke criteria?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: 2 major, OR 1 major + 3 minor, OR 5 minor, OR pathological proof. Possible IE = 1 major + 1 minor, or 3 minor.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What are the two MAJOR criteria of the Modified Duke criteria?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back:
• 1. Positive blood cultures (a typical organism — Staph aureus, Strep viridans, Enterococcus, HACEK — in ≥2 sets, or persistently positive ≥12h apart). Special case: a single positive blood culture for Coxiella burnetii, or a phase I IgG titre >1:800, counts as a major criterion on its own.
  • 2. Endocardial involvement (vegetation, abscess, or prosthetic dehiscence on echo; or new valvular regurgitation).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What are the 5 MINOR criteria of the modified Duke criteria for IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back:
• Predisposition (predisposing cardiac condition or IVDU)
  • Fever ≥38°C
  • Vascular phenomena (Janeway lesions, septic/arterial emboli, mycotic aneurysm, conjunctival/intracranial haemorrhage)
  • Immunologic phenomena (Osler's nodes, Roth spots, glomerulonephritis, +RF)
  • Microbiological evidence not meeting a major criterion.
There is NO echo minor criterion — echo counts only as a major criterion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What is the management principle in IE, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Prolonged IV bactericidal antibiotics — poor vascular penetration of the avascular vegetation requires high drug concentrations for weeks. Take blood cultures first and discuss with microbiology.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What is the blind/empirical antibiotic regimen for native-valve IE (and the penicillin-allergy/MRSA alternative)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Amoxicillin (± gentamicin); if penicillin-allergic or MRSA: vancomycin + gentamicin. For a prosthetic valve, empirical cover is broader: vancomycin + gentamicin + rifampicin.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What is the first-line antibiotic regimen for native-valve MSSA Staph aureus IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Flucloxacillin IV for 4–6 weeks (vancomycin + rifampicin if penicillin-allergic or MRSA).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What is the regimen for prosthetic-valve MSSA Staph IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Flucloxacillin + rifampicin + gentamicin (vancomycin + rifampicin + gentamicin if penicillin-allergic/MRSA).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What is the regimen for penicillin-sensitive Strep viridans IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Benzylpenicillin for 4 weeks (or 2 weeks with gentamicin); vancomycin + gentamicin if penicillin-allergic.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What is the regimen for Enterococcus IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Amoxicillin + gentamicin for 4–6 weeks (vancomycin + gentamicin if penicillin-allergic).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What is the regimen for MRSA IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Vancomycin plus rifampicin — at least 4 weeks for a native valve; for a prosthetic valve add gentamicin and treat for at least 6 weeks. Daptomycin is an alternative to vancomycin.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: List the indications for surgery in IE.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back:
• Severe HF (acute aortic/mitral regurgitation with haemodynamic compromise)
  • valve destruction (leaflet perforation, fistula)
  • aortic root/annulus abscess (especially if causing AV block)
  • recurrent systemic emboli despite antibiotics (especially vegetations >10mm)
  • resistant organisms (fungi, highly resistant bacteria)
  • prosthetic valve dehiscence or persistent bacteraemia despite treatment.
Urgency is graded: emergency (within 24 hours), urgent (within 3–5 days) and non-urgent (during the same admission) (ESC).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Which organisms causing IE are an indication for surgery due to resistance?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Fungi and highly resistant bacteria.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Exam pearl: what is the IVDU → IE pattern and its imaging finding?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: IVDU → tricuspid / right-sided IE → septic pulmonary emboli → cavitating lung lesions on CXR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Which organisms cause infective endocarditis on a pacemaker or ICD lead, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back:
Predominantly staphylococci — Staph epidermidis / coagulase-negative staphylococci and Staph aureus.
The pattern mirrors early prosthetic valve IE because the mechanism is the same: implanted foreign material colonised at or after the time of implantation, with biofilm formation on the hardware.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: A patient with a permanent pacemaker develops infective endocarditis on a pacing lead. Why is a prolonged antibiotic course alone insufficient?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back:
Because the hardware itself is colonised — bacteria form biofilm on the leads and generator that antibiotics cannot penetrate.
Treatment requires complete system extraction — generator and leads — alongside antibiotics.Same principle as an infected prosthetic valve: the foreign material has to go.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: List the indications for surgery or hardware removal in infective endocarditis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back:
• Severe heart failure — acute AR or MR with haemodynamic compromise
  • Valve destruction — leaflet perforation, fistula
  • Aortic root / annulus abscess — especially with AV block
  • Recurrent emboli despite antibiotics (especially vegetations >10 mm)
  • Resistant organisms — fungi, highly resistant bacteria
  • Prosthetic valve dehiscence or persistent bacteraemia
  • Infected cardiac device — complete system extraction

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: How is bradycardia defined, and what is the clinically important distinction?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: A heart rate <60 bpm. The clinically important distinction is symptomatic vs incidental — symptomatic bradycardia causes haemodynamic compromise (shock, syncope, ischaemia, heart failure) and needs treatment, whereas incidental bradycardia in an athlete or during sleep is physiologically normal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is the central organising principle for understanding bradycardias and heart block?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: The anatomical level of the block determines everything — the escape rate, QRS width, escape reliability, response to atropine, and whether pacing is needed.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What are the features of a block at the SA node level?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Sinus bradycardia and sick sinus syndrome. The SA node fires slowly (not a true escape); narrow QRS, and atropine works.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What are the features of a block at the AV node level?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: First-degree block and Mobitz I. Narrow QRS, usually benign, and atropine works.Conduction is maintained in both, so there is no escape rhythm — the junctional escape of 40–60 bpm is what emerges only if nodal block becomes complete.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What are the features of an infranodal (His-Purkinje) block?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Mobitz II and infranodal complete heart block (CHB) with a broad escape. Ventricular escape <40 bpm, broad QRS, and atropine is INEFFECTIVE — the patient must be paced.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: State the key principle linking the level of block to the escape rhythm.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: The lower the block, the slower and broader the escape rhythm — and the less reliable it is.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Why is atropine ineffective in an infranodal block?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Atropine acts on the AV node, not below it. An infranodal (His-Purkinje) block is below the AV node, so atropine cannot improve conduction there — pacing is required.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: How does QRS width relate to the level of a bradycardic block?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Higher blocks (SA node, AV node) preserve a narrow QRS because the His-Purkinje system still conducts normally; infranodal blocks produce a broad QRS as the escape arises distal to the block, within ventricular/distal Purkinje tissue.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Define sinus bradycardia on the ECG.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: HR <60 bpm with P waves of normal morphology preceding every QRS — the SA node fires, just slowly.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: In which physiological situations is sinus bradycardia expected and not treated?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: In athletes (enhanced vagal tone) and during sleep — no treatment is needed.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: List the drug (extrinsic) causes of sinus bradycardia.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back:
• Beta-blockers,
  • digoxin,
  • rate-limiting CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem), and
  • amiodarone/lithium.
The most dangerous is a combination — verapamil plus a β-blocker is additively negatively chronotropic and dromotropic and can precipitate complete heart block or asystole; the IV combination is contraindicated (BNF).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: List the systemic (extrinsic) causes of sinus bradycardia.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back:
• Hypothyroidism (myxoedema),
  • hypothermia,
  • raised ICP (Cushing's reflex — bradycardia + hypertension + irregular respirations), and
  • cholestasis (bile salts are vagotonic on the SA node).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is Cushing's reflex, and what triad does it produce?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: A response to raised intracranial pressure producing the triad of bradycardia, hypertension, and irregular respirations.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What are the intrinsic (within the heart) causes of sinus bradycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Acute ischaemia / inferior MI (the RCA supplies the SA node in ~60%; also vagally mediated), and sick sinus syndrome.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Why does an inferior MI commonly cause sinus bradycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: The right coronary artery supplies the SA node in ~60% of people, and inferior MI is also vagally mediated — so RCA-territory infarction frequently produces bradycardia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is sick sinus syndrome, and what patterns does it encompass?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back:
SA node dysfunction encompassing
  • idiopathic degenerative fibrosis (commonest; elderly),
  • persistent symptomatic sinus bradycardia,
  • prolonged pauses (SA exit block / sinus arrest), and
  • brady-tachy syndrome.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is the most common cause of sick sinus syndrome?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Idiopathic degenerative fibrosis of the SA node, typically in the elderly.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is brady-tachy syndrome?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: A form of sick sinus syndrome with alternating sinus bradycardia and paroxysmal AF or flutter — treating the tachy component can worsen the brady.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is the therapeutic dilemma in brady-tachy syndrome, and how is it resolved?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Antiarrhythmics used to treat the AF worsen the bradycardia. The resolution is to pace first — then it is safe to use antiarrhythmics.Anticoagulation is also given for the AF component.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: How is sick sinus syndrome managed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back:
• Treat the reversible cause (stop offending drugs, replace thyroid hormone),
  • give atropine for acute symptomatic episodes, and
  • implant a permanent pacemaker if symptomatic and the cause is not reversible.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Describe the V1 and V6 morphology of RBBB.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: RBBB shows an RSR' ('rabbit ears') in V1 and a broad slurred S wave in V6.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Describe the V1 and V6 morphology of LBBB.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: LBBB shows a deep S (dominant downward deflection) in V1 and a broad/notched R wave in V6.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is the key discriminator for classifying AV blocks, beyond just the degree?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Where in the conduction system the block sits — nodal vs infranodal.This determines the escape rhythm, atropine response and need for pacing.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Describe first-degree AV block and its management.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: PR >200 ms, fixed, with every P conducting to a QRS. It is at the AV node level, benign, and needs no treatment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Describe Mobitz I (Wenckebach) second-degree AV block.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Progressive PR lengthening until a QRS is dropped, then the cycle resets. It is at the AV node level, with a narrow QRS, and is usually benign.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Describe Mobitz II second-degree AV block and its key risks.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: A fixed PR interval with a sudden dropped QRS (no warning). It is INFRANODAL, usually with a broad QRS (may be narrow if the block is within the His bundle), carries a HIGH risk of progression to complete heart block, and requires a pacemaker.Beware 2:1 block: with every other P wave blocked you cannot see PR progression, so it cannot be classified as Mobitz I or II from the strip alone — judge by QRS width (narrow suggests nodal, broad suggests infranodal) and look for periods of 3:2 conduction on longer strips.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Describe third-degree (complete) heart block.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: P waves and QRS complexes are fully dissociated, with the ventricles driven by an escape rhythm only. A wide QRS escape indicates an infranodal (unreliable) origin.A pacemaker is mandatory.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Compare the PR interval across the four AV blocks.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back:
• 1st degree: fixed, prolonged >200 ms.
  • Mobitz I: progressive lengthening.
  • Mobitz II: constant (may be normal).
  • 3rd degree (CHB): no P–R relationship.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Compare the dropped-QRS pattern across the AV blocks.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back:
• 1st degree: none — all P waves conduct.
  • Mobitz I: dropped after maximal PR, then resets.
  • Mobitz II: sudden, no warning.
  • 3rd degree: all P waves fail — escape rhythm only.
