conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Compare QRS width and conduction level across the AV blocks.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back:
• 1st degree: narrow, AV node.
  • Mobitz I: narrow, AV node.
  • Mobitz II: broad (usually), infranodal.
  • 3rd degree (CHB): narrow if His-level escape, broad if Purkinje-level; AV node or infranodal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Compare the asystole risk across the four AV blocks.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back:
• 1st degree: none.
  • Mobitz I: low.
  • Mobitz II: HIGH.
  • 3rd degree (CHB): HIGH if there is a broad escape.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: In which AV blocks is atropine useful, and in which is it not?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back:
• Mobitz I: yes.
  • 1st degree: N/A.
  • Mobitz II: no.
  • 3rd degree (CHB): only if there is a narrow escape and the situation is acute.
Atropine works at the AV node, not below it.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Compare the treatment across the four AV blocks.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back:
• 1st degree: none.
  • Mobitz I: monitor / treat the cause.
  • Mobitz II: pacemaker.
  • 3rd degree (CHB): pacemaker.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is the memory hook for Mobitz II regarding atropine?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Fixed PR then sudden drop = INFRANODAL = atropine INEFFECTIVE.Atropine increases the atrial rate but cannot improve conduction below the AV node — it may paradoxically worsen the block ratio.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Why can atropine paradoxically worsen an infranodal block?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Atropine increases the atrial (sinus) rate, but the diseased infranodal tissue cannot conduct the extra impulses, so a greater proportion are blocked — worsening the block ratio.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: In complete heart block, what does ventricular output depend on, and what determines its reliability?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: It depends entirely on a spontaneous escape rhythm arising below the block. The anatomical level of that escape determines its reliability.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Describe the features of a NARROW escape (His bundle) in complete heart block.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back:
• Rate 40–60 bpm,
  • narrow QRS (<120 ms),
  • a reliable pacemaker,
  • often from inferior MI / a reversible cause,
  • may respond to IV atropine acutely.
Because the cause is usually reversible it is often transient — permanent pacing is frequently NOT needed once the cause is corrected.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Describe the features of a BROAD escape (His-Purkinje) in complete heart block.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back:
• Rate <40 bpm,
  • broad QRS (>120 ms),
  • unreliable (may fail without warning),
  • causes Stokes-Adams attacks,
  • atropine ineffective, and
  • a permanent pacemaker is mandatory.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is a Stokes-Adams attack?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: A sudden loss of consciousness from complete heart block due to transient asystole or VT, with rapid complete recovery and no post-ictal confusion. The patient goes pale then flushes as circulation restores.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: How can a Stokes-Adams attack be distinguished from an epileptic seizure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back:
• By the rapid, complete return to normal (no post-ictal confusion),
  • no tongue-biting and no incontinence,
  • with pallor then flushing as circulation restores.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Is bundle branch block a bradycardia, and what causes the wide QRS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: No — BBB is a conduction delay, not a bradycardia. The AV node and His bundle conduct normally; the delay is in one bundle branch, producing a wide QRS (>120 ms) with characteristic morphology.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What does the WiLLiaM mnemonic describe for LBBB?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: LBBB = WiLLiaM: a W in V1 (deep QS or rS wave) and an M in V5/V6 and I (broad notched R wave).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What are the additional features and significance of LBBB?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: QRS >120 ms; the axis is usually normal (marked left axis deviation indicates more extensive conduction disease, not LBBB itself). It is always pathological — causes include aortic stenosis, hypertension, IHD and cardiomyopathy. LBBB with ongoing ischaemic symptoms is treated as a STEMI equivalent → primary PCI.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What does the MaRRoW mnemonic describe for RBBB?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: RBBB = MaRRoW: an M in V1 (RSR' pattern, 'rabbit ears') and a W in V5/V6 and I (broad slurred S wave).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What are the additional features and causes of RBBB?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: QRS >120 ms with an rSR' ('M') pattern in V1 and a normal cardiac axis (right axis deviation suggests an additional left posterior fascicular block or RVH). Can be a normal variant in young people; other causes include PE (acute RV strain), RVH and congenital heart disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What are the five life-threatening (adverse) features in bradycardia that signify haemodynamic instability requiring immediate treatment?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back:
• Shock (hypotension, pallor, diaphoresis, cold extremities, confusion),
  • syncope (LOC from reduced cardiac output),
  • myocardial ischaemia (chest pain or ECG ischaemia related to the bradycardia),
  • severe heart failure (breathlessness, pulmonary oedema from low output), and
  • a bradyarrhythmia occurring immediately post-ROSC (Resus Council UK).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What are the four high-risk-of-asystole situations that warrant aggressive treatment even if the patient is currently stable?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back:
• (1) Recent asystole,
  • (2) Mobitz II,
  • (3) complete heart block with a broad QRS, and
  • (4) ventricular pauses >3 seconds.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What does Step 1 (stabilise) of the peri-arrest bradycardia algorithm involve?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back:
• ABCDE assessment,
  • oxygen,
  • IV access,
  • a 12-lead ECG,
  • continuous monitoring, and
  • identifying/treating reversible causes (electrolytes, hypoxia, hypothermia, drugs).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: If adverse features are present in bradycardia, what is the first-line drug, dose and regimen?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Atropine 500 mcg IV, repeated every 3–5 minutes to a maximum of 3 mg total.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is the mechanism of atropine, and when is it ineffective?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: It is an antimuscarinic that blocks vagal slowing of the SA/AV node. It is ineffective for Mobitz II, CHB, or a broad escape (all infranodal — below the vagally-innervated AV node).Never give it to a transplanted (denervated) heart — there is no vagal tone for it to block, and it can provoke high-degree AV block or sinus arrest; use aminophylline instead (Resus Council UK).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: If atropine gives an inadequate response in bradycardia, what interim escalation measures are available?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back:
• Isoprenaline IV starting at 5 mcg/min,
  • adrenaline 2–10 mcg/min IV,
  • aminophylline 100–200 mg by slow IV injection (for bradycardia in cardiac transplant or spinal cord injury),
  • transcutaneous pacing (a painful bridge that needs sedation), and
  • glucagon if the cause is a beta-blocker overdose — glucagon is also listed for CCB overdose in the algorithm, but IV calcium is the direct antidote in CCB poisoning.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Which drug overdoses have a specific antidote in refractory bradycardia, and what is it in each?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back:
• Beta-blocker overdose — glucagon, which bypasses the β-receptor to raise rate, contractility and AV conduction, when atropine and pacing are insufficient.
  • Calcium-channel-blocker overdose — IV calcium is the direct antidote, with high-dose insulin for myocardial depression; glucagon is an adjunct here, not the antidote.
  • Digoxin toxicity — digoxin-specific antibody fragments.
The peri-arrest algorithm lists glucagon for either overdose (Resus Council UK).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is transcutaneous pacing, and what are its drawbacks?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Defibrillator pads on the chest delivering pacing — it is fast but painful and needs sedation.It is a bridge only, used until a more definitive measure is available.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is transvenous pacing, and how does it compare to transcutaneous?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: A pacing wire passed via the subclavian/femoral/IJV to the right ventricle. It is more reliable than transcutaneous pacing and is used as a bridge to a permanent device (seek expert help).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is the definitive treatment for persistent/irreversible bradycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: A permanent pacemaker.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: If a bradycardic patient has NO adverse features, how is management decided?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back:
Assess asystole risk.
  • If high (Mobitz II, CHB + broad QRS, pauses >3s, recent asystole) → treat as unstable.
  • If low risk → observe and monitor with regular review.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What are the two forms of temporary pacing, and the role of each?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Transcutaneous (defibrillator pads on the chest — fast, painful, needs sedation, bridge only) and transvenous (pacing wire via subclavian/femoral to the RV — more reliable, used while awaiting a permanent device).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: List the indications for a permanent pacemaker.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back:
• Symptomatic sinus bradycardia (reversible causes excluded),
  • symptomatic sick sinus syndrome,
  • Mobitz II AV block,
  • complete (3rd-degree) heart block,
  • bifascicular/trifascicular block with symptoms,
  • recurrent Stokes-Adams attacks, and
  • carotid sinus hypersensitivity with recurrent syncope.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is the difference between a VVI and a DDD pacemaker?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: VVI paces and senses the ventricle only. DDD paces both the atrium and ventricle, maintaining AV synchrony (the atrial kick), which is important in impaired LV function.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Why is a permanent pacemaker indicated in Mobitz II regardless of symptoms?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Mobitz II (fixed PR then sudden dropped beat) carries a HIGH risk of progression to complete heart block, so a permanent pacemaker is indicated even if the patient is asymptomatic, provided reversible causes (drugs, ischaemia, electrolytes) have been excluded and corrected (ESC).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Compare the prognosis and escape rhythm of complete heart block in anterior MI vs inferior MI.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back:
• Anterior MI + CHB = His-Purkinje level, broad QRS, unreliable escape 30–40 bpm → urgent pacing; worse prognosis.
  • Inferior MI + AV block = AV nodal level, narrow QRS, usually transient, often responds to atropine and resolves with reperfusion; less alarming than anterior.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What are the early complications of permanent pacemaker insertion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back:
• Pneumothorax — from subclavian puncture; check the post-procedure CXR
  • Lead displacement — loss of capture or sensing, commonest in the first weeks
  • Pocket haematoma — especially in anticoagulated patients
  • Pocket-site infection

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What are the late complications of a permanent pacemaker?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back:
• Device / lead infection — can seed the leads and cause infective endocarditis
  • Lead fracture or insulation failure
  • Pacemaker syndrome — loss of AV synchrony with VVI pacing
  • Twiddler's syndrome — the patient rotates the generator in its pocket, twisting and dislodging the leads

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is pacemaker syndrome, and how is it treated?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back:
Symptoms caused by loss of AV synchrony in a VVI (single-chamber ventricular) paced patient — the atria contract against closed AV valves.
Features: fatigue, dizziness, breathlessness, and a sensation of neck pulsation from cannon A waves.Treatment: upgrade to a dual-chamber (DDD) device to restore the atrial kick.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Why can an infected pacing system not be treated with antibiotics alone?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back:
Because the hardware itself is colonised — bacteria form biofilm on the generator and leads, which antibiotics cannot penetrate.
It requires complete system extraction (generator and leads) plus antibiotics.Left untreated it can progress to lead-related infective endocarditis.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.front: What is the cardiac conducting system made of, and is the heartbeat neurogenic or myogenic?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.back: It is made of specialised (modified) cardiomyocytes — not nervous tissue; the heartbeat is myogenic (intrinsic), only modulated by autonomic nerves.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.front: List the components of the conduction pathway in order.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.back: SA node → AV node → Bundle of His → left and right bundle branches → Purkinje fibres → ventricular myocardium.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.front: Where is the SA node and what is its role?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.back: In the wall of the right atrium near the SVC/crista terminalis; it is the pacemaker (~60–100/min), made of small pale ovoid nodal (P) cells plus spindle-shaped transitional (T) cells with few myofibrils in fibrous stroma.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.front: Where is the AV node and what is its key function?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.back: In the floor of the right atrium (triangle of Koch, near the coronary sinus); it delays the impulse (~0.1 s) so the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.front: Why is the Bundle of His so important anatomically?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.back: It penetrates the fibrous skeleton and is the only electrical connection between the atria and ventricles (the fibrous skeleton insulates them elsewhere).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.front: Describe the histology of Purkinje fibres.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.back: Large, pale cells with glycogen-rich (clear) cytoplasm, sparse myofibrils pushed to the periphery, abundant gap junctions, located subendocardially — specialised for rapid conduction.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.front: Distinguish Mobitz I and Mobitz II second-degree AV block.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.back:
• Mobitz I (Wenckebach): progressive PR prolongation until a QRS is dropped — block in the AV node, usually benign and vagally mediated.
  • Mobitz II: constant PR with sudden dropped beats — block infranodal (His-Purkinje), often broad QRS with a high risk of progression to complete block, so it needs a pacemaker.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.front: Why do nodal cells have few myofibrils?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.back: Because they are specialised for generating and conducting impulses (signalling), not for contraction.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.front: What is the pacemaker hierarchy and its rates?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.back: SA node (~60–100/min) > AV node (~40–60) > His–Purkinje/ventricle (~20–40); if a higher pacemaker fails, a lower one takes over as an escape rhythm.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.front: How do the vagus and sympathetic nerves affect the conduction system?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.back: The vagus (parasympathetic) slows SA firing and AV conduction (↓ heart rate); the sympathetic speeds them (↑ heart rate and contractility).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.front: Which stain highlights the glycogen of Purkinje fibres?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.back: PAS (periodic acid–Schiff).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.front: What is heart block, and which structures are usually involved?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.back: Impaired AV conduction (1st, 2nd or 3rd/complete degree) due to disease of the AV node or Bundle of His.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.front: What is the accessory pathway in Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.back: The Bundle of Kent — an abnormal muscular connection that bypasses the AV node, causing pre-excitation (delta wave) and re-entry tachycardia.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.front: Why must AV-nodal blocking drugs be avoided in WPW with atrial fibrillation?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.back: Blocking the AV node (adenosine, verapamil/diltiazem, digoxin, beta-blockers) diverts rapid atrial impulses down the accessory pathway, risking very fast ventricular rates and degeneration to ventricular fibrillation; use flecainide or procainamide, or DC cardioversion if unstable.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.front: What ion current underlies the SA node's spontaneous depolarisation?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.back: The 'funny' current (If), a slow inward mixed Na+/K+ cation current through HCN channels activated on hyperpolarisation, which produces the unstable, gradually rising phase-4 pacemaker potential. (The nodal upstroke itself is L-type Ca2+, not fast Na+.)

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.front: What is the triangle of Koch and why does it matter?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.back: An anatomical landmark in the floor of the right atrium (bounded by the tricuspid annulus, coronary sinus and tendon of Todaro) marking the location of the AV node — important to avoid during ablation.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.front: Why is the internodal conduction faster than ordinary atrial muscle?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.back: Preferential atrial conduction (via fibre orientation — discrete anatomical internodal tracts are debated) carries the impulse from the SA to the AV node faster than ordinary atrial muscle; Bachmann's bundle carries it to the left atrium.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.front: What distinguishes nodal (P) cells from Purkinje cells histologically?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.back: Nodal cells are small, pale and fusiform with very few myofibrils; Purkinje cells are large, pale and glycogen-rich with peripheral myofibrils and abundant gap junctions.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.front: Rank conduction velocity through the parts of the conducting system.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.back: Purkinje fibres/His bundle are fastest (~2–4 m/s), then atrial and ventricular muscle, and the AV node is slowest (~0.05 m/s) — the source of the physiological AV delay. This velocity order is separate from the pacemaker-rate hierarchy.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.front: Which artery usually supplies the SA and AV nodes?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.back: The SA nodal artery arises from the RCA in ~60% and the left circumflex in ~40%; the AV nodal artery arises from the RCA in ~90% (right-dominant hearts) — so inferior (RCA) MIs classically cause AV nodal block.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.front: Why does the impulse spread from apex to base in the ventricles?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.back: Purkinje fibres deliver the impulse to the apex first, so contraction begins there and moves toward the base/outflow, ejecting blood efficiently.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.front: How do you distinguish a true abdominal aortic aneurysm from a mass that merely transmits the aortic pulse?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.back: An AAA is expansile — the palpating fingers are pushed outward / apart as well as up. A mass overlying the aorta only transmits the pulse and pushes the fingers upward, not apart.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.front: Where is an abdominal aortic aneurysm palpated?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.back: In the midline, above the umbilicus (epigastric / central). The infrarenal aorta bifurcates at about L4 (the level of the umbilicus), so most AAAs are felt above it.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.front: What is the classic triad of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.back:
• Abdominal / back / flank pain
  • a pulsatile (expansile) mass
  • and hypotension / collapse
In an older arteriopath with sudden pain and shock, assume a ruptured AAA until excluded.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.front: An unstable patient has a suspected ruptured AAA. Should they go to CT first?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.back: No. An unstable patient with a known or suspected AAA goes straight to theatre / vascular surgery with the major-haemorrhage protocol activated. CT angiography is only for the stable patient.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.front: At what diameter is an abdominal aortic aneurysm usually offered elective repair?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.back: At ≥5.5 cm, or if it is symptomatic / tender or growing rapidly (>1 cm per year). Below 5.5 cm and asymptomatic, it is kept under ultrasound surveillance.
A one-off abdominal ultrasound offered to men in the year they turn 65. Detected aneurysms enter a surveillance programme, with the interval determined by diameter.
A tender or rapidly expanding aneurysm causing pain (abdominal / back) but without haemodynamic collapse. It is a surgical emergency needing urgent repair, as it may rupture at any time.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.front: Which non-aortic masses classically transmit the aortic pulse and can be mistaken for an AAA?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.back: A pancreatic mass (epigastric, weight loss, jaundice), a gastric tumour, para-aortic / retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy (lymphoma), and a horseshoe or polycystic kidney — all lie over the aorta but are not expansile.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.front: A ballotable flank mass with haematuria and weight loss transmits the aortic pulse. What is the likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.back: A renal mass — classically renal cell carcinoma (the triad of flank mass, haematuria and loin pain). It is ballotable and bimanually palpable, unlike an expansile midline AAA.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.front: What is an aortoenteric fistula and how does it present?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.back: An abnormal communication between the aorta (usually a known AAA or aortic graft) and the bowel (typically duodenum), presenting as a massive gastrointestinal bleed — often a self-limiting ‘herald’ bleed before catastrophic haemorrhage.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.front: What is 'trash foot' in the context of an AAA?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.back: Distal embolisation of mural thrombus from the aneurysm sac, showering the toes / feet with debris → blue toes, livedo and digital ischaemia with preserved proximal pulses. A warning sign of an unstable aneurysm.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.front: Which aneurysms and conditions are associated with an AAA?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.back:
• Popliteal and femoral artery aneurysms (always palpate these pulses)
  • a first-degree family history
  • smoking and hypertension
  • and connective-tissue disease (Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos)
Inflammatory AAA is a distinct subtype.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.front: How does aortic dissection differ from an AAA in presentation?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.back: Dissection gives sudden tearing chest / interscapular pain radiating, often with an inter-arm blood-pressure difference or new aortic regurgitation; it may extend into the abdomen. An AAA is a focal expansile swelling that is dangerous when it ruptures.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.front: What is the first-line imaging to confirm and size a suspected AAA?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.back: Abdominal ultrasound — quick, bedside and accurate for diameter. A CT angiogram then defines morphology and the relationship to the renal / iliac vessels to plan repair in the stable patient.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.front: What defines an abdominal aortic aneurysm by diameter?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.back: An aortic diameter ≥3 cm (or >1.5× the expected normal). Normal infrarenal aorta is roughly 2 cm; 3–5.4 cm is under surveillance and ≥5.5 cm is repair territory.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.front: Why might a normal aorta be palpable, and how do you avoid over-diagnosing an AAA?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.back: In a thin, well person the normal aortic pulsation is easily felt. The distinction is that it is not expansile (fingers not pushed apart) and ultrasound shows a normal-calibre (<3 cm) aorta.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.front: What are the two elective repair options for an AAA?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.back:
• EVAR (endovascular aneurysm repair — a stent-graft via the femoral arteries)
  • and open surgical repair (laparotomy and graft)
Choice depends on anatomy, fitness and aneurysm morphology.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.front: A pulsatile epigastric mass is found with painless jaundice and weight loss. What is the likely cause and next test?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.back: A pancreatic head cancer transmitting the aortic pulse — the epigastric mass, painless obstructive jaundice and weight loss are the clue. Confirm with a CT abdomen / pancreas, not vascular imaging.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What is a thoracic aortic aneurysm, and why does location matter?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Dilatation of the thoracic aorta.Location matters — it drives both the symptoms (compression syndromes) and the repair thresholds.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What proportion of TAAs are at the ascending aorta/root, what causes them, and what is the repair threshold?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: 60%. Most common causes — Marfan's, bicuspid AV, syphilis. Repair threshold ≥5.5 cm (lower in CT disease).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What proportion of TAAs involve the aortic arch, and what features and threshold apply?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: 10%. Neck pain; high cerebral ischaemia risk during repair. Threshold ≥5.5 cm.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What proportion of TAAs are in the descending aorta, what causes them, and what is the threshold and preferred repair?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: ~35–40%. Posterior thoracic pain; atherosclerosis/dissection. Higher threshold — ≥5.5 cm if TEVAR is feasible, ≥6 cm if open repair is needed; prefer TEVAR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What proportion of TAAs are thoracoabdominal, and what is notable about repair?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: ~10% — but a subset of descending disease that extends below the diaphragm, not a separate 10% on top. Complex repair.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: How does TAA compare with AAA in terms of definition, physics, aetiology, and screening?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Shared definition (localised dilatation) and Laplace physics; different aetiology (CT disease/bicuspid/syphilis vs atherosclerosis) and different screening policy (no national TAA screening programme).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What is a true aneurysm, and which layers are involved?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: All 3 layers (intima, media, adventitia) are intact but dilated.This describes most TAAs.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What is a false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm), and what causes it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Intima + media rupture → blood contained only by adventitia. Caused by trauma, surgery, infection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What is a dissecting aneurysm?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Blood tracks into the tunica media via an intimal tear (see separate Aortic Dissection note).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What is the mechanism of TAA formation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Tunica media degeneration → loss of tensile strength → dilatation → increased wall tension (Laplace) → further dilatation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: List the main TAA-specific causes.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back:
• Connective-tissue disease (Marfan's [FBN1], Loeys-Dietz, vascular Ehlers-Danlos [COL3A1])
  • Turner syndrome
  • bicuspid aortic valve (a strong risk factor — most BAV patients develop aortic dilatation)
  • tertiary syphilis (classic ascending aneurysm — exam favourite)
  • trauma
  • aortic dissection
  • Takayasu's / giant cell arteritis

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: Why do patients with a bicuspid aortic valve need lifelong aortic surveillance?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: A large proportion develop ascending aortic dilatation — the aortopathy is part of the condition, not just a consequence of the valve.Hence lifelong surveillance and a lower repair threshold.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: Which TAA cause is the classic ascending aneurysm and an exam favourite?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Tertiary syphilis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What are the shared risk factors for TAA (with AAA)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back:
• Hypertension (key modifiable RF)
  • smoking
  • atherosclerosis
  • male sex
  • advanced age
  • family history
  • high BMI

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What is 'the discriminator' between TAA and AAA aetiology?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: TAA → think degenerative disease first (age, hypertension, atherosclerosis), but actively look for Marfan's / Loeys-Dietz / bicuspid AV / syphilis. AAA → think atherosclerosis.This contrast is frequently tested.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: How do most TAAs present?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Most are asymptomatic — found incidentally on CXR or cross-sectional imaging.There is no national screening programme.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What pain location corresponds to each TAA segment?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back:
• Ascending aorta → anterior chest pain
  • aortic arch → neck pain
  • descending aorta → posterior thoracic/back pain

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What compression syndrome arises from trachea/left bronchus involvement?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Cough, SOB, stridor.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What does LEFT recurrent laryngeal nerve compression cause in TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Hoarse voice.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What does oesophageal compression cause in TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Dysphagia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What does SVC compression cause in TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Distended neck veins, facial oedema, SVC obstruction syndrome.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What does aortic valve involvement cause in TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Aortic regurgitation → heart failure signs.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What does spinal compression cause in TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Back pain.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What are the key differentials for TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: PE, ACS, pneumothorax, aortic dissection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What routine bloods are taken in TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: FBC, U&Es, clotting.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What is the role of ECG in TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Exclude ACS; may show LVH from chronic HTN.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What CXR findings are seen in TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Widened mediastinal silhouette, enlarged aortic knob, tracheal deviation — often the incidental finding.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: Which is the preferred/definitive imaging modality in TAA, and what does it provide?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: CT angiogram — gives anatomy, size, extent, and TEVAR suitability.It is the definitive investigation for size, extent and surgical planning.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What does echo assess in TAA, and which modality is used for Marfan surveillance?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: TTE assesses aortic root diameter, valve involvement and AR, and is first-line surveillance in all Marfan's patients.TOE is reserved for peri-operative use and suspected dissection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What medical management applies to all TAA patients?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back:
• BP control with a beta-blocker (± ARB/losartan in Marfan) — key modifiable factor
  • statin and smoking cessation
  • optimise diabetes, hyperlipidaemia, weight
(antiplatelet only for coexistent atherosclerosis, not TAA itself).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What is the surgical threshold and procedure for an ascending/root TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back:
• Threshold ≥5.5 cm for degenerative disease
  • ≥5 cm in Marfan (≥4.5 cm with risk factors)
  • ≥4.5 cm in Loeys-Dietz
  • ≥4.5 cm if the patient is already having aortic valve surgery
Bicuspid AV is usually still ≥5.5 cm, falling to ≥5 cm only for the root phenotype or with risk factors. Dacron graft replacement; Bentall procedure if the root is involved (graft + prosthetic aortic valve).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What is the surgical threshold and procedure for an aortic arch TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Threshold ≥5.5 cm. Open graft replacement of the arch; the key risk is stroke from cerebral ischaemia or embolism while the great vessels are handled.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What is the surgical threshold and preferred procedure for a descending TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Threshold ≥5.5 cm if TEVAR is feasible, ≥6 cm if open repair is required. TEVAR (endovascular) is preferred where the anatomy allows.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: Why is the repair threshold lower in Marfan and Loeys-Dietz — and where does bicuspid AV actually sit?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: The media is structurally weaker, so dissection happens at smaller diameters — operate earlier: Marfan ≥5 cm (≥4.5 cm with risk factors), Loeys-Dietz ≥4.5 cm. Bicuspid AV is the trap: it is usually still ≥5.5 cm, dropping to ≥5 cm only for the root phenotype or with risk factors.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What is the Bentall procedure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Aortic root replacement + prosthetic valve — a key eponym to know.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: How is TEVAR performed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: A stent graft is delivered via catheter and deployed across the descending TAA, excluding the aneurysm from circulation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What happens when a TAA ruptures, and what determines the clinical picture?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Rupture causes bleeding into the mediastinum, with high mortality. The site of bleeding determines the clinical picture.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What does a ruptured TAA bleeding into the oesophagus, airway/lungs, or pericardial cavity each cause?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back:
• Oesophagus → haematemesis
  • airway/lungs → haemoptysis
  • pericardial cavity → cardiac tamponade

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What are the symptoms of a ruptured TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back:
• Severe acute-onset chest or back pain
  • collapse/syncope
  • haematemesis/haemoptysis (site-dependent)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What are the signs of a ruptured TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Haemodynamic instability — tachycardia + hypotension; signs of tamponade (raised JVP, muffled sounds, hypotension).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What is the management of a ruptured TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Emergency repair — open graft replacement for ascending/arch rupture (cardiac surgery); emergency TEVAR is usually preferred for a ruptured descending TAA where the anatomy allows.High mortality either way.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: Why does repair of a descending thoracic aortic aneurysm risk paraplegia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back:
The descending aorta gives off the intercostal arteries, which include the artery of Adamkiewicz — the dominant feeder of the anterior spinal artery.
Open repair sacrifices them and TEVAR covers them with the stent graft → anterior spinal artery territory infarction → paraplegia (with dorsal columns relatively spared).Risk is highest with long covered segments and previous AAA repair.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: How is spinal cord ischaemia prevented and treated during thoracic aortic repair?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back:
CSF drainage.
Spinal cord perfusion pressure = mean arterial pressure − CSF pressure. Draining CSF lowers the CSF pressure, so cord perfusion improves.Used both prophylactically in high-risk cases and therapeutically if paraplegia develops, alongside maintaining an adequate MAP.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What are the segment-specific risks of thoracic aortic aneurysm repair?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back:
• Ascending / Bentall: a prosthetic valve brings lifelong anticoagulation.
  • Arch: stroke — cerebral ischaemia or embolism while the great vessels are handled.
  • Descending (open or TEVAR): spinal cord ischaemia / paraplegia.
  • TEVAR generally: endoleak, graft migration, lifelong imaging surveillance, and retrograde type A dissection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: A patient is newly diagnosed with a thoracic aortic aneurysm. Why does this matter for their family?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back:
Because a large share of TAA is genetic — Marfan, Loeys-Dietz, vascular Ehlers-Danlos, bicuspid aortic valve, and familial TAA. Unlike AAA, the diagnosis is a finding about the family, not just the patient.
Action: image first-degree relatives (echo ± CT/MR aorta) and refer for genetic testing and counselling where a syndromic cause is suspected.There is no national screening programme for TAA, so relatives are only found if someone thinks of it.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Why is hypertension called the 'silent killer'?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: It is a sustained elevation of BP that is usually asymptomatic until end-organ damage occurs.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: How is hypertension diagnosed, and why is the confirmation step needed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Via clinic measurement, then confirmed with ABPM or HBPM (ambulatory/home) to exclude the white-coat effect.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What are the clinic BP and ABPM/HBPM thresholds for Stage 1 hypertension, and when is it treated?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Clinic ≥140/90, ABPM/HBPM ≥135/85. Treat if aged under 80 with target organ damage, established CVD, renal disease, diabetes (type 1 or 2), or a 10-year CV risk ≥10% (NICE). If aged 80 and over, treat stage 1 when clinic BP is over 150/90 (NICE). Also consider treatment in adults under 60 even if 10-year risk is below 10%, since 10-year risk underestimates lifetime risk (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What are the Stage 2 hypertension thresholds, and what is the treatment rule?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Clinic ≥160/100, ABPM/HBPM ≥150/95. Offer treatment regardless of other factors.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What defines Stage 3 / Severe hypertension, and what is the action?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
Clinic systolic ≥180 or diastolic ≥120. Assess for target organ damage as soon as possible, then three branches:
  • retinal haemorrhage/papilloedema or life-threatening symptoms → same-day referral (emergency)
  • target organ damage → start treatment immediately, no ABPM
  • neither → repeat clinic BP or arrange ABPM/HBPM with review within 7 days

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: State the key diagnostic rule linking clinic BP to confirmation and treatment threshold.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Clinic BP 140/90–180/120 → confirm with ABPM or HBPM before diagnosing. Treat to the lower ambulatory threshold. White-coat hypertension is common — ABPM prevents over-treatment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What proportion of hypertension is primary/essential, and what characterises it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: ~90%. No identifiable cause; polygenic (multiple genes + lifestyle).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: List the risk factors for primary hypertension.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• Age
  • obesity
  • high salt diet
  • alcohol
  • sedentary lifestyle
  • smoking
  • family history

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What is the proposed mechanism of primary hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• Increased RAAS activity
  • sympathetic overdrive
  • and impaired renal sodium excretion

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What is the commonest category of secondary hypertension, and which renal causes are included?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Renal (traditionally quoted as ~80% of secondary) — CKD, renovascular disease (RAS — especially if treatment-resistant), polycystic kidney disease. Note that primary aldosteronism is increasingly recognised as the commonest single secondary cause.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: List the endocrine causes of secondary hypertension.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• Conn's syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism)
  • phaeochromocytoma
  • Cushing's
  • acromegaly
  • and thyroid disease (hyper- or hypothyroidism)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Which 'other' (non-renal, non-endocrine) causes of secondary hypertension are listed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• Coarctation of the aorta (young patients)
  • pre-eclampsia
  • OSA

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Which drugs can cause secondary hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• NSAIDs
  • oestrogen (OCP)
  • alcohol
  • liquorice
  • cocaine
  • ciclosporin

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: When should you 'think secondary' hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Young, Resistant (≥3 drugs), or Sudden onset — especially patients under 40, those with refractory HTN, or an identifiable clinical clue (e.g. hypokalaemia → Conn's; episodic headache/sweating/palpitations → phaeochromocytoma).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Is primary hypertension symptomatic, and what do symptoms usually signify?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: It is largely asymptomatic; symptoms usually signify end-organ damage or an underlying secondary cause.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What are the neurological red flags of accelerated/malignant hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• Headache (occipital, morning)
  • visual disturbance
  • seizures
  • confusion
  • encephalopathy

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What retinal red flag confirms malignant hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Papilloedema, retinal haemorrhages, exudates — confirm malignant HTN.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What are the cardiac and renal red flags of malignant hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• Cardiac: chest pain (ACS / aortic dissection), breathlessness (acute LVF)
  • Renal: haematuria, oliguria — AKI from malignant HTN

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Renal/RAS as a secondary cause: what symptoms/signs and what clue?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• Symptoms/signs: renal bruit, peripheral oedema, resistant HTN
  • Clue: rising Cr on ACEi, asymmetric kidneys on USS

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Conn's syndrome as a secondary cause: what symptoms and what clue?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• Symptoms: muscle weakness, polyuria, cramps
  • Clue: hypokalaemia + HTN → primary hyperaldosteronism until proven otherwise

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Phaeochromocytoma as a secondary cause: what symptoms and what clue?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• Symptoms: episodic headache, sweating, palpitations, pallor
  • Clue: paroxysmal BP spikes; plasma free metanephrines, or 24h urinary fractionated metanephrines (not catecholamines)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Cushing's as a secondary cause: what symptoms and what clue?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• Symptoms: central obesity, striae, buffalo hump, moon face
  • Clue: 24h urinary free cortisol / overnight dexamethasone suppression

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Coarctation as a secondary cause: what symptoms and what clue?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• Symptoms: young patient, radiofemoral delay, weak femoral pulses
  • Clue: BP differential arms vs legs; chest X-ray rib notching

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Pre-eclampsia as a secondary cause: what symptoms and what clue?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• Symptoms: new HTN after 20 weeks plus proteinuria or other maternal organ dysfunction — proteinuria is not required and oedema is no longer part of the definition (NICE); headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain
  • Clue: pregnancy — screen for HELLP (haemolysis, raised LFTs, low platelets)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: On fundoscopy, how does a normal optic disc differ from papilloedema, and what does papilloedema indicate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Normal optic disc has a sharp disc margin; papilloedema has a blurred disc margin. Here it indicates malignant/accelerated hypertension (grade IV Keith-Wagener retinopathy) — it may coexist with hypertensive encephalopathy but is not primarily a raised-ICP sign.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What fundoscopy features make up hypertensive retinopathy, and which grade signifies a hypertensive emergency?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Haemorrhage (grade III), hard exudates (lipid deposits), soft exudates (cotton-wool spots = micro-infarcts), microaneurysms; grade III/IV = hypertensive emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Step 1 of diagnosis — how is the clinic measurement performed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
Clinic measurement ≥140/90:
  • use a validated device
  • check both arms (use the higher if they differ by >15 mmHg)
  • take a second reading and record the LOWER of the last two (NICE does not average)
If clinic BP is 140/90–180/120, confirm the diagnosis with ABPM (or HBPM if ABPM is declined or not tolerated) — not with a repeat clinic visit (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: How are ABPM and HBPM performed, and which threshold is used to diagnose?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• ABPM: at least 2 measurements per hour during waking hours; use the average of at least 14 readings
  • HBPM: two consecutive readings at least 1 minute apart, twice daily, for 4–7 days — discard day 1 and average the rest (NICE)
Diagnose using the lower ambulatory threshold (≥135/85 Stage 1).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: In the work-up, what are the two parallel goals?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• Assess end-organ damage
  • and identify secondary causes

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Which investigations assess end-organ damage in hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• Urine ACR (nephropathy/proteinuria)
  • U&E/Cr/eGFR (CKD, baseline before ACEi)
  • ECG (LVH — Sokolow-Lyon criteria, AF)
  • fundoscopy (retinopathy grading — Keith-Wagener)
  • fasting glucose/HbA1c (T2DM)
  • lipid profile (CV risk assessment)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Which investigations help identify secondary causes of hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• U&E (low K+ suggests Conn's or Cushing's)
  • aldosterone:renin ratio (Conn's if low K+ or resistant HTN — but a normal potassium does not exclude it, as most primary aldosteronism is normokalaemic)
  • plasma free metanephrines or 24h urinary fractionated metanephrines — not catecholamines (phaeochromocytoma)
  • renal USS ± Doppler (RAS, polycystic kidney disease)
  • overnight dexamethasone suppression (Cushing's)
  • TFTs (hypo/hyperthyroidism)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: How is QRISK3 used in hypertension management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Calculate the 10-year cardiovascular risk. If ≥10% → offer atorvastatin 20 mg (primary prevention). If already diagnosed with CVD → statin regardless of risk score, at the secondary-prevention dose of atorvastatin 80 mg (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Why is drug choice in hypertension driven by age and ethnicity?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: They predict renin status — the mechanism that determines which drug class works best.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Explain the renin logic that makes the ACD algorithm memorable.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• Younger/Caucasian = high-renin → RAAS-dependent → ACEi/ARB works
  • Older/Black African/Caribbean = low-renin → volume-dependent → CCB or diuretic works

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Step 1 monotherapy: what is first-line for a patient <55 yrs and not Black African/Caribbean?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: A — ACEi or ARB (e.g. ramipril or losartan); a high-renin state where RAAS blockade is most effective. T2DM at any age/ethnicity → A. In people of black African or African–Caribbean family origin, choose an ARB in preference to an ACEi (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Step 1 monotherapy: what is first-line for a patient ≥55 yrs or Black African/Caribbean (any age)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: C — calcium channel blocker (e.g. amlodipine, a dihydropyridine); a low-renin state where volume/vascular tone reduction is most effective.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What is the Step 2 (two-drug) combination in hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Add a CCB or a thiazide-like diuretic to the ACEi/ARB — NICE offers a choice, not a preference; a thiazide-like diuretic suits fluid overload or CCB intolerance (NICE). In people of black African or African–Caribbean family origin, choose an ARB in preference to an ACEi (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What is the Step 3 (three-drug) regimen, and what must be done before escalating?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: A + C + D — confirm adherence before escalating.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Step 4 resistant HTN (still ≥140/90 on A+C+D, adherence confirmed): what is added if K+ ≤4.5 mmol/L?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Add spironolactone 25 mg (aldosterone antagonist); check U&E before and 1 month after — risk of hyperkalaemia. Especially effective if a Conn's component is suspected.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Step 4 resistant HTN: what is added if K+ >4.5 mmol/L?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Add an alpha-blocker (doxazosin) or beta-blocker (bisoprolol); beta-blockers are less preferred due to metabolic side effects. Seek specialist advice.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What non-pharmacological measures apply at all stages of hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• Salt restriction (<6g/day)
  • DASH diet
  • aerobic exercise ≥150 min/week
  • weight loss
  • limit alcohol
  • stop smoking

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Class A — ACEi: give examples, key side effects, and key contraindications/cautions.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• Examples: ramipril, lisinopril, perindopril
  • Side effects: dry cough (10–15%), hyperkalaemia, angioedema (rare but serious), 1st-dose hypotension, raised Cr
  • Absolute CI: bilateral RAS, pregnancy
  • Caution: aortic stenosis, and CKD
Check U&E and eGFR before starting and 1–2 weeks after starting and after each dose increase (NICE). A creatinine rise under 30% or an eGFR fall under 25% is acceptable — recheck in 1–2 weeks. If creatinine rises ≥30% or eGFR falls ≥25%, look for another cause (volume depletion, NSAIDs) and, if none is found, reduce the dose or stop. Do not start if K+ is above 5.0 mmol/L; stop if K+ reaches 6.0 mmol/L (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Class A — ARB: examples, key side effects, and contraindications.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• Examples: losartan, candesartan, valsartan
  • Side effects: hyperkalaemia, raised Cr (no cough — use if ACEi cough)
  • CI: bilateral RAS, pregnancy; same CI profile as ACEi

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Class C — CCB (dihydropyridine): examples, key side effects, and caution.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• Examples: amlodipine, felodipine
  • Side effects: ankle oedema (most common), flushing, headache, reflex tachycardia
Note: amlodipine and felodipine are SAFE in HFrEF — it is the non-dihydropyridines (verapamil, diltiazem) that are negative inotropes and avoided in HFrEF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Class D — thiazide-like diuretic: examples, key side effects, and key CI/caution.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• Examples: indapamide, chlortalidone
  • Side effects: low K+, low Na+, raised urate (gout attacks), raised glucose, raised cholesterol, impotence
  • CI/caution: gout (relative CI); caution in T2DM

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Step 4 — aldosterone antagonist: example, key side effects, and key CI/caution.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• Spironolactone 25–50 mg
  • Side effects: hyperkalaemia, gynaecomastia (men), menstrual irregularity
  • CI/caution: K+ >4.5 before starting; eGFR <45 → caution; monitor U&E

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Alpha-blocker in hypertension: example, key side effect, and when it is useful.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• Doxazosin
  • Side effect: postural hypotension (1st dose), dizziness
  • Useful if BPH co-exists; caution with urinary incontinence

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Beta-blocker in hypertension: examples, key side effects, and cautions.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• Bisoprolol, atenolol
  • Side effects: fatigue, cold extremities, impotence, raised glucose, masks hypoglycaemia
  • Caution: asthma/COPD (relative); avoid abrupt cessation

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Which antihypertensives are used in pregnancy, and which classes are absolutely contraindicated?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• Labetalol first-line
  • modified-release nifedipine if labetalol is unsuitable
  • methyldopa if both are unsuitable (NICE)
Target BP in pregnancy is 135/85 (NICE). ACEi and ARBs are teratogenic — absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What are the clinic and ABPM/HBPM BP targets for patients <80 years?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Clinic <140/90; ABPM/HBPM <135/85.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What are the clinic and ABPM/HBPM BP targets for patients ≥80 years?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Clinic <150/90; ABPM/HBPM <145/85.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What is the clinic BP target for patients with CKD / Diabetes / CVD?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: <140/90 generally. Tighten to <130/80 only in CKD with ACR ≥70 mg/mmol (NICE). Type 2 diabetes takes the same target as everyone else — <140/90 (NICE); established CVD on its own does not lower the target.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Why is the BP target less aggressive in the elderly (>80 yrs)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Aggressive lowering risks falls, syncope and hypoperfusion, so the clinic target is <150/90 (ABPM/HBPM <145/85) regardless of established CVD (NICE). Only CKD with ACR ≥70 mg/mmol tightens the target to <130/80 (NICE); use clinical judgement in frailty or multimorbidity.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: How is a malignant / accelerated hypertensive emergency defined?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: BP ≥180/120 + evidence of end-organ damage. Severity is defined by the damage, not the number alone.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: In a hypertensive emergency, what are the encephalopathy/ICH features and the investigation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Headache, confusion, seizures, focal neurology — CT head urgently.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: In a hypertensive emergency, what retinal damage is seen and how is it confirmed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Papilloedema, flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots — fundoscopy confirms malignant HTN.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: In a hypertensive emergency, what are the ACS/aortic dissection features and management trigger?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Chest pain — ECG, troponin, CXR. If dissection → IV labetalol urgently.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: In a hypertensive emergency, what are the AKI / acute LVF features and investigations?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Raised Cr, haematuria, pulmonary oedema — U&E, CXR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Why must BP be lowered slowly in a hypertensive emergency, and what is the target rate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Rapid reduction causes cerebral and renal hypoperfusion. Reduce MAP by no more than 25% in the first hour, then cautiously towards 160/100 over 2–6 hours. Exception: acute aortic dissection needs rapid lowering to systolic 100–120 mmHg within about 20 minutes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Which IV agents are used in a hypertensive emergency (ITU/HDU setting)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• Labetalol IV (α and β blocker; first-line for most emergencies including dissection and pregnancy — but never before adequate alpha-blockade in suspected phaeochromocytoma, as unopposed alpha stimulation can precipitate a crisis)
  • GTN infusion (ACS / acute LVF component)
  • hydralazine IV (direct vasodilator, used in pregnancy/pre-eclampsia)
  • esmolol (very short-acting beta-blocker, critical-care setting)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What assessment and monitoring is done in a hypertensive emergency?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• Same-day referral to specialist centre
  • fundoscopy (grade retinopathy, confirms malignant)
  • U&E, Cr (baseline + AKI)
  • urinalysis / ACR (renal damage)
  • ECG (LVH, ischaemia)
  • CXR (pulmonary oedema, widened mediastinum for dissection)
  • CT head if neurological symptoms

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: On fundoscopy, what do cotton-wool spots represent and which retinopathy grade do they mark?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Soft exudates from retinal micro-infarcts due to arteriolar occlusion; a hallmark of grade III–IV hypertensive retinopathy in a hypertensive emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What are the cerebrovascular complications of untreated hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• Stroke (ischaemic and haemorrhagic)
  • TIA
  • vascular dementia
  • hypertensive encephalopathy

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What are the cardiac complications of untreated hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• LVH → heart failure (HFpEF)
  • IHD
  • AF
  • sudden cardiac death

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What are the renal complications of untreated hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: CKD, nephrosclerosis, proteinuria — hypertension is a major cause of end-stage kidney disease (diabetes is the commonest cause in the UK).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What are the retinal and vascular complications of untreated hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• Retinal: hypertensive retinopathy (grades 1–4) — grade 3/4 = malignant HTN
  • Vascular: PAD, AAA, aortic dissection, accelerated atherosclerosis

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Exam pearl: why does ACEi-induced dry cough occur, and what is the switch?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: ACEi dry cough in 10–15% → switch to ARB (same mechanism, no bradykinin accumulation → no cough).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Exam pearl: why is an ACEi contraindicated in bilateral renal artery stenosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: It reduces GFR by removing the efferent arteriolar tone that maintains filtration pressure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Exam pearl: which electrolyte/clinical combination should make you think Conn's, and what is the screening test?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Low K+ + HTN → think Conn's (primary hyperaldosteronism). The aldosterone:renin ratio is the screening test.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: A patient has a clinic BP of 190/125. What are the three possible branches of management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
• 1 · Same-day specialist referral — if there is retinal haemorrhage or papilloedema (accelerated hypertension), or life-threatening symptoms (new confusion, chest pain, signs of heart failure, AKI), or suspected phaeochromocytoma — labile or postural hypotension, headache, palpitations, pallor, abdominal pain or sweating (NICE).
  • 2 · Target organ damage found — start antihypertensive treatment immediately, without waiting for ABPM/HBPM.
  • 3 · No target organ damage — repeat clinic BP within 7 days (or ABPM/HBPM with clinical review within 7 days). Not an emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: When is it correct to start antihypertensive treatment WITHOUT waiting for ABPM or HBPM?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: When clinic BP is ≥180/120 and target organ damage is identified. This is the exception to the usual rule that hypertension is confirmed with ambulatory or home monitoring before diagnosis — waiting would delay treatment in someone already sustaining damage.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: A patient has a BP of 195/120 but no target organ damage and no symptoms. Why must the BP not be lowered rapidly?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back:
Because this is severe hypertension, not a hypertensive emergency — emergencies are defined by end-organ damage, not by the number.
Rapid reduction risks cerebral and renal hypoperfusion. Chronic hypertension shifts cerebral autoregulation, so a fast drop can cause watershed ischaemia.Correct action: oral treatment and repeat clinic BP within 7 days.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.front: What is a marfanoid habitus?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.back:
A tall, slender build with
  • long limbs (arm span > height),
  • arachnodactyly (long slender fingers),
  • a high-arched palate,
  • pectus and scoliosis, and
  • joint hypermobility.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.front: Why does a marfanoid habitus matter clinically?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.back: Because of the aorta — Marfan syndrome causes aortic root dilatation and aortic dissection / rupture, the leading cause of death. It also causes lens dislocation and mitral valve prolapse.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.front: What is the genetic basis and inheritance of Marfan syndrome?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.back: It is autosomal dominant, caused by mutations in the fibrillin-1 (FBN1) gene, which weakens connective tissue elastic fibres.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.front: What are the wrist and thumb signs?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.back:
Signs of arachnodactyly:
  • the wrist sign is overlap of the thumb and little finger when gripping the opposite wrist;
  • the thumb sign is the thumb tip projecting beyond the palm's ulnar border when the thumb is clenched in the fist.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.front: How does the direction of lens dislocation help distinguish Marfan from homocystinuria?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.back: In Marfan the lens dislocates upward (superotemporal); in homocystinuria it dislocates downward.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.front: What key features distinguish homocystinuria from Marfan syndrome?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.back: Homocystinuria is autosomal recessive and adds intellectual disability, a thromboembolic tendency and downward lens dislocation; it is confirmed with plasma (and urinary) homocysteine.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.front: What is the most important cardiovascular investigation in a marfanoid patient?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.back: Echocardiography of the aortic root, to detect and monitor aortic root dilatation (and associated mitral valve prolapse / aortic regurgitation).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.front: How is aortic root dilatation managed in Marfan syndrome?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.back:
• β-blockade or an angiotensin-receptor blocker to slow dilatation,
  • activity restriction (avoid heavy isometric / contact exertion),
  • serial echo, and
  • prophylactic surgery once the root reaches a threshold diameter.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.front: What criteria are used to diagnose Marfan syndrome?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.back:
The Ghent criteria, which weigh
  • aortic root dilatation,
  • ectopia lentis,
  • a systemic feature score,
  • family history and
  • FBN1 mutation.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.front: Which acute presentation in a marfanoid patient is an emergency until excluded?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.back: Acute tearing chest / back pain — assume aortic dissection until excluded (CT aortogram). Marfan patients are also prone to spontaneous pneumothorax.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.front: What is Loeys-Dietz syndrome and how does it differ from Marfan?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.back: A connective-tissue disorder with hypertelorism, a bifid uvula / cleft palate and arterial tortuosity, causing aggressive, early aortic aneurysms and dissections at smaller diameters than Marfan.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.front: Which endocrine syndrome can produce a marfanoid habitus with mucosal neuromas?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.back: MEN 2B — a marfanoid body habitus with mucosal neuromas and a high risk of medullary thyroid carcinoma (and phaeochromocytoma).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.front: What skeletal chest and spine features are part of the marfanoid habitus?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.back: Pectus excavatum or carinatum and scoliosis, along with pes planus (flat feet) and a high-arched (narrow) palate.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.front: Why should first-degree relatives of a Marfan patient be assessed?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.back: Because it is autosomal dominant, so each first-degree relative has a 50% chance of inheriting it and needs clinical, echo and genetic assessment to detect silent aortic disease early.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.front: Which heart valve lesion, besides aortic root disease, is commonly associated with Marfan syndrome?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.back: Mitral valve prolapse (a mid-systolic click ± late systolic murmur), and aortic regurgitation if the dilated root stretches the valve.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.front: How is arm span used in assessing a marfanoid habitus?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.back: An arm span greater than height (ratio > 1.05) indicates disproportionately long limbs, one of the systemic features supporting the diagnosis.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.front: At what aortic root diameter is prophylactic surgery offered in Marfan syndrome?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.back: Elective aortic root replacement is generally offered at about 5.0 cm, with a lower threshold (~4.5 cm) when there is a family history of dissection, rapid growth, planned pregnancy or Loeys-Dietz syndrome.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.front: What is the upper-to-lower segment ratio and how does it change in Marfan syndrome?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.back: The ratio of body length above versus below the pubic symphysis. In Marfan the legs are disproportionately long, giving a reduced upper:lower segment ratio (alongside arm span > height) — a Ghent systemic-score feature.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.front: Why is pregnancy high-risk in Marfan syndrome?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.back:
The haemodynamic load sharply raises the risk of aortic dissection.
  • Offer pre-pregnancy counselling,
  • consider aortic repair if the root is >4.0–4.5 cm,
  • continue β-blockade, and
  • monitor with serial echocardiography.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.front: How does vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome differ from Marfan syndrome?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.back: Vascular EDS (COL3A1) causes spontaneous arterial, bowel and uterine rupture with thin, translucent, easily-bruised skin and marked hypermobility, but no ectopia lentis and it is not primarily an aortic-root disorder.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.front: How and where is the JVP measured?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.back: Vertical height of the internal jugular vein pulsation above the sternal angle, patient at 45°, head turned slightly left.Normal ≤3 cm above the sternal angle (≈≤8 cmH₂O).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.front: How do you distinguish the JVP from the carotid pulse?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.back:
The JVP is
  • biphasic,
  • impalpable,
  • occludable,
  • fills from above,
  • falls on inspiration/sitting up,
  • and has a positive hepatojugular reflux.
The carotid is palpable, single, not occludable and unaffected by position.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.front: What does a raised JVP indicate?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.back:
Elevated right atrial pressure —
  • right heart failure,
  • fluid overload,
  • cardiac tamponade,
  • constrictive pericarditis,
  • pulmonary hypertension,
  • tricuspid regurgitation,
  • or SVC obstruction.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.front: What causes cannon ‘a’ waves?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.back:
The atrium contracting against a closed tricuspid valve (AV dissociation) —
  • complete heart block,
  • ventricular tachycardia,
  • or junctional rhythm.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.front: What causes large ‘a’ waves?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.back:
Forceful atrial contraction against resistance —
  • tricuspid stenosis,
  • pulmonary hypertension,
  • or right ventricular hypertrophy.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.front: What causes absent ‘a’ waves?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.back: Atrial fibrillation — no coordinated atrial contraction.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.front: What causes giant ‘cv’ / v waves in the JVP?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.back: Tricuspid regurgitation — regurgitant systolic flow into the venous system, often with a pulsatile liver.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.front: A prominent ‘x’ descent with an absent ‘y’ descent suggests?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.back: Cardiac tamponade (blunted diastolic filling).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.front: A steep, preserved ‘y’ descent (± pericardial knock) suggests?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.back: Constrictive pericarditis — rapid early diastolic filling that abruptly halts.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.front: What is Kussmaul’s sign and what causes it?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.back:
A paradoxical rise in the JVP on inspiration. Causes:
  • constrictive pericarditis,
  • right ventricular infarction,
  • restrictive cardiomyopathy.
Classically absent in uncomplicated tamponade.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.front: What is Beck’s triad?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.back: Hypotension + raised JVP + muffled heart sounds → cardiac tamponade.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.front: What does a fixed, non-pulsatile raised JVP indicate?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.back: SVC obstruction — the vein is distended but non-pulsatile and non-occludable; commonest cause is lung cancer / mediastinal mass.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.front: What is the hepatojugular reflux and what does a positive test mean?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.back: Sustained ≥4 cm rise in the JVP during 10 seconds of firm RUQ pressure → raised right heart filling pressure (e.g. right heart failure).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.front: What does the JVP ‘a’ wave represent?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.back: Atrial contraction (presystolic).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.front: What does the JVP ‘v’ wave represent?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.back: Atrial filling against a closed tricuspid valve during ventricular systole.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.front: What do the x and y descents represent?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.back: x descent = atrial relaxation (systole); y descent = tricuspid opening and early diastolic ventricular filling.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.front: What is the definitive investigation for a raised JVP of unclear cause?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.back: Echocardiography — assesses RV function, tamponade physiology, constriction, tricuspid regurgitation and pericardial effusion.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.front: Which echo findings confirm cardiac tamponade?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.back: Pericardial effusion with diastolic right atrial/ventricular collapse, a plethoric non-collapsing IVC, and exaggerated respiratory variation in valve inflow.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.front: A massive PE causes which JVP and cardiac signs?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.back: Raised JVP, tachycardia, hypotension, loud P2, RV heave, and a clear chest; ECG may show S1Q3T3 or right heart strain.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.front: An inferior STEMI with a raised JVP, clear lungs and hypotension suggests?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.back: Right ventricular infarction — preload-dependent and nitrate-sensitive; confirm with right-sided lead V4R.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.front: Why does tricuspid regurgitation produce giant v waves?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.back: Regurgitant flow from the right ventricle into the right atrium and great veins during systole transmits directly to the JVP.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.front: Besides a fixed JVP, what signs accompany SVC obstruction?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.back:
• Facial/arm swelling and plethora,
  • distended non-pulsatile neck and chest wall veins,
  • Pemberton’s sign,
  • and stridor (emergency).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.front: Explain the mechanism of Kussmaul’s sign.
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.back: Inspiration normally increases venous return and lowers the JVP; in constriction/RV infarction the right heart cannot accommodate the extra return, so venous pressure — and the JVP — rises instead.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.front: How do you convert JVP height to right atrial pressure?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.back: The sternal angle sits ~5 cm above the right atrium, so RA pressure (cmH₂O) ≈ JVP height above the sternal angle + 5.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.front: Which pulse sign accompanies tamponade and what is it?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.back: Pulsus paradoxus — an exaggerated (>10 mmHg) fall in systolic BP on inspiration.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.front: What ECG clues accompany a large pericardial effusion / tamponade?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.back: Low-voltage complexes and electrical alternans.
