signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.front: A raised JVP with a loud P2 and a left parasternal (RV) heave points to?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.back: Pulmonary hypertension / cor pulmonale (right ventricular pressure overload).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.front: What does the JVP ‘c’ wave represent?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.back: Bulging of the closed tricuspid valve into the right atrium at the onset of ventricular systole (rarely visible clinically).Normal relationship: a > v.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.front: Distinguish regular from irregular cannon ‘a’ waves.
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.back: Irregular cannon a → intermittent AV dissociation (complete heart block, VT). Regular cannon a → atrium and ventricle contracting together every beat (junctional/nodal rhythm, AVNRT).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What single pathological event unifies all three acute coronary syndromes?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Disruption (rupture or erosion) of an atheromatous plaque's fibrous cap, exposing thrombogenic material and triggering coronary thrombosis.The degree of resulting occlusion determines whether it presents as STEMI, NSTEMI, or unstable angina.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: A patient has total coronary occlusion. Which ACS does this produce, and what is the hallmark ECG change?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: STEMI — caused by complete (transmural) occlusion, producing ST elevation (or new LBBB).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Distinguish NSTEMI from unstable angina on the basis of troponin and myocardial damage.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Both involve partial occlusion. NSTEMI causes actual myocyte necrosis, so troponin rises. Unstable angina causes ischaemia without infarction, so troponin stays normal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Why are unstable angina and NSTEMI managed identically when a patient first arrives?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: They are clinically and electrocardiographically indistinguishable at presentation; only the troponin (which takes hours to rise) separates them.So both are treated the same until the troponin result is back.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Put the atherosclerosis sequence in order: foam cell formation, endothelial dysfunction, plaque rupture, fibrous cap formation.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: 1) Endothelial dysfunction → 2) fatty streak / foam cell formation → 3) fibrous cap (plaque) formation → 4) plaque rupture/erosion with thrombosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What turns a macrophage into a foam cell during early atherosclerosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: LDL infiltrates the subendothelial space and is oxidised; macrophages phagocytose the oxidised LDL and become lipid-laden foam cells, which then die and propagate inflammation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Where does the smooth muscle forming a fibrous cap come from?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Smooth muscle cells proliferate and migrate from the tunica media into the intima, laying down a fibrous cap over the lipid core.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: List the non-modifiable risk factors for ACS.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back:
• Increasing age
  • male sex
  • and a positive family history (1st-degree relative: male <55 or female <65)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: At what ages does a 1st-degree relative's cardiac event count as a positive family history for ACS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Male relative <55 years or female relative <65 years.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Name six modifiable risk factors for ACS.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back:
• Smoking
  • hypertension
  • diabetes mellitus
  • hypercholesterolaemia
  • obesity/metabolic syndrome
  • and a sedentary lifestyle

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Describe the classic character and radiation of ischaemic cardiac chest pain.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back:
• Central or left-sided
  • heavy/constricting/crushing
  • radiating to the jaw or left arm
  • occurring at rest or on exertion

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Which two patient groups may have a 'silent MI', and why does this matter?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Diabetics and the elderly may infarct with little or no chest pain due to autonomic neuropathy/atypical presentation.It matters because a normal pain history does not exclude MI in these groups.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What associated (non-pain) symptoms point towards ACS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back:
• Dyspnoea
  • diaphoresis (sweating)
  • nausea and vomiting
  • a feeling of impending doom
  • and palpitations or syncope

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: A new murmur appears after an MI. What complication should you suspect and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: New mitral regurgitation murmur — suggests papillary muscle rupture/dysfunction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What clinical signs suggest the MI has caused heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Bibasal crackles, a third heart sound (S3), and a raised JVP — signs of pump failure.The patient is also often pale and clammy with tachycardia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: How quickly should a 12-lead ECG be done in suspected ACS, and what if it is normal?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Within 10 minutes of presentation.If initially normal, repeat it — perform serial ECGs, as changes can evolve.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Why is a single early troponin insufficient to rule out ACS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Troponin only rises ~3–6 hours after symptom onset, so a negative early sample does not exclude an MI.Serial sampling (e.g. 0h and 1h, or 0h and 3h) is needed to detect a rise/fall pattern.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What pattern of troponin change confirms acute myocardial infarction (rather than chronic elevation)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: A dynamic rise and/or fall on serial sampling.A static raised troponin can reflect chronic causes (e.g. CKD).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Beyond troponin, what blood tests are routinely sent in suspected ACS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back:
• FBC
  • U&E
  • LFTs
  • glucose
  • lipid profile
  • HbA1c
  • coagulation
  • and group & save

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Give the ST-elevation thresholds that define a STEMI.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: ST elevation ≥1 mm in ≥2 contiguous leads — except V2–V3, where the threshold is ≥2 mm in men (≥2.5 mm if under 40) and ≥1.5 mm in women (Universal Definition of MI).LBBB with ischaemic symptoms also counts.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Match each ACS to its vessel occlusion: STEMI, NSTEMI, unstable angina.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back:
• STEMI = total occlusion
  • NSTEMI = partial occlusion (with necrosis)
  • unstable angina = partial occlusion/spasm (no necrosis, normal troponin)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: A patient with chest pain has a new left bundle branch block. How do you treat this?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Treat as a STEMI — activate the primary PCI (PPCI) pathway.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: An inferior STEMI is seen in leads II, III, aVF. What extra leads do you record and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Right-sided leads (V4R) to exclude right ventricular infarction — important because RV infarction makes the patient nitrate-sensitive (nitrates can cause profound hypotension).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What ECG findings indicate a posterior MI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: A dominant R wave in V1, ST depression in V1–V3, and an upright T wave in V1 — essentially the mirror image of an anterior STEMI.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What does the GRACE score do, and what does it change?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: It predicts mortality after an NSTEMI, and it is what determines HOW SOON the patient goes for angiography — the higher the risk, the earlier the catheter lab.It combines the things you would expect to matter: age, how sick they look haemodynamically, renal function, ECG changes and troponin.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What is the single most common cause of death in the first hour after an MI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Ventricular fibrillation / VT (a malignant ventricular arrhythmia).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Which territory of MI most commonly causes heart block, and which structures are responsible?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Inferior MI (right coronary artery territory) — the RCA supplies the AV node, so its occlusion causes heart block.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: List the early (<24h) complications of MI.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back:
• Ventricular fibrillation/VT
  • heart block
  • acute LV failure / pulmonary oedema
  • cardiogenic shock
  • and early pericarditis (often within 24–72h)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: A patient develops pericarditis, fever and a pericardial rub 3 weeks after an MI. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Dressler's syndrome — an autoimmune pericarditis occurring 2–6 weeks post-MI, with raised CRP/ESR.Treat with aspirin or an NSAID plus colchicine; steroids only if refractory; pericardiocentesis if tamponade (ESC).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Persistent ST elevation weeks after an MI suggests which complication?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Left ventricular aneurysm — which also carries a thrombus (and embolic) risk.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Differentiate the timing and murmur of papillary muscle rupture vs ventricular septal rupture post-MI.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Both occur ~3–5 days post-MI. Papillary muscle rupture → acute mitral regurgitation. VSD (septal rupture) → a pansystolic murmur.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What catastrophic mechanical complication of MI presents with tamponade and electromechanical dissociation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Free wall rupture — usually fatal, causing tamponade and pulseless electrical activity (electromechanical dissociation).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What does DAPT stand for, what does it consist of, and how long is it continued after ACS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Dual Antiplatelet Therapy = aspirin + a P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor or prasugrel first-line; clopidogrel if high bleeding risk/on an anticoagulant). Continued for 12 months post-ACS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Why is a CXR useful in the acute assessment of chest pain suggestive of ACS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: It can show pulmonary oedema (LV failure), cardiomegaly, and — importantly — a widened mediastinum, helping exclude aortic dissection as a differential.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What information does echocardiography add after ACS, once the patient is stable?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back:
• Assessment of LV function (ejection fraction)
  • regional wall motion abnormalities
  • and complications such as mitral regurgitation, VSD, or pericardial effusion

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What are the two roles of coronary angiography in ACS, and what is the preferred access route?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Diagnostic (defines coronary anatomy) and therapeutic (PCI at the same sitting). Radial access is preferred over femoral.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Why does a STEMI cause transmural (full-thickness) ischaemia rather than subendocardial?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: STEMI results from total coronary occlusion, cutting off blood flow to the entire wall thickness — producing transmural ischaemia.Partial occlusion (NSTEMI/UA) spares the outer layers.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: State the ST-elevation criteria for STEMI in limb leads versus precordial (chest) leads.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: ≥1 mm in ≥2 contiguous leads, including most chest leads — the exception is V2–V3, where the threshold is ≥2 mm in men (≥2.5 mm if under 40) and ≥1.5 mm in women (Universal Definition of MI).A new LBBB with symptoms is also treated as STEMI.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: When does troponin rise and peak after a STEMI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: It begins to rise at ~3–6 hours and peaks at ~12–24 hours.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Put the ECG evolution of a STEMI in order from earliest to latest.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: 1) Hyperacute tall, peaked T waves (minutes–hours) → 2) ST elevation, convex/tombstoning (0–12h) → 3) pathological Q waves (1–12h) → 4) ST returns to baseline with T-wave inversion (days) → 5) T waves normalise, persistent Q waves remain as scar (weeks–months).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What is the very first ECG change seen in an evolving STEMI, within minutes to hours?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Hyperacute tall, peaked T waves — these precede the ST elevation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Define a pathological Q wave on ECG.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: A Q wave that is >1 mm wide (>40 ms) or >25% of the height of the following R wave (QRS).It indicates established myocardial necrosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Weeks after a STEMI, which ECG change persists permanently as a marker of scar?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Persistent pathological Q waves.By this stage the T waves have normalised and the ST segment has returned to baseline.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF localises to which territory and culprit artery?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Inferior territory → right coronary artery (RCA).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: ST elevation in V1–V4 localises to which territory and culprit artery?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Anterior territory → left anterior descending (LAD) artery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: ST elevation in I, aVL, V5–V6 localises to which territory and culprit artery?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Lateral territory → left circumflex artery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: A dominant R wave in V1 with ST depression in V1–V3 indicates which STEMI territory, and which artery?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Posterior STEMI → RCA or circumflex.These anterior-lead changes are the mirror image of true posterior ST elevation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What does the MONA mnemonic stand for in immediate ACS management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Morphine, Oxygen, Nitrates, Aspirin.A memory aid only — aspirin 300 mg is for all, but oxygen (only if SpO₂<94%), nitrates and morphine are conditional, not routine.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Why must oxygen be given only if SpO₂ is below 94% in ACS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Hyperoxia causes coronary vasoconstriction and worsens infarct size, so supplemental oxygen is reserved for genuine hypoxia (SpO₂ <94%) — target 94–98%, or 88–92% if at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (BTS).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: In which two situations should nitrates be used with caution in ACS, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: If the patient is hypotensive, or has an inferior MI with RV involvement — nitrates reduce preload and can precipitate severe hypotension.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What dose of aspirin is given in acute ACS, and how should it be taken for fastest effect?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: 300 mg stat, chewed or crushed for rapid absorption.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Why is morphine used cautiously in ACS beyond its sedative/respiratory risks?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Morphine delays P2Y12 inhibitor absorption (slowing antiplatelet onset).It's reserved for severe pain and given with an anti-emetic such as metoclopramide.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: A STEMI is confirmed and aspirin given. PCI can be delivered within 120 minutes. What is the reperfusion strategy?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Primary PCI — the preferred reperfusion method when available within 120 minutes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: A STEMI is confirmed but PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes. What is the alternative, and name agents used.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Fibrinolysis — tenecteplase (a single weight-based bolus, and the usual UK pre-hospital agent; alteplase is an alternative), plus an antithrombin (fondaparinux/enoxaparin) and a second antiplatelet (clopidogrel — ticagrelor/prasugrel are reserved for primary PCI).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: After fibrinolysis, when is the ECG repeated, and what indicates failure requiring rescue PCI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Repeat the ECG at 60–90 minutes. Persistent ST elevation indicates failed lysis → proceed to rescue PCI.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Which second antiplatelet is given alongside aspirin for a patient going for primary PCI, and what is the exception?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Prasugrel 60 mg (or ticagrelor 180 mg). Not prasugrel if there is any history of stroke or TIA — that is an absolute contraindication.Aged 75 or over, or under 60 kg: weigh bleeding risk and use ticagrelor or clopidogrel instead. Use clopidogrel if the patient is on an oral anticoagulant (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What stent type and arterial access are preferred in primary PCI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: A drug-eluting stent, via radial access (preferred over femoral).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: List the '6 A's' of secondary prevention after ACS.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back:
• Aspirin (75 mg OD indefinitely)
  • Another antiplatelet (ticagrelor/clopidogrel for 12 months = DAPT)
  • Atorvastatin (80 mg OD)
  • ACE inhibitor (e.g. ramipril)
  • A beta-blocker (e.g. bisoprolol)
  • and Aldosterone antagonist (eplerenone if heart failure with LV systolic dysfunction post-MI)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What is the role of a beta-blocker (e.g. bisoprolol) in secondary prevention post-MI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Titrated up to reduce adverse ventricular remodelling (and improve prognosis).Continue indefinitely if LVEF is reduced; at least 12 months if LVEF is preserved (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: When is an aldosterone antagonist (eplerenone) indicated after an MI, and what must be monitored?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Indicated if there is heart failure AND LV systolic dysfunction after MI; start within 3–14 days, preferably after the ACE inhibitor (25 mg OD, titrate to 50 mg) (NICE). Monitor potassium, as it causes hyperkalaemia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Why is renal function and potassium monitoring essential when combining an ACE inhibitor with an aldosterone antagonist?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Both drugs cause hyperkalaemia and can impair renal function, so U&Es must be monitored when used together.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Beyond drugs, what additional steps are arranged as part of post-MI secondary prevention?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back:
• An echocardiogram (to assess LV function)
  • cardiac rehabilitation
  • and a diabetes/lipid review

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Why does an NSTEMI cause subendocardial rather than transmural ischaemia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: NSTEMI results from partial coronary occlusion. The subendocardium is the most distal, watershed region of perfusion, so it is the first to become ischaemic when flow is only partially reduced — sparing the outer wall.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What ECG findings are typical of an NSTEMI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back:
• ST depression
  • T-wave inversion
  • or a normal ECG
By definition there is no ST elevation and no new LBBB.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What single investigation distinguishes NSTEMI from unstable angina, and how?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Troponin — it is elevated in NSTEMI (myocyte necrosis) but normal in unstable angina (ischaemia without infarction).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Which risk-stratification tool is used in NSTEMI, and what decision does it guide?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: The GRACE score — it stratifies risk and guides the urgency/timing of coronary angiography.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: On the GRACE score, what threshold indicates the need for early angiography, and within what timeframe?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: GRACE returns a points score that maps to a predicted 6-month mortality. A predicted 6-month mortality above 3% (intermediate or higher risk) indicates angiography within 72 hours; clinically unstable patients go immediately (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What does the BATMAN mnemonic stand for in NSTEMI / unstable angina management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back:
• B – Base on GRACE score (risk-stratify for angiography/PCI timing)
  • A – Aspirin 300 mg stat
  • T – Ticagrelor 180 mg stat
  • M – Morphine (if severe pain + anti-emetic)
  • A – Antithrombin (fondaparinux/enoxaparin)
  • N – Nitrate (sublingual/IV GTN for ongoing pain)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: In the BATMAN approach, what does the 'B' represent and what does it determine?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: B = Base on GRACE — risk-stratification that determines angiography and PCI timing.It is the predicted 6-month mortality above 3%, not the points score itself, that triggers angiography within 72h (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What loading dose of aspirin is given in NSTEMI/UA, matching the 'A' in BATMAN?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Aspirin 300 mg stat.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: In BATMAN, what is the standard second antiplatelet and its dose, and what are the alternatives?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Ticagrelor 180 mg stat (first-line in NSTEMI). Prasugrel only once coronary anatomy is known and proceeding to PCI; clopidogrel 300 mg if high bleeding risk or on an anticoagulant.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Which antiplatelet is preferred in NSTEMI/UA if the patient has a high bleeding risk?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Clopidogrel 300 mg (instead of ticagrelor).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What antithrombin agents are used in NSTEMI/UA, and which is preferred?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Fondaparinux, unless high bleeding risk or going for immediate angiography.Use unfractionated heparin instead if renal function is significantly impaired; everyone going to the cath lab gets systemic UFH there as well (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: In the BATMAN protocol, when are nitrates given and by what route?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Nitrates (sublingual or IV GTN) are given for ongoing chest pain.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What is the defining feature of unstable angina in terms of myocardial damage?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Partial coronary occlusion causing ischaemia WITHOUT infarction — there is no myocyte necrosis, so troponin remains normal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What ECG findings can be seen in unstable angina?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: ST depression, T-wave inversion, or a normal ECG — the same range as NSTEMI, with no ST elevation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Describe the three classic symptom patterns that define unstable angina.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back:
• 1) New-onset chest pain
  • 2) angina occurring at rest
  • or 3) rapidly progressive (crescendo) exertional angina

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: How does the initial management of unstable angina compare with that of NSTEMI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: It is the same — the BATMAN protocol, with GRACE-score risk stratification to guide angiography timing.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: A patient describes stable exertional angina that has suddenly become more frequent and easily provoked over the past few days. What does this progression suggest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Crescendo (rapidly progressive) angina — a presentation of unstable angina, indicating an unstable plaque and warranting ACS workup.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What is the fundamental mechanism of pain in stable angina?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: A fixed atheromatous plaque causes flow-limiting stenosis, so myocardial oxygen demand exceeds supply (demand > supply) during exertion.The plaque is intact — no rupture.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What three features define 'stable' in stable angina?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back:
• It is predictable
  • brought on by exertion
  • and relieved by rest or GTN (typically within ~5 minutes)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Name the three characteristics used in the typicality ladder for angina.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back:
• 1) Constricting central/retrosternal pain ± radiation
  • 2) brought on by exertion or stress
  • 3) relieved by rest or GTN within ~5 minutes

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: How many of the three angina features are needed to classify chest pain as typical, atypical, or non-anginal?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back:
• Typical = all 3 features
  • atypical = 2 of 3
  • non-anginal = ≤1 of 3 (unlikely to be cardiac ischaemia)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: A patient has constricting central chest pain on exertion that settles with rest, but with no radiation noted. How is this classified on the typicality ladder?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Typical angina — all 3 features are present.Radiation is not a separate feature: criterion 1 is constricting central chest pain ± radiation, so absent radiation does not remove it.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What distinguishes the plaque behaviour in stable angina from that in ACS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: In stable angina the plaque is intact (fixed stenosis → ischaemia only on increased demand). In ACS the plaque ruptures → thrombus → partial or complete occlusion → ischaemia at rest, unpredictable.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Why does stable angina produce subendocardial (not transmural) ischaemia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: The fixed stenosis limits flow only when demand rises; the subendocardium — the watershed area — becomes ischaemic first, but the plaque does not occlude the vessel completely.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Why must LFTs be checked before starting a statin in stable angina?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: To establish a baseline, as statins can affect liver enzymes; LFTs are rechecked at 3 months and again at 12 months (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Is troponin a routine test in stable angina?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: No — troponin is only sent if there is an unstable or acute presentation, not in routine stable angina assessment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What can a resting ECG show in stable angina, and what is its main value?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: It is often normal between episodes, but may show old Q waves (previous MI), ST depression or T-wave changes. It is done in all patients mainly to help exclude other diagnoses.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: According to NICE, what is the first-line investigation for stable chest pain of suspected cardiac origin with no known CAD?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: CT coronary angiography (CTCA) — a non-invasive scan that identifies plaque burden and degree of stenosis, with an excellent negative predictive value for ruling out significant CAD.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What is the main strength of CTCA that makes it the first-line investigation for stable angina?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Its excellent negative predictive value — it effectively rules out significant coronary artery disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Give three examples of functional imaging used in stable angina, and when they are used.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back:
• Stress echocardiography (exercise/dobutamine, wall motion)
  • stress cardiac MRI (adenosine perfusion)
  • and myocardial perfusion imaging (MPI, nuclear)
Used if CTCA is non-diagnostic or to assess the functional significance of a stenosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What is the role of invasive coronary angiography in stable angina, and what does FFR add?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: It is the gold standard for coronary anatomy/severity and allows simultaneous PCI. Fractional flow reserve (FFR) measures the functional significance of a stenosis to guide whether to intervene.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: The stable angina management framework has three parallel arms. What are they?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back:
• Arm 1 — secondary prevention (modify risk / prevent MI)
  • Arm 2 — acute symptom relief (GTN)
  • Arm 3 — prophylactic symptom control (anti-anginal ladder)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: How does antiplatelet therapy in stable angina differ from that in ACS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Stable angina uses a SINGLE antiplatelet (aspirin 75 mg OD indefinitely, or clopidogrel if aspirin-intolerant). ACS uses DAPT (aspirin + a P2Y12 inhibitor).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What statin and dose is used for secondary prevention in stable angina, and what is its mechanism of benefit?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Atorvastatin 80 mg ON (high-intensity) — lowers LDL and stabilises plaque.Aim for LDL-C ≤2.0 mmol/L (non-HDL ≤2.6); add ezetimibe if not met. Check LFTs at baseline, 3 months and 12 months (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: When is an ACE inhibitor specifically indicated in stable angina?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: If there is co-existing diabetes, hypertension, CKD or heart failure — it is cardioprotective and reduces afterload/vascular tone.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Which single risk-factor modification is considered the most important in stable angina?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Smoking cessation.Other targets: BP control (<140/90; <150/90 if aged 80 or over — the tighter <130/80 applies only to type 1 diabetes or CKD with ACR ≥70 mg/mmol) (NICE), glycaemic control in diabetes, weight, exercise and diet.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Describe the mechanism by which sublingual GTN relieves angina.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: It is a nitric oxide donor causing venodilation → reduced preload → reduced myocardial oxygen demand; it also dilates the coronary arteries.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What is the patient-education GTN protocol for an acute angina attack?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Sit down and use GTN spray/tablet → wait 5 minutes → repeat dose if pain persists → wait 5 minutes → call 999 if still no relief (possible ACS).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What are the common side effects of GTN, and how should the spray be stored?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Headache (vasodilation), flushing and hypotension. Store away from light and heat, and note that GTN tablets expire about 8 weeks after the bottle is opened — a classic counselling point.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What are the two first-line options for prophylactic symptom control in stable angina?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: A beta-blocker (e.g. bisoprolol, atenolol — reduces HR and contractility, lowering O₂ demand) OR a rate-limiting calcium channel blocker (diltiazem, verapamil) if a beta-blocker is contraindicated/not tolerated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: If first-line monotherapy fails to control angina, what is the safe second-line combination, and which combination must be avoided?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Safe: beta-blocker + amlodipine (a dihydropyridine CCB). Never combine a beta-blocker with verapamil or diltiazem — risk of heart block/sinus arrest.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Why is the combination of a beta-blocker with verapamil or diltiazem dangerous?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Both suppress AV conduction and heart rate, so together they risk bradycardia, complete heart block or sinus arrest.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Name three add-on anti-anginal options beyond beta-blockers and CCBs, with a brief mechanism for each.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back:
• Long-acting nitrate (ISMN — isosorbide mononitrate, venodilation)
  • ivabradine (If-channel inhibitor, lowers HR, sinus rhythm only, if beta-blocker intolerant)
  • nicorandil (K-ATP channel opener + nitrate)
  • ranolazine (late sodium-channel inhibitor)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Why must rate-limiting CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem) be avoided in HFrEF, and what is the alternative?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: They are negative inotropes — reducing contractility can precipitate decompensation. Use amlodipine instead if a CCB is needed in heart failure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Under what circumstances is revascularisation considered in stable angina?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: For significant stenosis confirmed on imaging, or refractory symptoms despite optimal medical therapy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: When is PCI a suitable revascularisation choice, and what does it require afterwards?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: PCI (angioplasty + drug-eluting stent) suits single or discrete vessel disease — less invasive, shorter recovery. It requires DAPT (aspirin + clopidogrel) for 6 months post-stent in stable angina, shortened to 1–3 months if bleeding risk is high.The 12-month duration belongs to ACS, not to elective PCI.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: In which scenarios is CABG favoured over PCI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Left main stem disease, severe/multivessel disease, diabetes mellitus, and poor LV function (LV systolic dysfunction, typically EF ≤35%) — CABG gives better long-term outcomes in complex disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Which bypass graft is the gold standard, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: The LIMA (left internal mammary artery) → LAD graft.It stays open far longer than a saphenous vein graft, which is why it is used for the most important vessel — an artery grafted to an artery behaves better long-term than a vein does.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Distinguish a Type 1 from a Type 2 myocardial infarction.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back:
• Type 1 = acute atherothrombosis — plaque rupture or erosion → thrombus → coronary occlusion
  • Type 2 = supply–demand mismatch with no acute plaque event — the myocardium simply cannot get the oxygen it needs
Both raise troponin; only Type 1 is the classic 'heart attack' the ACS algorithm is built for.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Give five causes of a Type 2 myocardial infarction.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back:
Anything that tips myocardial oxygen supply below demand without a plaque rupture:
  • Tachyarrhythmia (fast AF, SVT) — shortens diastole
  • Anaemia — ↓oxygen content
  • Hypotension / shock — ↓coronary perfusion pressure
  • Sepsis — ↑demand + ↓SVR
  • Severe hypertension or hypoxaemia — ↑demand / ↓supply
Also: bradyarrhythmia, coronary spasm, dissection, embolism.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: How does the management of a Type 2 MI differ from that of a Type 1 MI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Treat the underlying cause — rate-control the AF, transfuse the anaemia, treat the sepsis, support the BP.It is not primarily a reperfusion/antithrombotic problem: DAPT, antithrombin and urgent angiography are usually inappropriate, and anticoagulating a septic bleeding patient can cause harm.⚠ The commonest error is running the full ACS pathway on a rising troponin that is actually demand ischaemia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: A 26-year-old presents with crushing chest pain and no conventional cardiac risk factors. What must you ask about, and why does it matter?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Ask about cocaine / stimulant use.It causes ACS by coronary vasoconstriction, ↑myocardial oxygen demand and a prothrombotic state — and it changes the algorithm: benzodiazepine first-line, and beta-blockers are avoided acutely.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Outline the acute management of cocaine-associated ACS.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back:
• 1. IV benzodiazepine (diazepam / lorazepam) — first-line
  • 2. GTN for chest pain + aspirin
  • 3. Primary PCI if there is ST elevation
  • 4. Avoid beta-blockers acutely — unopposed alpha stimulation worsens coronary vasoconstriction

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Why is a benzodiazepine first-line in cocaine-associated chest pain?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: It treats the sympathetic drive that is causing the ischaemia — the agitation, tachycardia and hypertension all raise myocardial oxygen demand.Settle the patient and you lower demand, lower BP and relieve coronary vasoconstriction in one step.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Why are beta-blockers avoided in the acute phase of cocaine-associated ACS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Unopposed α-adrenergic stimulation. Blocking β leaves α-mediated coronary vasoconstriction unchecked → worsening ischaemia and a rise in BP.Note this also means holding the usual prognostic bisoprolol (A5 of the 6 A's) in the acute setting.Newer data question how real this harm is, but 'avoid' remains the expected exam answer.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: When are the Sgarbossa criteria used?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: To help decide whether an acute MI is happening underneath an LBBB or a paced rhythm, where the baseline QRS/ST abnormality makes the usual ST-elevation criteria unreliable. You are not expected to apply the criteria yourself — what you need is the consequence: a new LBBB with ongoing ischaemic symptoms goes down the primary PCI pathway and is discussed with the PCI centre.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: A patient has had an ACS treated with successful PCI and drives a car (Group 1). When may they drive again, and must they tell the DVLA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: 1 week — provided all diseased vessels were treated, LVEF ≥40%, and no further revascularisation is planned. Otherwise 4 weeks. The DVLA need not be notified for Group 1.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What are the driving rules after an ACS for a Group 2 (HGV / PSV) licence holder?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back:
• Disqualified for at least 6 weeks.
  • They must notify the DVLA.
  • Re-licensing requires passing a functional (exercise) test and an LVEF ≥40%.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Before giving fibrinolysis for a STEMI, what must you screen for?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back:
Bleeding risk. Ask about
  • any previous haemorrhagic stroke or a recent ischaemic stroke
  • active bleeding or a known bleeding disorder
  • recent major surgery
  • serious trauma or head injury
  • suspected aortic dissection
  • and severe uncontrolled hypertension
If any apply, do not lyse - arrange transfer for primary PCI instead.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What is vasospastic (Prinzmetal / variant) angina, and how does it differ from ordinary angina?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Coronary artery SPASM rather than a plaque, occluding a vessel that may be near-normal. It causes pain at REST, often at night or early morning, with preserved exercise tolerance. ST elevation appears during the episode and resolves as the pain settles, without infarction - catching it on an ECG at the time is the diagnosis.Typically younger patients, often smokers; cocaine is an important precipitant.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: How is vasospastic angina treated, and which drug class should be avoided?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: A calcium channel blocker, with nitrates as needed, plus smoking cessation. AVOID beta-blockers - they leave alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed and can make the spasm worse.It is the same reasoning as avoiding beta-blockers in cocaine-associated chest pain.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: A patient presents 18 hours after the onset of STEMI pain and is now pain-free. Does he go for primary PCI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: No. Beyond 12 hours and pain-free with no ongoing ischaemia, primary PCI is no longer the reflex - he is admitted, medically managed and gets inpatient angiography.But instability overrides the clock: ongoing ischaemic pain, cardiogenic shock, heart failure or a life-threatening arrhythmia means immediate angiography regardless of how long it has been.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Where should a patient with suspected ACS be nursed, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: In a monitored bed - resus, CCU or equivalent - on continuous ECG monitoring with a defibrillator to hand.Ventricular fibrillation is the commonest cause of death in the first hour, and it is survivable in seconds if someone is watching for it.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What must a patient be told about their antiplatelets when they are discharged after a stent?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Never stop the second antiplatelet early, and never let another team stop it for a procedure without asking cardiology first.Stopping it early risks the stent thrombosing, which is frequently fatal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Beyond driving, what should post-MI discharge counselling cover?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back:
• Cardiac rehabilitation for everyone
  • return to work, usually within weeks after an uncomplicated MI and sooner for desk work than heavy manual work
  • resuming sex once they can manage ordinary exertion such as stairs - with an explicit warning that drugs for erectile dysfunction must NEVER be combined with nitrates
  • and flying, usually fine once stable but subject to the airline's rules

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: What is syncope?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back: A transient loss of consciousness due to global cerebral hypoperfusion, characterised by rapid onset, short duration and complete spontaneous recovery.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: What is pre-syncope?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back: The same process short of blacking out — light-headedness, greying/tunnelling of vision, weakness and impending collapse without full loss of consciousness.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: What are the three broad categories (buckets) of syncope?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back:
• Reflex (neurally-mediated)
  • orthostatic hypotension
  • and cardiac (arrhythmic or structural).
Always also exclude mimics (seizure, hypoglycaemia, functional).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: What are the features of vasovagal syncope?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back: A prodrome (warmth, nausea, sweating, tunnel vision) with a trigger (prolonged standing, pain, emotion, heat), a brief faint, and rapid full recovery.It is the commonest cause.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: What is situational syncope?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back: Reflex syncope triggered by a specific act — cough, micturition, swallowing or defecation — via a vagal surge.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: What is carotid sinus hypersensitivity?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back: An exaggerated vagal/vasodepressor response to carotid sinus stimulation (head-turning, a tight collar, shaving) causing syncope, typically in older patients.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: How is orthostatic hypotension defined?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back: A fall in systolic BP ≥20 mmHg or diastolic ≥10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing (or on a tilt), usually reproducing symptoms.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: What causes orthostatic hypotension?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back:
• Drugs (antihypertensives, diuretics, α-blockers, nitrates, antidepressants)
  • hypovolaemia (bleeding, dehydration)
  • and autonomic failure (diabetic neuropathy, Parkinson’s, multiple system atrophy).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: Why is exertional syncope a red flag?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back: It suggests a fixed obstruction to cardiac output during exercise — aortic stenosis or HOCM — or an exercise-induced arrhythmia; all risk sudden death and need urgent assessment.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: What history features suggest cardiac (dangerous) syncope?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back:
• Exertional or supine syncope
  • no prodrome
  • preceding palpitations
  • family history of sudden cardiac death <40
  • known structural/ischaemic heart disease
  • and an abnormal ECG.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: What is Stokes-Adams syndrome?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back: A transient complete heart block causing an abrupt syncopal episode with pallor, then a flushed reactive recovery — a form of arrhythmic syncope.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: Which primary electrical (channelopathy) causes of syncope must not be missed?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back: Long QT syndrome, Brugada syndrome, and catecholaminergic polymorphic VT — inherited causes of arrhythmic syncope and sudden death, often with a family history.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: Which structural cardiac lesions cause syncope?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back:
• Aortic stenosis
  • HOCM
  • massive pulmonary embolism
  • cardiac tamponade
  • aortic dissection
  • and (rarely) an atrial myxoma.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: What is the classic symptom triad of severe aortic stenosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back: Angina, syncope and dyspnoea (exertional) — the onset of any of these marks a poor prognosis without valve intervention.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: How do you distinguish syncope from a seizure?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back: Seizure — aura, lateral tongue biting, sustained rhythmic convulsions, a post-ictal confusional phase and slow recovery. Syncope — trigger/prodrome, brief, rapid full recovery.Incontinence is non-specific.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: What is convulsive syncope?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back: Brief myoclonic jerks occurring during a syncopal faint from cerebral hypoperfusion — it can mimic a seizure but is not epilepsy and lacks a true post-ictal phase.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: Which two bedside investigations are mandatory in everyone with syncope?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back: A 12-lead ECG and a lying & standing blood pressure.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: Which ECG findings are red flags in syncope?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back:
• Long QT
  • Brugada pattern
  • a delta wave (WPW)
  • bifascicular block/long PR
  • complete heart block or pauses
  • pathological Q waves
  • and S1Q3T3 (PE).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: When is echocardiography indicated in syncope?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back: When there is a murmur, an abnormal ECG, exertional syncope, or suspected structural disease — to assess aortic stenosis, HOCM and LV function.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: How are intermittent arrhythmic causes of syncope investigated?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back:
Ambulatory ECG matched to frequency —
  • Holter for frequent symptoms
  • an event/loop recorder for less frequent
  • and an implantable loop recorder for infrequent high-risk episodes.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: What is the tilt-table test used for?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back: To support a diagnosis of recurrent unexplained reflex (vasovagal) or orthostatic syncope when the history is unclear.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: What precaution applies to carotid sinus massage?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back: Avoid if a carotid bruit is present (or recent stroke/TIA) because of embolic/ischaemic risk; perform with ECG and BP monitoring, usually in older patients.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: What driving advice applies after syncope in the UK (DVLA)?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back:
• Simple faint (clear trigger + prodrome, unlikely sitting/lying) — no restriction, no notification.
  • Group 1 (car): unexplained/single with treatable cause off ~4 weeks, no cause found ~6 months.
  • Group 2 (HGV/PCV): stricter — typically 3–12 months off and DVLA notification.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: How does hypoglycaemia present as a syncope mimic?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back: Gradual light-headedness with sweating, tremor and hunger in a treated diabetic, relieved by glucose; check a capillary blood glucose in any collapse.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: How does the murmur of HOCM behave with manoeuvres, and why does it cause syncope?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back: The ejection systolic murmur gets louder on Valsalva/standing (reduced preload worsens dynamic LVOT obstruction); syncope arises from outflow obstruction or arrhythmia.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: What is the initial risk-stratification aim after a syncopal episode?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back: To separate low-risk reflex/orthostatic syncope (reassure) from high-risk cardiac syncope (admit, monitor, urgent cardiology), using history, examination and the ECG; structured aids include the San Francisco Syncope Rule and the Canadian Syncope Risk Score.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: How does massive pulmonary embolism cause syncope?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back: Acute obstruction of the pulmonary circulation raises RV afterload and drops left-heart preload and output, cutting cerebral perfusion; look for hypoxia, tachycardia, pleuritic pain and S1Q3T3/RV strain on ECG.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: What examination findings point to a structural cardiac cause of syncope?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back:
• An ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids with a slow-rising pulse (aortic stenosis)
  • a murmur louder on Valsalva (HOCM)
  • or signs of heart failure.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: Why must an ECG be done even when vasovagal syncope seems obvious?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back: To catch silent high-risk substrates (long QT, Brugada, WPW, heart block) that can present with a seemingly benign faint but risk sudden death.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: What simple advice reduces recurrence of vasovagal syncope?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back:
• Recognise the prodrome and lie down / physical counter-pressure manoeuvres (leg crossing, hand grip)
  • maintain hydration and salt
  • and avoid known triggers
  • review culprit drugs.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: What is the significance of syncope occurring while lying down (supine)?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back: Supine syncope cannot be reflex/orthostatic (no gravitational pooling) and strongly suggests a cardiac arrhythmia — a red flag.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: What features suggest psychogenic pseudosyncope?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back:
• Frequent or prolonged ‘collapses’
  • often with eyes closed and resisting opening
  • no injury or incontinence
  • and normal HR, BP and ECG during the event.
It is a functional disorder and a diagnosis of exclusion.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: How does posterior-circulation TIA / vertebrobasilar insufficiency differ from true syncope?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back: It causes transient focal neurology (diplopia, dysarthria, vertigo, ataxia) rather than a simple transient loss of consciousness from global hypoperfusion — a syncope mimic, not true syncope.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.front: What is subclavian steal syndrome and how does it cause syncope?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.back: Proximal subclavian stenosis so that arm exercise reverses vertebral-artery flow, causing posterior-circulation symptoms/syncope with an inter-arm BP/pulse difference and a subclavian bruit.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: What is the primary functional role of veins, and what proportion of blood volume do they hold?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back: Veins are capacitance (reservoir) vessels that return blood to the heart at low pressure; at rest they hold ~65–70% of the total blood volume.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: What is the single most useful contrast between an artery wall and a vein wall?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back: In an artery the tunica media is the thickest layer; in a vein the tunica adventitia is the thickest layer.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: Describe the tunica intima of a vein.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back: Endothelium with scant subendothelial connective tissue and no distinct internal elastic lamina; it folds inward to form the venous valves.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: Why is the tunica media of a vein thin?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back: Veins operate at low pressure and don't need thick muscular/elastic walls; they have little smooth muscle and elastic tissue in the media.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: What are venous sinusoids and where are they found?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back: Wide, irregular venous channels with a discontinuous endothelium and gaps in the basement membrane that let blood cells and macromolecules cross; found in the liver, splenic red pulp, bone marrow and adrenal cortex.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: List the venous hierarchy from capillary to heart.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back: Postcapillary venule → muscular (collecting) venule → small/medium vein → large vein (e.g. vena cava).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: What is distinctive about the postcapillary venule's structure and function?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back: It has endothelium plus pericytes and no true media; it is the main site of leukocyte emigration and fluid exchange, and the most responsive to histamine.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: What distinguishes the wall of a large vein such as the vena cava?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back: A thin media but an adventitia containing prominent longitudinal bundles of smooth muscle, with abundant vasa vasorum.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: How do venous valves work and what are they made of?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back: They are paired semilunar folds of the tunica intima (endothelium over a thin CT core) with cusps pointing toward the heart; they open with forward flow and snap shut on retrograde flow to prevent backflow.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: Where are venous valves most numerous and where are they absent?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back: Most numerous in the limb veins (working against gravity); absent from the venae cavae, portal vein, cerebral/dural venous sinuses and most visceral veins.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: Name the mechanisms that drive venous return.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back:
• The skeletal-muscle pump,
  • the respiratory (thoracic) pump,
  • sympathetic venoconstriction (venous tone),
  • and the residual pressure from the heart (vis a tergo).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: Why does venous return depend on external forces rather than the vein wall itself?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back: Venous pressure is low and the wall is thin/compliant, so blood is moved largely by muscle contraction, respiration and venous tone rather than by the vessel wall — hence immobility causes stasis.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: What happens when venous valves become incompetent?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back: Sustained venous hypertension develops, producing varicose veins and, over time, chronic venous insufficiency with venous (gaiter) ulceration.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: Why is the postcapillary venule called the 'inflammation vessel'?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back: It is the principal site of leukocyte rolling/adhesion/diapedesis and of histamine- and bradykinin-driven increased permeability that causes exudate and oedema.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: Outline the steps of leukocyte emigration across the postcapillary venule.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back: Rolling (selectins) → firm adhesion (integrins binding ICAM) → diapedesis between endothelial cells → chemotaxis into the tissue.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: What are high endothelial venules (HEVs) and where are they found?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back: Specialised postcapillary venules with tall cuboidal endothelium, found in lymph nodes and Peyer's patches, through which recirculating lymphocytes enter lymphoid tissue.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: On an elastic stain, how do veins differ from arteries?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back: Veins show sparse, scattered elastic fibres with no discrete internal or external elastic laminae, whereas arteries show crisp, well-defined elastic laminae.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: Which stain highlights the collagen-rich venous adventitia?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back: Masson trichrome (collagen stains blue/green).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: What is Virchow's triad and why is it relevant to veins?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back: Stasis, hypercoagulability and endothelial injury — the three factors predisposing to venous thrombosis (DVT), which can embolise to the lungs.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: Define chronic venous insufficiency and its skin changes.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back: Sustained venous hypertension (from valve failure or post-DVT damage) causing oedema, haemosiderin (brown) staining, lipodermatosclerosis and venous ulcers, typically in the gaiter area.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: What causes oesophageal varices?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back: Portal hypertension diverts blood through porto-systemic anastomoses, dilating submucosal veins at the gastro-oesophageal junction, which can rupture and bleed.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: What are telangiectasias/spider veins?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back: Dilated small dermal venules or capillaries visible at the skin surface.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: Contrast venous and arterial leg ulcers.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back:
• Venous ulcer: gaiter area/medial malleolus, shallow, exudative, surrounded by haemosiderin and lipodermatosclerosis, relatively painless, pulses present — treat with compression (after checking ABPI).
  • Arterial ulcer: distal/pressure points, 'punched-out', painful, cold pale limb, pulses absent, low ABPI — compression is contraindicated.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: What is a muscular (collecting) venule?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back: A venule that has acquired one to two layers of smooth muscle, draining the postcapillary venules on the way to small veins.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: Which endothelial immunomarkers help identify vascular (including venous) channels?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back: CD31 and CD34.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: Which layer carries the vasa vasorum in veins, and why are they prominent?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back: The tunica adventitia; vasa vasorum are more numerous and penetrate deeper in veins than in arteries because the deoxygenated, nutrient-poor luminal blood cannot supply the wall by diffusion, so the wall depends more on its own vessels.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: What are lines of Zahn, and how do venous and arterial thrombi differ?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back: Lines of Zahn are alternating pale platelet/fibrin and dark red-cell layers, indicating a thrombus formed in flowing (ante-mortem) blood. Venous ('red') thrombi are red-cell- and fibrin-rich (stasis, e.g. DVT); arterial ('white') thrombi are platelet-rich (high flow).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: Where does thrombophlebitis occur and what is it?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back: Thrombosis combined with inflammation of a vein, most often a superficial vein.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: Describe the superficial, deep and perforator venous systems of the leg.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back:
• Superficial veins (great and small saphenous) lie in subcutaneous fat;
  • deep veins accompany the arteries;
  • perforators connect the two, their valves directing flow from superficial to deep.
The calf-muscle pump plus competent valves drive venous return; perforator incompetence causes varicose veins and venous ulcers.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.front: What defines a portal venous system and why does it matter clinically?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.back: A portal system connects two capillary beds in series (hepatic portal: gut capillaries → liver sinusoids; also the hypophyseal portal system). It is valveless, so portal hypertension is transmitted directly to porto-systemic anastomoses, producing varices.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Define peripheral arterial disease (PAD).
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Atherosclerotic narrowing of the arteries supplying the limbs — the 'CAD of the legs.' It presents on a spectrum from stable claudication to limb-threatening emergencies.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Describe chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (CLTI) — features, ABPI, Fontaine stage, and urgency.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back:
• Rest pain and/or ulcers/gangrene.
  • ABPI <0.5.
  • Fontaine III–IV.
  • Needs urgent referral.
Now termed chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (CLTI).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Describe acute limb ischaemia — cause, key feature, time frame, and category.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back:
• Sudden occlusion
  • the 6 P's
  • hours to save the limb
  • an emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What is the key framing message about claudication patients?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Claudication patients don't lose their legs — they die of MI and stroke. PAD is a systemic atherosclerosis marker; treat the whole patient, not just the leg.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: How is the ABPI calculated, and where is it used?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Ankle-Brachial Pressure Index = ankle systolic BP ÷ brachial systolic BP. Used at every stage of PAD assessment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What does an ABPI >1.3 indicate, and what is the caveat?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Calcified/stiff incompressible arteries — falsely high. Common in diabetes, chronic kidney disease and advanced age (medial calcification). Do not rely on ABPI alone — use the toe-brachial index, Doppler waveform analysis or duplex.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What ABPI range is normal, and what does it mean?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: 0.9–1.3 = normal — no significant PAD.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What does an ABPI of 0.5–0.9 indicate and how is it managed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Claudication — conservative management, supervised exercise, risk factor modification.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What does an ABPI <0.5 indicate and what action is required?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Critical ischaemia / rest pain — urgent vascular referral for revascularisation or amputation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What ABPI value must be checked before applying venous compression, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back:
Full compression bandaging needs an ABPI of 0.8–1.3 — always check first.
  • 0.5–0.8 needs reduced/modified compression under specialist guidance
  • <0.5 (ischaemic leg) must not be compressed
  • >1.3 is falsely high from calcified vessels and is not a green light — get specialist assessment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What inspection findings are seen in PAD?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back:
• Pallor, cyanosis, dependent rubor (sunset foot)
  • muscle wasting, hair loss, dry skin
  • poor wound healing, ulcers, gangrene
  • scars (amputation, sternotomy, calf vein harvest from prior bypass).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What palpation findings occur in PAD?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back:
• Weak or absent pulses (femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial)
  • reduced skin temperature, prolonged capillary refill
  • reduced sensation (late sign — neuropathy or ischaemia).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Describe Buerger's test and what the angle signifies.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Elevate the limb → pallor (ischaemia); hang the leg down → dependent rubor (reactive hyperaemia). Buerger's angle <20° = severe ischaemia (the angle at which pallor appears on elevation).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What is the classic triad of Leriche syndrome (aortoiliac occlusion)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back:
• Buttock/thigh claudication
  • absent femoral pulses bilaterally
  • and erectile dysfunction (internal iliac involvement).
A high-yield exam eponym.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: How does intermittent claudication present (Fontaine II)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Cramping pain on walking, relieved by rest within minutes; a predictable claudication distance that reliably reproduces symptoms.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: How does the site of claudication map to the level of arterial disease?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back:
• Calf = femoropopliteal (SFA)
  • thigh = iliac
  • buttock = aortoiliac (buttock claudication + erectile dysfunction = Leriche).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What investigations are used in intermittent claudication?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back:
• ABPI (0.5–0.9 in claudication; baseline and follow-up)
  • duplex ultrasound (first-line imaging — identifies stenosis site and severity)
  • MRA/CTA (before surgical intervention — full anatomical map of disease).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What is the first-line imaging in claudication, and what does it identify?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Duplex ultrasound — identifies the stenosis site and severity.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What conservative (first-line) management applies in claudication?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back:
• Supervised exercise programme (2 hr/week × 3 months — first-line; improves walking distance)
  • smoking cessation (most important intervention)
  • diet, weight loss, glycaemic control.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What medical management is used in claudication?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back:
• Atorvastatin 80 mg (established CVD — secondary prevention)
  • clopidogrel 75 mg (first-line antiplatelet; aspirin if intolerant)
  • naftidrofuryl (vasodilator for claudication if the exercise programme fails)
  • optimise BP and diabetes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What is the first-line antiplatelet in PAD, and the alternative if intolerant?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Clopidogrel 75 mg first-line; aspirin if intolerant.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: When is naftidrofuryl used in claudication?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Only when a supervised exercise programme has not produced satisfactory improvement AND the patient prefers not to be referred for angioplasty or bypass (NICE). Review at 3–6 months and stop if there is no symptomatic benefit.Cilostazol and pentoxifylline are not recommended in the UK.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: When is surgery considered in claudication, and what are the two main options by lesion type?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Lifestyle-limiting symptoms only, after risk-factor advice, supervised exercise and medical therapy have failed and imaging confirms a suitable lesion. Angioplasty — short focal lesions; bypass/endarterectomy — long or multifocal disease. Primary stenting is not offered for claudication except in complete aortoiliac occlusion, where a bare-metal stent is used (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: How is chronic limb-threatening ischaemia — CLTI, formerly critical limb ischaemia (Fontaine III–IV) — defined?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Ischaemic rest pain >2 weeks requiring opiates, OR ischaemic ulceration/gangrene — WITH objective evidence of severe arterial disease (ABPI <0.5, ankle pressure <50 mmHg or toe pressure <30 mmHg). A low ABPI on its own is not CLTI.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Describe the rest pain of critical limb ischaemia.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back:
• Worse at night (loses gravity-assisted perfusion when supine)
  • the patient hangs the foot off the bed for relief
  • requires opiates.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What tissue loss and limb signs occur in critical limb ischaemia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Tissue loss: ischaemic ulcers (punched-out, distal) and gangrene — the end-stage of untreated CLI. Limb signs: pale, cold, absent pulses; atrophic shiny skin; absent hair; poor capillary refill.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Outline the management of critical limb ischaemia.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back:
• Urgent vascular referral (same-day if acute deterioration)
  • revascularisation (angioplasty/stent, or bypass/endarterectomy)
  • amputation (if the limb is unreconstructable or there is extensive necrosis/sepsis/limited life expectancy).
Thrombolysis has no role here — it is a treatment for ACUTE limb ischaemia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Define acute limb ischaemia and the signs that mean irreversible ischaemia is imminent.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Sudden arterial occlusion threatening limb viability within hours — irreversible muscle and nerve damage begins at roughly 6 hours. Paraesthesia = threatened limb (Rutherford IIa). Paralysis with sensory loss = immediately threatened (IIb) but still SALVAGEABLE — emergency revascularisation. It is irreversible (III) only when paralysis is joined by fixed non-blanching mottling, woody-hard rigid muscles and inaudible arterial AND venous Doppler signals — then primary amputation, not revascularisation. Act immediately.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What are the 6 P's of acute limb ischaemia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back:
• Pain (severe, sudden — worse on elevation)
  • pallor (skin white/waxy vs the other limb)
  • pulselessness (absent distal pulses — confirm with handheld Doppler)
  • perishing cold (poikilothermia — limb temperature = environment)
  • paraesthesia (numbness/tingling — early nerve ischaemia, threatened limb)
  • paralysis (motor loss — the limb is immediately threatened, Rutherford IIb: emergency revascularisation within hours).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Which two of the 6 P's signal a threatened limb, and what makes ischaemia irreversible?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Paraesthesia — early nerve ischaemia, threatened limb (Rutherford IIa). Paralysis — immediately threatened limb (IIb), the late sign demanding emergency revascularisation. It is irreversible only when paralysis is combined with fixed sensory loss and non-blanching mottling with woody-hard muscles.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: How does an embolic acute limb ischaemia differ from thrombosis in situ — onset and source?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back:
• Embolus: sudden onset (<24h), no prior claudication; source = AF, mural thrombus post-MI, AAA, prosthetic valve
  • Thrombosis in situ: prior claudication with acute deterioration; source = atherosclerotic plaque rupture.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: How does the contralateral leg help distinguish embolus from thrombosis in acute limb ischaemia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Embolus → normal pulses in the other leg (localised disease). Thrombosis → reduced pulses (widespread atherosclerosis).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: How does treatment differ between embolic and thrombotic acute limb ischaemia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Embolus → embolectomy / intra-arterial thrombolysis. Thrombosis → thrombolysis / angioplasty.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Outline the immediate management of acute limb ischaemia.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back:
• A–E
  • IV opioids (pain)
  • IV heparin (prevent propagation)
  • ECG (AF?), handheld Doppler, serum lactate, CT arteriogram
  • urgent vascular referral → embolectomy/thrombolysis/angioplasty.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Which medication is given in acute limb ischaemia to prevent clot propagation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: IV heparin.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What findings in acute limb ischaemia indicate an irreversible limb requiring amputation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Mottled non-blanching skin + woody hard muscles → amputation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What is reperfusion injury after revascularisation, and what does it cause?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back:
• Compartment syndrome (→ fasciotomy)
  • hyperkalaemia
  • metabolic acidosis
  • myoglobinuria → AKI.
This is why an irreversible limb (fixed mottling, rigid muscles, no Doppler) gets primary amputation — reperfusing dead muscle can cause fatal hyperkalaemia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Compare the cause and site of arterial, venous, and neuropathic leg ulcers.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back:
• Arterial: PAD/ischaemia; distal — toes, heel, pressure points
  • Venous: venous insufficiency (80% of ulcers); gaiter area (medial malleolus)
  • Neuropathic: neuropathy (diabetes, B12 deficiency); pressure points — sole, metatarsal heads.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Compare the appearance of arterial, venous, and neuropathic ulcers.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back:
• Arterial: deep, 'punched-out', well-defined, necrotic base
  • Venous: shallow, irregular, granulating base
  • Neuropathic: punched-out, surrounded by callus.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Compare the pain and surrounding skin of arterial, venous, and neuropathic ulcers.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Pain: arterial = painful (worse on elevation); venous = aching (better on elevation); neuropathic = painless. Surrounding skin: arterial = cold, hairless, reduced pulses; venous = haemosiderin staining, varicose eczema, lipodermatosclerosis, atrophie blanche, warm; neuropathic = warm, good pulses, sensory loss.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Compare the key management of arterial, venous, and neuropathic ulcers.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back:
• Arterial: revascularise (treat as PAD)
  • Venous: compression bandaging (check ABPI is 0.8–1.3 first)
  • Neuropathic: offload, glycaemic control, foot care, check for osteomyelitis.
