conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What is safety rule 1 regarding compression bandaging in leg ulcers?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back:
Always check ABPI before compression bandaging — full compression only if 0.8–1.3.
  • Never compress an ischaemic leg (<0.5)
  • 0.5–0.8 only under specialist guidance
  • >1.3 is unreliable (calcification), not safe.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What is safety rule 2 regarding deep neuropathic ulcers?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: X-ray any deep neuropathic ulcer for osteomyelitis. Visible bone or a positive probe-to-bone test makes osteomyelitis highly likely — MRI is the investigation of choice if the X-ray is normal or equivocal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What is gangrene, and what are its three types by cause?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Gangrene = irreversible tissue death — the endpoint of the ischaemia pathway (Fontaine IV / CLI's worst). Dry gangrene arises from ischaemia; wet gangrene from ischaemia plus superadded infection; gas gangrene from infection (Clostridium).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Describe dry gangrene and its management.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back:
• Ischaemic, aseptic
  • dehydrated, mummified, black
  • well-defined demarcation line
  • the classic PAD endpoint
  • typically affects digits.
Mx: revascularise where possible; allow auto-amputation or surgical amputation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Describe wet gangrene and its management.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back:
• Ischaemia + infection
  • moist, swollen, foul-smelling
  • no clear demarcation
  • a surgical emergency with rapid spread
  • common in diabetics.
Mx: urgent debridement + IV antibiotics + revascularisation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Describe gas gangrene — organism, trigger, signs, and management.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back:
• Clostridium perfringens
  • post-trauma/contaminated wound
  • crepitus on palpation + gas on X-ray
  • extremely rapid spread
  • life-threatening.
Mx: emergency radical surgical debridement (often amputation) + IV benzylpenicillin and clindamycin + critical care support.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What are the primary indications for amputation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back:
• Extensive weight-bearing necrosis
  • uncontrolled sepsis from an infected limb
  • irreversible ischaemia (fixed paralysis with fixed mottling and woody-hard muscles)
  • limited life expectancy (palliation)
  • failed/impossible revascularisation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What conservative measures apply in general PAD management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back:
• Smoking cessation (single biggest modifiable risk factor)
  • exercise (supervised programme for claudication)
  • diet, weight loss
  • optimise diabetes and hypertension.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What medical management applies in general PAD?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back:
• Atorvastatin 80 mg (all established CVD)
  • clopidogrel 75 mg (first-line antiplatelet; aspirin if intolerant)
  • naftidrofuryl oxalate only if supervised exercise has failed and the patient declines revascularisation, reviewed at 3–6 months
  • ACEi/ARB for BP control.
Beta-blockers are not contraindicated in stable PAD — old teaching; give them if there is a cardiac indication.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: In the surgical options table, what is angioplasty ± stent best for?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Short focal stenosis; less invasive. Primary stenting is not routinely offered for claudication.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What is a bypass graft/endarterectomy best for?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Long or multifocal disease; femoropopliteal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What is intra-arterial thrombolysis best for, and when is amputation indicated?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Intra-arterial thrombolysis: acute thrombotic occlusion, <14 days onset. Amputation: last resort — unreconstructable disease, extensive necrosis, sepsis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Why is a patient with intermittent claudication given a high-intensity statin and clopidogrel when the problem is their legs?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back:
Because PAD is a marker of systemic atherosclerosis — the same disease is in the coronaries and carotids.
A claudicant is far more likely to die of myocardial infarction or stroke than to lose the limb, so PAD is treated as a coronary risk equivalent.The medical therapy treats the disease that will actually kill them; revascularisation only treats the symptom.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Distinguish Buerger's test from Buerger's disease.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back:
Buerger's test — a bedside sign: elevate the leg to look for pallor (vascular angle <20° = severe ischaemia), then hang it down for dependent rubor.
Buerger's disease (thromboangiitis obliterans) — a distinct condition: a non-atherosclerotic segmental inflammatory disease of small and medium arteries and veins (which is why migratory superficial thrombophlebitis occurs) in young, heavy smokers.Same eponym, entirely different things.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: A 38-year-old man who smokes 30 a day has distal limb ischaemia and no atherosclerotic risk factors. What is the likely diagnosis and its treatment?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back:
Buerger's disease (thromboangiitis obliterans).
Clues: young man, heavy smoker, distal ischaemia (digits), often with migratory superficial thrombophlebitis and Raynaud-like features.
Treatment: absolute smoking cessation — nothing else reliably halts progression, and revascularisation usually fails because the affected vessels are too distal.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.front: What is a malar flush and which condition classically causes it?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.back: A dusky pink–plum discolouration over the cheekbones, the classic facial sign of severe mitral stenosis (low cardiac output with peripheral vasoconstriction and pulmonary hypertension).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.front: How do you distinguish a malar flush from the malar rash of lupus?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.back: A flush is a dusky, non-scaly discolouration over the cheekbones. The lupus rash is a raised, photosensitive butterfly erythema that spares the nasolabial folds.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.front: What are the auscultatory findings of mitral stenosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.back: A loud S1, an opening snap, and a low-pitched rumbling mid-diastolic murmur at the apex — best heard with the bell, in the left lateral position, on expiration.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.front: Why does mitral stenosis so commonly cause atrial fibrillation?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.back: Obstruction at the mitral valve raises left atrial pressure and dilates the left atrium, which disrupts atrial conduction — producing AF. Loss of the atrial kick can then precipitate pulmonary oedema.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.front: What is the most common cause of mitral stenosis worldwide?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.back: Rheumatic heart disease (>90%) — typically a young woman from an endemic area with a history of rheumatic fever (sore throat, Sydenham's chorea).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.front: Why are patients with mitral stenosis at high risk of stroke?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.back: The dilated, often fibrillating left atrium promotes stasis and thrombus formation, which can embolise systemically. Anticoagulation is indicated, especially once AF develops.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.front: What signs indicate pulmonary hypertension has developed in mitral stenosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.back:
• A loud P2,
  • a right ventricular (parasternal) heave,
  • a raised JVP and
  • eventually signs of right heart failure (peripheral oedema, hepatomegaly).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.front: Which investigation confirms mitral stenosis and what does it assess?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.back: Echocardiography — it measures the valve area and transvalvular gradient, left atrial size, and estimates pulmonary artery pressure.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.front: What ECG changes are seen in mitral stenosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.back: P mitrale (a broad, bifid P wave from left atrial enlargement) in sinus rhythm, and frequently atrial fibrillation; right axis deviation / RVH if pulmonary hypertension is present.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.front: Why can pregnancy unmask or decompensate mitral stenosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.back: The increased cardiac output and heart rate of pregnancy raise flow across a fixed, narrowed valve, sharply increasing left atrial pressure and precipitating pulmonary oedema.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.front: What causes haemoptysis in mitral stenosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.back: High left atrial and pulmonary venous pressure can rupture dilated bronchial veins, and pulmonary congestion / oedema also produces blood-tinged (pink, frothy) sputum.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.front: How does the flushing of carcinoid syndrome differ from a malar flush?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.back: Carcinoid flushing is episodic / paroxysmal and accompanied by diarrhoea and wheeze, whereas a malar flush is a fixed discolouration tied to a diastolic murmur.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.front: What is a tapping apex beat?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.back: A palpable first heart sound — a non-displaced but unusually forceful apex — caused by the loud S1 of mitral stenosis.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.front: What facial sign might polycythaemia produce, and how is it distinguished?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.back: A ruddy facial plethora with aquagenic pruritus (itch after a hot bath). It is distinguished from a malar flush by the absence of a diastolic murmur and by a raised haematocrit.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.front: How is atrial fibrillation in mitral stenosis managed?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.back: Anticoagulation (the stroke risk is high — this is 'valvular' AF, warranting a vitamin-K antagonist) plus rate control; definitive treatment addresses the stenosed valve.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.front: What are the definitive treatment options for severe symptomatic mitral stenosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.back:
• Percutaneous balloon mitral valvotomy (for suitable pliable valves) or
  • surgical valve repair / replacement.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.front: What are the chest X-ray findings of mitral stenosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.back: Left atrial enlargement — a double right-heart border (double density), a splayed carina, straightening of the left heart border and a prominent left atrial appendage — with upper-lobe venous diversion, Kerley B lines and pulmonary congestion.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.front: Besides rheumatic disease, name a rare cause of mitral stenosis or its mimic.
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.back:
• Heavy mitral annular calcification,
  • congenital mitral stenosis, or
  • a left atrial myxoma obstructing the valve and mimicking the murmur (with positional symptoms and constitutional features).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.front: What is the Graham Steell murmur?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.back: An early diastolic murmur of pulmonary regurgitation secondary to severe pulmonary hypertension (as in mitral stenosis), heard at the left sternal edge and louder on inspiration.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.front: Which auscultatory features indicate that mitral stenosis is more severe?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.back: A shorter A2–opening snap interval (higher left atrial pressure opens the valve sooner) and a longer mid-diastolic murmur. Presystolic accentuation is present in sinus rhythm and lost once AF develops.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.front: What is Ortner's syndrome in mitral stenosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Malar Flush.back: Hoarseness from compression of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve by a massively enlarged left atrium (cardiovocal syndrome).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Every valve lesion in this reference follows the same revision template. What are the six steps in order?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Aetiology → Pathophysiology → Symptoms → Signs → Investigations → Management.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: A murmur is ejection systolic, crescendo-decrescendo, heard best at the right 2nd intercostal space and radiates to the carotids. Name the lesion.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Aortic stenosis (AS).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Which valve lesion produces a pansystolic, blowing, high-pitched murmur best heard at the apex and radiating to the axilla?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Mitral regurgitation (MR).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: A mid-diastolic rumbling murmur with an opening snap is heard at the apex, loudest with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position on expiration. What is the lesion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Mitral stenosis (MS).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: An early-diastolic, blowing, high-pitched murmur is heard at the left sternal edge, best with the patient sitting forward in expiration. Name it.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Aortic regurgitation (AR).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Which lesion gives a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge that gets louder on inspiration?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Tricuspid regurgitation (TR).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: List the key added peripheral features that point to aortic stenosis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back:
• Slow-rising pulse,
  • narrow pulse pressure,
  • soft S2,
  • and an S4.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Beyond the murmur, what three findings flag mitral regurgitation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back:
• Soft S1,
  • an S3,
  • and a displaced apex beat.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Which auscultatory and clinical extras accompany mitral stenosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back:
• Loud S1,
  • an opening snap,
  • malar flush,
  • and atrial fibrillation (AF).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What peripheral signs go with aortic regurgitation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back:
• Wide pulse pressure,
  • a collapsing (water-hammer) pulse,
  • and a displaced apex.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Which added features signal tricuspid regurgitation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back:
• Giant V waves in the JVP,
  • a pulsatile liver,
  • and a raised JVP.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Which valve lesions produce a systolic murmur?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Systolic murmurs: AS, MR, MVP, VSD, TR, HOCM.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Which valve lesions produce diastolic murmurs?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Aortic & pulmonary regurgitation (early diastolic) and mitral & tricuspid stenosis (mid-diastolic) — i.e. regurgitation of the outflow (semilunar) valves plus stenosis of the inflow (AV) valves.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: In what order of frequency does rheumatic fever affect the heart valves?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Mitral (most common) → Aortic → Tricuspid → Pulmonary (pulmonary involvement is rare). Note that the letters of "MAPT" do not encode the true frequency order.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: On a murmur-timing diagram, which lesion shows a crescendo-decrescendo 'diamond' shape filling systole?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Aortic stenosis (ejection systolic).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Which lesion appears as a uniform band of sound occupying the whole of systole between S1 and S2?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Mitral regurgitation (pansystolic).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: On the timing diagram, what shape and position identifies aortic regurgitation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Early-diastolic, decrescendo murmur beginning immediately after S2.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Mitral stenosis sits where in the cardiac cycle on a timing diagram?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Mid-diastolic — a rumble after the opening snap.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: A patent ductus arteriosus produces a murmur with a distinctive timing. Describe it.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: A continuous 'machinery' murmur spanning both systole and diastole.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: The mnemonic RILE summarises manoeuvre effects. What does it stand for?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Right-sided murmurs louder on Inspiration; Left-sided murmurs louder on Expiration.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Mechanistically, why does inspiration make right-sided murmurs louder?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart, raising right-sided flow and therefore murmur intensity.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Which murmurs get louder on inspiration?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Right-sided murmurs — tricuspid regurgitation, tricuspid stenosis, and pulmonary murmurs.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Why does expiration accentuate left-sided murmurs?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Expiration increases pulmonary venous return to the left heart, raising left-sided flow.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Which murmurs are loudest in expiration?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: AS, MR, MS, and AR (all left-sided).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Beyond expiration, what extra manoeuvre maximises the mitral stenosis murmur, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Left lateral decubitus position — it brings the apex closer to the chest wall.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is the optimal positioning to hear aortic regurgitation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Patient sitting forward with breath held in expiration.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: How do Valsalva, squatting and handgrip differ in their effect on murmurs?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back:
• Valsalva decreases preload and makes HOCM & MVP murmurs louder; squatting increases preload and makes them quieter.
  • Sustained handgrip raises afterload — it makes MR, AR and VSD louder and AS and HOCM quieter, which is how you separate AS from MR at the bedside.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Two murmurs have signature radiation patterns you should always check. Name them.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: AS radiates to the carotids; MR radiates to the axilla.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What causes the first heart sound (S1), and which lesion makes it louder versus softer?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: S1 = mitral and tricuspid valve closure (start of systole). Louder in MS (rigid but still mobile valves snap shut); softer in MR (valve doesn't close properly).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What produces S2, and what makes it split on inspiration?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: S2 = aortic and pulmonary valve closure. It splits on inspiration because the pulmonary valve closes slightly later.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: In which valve lesion is S2 soft or absent, and which condition gives a wide fixed split of S2?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: S2 is soft/absent in severe AS; a wide fixed split occurs in ASD. S2 is loud in pulmonary hypertension.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What does S3 represent, when is it physiological, and when is it pathological?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: S3 = rapid ventricular filling. Physiological in the young, athletic, and in pregnancy. Pathological in heart failure (LV dilatation) and severe MR — gives a 'gallop' rhythm.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Why is S4 always pathological, and what generates it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: S4 is atrial contraction against a stiff, non-compliant ventricle — this never occurs normally. Heard in AS (pressure overload), HCM, hypertension, and ischaemic disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: An opening snap follows S2 in mitral stenosis. What does a shorter S2–snap interval indicate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: The earlier the snap occurs after S2, the higher the left atrial pressure and the more severe the stenosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: A pericardial knock can be mistaken for an S3. How does it differ, and what causes it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: It sounds like S3 but occurs earlier and is louder; it is caused by abrupt halting of ventricular filling in constrictive pericarditis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is a slow-rising (parvus et tardus) pulse, and which lesion produces it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: A slow, low-amplitude aortic upstroke caused by obstruction to LV outflow — characteristic of aortic stenosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Explain the mechanism of the narrow pulse pressure in aortic stenosis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Reduced stroke volume lowers the systolic BP while the arterial diastolic pressure is relatively preserved — narrowing the gap between them.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Which lesion gives a collapsing (water-hammer) pulse, and what is the underlying mechanism?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Aortic regurgitation — regurgitation lowers diastolic pressure while compensatory increased stroke volume raises systolic, producing a wide pulse pressure and bounding, collapsing pulse.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: A patient with mitral stenosis has a low-volume pulse and malar flush. Explain both.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Fixed valve obstruction reduces cardiac output (low-volume pulse); the malar flush reflects chronically low cardiac output plus pulmonary hypertension.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What produces giant V waves in the JVP, and which lesion causes them?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Systolic regurgitation of blood into the right atrium produces a large V wave in the venous waveform — seen in tricuspid regurgitation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Why does tricuspid regurgitation cause a pulsatile, enlarged liver?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Systolic regurgitant pressure is transmitted backwards through the right atrium into the hepatic veins.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Two lesions cause a displaced, thrusting apex beat. Which, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: MR and AR — both are volume-overload states; LV dilatation pushes the apex down and out.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: How does the apex beat in aortic stenosis differ from that in MR/AR, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: AS gives a heaving, non-displaced apex (concentric LV hypertrophy from pressure overload — forceful but not dilated), whereas MR/AR give a displaced, thrusting apex from volume-overload dilatation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is the most common valvular lesion in developed countries, and what murmur defines it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Aortic stenosis — an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: The symptoms of aortic stenosis are captured by the mnemonic SAD. What are they?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Syncope, Angina, Dyspnoea.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Which is the most common overall cause of aortic stenosis, who gets it, and what's the underlying pathology?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Senile calcific AS — affects the elderly (>65 yrs); calcium deposits form on a normal tricuspid valve.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: A patient aged 40–60 presents with aortic stenosis. Which congenital cause should you suspect, and what else can it cause?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Bicuspid aortic valve — presents in middle age; congenital; can also cause aortic regurgitation (AR).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: How does rheumatic fever cause aortic stenosis, and what valve does it tend to affect first?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Post-streptococcal; causes commissural fusion. It tends to affect the mitral valve first.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: HOCM can mimic the AS murmur. How do you distinguish it on dynamic manoeuvres and radiation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: HOCM is a dynamic obstruction — the murmur increases with Valsalva and decreases with squatting, and it does NOT radiate to the carotids.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Supravalvular AS is a mimic of true AS. What kind of lesion is it and which syndrome is it associated with?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: A coarctation-type lesion above the valve, associated with Williams syndrome.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is subvalvular AS, and what is it associated with?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: A fibromuscular shelf below the valve, associated with aortic regurgitation (AR).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Aortic sclerosis is a mimic of AS. How is it distinguished by S2 and symptoms?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: It is calcification without obstruction — gives a normal S2 and no symptoms.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Walk through the core pathophysiological cascade of aortic stenosis from narrowed valve to low cardiac output.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Narrowed valve → fixed outflow obstruction → LV must generate increased pressure to eject → concentric LV hypertrophy (compensatory; preserves wall stress) → increased oxygen demand → subendocardial ischaemia → eventually LV fails → reduced stroke volume → reduced cardiac output.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Why is concentric LV hypertrophy described as compensatory in AS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: It develops in response to the pressure load and preserves wall stress.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Trace the pressure-overload pathway in AS and the symptom it ultimately produces.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Pressure overload → concentric hypertrophy → stiff, non-compliant LV → raised LVEDP → diastolic dysfunction → dyspnoea.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: How can AS cause angina even when the coronary arteries are normal?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Subendocardial ischaemia produces angina even with normal coronaries.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is the mechanism and prognosis of syncope in aortic stenosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Exertional syncope: fixed cardiac output plus peripheral vasodilation causes cerebral underperfusion. Once symptomatic, prognosis worsens — syncope ~3 years, angina ~5 years, and heart failure/dyspnoea carries the WORST prognosis at ~2 years.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Describe the mechanism and survival associated with angina in AS.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Exertional angina from subendocardial ischaemia (increased demand plus reduced supply). Survival ~5 years.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What drives dyspnoea in AS, and what is its prognostic significance?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea/PND from LV failure and raised LVEDP. It has the worst median survival — ~2 years.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: State the key prognostic principle linking symptoms to outcome in AS.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Once symptoms develop, prognosis is poor without surgery. Asymptomatic AS (even if severe) has a much better prognosis than symptomatic AS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Fully describe the aortic stenosis murmur, including where it is loudest and where it radiates.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Ejection systolic (crescendo-decrescendo), loudest at the right 2nd ICS, radiating to the carotids.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: When is the AS murmur preceded by an ejection click, and when is it absent?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: When the valve is still mobile and non-calcified — classically a bicuspid valve in a younger patient. The click disappears once the valve calcifies and stiffens.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What are the three components of the AS triad on pulse/sounds?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back:
• Slow-rising (parvus et tardus) pulse — small amplitude, slow upstroke;
  • narrow pulse pressure (from reduced stroke volume);
  • soft/absent S2 (calcified immobile valve can't produce a crisp closure sound).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Why does AS produce an S4 and a heaving apex beat?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: S4 = atrial kick against a stiff, hypertrophied LV; the heaving (sustained, non-displaced) apex beat reflects concentric hypertrophy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What additional palpable sign indicates severe AS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: A systolic thrill at the base.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Why can the AS murmur become quieter as the disease becomes very severe, and what's the clinical warning?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Failing LV → reduced stroke volume → less turbulence, so the murmur softens. Do not be reassured by a soft murmur in a sick patient.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: On echo, which Doppler measurements define severe aortic stenosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Mean gradient >40 mmHg / peak velocity >4 m/s (peak gradient >64 mmHg), and aortic valve area (AVA) <1 cm². Beware low-flow low-gradient AS: with a small or failing LV the gradient can be <40 mmHg despite an AVA <1 cm² and a stroke volume index <35 mL/m² — low-dose dobutamine stress echo distinguishes true severe from pseudo-severe AS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Besides the Doppler gradient, what else does echo assess in AS, and how often should it be repeated in asymptomatic severe disease?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: LV hypertrophy, function and wall motion, plus bicuspid valve morphology. Serial echo ~6-monthly if asymptomatic severe (yearly for moderate, 2–3-yearly for mild).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What ECG changes are seen in aortic stenosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: LVH (tall R in V5–6, deep S in V1–2) and a strain pattern — ST depression plus T-wave inversion in the lateral leads.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What might you see on CXR in aortic stenosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Calcified aortic valve (lateral film), post-stenotic dilatation of the ascending aorta, and LVH (heart size is often normal — a boot-shaped heart is Tetralogy of Fallot, not AS).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is the role of cardiac catheterisation in AS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Used if echo is inconclusive, and for pre-op coronary angiography.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: How is BNP useful in aortic stenosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: A rising BNP in asymptomatic AS predicts symptom onset.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Surgical AVR (SAVR) is the gold standard for most AS patients. What are the indications?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Symptomatic severe AS (SAD criteria). In the asymptomatic patient, consider referral if LVEF <55%, peak jet velocity >5 m/s, AVA <0.6 cm², or BNP/NT-proBNP more than twice the upper limit of normal (NICE) — also if exercise testing unmasks symptoms, or the patient is having other cardiac surgery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: How do you choose between a mechanical and a bioprosthetic valve in SAVR?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Mechanical = durable but commits the patient to lifelong warfarin; bioprosthetic = no long-term anticoagulation but degenerates over ~10–15 years and may need redo surgery. Age is only a proxy for that trade-off. Pregnancy plans matter because warfarin is teratogenic.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is TAVI and which AS patients is it for?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Transcatheter (transfemoral, catheter-based) aortic valve implantation. UK practice is risk-based, not age-based: surgery first-line at low or intermediate surgical risk; TAVI for high surgical risk or when surgery is unsuitable, and for non-bicuspid valves (NICE). European guidance additionally favours TAVI from around 70 years upward (ESC). Always a heart-team/MDT decision. No open-chest surgery required.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is the role and limitation of balloon aortic valvuloplasty in AS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: A temporary measure only with a high restenosis rate; serves as a bridge to definitive AVR/TAVI in haemodynamically unstable patients. Not a definitive treatment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Summarise the medical management of aortic stenosis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: No drug is proven to slow AS progression; diuretics are for symptoms only.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Why are vasodilators and nitrates relatively contraindicated in aortic stenosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: The obstruction is fixed — dropping afterload can cause severe hypotension.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What murmur defines mitral regurgitation, and what is the key clinical distinction in how it presents?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: A pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla. Chronic MR is well-tolerated; acute MR is an emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is the most common cause of mitral regurgitation in the developed world, and what is its underlying pathology and murmur?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Mitral valve prolapse (MVP) — from myxomatous degeneration; gives a click plus a late systolic murmur (Barlow's).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is the most common cause of mitral regurgitation worldwide, and how does it damage the valve?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Rheumatic fever — causes fibrosis plus commissural fusion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: How can infective endocarditis cause mitral regurgitation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Valve leaflet destruction; it can cause acute MR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Distinguish the acute from the chronic mechanism by which ischaemia causes mitral regurgitation.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Papillary muscle rupture causes acute MR (post-STEMI); ischaemia causes chronic functional MR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Which connective tissue disorders predispose to mitral regurgitation, and via what mechanism?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Marfan's and Ehlers-Danlos — through myxomatous change.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is functional mitral regurgitation, and why are the leaflets normal?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: LV dilatation (from any cause of DCM) stretches the annulus → annular dilatation, but the leaflets themselves are normal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: In acute MR, why does sudden regurgitation lead to acute pulmonary oedema and emergency surgery?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Causes include IE, papillary muscle rupture, and chest trauma; the LV and LA have no time to dilate → sudden rise in LA pressure → acute pulmonary oedema → needs emergency surgery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Why is chronic MR tolerated for years before symptoms appear?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Gradual LV and LA dilatation (compensatory) accommodates the large regurgitant volume for years, until the LV eventually fails from volume overload — then exertional dyspnoea, AF and emboli appear.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Trace the full pathophysiological cascade of mitral regurgitation from incompetent valve to right heart failure.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Incompetent mitral valve → systolic regurgitation into the LA → increased LA volume and pressure → LA dilatation → AF → pulmonary hypertension → right heart failure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: How does the LV compensate in chronic MR, and what is the eventual outcome?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: The LV handles increased preload via eccentric LV dilatation (volume overload); increased stroke volume compensates, until the LV eventually fails.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is the regurgitant fraction in MR, and how high can it get in severe disease?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: The proportion of stroke volume going backwards into the LA. In severe MR it can be >50% — the LV ejects twice what it needs to maintain forward output.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Explain why AF develops in MR and why anticoagulation becomes relevant.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: LA dilatation stretches the atrial myocardium → triggers AF. Once AF develops there is LA thrombus + embolic risk → anticoagulate.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: List the symptoms of chronic mitral regurgitation.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back:
• Exertional dyspnoea (progressive),
  • fatigue (reduced forward CO),
  • palpitations (AF),
  • peripheral oedema (RHF),
  • embolic events (AF + LA thrombus);
often asymptomatic for many years.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What are the hallmark features of acute MR as an emergency?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back:
• Sudden severe pulmonary oedema and cardiogenic shock;
  • cause usually evident (IE, post-MI papillary muscle rupture, trauma);
  • murmur may be soft or inaudible (equalisation of pressures);
  • requires urgent surgical repair/replacement.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Why might the murmur be soft or inaudible in acute MR?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Equalisation of pressures between the LV and LA reduces turbulent flow.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Fully describe the mitral regurgitation murmur, including timing, character, site, radiation, and maximising manoeuvres.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Pansystolic (throughout systole, from S1 to S2), blowing, high-pitched, at the apex, radiating to the axilla. Louder in expiration and with the patient in left lateral decubitus.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Why is S1 soft in mitral regurgitation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: The valve doesn't close completely, so the closure sound is attenuated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What does an S3 signify in mitral regurgitation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Rapid ventricular filling from the enlarged LA — a sign of significant MR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Describe the apex beat in mitral regurgitation and the reason for it.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Displaced, diffuse apex beat — LV volume overload → eccentric dilatation; the apex moves down and out.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What additional signs may be present in MR relating to rhythm and advanced disease?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Signs of AF (irregularly irregular pulse), and signs of pulmonary HTN / right HF in severe chronic MR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is the key investigation in MR and what does it assess?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Echo — quantifies severity (regurgitant fraction, vena contracta, ERO area), assesses LV dimensions and function (triggers for surgery); TOE if TTE is inadequate or pre-operative; serial echo 6–12 monthly in moderate-severe.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What ECG findings occur in mitral regurgitation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: AF; P mitrale (bifid P if in sinus); LVH. The broad notched P wave reflects LA enlargement from volume overload, and AF is common in chronic MR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What CXR findings are seen in mitral regurgitation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: LA enlargement (double heart border, widened carina); pulmonary oedema; cardiomegaly.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is the role of cardiac MRI and BNP in MR?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Cardiac MRI quantifies regurgitant volume if echo is inadequate; BNP is a useful marker of LV stress.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Outline the medical management of mitral regurgitation.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back:
• Treat heart failure: ACEi/ARB (reduce afterload, lower regurgitant fraction), diuretics, beta-blockers;
  • rate control/anticoagulation if AF (CHA₂DS₂-VASc);
  • serial echo surveillance;
  • IE prophylaxis not routinely recommended (UK).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What are the surgical indications in mitral regurgitation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back:
• Symptomatic severe MR with preserved EF;
  • asymptomatic severe MR with LVESD ≥40 mm (or indexed LVESD ≥20 mm/m²), EF ≤60%, AF or pulmonary HTN;
  • acute severe MR → emergency surgery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Why is repair preferred over replacement in MR when feasible?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: When anatomically feasible, repair gives lower mortality and avoids the need for anticoagulation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is MitraClip and who is it for?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Percutaneous leaflet repair; an option for very high surgical risk patients with severe symptomatic MR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is the single overwhelming cause of mitral stenosis, and what murmur and manoeuvre characterise it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Rheumatic (almost always). It gives a mid-diastolic rumble plus an opening snap, louder leaning left, on expiration.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What proportion of mitral stenosis is rheumatic in origin, and what is the typical time lag from the initial illness?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Almost all MS is rheumatic — often 10–20 years after the initial illness.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Explain how post-streptococcal pharyngitis leads to mitral stenosis at the valve level.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Post-streptococcal Group A (GAS) pharyngitis triggers immune-mediated cardiac inflammation → valve fibrosis + commissural fusion + chordal shortening.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: In rheumatic heart disease, how often is the mitral valve involved, and what other lesion often coexists?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: The mitral valve is affected in >90% of rheumatic heart disease; often with MR also.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Name some rare non-rheumatic causes (or mimics) of mitral stenosis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back:
• Congenital MS,
  • a large LA myxoma (mimics MS),
  • and Libman-Sacks endocarditis in SLE (usually causes MR, only rarely true MS).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Why is mitral stenosis becoming rare in developed countries but still common elsewhere?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Rheumatic fever rates have fallen in developed countries; MS remains prevalent in the developing world.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Trace the full pathophysiology of mitral stenosis from the fused valve through to right heart failure.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Fibrotic, fused mitral valve → fixed obstruction to LA emptying → increased LA pressure → LA dilatation → AF → LA thrombus/emboli. Simultaneously: raised LA pressure → pulmonary venous hypertension → pulmonary arterial hypertension → right heart failure. The LV is actually underfilled and often normal or small.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: In mitral stenosis, what is the state of the LV, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: The LV is underfilled and often normal or small, because the stenotic valve limits filling.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What complication does LA dilatation in MS lead to, and what is its downstream risk?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: LA dilatation → AF → thrombus → systemic embolism (stroke).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Trace the pulmonary HTN pathway in mitral stenosis and its endpoint.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Pulmonary HTN → RV pressure overload → RV hypertrophy → RHF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: How does reduced LV filling in MS translate into symptoms?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Reduced LV filling → reduced cardiac output → fatigue and exertional dyspnoea.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: List the symptoms of mitral stenosis arising from raised LA pressure.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back:
• Exertional dyspnoea (progressive) → orthopnoea, PND;
  • haemoptysis (pulmonary venous congestion);
  • pulmonary oedema (especially with tachycardia, pregnancy, infection);
  • right heart failure symptoms — oedema, ascites.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What symptoms in MS arise from AF / emboli, and which patients may stay asymptomatic?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back:
• Palpitations (AF — irregular, often precipitates acute decompensation);
  • stroke/TIA/peripheral emboli (LA thrombus);
  • fatigue (reduced CO).
Patients may remain asymptomatic for years if mild-moderate.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Why can pregnancy, tachycardia or infection precipitate pulmonary oedema in mitral stenosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: These states shorten diastolic filling time and increase demand, raising LA pressure and tipping into pulmonary oedema.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Fully describe the mitral stenosis murmur, including how it is best heard and what presystolic accentuation indicates.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Mid-diastolic, low-pitched rumble, best heard at the apex with the patient in left lateral decubitus, using the bell, on expiration. Presystolic accentuation occurs if in sinus rhythm (atrial kick).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Where is the opening snap heard in MS, and what does the timing of the snap indicate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Just after S2. An earlier snap means higher LA pressure = more severe stenosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Why is S1 loud in mitral stenosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Forceful closure of the stiff (but still mobile) mitral leaflets.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Why does mitral stenosis produce a low-volume pulse?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Fixed obstruction reduces stroke volume.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is malar flush in MS and what is its mechanism?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Mitral facies — dusky malar flush; from chronic low CO + pulmonary HTN → peripheral vasoconstriction / cutaneous cyanosis with dilated malar capillaries.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What pulse and advanced-disease signs occur in mitral stenosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Irregularly irregular pulse (AF is very common); signs of right HF in advanced disease (raised JVP, oedema, hepatomegaly).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Describe the apex beat in mitral stenosis and why it is non-displaced.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: A tapping apex beat — a palpable loud S1; non-displaced because the LV is normal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What does echo assess in mitral stenosis, including the values that define severe disease?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back:
• Leaflet thickening/calcification, subvalvular disease, commissural fusion;
  • mitral valve area (MVA) — severe if <1 cm²;
  • mean gradient across valve (severe: >10 mmHg);
  • LA size (dilatation), LA thrombus (TOE more sensitive);
  • pulmonary artery pressure estimate.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What ECG findings occur in mitral stenosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: P mitrale — bifid (notched) P wave in II (>120 ms), broad P in V1; AF; right axis deviation (RVH from pulmonary HTN). AF is very common in chronic MS due to atrial dilatation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What CXR findings are seen in mitral stenosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back:
• LA enlargement (left atrial appendage, double right heart border, widened carina);
  • pulmonary venous congestion (Kerley B lines);
  • pulmonary oedema;
  • mitral valve calcification.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is the role of cardiac catheterisation in mitral stenosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Used if echo is insufficient; measures pulmonary capillary wedge pressure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Outline the medical management of mitral stenosis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back:
• Rate control (beta-blocker, digoxin, rate-limiting CCB) — slowing HR allows more time for diastolic filling across the stenotic valve;
  • anticoagulation with warfarin for all patients with MS + AF, because DOACs are contraindicated in moderate-to-severe rheumatic MS;
  • diuretics for congestion;
  • penicillin prophylaxis if there is a history of rheumatic fever.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is notable about anticoagulation thresholds in MS with AF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: All patients with MS + AF are anticoagulated — high embolic risk even with a CHA₂DS₂-VASc score of 0. Use warfarin: DOACs are contraindicated in moderate-to-severe rheumatic MS. "Valvular AF" means exactly these two situations — a mechanical valve or moderate-to-severe rheumatic MS. AF with any other valve lesion is anticoagulated as ordinary AF, where a DOAC is appropriate.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is the first-line interventional treatment for mitral stenosis and what anatomy must be suitable?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Percutaneous balloon mitral valvotomy (valvuloplasty) — first-line if anatomy is suitable (pliable non-calcified leaflets, no significant MR, no LA thrombus); gives immediate haemodynamic improvement.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: When is surgical mitral commissurotomy / valve replacement used in MS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: If anatomy is unsuitable for balloon, or if severe MR coexists.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What are the indications for intervention in mitral stenosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Significant MS (MVA ≤1.5 cm²) that is symptomatic; or, if asymptomatic, when there is pulmonary hypertension, new-onset AF, previous embolism, or a desire for pregnancy — intervene before conceiving, because pregnancy reliably decompensates significant MS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What single haemodynamic fact underlies aortic regurgitation, and what murmur and positioning characterise it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Wide pulse pressure → all the eponymous signs. The murmur is early diastolic at the left sternal edge, with the patient leaning forward in expiration. This is chronic AR: in acute AR the pulse pressure is normal or narrow and the murmur is short and soft.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: List the valve/leaflet causes of aortic regurgitation.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back:
• Rheumatic fever (fibrosis + retraction of leaflets, often with MS);
  • bicuspid aortic valve (congenital; causes both AS and AR);
  • infective endocarditis (leaflet perforation/destruction; acute AR);
  • collagen vascular disease (SLE, RA).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: List the aortic root (dilatation) causes of aortic regurgitation.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back:
• Aortic dissection (acute emergency; dissection extends to aortic root);
  • Marfan syndrome (cystic medial necrosis → aortic root dilatation);
  • syphilitic aortitis (obliterative endarteritis of vasa vasorum; classic cause);
  • hypertension (chronic aortic root dilatation);
  • ankylosing spondylitis, Reiter's syndrome, relapsing polychondritis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Which two emergencies cause acute AR, and why do they require emergency surgery?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: IE (leaflet destruction) and aortic dissection (root involvement) — both cause acute haemodynamic collapse, requiring emergency surgery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Trace the pathophysiology of chronic aortic regurgitation from incompetent valve to LV failure.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Incompetent aortic valve → diastolic regurgitation into the LV → increased LV end-diastolic volume → eccentric LV dilatation (volume overload, same as MR) → compensatory increased stroke volume → maintains forward output for years → LV eventually dilates and fails.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Explain the mechanism of the wide pulse pressure in aortic regurgitation.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Regurgitation lowers diastolic BP (blood runs back into the LV); compensatory increased stroke volume raises systolic BP. All peripheral signs flow from this single haemodynamic fact.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Why is acute AR so dangerous, and why might its murmur be short or soft?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: The LV has no time to dilate → acute rise in LVEDP → marked rise in LA pressure → acute pulmonary oedema. The murmur may be short/soft as pressures equalise rapidly.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: List the symptoms of chronic aortic regurgitation.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back:
• Asymptomatic for years (compensated LV dilatation);
  • exertional dyspnoea (progressive as LV fails);
  • awareness of heartbeat (wide pulse pressure, hyperdynamic circulation);
  • angina (increased O₂ demand + reduced diastolic coronary filling pressure);
  • orthopnoea/PND (LV failure).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What are the features of acute AR as an emergency?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back:
• Sudden-onset acute pulmonary oedema;
  • cardiogenic shock;
  • cause is IE or aortic dissection;
  • emergency surgery required.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Why does aortic regurgitation cause angina even with normal coronaries?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Increased O₂ demand combined with reduced diastolic coronary filling pressure (from the low diastolic BP).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Fully describe the aortic regurgitation murmur, including positioning and the accompanying systolic murmur.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Early diastolic, blowing, high-pitched, decrescendo — best heard at the left sternal edge, with the patient sitting forward, breath held in expiration, using the diaphragm. There is also a systolic ejection murmur (from increased flow across the aortic valve from the large stroke volume).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is the Austin Flint murmur, what causes it, and how is it distinguished from true MS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: A mid-diastolic rumble at the apex — the regurgitant jet impinges on the anterior mitral leaflet, causing functional MS. It can be confused with true MS, but there is no opening snap in Austin Flint.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is Corrigan's / water-hammer pulse?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Rapid upstroke and collapse, felt at the wrist and carotids; lifting the arm exaggerates the pulsation. It is the collapsing pulse.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is Quincke's sign?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Capillary pulsation visible at the nail-bed (press lightly on the nail) — systolic flushing plus diastolic blanching from the wide pulse pressure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is de Musset's sign?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Head nodding with each heartbeat — carotid hyperdynamic pulsation moves the head. (de Musset was a French poet with AR.)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is Duroziez's sign?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: A systolic and diastolic murmur heard over the femoral artery on partial compression with the stethoscope — from retrograde diastolic flow.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is Traube's sign?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: A 'pistol-shot' sound heard over the femoral artery — from hyperdynamic systolic pulsation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is Hill's sign and when is it significant?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Popliteal systolic BP exceeds brachial systolic by more than 20 mmHg (a small difference is normal) — the wider the gap, the more severe the AR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Describe the apex beat in aortic regurgitation and its mechanism.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Displaced, diffuse, thrusting/hyperdynamic apex beat — down and out (volume overload → eccentric LV dilatation). ('Heaving' is reserved for pressure overload/AS.)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What does echo assess in aortic regurgitation, including the LV dimensions that trigger surgery?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back:
• Quantifies regurgitation severity;
  • assesses LV size — progressive LV dilatation on serial echo is a surgical trigger;
  • LV systolic function (EF <50%) — the key surgical trigger;
  • aortic root diameter and morphology;
  • serial 6–12 monthly if moderate-severe.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What ECG and CXR findings occur in aortic regurgitation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: ECG: LVH (volume overload pattern — tall voltage, without strain); AF possible. CXR: cardiomegaly (LV dilatation); ± aortic root dilatation/unfolded aorta. A strain pattern (ST depression and T-wave inversion laterally) indicates pressure overload — AS or hypertension — rather than the volume overload of AR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: When are CT aorta and cardiac MRI used in aortic regurgitation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: CT aorta if dissection is suspected or root dilatation (>45 mm); cardiac MRI is the most accurate for quantifying regurgitant volume.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Outline the medical management of aortic regurgitation.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Vasodilators/ACEi — reduce afterload → lower regurgitant fraction; indicated if LV dilatation/hypertension and not a surgical candidate. Diuretics for symptoms. Monitor BP — aortic root dilatation, target <130/80.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Why are beta-blockers generally avoided in aortic regurgitation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: They increase diastolic time (prolonging the regurgitation), so aren't first-line for the leak itself — but are used when there is aortic root dilatation/Marfan.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What are the surgical AVR indications in aortic regurgitation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back:
• Symptomatic severe AR;
  • asymptomatic severe AR with EF <50%, LVESD >50 mm, or indexed LVESD >24 mm/m²;
  • acute severe AR (IE, dissection) → emergency surgery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Why should AVR in AR be done before irreversible LV dysfunction?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Once EF falls, surgery is still beneficial but the risk increases — so operate before irreversible LV dysfunction sets in.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is the most common cause of tricuspid regurgitation, and why are the leaflets normal?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Functional TR — RV dilatation from any cause (pulmonary HTN, RV failure) → annular dilatation; the leaflets themselves are normal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: List the causes of tricuspid regurgitation beyond functional.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back:
• Rheumatic fever (usually with MS/MR);
  • IE — especially IVDU (right-sided IE);
  • carcinoid syndrome (plaques on tricuspid/pulmonary valves);
  • congenital (Ebstein's anomaly — tricuspid displaced into RV).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Why is right-sided IE particularly associated with IVDU?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Intravenous drug use predisposes to right-sided infective endocarditis, a cause of TR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: How does carcinoid syndrome cause tricuspid regurgitation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: It deposits plaques on the tricuspid/pulmonary valves.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is Ebstein's anomaly?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: A congenital cause of TR — the tricuspid valve is displaced into the RV.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Describe the tricuspid regurgitation murmur and its key clinical features.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back:
• Pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge, louder on inspiration;
  • giant V waves in the JVP (systolic regurgitation into RA → large V wave);
  • pulsatile/enlarged liver (systolic regurgitation transmitted to hepatic veins);
  • peripheral oedema, ascites (RHF);
  • raised JVP.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: How is tricuspid regurgitation managed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back:
• Treat the underlying cause;
  • diuretics;
  • surgery if severe and refractory.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is the cause and core haemodynamic lesion of tricuspid stenosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Rare; almost always rheumatic (almost always with MS). Fixed obstruction → increased RA pressure → RA dilatation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What JVP and murmur findings occur in tricuspid stenosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Giant a waves in the JVP (prominent atrial contraction against obstruction); a diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge, louder on inspiration.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Why does tricuspid stenosis cause hepatomegaly, ascites and oedema without pulmonary congestion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: The obstruction is upstream of the lungs (blocked before blood reaches them), so congestion is systemic (hepatomegaly, ascites, oedema) rather than pulmonary.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: How is tricuspid stenosis treated?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Balloon valvuloplasty or surgical commissurotomy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is the Graham Steell murmur, where is it heard, and what most commonly causes it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: An early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge, due to pulmonary regurgitation secondary to pulmonary hypertension (the most common cause).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Besides pulmonary HTN, what other causes of pulmonary regurgitation are noted, and what is its natural history?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Congenital; post-surgical (ToF repair). Usually benign but can cause RV dilatation and failure over time; louder on inspiration.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: How does pulmonary stenosis usually arise, and what conditions is it part of?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Usually congenital — isolated or part of Fallot's tetralogy or Noonan's.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Describe the pulmonary stenosis murmur and associated signs.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Ejection systolic murmur at the upper left sternal edge plus an ejection click; the murmur is louder on inspiration (the pulmonary ejection click uniquely softens on inspiration); signs of RV pressure overload (heave, raised JVP).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is the prognosis and treatment of pulmonary stenosis by severity?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Mild-moderate: excellent prognosis. Severe: balloon valvuloplasty.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Exam pearl: which two murmurs have signature radiation, and what does it remind you to do?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: AS → carotids; MR → axilla. Always examine the neck and axilla when you hear a murmur.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Exam pearl: state the RILE rule for maximising murmurs on examination.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back:
• Right-sided louder on Inspiration,
  • Left-sided louder on Expiration.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Exam pearl: summarise the AS symptom mnemonic and its prognostic implication.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: AS symptoms = SAD (Syncope, Angina, Dyspnoea — all exertional). Once SAD develops, prognosis is poor without surgery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Exam pearl: recall the AS triad and the origin of its S4.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Slow-rising pulse + narrow pulse pressure + soft S2; S4 from the stiff hypertrophied LV.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Exam pearl: which lesion produces a wide pulse pressure, and what does that single fact explain?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Chronic AR — all the eponyms (Corrigan's, Quincke's, de Musset's, Duroziez's, Hill's) are explained by the wide pulse pressure alone. In acute AR there is no time to compensate, so the wide pulse pressure and every eponym are absent — a normal pulse pressure does not exclude severe AR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Exam pearl: contrast P mitrale with the Austin Flint murmur.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: P mitrale = MS (bifid P in lead II, >120 ms). Austin Flint murmur = AR mimicking MS (no opening snap).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Exam pearl: what does a bicuspid aortic valve cause across the lifespan, and what must you screen for?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: AS in middle age (calcification) AND AR (leaflet dysfunction). Screen for aortic root dilatation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Exam pearl: which acute valve lesions are emergencies, and what are their causes?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Acute severe MR or AR = emergency (pulmonary oedema). Causes: IE (leaflet destruction), aortic dissection (AR), papillary muscle rupture (MR).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Exam pearl: trace the rheumatic fever valve thread and the prophylaxis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: MS → MR → AR → TS/TR. Almost all MS is rheumatic; treat with penicillin prophylaxis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Exam pearl: what does the timing of the opening snap in MS tell you, and what does its absence imply?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Earlier snap = higher LA pressure = more severe stenosis. No opening snap = heavily calcified immobile leaflets.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Exam pearl: when should you operate on AR, even in an asymptomatic patient?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Operate on AR before irreversible LV dysfunction: if EF <50%, LVESD >50 mm, or indexed LVESD >24 mm/m², even if asymptomatic — don't wait for symptoms.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is the real trade-off between a mechanical and a bioprosthetic valve?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back:
• Mechanical: durable (lasts decades) but commits the patient to lifelong warfarin.
  • Bioprosthetic: no long-term anticoagulation, but structurally degenerates over roughly 10–15 years and may need redo surgery.
Age is only a proxy for this trade-off — a younger patient has more years for a tissue valve to fail, an older one has fewer years of warfarin risk. Plans for pregnancy also count, since warfarin is teratogenic.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Which anticoagulant is used for a mechanical heart valve, and which must be avoided?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Warfarin — with the target INR set by the valve type and its position. DOACs are contraindicated. In trials against mechanical valves they performed worse than warfarin, with more valve thrombosis and more bleeding.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What are the important complications of a prosthetic heart valve?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back:
• Valve thrombosis / obstruction
  • Prosthetic valve endocarditis
  • Structural degeneration (bioprosthetic valves)
  • Haemolysis from a paravalvular leak
A new or changed prosthetic murmur, or unexplained fever, warrants urgent assessment.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.back: Small, tender, purplish nodules on the pulps of the fingers and toes — an immune-complex / vasculitic phenomenon of infective endocarditis. Mnemonic: “Osler = Ouch” (tender).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.front: How do Osler's nodes differ from Janeway lesions?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.back:
• Osler’s — tender nodules on the finger/toe pulps, immune-complex, more subacute
  • Janeway — painless macules on the palms/soles, septic emboli, more acute (S. aureus)

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.front: What condition do Osler's nodes point to, and what is their Duke status?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.back: Infective endocarditis — they count as a minor (immunologic) criterion in the modified Duke criteria.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.front: What is the pathophysiology of Osler's nodes?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.back: Immune-complex deposition causing a small-vessel vasculitis in the digital pulps (hence tender).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.front: Which organisms cause subacute infective endocarditis (the setting for Osler's nodes)?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.back: Strep viridans (poor dentition/dental work), Enterococcus (GU/GI source), and Strep gallolyticus (bovis) — the last mandates colonoscopy to exclude colorectal cancer.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.front: Why does Streptococcus gallolyticus (bovis) endocarditis require a colonoscopy?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.back: It is strongly associated with colorectal cancer (and other colonic pathology) — “bovis in the blood, cancer in the bowel” — so it warrants lower GI investigation.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.front: Besides Osler's nodes, what other peripheral signs suggest infective endocarditis?
What is the first investigation when infective endocarditis is suspected in a stable patient?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.back: Three sets of blood cultures from separate sites, taken before antibiotics (an unstable/septic patient is treated empirically without delay).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.front: Which imaging confirms infective endocarditis, and which is more sensitive?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.back: Echocardiography — transthoracic (TTE) first; transoesophageal (TOE) is more sensitive for vegetations, abscess and prosthetic valves.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.front: What are the two major modified Duke criteria?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.back: Typical positive blood cultures and echocardiographic endocardial involvement (vegetation, abscess, new valve regurgitation).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.front: What does a new PR prolongation / AV block indicate in infective endocarditis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.back: An aortic root abscess (peri-valvular extension) — an indication for urgent surgery.
Immune-complex glomerulonephritis (and/or septic renal emboli) — supporting the immune-complex picture alongside Osler’s nodes.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.front: What are the main risk factors for infective endocarditis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.back:
• IV drug use
  • a prosthetic or abnormal native valve
  • previous endocarditis
  • congenital heart disease
  • and recent dental/instrumentation with poor dentition

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.front: Which non-endocarditis conditions cause Osler-like tender acral nodules?
In an IV drug user with fever, which valve and organism are typical?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.back: The tricuspid valve (right-sided), classically Staphylococcus aureus, with septic pulmonary emboli.
Retinal haemorrhages with pale centres on fundoscopy — an immune peripheral sign of infective endocarditis.
Prior antibiotics (commonest), and fastidious organisms — HACEK group, Coxiella burnetii (Q fever), Bartonella, Brucella and fungi.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.front: Which peripheral signs of endocarditis are immune-complex vs embolic?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.back:
• Immune-complex — Osler’s nodes, Roth spots, glomerulonephritis
  • Embolic — Janeway lesions, splinter haemorrhages, systemic/septic emboli

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What is the mechanism of acute heart failure (AHF)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: An acute event leaves the heart unable to meet the circulation's demands. Most commonly the LV cannot pump forward → backlog into the left atrium, pulmonary veins and lungs → pulmonary oedema. AHF occurs with reduced OR preserved ejection fraction — flash pulmonary oedema in a hypertensive elderly patient with a normal EF is a common presentation — and can also be predominantly right-sided (raised JVP with clear lungs) or low-output with hypoperfusion rather than florid congestion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What is de novo acute heart failure, and what are its typical causes?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: A first-ever presentation with no prior HF diagnosis. Often caused by a new MI, hypertensive emergency, or acute valve rupture.It requires a full diagnostic workup.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What is decompensated chronic heart failure, and how common is it relative to de novo AHF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Known HF that is acutely worsened by a trigger — it is the more common form.Management involves identifying and treating the trigger while optimising chronic therapy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: How does the acute management of de novo AHF differ from decompensated AHF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: The acute management is the same, but de novo AHF additionally needs a full diagnostic workup to find the cause.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: List the common triggers that precipitate decompensated chronic heart failure.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back:
• MI/ACS
  • new AF or arrhythmia
  • hypertensive emergency
  • sepsis/infection
  • iatrogenic IV fluids
  • non-compliance with medications
  • anaemia/PE
  • and valvular rupture

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What are the SYMPTOMS of acute heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back:
• Acute shortness of breath (worse lying flat, improves sitting up)
  • cough with frothy white/pink sputum
  • raised respiratory rate with reduced O₂ sats
  • and extreme anxiety / sense of impending doom

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What are the SIGNS of acute heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back:
• Tachycardia and tachypnoea
  • a 3rd heart sound
  • bilateral basal crackles
  • hypotension in severe cases (cardiogenic shock)
  • signs of the underlying cause (chest pain in ACS, fever in sepsis, palpitations in arrhythmia)
  • and — if right-sided HF too — raised JVP and peripheral oedema

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What does hypotension signify in acute heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: It marks severe disease and should prompt an immediate assessment for cardiogenic shock — hypotension plus hypoperfusion (cool clammy peripheries, mottling, oliguria, confusion, rising lactate).Hypotension alone is not shock, and shock can occur with a near-normal blood pressure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What is the role of an ECG in acute heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: To look for arrhythmias (AF), ischaemia (STEMI/NSTEMI) and LBBB — it helps identify the trigger.
