conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: Which bloods are sent in acute heart failure, and what is each looking for?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back:
• FBC (anaemia)
  • U&E (renal function)
  • BNP/NT-proBNP
  • troponin
  • and CRP/cultures (sepsis)
D-dimer only if PE is clinically suspected (not routine).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What is the role of an arterial blood gas (ABG) in acute heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: To assess the degree of hypoxia and hypercapnia, guiding the need for NIV or intubation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What does echocardiography assess in acute heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: LV function and structural abnormalities — it identifies the cause (e.g. valve rupture, wall motion abnormality).In new suspected acute heart failure, do it within 48 hours of admission (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What level of care does acute heart failure require, and when is HDU/ITU needed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: It requires hospital admission. Severe pulmonary oedema or cardiogenic shock warrants HDU or ITU.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What does the SODIUM mnemonic stand for in first-line AHF management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back:
• S – Sit up
  • O – Oxygen
  • D – IV Diuretic
  • I – IV fluids stop
  • U – Underlying cause (treat the trigger)
  • M – Monitor

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: In the SODIUM approach, why is sitting the patient up beneficial?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: It reduces venous return (preload) to the failing ventricle and lets the diaphragm move more freely, easing the work of breathing and improving gas exchange.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What is the oxygen target in AHF, and what is added if it is not achieved on oxygen alone?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Give oxygen only if hypoxic, targeting SpO₂ 94–98% (88–92% if at risk of CO₂ retention). Escalate to CPAP/NIV if refractory.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What IV diuretic and dose is used in AHF, and how does it help?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: IV furosemide — increases urine output and reduces circulating volume. 40 mg IV is the usual starting dose in someone diuretic-naive (BNF: 20–50 mg by slow IV injection, increasing in 20 mg steps; give by infusion above 50 mg); if already on a loop diuretic, give at least their usual total daily oral dose intravenously.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: Why are IV fluids stopped in acute heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: The patient is fluid-overloaded; all IV fluid infusions should be stopped (the 'I' in SODIUM).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What does 'Monitor' (M in SODIUM) involve in AHF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Monitoring urine output, observations, U&E, and fluid balance.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: In the BP-stratified approach to AHF, what is the strategy when SBP is >100 mmHg?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: The IV loop diuretic remains the cornerstone. Add IV GTN only if there is hypertension, ischaemia or severe congestion — not routinely — and with close BP monitoring. Add CPAP/NIV for respiratory failure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: In the BP-stratified approach to AHF, what is the strategy when SBP is 90–100 mmHg?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Treat cautiously with a diuretic. Inotropes only if there is hypoperfusion — cool peripheries, mottling, oliguria, confusion, rising lactate — not for a low number alone (NICE), and given where level 2 or 3 care is available.Vasodilators are usually unsafe here; low-dose GTN only under continuous BP monitoring.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: In the BP-stratified approach to AHF, what is the strategy when SBP is <90 mmHg (cardiogenic shock)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back:
Inotrope/vasopressor ± mechanical support:
  • dobutamine (↑contractility, ↑CO)
  • noradrenaline (vasopressor, ↑SVR)
  • and consider specialist mechanical circulatory support if no response

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: Why is IV morphine no longer routinely recommended in acute heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Although historically used for anxiolysis and preload reduction, evidence shows harm (increased ventilation rates and mortality in registries).Avoid unless in a palliative context.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: Which non-invasive modality comes first in cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, when is the other added, and when is invasive ventilation needed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: CPAP is the usual first modality — use it early if oxygen alone is insufficient. The PEEP recruits alveoli, reduces work of breathing, and lowers preload and afterload, improving oxygenation. BiPAP (NIV proper) is added mainly if the patient is hypercapnic or tiring, often with coexisting COPD.Invasive ventilation is reserved for refractory cases.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: In which specific situations is IV GTN indicated in acute heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Not routine. Consider an IV nitrate where there is concomitant myocardial ischaemia, severe hypertension, or regurgitant aortic or mitral valve disease, and only with close BP monitoring in a setting providing at least level 2 care (NICE).Avoid if SBP is low, and avoid in suspected right ventricular infarction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: How does fluid management in cardiogenic shock differ from septic shock?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: In septic shock, fluid resuscitation is the priority. In cardiogenic shock the problem is pump failure, not volume: do not fluid-load a congested patient — give inotropes and arrange urgent revascularisation.A cautious fluid challenge is appropriate where there are no signs of fluid overload (ESC), and is specifically indicated in right ventricular infarction (inferior MI + hypotension + clear lungs).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What are dobutamine and noradrenaline each used for in cardiogenic shock?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Dobutamine is an inotrope (↑contractility, ↑CO); noradrenaline is a vasopressor (↑SVR).Specialist mechanical circulatory support is considered if there is no response.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What is the definition of acute heart failure (AHF)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Rapid onset or worsening of symptoms/signs of HF requiring urgent therapy — includes de-novo AHF and acute decompensation of chronic HF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What is cardiogenic shock?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Tissue hypoperfusion due to cardiac failure: SBP <90 mmHg + signs of low output (cold/clammy, oliguria, altered consciousness) despite adequate filling.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What are the key bedside findings in pulmonary oedema?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Severe dyspnoea, tachypnoea, orthopnoea, pink frothy sputum, widespread crepitations, hypoxia — life-threatening.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What does the chest X-ray show in AHF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back:
ABCDE:
  • Alveolar oedema (bat-wing)
  • Kerley B lines
  • Cardiomegaly
  • upper-lobe Diversion (vascular redistribution)
  • Effusion (pleural)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What is the first-line acute pharmacological treatment for AHF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back:
• IV loop diuretics (furosemide) — reduce preload
  • IV/SL nitrates if hypertensive
  • O₂ if SpO₂ <94%
  • opiates no longer routinely recommended

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: When is non-invasive ventilation (NIV/CPAP) used in AHF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Pulmonary oedema with severe dyspnoea and acidaemia, or respiratory failure not responding to oxygen and medical therapy — start it without delay (NICE).It relieves breathlessness and the work of breathing quickly; UK trial evidence has not shown that it reduces intubation or mortality.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What inotropes are used in cardiogenic shock?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Dobutamine (first-line); noradrenaline if the patient is vasodilated.Refractory shock is a critical-care referral.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What is BNP/NT-proBNP used for in AHF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Chiefly to RULE OUT: a normal BNP/NT-proBNP makes acute heart failure very unlikely. A raised level supports it but is non-specific — it also rises in PE, sepsis, AF and renal impairment.See Cardiac Markers for the thresholds used in the UK.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What are the precipitants of acute decompensation in chronic HF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back:
FAILURE:
  • Forgot medications
  • Arrhythmia (AF)
  • Ischaemia/Infection
  • Lifestyle (salt/fluid)
  • Uraemia
  • Reduced EF progression
  • Embolism (PE)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: EXAM PEARL: What distinguishes cardiogenic from non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Cardiogenic: cardiomegaly, upper-lobe diversion and Kerley B lines on CXR, a raised BNP, and it improves with diuresis. Non-cardiogenic (ARDS): bilateral infiltrates with a normal heart size, a lung-injury precipitant, and no response to diuresis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: A patient with acute heart failure is not responding to IV furosemide. What is the escalation ladder?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back:
• 1. Double the IV bolus (e.g. 40 mg → 80 mg)
  • 2. Switch to a continuous IV infusion rather than intermittent boluses
  • 3. Add a thiazide or thiazide-like diuretic (metolazone — thiazide-like; or bendroflumethiazide — a true thiazide) — sequential nephron blockade
  • 4. Consider ultrafiltration if diuretic resistance is confirmed — escalation beyond the usual dose ceiling, or a dose near the daily maximum, without incremental diuresis (NICE); a specialist decision

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What is sequential nephron blockade, and which drugs achieve it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back:
Blocking two different sites along the nephron at once.
A loop diuretic (furosemide — thick ascending limb) plus a thiazide-like diuretic (metolazone or bendroflumethiazide — distal convoluted tubule).The thiazide blocks the distal sodium reabsorption that otherwise compensates for the loop diuretic, so the combination is far more potent than either alone — which is why it works in diuretic resistance.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What must be monitored when a thiazide is added to a loop diuretic in acute heart failure, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back:
U&E — closely.
Sequential nephron blockade is potent and readily causes hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia and AKI from over-diuresis.Also track urine output, daily weight and fluid balance.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: A patient with acute breathlessness has a widespread wheeze. Does this rule out acute heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: No - this is 'cardiac asthma'. Interstitial fluid narrows the small airways, so pulmonary oedema can wheeze. It matters because the treatments oppose each other: nebulised salbutamol and steroids do nothing for the fluid, and the tachycardia salbutamol causes makes the failing heart worse.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: Which features point to pulmonary oedema rather than an asthma or COPD exacerbation in an acutely wheezing patient?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back:
• Orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea
  • a raised JVP
  • a third heart sound
  • a displaced apex beat
  • pink frothy sputum
  • known ischaemic or valve disease
  • and a chest X-ray showing oedema rather than hyperinflation
A long history of the same illness, prolonged expiration, a barrel chest and hyperinflated lung fields point the other way.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: A patient with decompensated chronic heart failure already takes furosemide 80 mg twice daily. Is 40 mg IV furosemide an adequate starting dose?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: No - it will do essentially nothing. If a patient is already on a loop diuretic, give at least the equivalent of their total daily oral dose intravenously. The usual 40 mg starting dose is only for someone who is diuretic-naive.Under-dosing here is a common and consequential F1 prescribing error.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: Why is blood pressure alone an inadequate way to assess a patient with acute heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Because perfusion and pressure are different questions. A patient can be badly hypoperfused with a blood pressure that looks acceptable. Look for cool clammy peripheries, mottled skin, oliguria, confusion and a rising lactate - those are what tell you the patient needs inotropic support, not the systolic number on its own.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What must you do before a patient with acute heart failure goes home?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back:
• Convert the IV diuretic to oral once they are euvolaemic and the weight has settled
  • start or uptitrate the disease-modifying drugs before discharge rather than deferring to clinic — the four pillars in HFrEF, or an SGLT2 inhibitor and an MRA plus treatment of the comorbidities in HFpEF and HFmrEF (NICE)
  • restart the beta-blocker if it was withheld
  • and refer to the specialist heart-failure team for review within 2 weeks of discharge (NICE), because the weeks after an admission are the highest-risk period for readmission.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.back:
• HFrEF: EF <40%
  • HFmrEF: 40–49%
  • HFpEF: ≥50%
Ventricular wall stress (volume/pressure overload) from ventricular myocardium

  • 400–2000: echo in 6 weeks
  • >2000: echo in 2 weeks

Aldosterone antagonist (spironolactone/eplerenone) if still symptomatic
Sacubitril/valsartan (replace ACEi — 36h washout) OR ivabradine (HR >75, sinus rhythm)
Reduces hospitalisation + mortality — now standard of care in HFrEF regardless of diabetes

  • Oxygen
  • Diuretics IV

  • Underlying cause
  • Monitor

Symptoms at rest
Symptoms with less than ordinary activity

  • Thyrotoxicosis

  • Beriberi (B1 deficiency)
  • Paget's disease

May be mildly elevated from myocardial stretch — not necessarily ACS. Serial troponins needed.
Annual influenza + one-off pneumococcal vaccine (respiratory infections precipitate decompensation)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.front: What is heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.back: HFrEF = EF <40% — pump failure (systolic dysfunction). The 'classic' HF treated with the 'fantastic four'.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.front: What is heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.back: HFpEF = EF ≥50% with symptoms and diastolic dysfunction. Common in elderly, hypertensive, obese, diabetic patients. Fewer proven therapies.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.front: What is the 'fantastic four' in HFrEF management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.back: ACE inhibitor (or ARB/ARNI), beta-blocker, MRA (spironolactone/eplerenone), SGLT2 inhibitor — all reduce mortality.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.front: What does ARNI stand for and what is the example?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.back: Angiotensin Receptor-Neprilysin Inhibitor — sacubitril-valsartan (Entresto). Replaces ACE inhibitor in HFrEF if still symptomatic — reduces hospitalisation and mortality.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.front: What is the role of SGLT2 inhibitors in heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.back: Dapagliflozin/empagliflozin reduce hospitalisation and cardiovascular death in HFrEF (and increasingly HFpEF) — even in non-diabetics. Diuretic-like effect.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.front: What are indications for cardiac resynchronisation therapy (CRT)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.back: HFrEF (EF ≤35%) + LBBB with QRS ≥130 ms + NYHA II–IV despite optimal medical therapy — restores synchronised ventricular contraction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.front: What are indications for ICD in heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.back: Primary prevention: EF ≤35% + NYHA II–III + ≥3 months optimal therapy — ICD reduces sudden cardiac death from VT/VF.Secondary prevention: prior cardiac arrest, sustained VT or VF — regardless of EF.

• I: No symptoms
  • II: Symptoms on moderate exertion
  • III: Symptoms on mild exertion
  • IV: Symptoms at rest

• Ischaemic cardiomyopathy (most common — post-MI)
  • dilated cardiomyopathy
  • hypertension
  • valve disease
  • arrhythmia (tachycardia-induced)
  • toxins (alcohol, chemotherapy)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.front: What are loop diuretics used for in heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.back: Symptom relief — reduce fluid overload (oedema, pulmonary congestion). Furosemide is first-line. Do NOT reduce mortality.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.front: Why are CCBs (except amlodipine/felodipine) contraindicated in HFrEF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.back: Negative inotropes — worsen systolic function. Amlodipine/felodipine are vascular-selective and safe if needed for angina/hypertension in HFrEF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.front: What is the role of digoxin in heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.back: Rate control in AF + HF (no longer first-line for sinus rhythm HFrEF). Reduces hospitalisation but no mortality benefit. Narrow therapeutic window.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.front: What is the target heart rate in heart failure on beta-blocker?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.back: Resting HR 50–70 bpm on beta-blocker. Evidence-based doses: bisoprolol 10 mg, carvedilol 25–50 mg, nebivolol 10 mg.
Right heart failure secondary to pulmonary hypertension from lung disease — RV hypertrophy/dilatation. Causes: COPD, PE, OSA, pulmonary fibrosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the single most important prognostic intervention in HFrEF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.back: ACE inhibitor (or ARNI) + beta-blocker + MRA + SGLT2i = the fantastic four — ALL reduce mortality independently. Start all four at lowest doses and uptitrate.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.front: Name the three layers of the heart wall from inside out and their vessel equivalents.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.back:
• Endocardium (≈ tunica intima),
  • myocardium (≈ tunica media)
  • and epicardium (≈ tunica adventitia).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.front: What does the endocardium consist of?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.back: An endothelial lining on subendothelial connective tissue, plus a deeper subendocardial layer that contains the Purkinje fibres; it lines the chambers and valves.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.front: Why is the endocardium smooth?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.back: To minimise turbulence and the risk of thrombosis as blood flows through the chambers.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.front: What is the myocardium and where is it thickest?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.back: The middle layer of cardiac muscle — the thickest layer, greatest in the left ventricle because it pumps against systemic pressure.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.front: What is the epicardium?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.back: The outer layer = the visceral layer of the serous pericardium: mesothelium + connective tissue + fat, carrying the coronary vessels and nerves.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.front: Describe the histology of cardiac muscle.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.back: Branching, striated cardiomyocytes with a single central nucleus, joined end-to-end by intercalated discs; mitochondria-rich, involuntary.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.front: What are intercalated discs and what do they contain?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.back: The junctions joining cardiomyocytes end-to-end, seen as dark cross-lines; they contain desmosomes/fascia adherens (mechanical adhesion) and gap junctions (electrical coupling).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.front: Why does the myocardium behave as a functional syncytium?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.back: Gap junctions in the intercalated discs electrically couple the cells, so an impulse spreads cell-to-cell and each of the atrial and ventricular masses contracts as a coordinated unit — the fibrous skeleton separates the two, sequenced by the AV node.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.front: How do you distinguish cardiac, skeletal and smooth muscle histologically?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.back:
• Cardiac = branching, central nucleus, intercalated discs;
  • skeletal = unbranched, multinucleate with peripheral nuclei;
  • smooth = spindle cells with a single central nucleus and no striations.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.front: What is the structure of a heart valve?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.back: A core of dense fibrous connective tissue covered by endocardium/endothelium; valves are avascular and anchored to the fibrous skeleton.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.front: Describe the layers of the pericardium.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.back: An outer tough fibrous pericardium, and a serous pericardium with a parietal layer (lining the fibrous sac) and a visceral layer (the epicardium); the pericardial cavity between them contains serous fluid.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.front: What lines the serous pericardial surfaces, and what is the pericardial fluid for?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.back: Mesothelium (simple squamous) lines them; the serous fluid in the pericardial cavity lets the heart beat without friction.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.front: What is the fibrous (cardiac) skeleton and its two roles?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.back: Dense connective-tissue rings (annuli fibrosi) around the valves; they anchor the valves and muscle and electrically insulate the atria from the ventricles (only the Bundle of His crosses).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.front: Why does the heart heal by scar after a myocardial infarction?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.back: Cardiac muscle is a permanent tissue with negligible regenerative capacity, so dead myocytes are replaced by fibrous (collagenous) scar.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.front: How do Purkinje fibres look histologically, and why?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.back: Larger and paler than working cardiomyocytes, glycogen-rich with sparse, peripherally-placed myofibrils and abundant gap junctions — specialised for rapid impulse conduction rather than force. They lie in the subendocardium.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.front: What is infective endocarditis and why are valves hard to clear of infection?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.back: Infection producing vegetations on the endocardium/valves; because valves are avascular, antibiotics and immune cells reach them poorly.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.front: What is cardiac tamponade?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.back: Accumulation of fluid or blood in the pericardial cavity that compresses the heart and impairs filling, causing obstructive shock.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.front: What are T-tubules and where are they located in cardiac muscle?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.back: Invaginations of the sarcolemma at the Z-line that carry the action potential deep into the fibre for uniform calcium release and contraction.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.front: Why is cardiac muscle so rich in mitochondria?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.back: Because it contracts continuously and relies almost entirely on aerobic metabolism — making it very sensitive to ischaemia.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.front: What is the difference between the fascia adherens and desmosomes within an intercalated disc?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.back: The fascia adherens anchors actin filaments (transverse regions of the disc); desmosomes anchor intermediate filaments — together they provide mechanical adhesion, while gap junctions provide electrical coupling.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.front: What is a fibrinous ('bread-and-butter') pericardium?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.back: Pericarditis in which fibrin exudate coats the roughened pericardial surfaces, producing a friction rub.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.front: Why can chronic pericarditis cause constrictive physiology?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.back: Fibrosis and sometimes calcification of the pericardium stiffen the sac, restricting ventricular filling.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.front: Name the three layers of a heart valve cusp and their roles.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.back:
• Fibrosa (dense collagen on the outflow side — main strength),
  • spongiosa (loose GAG-rich central layer — shock absorber),
  • and ventricularis/atrialis (elastin-rich on the inflow side).
Expansion of the spongiosa causes myxomatous degeneration / mitral valve prolapse.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.front: What do atrial cardiomyocytes secrete, and why does it matter?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.back: They contain atrial natriuretic granules and secrete ANP (and the atria/ventricles secrete BNP) in response to wall stretch → natriuresis, diuresis and vasodilation, lowering blood volume/pressure; BNP/NT-proBNP is a key heart-failure marker.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.front: Outline the histological evolution of a myocardial infarct over time.
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.back:
• 0–24 h: coagulative necrosis with wavy fibres and contraction bands.
  • 1–3 days: neutrophil infiltration.
  • 3–14 days: macrophages remove debris and granulation tissue forms — the wall is weakest, risking free-wall, papillary-muscle or septal rupture.
  • Weeks onward: a dense collagenous scar, the substrate for aneurysm, mural thrombus and re-entry arrhythmia.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.front: What tethers the atrioventricular valve leaflets and prevents them prolapsing?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.back: Collagenous chordae tendineae running from the valve fibrosa to the papillary muscles of the ventricular myocardium; papillary-muscle rupture after an MI causes acute mitral regurgitation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is a pericardial effusion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Abnormal accumulation of fluid in the pericardial sac. Causes range from infection to malignancy to metabolic disorders. The clinical significance depends on the rate of accumulation, not just the volume.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is cardiac tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Life-threatening compression of the heart by pericardial fluid → impaired ventricular filling → reduced cardiac output. It is a clinical diagnosis confirmed by echo.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is Beck's triad?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Hypotension + raised JVP + muffled heart sounds — the classic triad of cardiac tamponade, pointing to urgent pericardiocentesis. All three together are found in only a minority of cases (most often acute/traumatic).Echo confirms the diagnosis and guides drainage — use bedside echo wherever it is immediately available, but in peri-arrest it must not delay drainage.An incomplete triad does not exclude tamponade.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: Why does rapid accumulation cause tamponade at a low volume?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: The fibrous pericardium cannot stretch acutely, so rate matters more than volume. 150–200 mL accumulating quickly can cause tamponade; a chronic effusion may reach 1–2 L before tamponade because the pericardium slowly distends.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is pulsus paradoxus?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: An exaggerated fall in systolic BP of >10 mmHg on inspiration — the key sign of tamponade physiology.Mechanism: inspiration → RV expands → interventricular septum shifts left → LV filling reduced → BP falls.Absent despite tamponade in aortic regurgitation (so typically absent in Type A dissection), ASD, severe LV dysfunction and profound hypotension. Present without tamponade in severe asthma, COPD, tension pneumothorax and massive PE.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What are the ECG findings in cardiac tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Low-voltage QRS complexes + electrical alternans (beat-to-beat alternation in QRS amplitude, and often axis, as the heart swings in the effusion) + sinus tachycardia — together, tamponade until proven otherwise.All three are specific but not sensitive: most tamponades do not show them, so a bland ECG never excludes tamponade.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What does electrical alternans indicate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Cardiac tamponade — the swinging movement of the heart within the effusion causes beat-to-beat variation in the QRS axis and amplitude.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What does CXR show in a large pericardial effusion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Globular/flask-shaped ('water-bottle') cardiac silhouette. Lung fields are typically clear (differentiates from pulmonary oedema).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is the first-line and most sensitive investigation for pericardial effusion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Echocardiography — it detects even small effusions, quantifies them, and assesses for tamponade physiology.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is the earliest echocardiographic sign of tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Right atrial collapse (late diastole/early systole) — the RA is the lowest-pressure chamber, so it is the earliest and most sensitive sign. Right ventricular diastolic collapse appears later but is more specific.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What are the common causes of pericardial effusion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back:
• Idiopathic/viral pericarditis (commonest)
  • malignancy (lung, breast, lymphoma — leading identified cause of effusions needing drainage)
  • TB (commonest worldwide)
  • uraemia
  • post-MI (Dressler's)
  • post-cardiac surgery
  • trauma
  • hypothyroidism
  • autoimmune (SLE, RA)
  • aortic dissection

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: Which cause of tamponade is a contraindication to pericardiocentesis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Aortic dissection — the haemopericardium is tamponading the dissection site. Draining it removes the protective tamponade and can cause fatal exsanguination. Requires emergency surgery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is the emergency treatment for cardiac tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Pericardiocentesis (needle aspiration) — urgent, life-saving. Echo-guided: enter at the point where fluid is deepest and closest to the probe with nothing vital in the way, in practice often apical/parasternal (ESC). Subxiphoid, needle aimed at the left shoulder, is the landmark (blind) route used when echo is unavailable. Even 30–50 mL dramatically improves haemodynamics. NOT in Type A aortic dissection — that goes straight to theatre.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is a pericardial window and when is it used?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Surgical creation of a communication between the pericardial sac and the pleural/peritoneal space to allow continuous drainage. Used for recurrent effusions not amenable to repeated aspiration (malignancy, post-surgical), or where the fluid is loculated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: How does tamponade differ from constrictive pericarditis on examination?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back:
• Both: raised JVP, reduced cardiac output, peripheral oedema.
  • Constrictive: Kussmaul's sign (JVP rises on inspiration), calcification on X-ray, gradual onset.
  • Tamponade: pulsus paradoxus, JVP falls on inspiration, acute onset.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is Kussmaul's sign and in which pericardial condition is it seen?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Paradoxical rise in JVP on inspiration (normally the JVP falls). Seen in constrictive pericarditis, restrictive cardiomyopathy and right heart failure — NOT in cardiac tamponade.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What supports the diagnosis of tamponade on echo beyond the effusion itself?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back:
• RV diastolic collapse
  • RA systolic collapse
  • dilated IVC with <50% inspiratory collapse (elevated RA pressure)
  • respirophasic variation in mitral/tricuspid inflow
  • interventricular septal shift/bounce

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is uraemic pericardial effusion and how is it managed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Caused by uraemic toxins irritating the pericardium. Managed by urgent dialysis — pericardiocentesis is reserved for tamponade.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is Dressler's syndrome?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Post-MI or post-cardiac surgery pericarditis (immune-mediated) occurring weeks to months later — can cause a pericardial effusion. Treated with NSAIDs/colchicine.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: EXAM PEARL: How does CXR differentiate large effusion from pulmonary oedema?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back:
• Large effusion = globular heart + CLEAR lung fields.
  • Pulmonary oedema = normal/enlarged heart + bilateral infiltrates/bat-wing shadowing.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What are the symptoms of pericardial effusion / tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back:
• Small effusion: often asymptomatic.
  • Larger/tamponade: dyspnoea, orthopnoea, chest heaviness, fatigue, syncope.
  • Severe tamponade: hypotension, confusion, cardiogenic shock.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is the pathophysiology of cardiac tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Fluid in the pericardial space → increased intrapericardial pressure → external cardiac compression → reduced ventricular filling → reduced cardiac output → shock.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is haemopericardium?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back:
Blood in the pericardial space — causes include
  • aortic dissection (most serious)
  • trauma
  • cardiac rupture post-MI
  • iatrogenic (pacemaker/ablation)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What fluid is sent from pericardiocentesis aspirate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back:
• Cytology (malignancy)
  • microbiology (culture + AFB for TB)
  • LDH + protein (exudate vs transudate)
  • pH
  • glucose

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is chronic constrictive pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Fibrotic, calcified, rigid pericardium constraining ventricular filling — late complication of TB, post-cardiac surgery, radiation. Treated by pericardiectomy.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.question: A 55-year-old man is found to have an ejection-systolic murmur loudest at the right 2nd intercostal space, radiating to both carotids. His pulse is slow-rising and the second heart sound is soft. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.explanation: Ejection-systolic at the right 2nd space radiating to the carotids, with a slow-rising pulse and a soft S2, is aortic stenosis. The soft S2 and a narrow pulse pressure are markers of SEVERITY. Beware the trap that loudness does not track severity - severe stenosis can be quiet once stroke volume falls.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.question: Which murmur characteristic is ALWAYS pathological and never innocent?
options: A murmur that varies with posture
A murmur present only during a fever
A continuous murmur heard in the neck
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.explanation: There is no such thing as an innocent purely diastolic murmur. Note the last option is a trap: a continuous murmur in the neck is most likely a VENOUS HUM, which is innocent and disappears on lying the child flat, turning the head, or compressing the jugular vein.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.question: A 6-year-old girl is noted to have a soft, systolic, musical/vibratory murmur at the left sternal edge that becomes quieter when she stands. She is asymptomatic with normal heart sounds, no radiation and no thrill. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Reassure the parents - this is an innocent murmur
Commence a beta-blocker and review in clinic
Refer urgently to paediatric cardiology for an echo
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.answer: Reassure the parents - this is an innocent murmur
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.explanation: A soft, systolic, musical murmur at the left sternal edge that quietens on standing, in a well child with normal sounds and no radiation or thrill, is the commonest innocent murmur of childhood. It needs reassurance, not investigation. A murmur in an infant under 3 months is different and does warrant referral.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.question: A pansystolic murmur is heard loudest at the apex and radiates to the axilla. Which valve lesion does this describe?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.explanation: Pansystolic at the apex radiating to the axilla is mitral regurgitation. One caveat worth knowing: in ACUTE severe regurgitation the murmur may be short, soft or even absent, with pulmonary oedema and a normal-sized heart - so a quiet murmur does not exclude it.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.question: Which single investigation is the key test to characterise and grade a valve lesion causing a murmur?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.explanation: Echo characterises and grades the lesion. ECG and chest X-ray support the assessment but cannot define valve anatomy or severity.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.question: A 24-year-old athlete reports exertional syncope. On examination there is an ejection-systolic murmur at the left sternal edge that becomes LOUDER when he performs a Valsalva manoeuvre. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Aortic stenosis on a bicuspid aortic valve
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.explanation: Reducing preload shrinks the ventricular cavity and worsens outflow obstruction, so the murmur gets louder - the opposite of aortic stenosis. The pulse is jerky rather than slow-rising, and the murmur does not radiate to the carotids. Mitral valve prolapse responds to manoeuvres the same way, but gives a mid-systolic click and a late murmur.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.question: Right-sided murmurs are accentuated by which manoeuvre?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.explanation: Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart, so right-sided murmurs get louder - the RILE rule, Right on Inspiration, Left on Expiration. It is a useful heuristic rather than an absolute.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.question: An early-diastolic murmur is heard at the left sternal edge with the patient sitting forward in expiration. Examination reveals a collapsing pulse and a wide pulse pressure. Which lesion is this?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.explanation: Early-diastolic at the left sternal edge with a collapsing pulse and wide pulse pressure is aortic regurgitation. If the cause is aortic ROOT disease the murmur is classically louder at the RIGHT sternal edge instead.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.question: A 68-year-old woman with a prosthetic mitral valve develops a new murmur, fever and splinter haemorrhages. What are the two most important initial investigations?
options: Thyroid function tests and an ECG
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.explanation: A new murmur with fever is endocarditis until proven otherwise, and a prosthetic valve raises the stakes further. Take cultures before antibiotics, and image the valve. If she is acutely septic, two sets within an hour then treat - do not wait to complete three.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.question: Which set of features best describes an innocent flow murmur?
options: Soft, systolic, asymptomatic, no radiation, normal sounds
A loud pansystolic murmur radiating right into the axilla
A mid-diastolic rumble with an opening snap
A continuous machinery murmur with a wide pulse pressure
An ejection-systolic murmur with a slow-rising pulse
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.answer: Soft, systolic, asymptomatic, no radiation, normal sounds
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.explanation: Innocent murmurs are soft, short, systolic, symptomless, vary with posture and come with normal sounds. Remember the category is much weaker in adults - a newly heard murmur in an older adult, or any murmur with symptoms, an abnormal S2 or an abnormal ECG, earns an echo.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.question: A mid-diastolic rumbling murmur with an opening snap is heard at the apex, loudest in the left lateral position using the bell. There is a loud S1 and the patient is in atrial fibrillation. What is the diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.explanation: A mid-diastolic rumble with an opening snap at the apex, with AF, is mitral stenosis. Note the loud S1 and the snap depend on a still-pliable valve; once it calcifies, S1 softens and the snap disappears, so their absence does not mean mild disease.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.question: Which of the following is a red flag around a murmur that mandates echocardiography and cardiology referral?
options: A murmur associated with exertional syncope
A grade 1/6 systolic murmur in a febrile child
A murmur that disappears on standing up
A soft systolic murmur in pregnancy with normal sounds
A continuous neck murmur abolished by turning the head
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.answer: A murmur associated with exertional syncope
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.explanation: A systolic murmur with exertional syncope points to severe aortic stenosis or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and needs specialist assessment within two weeks. The last option describes a venous hum, which is innocent precisely because the manoeuvre abolishes it.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.question: A pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge becomes louder on inspiration, and the JVP shows giant V waves with a pulsatile liver. Which lesion is this?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.explanation: Pansystolic at the left sternal edge, louder on inspiration, with giant systolic waves in the JVP and a pulsatile liver, is tricuspid regurgitation. Inspiration is what separates it from a left-sided pansystolic murmur at the bedside.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.question: Which murmur becomes QUIETER on both squatting and sustained handgrip?
options: Mitral regurgitation with a flail leaflet
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.explanation: Squatting raises preload AND afterload, and handgrip raises afterload alone; both enlarge the ventricular cavity or oppose ejection, easing the outflow obstruction. The other murmurs get louder. Note that handgrip changes aortic stenosis little, which is how those two are separated.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.question: A continuous machinery murmur is heard at the left infraclavicular region in a child, with a wide pulse pressure. Which statement is correct?
options: This is a patent ductus arteriosus and needs an echo
This is a venous hum and can safely be reassured
Continuous murmurs are always pathological, without exception
It is best heard in the left lateral position using the bell
The findings indicate significant aortic stenosis
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.answer: This is a patent ductus arteriosus and needs an echo
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.explanation: The machinery quality, the site and the wide pulse pressure make this a persistent ductus. The key bedside discriminator is that a VENOUS HUM - the innocent continuous murmur - is abolished by lying the child flat, turning the head or compressing the jugular vein, whereas this is not. So continuous murmurs are not always pathological, but this one is.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.question: A 30-year-old woman with a soft systolic murmur is pale and fatigued. Which first-line blood tests would identify a high-output cause?
options: Full blood count and thyroid function tests
Serum ferritin and vitamin B12 alone
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.answer: Full blood count and thyroid function tests
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Murmur (Inc.explanation: Anaemia and thyrotoxicosis drive flow across a normal valve and produce a soft systolic murmur, as do pregnancy and fever. Correcting the high-output state makes the murmur disappear.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.question: A 79-year-old has an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids and a slow-rising pulse. The apex beat is forceful and sustained but not displaced. What does the apex character indicate?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.explanation: A heaving, sustained, undisplaced apex is the signature of LV pressure overload — here severe aortic stenosis (ESM to carotids, slow-rising pulse). Volume overload (AR/MR) gives a displaced, thrusting apex instead.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.question: A 40-year-old has a collapsing pulse, wide pulse pressure and an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. The apex beat is displaced, diffuse and hyperdynamic. Which lesion best fits?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.explanation: A thrusting, displaced (volume-loaded) apex with a collapsing pulse, wide pulse pressure and an early diastolic murmur is aortic regurgitation. AS gives a heaving, undisplaced apex; MS gives a tapping apex.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.question: A 55-year-old woman has a tapping apex beat, a loud S1 and a rumbling mid-diastolic murmur with malar flush. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.explanation: A tapping apex is a palpable loud S1 — the classic sign of mitral stenosis, supported by the mid-diastolic murmur and malar (mitral) facies. MR gives a pansystolic murmur with a displaced/thrusting apex; AS a heaving apex with an ejection murmur to the carotids; HOCM a dynamic murmur; DCM a displaced apex with an S3.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.question: A 22-year-old with a family history of sudden cardiac death has a double apical impulse and an ejection systolic murmur that gets louder on Valsalva. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.explanation: A double apical impulse with a murmur that intensifies on Valsalva (reduced preload worsens dynamic LVOT obstruction), plus a family history of sudden death, indicates HOCM. In fixed AS the murmur softens with Valsalva.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.question: A 68-year-old is hypotensive with a raised JVP, muffled heart sounds and an impalpable apex beat. What is the most appropriate immediate investigation?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.explanation: An impalpable apex with Beck's triad (hypotension, raised JVP, muffled sounds) suggests a pericardial effusion / tamponade. Bedside echocardiography is the immediate investigation and guides pericardiocentesis. A CXR may show a globular heart but cannot diagnose tamponade; coronary angiography, an exercise ECG and MRI are all inappropriate in a haemodynamically unstable patient.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.question: A 25-year-old man is acutely breathless. The trachea is deviated to the left, the right hemithorax is hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds, and the apex beat is impalpable in its normal position. What is the most likely cause of the apex findings?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.explanation: The hyper-resonant, silent right hemithorax pushing the trachea and apex to the left is mediastinal shift from a tension pneumothorax — a respiratory emergency; the displaced apex is a consequence, not primary heart disease. A massive effusion also pushes but is stony dull, not hyper-resonant; lobar collapse pulls the trachea toward the lesion; a pericardial effusion muffles heart sounds without a silent hemithorax; dextrocardia is congenital with a right-sided apex and normal breath sounds.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.question: A 60-year-old with breathlessness has a displaced apex beat, bilateral basal crepitations, a raised JVP and a third heart sound. Which investigation best confirms the underlying cause?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.explanation: A displaced apex with an S3 and congestion suggests a dilated, failing LV (dilated cardiomyopathy / heart failure). Echocardiography confirms chamber size and ejection fraction and is the key investigation. Troponin, D-dimer, CT coronary angiography and a 24-hour tape address ischaemia, PE, coronary anatomy and arrhythmia respectively — none characterises ventricular size and function as echo does.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.question: A patient has a dyskinetic apical impulse six weeks after an anterior STEMI, with persistent ST elevation on the ECG. What complication does this suggest?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.explanation: A dyskinetic (paradoxically bulging) apex weeks after an anterior MI, with persistent ST elevation, indicates a left-ventricular aneurysm. Echo/cardiac MRI confirm it. VSD and free-wall rupture are early mechanical complications (days, with a new murmur or tamponade); Dressler's is pericarditic (pleuritic pain, rub); recurrent STEMI gives new dynamic ECG changes, not fixed persistent ST elevation.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.question: Before documenting an apex beat as 'displaced', which single check is most important?
options: Auscultate for a third heart sound
Measure the blood pressure in both arms
Palpate for a left parasternal heave
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.explanation: An apex can appear 'displaced' simply because the whole mediastinum is shifted (effusion, pneumothorax, collapse) or because of dextrocardia. Checking the trachea (and excluding dextrocardia) tells you whether the displacement is cardiac or non-cardiac.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.question: A 58-year-old with COPD is breathless. There is a sustained lift at the left sternal edge, a loud pulmonary second sound and a raised JVP; the apex beat is normally placed. What does the parasternal finding indicate?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.explanation: A sustained left parasternal (RV) heave with a loud P2 and a raised JVP indicates right ventricular pressure overload — here cor pulmonale / pulmonary hypertension from COPD. It is felt at the sternal edge, not the apex, which excludes left-sided lesions (LV pressure or volume overload, mitral stenosis); a pericardial effusion muffles the heart sounds and makes the apex impalpable rather than producing a heave.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.question: A 62-year-old has a displaced, thrusting apex beat and a pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla with a soft first heart sound. Which valve lesion best fits?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.explanation: A displaced, thrusting (volume-loaded) apex with a pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla and a soft S1 is chronic mitral regurgitation. AS gives a heaving undisplaced apex with an ejection murmur to the carotids; MS a tapping apex with a diastolic rumble; AR a displaced apex with an early diastolic murmur; TR a left parasternal heave with a murmur at the lower sternal edge that rises on inspiration.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.question: A 24-year-old has an ejection systolic murmur that becomes louder on standing and on Valsalva, and softer on squatting. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.explanation: A murmur that intensifies when preload falls (standing, Valsalva) and softens when preload/afterload rise (squatting) reflects dynamic LVOT obstruction — HOCM. Fixed AS and PS behave oppositely (louder on squatting); MR (a regurgitant murmur) rises with handgrip; an innocent murmur has no structural basis and varies little in this pattern.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.question: A 70-year-old hypertensive man has a sustained, undisplaced apex with a palpable presystolic impulse producing a double beat. What does the presystolic impulse represent?
options: A palpable third heart sound from a dilated LV
A palpable S4 from a stiff, hypertrophied LV
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.explanation: A presystolic (atrial) impulse in a pressure-loaded, hypertrophied LV is a palpable S4 — the atrium contracting against a stiff ventricle. A palpable S3 signals a dilated, failing/volume-loaded LV; an opening snap (MS), pericardial knock (constriction) and tumour plop (atrial myxoma) are early-diastolic sounds, not presystolic impulses.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.question: A thin, anxious 21-year-old woman has a forceful but undisplaced, non-sustained apex beat; ECG and echocardiogram are normal. What is the best interpretation?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.explanation: A forceful apex that is undisplaced and non-sustained with normal investigations is typically physiological — a thin chest wall or a high-output state (anxiety, anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, pregnancy). Pressure overload (AS/HTN) gives a sustained heaving apex, volume overload a displaced thrusting one, and an RV heave is felt at the sternal edge, not the apex.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.question: A 66-year-old with COPD has a left parasternal heave, a loud pulmonary second sound and peripheral oedema. What process best explains these findings?
options: Severe mitral regurgitation with LV failure
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.explanation: An RV heave with a loud P2 and right-sided fluid overload in chronic lung disease is cor pulmonale — RV pressure overload from pulmonary hypertension. LV failure and MR affect the left heart/apex; MS causes a tapping apex; tamponade gives an impalpable apex with Beck's triad, not a heave.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.question: A patient has a heaving, sustained, undisplaced apex beat. Which ECG finding would best support the expected diagnosis?
options: Deep S in V1 plus tall R in V5–V6 exceeding 35 mm
A delta wave with a short PR interval (pre-excitation)
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.explanation: A heaving apex reflects LV pressure overload/hypertrophy, supported by LVH voltage criteria (Sokolow–Lyon: S-V1 + R-V5/6 > 35 mm). Tented T waves suggest hyperkalaemia; a delta wave indicates pre-excitation; RBBB is a conduction defect; low voltages suggest an effusion or infiltration — none reflects LV hypertrophy.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.question: Which chest X-ray appearance suggests a pericardial effusion?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.explanation: A pericardial effusion enlarges the cardiac shadow into a globular 'water-bottle' silhouette with clear lungs. A boot-shaped heart suggests tetralogy of Fallot; upper-lobe diversion indicates LV failure/pulmonary venous congestion; a right-sided apex indicates dextrocardia; hyperexpanded lungs indicate COPD.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.question: A patient has a collapsing pulse, a wide pulse pressure and head-bobbing. Which apex-beat character would you expect to find?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.explanation: These peripheral signs indicate aortic regurgitation — a volume-loaded LV, giving a displaced, thrusting apex. A heaving undisplaced apex is pressure overload (AS/HTN); a tapping apex is mitral stenosis; an impalpable apex suggests effusion/hyperinflation; a normal apex would not fit gross volume overload.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.question: To best elicit the tapping apex and diastolic murmur of mitral stenosis, in which position should you examine the patient?
options: Left lateral decubitus, using the bell, in held expiration
Right lateral decubitus, using the bell, in full inspiration
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.explanation: MS signs are accentuated in the left lateral decubitus position with the bell in expiration, which brings the apex against the chest wall. Sitting forward in expiration is for the aortic regurgitation murmur; the other positions do not optimise a low-pitched apical diastolic murmur.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.question: A 68-year-old with cardiac tamponade has hypotension, a raised JVP and an impalpable apex. Which additional pulse sign supports the diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Apex Bea.explanation: Tamponade classically causes pulsus paradoxus — a >10 mmHg inspiratory fall in systolic BP. A collapsing pulse indicates aortic regurgitation; a slow-rising pulse aortic stenosis; a bisferiens pulse mixed aortic valve disease; pulsus alternans severe LV systolic failure.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.question: A 74-year-old presents with an irregularly irregular pulse; the apical rate is 96 but the radial rate is 78. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.explanation: An irregularly irregular rhythm with an apex–radial deficit (apical > radial) indicates atrial fibrillation — weak beats fail to reach the wrist. Mobitz I and ectopics give a regularly irregular pulse without a large deficit; sinus arrhythmia varies with respiration; pulsus alternans is a regular rhythm with alternating volume.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.question: A 70-year-old with exertional syncope has a slow-rising, small-volume carotid pulse and a narrow pulse pressure. Which lesion is most likely?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.explanation: A slow-rising (plateau) pulse with a narrow pulse pressure is the hallmark of aortic stenosis. AR gives a collapsing pulse with a wide pulse pressure; HOCM gives a jerky/bisferiens pulse; MR and MS do not alter the carotid upstroke in this way.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.question: A 40-year-old has a collapsing, water-hammer pulse that becomes more obvious when the arm is raised, with a wide pulse pressure. Which lesion is most likely?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.explanation: A collapsing (water-hammer) pulse with a wide pulse pressure, exaggerated on raising the arm, indicates aortic regurgitation (or a high-output state). AS gives the opposite (slow-rising, narrow pulse pressure); the other lesions do not produce a collapsing pulse.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.question: A 68-year-old with a recent large anterior MI is found to have a regular pulse in which the beats alternate strong and weak. What does this indicate?
options: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.explanation: Pulsus alternans — a regular rhythm with alternating pulse volume — indicates severe LV systolic dysfunction. AF is irregularly irregular; complete heart block is slow with cannon a waves; tamponade gives pulsus paradoxus; bigeminy is a regularly irregular rhythm from alternating ectopics.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.question: A 30-year-old with pericardial effusion is hypotensive; the radial pulse disappears during inspiration and systolic BP falls by 18 mmHg. What is this sign and its cause?
options: Pulsus paradoxus due to cardiac tamponade
Pulsus alternans due to LV failure
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.explanation: An inspiratory systolic BP fall >10 mmHg is pulsus paradoxus, here due to cardiac tamponade (also severe asthma, massive PE). Pulsus alternans alternates volume at a regular rhythm; Kussmaul’s is a JVP sign; bisferiens has two systolic peaks; bigeminus is coupled ectopics.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.question: A 25-year-old woman has a large-volume, bounding, collapsing pulse with warm peripheries, a fine tremor and a smooth goitre. What is the most likely cause?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.explanation: A bounding, collapsing pulse with warm peripheries, tremor and a goitre points to thyrotoxicosis, a high-output state. AR would give a diastolic murmur without goitre/tremor; anaemia and sepsis can give bounding pulses but not a goitre and tremor; an AV fistula gives a localised thrill/bruit.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.question: A patient has a pulse with two distinct systolic peaks (bisferiens) and an ejection systolic murmur that gets louder on Valsalva. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.explanation: A bisferiens/jerky pulse with a murmur that increases on Valsalva (reduced preload worsens dynamic obstruction) indicates HOCM. Isolated AS softens with Valsalva; a bisferiens pulse can also occur in mixed AS+AR, but the Valsalva response points to HOCM; MVP and PDA give different signs.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.question: A 40-year-old is shocked after a major haemorrhage — pulse 130/min with cold, clammy peripheries. Which pulse character best fits this state?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.explanation: Hypovolaemic shock gives a thready, low-volume pulse from a reduced stroke volume with compensatory tachycardia and vasoconstriction. Bounding/collapsing pulses occur in high-output states or AR (warm peripheries); a slow-rising pulse indicates aortic stenosis; alternating strong–weak beats (pulsus alternans) indicate severe LV failure.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.question: An 80-year-old presents with recurrent syncope and a persistently slow, regular pulse of 34/min with intermittent cannon a waves in the neck. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Atrial fibrillation with slow ventricular response
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.explanation: A slow, regular pulse with intermittent cannon a waves (AV dissociation) and syncope indicates complete heart block. AF is irregular; sinus bradycardia has normal a waves and P–QRS relationship; carotid sinus hypersensitivity gives situational syncope; VT is fast.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.question: A patient has a regularly irregular pulse in which every strong beat is followed by a weak premature beat (pulsus bigeminus). Which underlying cause is most likely?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.explanation: Pulsus bigeminus — coupled sinus-then-ectopic beats — is classically caused by digoxin toxicity (also frequent ventricular ectopics). Hypothyroidism slows the rate without coupling; aortic stenosis alters character not coupling; atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular; hypercalcaemia shortens the QT but does not cause bigeminy.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.question: A patient has an irregular pulse. The 12-lead ECG is normal but symptoms are intermittent. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.explanation: Intermittent (paroxysmal) symptoms with a normal resting ECG are best captured by ambulatory ECG monitoring to document the arrhythmia. Echo assesses structure but not the rhythm event; exercise testing and angiography assess ischaemia; an EP study is invasive and reserved for selected cases.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.question: A patient has a raised JVP, hypotension, muffled heart sounds and pulsus paradoxus. Which investigation should be performed most urgently?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.explanation: This is cardiac tamponade (Beck’s triad + pulsus paradoxus); urgent echocardiography confirms the effusion and diastolic RA/RV collapse and guides pericardiocentesis. CXR is non-specific; angiography, D-dimer and MRI would dangerously delay treatment.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.question: A 65-year-old smoker has calf pain on walking that eases with rest, a cool hairless foot and absent pedal pulses; ABPI is 0.6. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.explanation: Intermittent claudication with weak foot pulses and an ABPI of 0.6 indicates chronic peripheral arterial disease. Acute limb ischaemia is sudden with the 6 Ps; DVT gives a swollen warm calf; spinal claudication eases on leaning forward with normal pulses; venous insufficiency gives oedema and venous ulcers with intact pulses.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.question: A 72-year-old with AF develops a sudden cold, pale, painful right leg with absent pulses and reduced sensation. What is the most appropriate immediate step?
options: IV heparin then outpatient duplex in 2 weeks
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.explanation: The 6 Ps indicate acute limb ischaemia (embolic from AF) — give immediate IV heparin and refer urgently for revascularisation (embolectomy/thrombolysis) within ~6 h. Deferring to outpatient duplex or discharge risks the limb; blind systemic thrombolysis without imaging/vascular input is inappropriate; elevation/analgesia alone treats nothing.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.question: A 55-year-old with sudden severe chest pain radiating to the back has a systolic BP of 168 in the right arm and 132 in the left, with a delayed left radial pulse. What is the most important diagnosis to exclude?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.explanation: An inter-arm systolic BP difference >20 mmHg with radio-radial delay and tearing interscapular pain strongly suggests aortic dissection — image (CT aortography) before anticoagulation or thrombolysis. ACS and PE do not cause this asymmetry; PAD is chronic; coarctation gives radio-femoral delay and presents earlier in life.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.question: A 20-year-old with hypertension in the arms has weak femoral pulses and a radio-femoral delay. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.explanation: Radio-femoral delay with upper-limb hypertension in a young person is classic for coarctation of the aorta (also rib notching and a murmur over the back). Dissection gives radio-radial delay and acute pain; PAD is uncommon at this age; Takayasu gives absent upper-limb pulses; fibromuscular dysplasia typically causes renovascular hypertension.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.question: A 28-year-old woman has an absent left radial pulse, a left subclavian bruit, an inter-arm BP difference and a raised ESR. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.explanation: Absent/asymmetric upper-limb pulses ('pulseless disease') with bruits, an inter-arm BP difference and a raised ESR in a young woman indicate Takayasu arteritis, a large-vessel vasculitis. Dissection is acutely painful; thoracic outlet and subclavian steal are positional; giant cell arteritis affects older patients with cranial symptoms.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.question: A 70-year-old man has a central, pulsatile abdominal mass that pushes the examiner's hands apart. He is asymptomatic. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.explanation: An expansile pulsatile mass is an abdominal aortic aneurysm; abdominal ultrasound is the first-line test for diagnosis and surveillance. CT angiography defines size and leak before repair but is not the initial screen; plain X-ray and MRI are not first-line; DSA is invasive.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.question: A patient with intermittent claudication has absent foot pulses. Which bedside test best quantifies the severity of the arterial insufficiency?
options: Handheld Doppler waveform of the foot
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.explanation: The ankle-brachial pressure index gives a reproducible number that grades severity (<0.9 = PAD; <0.5 = critical ischaemia; >1.3 = calcified non-compressible vessels). Buerger’s test, capillary refill, a Doppler waveform and skin temperature give qualitative clues but do not quantify severity as the ABPI does.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.question: A diabetic patient with claudication has an ABPI of 1.4. How should this be interpreted?
options: Normal, reliably excluding peripheral arterial disease
An artefact requiring no further action
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.explanation: An ABPI >1.3 suggests calcified, non-compressible vessels (common in diabetes/CKD), which can mask underlying PAD — it does not exclude disease, so use toe-pressures or duplex. It is not normal reassurance, nor does it indicate critical or acute ischaemia by itself.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.question: A 60-year-old reports left arm heaviness on exertion and dizziness when using the arm; there is a left subclavian bruit and a 30 mmHg lower BP in the left arm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.explanation: Arm claudication with posterior-circulation symptoms provoked by arm use, a subclavian bruit and an inter-arm BP difference indicate subclavian steal syndrome (proximal subclavian stenosis reversing vertebral flow). Dissection is acute; Takayasu affects young women with a raised ESR; thoracic outlet and radiculopathy are neurological/positional.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.question: On examination a patient has a strong femoral pulse but absent popliteal and foot pulses on the same side. Which level of arterial disease does this localise to?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.explanation: A present femoral but absent popliteal/foot pulses localises disease to the femoropopliteal segment. Absent femorals would indicate aortoiliac disease; absent foot pulses with a normal popliteal indicate distal/tibial disease; renal and subclavian arteries do not supply the leg.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.question: A 78-year-old collapses with sudden severe abdominal and back pain; he is hypotensive with a tender, expansile pulsatile abdominal mass. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Immediate surgical referral for a ruptured AAA
Rapid CT then repair if haemodynamically stable
Analgesia and discharge with GP follow-up
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.explanation: A tender, expansile pulsatile mass with pain and hypotension is a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm — an immediate surgical emergency; an unstable patient goes straight to theatre (a stable patient may have a rapid CT first). Surveillance, antibiotics or discharge would be fatal.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.question: A 68-year-old smoker with longstanding intermittent claudication develops a cold, painful left leg worsening over a day; foot pulses are absent in both legs and he is in sinus rhythm. Which mechanism is most likely?
options: Embolic from a proximal cardiac source
Thrombosis on a background of PAD
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abnormal Pulse.explanation: A gradual onset on a background of claudication, bilateral absent pulses (diffuse disease) and sinus rhythm (no embolic source) points to acute-on-chronic thrombotic limb ischaemia. An embolic cause is sudden with a cardiac source (AF/MI) and normal contralateral pulses; DVT gives a swollen warm leg; vasospasm and compartment syndrome do not abolish pulses like this.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.question: A 24-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of a rapid, regular heartbeat that start and stop abruptly and sometimes stop when she bears down. Between episodes she is well with a normal ECG. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.explanation: Abrupt on/off, regular, fast palpitations that terminate with Valsalva are classic paroxysmal SVT (AVNRT/AVRT). AF is irregular; VT usually occurs with structural disease and instability; sinus tachycardia has gradual onset/offset with a driver; anxiety is a diagnosis of exclusion.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.question: A 70-year-old describes a fast, completely irregular heartbeat; the pulse is irregularly irregular and the ECG shows no P waves with an irregular baseline. What is the diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.explanation: An irregularly irregular pulse with absent P waves and a fibrillating baseline is atrial fibrillation. Flutter is usually regular with sawtooth waves; SVT is regular; MAT shows ≥3 P-wave morphologies; VT is broad-complex.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.question: A 62-year-old man with a previous myocardial infarction has palpitations and presyncope; the ECG shows a regular broad-complex tachycardia at 170 bpm. What is the most appropriate assumption?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.explanation: A regular broad-complex tachycardia, especially with prior MI and presyncope, must be treated as ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise; assuming SVT with aberrancy and giving a nodal blocker can be fatal.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.question: A 30-year-old reports occasional ‘skipped beats’ and thumps in the chest, worse when resting in the evening and gone when he exercises. Examination and ECG are normal. What is the most likely cause?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.explanation: Isolated skipped/thumping beats that are worse at rest and abolished by exercise, with a structurally normal heart, are benign ectopic beats. The extrasystole and compensatory pause are felt as a skip then a thump; reassurance and trigger avoidance suffice.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.question: A 45-year-old woman has palpitations with weight loss, heat intolerance, a fine tremor and a smooth goitre. Which investigation is most likely to reveal the cause?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.explanation: The picture is thyrotoxicosis; thyroid function tests (suppressed TSH, raised free T4/T3) reveal it. A Holter documents the rhythm but not the cause; echo, troponin and CXR do not address the thyroid.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.question: A 28-year-old presents with palpitations, peri-oral tingling, carpopedal spasm and a sense of impending doom during a stressful event; ECG and examination are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.explanation: Situational palpitations with hyperventilation-related paraesthesiae and carpopedal spasm and a normal ECG suggest a panic attack (hyperventilation causes a respiratory alkalosis and transient reduction in ionised calcium). It remains a diagnosis of exclusion once arrhythmia and thyrotoxicosis are ruled out.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.question: A patient's palpitations are infrequent (roughly once a month) and the resting 12-lead ECG is normal. What is the most appropriate investigation to capture the rhythm?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.explanation: For infrequent palpitations a patient-activated event/loop recorder (or implantable loop recorder) maximises the chance of capturing an episode. A 24-hour Holter is likely to miss monthly symptoms; a repeat resting ECG, echo and exercise test do not document intermittent rhythm.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.question: A 19-year-old with palpitations has an ECG showing a short PR interval and a delta wave, then develops fast atrial fibrillation. Which option is contraindicated in the acute management?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.explanation: The ECG shows Wolff-Parkinson-White. In pre-excited (WPW) atrial fibrillation, AV-nodal blockers such as verapamil (also digoxin/adenosine) can accelerate accessory-pathway conduction and precipitate VF. Flecainide or procainamide, or DC cardioversion if unstable, are appropriate; vagal manoeuvres are harmless.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.question: A haemodynamically stable 25-year-old has a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 190 bpm. After failed vagal manoeuvres, what is the first-line pharmacological treatment?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.explanation: For stable regular narrow-complex SVT after failed vagal manoeuvres, IV adenosine is first-line. Verapamil or a beta-blocker are later options; DC cardioversion is reserved for instability (shock, syncope, ischaemia, heart failure).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.question: A 68-year-old with palpitations is found to be in atrial fibrillation. Beyond rate/rhythm control, which assessment is essential?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.explanation: AF markedly raises stroke risk, so CHA₂DS₂-VASc (weighed against bleeding risk) guides anticoagulation. Angiography, EP study, metanephrines and tilt testing are not routine in uncomplicated AF.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.question: A 55-year-old has palpitations only on exertion, with one episode of exertional syncope; there is a family history of sudden cardiac death. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Start a beta-blocker and review in 6 months
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.explanation: Exertional palpitations with exertional syncope and a family history of sudden death suggest a cardiomyopathy (e.g. HOCM) or channelopathy — arrange echocardiography and specialist referral (± exercise testing, cardiac MRI). Reassurance or empirical treatment without imaging would be unsafe.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.question: A 40-year-old has episodic palpitations accompanied by pounding headaches, drenching sweats and blood pressure surges to 220/120. Which diagnosis must be excluded?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.explanation: Paroxysmal palpitations + headache + sweating + episodic severe hypertension is the classic triad of phaeochromocytoma; confirm with plasma/urinary metanephrines. Panic and essential hypertension do not give catecholamine surges; thyroid storm and carcinoid have other features.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Palpitations.question: A 20-year-old athlete reports occasional palpitations; resting ECG is normal, and you want to reproduce symptoms that occur during running. Which test is most appropriate?
