conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: It is always a response to something — identify and treat the cause rather than blindly slowing the rate
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Sinus tachycardia is physiologically appropriate; rate-blocking without addressing the underlying driver can be dangerous.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which ECG feature is characteristic of sinus tachycardia rather than another regular narrow tachycardia?
options: A normal upright P wave before every QRS with identical morphology, and gradual onset/offset
P waves completely buried within each QRS complex and never visible anywhere on the surface ECG
Sawtooth flutter waves seen best in the inferior leads at an atrial rate of around 300 per minute
A slurred delta wave preceding a broadened QRS with a characteristically short PR interval
An abrupt on-off pattern, with the tachycardia starting and stopping instantaneously at full rate
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: A normal upright P wave before every QRS with identical morphology, and gradual onset/offset
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Sinus tachycardia has a normal upright P before every QRS (identical morphology), a normal PR interval, and gradual (not abrupt) onset and offset, with the rate varying with respiration and activity.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: In the PIRATES mnemonic for sinus tachycardia causes, what does the 'A' represent?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Anaemia, Anxiety, Alcohol withdrawal
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: PIRATES: Pain/PE/Pneumothorax, Infection/Sepsis/Inflammation, Respiratory failure (hypoxia), Anaemia/Anxiety/Alcohol withdrawal, Thyrotoxicosis/Tamponade, Exercise/Electrolyte imbalance, Shock/Stimulants.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is the unifying question that determines management across all regular narrow-complex tachycardias?
options: Is the AV node part of the circuit?
Is the patient young or old?
Is the rhythm broad or narrow?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Is the AV node part of the circuit?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Yes → terminate (Group A: vagal/adenosine/ablation). No, but conduction via it → rate control (Group B; adenosine is diagnostic only). No, physiological → treat the cause (Group C: sinus tachycardia).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is the 'Golden Rule' for any regular broad-complex tachycardia?
options: Assume SVT with aberrancy and give IV verapamil to block the AV node and terminate the tachycardia
Treat as VT until proven otherwise — misdiagnosing VT as SVT and giving a nodal blocker can be fatal
Treat it as sinus tachycardia and focus on identifying and correcting the underlying physiological cause
Always give a rapid intravenous bolus of adenosine first to unmask and terminate the underlying rhythm
Only bother treating the rhythm at all once the patient becomes haemodynamically unstable or collapses
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Treat as VT until proven otherwise — misdiagnosing VT as SVT and giving a nodal blocker can be fatal
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Treating SVT as VT is almost always safe — the exception is pre-excited AF, where amiodarone is not benign — but misdiagnosing VT as SVT and giving a nodal blocker (verapamil/diltiazem) can be fatal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which of the following is one of the three causes of a regular broad-complex tachycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: SVT with aberrancy (bundle branch block)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: The three causes are VT (most common, default assumption), SVT with aberrancy (SVT + BBB), and SVT with pre-excitation (antidromic AVRT).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Why does ventricular tachycardia produce a wide QRS?
options: The impulse originates below the His bundle and spreads cell-to-cell (not via His-Purkinje), causing slow abnormal depolarisation
The impulse travels through the His-Purkinje system extremely rapidly, activating both ventricles at once and widening the QRS
An accessory pathway pre-excites the ventricle early, so the impulse bypasses the AV node and produces a broad slurred complex
The AV node conducts far too quickly, overwhelming the His-Purkinje system and forcing slow abnormal ventricular depolarisation
The atria depolarise the ventricles directly across the valve rings, bypassing the conduction system and broadening the QRS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: The impulse originates below the His bundle and spreads cell-to-cell (not via His-Purkinje), causing slow abnormal depolarisation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: VT arises below the His bundle in ventricular myocardium and spreads cell-to-cell rather than via the fast His-Purkinje system, producing slow depolarisation and a wide QRS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is the most common substrate for ventricular tachycardia?
options: An accessory pathway conducting antegrade to pre-excite the ventricle
A prolonged QT interval triggering early afterdepolarisations
Re-entry around scar from a prior MI / ischaemic heart disease
An automatic ectopic atrial focus firing faster than the sinus node
Enhanced automaticity within the AV node driving the ventricles
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Re-entry around scar from a prior MI / ischaemic heart disease
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Re-entry around scar tissue from a prior MI or ischaemic heart disease is the most common substrate for VT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: In a patient with known ischaemic heart disease, what is the approximate pre-test probability that a regular broad-complex tachycardia is VT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Over 95%
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: In a patient with known IHD or prior MI, the scar provides the re-entry substrate, raising the pre-test probability of VT to >95%. It is VT until definitively proven otherwise.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: A patient in a regular broad-complex tachycardia is haemodynamically stable and chatting comfortably. What does this tell you about the diagnosis?
options: Haemodynamic stability does NOT rule out VT — a common, dangerous trap
It confirms SVT with aberrancy conducting through an intact His-Purkinje system
It reliably rules out VT, since true VT always causes haemodynamic collapse
It means the underlying rhythm is entirely benign and needs no urgent treatment
It indicates the AV node forms part of the re-entry circuit driving the rhythm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Haemodynamic stability does NOT rule out VT — a common, dangerous trap
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Patients can be in VT and remain haemodynamically stable. Stability does not exclude VT and must not be used to downgrade the diagnosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which ECG finding has HIGH specificity for VT (rather than merely supporting it)?
options: AV dissociation (P waves and QRS marching independently)
An extreme north-west (superior) frontal QRS axis
A broad QRS duration measuring greater than 140 ms
A documented history of previous myocardial infarction
An atypical bundle branch block QRS morphology pattern
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: AV dissociation (P waves and QRS marching independently)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: AV dissociation, capture beats, fusion beats and concordance are high-specificity (near-diagnostic) features. A very broad QRS, extreme axis, prior MI and atypical BBB are supportive but less specific.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is a capture beat, and what does it indicate?
options: A hybrid intermediate QRS formed when two impulses collide and merge together — indicates simple SVT
A beat carrying a slurred delta wave and short PR interval — indicates underlying Wolff-Parkinson-White
A QRS that widens further only at faster ventricular rates — indicates rate-dependent aberrant conduction
An occasional narrow QRS when a sinus impulse briefly captures the ventricles — diagnostic of VT
A completely dropped beat with a missing QRS after a P wave — indicates underlying high-grade AV block
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: An occasional narrow QRS when a sinus impulse briefly captures the ventricles — diagnostic of VT
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: A capture beat is a rare narrow QRS amid the broad complexes, occurring when a sinus impulse briefly captures the ventricles. With fusion beats, it is diagnostic of VT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: A patient in stable, sustained monomorphic VT is to be treated pharmacologically (first-line UK). Which drug and regimen is used?
options: Adenosine 6 mg by rapid intravenous bolus, then 12 mg
Verapamil 5 mg by slow intravenous injection over 2 min
Magnesium sulphate 2 g intravenously given over 10 min
Amiodarone 300 mg IV over 20–60 min, then 900 mg over 24h
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Amiodarone 300 mg IV over 20–60 min, then 900 mg over 24h
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: First-line UK treatment of stable VT is amiodarone 300 mg IV over 20–60 min, then 900 mg over 24h maintenance, with electrolyte correction. Procainamide or lidocaine are alternatives.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: A patient in VT becomes hypotensive and confused (unstable). What is the immediate management?
options: Amiodarone 300 mg IV over 20-60 minutes via central line
Synchronised DC cardioversion (sedate first if conscious)
Adenosine 12 mg by rapid intravenous bolus into a large vein
Vagal manoeuvres such as carotid sinus massage or Valsalva
Oral beta-blockade with bisoprolol for urgent rate control
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Synchronised DC cardioversion (sedate first if conscious)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Unstable VT requires immediate synchronised DC cardioversion (sedate first if conscious). If pulseless, treat as VF with unsynchronised defibrillation and CPR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is the mechanism of SVT with aberrancy?
options: A ventricular focus firing below the His bundle and spreading cell-to-cell through myocardium, giving a broad abnormal QRS
A markedly prolonged QT interval triggering early afterdepolarisations and degenerating into polymorphic ventricular tachycardia
An accessory pathway conducting antegrade to pre-excite the ventricle ahead of the AV node, producing a broad slurred QRS
Multiple chaotic atrial wavelets bombarding the AV node irregularly and conducting down with variable aberrancy → broad QRS
A supraventricular rhythm conducting normally to the AV node, then blocked/delayed in one bundle branch below it → broad QRS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: A supraventricular rhythm conducting normally to the AV node, then blocked/delayed in one bundle branch below it → broad QRS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: In SVT with aberrancy the supraventricular impulse reaches the AV node normally, but below it conduction is blocked/delayed in one bundle branch, so the ventricle depolarises via the opposite bundle → slow spread → broad QRS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which feature would favour SVT with aberrancy rather than VT?
options: Clear AV dissociation with P waves marching through the QRS
Intermittent capture beats and fusion beats during the run
Classic RBBB or LBBB morphology with P waves 1:1 to the QRS
Positive concordance across all six precordial chest leads
QRS duration over 140 ms with an extreme north-west axis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Classic RBBB or LBBB morphology with P waves 1:1 to the QRS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Classic RBBB/LBBB morphology, 1:1 P:QRS, no AV dissociation/capture/fusion, identity to a prior ECG with BBB, and termination with adenosine all favour SVT with aberrancy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Adenosine is being considered to help diagnose a broad-complex tachycardia. When is this acceptable?
options: In all broad-complex tachycardias, since adenosine is a safe universal first-line agent whatever the mechanism
Only if the patient is haemodynamically unstable, when adenosine works faster and more safely than a DC shock
Only if you are confident it is NOT VT (old ECG showing BBB, no structural disease, stable, classic SVT history)
Never under any circumstances, because adenosine is absolutely contraindicated in every broad-complex rhythm
Only when the ventricular rate exceeds 200 bpm, as adenosine is ineffective at any slower tachycardia rate
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Only if you are confident it is NOT VT (old ECG showing BBB, no structural disease, stable, classic SVT history)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Adenosine can be diagnostically useful in suspected SVT with aberrancy, but only when you are confident it is not VT. When in doubt, treat as VT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which describes the classic RBBB vs LBBB morphology used to identify aberrancy?
options: RBBB: rS in V1, R in V6; LBBB: rSR' in V1, qRs in V6
RBBB: AV dissociation; LBBB: capture beats
Both show a delta wave in V1
RBBB: rSR' in V1, qRs in V6; LBBB: rS in V1, R in V6
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: RBBB: rSR' in V1, qRs in V6; LBBB: rS in V1, R in V6
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Classic RBBB shows rSR' in V1 and qRs in V6; classic LBBB shows rS in V1 and R in V6. Atypical morphology that doesn't fit these patterns favours VT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: In antidromic AVRT, what is the path of conduction and the resulting QRS?
options: Antegrade down the accessory pathway, retrograde up the His-AV node → very broad, slurred QRS
Antegrade down the AV node and His-Purkinje, retrograde up the accessory pathway → narrow, normal QRS
Macro-re-entry circling the tricuspid annulus in the right atrium → sawtooth flutter waves at ~300 bpm
Re-entry confined within the compact AV node using dual pathways → narrow QRS with a pseudo-R' in V1
Impulse arising entirely within ventricular myocardium below the His → broad QRS with AV dissociation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Antegrade down the accessory pathway, retrograde up the His-AV node → very broad, slurred QRS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Antidromic AVRT conducts antegrade down the accessory pathway (maximal pre-excitation of the ventricle → very broad, slurred QRS) and retrograde up the His-AV node. It is the opposite of orthodromic AVRT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Why are AV nodal blockers dangerous in antidromic AVRT / pre-excited WPW?
options: They would terminate a pure antidromic AVRT, but risk VF if the rhythm is (or becomes) pre-excited AF conducting rapidly down the accessory pathway
They markedly prolong the QT interval and trigger polymorphic torsades de pointes by blocking the cardiac potassium channels responsible for repolarisation
They cause only profound sinus bradycardia and prolonged asystole from excessive AV nodal suppression, with no additional risk to the ventricles
They are simply pharmacologically ineffective at the accessory pathway and carry no real danger whatsoever to the patient in any rhythm
They precipitate severe bronchospasm and acute respiratory compromise through beta-2 receptor blockade in the airways of susceptible patients
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: They would terminate a pure antidromic AVRT, but risk VF if the rhythm is (or becomes) pre-excited AF conducting rapidly down the accessory pathway
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: In pre-excited AF the AV node is the protective 'brake'; blocking it (adenosine, verapamil, beta-blockers) lets impulses conduct unopposed down the accessory pathway → very fast ventricular rates → VF. (In a pure antidromic AVRT a nodal blocker would actually terminate it, but the rhythm cannot always be assumed pure.)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which clue on the baseline ECG points towards antidromic AVRT as the cause of a broad-complex tachycardia?
options: A markedly prolonged QT interval on the baseline ECG
Sawtooth flutter waves seen in the inferior leads
A history of WPW or a delta wave on the baseline ECG
An irregularly irregular rhythm with no clear P waves
A pathological Q wave from a previous old infarct
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: A history of WPW or a delta wave on the baseline ECG
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: A history of WPW or a δ-wave on the baseline ECG is a diagnostic clue. Antidromic AVRT shows no AV dissociation, as the AV node is part of the circuit retrogradely.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which set of features all FAVOUR VT in the VT-vs-SVT decision?
options: AV dissociation, capture/fusion beats, concordance, QRS >140 ms, known IHD
Classic RBBB/LBBB, 1:1 P:QRS, terminates with adenosine, young patient
Short PR, delta wave, narrow QRS, no structural disease
f-waves, no P waves, irregular rhythm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: AV dissociation, capture/fusion beats, concordance, QRS >140 ms, known IHD
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Features favouring VT include AV dissociation, capture/fusion beats, precordial concordance, QRS >140 ms, extreme/north-west axis, known IHD/prior MI, structural heart disease and atypical BBB morphology.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: You cannot confidently exclude VT in a stable broad-complex tachycardia. What is the safest approach?
options: Treat as VT (amiodarone IV); never give verapamil/diltiazem blindly to a broad-complex rhythm
Give IV verapamil to test the response and terminate the rhythm if it is a supraventricular tachycardia
Give a rapid IV adenosine bolus to unmask atrial activity and terminate it if it is truly supraventricular
Discharge home the same day with routine outpatient cardiology follow-up and an ambulatory Holter monitor
Start regular oral flecainide as a pill-in-the-pocket to chemically suppress the broad-complex rhythm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Treat as VT (amiodarone IV); never give verapamil/diltiazem blindly to a broad-complex rhythm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Doubt = VT. If you cannot confidently exclude VT, treat it as VT and never give verapamil or diltiazem blindly to a broad-complex tachycardia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What are the three safety rules summarising the VT-vs-SVT approach?
options: Rate-control the ventricular response, anticoagulate to prevent thromboembolic stroke, then electively cardiovert
Adenosine first to break the circuit, verapamil second for rate control, then amiodarone third if both fail
Stability first (unstable → synchronised DC cardioversion); doubt = VT; the unifying question 'Could this be VT?'
Always attempt vagal manoeuvres first, then a trial of IV adenosine, and finally a synchronised DC shock
Identify buried P waves, measure the PR interval, and assess the frontal-plane QRS axis to reach a diagnosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Stability first (unstable → synchronised DC cardioversion); doubt = VT; the unifying question 'Could this be VT?'
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: The three rules: (1) stability first — unstable → immediate synchronised DC cardioversion regardless of diagnosis; (2) doubt = VT — treat as VT if VT cannot be excluded; (3) the unifying question — 'Could this be VT?' If yes, treat as VT and step down only with clear evidence and specialist input.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is the danger instinct to apply to any irregular broad-complex tachycardia?
options: Assume ordinary AF with a rate-related bundle branch block and give an IV beta-blocker for rate control
Assume it is simply sinus tachycardia with aberrancy and focus solely on treating the underlying cause
Think pre-excited AF or polymorphic VT until proven otherwise; never reflexively give AV-nodal blockers
Give a rapid IV adenosine bolus to terminate the re-entrant circuit and restore sinus rhythm promptly
Treat every case as torsades de pointes and empirically give IV magnesium sulphate to all such patients
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Think pre-excited AF or polymorphic VT until proven otherwise; never reflexively give AV-nodal blockers
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Irregular + broad narrows to a short list of high-risk rhythms; reflexively giving AV-nodal blockers can be fatal (especially in pre-excited AF).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which are the three causes of an irregular broad-complex tachycardia?
options: VT, SVT with aberrancy, antidromic AVRT
Pre-excited AF, polymorphic VT/torsades, AF with BBB
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Pre-excited AF, polymorphic VT/torsades, AF with BBB
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: The three causes are 5A pre-excited AF (WPW+AF), 5B polymorphic VT/torsades, and 5C AF with BBB.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Why are the ventricles bombarded at near-atrial rates in pre-excited AF?
options: The AV node abnormally conducts far faster than normal, losing its decremental delay and passing every atrial impulse straight through
The sinoatrial node itself fires at an extremely rapid rate and drives the ventricles directly at near-atrial frequencies throughout
The His-Purkinje conduction system fails and depolarises passively, letting the rapid atrial impulses flood the ventricles unchecked
The chaotic atrial impulses conduct directly down the accessory pathway, bypassing the AV node's protective rate-limiting gating
The patient's regular oral beta-blockers have worn off, removing the pharmacological brake that normally slows AV nodal conduction
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: The chaotic atrial impulses conduct directly down the accessory pathway, bypassing the AV node's protective rate-limiting gating
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: In WPW, AF impulses bypass the AV node's gating and conduct directly down the accessory pathway, so the ventricles are bombarded at near-atrial rates (often >200 bpm ventricular).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which ECG features are characteristic of pre-excited AF?
options: Perfectly regular rhythm, narrow QRS complexes, and clear sawtooth flutter waves between the beats
QRS complexes that twist and rotate around the baseline on a background of a markedly prolonged QT
Irregular R-R, broad QRS, very fast (>200 bpm), varying QRS width beat-to-beat, no organised P waves
Regular 1:1 P-to-QRS relationship with a classic broad left bundle branch block morphology throughout
Regular broad complexes at a fixed rate with clear AV dissociation and occasional capture beats seen
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Irregular R-R, broad QRS, very fast (>200 bpm), varying QRS width beat-to-beat, no organised P waves
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Pre-excited AF shows irregular R-R (underlying AF), broad QRS (via the accessory pathway), a very fast ventricular rate (>200 bpm), beat-to-beat varying QRS width (fusion), and no organised P waves.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which drugs must NEVER be given in pre-excited AF?
options: AV-nodal blockers — adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blockers, digoxin
The class I antiarrhythmic drugs flecainide, procainamide and disopyramide
Electrolyte replacement with IV magnesium sulphate and potassium chloride
The class III agent amiodarone together with the class Ib drug lidocaine
Supplemental high-flow oxygen together with intravenous crystalloid fluids
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: AV-nodal blockers — adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blockers, digoxin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: These block the AV node and force all conduction down the accessory pathway → extreme rate acceleration → VF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: A stable patient with pre-excited AF and no structural heart disease needs pharmacological treatment. What is first-line?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Flecainide IV
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Of the options offered, only flecainide is safe — the other four are all AV-nodal blockers, which are dangerous in pre-excited AF. In UK practice the RCUK algorithm advises seeking expert help and considering amiodarone; flecainide (no structural heart disease) and procainamide are the ESC/AHA options where available. AV-nodal blockers (verapamil, beta-blockers, digoxin, adenosine) must never be given. Note that ESC classes IV amiodarone as not recommended and potentially harmful here, while the UK algorithm still lists it as a consider-with-expert-help option — for UK practice, follow the UK position.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: How is unstable pre-excited AF managed?
options: A rapid IV adenosine bolus of 12 mg via a large-bore cannula to break the accessory-pathway circuit
A loading dose of oral flecainide as a pill-in-the-pocket to chemically restore sinus rhythm
Slow IV verapamil 5 mg for rate control, repeated to 10 mg if the fast ventricular rate persists
Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion (unsynchronised defibrillation + CPR if it degenerates to VF)
Vagal manoeuvres such as carotid sinus massage and a modified Valsalva to terminate the tachycardia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion (unsynchronised defibrillation + CPR if it degenerates to VF)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Unstable pre-excited AF requires immediate synchronised DC cardioversion; if it degenerates to VF, give unsynchronised defibrillation and CPR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What specifically defines torsades de pointes (as opposed to other polymorphic VT)?
options: Polymorphic VT arising on a background of an entirely normal QT interval
Pre-excited AF conducting down an accessory pathway in WPW syndrome
Monomorphic VT occurring in a patient with structural heart disease
Irregularly irregular AF conducting with a broad bundle-branch QRS
Polymorphic VT occurring on a background of a prolonged QT interval
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Polymorphic VT occurring on a background of a prolonged QT interval
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Torsades de pointes is polymorphic VT (continuously varying QRS morphology/axis, 'twisting around the baseline') occurring on a background of prolonged QT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What corrected QT (QTc) values are considered prolonged?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: >440 ms (men) / >460 ms (women)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: QT is measured from the start of the QRS to the end of the T wave; a QTc >440 ms in men or >460 ms in women is prolonged.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which is a recognised drug cause of a prolonged QT predisposing to torsades?
options: The cardioselective beta-blocker bisoprolol given once daily
The ACE inhibitor ramipril used widely in hypertension
Low-dose aspirin used for cardiovascular prevention
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Macrolide antibiotics (e.g. erythromycin, clarithromycin)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: High-yield QT-prolonging drugs include antiarrhythmics (sotalol, amiodarone), antipsychotics, antidepressants (citalopram, TCAs), macrolides, antiemetics (ondansetron) and antimalarials.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which is the MOST common electrolyte cause of a prolonged QT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Hypokalaemia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Hypokalaemia is the most common electrolyte cause; hypomagnesaemia and hypocalcaemia also prolong the QT by impairing repolarisation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is the first-line treatment for stable torsades de pointes, and the key point about it?
options: IV amiodarone 300 mg over 20-60 min as the definitive first-line rhythm control
IV magnesium sulphate 2 g over 10 min — given even if the serum Mg²⁺ is normal
A rapid IV adenosine 6 mg bolus to break the re-entrant circuit and restore sinus
Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion under sedation as the first-line treatment
IV flecainide as a class Ic agent to chemically terminate the arrhythmia at once
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: IV magnesium sulphate 2 g over 10 min — given even if the serum Mg²⁺ is normal
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: IV magnesium sulphate 2 g over 10 min is first-line, given even with a normal serum Mg²⁺ because it stabilises cardiac membranes. Do not wait for a low level before giving it.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which drug should be AVOIDED in torsades de pointes, and why?
options: Magnesium, because it lowers the heart rate
Amiodarone, because it itself prolongs the QT
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Amiodarone, because it itself prolongs the QT
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Amiodarone is avoided in torsades because it prolongs the QT, which is the underlying problem. Stop all QT-prolonging drugs and correct electrolytes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Why is sotalol an important exception when considering beta-blockers in long QT?
options: Sotalol usefully shortens the QT interval, making it the safest beta-blocker to use in patients with congenital long QT
Sotalol works mainly by blocking conduction through the accessory pathway, which is why it is favoured in long QT syndrome
Sotalol is the recommended first-line drug for actively terminating torsades de pointes and preventing its recurrence
Sotalol prolongs the QT and can cause torsades, unlike other beta-blockers which are safe and used in congenital LQTS
Sotalol is absolutely contraindicated in every arrhythmia and must never be used for rhythm or rate control at all
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Sotalol prolongs the QT and can cause torsades, unlike other beta-blockers which are safe and used in congenital LQTS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Sotalol prolongs the QT and can cause torsades, so it must not be confused with other beta-blockers, which are QT-safe and actually used in congenital LQTS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which device intervention can be used acutely in torsades because it shortens the QT?
options: A permanent pacemaker set to a slow rate
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Temporary (overdrive) pacing
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Temporary overdrive pacing increases the heart rate, which shortens the QT and can suppress torsades. An ICD is used for recurrent or congenital LQTS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is the mechanism of AF with bundle branch block?
options: Fibrillatory AF impulses conduct rapidly down an accessory pathway, bypassing the AV node and pre-exciting the ventricles broadly
Ordinary AF (irregular atrial activity) plus a pre-existing or rate-related BBB providing the broad QRS, with the AV node intact
A single irritable ventricular ectopic focus firing irregularly and driving the ventricles independently of any atrial activity
Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia arising on a background of a markedly prolonged QT interval producing broad varying complexes
Macro-re-entry circling the tricuspid annulus with variable AV block giving irregular broad conducted complexes at the ventricle
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Ordinary AF (irregular atrial activity) plus a pre-existing or rate-related BBB providing the broad QRS, with the AV node intact
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: AF provides the irregularity and the BBB provides the broad QRS. The AV node remains intact and rate-limiting (ventricular rate rarely >180 bpm) — it's 'just AF that looks broad'.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: How can pre-excited AF be distinguished from AF with BBB?
options: AF with BBB is the faster of the two, consistently exceeding 200 bpm with beat-to-beat variation in QRS width, whereas pre-excited AF stays slower with a fixed morphology
Pre-excited AF is very fast (>200 bpm) with varying beat-to-beat QRS width and a WPW/δ-wave history; AF with BBB is slower (<180 bpm) with fixed BBB morphology
Both conditions show completely identical ventricular rates and identical fixed QRS morphology, so they simply cannot be told apart on the surface ECG at all
Pre-excited AF characteristically shows a single fixed bundle branch block morphology at a slow rate, while AF with BBB varies its QRS width markedly beat to beat
AF with BBB reliably shows a slurred delta wave and a short PR on the baseline tracing, which is the key feature separating it from pre-excited AF conduction
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Pre-excited AF is very fast (>200 bpm) with varying beat-to-beat QRS width and a WPW/δ-wave history; AF with BBB is slower (<180 bpm) with fixed BBB morphology
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Pre-excited AF: rate >200, varying QRS width, WPW/δ-wave history, treat with flecainide/DC. AF with BBB: rate <180, fixed BBB morphology, known BBB/structural disease, treat with rate control + anticoagulation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Once pre-excited AF is confidently excluded, how is AF with BBB managed?
options: Give a rapid IV adenosine bolus to terminate the rhythm and restore normal sinus conduction
Use IV flecainide to slow conduction through the accessory pathway and safely narrow the QRS
Give IV magnesium sulphate and institute overdrive pacing to suppress the irregular broad rhythm
Manage as AF — rate control (beta-blocker/CCB/digoxin) and anticoagulate per CHA₂DS₂-VASc
No specific treatment is required, as the rhythm reliably self-terminates without intervention
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Manage as AF — rate control (beta-blocker/CCB/digoxin) and anticoagulate per CHA₂DS₂-VASc
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Once pre-excited AF is excluded, AF with BBB is managed as ordinary AF: rate control and anticoagulation per CHA₂DS₂-VASc. If in doubt, treat as pre-excited AF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is the safety rule about AV-nodal blockers in any irregular broad-complex tachycardia?
options: They are safe and first-line in all cases of irregular broad-complex tachycardia for prompt rate control
Give them only when the ventricular rate is below 180 bpm and the complexes look reasonably uniform
Only beta-blockers among the AV-nodal agents are safe to give, while the others must be strictly avoided
They are perfectly safe to give provided the patient is haemodynamically stable and not compromised
Never give adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blockers or digoxin until pre-excited AF is excluded
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Never give adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blockers or digoxin until pre-excited AF is excluded
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: AV-nodal blockers must be withheld in any irregular broad-complex tachycardia until pre-excited AF is confidently excluded, because of the VF risk.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which two irregular broad-complex rhythms can both degenerate to VF, mandating an immediately available defibrillator?
options: AF with BBB and sinus tachycardia
Pre-excited AF and torsades de pointes
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Pre-excited AF and torsades de pointes
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Both pre-excited AF and torsades can degenerate to VF, so a defibrillator must be immediately available. Stability-first and no-nodal-blocker rules also apply.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: A 68-year-old with a previous anterior MI is successfully cardioverted from sustained monomorphic VT. Echo shows an LVEF of 30% with an apical scar. Electrolytes are normal and he is on no proarrhythmic drugs; angiography shows no new culprit lesion. What is the most appropriate long-term management?
options: No specific long-term therapy as the VT has been terminated
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator for secondary prevention
explanation: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator for secondary prevention — he had sustained VT with no completely reversible cause, arising from established infarct scar with impaired LV function. That is the classic secondary-prevention ICD indication.
Amiodarone alone — reduces episodes and is a useful adjunct, but it does not abort a lethal arrhythmia and is not a substitute for an ICD.
Permanent pacemaker — treats bradycardia, not ventricular tachyarrhythmia; it cannot defibrillate.
No long-term therapy — the scar substrate remains, so recurrence risk is high; terminating the episode addresses only half the problem.
Flecainide — a class Ic agent, contraindicated in structural heart disease and post-MI, where it increases mortality).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: A 74-year-old with stable AVNRT is about to have vagal manoeuvres attempted. Which finding would make carotid sinus massage inappropriate?
options: A history of previous AVNRT terminated by adenosine
A narrow QRS complex on the ECG
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: An audible carotid bruit
explanation: An audible carotid bruit — this suggests carotid atheroma, and massage risks dislodging plaque and causing a stroke. Known carotid stenosis or a TIA/stroke in the preceding 3 months are equally contraindications, and both sides must never be massaged at once.
BP 130/80 — a normal, stable blood pressure; this patient is haemodynamically stable and suitable for vagal manoeuvres.
Heart rate 170 bpm — the expected rate in AVNRT and precisely the rhythm vagal manoeuvres are used for.
Previous AVNRT terminated by adenosine — reassuring history supporting the diagnosis, not a contraindication.
Narrow QRS — confirms a supraventricular origin, which makes vagal manoeuvres and adenosine appropriate.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: Which statement best defines a cardiomyopathy?
options: Myocardial dysfunction caused directly by obstructive coronary artery disease
Inflammation of the visceral and parietal pericardial layers
Progressive fibrosis and calcification of the cardiac valve leaflets
A primary disorder of heart muscle not explained by coronary, valve or hypertensive disease
Ischaemic damage confined to the specialised conduction system
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.answer: A primary disorder of heart muscle not explained by coronary, valve or hypertensive disease
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: Cardiomyopathy is a primary disease of the myocardium itself, by definition not attributable to coronary, valvular, hypertensive or congenital heart disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: Which is the commonest type of cardiomyopathy?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: Dilated cardiomyopathy is the commonest pattern, producing a dilated, poorly-contracting ventricle and systolic heart failure (HFrEF). HCM is the commonest INHERITED disorder but not commonest overall.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: Hypertrophic and restrictive cardiomyopathies primarily cause which type of ventricular dysfunction?
options: Systolic dysfunction with a reduced ejection fraction
Isolated valvular dysfunction with normal myocardium
Diastolic with impaired filling and preserved EF
Pure conduction dysfunction with normal filling
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.answer: Diastolic with impaired filling and preserved EF
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: HCM (stiff, hypertrophied) and RCM (rigid walls) impair filling → diastolic dysfunction with preserved EF; dilated cardiomyopathy causes systolic dysfunction (HFrEF).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: A 33-year-old woman develops heart failure with a dilated, poorly-contracting LV in the last month of pregnancy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is heart failure from LV systolic dysfunction developing towards the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery, with no other cause found. EF is nearly always below 45% and the LV is usually, though not always, dilated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: Which drug characteristically causes a dose-dependent dilated cardiomyopathy, prompting EF monitoring?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: Anthracyclines such as doxorubicin cause dose-dependent, largely irreversible cardiotoxicity leading to dilated cardiomyopathy. Trastuzumab causes a separate injury that is NOT dose-dependent and is usually reversible on stopping. Serial echo/EF monitoring is used for both.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: A young man with dilated cardiomyopathy develops atrial fibrillation. Which therapy most importantly prevents a common complication?
options: A long-acting nitrate for afterload reduction
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: The dilated, akinetic ventricle predisposes to mural thrombus and systemic embolism; anticoagulate when there is AF or intracardiac thrombus.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: Which is the correct standard therapy for the heart failure of dilated cardiomyopathy?
options: A nitrate plus digoxin, with no disease-modifying therapy
Calcium-channel blocker monotherapy for rate control
Aspirin and a statin only, as for ischaemic disease
No pharmacological therapy — transplant assessment alone
ACE inhibitor/ARB, beta-blocker, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.answer: ACE inhibitor/ARB, beta-blocker, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: DCM causes HFrEF, treated with the standard quadruple therapy (ACEi/ARB or ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor) plus diuretics; ICD/CRT where indicated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: What is the inheritance pattern and gene type in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: HCM is autosomal dominant with sarcomere-gene mutations. Desmosomal genes cause ARVC; dystrophin causes Duchenne-associated DCM.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: What is the commonest structural (inherited myocardial) cause of sudden cardiac death in a young athlete?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: HCM is the commonest structural cause of sudden cardiac death in young people and athletes, via ventricular arrhythmia; exertional syncope is a red flag. In UK autopsy series the single commonest finding overall is a morphologically normal heart (sudden arrhythmic death syndrome).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: How does the murmur of obstructive HCM change with the Valsalva manoeuvre?
options: Louder — reduced preload shrinks the LV cavity and worsens obstruction
Softer, because reduced preload widens the outflow tract
Unchanged, as the obstruction is fixed
Disappears completely during the strain phase
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.answer: Louder — reduced preload shrinks the LV cavity and worsens obstruction
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: Reducing preload (Valsalva/standing) increases dynamic LVOT obstruction, making the murmur louder — the opposite of aortic stenosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: Which drug should be AVOIDED in obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: Nitrates — along with ACE inhibitors, diuretics and digoxin — reduce preload or afterload and worsen the dynamic outflow obstruction. Negative inotropes are used instead: a beta-blocker first-line, with verapamil second-line if a beta-blocker is not tolerated (though verapamil is itself cautioned in severe obstruction with a high gradient, because it is also a vasodilator). Amiodarone is appropriate for atrial fibrillation in HCM, and cautious fluid is the right response to hypotension in a preload-dependent ventricle.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: What is the first-line pharmacological treatment of symptomatic obstructive HCM?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: A beta-blocker is first-line: as a negative inotrope it reduces the outflow gradient and relieves symptoms. Verapamil is the second-line option where a beta-blocker is not tolerated, but it is cautioned or avoided in severe obstruction with a high gradient and hypotension, because it is also a vasodilator and can worsen the obstruction. Nitrates, ACE inhibitors, diuretics and digoxin are all avoided in obstructive HCM — they reduce preload or afterload and worsen the dynamic obstruction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: Which echocardiographic finding is characteristic of HCM?
options: Four-chamber dilatation with global hypokinesia and a low EF
Asymmetric septal hypertrophy with systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve
A large pericardial effusion with right ventricular diastolic collapse
Mitral valve vegetations with valve destruction
A bicuspid aortic valve with a dilated root
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.answer: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy with systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: HCM shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy with systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve and a dynamic LVOT gradient ('MR SAM ASH').

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: Which ECG changes are typical of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
options: A delta wave with a short PR interval and wide QRS
Widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation with PR depression
LVH with deep T-wave inversion and dagger-like septal Q waves
An epsilon wave in leads V1–V3 with T-wave inversion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.answer: LVH with deep T-wave inversion and dagger-like septal Q waves
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: HCM shows LVH, deep T-wave inversion and narrow 'dagger' septal Q waves. Saddle ST elevation = pericarditis; electrical alternans = large effusion; epsilon = ARVC.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: Which feature is used to guide ICD implantation in HCM?
options: A family history of sudden cardiac death
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.answer: A family history of sudden cardiac death
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: The validated 5-year risk score (ESC) is built from age, maximal LV wall thickness, left atrial size, LVOT gradient, family history of sudden death, non-sustained VT and unexplained syncope — a family history of sudden cardiac death is one of its variables. An abnormal exercise BP response is a supporting consideration, not part of the score.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: What invasive procedure relieves refractory LV outflow obstruction in HCM?
options: Catheter ablation of the AV node
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: Refractory LVOT obstruction is treated by reducing the bulk of the septum, either surgically or by catheter.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: What is the commonest cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: Amyloidosis (AL and ATTR) is the commonest cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: Restrictive cardiomyopathy closely mimics which surgically curable condition?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: RCM and constrictive pericarditis both cause diastolic right heart failure; constriction shows pericardial thickening/calcification and is curable by pericardiectomy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: Which histological finding confirms cardiac amyloidosis?
options: Non-caseating granulomas with Langhans giant cells
Multinucleated giant cells with lymphocytic infiltrate
Congo red staining with apple-green birefringence
Fibrofatty replacement of the ventricular myocardium
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.answer: Congo red staining with apple-green birefringence
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: Amyloid stains with Congo red and shows apple-green birefringence under polarised light. Granulomas = sarcoid; giant cells = giant-cell myocarditis; fibrofatty = ARVC.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: Which echo finding suggests restrictive cardiomyopathy?
options: Non-dilated ventricles with marked biatrial enlargement and preserved EF
Dilated ventricles with a globally reduced ejection fraction
Asymmetric septal hypertrophy with outflow obstruction
A flail mitral leaflet with severe regurgitation
A bicuspid aortic valve with a dilated aortic root
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.answer: Non-dilated ventricles with marked biatrial enlargement and preserved EF
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: RCM shows normal-sized ventricles with big atria and preserved EF, reflecting diastolic dysfunction. Wall thickness is normal in idiopathic RCM but increased in infiltrative causes such as amyloid.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: A 68-year-old woman develops chest pain, anterior ST elevation and a raised troponin after her husband's death; angiography is normal and echo shows apical ballooning. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy: catecholamine-driven transient apical ballooning after stress that mimics ACS but with unobstructed coronaries; usually recovers fully.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: What is the typical outcome of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy?
options: Progressive irreversible heart failure requiring transplant
Immediate need for cardiac transplantation assessment
Permanent complete heart block requiring pacing
Full recovery of LV function over days to weeks with supportive care
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.answer: Full recovery of LV function over days to weeks with supportive care
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: Takotsubo is usually reversible: supportive management (treat as heart failure, avoid catecholamines) with recovery of LV function in weeks.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: Which ECG finding is characteristically associated with ARVC?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: ARVC classically shows an epsilon wave with T-wave inversion in V1–V3. Delta wave = WPW; J wave = hypothermia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: What is the underlying pathology of ARVC?
options: Sarcomere protein disarray with myocyte hypertrophy
Amyloid deposition in the ventricular myocardium
Myocardial iron overload from repeated transfusion
Fibrofatty replacement of the right ventricular myocardium
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.answer: Fibrofatty replacement of the right ventricular myocardium
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: ARVC is an autosomal-dominant desmosomal disorder with fibrofatty replacement of the RV, predisposing to ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: What is the key first-line/bedside investigation for suspected cardiomyopathy?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: Echocardiography is the key bedside test (with ECG, CXR, BNP), assessing chamber size, wall thickness, EF, diastolic function and gradients.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: What is the main role of cardiac MRI in cardiomyopathy?
options: To measure serum troponin more accurately
To replace echocardiography for measuring ejection fraction
Tissue characterisation with late gadolinium enhancement
To screen for obstructive coronary artery disease
To guide anticoagulation dosing in atrial fibrillation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.answer: Tissue characterisation with late gadolinium enhancement
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: Cardiac MRI provides tissue characterisation (LGE) for phenotyping and risk/prognosis and is increasingly the gold-standard imaging test.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: A 31-year-old at 36 weeks' gestation presents with orthopnoea and ankle oedema. Echo shows a dilated left ventricle with an LVEF of 32%; no other cause is found. Which treatment is CONTRAINDICATED at this stage?
explanation: Ramipril — ACE inhibitors (and ARBs, ARNI) are teratogenic and must be withheld while the patient is pregnant. They can be introduced after delivery, with the choice adjusted if she is breastfeeding.
Bisoprolol — beta-1 selective beta-blockers are a backbone of antenatal treatment and are appropriate here.
Hydralazine — used with a nitrate to provide afterload reduction in place of an ACE inhibitor during pregnancy.
Furosemide — a loop diuretic is appropriate for congestion, used judiciously to avoid compromising placental perfusion.
Isosorbide dinitrate — the nitrate partner to hydralazine, providing safe afterload and preload reduction antenatally.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: A woman recovering from peripartum cardiomyopathy asks about future pregnancies. Her LVEF remains 42% at one year. What is the most appropriate counselling?
options: A further pregnancy carries high maternal risk while LV function remains impaired
There is no increased risk provided she takes a beta-blocker throughout
Recurrence occurs only if the first episode required intensive care
She can safely conceive as soon as she is symptom-free, regardless of ejection fraction
Risk is eliminated by planned early caesarean delivery
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.answer: A further pregnancy carries high maternal risk while LV function remains impaired
explanation: A further pregnancy carries high maternal risk and is generally advised against while LV function remains impaired — persistent LVEF below 50% places a subsequent pregnancy in the highest maternal-risk category, where it is considered contraindicated.
No increased risk on a beta-blocker — incorrect; medication does not abolish the recurrence risk conferred by unrecovered ventricular function.
Recurrence only after severe first episodes — recurrence relates principally to residual LV function, not the severity of the index admission.
Symptom-free regardless of EF — symptoms are an unreliable guide; the ejection fraction is what determines risk.
Early caesarean eliminating risk — delivery planning matters but does not remove the haemodynamic burden of pregnancy itself.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: What are varicose veins?
options: Thrombosed deep veins of the calf
Dilated arteries of the lower limb
Dilated, tortuous superficial leg veins from incompetent valves and venous hypertension
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.answer: Dilated, tortuous superficial leg veins from incompetent valves and venous hypertension
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: Varicose veins are dilated, tortuous superficial leg veins (>3 mm) caused by incompetent venous valves and venous hypertension.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: Normal venous return from the leg depends on all of the following EXCEPT:
options: High arterial pressure driving venous flow
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.answer: High arterial pressure driving venous flow
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: Venous return relies on competent valves, the calf muscle pump and patent deep veins; failure of any of these causes venous hypertension. Arterial pressure is not the mechanism.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: Which vein and junction are most commonly involved in varicose veins?
options: Small saphenous vein at the saphenopopliteal junction
Femoral vein at the common femoral vein
Great saphenous vein at the saphenofemoral junction
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.answer: Great saphenous vein at the saphenofemoral junction
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: The great saphenous vein (medial), refluxing at the saphenofemoral junction, is most commonly involved.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: Which is the commonest type of varicose veins?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: Most varicose veins are primary (idiopathic valve/vein-wall weakness); risk factors include age, female sex, family history, pregnancy, obesity and prolonged standing.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: Which is an important SECONDARY cause of varicose veins to ask about?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: A previous DVT (post-thrombotic syndrome) damages the deep valves and is a key secondary cause — always ask about it.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: How do the symptoms of varicose veins typically behave?
options: Worse on elevation, better on standing
Worse on standing/at the end of the day, relieved by elevation
Worse after exercise, better on standing
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.answer: Worse on standing/at the end of the day, relieved by elevation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: Aching, heaviness and throbbing are worse on standing/at the end of the day and are relieved by leg elevation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: The 'inverted champagne bottle' leg of chronic venous insufficiency is due to:
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: Lipodermatosclerosis (fibrosis of the skin/subcutaneous tissue) produces the 'inverted champagne bottle' appearance; other CVI signs include haemosiderin, venous eczema and atrophie blanche.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: A lump at the saphenofemoral junction gives a cough impulse and disappears on lying down. What is it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: A saphena varix (a dilatation at the SFJ) gives a cough impulse and disappears on lying — an important mimic of a femoral hernia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: What is the investigation of choice for varicose veins?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: Duplex ultrasound is the investigation of choice — it confirms reflux, localises the incompetence and excludes deep venous obstruction/DVT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: What must be checked before applying compression therapy to a leg?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: ABPI must be measured first to exclude significant arterial disease — compression on an ischaemic leg is harmful.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: According to NICE, what is the first-line interventional treatment for varicose veins?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: Endothermal ablation (radiofrequency or endovenous laser) is first-line; foam sclerotherapy is second-line and surgery third-line.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: If endothermal ablation is unsuitable, what is the next interventional option for varicose veins?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: The NICE interventional ladder is: endothermal ablation → ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy → surgery (ligation/stripping ± avulsions).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: Which of the following is a NICE criterion for referral of varicose veins to a vascular service?
options: A venous leg ulcer (active or healed)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.answer: A venous leg ulcer (active or healed)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: Referral criteria include symptomatic primary/recurrent varicose veins, CVI skin changes, superficial vein thrombosis with suspected incompetence, and a venous leg ulcer (active or healed).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: What is the mainstay of treatment for a venous leg ulcer (once arterial disease is excluded)?
options: Bed rest with the leg dependent
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: Compression bandaging (after excluding arterial disease with ABPI) plus wound care is the mainstay; treating venous incompetence reduces recurrence.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: Which set of features best describes a VENOUS ulcer?
options: Gaiter area, shallow, exudative, ABPI normal
On the toes, dry, with weak pulses
Over the sacrum with necrotic base
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.answer: Gaiter area, shallow, exudative, ABPI normal
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: Venous ulcers are in the gaiter area, large/shallow/exudative, with surrounding haemosiderin/eczema and an ABPI ≥0.8 (compression safe; normal 0.9–1.3).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: Which set of features best describes an ARTERIAL ulcer?
options: Gaiter area, shallow, exudative, ABPI normal
Above the medial malleolus with haemosiderin
Punched-out, deep, very painful, ABPI <0.8, on toes/pressure points
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.answer: Punched-out, deep, very painful, ABPI <0.8, on toes/pressure points
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: Arterial ulcers are small, deep and 'punched-out', very painful (worse on elevation), on the toes/pressure points, with cold hairless skin and a reduced ABPI (<0.8).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: An 82-year-old woman is found at home with brisk bleeding from a varicosity on her lower leg. She is sitting in her armchair with blood pooling on the floor. What is the immediate management?
options: Sit her upright and apply a tourniquet above the knee
Lie her flat, elevate the leg above the level of the heart and apply firm direct pressure
Apply a haemostatic dressing and arrange urgent surgical ligation
Insert two large-bore cannulae and start a rapid fluid bolus before addressing the leg
Apply a high-compression bandage over the bleeding point with the leg dependent
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.answer: Lie her flat, elevate the leg above the level of the heart and apply firm direct pressure
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: This is venous, pressure-driven bleeding, so it stops as soon as the leg is raised above the heart and direct pressure is applied — a manoeuvre that needs no equipment. Leaving the patient sitting up (or leaving the leg dependent) keeps venous pressure in the leg high and the bleeding continues; deaths have been reported from bleeding varices in elderly people for exactly this reason. A tourniquet is unnecessary and harmful. Resuscitation follows once the bleeding is controlled, and the underlying incompetence is treated later because the varix will bleed again.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: A 58-year-old man presents with a tender, hard, erythematous cord along a varicose great saphenous vein in the thigh. Duplex confirms a 9 cm superficial vein thrombosis with no DVT, extending to within 6 cm of the saphenofemoral junction. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Therapeutic anticoagulation for 3 months as for a provoked DVT
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: Symptomatic superficial vein thrombosis at least 5 cm long is treated with a prophylactic dose of fondaparinux (or LMWH) for 45 days, which reduces extension into the deep system and recurrence. Antibiotics have no role — this is thrombosis, not infection, however red the leg looks. Reassurance alone under-treats a segment of this length and proximity. Full therapeutic anticoagulation is reserved for a confirmed DVT or thrombus reaching the junction itself, and surgery is not the first response.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: What is the defining pathology of aortic dissection?
options: Symmetrical dilatation of all three intact aortic wall layers, forming a true aneurysmal sac
Occlusive thrombosis filling the true aortic lumen, arising on a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque
Rupture of an atheromatous plaque within a coronary artery, causing acute thrombotic occlusion
Progressive calcific degeneration of the aortic valve cusps, restricting leaflet opening in systole
A tear in the aortic intima → blood between intima and media → a propagating false lumen
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: A tear in the aortic intima → blood between intima and media → a propagating false lumen
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Aortic dissection is a tear in the intima allowing blood between intima and media, creating a false lumen that propagates along the aortic wall.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: Why is a Type A dissection so time-critical?
options: Type A mortality rises ~1–2%/hour without surgery
Mortality is highest at 48–72 hours, so early surgery gains little
Mortality is roughly 1–2% per day, allowing overnight transfer
Mortality is driven by rupture alone, which is rare in the first week
Mortality is comparable to Type B, which is managed medically
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Type A mortality rises ~1–2%/hour without surgery
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Type A dissection mortality rises ~1–2% per hour without surgery, making it a time-critical emergency; management hinges on Stanford A vs B.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: Retrograde propagation of a dissection toward the aortic root can cause which complications?
options: Lower limb ischaemia and renal malperfusion from distal spread
Acute iliac artery occlusion causing sudden painful leg ischaemia
Isolated mesenteric ischaemia from superior mesenteric involvement
Paraplegia caused by occlusion of a spinal segmental artery
Aortic regurgitation, coronary involvement, cardiac tamponade
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Aortic regurgitation, coronary involvement, cardiac tamponade
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Retrograde propagation to the aortic root causes aortic regurgitation, coronary involvement and cardiac tamponade; anterograde propagation causes limb ischaemia and renal/mesenteric malperfusion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: How is aortic dissection classified by time from symptom onset?
options: Acute <7 days; subacute 8–30 days; chronic >30 days
Acute ≤14 days; subacute 15–90 days; chronic >90 days
Acute <30 days; subacute 31–180 days; chronic >180 days
Acute <48 hours; subacute 3–14 days; chronic >14 days
Acute ≤14 days; chronic >14 days, with no subacute phase
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Acute ≤14 days; subacute 15–90 days; chronic >90 days
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Time from symptom onset: acute ≤14 days, subacute 15–90 days, chronic >90 days (the first 24 hours is termed hyperacute). The subacute window matters because it influences the timing of intervention in Type B disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: Which classification matters clinically because it determines surgical vs medical management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Stanford
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: The Stanford classification is the clinically important one — it directly determines surgical vs medical management.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: A Stanford Type A dissection is defined how, and how is it managed?
options: Involves the ascending aorta — surgical emergency
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Involves the ascending aorta — surgical emergency
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Stanford Type A involves the ascending aorta (± arch/descending) and is a surgical emergency; Type B spares the ascending aorta and is managed medically if uncomplicated. Note that "distal to the left subclavian" is the narrower DeBakey III definition — Stanford B may still involve the arch.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: Which DeBakey types correspond to Stanford A?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: DeBakey I and II
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: DeBakey I (ascending + arch + beyond) and II (ascending only) = Stanford A; DeBakey III (descending only) = Stanford B.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: What is the most important modifiable risk factor for aortic dissection, and which surges are especially dangerous?
options: Hypertension — transient surges from cocaine use and heavy weightlifting
Hyperlipidaemia — post-prandial triglyceride surges after heavy fatty meals
Diabetes — autonomic catecholamine surges triggered by severe hypoglycaemia
Smoking — transient catecholamine and nicotine spikes with each cigarette
Obesity — repeated pressure surges provoked by episodes of heavy overeating
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Hypertension — transient surges from cocaine use and heavy weightlifting
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Hypertension is the most important modifiable risk factor; transient surges from cocaine use and heavy weightlifting are especially dangerous.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: How does a bicuspid aortic valve predispose to dissection?
options: Associated aortopathy — intrinsic media weakness independent of valve haemodynamics
Through turbulent transvalvular flow alone, mechanically eroding the ascending aortic wall
By directly causing systemic hypertension that raises wall stress on the ascending aorta
Through showering of valvular thrombus emboli into the coronary and aortic wall vessels
By accelerating atherosclerosis of the aortic wall only, without any medial weakness
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Associated aortopathy — intrinsic media weakness independent of valve haemodynamics
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: A bicuspid aortic valve carries an associated aortopathy with intrinsic media weakness, independent of valve haemodynamics.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: What is the cardinal symptom of aortic dissection, and how does it differ from MI?
options: Gradual crushing central chest pain that builds over minutes with exertion, exactly like myocardial infarction
Sharp pleuritic chest pain, worse on inspiration and relieved by sitting up and leaning forward
Sudden-onset, severe 'tearing' or 'ripping' chest pain, maximal at onset (unlike MI which builds)
Burning epigastric pain radiating upward after meals, eased somewhat by antacids and belching
Positional interscapular ache that worsens with movement and eases with rest and simple analgesia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Sudden-onset, severe 'tearing' or 'ripping' chest pain, maximal at onset (unlike MI which builds)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: The cardinal symptom is sudden-onset, severe tearing/ripping chest pain that is maximal at onset, unlike MI pain which builds.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: Where is the pain typically felt in Type A versus Type B dissection?
options: Type A → back; Type B → anterior chest
Type A → anterior chest; Type B → interscapular/back
Type A → neck; Type B → abdomen
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Type A → anterior chest; Type B → interscapular/back
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Type A causes anterior chest pain (ascending aorta); Type B causes interscapular/back pain (descending aorta).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: What causes a pulse deficit in aortic dissection?
options: The false lumen occluding a branch — absent or weak carotid/brachial/femoral pulse
Chronic atherosclerosis of the peripheral arteries causing gradual narrowing and weak pulses
Cardiac tamponade reducing stroke volume, producing weak and thready peripheral pulses
Aortic regurgitation causing a collapsing pulse from rapid diastolic runoff into the ventricle
Coronary ostium occlusion reducing cardiac output and thereby weakening all peripheral pulses
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: The false lumen occluding a branch — absent or weak carotid/brachial/femoral pulse
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: A pulse deficit results from the false lumen occluding a branch, giving an absent or weak carotid/brachial/femoral pulse.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: A >20 mmHg inter-arm BP difference in a chest pain patient is the classic discriminating sign of what, and what should be done?
options: MI — give thrombolysis without delay to restore coronary perfusion
Pericarditis — give high-dose NSAIDs with colchicine for symptom relief
PE — start therapeutic anticoagulation with low-molecular-weight heparin
Dissection with subclavian involvement — check both arms in every chest pain
Musculoskeletal chest wall pain — reassure the patient and discharge home
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Dissection with subclavian involvement — check both arms in every chest pain
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: A >20 mmHg inter-arm BP difference indicates subclavian involvement in dissection — the classic discriminating sign; check both arms in every chest pain. It is present in only a minority of dissections and also occurs in patients without one, so it raises suspicion but neither confirms nor excludes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: Why might a new aortic regurgitation murmur appear in aortic dissection?
options: Retrograde dissection to the aortic root → aortic regurgitation
Anterograde dissection extending down toward the iliac arteries
Coronary ostium occlusion by the dissection flap → acute ischaemia
Occlusion of the anterior spinal artery causing cord ischaemia
Renal artery involvement producing malperfusion and hypertension
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Retrograde dissection to the aortic root → aortic regurgitation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Retrograde dissection to the aortic root causes aortic regurgitation, producing a new early diastolic murmur.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: Hypotension and tachycardia in a dissection patient should be assumed to be which type until proven otherwise?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Type A
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Hypotension/tachycardia (from blood loss, cardiac tamponade or severe AR) indicates haemodynamic instability = Type A until proven otherwise.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: Which end-organ effect results from coronary ostium involvement in dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: MI
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Coronary ostium involvement causes MI; other malperfusion effects include stroke (carotid), paraplegia (spinal artery), limb ischaemia (iliac/femoral), AKI (renal) and mesenteric ischaemia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: Why must a suspected aortic dissection never be thrombolysed or anticoagulated?
options: Because a dissection almost always seals and resolves spontaneously, so intervention only adds needless bleeding risk
Because it has no haemodynamic effect at all, so anticoagulation is merely wasted rather than being harmful
Because thrombolysis dangerously raises the blood pressure and thereby accelerates propagation of the false lumen
Because it produces sharp pleuritic pain that anticoagulation and thrombolysis characteristically make far worse
Because dissection can cause MI via coronary involvement and mimics it — anticoagulation/thrombolysis is fatal
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Because dissection can cause MI via coronary involvement and mimics it — anticoagulation/thrombolysis is fatal
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Dissection can cause MI via coronary involvement and mimics ACS, but the key danger is that thrombolysis/anticoagulation causes catastrophic haemorrhage into the false lumen (rupture, tamponade, exsanguination) — rapidly fatal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: How does pericarditis differ from aortic dissection in its pain character?
options: Sudden tearing chest pain maximal at the very onset, radiating through to the interscapular region
Sharp positional chest pain, pleuritic, relieved by leaning forward, no tearing quality
Chest pain with a measurable inter-arm systolic blood pressure difference of more than 20 mmHg
Chest pain accompanied by an obvious pulse deficit in one carotid, brachial or femoral artery
Severe chest pain radiating downward to the groin as the process extends toward the iliac vessels
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Sharp positional chest pain, pleuritic, relieved by leaning forward, no tearing quality
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Pericarditis gives sharp positional, pleuritic chest pain relieved by leaning forward with no tearing quality, unlike dissection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: What is the safety rule regarding dissection and anticoagulation for suspected MI/PE?
options: Always anticoagulate immediately with heparin, since prompt clot prevention outweighs any small dissection risk in chest pain
Give aspirin and discharge the patient home, arranging routine outpatient follow-up imaging over the next several weeks
Thrombolyse straight away and simply observe, as reperfusion is the priority and dissection features can be reviewed later
Exclude dissection first — CT angiogram if any dissection features (tearing pain, inter-arm BP difference, pulse deficit)
Anticoagulate unless the resting ECG is entirely normal, treating a clean tracing as enough to exclude a dissection
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Exclude dissection first — CT angiogram if any dissection features (tearing pain, inter-arm BP difference, pulse deficit)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Exclude dissection before anticoagulating for suspected MI/PE — get a CT angiogram first if any dissection features are present (tearing pain, inter-arm BP difference, pulse deficit).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: What is the role of ECG in aortic dissection?
options: It is diagnostic of dissection, showing a characteristic pattern of diffuse ST depression across all precordial leads
Often normal or non-specific — used to exclude/identify MI; a normal ECG in severe chest pain raises dissection
