conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.answer: ICD (implantable cardioverter defibrillator) — secondary prevention post-VT/VF arrest
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.explanation: ICD is indicated for secondary prevention after a VT/VF cardiac arrest regardless of EF — an EF threshold applies only to sustained VT without syncope or arrest (NICE). Primary prevention: EF ≤35%, NYHA I–III, on optimal medical therapy. If also wide QRS with LBBB: CRT-D.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the significance of an elevated NT-proBNP in a patient with dyspnoea?
options: NT-proBNP is only useful in acute heart failure and has no role in the diagnosis, referral or monitoring of chronic heart failure at any level
A level below 500 ng/L effectively excludes any possibility of heart failure, whatever the clinical picture and whatever treatment the patient is on
An NT-proBNP above 50 ng/L is diagnostic of heart failure and warrants immediate initiation of drug treatment without any need for echocardiography
NT-proBNP 400–2000 ng/L supports referral for echo (within 6 weeks); >2000 ng/L warrants urgent (2-week) assessment — use to guide diagnosis and monitor treatment
NT-proBNP elevation is entirely non-specific, adds nothing useful to the assessment of suspected heart failure, and should not influence referral
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.answer: NT-proBNP 400–2000 ng/L supports referral for echo (within 6 weeks); >2000 ng/L warrants urgent (2-week) assessment — use to guide diagnosis and monitor treatment
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.explanation: NT-proBNP (or BNP) is the heart-failure biomarker. NICE: <400 ng/L in an untreated person makes HF less likely — it does NOT exclude it; 400–2000 ng/L → echo within 6 weeks; >2000 ng/L → urgent echo within 2 weeks. Obesity, African/African-Caribbean family background and treatment with diuretics, ACEi, ARB, beta-blockers or MRAs all lower the level, so if clinical suspicion persists discuss with a heart failure specialist (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.question: A 68-year-old with HFrEF (EF 30%) remains symptomatic on optimal four-pillar therapy. Bloods: Hb 131 g/L (normal), with iron studies showing iron deficiency. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: No action — he is not anaemic
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.answer: IV ferric carboxymaltose
explanation: IV ferric carboxymaltose — ferritin <100 µg/L defines iron deficiency in heart failure, and it is treated irrespective of anaemia because iron is required by skeletal and cardiac muscle independently of haemoglobin. It improves symptoms, quality of life and reduces HF hospitalisation.
Oral ferrous sulfate — ineffective in HF: chronic inflammation raises hepcidin, which blocks intestinal absorption and traps iron in macrophages.
No action as he is not anaemic — the commonest error; the indication is iron deficiency, not anaemia.
Blood transfusion — has no role with a normal haemoglobin and carries volume-overload risk in HF.
Erythropoiesis-stimulating agent — not indicated, and ESAs increase thromboembolic risk without improving outcomes in HF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.question: A 60-year-old with HFrEF has an ICD implanted for primary prevention. He holds an ordinary car licence and asks when he can drive. What is the correct advice?
options: Stop for 1 month and notify the DVLA
Stop for 6 months and notify the DVLA
Stop for 1 week; the DVLA need not be notified
No restriction; the DVLA need not be notified
He is permanently barred from driving any vehicle
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.answer: Stop for 1 month and notify the DVLA
explanation: Stop for 1 month and notify the DVLA — a Group 1 licence holder stops for 1 month after an ICD implanted for primary prevention, and the DVLA must be notified for every ICD.
6 months — this is the rule for an ICD implanted for secondary prevention (after VT/VF), or following any appropriate shock.
1 week without notifying — these are the rules for a simple pacemaker or CRT-P, not an ICD.
No restriction — incorrect; every ICD carries both an off-road period and a duty to notify.
Permanently barred from all driving — an ICD permanently bars Group 2 (HGV/PSV) only; Group 1 driving resumes after the relevant interval.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.question: A 78-year-old with HFrEF is on optimal four-pillar therapy but has had three admissions with decompensation in six months, is NYHA IV at rest and has lost weight. He has an ICD in situ. Which is the most appropriate addition to his care?
options: Withdraw all heart failure medication and refer to palliative care instead of continuing disease-modifying treatment
Involve palliative care alongside his current treatment, and discuss advance care planning including ICD deactivation
Defer any palliative care discussion until he is clearly in the last days of life
Increase his beta-blocker dose to improve symptom control and reduce further admissions
Refer for cardiac transplantation without further discussion of his goals of care
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.answer: Involve palliative care alongside his current treatment, and discuss advance care planning including ICD deactivation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.explanation: Palliative care in heart failure runs in parallel with disease-modifying treatment rather than replacing it, and this patient has three clear triggers: severe symptoms despite optimal therapy, repeated admissions and cardiac cachexia. Advanced heart failure has a prognosis worse than many cancers but is referred far less often. The conversation covers refractory breathlessness, what matters to the patient, ceilings of treatment and a DNACPR decision - and it must explicitly include ICD deactivation, since a device that goes on shocking a dying patient is an avoidable harm. Deferring until the last days of life is the commonest error, because the trajectory of gradual decline punctuated by crises means the opportunity is often missed.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.question: A 68-year-old woman has a shallow, exudative ulcer just above the medial malleolus. The surrounding skin is brown-stained and firm, with pitting oedema. Ankle pulses are present and the ABPI is 0.95. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.explanation: Gaiter-region site, shallow exudative ulcer, haemosiderin + lipodermatosclerosis and an ABPI >0.8 are classic venous disease. Arterial ulcers are distal, punched-out and pulseless with a low ABPI; neuropathic ulcers sit on plantar pressure points and are painless; Marjolin's shows a rolled edge; pyoderma has a violaceous undermined border.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.question: A 74-year-old smoker with a deep, punched-out ulcer on the lateral malleolus describes severe pain that is worse in bed at night and relieved by hanging the leg out of bed. The foot is cold and pulseless. Which diagnosis best fits?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.explanation: Distal, punched-out, painful ulcer with rest pain relieved by dependency on a cold, pulseless leg is arterial. The night pain eased by hanging the leg down is the hallmark of critical ischaemia. Venous ulcers ache and improve with elevation; neuropathic ulcers are painless; vasculitic ulcers have palpable purpura; sickle-cell ulcers occur in young patients with known haemoglobinopathy.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.question: A leg ulcer looks venous, but the ABPI measures 0.4. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Start a two-week course of oral antibiotics
Withhold compression and refer to vascular
Reassure and review in three months
Begin high-dose diuretics for the leg oedema
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.explanation: An ABPI of 0.4 is below 0.5 and indicates critical (limb-threatening) ischaemia: withhold all compression and refer urgently to vascular. (Between 0.5 and 0.8 full compression is still unsafe — only reduced compression under specialist supervision.) Antibiotics are only for clinical infection; diuretics do not treat the ulcer; delay risks limb loss.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.question: A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has a painless ulcer beneath the first metatarsal head, ringed by thick callus. The foot is warm with bounding pulses but he cannot feel a 10 g monofilament. What is the diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.explanation: A painless ulcer on a plantar pressure point with callus, a warm well-perfused foot and loss of protective sensation is a neuropathic (diabetic) ulcer. Arterial ulcers are painful and pulseless; venous ulcers sit in the gaiter area; a pressure ulcer overlies a bony prominence in an immobile patient; pyoderma has a violaceous undermined edge.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.question: A diabetic patient with a foot ulcer has an ABPI of 1.4. How should this be interpreted?
options: Normal arterial supply, compression is fully safe
Arterial disease is excluded with certainty
Vessels are calcified and the value is unreliable
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.explanation: An ABPI >1.3 indicates medial calcification (Mönckeberg), which makes vessels incompressible and the reading falsely high / unreliable — use toe pressures. It does NOT prove a healthy or disease-free circulation, and a high ABPI is not a marker of venous disease or critical ischaemia (which gives a low ABPI).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.question: A venous ulcer present for 15 years has recently stopped responding to compression and developed a raised, rolled, everted edge with heaped-up tissue. What is the most important next step?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.explanation: A chronic ulcer that will not heal and develops a rolled / everted edge is suspicious for a Marjolin's ulcer (SCC) and must be biopsied. More compression or antibiotics ignore the malignancy; immunosuppression treats pyoderma; offloading is for neuropathic ulcers.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.question: A 35-year-old with ulcerative colitis has a rapidly enlarging, very painful ulcer with a violaceous, undermined border. It grew larger after surgical debridement. What is the diagnosis and correct management?
options: Marjolin's ulcer — wide local surgical excision
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.explanation: Rapid growth, a violaceous undermined border, severe pain, pathergy (worsening after debridement) and the IBD association are classic pyoderma gangrenosum, treated with immunosuppression; surgery/debridement worsens it. The other options describe different ulcer types with different management.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.question: A patient presents with a new leg ulcer that looks venous. Before starting treatment, which single investigation is essential?
options: Punch biopsy of the ulcer edge
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.explanation: The ABPI must be measured before compression to exclude arterial disease. A swab is only for clinical infection; biopsy is reserved for atypical/non-healing ulcers; duplex assesses venous reflux but does not decide compression safety; X-ray is for suspected osteomyelitis.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.question: Which investigation best confirms the underlying venous incompetence responsible for a venous leg ulcer?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.explanation: Venous duplex ultrasound maps reflux and incompetence and guides intervention. ABPI screens the arterial supply; CT angiography assesses arteries; D-dimer is for acute VTE; invasive venous pressure studies are rarely needed in practice.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.question: An ulcer shows mixed venous and arterial features and the ABPI is 0.7. What is the safest management approach?
options: Full multilayer compression as for a venous ulcer
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.explanation: An ABPI of 0.5–0.8 indicates a mixed ulcer where full compression is unsafe but some support may help — use reduced compression under specialist supervision. Full compression risks ischaemic damage; amputation work-up is premature; immunosuppression and casting treat different ulcer types.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.question: A patient with a foot ulcer has rest pain, a cold pulseless foot and an ABPI of 0.3. What does this represent and what is required?
options: Critical limb ischaemia — urgent vascular referral
Uncomplicated venous disease — apply full compression
Cellulitis — a course of oral antibiotics
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.explanation: Rest pain, a cold pulseless foot and ABPI <0.5 define critical limb ischaemia — a limb-threatening emergency needing urgent vascular referral for revascularisation. Compression would be dangerous; offloading and antibiotics do not restore perfusion; this is arterial, not venous thrombosis.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.question: What is the mainstay of treatment for a confirmed venous leg ulcer with an ABPI of 0.9?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Ulcers.explanation: With arterial disease excluded (ABPI ≥0.8), multilayer compression bandaging is the mainstay of venous ulcer healing, alongside elevation and treating incompetence. Antibiotics are only for infection; bypass is for arterial disease; casting offloads neuropathic ulcers; steroids are for inflammatory ulcers such as pyoderma.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.question: A thin-walled vascular channel on H&E has a wide, irregular, collapsed lumen that is empty apart from a few lymphocytes and contains no red blood cells. It is most likely a:
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.explanation: An empty, thin-walled, red-cell-free channel with an irregular lumen is characteristic of a lymphatic. Blood vessels are typically filled with red cells.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.question: Which feature is characteristic of a lymphatic capillary but NOT a blood capillary?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.explanation: Lymphatic capillaries are blind-ended and possess anchoring filaments and a discontinuous/absent basement membrane, unlike blood capillaries.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.question: Anchoring filaments of lymphatic capillaries function to:
options: Contract the vessel to pump lymph
Pull the vessel open when interstitial pressure rises
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.explanation: Anchoring filaments tether endothelium to the ECM; when tissue swells they pull the overlapping endothelial flaps apart, increasing uptake precisely when interstitial fluid is high.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.question: The functional contractile unit of a collecting lymphatic vessel, lying between two valves, is called a:
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.explanation: A lymphangion is the segment between two valves; its intrinsic contraction is the main pump moving lymph forward.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.question: A milky, triglyceride-rich lymph is absorbed from the gut by which structure?
options: The central lacteal of the villus
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.explanation: Long-chain dietary fats are packaged as chylomicrons and absorbed into the central lacteal (a lymphatic capillary) of each villus, forming chyle.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.question: The thoracic duct returns lymph to the venous system at the:
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.explanation: The thoracic duct drains all but the right upper quadrant and empties at the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.question: Which immunohistochemical marker is most useful for specifically identifying lymphatic endothelium (e.g. to detect lymphovascular invasion)?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.explanation: D2-40 (podoplanin) is a specific lymphatic endothelial marker. CD31 stains both blood and lymphatic endothelium and CD34 favours blood vessels.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.question: A woman develops chronic arm swelling after mastectomy with axillary lymph-node clearance. This is best classified as:
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.explanation: Removal/disruption of lymph nodes and vessels causes secondary lymphoedema. Primary lymphoedema (e.g. Milroy disease) is congenital/heritable.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.question: Which statement about lymph propulsion is correct?
options: A central lymphatic heart pumps lymph
Lymph moves by arterial pressure alone
Lymph flow is driven by lymphangion contraction plus muscle and respiratory pumps, kept unidirectional by valves
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.explanation: There is no central pump; intrinsic lymphangion contraction plus the skeletal-muscle and respiratory pumps move lymph, with valves ensuring one-way flow.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.question: A chylothorax (milky pleural effusion) most directly indicates injury or obstruction of the:
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.explanation: The thoracic duct carries fat-rich chyle; its injury or obstruction leaks chyle into the pleural space, producing a chylothorax.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.question: Compared with a blood capillary, the lymphatic capillary has:
options: A continuous basement membrane and pericytes
Higher permeability with absent/discontinuous basement membrane
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.explanation: Lymphatic capillaries lack a continuous basement membrane and pericytes, making them far more permeable so proteins and whole cells can enter.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.question: Massive lower-limb and scrotal swelling (elephantiasis) due to lymphatic obstruction is classically caused by:
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.explanation: Filarial infection with Wuchereria bancrofti blocks lymphatics, causing gross secondary lymphoedema (elephantiasis) - the leading global cause.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.question: The overlapping endothelial cells of the initial lymphatic act as:
options: One-way primary valves admitting fluid and cells
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.explanation: The loosely overlapping endothelial flaps behave as one-way primary valves, opening inward to admit interstitial fluid, protein and cells, then closing to prevent escape.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.question: Sentinel lymph node biopsy in breast cancer exploits which biological principle?
options: Lymphatic (lymphovascular) spread of carcinoma to the first draining node
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.explanation: Carcinomas typically spread first via lymphatics to the first (sentinel) draining node; its status guides staging and further nodal surgery.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.question: Which cell/marker relationship is correct?
options: Prox1 is the master transcription factor of lymphatic endothelium
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.explanation: Prox1 is the master regulator specifying lymphatic endothelial identity. D2-40/LYVE-1 mark lymphatics; CD34 favours blood endothelium; CD31 stains both.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.question: Tender red streaks tracking up the forearm toward the axilla from an infected wound represent:
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.explanation: Infection spreading along lymphatic vessels causes lymphangitis - visible red streaks tracking toward the draining nodes.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.question: A cystic, fluid-filled swelling in the posterior neck of an infant, composed of dilated endothelial-lined lymphatic spaces, is a:
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.explanation: A cystic hygroma is a benign lymphatic malformation (lymphangioma) of dilated lymphatic channels, classically in the neck of infants.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.question: Roughly what fraction of the fluid filtered by blood capillaries is returned to the circulation by the lymphatics?
options: None - it is all reabsorbed by venules
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.explanation: Around 90% of filtrate is reabsorbed by the venular end of capillaries; the remaining ~10% (with escaped protein) is returned by the lymphatics - roughly 3 L/day.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.question: Which of the following normally contains valves and shows a beaded appearance?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.explanation: Collecting lymphatics have numerous closely spaced valves giving a beaded look; the initial lymphatic capillaries and lacteals rely on overlapping-flap primary valves.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.question: Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to:
options: An angiosarcoma (lymphangiosarcoma) arising in chronic lymphoedema
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.explanation: Stewart-Treves syndrome is a lymphangiosarcoma/angiosarcoma developing in a chronically lymphoedematous limb, classically after mastectomy with axillary clearance.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.question: An enlarged, hard left supraclavicular lymph node (Troisier sign) is a classic sign of:
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.explanation: Virchow's node (left supraclavicular) drains via the thoracic duct and is classically enlarged by metastatic gastric or other abdominal/GI/pelvic carcinoma — Troisier's sign.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.question: Medium-chain triglycerides are useful in chylothorax because these fats are absorbed:
options: Directly into villus blood capillaries and the portal vein
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lymphatic Ves.explanation: Short- and medium-chain fatty acids enter the villus blood capillaries and drain to the portal vein directly, bypassing the lacteals and thoracic duct — reducing chyle flow in chylothorax.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.question: A 64-year-old man presents with sudden, severe interscapular chest pain that was maximal at onset. BP is 178/96 mmHg in the right arm and 146/78 mmHg in the left. There is a new early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. What is the most appropriate definitive investigation?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.explanation: Tearing/interscapular pain maximal at onset, an inter-arm systolic BP difference >20 mmHg and a new aortic-regurgitation murmur (retrograde extension to the aortic root) point to aortic dissection. CT angiography of the aorta is the definitive investigation (TOE if too unstable to transfer). D-dimer/CTPA target PE; an exercise test is contraindicated in acute chest pain. Crucially, do NOT anticoagulate until dissection is excluded.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.question: A 58-year-old man has 45 minutes of crushing central chest pain. ECG shows 3 mm ST elevation in V1–V4. He can reach a primary-PCI centre within 90 minutes. What is the most appropriate immediate reperfusion strategy?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.explanation: Anterior STEMI — ST-segment elevation indicating acute total coronary occlusion. (LBBB with ongoing ischaemic symptoms is managed the same way, down the primary PCI pathway; Sgarbossa criteria help only where the picture is equivocal.) Primary PCI is first-line reperfusion when it can be delivered within 120 minutes of the time fibrinolysis could otherwise be given — here 90 minutes, so PCI. Fibrinolysis is the fallback only if timely PCI is unavailable. An exercise test is dangerous in acute STEMI.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.question: A 70-year-old with chest pain has an ECG showing ST depression and T-wave inversion in the lateral leads, and a raised troponin. There is no ST elevation. Which is the single best diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.explanation: Partial (non-occlusive) coronary thrombus causing myocardial necrosis gives a troponin rise with ST depression / T-wave inversion but no ST elevation = NSTEMI. Unstable angina has the same ECG picture but a NORMAL troponin. STEMI requires ST-segment elevation — or LBBB with ongoing ischaemic symptoms, which is managed down the same primary PCI pathway. This is the NSTEMI vs UA distinction from the ACS note.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.question: A 34-year-old presents with sharp retrosternal chest pain that is worse on lying flat and relieved by sitting forward, following a viral illness. A scratchy sound is heard at the left sternal edge. Which ECG finding is most characteristic?
options: ST elevation confined to contiguous leads with reciprocal ST depression
Widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation with PR depression
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.explanation: Positional pleuritic pain (worse supine, relieved leaning forward), a post-viral prodrome and a friction rub are classic acute pericarditis. Its hallmark ECG is widespread (not territorial) saddle ST elevation with PR depression. Territorial ST elevation with reciprocal change indicates STEMI; S1Q3T3 suggests PE.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.question: A 42-year-old woman has pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness 5 days after a long-haul flight. She is haemodynamically stable and her two-level PE Wells score is 3 (‘PE unlikely’). What is the most appropriate next investigation?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.explanation: With a Wells score in the ‘PE unlikely’ range, a D-dimer is the correct next step: if negative it excludes PE, if positive proceed to CTPA. A CTPA first-line is reserved for ‘PE likely’ (Wells >4). V/Q is used when CTPA is contraindicated (renal impairment, contrast allergy, pregnancy).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.question: A 55-year-old with a confirmed large PE has a systolic BP of 78 mmHg, is tachycardic and has signs of right-heart strain. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Observation with repeat CTPA in 24 hours
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.explanation: This is a massive (high-risk) PE — haemodynamic instability from obstructive shock. The management fork is: stable → anticoagulate; unstable → thrombolyse. A DOAC is appropriate for a stable PE, not one with shock. IVC filters are for when anticoagulation is contraindicated.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.question: A 25-year-old man becomes acutely breathless during central-line insertion. He is hypotensive with a deviated trachea, absent breath sounds and a hyper-resonant percussion note on the right. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Urgent portable chest X-ray, then chest drain
Intravenous fluids and reassess in 30 minutes
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.explanation: This is a tension pneumothorax — a clinical diagnosis (iatrogenic cause, tracheal deviation, hyper-resonance, absent breath sounds, shock). Treat immediately with decompression — do NOT wait for a CXR. Imaging first risks cardiac arrest. A chest drain is then placed definitively.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.question: Which single finding best distinguishes a pneumothorax from a pleural effusion on examination of the affected side?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.explanation: Both reduce breath sounds and expansion, but percussion separates them: hyper-resonant = pneumothorax (air), stony-dull = effusion (fluid). Bronchial breathing and increased fremitus indicate consolidation, not either of these.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.question: A 60-year-old man develops severe chest pain and subcutaneous emphysema after a bout of forceful vomiting following an alcohol binge. He is septic. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.explanation: Severe pain after forceful vomiting with surgical emphysema and sepsis is Boerhaave syndrome — spontaneous full-thickness oesophageal rupture (the oesophagus has no serosa, so contents leak into the mediastinum → mediastinitis). Mackler's triad = vomiting + chest pain + subcutaneous emphysema. It is frequently misdiagnosed as MI, PE or dissection.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.question: What is the commonest cause of oesophageal perforation overall?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.explanation: Iatrogenic perforation (~50%) — from OGD, especially with dilatation/stenting, plus TOE and NG-tube insertion — is the commonest cause overall, tending to occur at the anatomical narrowings. Boerhaave (spontaneous) accounts for ~15%.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.question: A 68-year-old, 3 days after an anterior MI, becomes hypotensive with a raised JVP and muffled heart sounds. There is a >15 mmHg fall in systolic BP on inspiration (pulsus paradoxus). What is the most appropriate immediate investigation?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.explanation: Beck's triad (hypotension, raised JVP, muffled sounds) plus pulsus paradoxus after MI indicates cardiac tamponade (e.g. free-wall rupture / haemorrhagic effusion). Echocardiography is the immediate investigation (effusion with diastolic right-heart collapse) and guides urgent pericardiocentesis.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.question: A 64-year-old with central chest pain also describes an episode of tearing pain radiating to the back. BP is 182/96 mmHg in the right arm and 150/80 mmHg in the left. What is the most appropriate immediate step?
options: Arrange CT aortography before giving any anticoagulation
Give aspirin, clopidogrel and treatment-dose LMWH now
Start a heparin infusion and repeat the troponin
Give GTN and admit for serial ECGs
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.explanation: The inter-arm systolic BP difference (>20 mmHg) and tearing/interscapular pain point to aortic dissection. Antiplatelets, anticoagulation or thrombolysis (B–D) can be fatal if it is a dissection, so imaging (CT aortography) must come first. GTN with serial ECGs (E) neither confirms nor excludes it. This is the anchoring trap — check both-arm BP and image before committing to the ACS pathway.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.question: A 48-year-old has troponin elevation during an episode of fast atrial fibrillation and severe sepsis, with no evidence of acute plaque rupture. Which is the single best classification?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.explanation: Under the 4th Universal Definition, a troponin rise from supply–demand mismatch (tachyarrhythmia, anaemia, hypotension, sepsis) without acute atherothrombosis is a Type 2 MI. Management targets the underlying cause (rate control, treat sepsis), not primary-PCI. Type 1 is acute plaque rupture/erosion with thrombus.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.question: A 55-year-old with exertional central chest tightness relieved by rest within minutes has a normal resting ECG and troponin. According to NICE, what is the most appropriate first-line investigation for stable chest pain of suspected cardiac origin?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.explanation: The stem describes stable angina. NICE recommends CT coronary angiography as the first-line investigation for stable chest pain of suspected coronary origin (it images anatomy/atheroma). The exercise ECG is no longer recommended for diagnosis; invasive angiography and functional imaging are second-line.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.question: An 80-year-old presents with exertional chest pain and an episode of exertional syncope. Examination reveals an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids and a slow-rising pulse. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.explanation: Exertional angina, syncope and dyspnoea with an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids and a slow-rising (plateau) pulse is the classic triad of severe aortic stenosis — a cardiac cause of chest pain that must not be missed.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.question: A 30-year-old has chest pain that is fully reproducible on palpation of the costochondral junctions; observations are normal. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Arrange urgent outpatient CT coronary angiography
Diagnose costochondritis and discharge without an ECG
Reassure and treat with oral NSAIDs alone
Record an ECG; tenderness does not exclude ACS
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.explanation: Reproducible chest-wall tenderness raises the probability of a musculoskeletal cause but does not exclude ACS or other serious pathology, so an ECG and clinical assessment come first. Discharging without an ECG or giving NSAIDs alone risks missing ACS; urgent CT coronary angiography and rheumatology referral are not the immediate step.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.question: A 68-year-old with COPD suddenly develops right-sided pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. Examination shows reduced expansion and a hyper-resonant right hemithorax. Which is the single most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.explanation: A pneumothorax occurring in a patient with underlying lung disease (COPD is the commonest) is a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax — these have worse outcomes and a lower threshold to drain/admit. Primary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs in tall, thin young people with NO lung disease.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.question: A 26-year-old man reports a 3-day history of a burning, band-like pain across the left chest in a single dermatome; today a vesicular rash has appeared over the same area. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.explanation: A dermatomal, burning pain that precedes a vesicular rash in the same distribution is herpes zoster (reactivation of varicella-zoster virus). The pain can predate the rash by days and mimic other causes of chest pain until the rash appears.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.question: A 78-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes presents with 2 hours of breathlessness, nausea and epigastric discomfort but no chest pain. ECG shows new lateral ST depression and troponin is elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.explanation: Diabetics, the elderly and women frequently have atypical or silent MI — breathless, nauseated or epigastric presentations without classic chest pain. Dynamic ischaemic ECG changes plus a troponin rise indicate NSTEMI. A normal pain story does not exclude ACS.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.question: A 60-year-old man has an inferior STEMI (ST elevation in II, III and aVF). He becomes profoundly hypotensive shortly after a dose of GTN. What is the most likely explanation?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.explanation: Inferior MIs (RCA territory) often involve the right ventricle. The RV is preload-dependent, so nitrates — which drop preload — can precipitate profound hypotension. Suspect RV infarction (confirm with right-sided lead V4R), give fluids and use nitrates cautiously.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.question: A 24-year-old has recurrent episodes of sharp left-sided chest pain with palpitations, perioral tingling and breathlessness during stressful situations. ECG, troponin and examination are normal. What is the most appropriate conclusion?
options: Chest pain in the young never needs investigation
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.explanation: Situational chest pain with hyperventilation and paraesthesiae suggests anxiety/panic — a common benign cause but a diagnosis of exclusion. Here ACS (normal ECG/troponin) and other serious causes have been considered. Absolute statements (E) are wrong; angina/PE are not supported by the picture.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.question: A 52-year-old smoker with hypertension describes burning retrosternal pain after meals, worse lying flat and partially relieved by antacids. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Record an ECG to exclude ACS first
Prescribe a proton-pump inhibitor and discharge without an ECG
Arrange urgent OGD as the first investigation
Reassure the patient that antacid relief confirms GORD
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chest Pain.explanation: Reflux-type features and antacid relief do not exclude ACS — cardiac and oesophageal pain overlap and this patient has cardiac risk factors. An ECG (± troponin) to exclude ACS comes first; antacid relief is not confirmatory (D). OGD, PPI and H. pylori therapy are not the immediate priority.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.question: A 38-year-old man has nodular thickening of both Achilles tendons and a corneal arcus. His father died of a myocardial infarction at 42. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.explanation: Tendon xanthomata plus premature arcus and a strong family history of early MI are near-diagnostic of familial hypercholesterolaemia. Arcus senilis is age-related; rheumatoid nodules and tophi are not lipid deposits.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.question: A 30-year-old with poorly controlled diabetes has crops of small yellow papules over the buttocks and elbows. His serum is lipaemic. What do these lesions indicate?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.explanation: Eruptive xanthomata with lipaemic serum indicate severe hypertriglyceridaemia (often >10 mmol/L), which also carries a risk of acute pancreatitis. Cholesterol-driven deposits are xanthelasma, arcus and tendon xanthomata.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.question: An 82-year-old has a white ring around the edge of both corneas and normal lipids. What is the appropriate interpretation?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.explanation: A corneal arcus in an elderly patient with normal lipids is benign arcus senilis, needing no action. Arcus under 45 (arcus juvenilis) would instead suggest pathological hyperlipidaemia.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.question: Which physical sign is most specific for familial hypercholesterolaemia?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.explanation: Tendon xanthomata (Achilles, knuckle extensors) are the most specific sign, being near-diagnostic of familial hypercholesterolaemia. Xanthelasma and arcus are less specific, and eruptive / palmar xanthomata point to triglyceride disorders.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.question: A patient with eruptive xanthomata and a triglyceride level of 40 mmol/L is at particular risk of which acute complication?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.explanation: Severe hypertriglyceridaemia (marked by eruptive xanthomata) is a recognised cause of acute pancreatitis, so urgent triglyceride lowering is needed. Cardiovascular risk is also raised, but pancreatitis is the acute danger here.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.question: Which set of blood tests best screens for secondary causes of dyslipidaemia?
options: TFTs, glucose/HbA1c, renal function and LFTs
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.explanation: Secondary dyslipidaemia is commonly caused by hypothyroidism, diabetes, nephrotic syndrome and cholestasis, so TFTs, glucose/HbA1c, renal function and LFTs are the appropriate screen. The other panels do not target these causes.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.question: Yellow lipid deposits confined to the palmar creases are most characteristic of which disorder?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.explanation: Palmar crease (striae) xanthomata are characteristic of remnant (type III) hyperlipidaemia (dysbetalipoproteinaemia). Tendon xanthomata point to familial hypercholesterolaemia instead.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.question: A patient is found to have xanthelasma. Which statement is correct?
options: It is a benign finding of no cardiovascular relevance
It can occur with normal lipids but still matters
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.explanation: Xanthelasma can occur with normal serum lipids yet still carries a modest independent cardiovascular risk, so risk assessment (and a lipid profile) is appropriate. It is neither diagnostic of FH nor irrelevant.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.question: What is the most appropriate first-line drug for a patient found to have hypercholesterolaemia and raised cardiovascular risk?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.explanation: A statin is first-line for hypercholesterolaemia and cardiovascular risk reduction. Fibrates target predominant hypertriglyceridaemia; ezetimibe and other agents are usually add-ons when statins are insufficient or not tolerated.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.question: After diagnosing a patient with familial hypercholesterolaemia, what key public-health step should follow?
options: Cascade screening of first- and second-degree relatives
Routine coronary angiography of all relatives
No further action once the index case is treated
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.explanation: Cascade screening of first- and second-degree relatives identifies other gene carriers so they can be treated early to prevent premature coronary disease. It is the defining follow-up step in familial hypercholesterolaemia.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.question: A 45-year-old with new hyperlipidaemia also reports fatigue, weight gain and cold intolerance, with a pulse of 52. Which secondary cause is most likely?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.explanation: Fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance and bradycardia point to hypothyroidism, a classic and treatable secondary cause of hyperlipidaemia. Treating the thyroid deficiency improves the lipid profile.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.question: Which of the following lipid stigmata reflects a triglyceride disorder rather than a cholesterol disorder?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.explanation: Eruptive xanthomata reflect high triglycerides. Tendon xanthomata, corneal arcus and xanthelasma reflect elevated cholesterol / LDL.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.question: A 40-year-old man is diagnosed with familial hypercholesterolaemia. How should his cardiovascular risk be managed?
options: Calculate QRISK and treat only if it exceeds 10%
No treatment until he develops symptoms
Treat as high-risk with atorvastatin, ignoring QRISK
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Stigmata.explanation: Familial hypercholesterolaemia confers lifelong high risk, so QRISK is not used; patients are treated as high-risk with a high-intensity statin (atorvastatin) aiming for a ≥50% LDL reduction, adding ezetimibe / PCSK9 inhibitors as needed. Fibrates target hypertriglyceridaemia, not FH.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.question: A 68-year-old, 6 days after a hip replacement, has a swollen, warm, tender left calf that is 4 cm larger than the right. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.explanation: Unilateral warm, tender calf swelling with a >3 cm difference and a strong provoking factor (recent surgery / immobility) is a DVT until excluded. Cellulitis is redder with a portal of entry; a ruptured Baker's cyst usually has known knee arthritis; CVI and lipoedema are chronic and bilateral / non-acute.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.question: Both a DVT and cellulitis can cause a hot, swollen leg. Which feature most favours cellulitis?
options: A portal of entry with spreading erythema
A palpable tender cord in a superficial vein
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.explanation: A portal of entry (tinea, ulcer) with spreading erythema and systemic upset favours cellulitis. A recent flight is a VTE risk factor (DVT); a palpable cord is superficial thrombophlebitis; Stemmer's sign indicates lymphoedema.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.question: A 74-year-old has bilateral pitting ankle oedema, a raised JVP, orthopnoea and bibasal crepitations. What is the most likely cause?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.explanation: Bilateral pitting oedema with a raised JVP, orthopnoea and basal crepitations indicates heart failure. Nephrotic and hepatic oedema do not raise the JVP; lymphoedema is non-pitting; DVT is unilateral.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.question: A 30-year-old has bilateral leg and periorbital oedema, frothy urine, and a serum albumin of 18 g/L. What is the diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.explanation: Oedema with periorbital swelling, frothy (proteinuric) urine and a low albumin is nephrotic syndrome (heavy urinary protein loss → low oncotic pressure). Heart failure raises the JVP; CVI has skin changes; hypothyroid oedema is non-pitting; cellulitis is unilateral and red.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.question: A 55-year-old woman has painless, non-pitting swelling of one leg including the toes, and you cannot pinch the skin at the base of the second toe. She had pelvic radiotherapy. What is the diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.explanation: Non-pitting swelling that includes the foot / toes with a positive Stemmer's sign after pelvic radiotherapy is secondary lymphoedema. Lipoedema spares the feet and is bilateral; DVT is acute and tender; CVI pits and shows skin changes; heart failure is bilateral with a raised JVP.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.question: A 62-year-old develops bilateral ankle oedema two weeks after starting a new antihypertensive. Examination and bloods are otherwise normal. What is the most likely cause?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.explanation: Bilateral ankle oedema shortly after starting an antihypertensive, with normal bloods and a normal JVP, is typical calcium-channel blocker (amlodipine) oedema — from precapillary arteriolar dilatation. It resolves on stopping / switching the drug.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.question: A 60-year-old with knee osteoarthritis feels a sudden pop and pain behind the knee, then rapid calf swelling and bruising around the ankle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.explanation: Sudden posterior knee pain and calf swelling with ankle bruising in a patient with knee OA is a ruptured Baker's cyst (pseudothrombophlebitis). It mimics a DVT, which must still be excluded, but the mechanism and crescent bruise point to the cyst.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.question: A patient has a swollen leg and a two-level Wells score in the 'DVT unlikely' range. What is the most appropriate next test?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.explanation: In the 'DVT unlikely' category a D-dimer is done first: if negative it excludes DVT, if positive proceed to compression Doppler ultrasound. A scan first-line is for the 'DVT likely' group; venography and echo are not first-line.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.question: A 28-year-old at 34 weeks' gestation has rapid leg and facial swelling, a BP of 158/104 and proteinuria. What is the diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.explanation: New hypertension and proteinuria after 20 weeks with rapid oedema is pre-eclampsia, not benign physiological swelling. It is dangerous to mother and fetus and needs urgent obstetric assessment.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.question: A 58-year-old has bilateral non-pitting, doughy leg swelling with tiredness, cold intolerance, weight gain and a slow pulse. What is the most likely cause?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.explanation: Non-pitting, doughy swelling with fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain and bradycardia is myxoedema from hypothyroidism. CVI pits and shows venous skin changes; lymphoedema gives a positive Stemmer's sign; nephrotic and cardiac oedema pit.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.question: A 55-year-old with alcohol excess has bilateral pitting leg oedema, ascites, jaundice and spider naevi. What is the mechanism of the oedema?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.explanation: Cirrhosis reduces albumin synthesis; the resulting low oncotic pressure (with portal hypertension / sodium retention) causes pitting oedema and ascites. The stigmata of chronic liver disease point to the cause; it is not a raised-JVP cardiac picture.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.question: A patient presents with a hot, swollen, tender left calf. What is the single most important immediate priority?
options: Elevate the leg and review in a week
Start empirical oral antibiotics for cellulitis
Assess DVT probability and exclude a DVT
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Swollen Leg.explanation: The priority in an acute unilateral hot, swollen, tender leg is to assess DVT probability (Wells) and exclude a DVT because of the PE risk. Empirical antibiotics, diuretics or compression without excluding DVT can delay a dangerous diagnosis or (compression) be unsafe.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: A 66-year-old smoker has cramping right calf pain after walking ~200 m that settles within 2 minutes of standing still. Foot pulses are absent and the ABPI is 0.6. What is the diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: A fixed-distance calf cramp relieved by standing still, with absent pulses and an ABPI of 0.6, is vascular intermittent claudication. Neurogenic claudication has normal pulses and is relieved by flexion; OA pain is joint-based; venous claudication is bursting with prior DVT; compartment syndrome affects young athletes with normal pulses.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: A 60-year-old man reports buttock and thigh pain on walking, erectile dysfunction, and absent femoral pulses. Which diagnosis best fits?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: Buttock/thigh claudication + erectile dysfunction + absent femoral pulses is the triad of Leriche syndrome (aortoiliac occlusion). Femoropopliteal disease gives calf claudication with present femorals; the others do not produce this pattern with absent femorals.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: A 70-year-old has leg heaviness on walking that also comes on when standing and is relieved by sitting or leaning forward on a trolley; foot pulses are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: Symptoms on standing and walking, relieved by lumbar flexion (sitting / leaning forward) with normal pulses, indicate neurogenic claudication from spinal stenosis. Vascular causes give absent pulses and relief only on stopping; venous claudication follows DVT with bursting pain.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: Which single feature best distinguishes neurogenic from vascular claudication?
options: Relief by sitting or leaning forward
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: Relief by lumbar flexion (sitting / leaning forward), rather than by merely stopping, is the hallmark of neurogenic claudication; the distance is also variable and the pulses normal. A fixed distance, calf site, relief on stopping and absent pulses all point to vascular disease.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: A diabetic patient with claudication-type pain has an ABPI of 1.4. How should this be interpreted?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: An ABPI >1.3 reflects medial calcification (common in diabetes / CKD) making vessels incompressible and the value falsely high / unreliable — it does not exclude PAD, so use toe pressures or duplex. Critical and acute ischaemia give low ABPIs.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: A 65-year-old with stable intermittent claudication (ABPI 0.7) has no rest pain or tissue loss. What is the most appropriate first-line management?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: Stable claudication is managed first with a supervised exercise programme and risk-factor modification (smoking cessation, statin, antiplatelet, BP / glucose control). Revascularisation is for lifestyle-limiting or conservative-failed disease; anticoagulation and amputation are not indicated here.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: A patient with known claudication now has foot pain at rest that wakes him at night and eases when he hangs the foot out of bed; ABPI is 0.3. What does this indicate?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: Rest / night pain relieved by dependency with an ABPI of 0.3 is critical limb ischaemia — a limb-threatening emergency needing urgent vascular referral for revascularisation. The other options do not give a critically low ABPI with dependency-relieved rest pain.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: A patient describes calf pain on walking that is relieved by rest. Which is the most appropriate first investigation?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: The ankle-brachial pressure index is the first-line bedside test — cheap, quick, and it confirms and grades arterial disease. Duplex and CT/MR angiography map disease before intervention; MRI spine and joint X-rays are for neurogenic or OA causes.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: A 55-year-old with a previous extensive iliofemoral DVT has bursting leg pain on walking, relieved slowly by elevation, with chronic swelling; foot pulses are present. What type of claudication is this?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: Bursting pain after prior DVT / outflow obstruction, with swelling and slow relief on elevation and present pulses, is venous claudication. Arterial claudication has absent pulses and quick relief on stopping; the others do not fit a post-thrombotic swollen limb.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: A 68-year-old has right groin pain that is worst on the first steps after rest and after activity, with reduced hip rotation and crepitus; foot pulses are normal. What is the most likely cause?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: Groin pain worst on the first steps, with reduced hip rotation, crepitus and normal pulses, is hip osteoarthritis. Aortoiliac claudication gives buttock/thigh pain with absent femorals; trochanteric bursitis causes lateral hip tenderness; a hernia gives a lump, not activity-related joint pain.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: A 34-year-old man who smokes heavily has painful ischaemia of the toes and fingertips with distal claudication; proximal pulses and vessels are normal. What is the diagnosis and its key treatment?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: Distal digit ischaemia in a young heavy smoker with normal proximal vessels is Buerger's disease (thromboangiitis obliterans); the one essential, disease-modifying treatment is complete smoking cessation. The other pairings describe different conditions.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: A patient with intermittent claudication asks what will most reduce his risk of dying. What is the most important intervention?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: Claudication signals systemic atherosclerosis, so the greatest mortality reduction comes from secondary prevention — smoking cessation, a statin and an antiplatelet. Exercise and angioplasty improve the leg symptoms but do not cut cardiovascular death as much; stockings and vitamin E do not.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: A 72-year-old smoker is woken each night by pain in the toes of the right foot, relieved by hanging the foot out of bed. The foot is cold with absent pulses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: Forefoot pain at night relieved by dependency, with a cold, pulseless foot, is ischaemic rest pain from critical limb ischaemia. Neuropathy and restless legs leave the foot warm and pulses intact; cramps give a muscle knot relieved by stretch; radicular pain is dermatomal and positional to the spine.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: A 68-year-old with critical limb ischaemia has an ABPI of 1.4 despite a cold, pulseless foot. What best explains this discrepancy?
options: Medial calcification of incompressible ankle vessels
A reassuring sign that arterial inflow is preserved
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: In diabetes and renal disease, medial calcification makes the ankle arteries incompressible, so the cuff cannot occlude them and the ABPI is falsely high (>1.3). It does not exclude ischaemia — use toe-brachial pressures or duplex.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: A 60-year-old diabetic describes burning, tingling pain in both feet at night in a stocking distribution. The feet are warm with palpable pulses and reduced monofilament sensation. What is the diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: Symmetrical burning stocking-distribution pain with warm feet, intact pulses and reduced monofilament is diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Critical ischaemia gives a cold, pulseless foot; the other options do not fit the sensory pattern.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: A 45-year-old feels an irresistible urge to move her legs each evening, with a crawling sensation relieved by walking about. Examination is normal. What single investigation is most useful?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: The picture is restless legs syndrome, and iron deficiency is a common, treatable driver, so ferritin / iron studies are the key test (replace iron if low). ABPI and duplex address vascular disease, which is not suggested by a normal exam.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: A 34-year-old male heavy smoker with distal digital ischaemia undergoes angiography showing abrupt small-vessel occlusions with ‘corkscrew’ collaterals and normal proximal arteries. What is the diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: Corkscrew collaterals with abrupt distal small/medium-vessel occlusion and normal proximal arteries in a young heavy smoker are characteristic of Buerger’s disease (thromboangiitis obliterans); management centres on complete smoking cessation.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: An 80-year-old is woken by sudden painful tightening of the calf that resolves when she stretches the muscle. Pulses are normal and the foot is warm. What is the most likely cause?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: A sudden painful muscle contraction relieved by stretching, with a warm, well-perfused foot, is a benign nocturnal leg cramp. Ischaemic rest pain gives a cold pulseless foot with dependent relief, not a muscle knot eased by stretch.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: Which single bedside feature most reliably separates ischaemic rest pain from its neuropathic and benign mimics?
options: The exact time of night the pain occurs
The state of the foot pulses and perfusion
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: The foot pulses and perfusion are decisive: ischaemic rest pain has a cold, pulseless foot, whereas neuropathy, cramps and restless legs leave a warm foot with intact pulses. Age, timing and diabetes are supportive but not discriminating on their own.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: A patient has forefoot rest pain for three weeks and a small necrotic ulcer over the first toe, with an ankle pressure of 40 mmHg. How should this be managed?
options: Review in the community clinic in 6 weeks
Start a neuropathic analgesic and reassure
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: Rest pain >2 weeks with tissue loss and an ankle pressure <50 mmHg is chronic limb-threatening ischaemia — an urgent vascular referral for revascularisation to avoid amputation. Delay, neuropathic analgesia or compression would risk the limb.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: Why is ischaemic rest pain characteristically worse at night and relieved by dangling the leg?
options: Flat loses gravity-assisted inflow; dependency restores it
Cold ambient temperature at night causes vasodilatation
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: When lying flat the foot loses the gravitational boost to arterial inflow, so a critically perfused foot tips into pain; hanging it down (dependency) restores perfusion and eases the pain. This is why patients sleep with the leg out of bed or in a chair.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: A 58-year-old reports shooting pain from the buttock down the back of the leg, worse when bending forward and coughing, with normal foot pulses. What is the most likely cause?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: Dermatomal shooting pain provoked by spinal movements / coughing, with normal pulses, is lumbar radiculopathy (sciatica) from nerve-root compression. Vascular rest pain is in the forefoot and depends on limb position, not spinal position.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: On examination of a patient with suspected critical limb ischaemia, the foot goes pale when elevated and dusky red when hung down. What is this sign called and what does it indicate?
options: Dependent rubor + elevation pallor; severe ischaemia
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: Elevation pallor with dependent rubor (a positive Buerger's test) indicates severe arterial insufficiency — poor inflow cannot overcome gravity on elevation, and maximal reactive vasodilatation reddens the dependent foot. The other signs relate to venous / lymphatic disease.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: A diabetic patient has painful burning feet at night with intact pulses. Which treatment is most appropriate for the pain?
options: Therapeutic anticoagulation with a heparin infusion
A neuropathic agent such as amitriptyline or gabapentin
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: Warm feet with intact pulses point to painful diabetic neuropathy, treated with neuropathic agents (amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin) and tighter glycaemic control. Revascularisation and anticoagulation address vascular disease, which is not the problem here.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: A 74-year-old with atrial fibrillation develops a sudden, severely painful, cold, white right leg over minutes. The left leg pulses are all normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Critical limb ischaemia from chronic PAD
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: Sudden onset in a patient with AF and a normal contralateral leg is an embolic acute limb ischaemia (usually a cardiac clot). Thrombotic ischaemia comes on over hours-days on a background of claudication with bilateral disease; DVT gives a swollen warm leg.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: A 66-year-old smoker with longstanding claudication develops a painful, cold left leg over two days. Pulses are absent in both legs. What is the most likely mechanism?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: A gradual deterioration on a background of claudication with bilaterally absent pulses points to in-situ thrombosis of an already diseased artery, not a fresh cardiac embolus onto a healthy tree. This distinction changes management from embolectomy to angiography-guided revascularisation.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: Which pair of the 6 Ps, if present, indicates an immediately threatened limb?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: Paraesthesia and paralysis are the late Ps: sensory loss beyond the toes and motor weakness mean the nerve and muscle are failing, so the limb is immediately threatened and needs revascularisation within hours. The other Ps appear earlier and do not by themselves imply a threatened limb.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: A patient has an acutely ischaemic leg with fixed, non-blanching mottling and hard, tender, paralysed calf muscles. What does this indicate?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: Fixed mottling that does not blanch with woody, paralysed muscle is Rutherford III — irreversible ischaemia. The limb is not salvageable and needs amputation; attempting reperfusion risks fatal reperfusion injury (hyperkalaemia, rhabdomyolysis).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: A patient is diagnosed with acute limb ischaemia. Before any imaging, what is the single most important immediate drug treatment?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: IV unfractionated heparin is given immediately to limit clot propagation while arranging urgent vascular referral and imaging. Thrombolysis is a planned revascularisation option decided with vascular surgery, not the first bedside step; antibiotics and diuretics have no role.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: A 70-year-old has a cold, pulseless right leg. The contralateral leg has strong palpable pulses. Which single feature most strongly suggests an embolic rather than thrombotic cause?
options: Absent pulses in the contralateral leg
Normal pulses in the contralateral leg
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: Normal pulses in the other leg imply a healthy vascular tree, so the occlusion is most likely a fresh embolus onto an otherwise normal vessel. Claudication, contralateral absent pulses, bruits and a gradual onset all indicate underlying disease and favour in-situ thrombosis.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: A 55-year-old presents with a blue, tensely swollen, painful left leg. It is not pale, and the foot is warm with a Doppler arterial signal present. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: A blue, tensely swollen leg that is not pale, with arterial signals present, is phlegmasia cerulea dolens — a massive iliofemoral DVT obstructing venous outflow. Arterial ischaemia makes the leg pale and pulseless, not swollen and blue.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: Three days after femoral angiography, a patient develops painful blue toes and livedo reticularis, but the foot pulses remain palpable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: Blue toes with livedo but preserved pulses after an arterial procedure is cholesterol atheroembolism (trash foot) — showers of cholesterol crystals occlude the digital vessels while larger arteries stay patent. Large-vessel ischaemia would abolish the pulses.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: Six hours after successful embolectomy for acute limb ischaemia, the leg becomes tensely swollen with severe pain on passive stretch of the foot, though pulses are present. What complication should you suspect?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: Pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch and a tense compartment after reperfusion indicate compartment syndrome, which needs urgent fasciotomy. Distal pulses are often preserved early, so a present pulse does not exclude it.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: A 68-year-old presents with a cold, pulseless left leg, tearing interscapular pain and a 30 mmHg difference in blood pressure between the arms. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: A cold, pulseless leg with tearing chest / back pain and an inter-arm BP difference is aortic dissection extending into the iliac vessels. It must be confirmed with a CT aortogram before anticoagulation, since heparin would be dangerous.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: In a patient with a threatened but viable acutely ischaemic limb, which investigation best guides the choice of revascularisation?
options: CT / catheter angiography of the limb
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: CT or catheter angiography maps the level and extent of the occlusion and the distal run-off, guiding embolectomy versus angioplasty / thrombolysis / bypass. Venous duplex and D-dimer address DVT; ABPI and plain films do not plan arterial revascularisation.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.question: Immediately after revascularising a prolonged ischaemic limb, the patient develops a peaked-T-wave arrhythmia and dark urine. What is the mechanism?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Leg Pain.explanation: Restoring flow washes out potassium, myoglobin and acid from dead muscle → hyperkalaemia (peaked T waves / arrhythmia) and rhabdomyolysis (dark, myoglobinuric urine) risking AKI. It is managed with U&E / ECG / CK monitoring, treatment of hyperkalaemia and consideration of fasciotomy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: Acute pericarditis is the start of a spectrum. What is the correct progression?
options: Acute pericarditis → cardiac tamponade first → then a slowly accumulating effusion
Acute pericarditis → constrictive scarring → then a large pericardial effusion forms
Effusion forms first → then acute pericarditis develops → progressing to constriction
Acute pericarditis → effusion → tamponade, and separately → constrictive pericarditis
Tamponade → a resolving effusion → then late-onset acute fibrinous pericarditis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Acute pericarditis → effusion → tamponade, and separately → constrictive pericarditis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: Acute pericarditis can progress to an effusion and then tamponade, and separately may lead to constrictive pericarditis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: What is the commonest INFECTIVE cause of acute pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Viral (e.g. Coxsackievirus B)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: Viral infection (Coxsackievirus B, enteroviruses, EBV, CMV) is the commonest infective cause; idiopathic (presumed viral) is the largest single group overall.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: Which infective cause of pericarditis should be suspected with any exudative effusion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Tuberculosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: TB should be suspected with any exudative pericardial effusion and is also the leading cause of constrictive pericarditis worldwide.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: A patient develops fibrinous pericarditis from direct irritation 2 days after an MI. What is this, and how does it differ from Dressler's?
options: Dressler's syndrome; an autoimmune reaction that typically occurs early, within the first 2–3 days after an MI
Constrictive pericarditis; a fibrotic late complication months after MI, distinct from Dressler's autoimmune type
Early post-MI pericarditis (1–3 days, direct irritation); Dressler's is late (weeks–months, autoimmune)
Uraemic pericarditis; driven by renal failure and retained toxins, entirely unrelated to MI or the post-infarct period
Both are the same entity; early post-MI pericarditis and Dressler's share one autoimmune mechanism and the same timing
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Early post-MI pericarditis (1–3 days, direct irritation); Dressler's is late (weeks–months, autoimmune)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: Early post-MI pericarditis (1–3 days) is fibrinous, from direct irritation; Dressler's syndrome is a late (weeks–months) autoimmune pericarditis with fever and pleurisy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: Which of the following is a recognised systemic/inflammatory cause of pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Uraemia (renal failure)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: Systemic causes include SLE, RA and other connective tissue diseases, uraemia (pericardial rub in renal failure), hypothyroidism, and malignancy (lung, breast).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: What is the defining symptom of acute pericarditis and its character?
options: Crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw, relieved by rest
Sharp, pleuritic, retrosternal chest pain worsened by inspiration and movement
Burning epigastric pain relieved by antacids
Dull constant pain unaffected by position
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Sharp, pleuritic, retrosternal chest pain worsened by inspiration and movement
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: The defining symptom is sharp, pleuritic, retrosternal chest pain worsened by deep inspiration and movement.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: Which positional feature of pericarditic chest pain is key in distinguishing it from ACS?
options: Relieved by sitting/leaning forward and worse lying flat
Worse on sitting or leaning forward, and eased by lying flat
Relieved by lying flat and made worse by leaning forward
Completely unaffected by posture or body position changes
Worse only on exertion and unrelated to body posture
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Relieved by sitting/leaning forward and worse lying flat
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: Pericarditic pain is relieved by leaning forward (lifting the inflamed pericardium off the diaphragm) and worse lying flat — a key feature distinguishing it from ACS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: What is the cardinal clinical sign of acute pericarditis, and how is it best heard?
options: A mid-diastolic rumbling murmur — low-pitched, best heard at the cardiac apex with the patient rolled into the left lateral position
A continuous machinery murmur — loudest beneath the left clavicle in systole and diastole, best heard sitting the patient forward
A pansystolic blowing murmur — high-pitched at the apex, radiating to the axilla and best heard in the left lateral position
An ejection systolic murmur — crescendo–decrescendo at the right sternal edge, radiating to the carotids and best heard sitting forward
A pericardial friction rub — scratchy/high-pitched at the left sternal edge, best heard leaning forward in end-expiration
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: A pericardial friction rub — scratchy/high-pitched at the left sternal edge, best heard leaning forward in end-expiration
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: The cardinal sign is a scratchy, high-pitched pericardial friction rub at the left sternal edge, best heard leaning forward in end-expiration; it may be triphasic.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: Why might a pericardial friction rub disappear as the illness progresses?
options: The pericardial inflammation has fully resolved and the layers no longer rub together
A large effusion develops, and the fluid separates the two inflamed layers
The patient is now lying flat, a position which silences the friction rub entirely
The heart rate has slowed, and the rub is only generated at faster heart rates
The rub becomes inaudible at faster heart rates and returns once bradycardia sets in
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: A large effusion develops, and the fluid separates the two inflamed layers
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: The rub is transient — it disappears once a large effusion develops, because the accumulating fluid separates the two inflamed pericardial layers.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: What are the four diagnostic criteria for acute pericarditis, and how many are required?
options: Chest pain, troponin rise, fever, friction rub — any 1
Friction rub, raised CRP, effusion, fever — all 4
Chest pain, friction rub, ECG changes, pericardial effusion — any ≥2
ECG changes and troponin rise — both required
Chest pain and effusion only — both required
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Chest pain, friction rub, ECG changes, pericardial effusion — any ≥2
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: Diagnosis requires ≥2 of 4: characteristic chest pain, pericardial friction rub, ECG changes (saddle ST + PR depression), and a pericardial effusion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: Why is TTE (echo) recommended in all suspected cases of acute pericarditis?
options: To measure the left ventricular ejection fraction only, with no other purpose
To exclude a pulmonary embolism as the true source of the chest pain
To confirm the underlying viral cause by visualising the causative organism
To replace the ECG entirely as the single first-line diagnostic test
To exclude a pericardial effusion and assess for myocardial involvement
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: To exclude a pericardial effusion and assess for myocardial involvement
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: TTE is recommended in all suspected cases to exclude an effusion and assess for associated myocardial involvement (myopericarditis).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: Which pair of ECG changes are the two hallmarks of acute pericarditis?
options: Convex ST elevation and reciprocal depression
Saddle-shaped (concave) ST elevation and PR depression
Pathological Q waves and T inversion
Delta waves and a short PR
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Saddle-shaped (concave) ST elevation and PR depression
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: The two hallmark ECG changes are widespread saddle-shaped (concave) ST elevation and PR depression (the latter highly specific).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: Why is PR depression an important ECG finding in acute pericarditis?
options: It indicates an acute STEMI, reflecting transmural ischaemia; reciprocal ST depression appears in the opposing leads as confirmation
It signifies hyperkalaemia, reflecting a raised serum potassium; peaked T waves and a widened QRS complex typically accompany it
It indicates first-degree AV block, reflecting delayed conduction through the AV node, with the PR interval prolonged beyond 200 ms
It is a benign normal variant with no clinical significance, seen commonly in healthy young athletes and requiring no investigation
It is highly specific for pericarditis, reflecting atrial epicardial involvement; PR elevation appears in aVR (mirror image)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: It is highly specific for pericarditis, reflecting atrial epicardial involvement; PR elevation appears in aVR (mirror image)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: PR depression is highly specific for pericarditis (atrial epicardial involvement), with PR elevation in aVR as the mirror image; it may precede the ST changes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: How do the ST shape and distribution typically differ between pericarditis and STEMI?
options: Pericarditis: convex and territorial; STEMI: concave and widespread
Both show convex (tombstone) ST elevation in a territorial distribution
Both show concave (saddle) ST elevation across most of the leads
Pericarditis: territorial ST elevation; STEMI: widespread ST elevation
Pericarditis: concave (saddle), widespread; STEMI: convex (tombstone), territorial
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Pericarditis: concave (saddle), widespread; STEMI: convex (tombstone), territorial
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: Pericarditis shows concave (saddle/smiley) ST elevation across most leads; STEMI shows convex (tombstone) ST elevation in a territorial distribution.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: Regarding reciprocal changes and Q waves, how does pericarditis differ from STEMI?
options: Pericarditis: reciprocal changes and pathological Q waves both present; STEMI: neither reciprocal changes nor Q waves ever develop
Pericarditis: no reciprocal changes and no Q waves; STEMI: reciprocal changes present and pathological Q waves develop
Both pericarditis and STEMI reliably develop pathological Q waves along with matching reciprocal ST-segment changes on the ECG
Both pericarditis and STEMI characteristically show reciprocal ST-segment changes in the opposing leads on the surface ECG
Pericarditis develops pathological Q waves and reciprocal changes, whereas STEMI does neither and shows only diffuse ST elevation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Pericarditis: no reciprocal changes and no Q waves; STEMI: reciprocal changes present and pathological Q waves develop
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: Pericarditis lacks reciprocal changes and Q waves — the exception is aVR (± V1), which shows ST depression and PR elevation; STEMI shows reciprocal ST depression and develops pathological Q waves.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: How does troponin typically behave in pericarditis versus STEMI?
options: Markedly and steeply raised in pericarditis, yet remaining completely normal throughout an acute STEMI
Always entirely normal in both pericarditis and STEMI, so troponin cannot help distinguish the two
Unreliable as a discriminator — may be raised in pericarditis, and often normal at presentation in STEMI
