Always markedly and equally raised in both pericarditis and STEMI, giving identical troponin curves
Raised only in pericarditis and never in STEMI, where the troponin level stays firmly normal
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Unreliable as a discriminator — may be raised in pericarditis, and often normal at presentation in STEMI
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: In pericarditis troponin may be mildly raised (a myopericarditis component); in STEMI it is significantly raised.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: What is the first-line drug treatment for acute pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: An NSAID (e.g. ibuprofen) plus colchicine
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: First-line is an NSAID at attack dose until symptoms settle and CRP normalises (typically 1–2 weeks) then tapered, plus colchicine continued for 3 months to reduce recurrence.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: What is the main benefit of adding colchicine to NSAID therapy in pericarditis?
options: It provides markedly faster relief of the chest pain
It fully replaces the need for exercise restriction
It directly treats the underlying viral infection
It reliably prevents progression to cardiac tamponade
It reduces (roughly halves) the risk of recurrence
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: It reduces (roughly halves) the risk of recurrence
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: Colchicine added to an NSAID roughly halves the recurrence risk and is continued for 3 months.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: Why are non-aspirin NSAIDs avoided in pericarditis occurring in the early post-MI period?
options: They cause dangerous hyperkalaemia in the early post-MI period, precipitating fatal arrhythmias
They worsen the pericardial effusion and hasten progression to tamponade in the early post-MI phase
Non-aspirin NSAIDs impair infarct healing; aspirin at anti-inflammatory doses is used instead
They cause high-grade AV block by suppressing conduction through the AV node soon after an MI
They lose all anti-inflammatory effect in the post-MI setting and so provide no symptom benefit
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Non-aspirin NSAIDs impair infarct healing; aspirin at anti-inflammatory doses is used instead
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: Non-aspirin NSAIDs are avoided in early post-MI pericarditis because they impair infarct healing (rupture risk). Aspirin — itself an NSAID — is used at anti-inflammatory doses instead (e.g. for Dressler's syndrome).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: Why are corticosteroids used only with caution in acute pericarditis?
options: They cause immediate cardiac tamponade by rapidly expanding any existing pericardial effusion
They mask the pericardial friction rub and so obscure the key diagnostic sign on auscultation
They are entirely ineffective at reducing pericardial inflammation and provide no symptom relief
They directly cause myocardial free-wall rupture, especially in the early post-infarct period
They increase the recurrence risk, so are reserved for autoimmune causes or refractory disease
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: They increase the recurrence risk, so are reserved for autoimmune causes or refractory disease
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: Corticosteroids increase the recurrence risk, so they are reserved for an autoimmune cause (SLE/RA), refractory disease, or where NSAIDs/colchicine are contraindicated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: Which of the following is a high-risk feature warranting admission in acute pericarditis?
options: Mild pleuritic chest pain that is promptly relieved by sitting and leaning forward
A completely normal ECG with no ST elevation or PR-segment depression at all
A single self-limiting episode of viral pericarditis in an otherwise well young patient
Fever >38°C, a large effusion or tamponade, or elevated troponin (myopericarditis)
A rapid and complete symptomatic response to standard NSAID therapy within days
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Fever >38°C, a large effusion or tamponade, or elevated troponin (myopericarditis)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: High-risk features include fever >38°C, large effusion/tamponade, elevated troponin, immunosuppression/anticoagulation, and subacute onset or NSAID failure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: What is the most common complication of acute pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Pericardial effusion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: Pericardial effusion is the most common complication; others include constriction (chronic, especially TB), recurrence (~30% without colchicine, roughly halved by colchicine), and myopericarditis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: What is a pericardial effusion, and where does it sit in the disease spectrum?
options: Accumulation of fluid in the pericardial sac; the bridge between acute pericarditis and tamponade
Fibrosis and rigid scarring of the pericardium; the irreversible end stage following chronic constriction
Inflammation confined to the myocardium itself; a distinct entity entirely unrelated to any pericardial disease
A congenital defect or absence of the pericardium present from birth, unrelated to acute pericarditis
A primary tumour arising within the pericardium, sitting outside the acute-pericarditis disease spectrum
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Accumulation of fluid in the pericardial sac; the bridge between acute pericarditis and tamponade
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: A pericardial effusion is fluid accumulation in the pericardial sac, resulting from any cause of pericarditis, and forms the bridge between acute pericarditis and tamponade.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: On examination of a large pericardial effusion, what is Ewart's sign?
options: Dullness to percussion below the left scapula (from left lung base compression)
A loud pansystolic murmur at the cardiac apex radiating into the left axilla
A large-volume collapsing pulse felt at the wrist with each cardiac cycle
A raised JVP showing a prominent and sharply steep y descent on inspection
A loud and palpable pulmonary component of the second heart sound (P2)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Dullness to percussion below the left scapula (from left lung base compression)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: Ewart's sign is dullness to percussion below the left scapula in large effusions, due to compression of the left lung base.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: What is electrical alternans on the ECG, and what does it signify?
options: Alternating PR-interval length beat-to-beat as conduction fluctuates through the AV node; signifies high-grade AV block
QRS axis/amplitude alternating beat-to-beat as the heart swings in fluid; specific for a large effusion/tamponade
Alternating T-wave amplitude and morphology from beat to beat during exertion; signifies subendocardial myocardial ischaemia
A tall bifid (M-shaped) P wave alternating in height across beats; signifies left atrial enlargement or overload
Alternating left and right bundle branch block morphology on successive beats; signifies advanced His-Purkinje conduction disease
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: QRS axis/amplitude alternating beat-to-beat as the heart swings in fluid; specific for a large effusion/tamponade
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: Electrical alternans is the beat-to-beat alternation of the QRS as the heart swings within the fluid, and is specific for a large pericardial effusion (tamponade until proven otherwise).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: What is the classic CXR finding in a pericardial effusion, and the volume threshold?
options: Bilateral blunting of costophrenic angles from pleural effusions, seen at essentially any volume
A bilateral perihilar bat-wing pattern of alveolar pulmonary oedema, at essentially any volume
A globular (water-bottle) heart when the effusion is >250 mL, with clear lung fields
A widened mediastinal silhouette once the effusion exceeds 100 mL, with congested lung fields
A completely normal cardiac silhouette regardless of the effusion volume present
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: A globular (water-bottle) heart when the effusion is >250 mL, with clear lung fields
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: A globular (water-bottle) cardiac silhouette appears when the effusion exceeds ~250 mL; clear lung fields help distinguish it from heart failure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: What is the gold-standard investigation for a pericardial effusion?
options: Echo (showing an echo-free space around the heart)
CXR (showing an enlarged globular cardiac silhouette)
ECG (showing low-voltage complexes and sinus tachycardia)
CT coronary angiography of the epicardial vessels
Cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement imaging
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Echo (showing an echo-free space around the heart)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: Echo is the gold standard, showing an echo-free space around the heart, quantifying the size and guiding pericardiocentesis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: Why does the rate of fluid accumulation determine the haemodynamic impact of an effusion?
options: Slow accumulation lets the pericardium stretch to hold 1–2 L, whereas rapid accumulation of even 150–200 mL can cause tamponade
Faster accumulation is always better tolerated, as the pericardium rapidly stretches to accommodate the extra fluid without raising pressure
The rate of accumulation has no effect on tamponade risk; only the underlying cause of the effusion determines haemodynamic compromise
Only the absolute volume matters, so any effusion below roughly 500 mL is safe regardless of how quickly the fluid collects in the sac
Slow accumulation always causes tamponade, because the gradually stretched pericardium eventually loses all of its reserve compliance
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Slow accumulation lets the pericardium stretch to hold 1–2 L, whereas rapid accumulation of even 150–200 mL can cause tamponade
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: A slowly accumulating effusion allows the pericardium to stretch and tolerate 1–2 L, but rapid accumulation of even 150–200 mL can precipitate tamponade.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: What is the mainstay of management for most pericardial effusions?
options: Immediate surgical pericardiectomy in every patient
Lifelong high-dose loop diuretics to offload the heart
Treating the underlying cause — most resolve with this alone
Routine pericardiocentesis with drainage for all patients
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Treating the underlying cause — most resolve with this alone
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: Most effusions resolve once the underlying cause is treated; pericardiocentesis is reserved for symptomatic or large effusions.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: What is the underlying mechanism of cardiac tamponade?
options: A slowly fibrosing, thickened pericardium that progressively stiffens over years and prevents adequate diastolic filling of the ventricles, gradually reducing stroke volume
Chronically elevated pulmonary arterial pressure that overloads and dilates the right ventricle, eventually impairing its filling, contraction and forward output
Infarction of the right ventricular free wall causing acute RV failure, raised filling pressures and a fall in left-sided preload, output and systemic blood pressure
Acute traumatic rupture of an aortic valve cusp producing torrential regurgitation, volume overload of the left ventricle and rapid cardiogenic pulmonary oedema
Fluid accumulating faster than the pericardium can stretch → rising pressure compresses all four chambers → impaired filling → reduced output → obstructive shock
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Fluid accumulating faster than the pericardium can stretch → rising pressure compresses all four chambers → impaired filling → reduced output → obstructive shock
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: In tamponade, fluid accumulates faster than the pericardium can stretch, raising intrapericardial pressure that compresses all four chambers, impairing diastolic filling and causing obstructive shock.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: What is Beck's triad of cardiac tamponade?
options: Hypotension, bounding pulse, loud heart sounds
Hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: Beck's triad is hypotension (low output), raised JVP (impaired venous return), and muffled heart sounds (insulating fluid).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: What is pulsus paradoxus, and what is the threshold in tamponade?
options: A rise in systolic BP on inspiration of any amount
A pulse that varies with posture only
An exaggerated inspiratory fall in systolic BP >10 mmHg
A fall in diastolic BP >20 mmHg on expiration
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: An exaggerated inspiratory fall in systolic BP >10 mmHg
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: Pulsus paradoxus is an exaggerated inspiratory fall in systolic BP >10 mmHg; on inspiration, increased RV volume pushes the septum into the LV, impairing LV output.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: Why is the JVP y descent absent in cardiac tamponade?
options: The tricuspid valve is stenosed, so blood cannot empty from the right atrium during early diastole
The pericardium is calcified and rigid, abruptly halting ventricular filling in mid-diastole
The right atrium is fibrillating, so there is no coordinated atrial emptying in early diastole
The heart volume is fixed by surrounding fluid, so venous inflow cannot increase in diastole
The JVP is simply not visible because the raised venous pressure pushes the column above the jaw
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: The heart volume is fixed by surrounding fluid, so venous inflow cannot increase in diastole
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: In tamponade the surrounding fluid fixes the heart volume, so venous inflow cannot increase in early diastole — abolishing the y descent.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: Which bedside sign is ABSENT in tamponade and helps distinguish it from constrictive pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Kussmaul's sign
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: Kussmaul's sign is absent in tamponade but present in constrictive pericarditis, making it a key discriminator.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: What is the most sensitive echo sign of cardiac tamponade?
options: A septal bounce on the parasternal view
A dilated left atrium with normal filling
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Right atrial collapse (late diastole/early systole)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: Right atrial collapse is the earliest and most sensitive echo sign — the RA is the lowest-pressure chamber. Right ventricular diastolic collapse appears later but is more specific. Echo also guides pericardiocentesis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: What is the definitive treatment of cardiac tamponade?
options: IV fluid resuscitation with close haemodynamic observation
High-dose intravenous loop diuretics to reduce preload
Intravenous thrombolysis to dissolve the effusion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Urgent echo-guided pericardiocentesis (needle aspiration)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: The definitive treatment is urgent echo-guided pericardiocentesis; even draining small volumes produces immediate haemodynamic improvement.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: What is the underlying pathology of constrictive pericarditis, and the leading cause worldwide?
options: Chronic fluid accumulation in the pericardial space; viral pericarditis
A rigid fibrotic pericardium preventing diastolic filling; TB worldwide
Diffuse myocardial fibrosis stiffening the ventricle; idiopathic
Fatty infiltration and thickening of the pericardium; obesity
Congenital partial or complete absence of the pericardium; inherited
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: A rigid fibrotic pericardium preventing diastolic filling; TB worldwide
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: Constrictive pericarditis is a rigid fibrotic pericardium that prevents diastolic filling; TB is the most important cause worldwide.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: What is Kussmaul's sign, and why does it occur in constrictive pericarditis?
options: A fall in the JVP on inspiration, due to a stiff right ventricle that cannot accommodate the extra venous return during inspiration
A paradoxical rise in systemic blood pressure on expiration, produced by the rigid pericardium impairing ventricular filling
A paradoxical rise in JVP on inspiration, because the rigid pericardium cannot accommodate the increased venous return
A completely absent JVP a wave, reflecting loss of effective atrial contraction against the rigid, non-compliant pericardium
A double apical impulse on palpation, caused by the ventricle striking the rigid, thickened pericardium during diastolic filling
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: A paradoxical rise in JVP on inspiration, because the rigid pericardium cannot accommodate the increased venous return
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: Kussmaul's sign is a paradoxical rise in JVP on inspiration; the rigid pericardium cannot accommodate the inspiratory increase in venous return.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: What is a pericardial knock, and what causes it?
options: A mid-systolic click from a prolapsing, myxomatous mitral valve leaflet bulging back into the left atrium
A high-pitched early-diastolic opening snap produced by a stenosed, thickened mitral valve leaflet opening
A loud early S3 from abrupt cessation of ventricular filling as the ventricle hits the rigid pericardium
A scratchy three-component friction rub of acute pericarditis from inflamed pericardial surfaces rubbing together
A low-pitched fourth heart sound from atrial contraction against a stiff, poorly compliant left ventricle
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: A loud early S3 from abrupt cessation of ventricular filling as the ventricle hits the rigid pericardium
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: A pericardial knock is a loud early S3 caused by the sudden halt of ventricular filling as the ventricle meets the rigid pericardium.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: How does the JVP waveform differ between constriction and tamponade?
options: Constriction: y descent absent; tamponade: prominent x and y
Constriction: absent a wave; tamponade: giant a wave
Both have an absent y descent
Both have prominent x and y descents
Constriction: prominent x AND y descents; tamponade: y descent absent
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Constriction: prominent x AND y descents; tamponade: y descent absent
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: Constriction shows prominent x and y descents, whereas tamponade has an absent y descent — the y descent is the key contrast.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: Regarding pulsus paradoxus and Kussmaul's sign, how do tamponade and constriction differ?
options: Tamponade: both pulsus paradoxus and Kussmaul's sign absent; constriction: both pulsus paradoxus and Kussmaul's sign present
Tamponade: pulsus paradoxus present, Kussmaul's absent; constriction: pulsus paradoxus usually absent, Kussmaul's present
Both conditions: pulsus paradoxus and Kussmaul's sign are consistently present, making them useless for distinguishing the two
Tamponade: Kussmaul's sign present, pulsus paradoxus absent; constriction: pulsus paradoxus present, Kussmaul's sign absent
Both conditions: pulsus paradoxus is present while Kussmaul's sign is characteristically absent in each of them
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Tamponade: pulsus paradoxus present, Kussmaul's absent; constriction: pulsus paradoxus usually absent, Kussmaul's present
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: Tamponade has pulsus paradoxus (present) and Kussmaul's (absent); constriction has pulsus paradoxus (usually absent) and Kussmaul's (present).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: Comparing CXR findings, how do tamponade and constriction differ?
options: Tamponade: normal-sized heart with pericardial calcification; constriction: enlarged globular heart without any calcification
Tamponade: a heavily calcified rigid pericardium; constriction: an enlarged globular water-bottle cardiac silhouette
Both conditions: enlarged globular cardiac silhouettes with visible pericardial calcification on the plain chest film
Both conditions: normal cardiac silhouette size with no pericardial calcification seen on the plain chest radiograph
Tamponade: enlarged (globular) heart, no calcification; constriction: normal heart size, calcification may be present
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Tamponade: enlarged (globular) heart, no calcification; constriction: normal heart size, calcification may be present
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: Tamponade gives an enlarged globular heart without calcification; constriction shows a normal heart size with possible pericardial calcification.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: What is the 'square root sign' on cardiac catheterisation, and in which condition is it seen?
options: A rapid systolic pressure upstroke on the ventricular tracing; aortic stenosis
A giant regurgitant v wave on the atrial pressure trace; mitral regurgitation
A dip-plateau pattern in ventricular pressure; constrictive pericarditis
A slow, blunted y descent on the atrial pressure trace; cardiac tamponade
Equalisation of all four cardiac chamber pressures; acute myocarditis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: A dip-plateau pattern in ventricular pressure; constrictive pericarditis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: The square root sign is a dip-plateau pattern in the ventricular pressure trace, seen in constrictive pericarditis when imaging is inconclusive.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: What is the only definitive treatment for constrictive pericarditis, and a key risk?
options: Needle pericardiocentesis and drainage; risk of fluid re-accumulation
Long-term therapeutic anticoagulation; risk of major bleeding
Lifelong high-dose loop diuretics; risk of acute kidney injury
Orthotopic heart transplantation; risk of graft rejection
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Pericardiectomy (surgical excision); a high-risk operation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: Pericardiectomy is the only definitive treatment, reserved for severe or progressive disease. It is a high-risk operation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: Why can constrictive pericarditis not be distinguished clinically from restrictive cardiomyopathy?
options: They produce identical murmurs on auscultation
Restrictive cardiomyopathy never causes a raised JVP
Constrictive pericarditis produces no physical signs at all
They share the same haemodynamic profile, so imaging is essential
They occur in entirely different age groups only
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: They share the same haemodynamic profile, so imaging is essential
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: Constriction and restrictive cardiomyopathy share the same haemodynamic profile, so imaging (CT/MRI showing pericardial thickening/calcification) is essential to distinguish them — and only constriction has a surgical fix.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: Exam pearl: what does pericardial calcification on CXR/CT indicate, and what is the surgical caveat?
options: Cardiac tamponade; urgent needle pericardiocentesis drains the fluid and completely cures the condition
Constriction; pericardiectomy cures constriction, but there is no surgical fix for restrictive cardiomyopathy
A large pericardial effusion; simple catheter drainage of the fluid completely and permanently cures it
Acute viral pericarditis; a course of high-dose NSAIDs with colchicine fully cures the calcified pericardium
Acute myocarditis; there is no effective treatment and the calcified myocardium cannot be surgically removed
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Constriction; pericardiectomy cures constriction, but there is no surgical fix for restrictive cardiomyopathy
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.explanation: Pericardial calcification points to constriction, which pericardiectomy can cure; restrictive cardiomyopathy (the haemodynamic mimic) has no surgical fix.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: A 61-year-old is hypotensive (BP 82/60) with a raised JVP, muffled heart sounds and pulsus paradoxus. Bedside echo shows a large pericardial effusion with diastolic right atrial collapse. The cardiology team is 15 minutes away. Which is the most appropriate immediate supportive measure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: A cautious IV fluid bolus
explanation: A cautious IV fluid bolus — raising preload helps maintain ventricular filling against the elevated intrapericardial pressure and buys time until pericardiocentesis.
IV furosemide — the classic and dangerous error. The raised JVP mimics heart failure, but diuresis strips the preload the compressed heart depends on and can precipitate arrest.
Sublingual GTN — a vasodilator; it reduces preload for the same reason and is contraindicated here.

Intubation and mechanical ventilation — positive-pressure ventilation further reduces venous return, and induction in untreated tamponade is a recognised cause of peri-induction arrest. Drain first where possible.
Sitting fully upright — reduces venous return; the patient should be kept flat.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: A patient develops cardiac tamponade following penetrating chest trauma. Needle pericardiocentesis produces transient improvement, but hypotension recurs within minutes. What is the definitive management?
options: Repeat needle pericardiocentesis every time symptoms recur
Insertion of a pericardial drain and observation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Emergency surgical thoracotomy
explanation: Emergency surgical thoracotomy — in traumatic tamponade the pericardium is filling with clotting blood from an ongoing injury. Needle drainage is only a temporising bridge; the bleeding source must be controlled surgically.
Repeat needle aspiration — clotted blood drains poorly and the source keeps bleeding, so this only delays definitive control.
Loop diuretics — reduce preload in a patient dependent on filling pressure; contraindicated.
Pericardial drain and observation — inadequate for ongoing haemorrhage, and blood clot readily blocks the drain.
Thrombolysis — would worsen bleeding catastrophically in a trauma patient.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.question: A 34-year-old has had three episodes of idiopathic pericarditis in 18 months despite adherent NSAID and colchicine therapy. Inflammatory markers are raised during attacks. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.answer: Refer to cardiology
explanation: Refer to cardiology — recurrent, colchicine-resistant pericarditis needs specialist assessment. Second-line agents beyond NSAIDs and colchicine are specialist decisions and are not licensed for pericarditis in the UK.

Prolonged high-dose prednisolone — corticosteroids control symptoms but are themselves associated with more recurrence, so they are reserved for an autoimmune cause, refractory disease, or where first-line agents are contraindicated.
Switching NSAID — unlikely to alter the natural history; the problem is recurrent inflammation, not the choice of NSAID.
Pericardiectomy — a last resort, and it is the definitive treatment for constrictive pericarditis rather than recurrent pericarditis.
Stopping colchicine — the opposite of what is needed; colchicine roughly halves recurrence and should be continued 6–12 months in recurrent disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A 68-year-old woman with AF has a CHA₂DS₂-VASc score of 3. What is the most appropriate management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 = oral anticoagulation required, and NICE applies that same threshold to both sexes; a score of 1 in a man is a ‘consider’ decision. DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran) are first-line over warfarin for non-valvular AF due to better safety profile, fixed dosing, and no routine INR monitoring.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A 55-year-old presents with new-onset AF for 30 hours. He is haemodynamically stable with HR 135bpm. What is the appropriate management?
options: Rate control only, because atrial fibrillation lasting beyond 24 hours can no longer be cardioverted safely
Immediate DC cardioversion with no anticoagulation cover, as the embolic stroke risk here is negligible
Rhythm control is appropriate — anticoagulate with heparin and cardiovert
Rate control for three weeks first, then arrange a purely elective outpatient cardioversion later
Digoxin alone for rapid rate control, then cardiovert once the ventricular response has settled
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: AF <48h in a haemodynamically stable patient → rhythm control is appropriate. Anticoagulate with heparin immediately before cardioversion (no need for 3 weeks prior anticoagulation if <48h), then continue anticoagulation for minimum 4 weeks after cardioversion. DC cardioversion or flecainide.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A patient with AF and structural heart disease needs pharmacological cardioversion. Which drug is most appropriate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Amiodarone is the drug of choice for pharmacological cardioversion or rhythm control in AF with structural heart disease (IHD, HF, LV dysfunction). Flecainide is contraindicated in structural heart disease (proarrhythmic risk). Digoxin is for rate control only. Adenosine treats SVT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: What is the ventricular rate in typical 2:1 atrial flutter?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Atrial rate in flutter = ~300bpm. With 2:1 AV block, every other atrial impulse conducts → ventricular rate = 300/2 = 150bpm. 3:1 block → 100bpm. Sawtooth flutter waves (F waves) are diagnostic on ECG.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A patient's warfarin INR is 4.8. They are asymptomatic with no bleeding. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Temporarily withhold warfarin, recheck INR in 1–2 days
Continue warfarin at same dose, recheck in 1 week
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: INR 4.8 with no bleeding → temporarily withhold 1–2 doses of warfarin and recheck INR in 1–2 days. Target INR 2–3. Vitamin K is used if INR >5 or bleeding present. Emergency FFP/PCC for major bleeding with supratherapeutic INR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: Which of the following is NOT an indication for immediate DC cardioversion in AF?
options: New-onset AF for 72 hours in a stable patient
Acute chest pain with rapid AF
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Immediate DC cardioversion is for haemodynamically unstable AF (shock, acute LVF, severe chest pain) or WPW+AF (risk of VF via accessory pathway). Stable AF of 72h duration does not need emergency cardioversion — rate control and elective cardioversion after 3 weeks anticoagulation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: What is the main risk of using flecainide in atrial flutter?
options: Marked QT prolongation precipitating torsades de pointes
1:1 AV conduction causing rapid ventricular response
Profound sinus bradycardia with a junctional escape rhythm
Acute renal failure with dangerous accumulation of the drug
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Flecainide slows the atrial rate in flutter from ~300 to ~200bpm. This can paradoxically make it easier for the AV node to conduct every impulse (1:1), causing a dangerous ventricular rate of 200bpm. Avoid flecainide in flutter — use DC cardioversion or amiodarone instead.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A 42-year-old athlete with no structural heart disease has paroxysmal AF and wants to self-manage episodes. What is the most appropriate approach?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Pill-in-the-pocket with flecainide is appropriate for young patients with infrequent, well-tolerated paroxysmal AF and no structural heart disease. They take flecainide at onset of symptoms. Catheter ablation is considered if pharmacological rhythm control fails. Long-term amiodarone has significant side effects and is not first-line.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: Amiodarone causes thyroid dysfunction. What monitoring is required?
options: TFTs only if symptoms of thyroid disease develop
No monitoring needed unless symptoms develop
TFTs before treatment, then every 6 months
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Amiodarone contains iodine and can cause BOTH hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism. TFTs must be checked before starting, then every 6 months during treatment. Also monitor: LFTs, CXR (pulmonary fibrosis), eye exam (corneal deposits), peripheral nerve exam.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A 78-year-old woman with AF and CHA₂DS₂-VASc score of 2 starts warfarin. Her target INR should be:
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Target INR for AF anticoagulation with warfarin is 2–3 (not higher — increased bleeding risk). INR 2.5–3.5 is for mechanical heart valves. An INR <2 is subtherapeutic for AF stroke prevention.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: Which of the following is a direct thrombin inhibitor DOAC used in AF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Dabigatran is the only direct thrombin inhibitor (DTI) used in AF. Rivaroxaban, apixaban, and edoxaban are all direct factor Xa inhibitors. Dabigatran is reversed by idarucizumab; Xa inhibitors by andexanet alfa.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: What is the preferred pharmacological treatment for rate control in AF with concurrent heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Beta-blockers (bisoprolol, carvedilol) are first-line for rate control in AF with HF. Rate-limiting CCBs (diltiazem, verapamil) are contraindicated in HFrEF — negative inotropic effect worsens heart failure. Digoxin can be added as adjunct but is not first-line alone.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A 60-year-old with AF and a CHA₂DS₂-VASc of 0 (male, no risk factors). What is the recommended anticoagulation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: CHA₂DS₂-VASc = 0 in a male → no antithrombotic therapy recommended. The annual stroke risk is very low (<1%) and the bleeding risk from anticoagulation outweighs the benefit. Aspirin is no longer recommended for AF stroke prevention (ineffective and still causes bleeding).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: What distinguishes AF from atrial flutter on a rhythm strip?
options: AF produces the sawtooth flutter waves, whereas atrial flutter shows chaotic fibrillatory f waves
AF gives a perfectly regular ventricular rate, whereas atrial flutter is the irregularly irregular rhythm
AF is irregularly irregular; flutter has regular F waves and typically a regular ventricular rate
Both lack P waves, but AF is distinguished by a characteristically broad QRS complex on the ECG
AF has a much slower atrial rate than flutter, usually well under 200 beats per minute
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: AF: irregularly irregular rhythm, fine fibrillation (f) waves, no true P waves. Atrial flutter: regular sawtooth F waves at ~300bpm, regular ventricular rate (e.g. 150bpm in 2:1 block). Both can have narrow QRS unless aberrant conduction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A patient who had electrical cardioversion 6 weeks ago for AF now develops palpitations. ECG shows AF again. What is the appropriate rhythm control drug given they have no structural heart disease?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Flecainide is first-line for rhythm control (prevention of AF recurrence) in patients WITHOUT structural heart disease. Amiodarone is used if structural heart disease is present. Digoxin and verapamil are for rate control, not rhythm control.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: In AF with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, which drug is absolutely contraindicated?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: In WPW with AF, all AV-nodal blocking drugs are absolutely contraindicated — verapamil (and diltiazem), beta-blockers, digoxin and adenosine. Blocking the AV node forces conduction down the accessory pathway at the full atrial rate, risking VF. Treatment is synchronised DC cardioversion (if unstable) or a class Ia/Ic agent such as procainamide or flecainide (amiodarone with caution).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: How long should anticoagulation be continued AFTER successful cardioversion of AF?
options: No anticoagulation needed if sinus rhythm restored
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Anticoagulation must continue for a MINIMUM of 4 weeks after cardioversion regardless of CHA₂DS₂-VASc score — atrial stunning occurs after cardioversion and thromboembolism risk persists for 4 weeks even if sinus rhythm is maintained. Thereafter, anticoagulation continues based on CHA₂DS₂-VASc.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: What is the AV node ablation ('ablate and pace') strategy used for?
options: Patients with HF and AF awaiting catheter ablation
Elderly patients with poor rate control despite optimal medical therapy
Patients with paroxysmal AF refractory to one antiarrhythmic drug
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Ablate and pace = AV node ablation to create complete heart block + permanent pacemaker implantation. Used for elderly patients with permanent AF and poor ventricular rate control despite optimal drug therapy. Provides definitive rate control but makes patient pacemaker-dependent.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A 75-year-old woman with AF has a CHA₂DS₂-VASc score of 5. She has a history of falls. What is the most appropriate approach to anticoagulation?
options: Withhold anticoagulation due to fall risk
Start anticoagulation — fall risk does not outweigh stroke risk
Give aspirin instead as safer option
Refer for catheter ablation before deciding
Refer for left atrial appendage occlusion device instead
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Falls alone are not a contraindication to anticoagulation in AF. The stroke risk at CHA₂DS₂-VASc 5 (~6.7%/year) far outweighs the annual bleeding risk from falls (very high number of falls needed to equal the harm from a major stroke). Assess a validated bleeding score for bleeding risk; optimise fall prevention.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: Which of the following correctly describes how to calculate CHA₂DS₂-VASc?
options: Stroke/TIA scores 1 point; age ≥75 scores 1 point
All factors score 1 point each except female sex which scores 0
Age ≥75 scores 2 points; Stroke/TIA scores 2 points; female sex scores 1 point
Heart failure and diabetes each score 2 points
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: CHA₂DS₂-VASc: C(1), H(1), A₂ age≥75(2), D(1), S₂ stroke/TIA(2), V vascular disease(1), A age 65-74(1), Sc female sex(1). Stroke/TIA and age ≥75 are the highest-weighted factors at 2 points each. Maximum score is 9.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A patient with AF is on digoxin for rate control. Which finding would suggest digoxin toxicity?
options: A resting heart rate of around 90 beats per minute
Bilateral pitting ankle oedema up to the knees
Peripheral oedema with several kilograms of weight gain
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Digoxin toxicity: nausea, vomiting, anorexia, visual disturbances (yellow-green halos, blurred vision — classic), bradycardia, heart block, arrhythmias. Hypokalaemia increases toxicity risk. Digoxin has a narrow therapeutic index — monitor drug levels and renal function.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: After starting amiodarone for AF, a patient develops exertional breathlessness and a dry cough 6 months later. What is the most likely cause?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Amiodarone-induced pulmonary toxicity (pneumonitis/fibrosis) presents with dyspnoea, dry cough, reduced transfer factor, and bilateral infiltrates on CXR/CT. It can occur months to years after starting. Diagnosis: CXR, CT chest, PFTs. Treat: stop amiodarone, consider steroids.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A 65-year-old man with paroxysmal AF has CHA₂DS₂-VASc of 1 (hypertension only). What is the recommended management?
options: Consider oral anticoagulation — discuss risks and benefits
Anticoagulation only if additional risk factor develops
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: CHA₂DS₂-VASc = 1 in a male: anticoagulation may be considered (1-2% annual stroke risk). Discuss with patient. Score 0 in male = no treatment. Score ≥2 in male = anticoagulate. Female sex adds 1 point but is not independently sufficient to mandate treatment (need ≥2 in females for definite indication).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A patient with AF has a CHA₂DS₂-VASc of 4. a validated bleeding score is 5 (high bleeding risk). What is the correct approach?
options: Withhold anticoagulation entirely because the bleeding risk outweighs any stroke benefit
Use aspirin monotherapy instead, as it protects against stroke with much less bleeding risk
Start anticoagulation — high stroke risk outweighs even high bleeding risk
Refer for AF ablation first and postpone the anticoagulation decision until afterwards
Switch to warfarin, which is inherently safer than DOACs at high bleeding risk
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Even with high a validated bleeding score, the annual stroke risk at CHA₂DS₂-VASc 4 (~4%/year) usually outweighs the bleeding risk. Anticoagulate and MODIFY bleeding risk factors (optimise BP, review interacting drugs, manage anaemia). Bleeding risk scores guide risk modification — they are NOT contraindications to anticoagulation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: Which factor Xa inhibitor is taken TWICE daily for AF stroke prevention?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Apixaban (a factor Xa inhibitor) is 5 mg TWICE DAILY, reduced to 2.5 mg twice daily if two of: age 80 or over, weight 60 kg or under, creatinine 133 micromol/L or more. Rivaroxaban is once daily with the evening meal and edoxaban once daily. Dabigatran is also twice daily, but it is a direct thrombin inhibitor rather than a factor Xa inhibitor.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A patient with permanent AF develops an ischaemic stroke. She was not anticoagulated as her GP felt her fall risk was too high. Was this correct?
options: Yes — a significant falls risk is a firm, well-established contraindication that should always preclude anticoagulation
It depends entirely on the severity; only recurrent major injurious falls should ever preclude anticoagulation
No — a patient would need to fall approximately 300 times per year to offset the benefit of anticoagulation in preventing strokes
Yes, provided the CHA2DS2-VASc score is only 2, in which case the fall risk tips the balance against treatment
Yes, particularly once the patient is over 80, when advancing age makes falls an absolute contraindication
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: IMPORTANT: a patient needs to fall approximately 295 times per year for the fall risk to outweigh the stroke prevention benefit of anticoagulation. Fall risk alone is NOT a contraindication to anticoagulation in AF. Address fall risk (physio, medication review, home hazard assessment) rather than withholding anticoagulation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: What distinguishes permanent AF from persistent AF from paroxysmal AF?
options: Permanent AF is simply defined as any episode continuing unbroken for at least twelve months
Paroxysmal: self-terminates <48h; persistent: >7 days not self-terminating; permanent: cardioversion not pursued/failed
Paroxysmal AF cannot be cardioverted, persistent AF can, and permanent AF is cardioverted routinely
Duration is completely irrelevant; the categories are distinguished purely by how symptomatic the patient feels
Long-standing persistent AF means over 6 months, at which point cardioversion becomes technically impossible
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: AF classification: Paroxysmal = self-terminates <48h (usually). Persistent = lasts >7 days, not self-terminating, can be cardioverted. Long-standing persistent = >12 months, cardioversion still considered. Permanent = cardioversion not pursued (patient and doctor decision) — rate control only.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A 50-year-old with paroxysmal AF wants pharmacological cardioversion. She has no structural heart disease. What drug is used?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Flecainide is first-line for pharmacological cardioversion and rhythm control in paroxysmal AF WITHOUT structural heart disease. Dose: 200-300mg oral (pill-in-pocket) or IV. Contraindicated in structural heart disease (IHD, HF, LVH) due to proarrhythmic risk. Amiodarone used if structural disease present.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: What is the mechanism of atrial flutter and what defines its ECG?
options: Organised re-entry circuit (usually around tricuspid valve) — regular sawtooth F waves at 300bpm
Random re-entry throughout atria — fine fibrillatory baseline
Multiple ectopic foci — irregular tachycardia with P waves
AV nodal re-entry — regular narrow complex tachycardia with P behind QRS
Triggered activity from pulmonary veins — irregular sawtooth baseline
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Atrial flutter: single organised re-entry circuit (most commonly around the tricuspid annulus — cavotricuspid isthmus flutter). Atrial rate ~300bpm → regular sawtooth F waves on ECG (best in II, III, aVF, V1). AV node usually blocks 2:1 → ventricular rate ~150bpm. Radiofrequency ablation is curative.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: Rate control with digoxin in AF is MOST appropriate in which patient?
options: Active young patient with lone AF
Patient with AF and acute myocardial infarction
Elderly sedentary patient with AF and low activity level
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Digoxin for rate control in AF: most appropriate in elderly sedentary/inactive patients. It is ineffective during exertion (primarily vagotonic — reduces resting rate but inadequate rate control during exercise). Not first-line. Better options for active patients: beta-blocker or rate-limiting CCB. Also useful in AF + HF (where CCBs are contraindicated).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A patient with AF undergoes successful DC cardioversion to sinus rhythm. What is the minimum post-cardioversion anticoagulation duration?
options: 2 weeks if sinus rhythm confirmed on ECG
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: MINIMUM 4 weeks anticoagulation after ALL cardioversions (electrical or pharmacological). 'Atrial stunning' post-cardioversion → high clot formation risk in left atrial appendage for 4 weeks even in sinus rhythm. After 4 weeks → continue based on CHA₂DS₂-VASc. If patient is at high stroke risk, anticoagulate indefinitely.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: What is the key distinction between AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT) and AF on ECG?
options: AVNRT has no P waves at all, whereas AF shows clearly visible, normal upright P waves before each QRS
AVNRT always needs DC cardioversion to terminate, whereas AF can simply be rate-controlled
AVNRT always runs at a substantially faster ventricular rate than atrial fibrillation does
AVNRT is regular, narrow complex; AF is irregularly irregular with no true P waves
AVNRT produces a broad-complex QRS, whereas atrial fibrillation is always narrow-complex
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: AVNRT: rapid, REGULAR narrow QRS tachycardia (HR typically 150–250bpm), P waves buried in or just after QRS. AF: IRREGULARLY IRREGULAR, no true P waves (only fibrillation f waves). Regularity is the key distinction — regular narrow complex = SVT (AVNRT, AT, flutter); irregular = AF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: Which anticoagulant is preferred when a patient with AF also has significant renal impairment (CrCl 20 mL/min)?
options: Apixaban — least renally excreted, preferred in CKD
Edoxaban — once daily and safest in CKD
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Apixaban has the LEAST renal excretion (~27%) among DOACs — preferred when eGFR is significantly reduced. Dabigatran is predominantly renally excreted (~80%) — contraindicated in severe CKD. Rivaroxaban ~33% renal. Warfarin: metabolised hepatically, but monitoring is complex. DOACs generally preferred over warfarin in CKD if CrCl >15-25.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: How does idarucizumab reverse dabigatran?
options: It works by directly inhibiting factor Xa, thereby reducing thrombin generation and stopping the bleed
It reverses the anticoagulant by strongly activating antithrombin III within the coagulation cascade
Monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran with high affinity, reversing its anticoagulant effect
It simply provides concentrated clotting factors that directly override the drug's anticoagulant effect
It competitively displaces dabigatran from the thrombin active site, thereby restoring normal clotting
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Idarucizumab (Praxbind): humanised monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran with 350x greater affinity than thrombin → completely neutralises dabigatran within minutes. Used for life-threatening bleeding or urgent surgery in patients on dabigatran. Andexanet alfa reverses factor Xa inhibitors (rivaroxaban, apixaban).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A patient with new-onset AF (duration unknown) needs rate control while awaiting elective cardioversion. What must be started simultaneously with rate control?
options: Nothing additional — rate control alone is sufficient
Beta-blocker AND CCB together for faster rate control
Anticoagulation for minimum 3 weeks before cardioversion
TOE to exclude LAA thrombus — mandatory before any cardioversion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: If AF duration >48h or unknown → risk of left atrial appendage thrombus. Must anticoagulate for MINIMUM 3 WEEKS before elective cardioversion (to allow any existing thrombus to organise/dissolve). Alternative: TOE to exclude LAA thrombus → early cardioversion with pre-procedure anticoagulation. Then 4 weeks post-cardioversion regardless.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: What is the role of pulmonary vein isolation in AF?
options: It surgically removes the sinoatrial node itself, which permanently prevents any future atrial fibrillation arising
It creates an extensive surgical maze of atrial scars that channels every impulse along fixed protected corridors
Ablates the pulmonary vein ostia — site of ectopic triggers for paroxysmal AF — electrically isolating them from the left atrium
It implants an intracardiac device that continuously monitors for and automatically shocks any AF episode developing
It deliberately occludes the coronary sinus to interrupt the re-entrant circuits that sustain atrial fibrillation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Pulmonary vein isolation (PVI): catheter ablation targeting the pulmonary vein ostia (PVs) where ectopic atrial beats triggering AF originate. Radiofrequency or cryoenergy creates encircling lesions isolating PVs from LA. Success rates: ~50-80% for paroxysmal AF at 1 year. Indicated: symptomatic AF failed antiarrhythmic drugs.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: Which of the following is a side effect UNIQUE to amiodarone due to its iodine content?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Amiodarone contains ~37% iodine by weight → can cause BOTH hypothyroidism (iodine load inhibits thyroid hormone synthesis — Wolff-Chaikoff effect) AND hyperthyroidism (iodine provides substrate for autonomous thyroid production). Check TFTs before starting and every 6 months during treatment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A patient's CHA₂DS₂-VASc score components are: age 72 (1pt), hypertension (1pt), previous TIA (2pts), female (1pt). Total score?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: C=0 (no HF), H=1 (HTN), A₂=1 (age 65-74, NOT ≥75 so 1pt), D=0, S₂=2 (TIA), V=0, A=1 (age 65-74), Sc=1 (female). Total = 0+1+1+0+2+0+1+1 = 6. Wait — age 72 = A₂ component (65-74) = 1 point. Score = 1+2+1+1 = 5. Requires anticoagulation (score ≥3 in female).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: What is meant by 'rate versus rhythm control' — and what does the evidence show?
options: Rhythm control is always superior — reduces mortality
Rate control is superior — lower mortality and fewer adverse effects
Both strategies have similar mortality — choose based on patient symptoms and preference
Rhythm control is superior only in patients <65 years
Rhythm control is superior only in patients with HFrEF
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Rate control (HR <80bpm, remain in AF) vs rhythm control (cardioversion to maintain sinus rhythm) in AF. RESULT: similar mortality between strategies, but rhythm control patients had MORE hospitalisations and drug side effects. Rate control preferred in older, less symptomatic patients. Rhythm control for younger, symptomatic, or HF patients.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A 55-year-old man with recent-onset AF <24h is haemodynamically stable but very symptomatic (severe palpitations). What is the most appropriate rhythm management?
options: Rhythm control — can cardiovert with anticoagulation cover — amiodarone or flecainide (if no SHD)
Urgent DC cardioversion without anticoagulation is safe and appropriate
Anticoagulate for 3 weeks then elective cardioversion
Rate control with bisoprolol plus anticoagulation for 3 weeks before considering rhythm control
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: AF <48h in a STABLE patient: rhythm control is appropriate. Can cardiovert (pharmacological or DC) with anticoagulant cover (heparin pre-procedure), then continue anticoagulation for 4 weeks. Urgent DC cardioversion without anticoagulation is reserved for HAEMODYNAMICALLY UNSTABLE patients only.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A 28-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of sudden-onset rapid regular palpitations terminating abruptly. ECG during episode: HR 185bpm, regular, narrow QRS, P waves not visible. No delta wave in sinus rhythm. What is the diagnosis and first-line acute treatment?
options: Atrial fibrillation — immediate rate control with oral bisoprolol
AVNRT — vagal manoeuvres (Valsalva) then adenosine 6mg IV
Ventricular tachycardia — a 300mg IV amiodarone loading dose
AVRT with pre-excitation — urgent synchronised DC cardioversion
Atrial flutter — first-line rate control using intravenous digoxin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: AVNRT: most common SVT. Regular narrow complex tachycardia, abrupt onset/termination, P waves hidden in QRS. No delta wave (not WPW). First-line: vagal manoeuvres (Valsalva). If fails → adenosine 6mg IV (12mg, 18mg). Monitor ECG continuously. If haemodynamically unstable → synchronised DC cardioversion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A 22-year-old presents with SVT. ECG in sinus rhythm shows a short PR interval of 90ms and a slurred upstroke of the QRS. He is now in AF with a rapid irregular broad complex tachycardia. What should NOT be given?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: WPW + AF: NEVER give adenosine, beta-blockers, verapamil, or diltiazem. These block the AV node → all conduction forced through the accessory pathway at the full rapid atrial rate → extremely fast ventricular response → VF → cardiac arrest. Treatment: DC cardioversion (if unstable) or procainamide/flecainide (if stable). Amiodarone has been used but may worsen in some cases.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: Adenosine 6mg is given rapidly IV for SVT. The patient has a brief period of chest tightness and asystole, then sinus rhythm returns. Was the response appropriate?
options: No — the adenosine has caused a genuine cardiac arrest, so start CPR and give adrenaline immediately
No — adenosine should never produce any asystole, so this indicates a serious dosing or delivery error
Yes — transient asystole and chest tightness are expected effects. Sinus rhythm returned = successful.
No — this appearance means the patient urgently needs full anticoagulation before anything else is done
No — the chest tightness signals an acute adenosine allergy, so treat with antihistamine and steroids
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Adenosine causes transient AV block → brief asystole (seconds) before sinus rhythm restores. Patients commonly experience: chest tightness, facial flushing, breathlessness, and a sense of impending doom (lasting 10–30 seconds). This is expected and transient due to adenosine's very short half-life (<10 seconds). Warn patients before administration.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: Carotid sinus massage is being considered for SVT. What must be checked first?
options: Listen for carotid bruits / history of TIA or stroke — contraindicated if carotid stenosis present
Simply check the blood pressure, as this is the only safety step needed before the manoeuvre
Check the serum potassium level first, since this is the key safety check before proceeding
Perform a 12-lead ECG first purely to exclude atrial fibrillation before attempting the manoeuvre
Check the INR beforehand, as a deranged clotting result is the main contraindication here
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Carotid sinus massage contraindicated in patients with carotid artery stenosis (risk of dislodging atherosclerotic plaque → stroke) or recent TIA/stroke. Always auscultate for carotid bruits before performing carotid sinus massage. If bruits present → avoid bilateral massage. Perform on one side only for 5–10 seconds. Can be repeated on the other side if needed.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: What is synchronised DC cardioversion and why is synchronisation important?
options: Shock delivered on the P wave to reset atrial activity
Shock synchronised with the R wave to avoid shocking during the T wave (which would cause VF)
Shock given continuously throughout the cardiac cycle
Shock given at a random point to maximise energy delivery
Shock delivered asynchronously at maximum energy to terminate arrhythmia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Synchronised cardioversion: the defibrillator detects QRS complexes and delivers the shock at the peak of the R wave. This is critical because shocking during the T wave (vulnerable period of ventricular repolarisation) can trigger VF. This is why synchronisation is used for PULSED arrhythmias. Pulseless VT/VF: no synchronisation (unsynchronised defibrillation) as there are no organised QRS complexes to sync to.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: Long-term management of recurrent AVNRT is required for a 35-year-old professional musician. He has had 5 hospital admissions in 2 years. What is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
options: Commit the patient to lifelong daily flecainide as the definitive long-term solution
Prescribe a beta-blocker indefinitely, which is regarded here as the curative treatment
Radiofrequency catheter ablation of the slow AV nodal pathway — curative in >95% of cases
Arrange routine annual DC cardioversion sessions to keep the arrhythmia suppressed
Implant a permanent pacemaker, which definitively cures the underlying re-entry circuit
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Radiofrequency ablation is the definitive curative treatment for AVNRT (slow AV nodal pathway ablation). Success rate >95%. Preferred for patients with frequent recurrences, drug intolerance, or who prefer a cure over lifelong medication. Performed under sedation/GA via femoral vein in the catheter lab. Risk of AV block ~1%.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A patient with regular narrow complex tachycardia at 150bpm has sawtooth baseline activity visible in leads II, III, and aVF. What is the diagnosis?
options: AVNRT — terminate it acutely with a rapid IV adenosine bolus
Ventricular tachycardia — give adenosine then IV amiodarone
Atrial fibrillation — simple long-term ventricular rate control
Sinus tachycardia driven by pain — treat the underlying cause
Atrial flutter — rate control and consider cardioversion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Regular sawtooth F waves at 300bpm + ventricular rate 150bpm (2:1 conduction) = atrial flutter. The sawtooth pattern is most visible in inferior leads (II, III, aVF) and V1. Management: rate control (beta-blocker, diltiazem) and rhythm control (DC cardioversion or pharmacological). Radiofrequency ablation of the cavotricuspid isthmus is curative (>95% success for typical flutter).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: Acute rheumatic fever typically develops after which infection, and after how long?
options: A streptococcal skin infection, within 24 hours
A urinary tract infection, 1 week later
A group A streptococcal sore throat, 2–4 weeks later
An untreated dental abscess, 6 weeks later
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: A group A streptococcal sore throat, 2–4 weeks later
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: ARF is a multisystem immune-mediated disease that develops 2–4 weeks after a group A β-haemolytic streptococcal (S. pyogenes) throat infection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: Rheumatic fever characteristically follows streptococcal infection at which site?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: The throat (pharyngitis)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: Rheumatic fever follows strep PHARYNGITIS (throat), unlike post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, which can follow throat or skin infection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: What is the underlying mechanism of tissue damage in rheumatic fever?
options: IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity to streptococcal antigen
Direct streptococcal invasion of the myocardium and valves
Molecular mimicry — cross-reactive antibodies against streptococcal M protein
Immune-complex deposition in the valve endothelium
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Molecular mimicry — cross-reactive antibodies against streptococcal M protein
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: Molecular mimicry (predominantly type II antibody-mediated with a type IV T-cell component): antibodies and T cells against the streptococcal M protein cross-react with human antigens in the heart, joints, brain and skin.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: What is the pathognomonic histological finding of rheumatic carditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Aschoff bodies with Anitschkow cells
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: Aschoff bodies — granulomatous nodules containing Anitschkow (‘caterpillar’) macrophages — in the myocardium are pathognomonic of rheumatic carditis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: According to the Jones criteria, what is needed to diagnose a FIRST episode of rheumatic fever?
options: Any single major criterion, with no evidence of preceding strep
Evidence of preceding strep PLUS 2 major, or 1 major + 2 minor
Three minor criteria alone, with no major criterion required
A positive throat swab alone, with no clinical criteria needed
A raised ESR plus fever, with no other criteria required
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Evidence of preceding strep PLUS 2 major, or 1 major + 2 minor
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: A first episode requires evidence of a preceding group A strep infection PLUS either 2 major criteria or 1 major + 2 minor. (For a recurrent attack in someone with previous ARF or established RHD, 3 minor criteria alone will also do.)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: Which of the following is a MAJOR Jones criterion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Sydenham’s chorea
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: Sydenham’s chorea is a major criterion (JONES: Joints, Carditis, Nodules, Erythema marginatum, Sydenham’s chorea). Fever, arthralgia, raised markers and prolonged PR are minor criteria.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: Which of the following is a MINOR Jones criterion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Prolonged PR interval
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: A prolonged PR interval is a minor criterion. Migratory polyarthritis, carditis, nodules and erythema marginatum are major criteria.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: Because rheumatic fever presents weeks after the sore throat, which investigation best confirms preceding streptococcal infection?
options: Throat swab culture taken on presentation
Raised or rising ASO titre and anti-DNase B
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Raised or rising ASO titre and anti-DNase B
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: Swabs are often already negative by presentation, so raised/rising anti-streptococcal antibody titres (ASO and anti-DNase B) are the more reliable evidence of recent infection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: Which best describes the arthritis of rheumatic fever?
options: A symmetrical small-joint arthritis with erosions and morning stiffness
A monoarthritis with a hot, red joint and negatively birefringent crystals
A chronic deforming arthritis of the hands, sparing the large joints
A seronegative sacroiliitis with enthesitis and no peripheral joint pain
A migratory large-joint polyarthritis, aspirin-responsive, leaving no damage
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: A migratory large-joint polyarthritis, aspirin-responsive, leaving no damage
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: The arthritis is a migratory polyarthritis of large joints, hot and tender, dramatically responsive to aspirin/NSAIDs, and leaves no permanent joint damage.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: Which single manifestation of rheumatic fever is responsible for its long-term sequelae?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Carditis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: Carditis (a pancarditis) is the only manifestation with lasting sequelae, leading to chronic rheumatic heart disease (classically mitral stenosis).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: A soft mid-diastolic murmur of acute mitral valvulitis in rheumatic carditis is known as:
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Carey Coombs murmur
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: The Carey Coombs murmur is the soft mid-diastolic murmur of active mitral valvulitis; the commonest acute murmur overall is mitral regurgitation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: Which statement about Sydenham’s chorea is correct?
options: It is a late feature (1–6 months) and may be the only manifestation
It presents in the first 48 hours of infection
It causes a permanent movement disorder in most affected children
It occurs only in boys and never in girls of the same age
It is a minor Jones criterion rather than a major one
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: It is a late feature (1–6 months) and may be the only manifestation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: Sydenham’s chorea is a late feature (1–6 months), can be the sole manifestation, is commoner in girls, and is self-limiting; it is a MAJOR criterion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: Which description matches erythema marginatum?
options: A malar (butterfly) facial rash sparing the nasolabial folds
A painful vesicular rash confined to a single dermatome
Pink rings with central clearing on the trunk, sparing the face
Palpable purpura over the extensor surfaces of the legs
Target lesions on the palms and soles with mucosal involvement
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Pink rings with central clearing on the trunk, sparing the face
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: Erythema marginatum is pink rings with central clearing on the trunk and proximal limbs, characteristically sparing the face.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: Subcutaneous nodules in rheumatic fever are associated with:
options: Mild disease with a good prognosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Severe carditis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: The painless, firm subcutaneous nodules over extensor surfaces are associated with severe carditis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: What is the role of echocardiography in suspected rheumatic fever?
options: It is not indicated unless a murmur is audible on examination
Recommended in all suspected cases, including for subclinical carditis
It replaces the Jones criteria as the sole basis for diagnosis
It is used only at 6 months to look for established valve damage
It is used solely to measure left ventricular ejection fraction
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Recommended in all suspected cases, including for subclinical carditis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: Echocardiography is recommended in all suspected cases; it detects valvulitis/regurgitation and subclinical carditis, plus any pericardial effusion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: What is the recommended antibiotic to eradicate the streptococcus in acute rheumatic fever?
options: 10 days of oral penicillin V, or one IM benzathine dose
No antibiotic — the infection has resolved
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: 10 days of oral penicillin V, or one IM benzathine dose
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: A 10-day course of oral phenoxymethylpenicillin (penicillin V) is the usual UK course; a single dose of IM benzathine benzylpenicillin is the WHO/international standard, preferred where adherence is a concern. A macrolide is used if penicillin-allergic.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: Rheumatic fever is one of the few paediatric settings where which drug is deliberately used despite the usual Reye’s syndrome caution?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Aspirin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: High-dose aspirin is deliberately used for the arthritis/fever of rheumatic fever (as in Kawasaki disease), despite the usual caution about Reye’s syndrome in children.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: What is the mainstay of secondary prevention after rheumatic fever?
options: A single further course of antibiotics at the time of the attack
Lifelong low-dose aspirin to prevent valve inflammation
Long-term penicillin prophylaxis — IM benzathine 3–4 weekly or oral V
Annual influenza and pneumococcal vaccination alone
No specific prophylaxis beyond treating recurrences
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Long-term penicillin prophylaxis — IM benzathine 3–4 weekly or oral V
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: Long-term penicillin prophylaxis — IM benzathine penicillin every 3–4 weeks (or oral penicillin V twice daily) — prevents recurrence and further valve damage; duration depends on carditis and residual valve disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: In rheumatic heart disease, which valve and lesion are classically involved?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Mitral stenosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: The mitral valve is most commonly affected, classically producing mitral stenosis; the aortic valve is the next most involved.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: A 9-year-old is admitted with fever and a single hot, swollen, exquisitely tender knee that she refuses to weight-bear on. She had a sore throat three weeks ago. What is the most important next step?
options: Start high-dose aspirin for presumed rheumatic fever
Aspirate the joint and take blood cultures before antibiotics
Send an ASO titre and await the result
Start oral penicillin V and review in 48 hours
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Aspirate the joint and take blood cultures before antibiotics
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: A febrile child with a hot joint is septic arthritis until proven otherwise, and a missed septic joint destroys cartilage within days. The pattern is the discriminator: rheumatic fever arthritis is polyarticular and migratory, whereas this joint is monoarticular, non-migratory and non-weight-bearing. Aspiration (Gram stain, culture, cell count) plus blood cultures before antibiotics is the priority. Starting aspirin now would also abolish the fever and migratory pattern the Jones criteria depend on.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: A 12-year-old develops an additive, non-migratory arthritis of the knees and ankles 7 days after a streptococcal sore throat. It has persisted for six weeks and responded only sluggishly to ibuprofen. There is no murmur and the echocardiogram is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate management?
options: Acute rheumatic fever — 10 years of penicillin prophylaxis or until age 21
Post-streptococcal reactive arthritis — NSAIDs, echo, and about 12 months of prophylaxis
Reactive arthritis — check HLA-B27 and treat symptomatically only
Septic arthritis — urgent joint aspiration and washout under anaesthetic
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Post-streptococcal reactive arthritis — NSAIDs, echo, and about 12 months of prophylaxis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: The short latency (≤10 days rather than 2–4 weeks), the additive non-migratory pattern, the prolonged course and the blunted NSAID response all point to post-streptococcal reactive arthritis rather than acute rheumatic fever, whose arthritis flits between joints, settles within days and responds dramatically to salicylates. PSRA does not meet the Jones criteria, but because a minority later declare valve disease, practice is to echo the patient and give secondary penicillin prophylaxis for about 12 months before reassessing.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What is the organising principle that governs every event of the cardiac cycle?
options: Valves open and close through active muscular effort, the papillary muscles prising each leaflet apart at the right time
Volume determines valve position independent of pressure, so valves open and shut by chamber filling, not gradient
Blood flows up pressure gradients driven by the atria, which supply the force pushing blood forward through the heart
Electrical events follow the mechanical contractions that trigger them, occurring only after the muscle has shortened
Blood flows down pressure gradients and valves open/close passively when the pressure either side reverses
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: The organising principle is that blood flows down pressure gradients and valves open/close passively when the pressure either side reverses — every event follows from which chamber now has the higher pressure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: During isovolumetric contraction, what is the state of the valves and the pressure relationship?
options: Aortic valve open, mitral closed; ventricular pressure now exceeds the aortic
All four valves lie open at once with equal pressures in every chamber
Mitral valve open, aortic closed; atrial pressure exceeds the ventricular
All valves closed; ventricular P rising but not yet greater than aortic
Aortic and mitral both open together as ventricular pressure falls fast
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: In isovolumetric contraction the ventricle contracts with all valves shut, so pressure rises sharply with no volume change; ventricular pressure is rising but not yet greater than aortic.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What triggers the aortic valve to open, beginning ejection?
options: Ventricular pressure falling below atrial pressure
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: In rapid + reduced ejection, ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure, so the aortic valve opens and blood is ejected (aortic open, mitral closed).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: The 'atrial kick' during atrial systole contributes approximately what proportion of ventricular filling?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Atrial systole provides the final 'top-up' of filling — the 'atrial kick' — contributing about 20-30%, with the mitral open and aortic closed (atrial P > ventricular P).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Which phases make up systole, and which make up diastole?
options: Systole = atrial systole plus ventricular filling; diastole = the single ejection phase when blood is expelled into the great arteries
Systole = phases 2-3 (isovolumetric contraction + ejection); diastole = phases 4-5 + atrial systole (relaxation + filling)
Systole = phases 4-5 (relaxation and filling); diastole = phases 2-3 (isovolumetric contraction and ejection of blood into the aorta)
Systole consists of ventricular filling only, whereas diastole consists solely of the ejection of blood into the aorta and pulmonary artery
