Deliver immediate unsynchronised defibrillation at 150 J, treating the rhythm as shockable regardless of the breath sounds
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Immediate finger (open) thoracostomy — preferred in the ventilated or arrested patient → then a chest drain
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Tension pneumothorax needs immediate decompression. In a ventilated or arrested patient a finger (open) thoracostomy is preferred — needle decompression often fails — followed by a definitive chest drain.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What is Beck's triad, and which reversible cause does it point to?
options: Unequal breath sounds, tracheal deviation, hyper-resonance — tension pneumothorax
Bradycardia, hypertension, irregular breathing — raised ICP
Raised JVP, hypotension, muffled heart sounds — cardiac tamponade
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Raised JVP, hypotension, muffled heart sounds — cardiac tamponade
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Beck's triad (raised JVP, hypotension, muffled heart sounds) points to cardiac tamponade, treated with US-guided pericardiocentesis (or emergency thoracotomy in traumatic arrest).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: Which antidote is correctly matched to its toxin in cardiac arrest?
options: Opioid overdose → atropine as the specific antidote
Organophosphate poisoning → naloxone as the antidote
Digoxin toxicity → flumazenil to reverse it
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Local anaesthetic toxicity → 20% lipid emulsion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Local anaesthetic toxicity is treated with 20% lipid emulsion. Other pairings: organophosphates → atropine; opioids → naloxone; digoxin → digoxin-specific antibody fragments (DigiFab).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: When should activated charcoal be considered in a poisoned patient?
options: In all poisoned patients regardless of timing
In any unconscious patient once IV access is secured
Only if the toxin is unknown
Only if the patient is alert and within 1 hour of ingestion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Only if the patient is alert and within 1 hour of ingestion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Activated charcoal is appropriate only if the patient is alert and within 1 hour of ingestion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What can POCUS distinguish during the arrest pulse-check window, and what is the time constraint?
options: The coronary artery anatomy and site of the occlusion; the operator has under 60 seconds during the pulse check to obtain the views needed
The exact left-ventricular ejection fraction as a precise percentage, which can be carefully measured with no time limit during the arrest
The serum potassium and other electrolyte abnormalities driving the arrest; this must be assessed within 30 seconds at the pulse check
Cardiac motion (fine VF vs true asystole), pericardial effusion, flat IVC, and pleural fluid; requires <10 seconds at the pulse check
Only the underlying heart rate, counted directly off the screen; up to 5 minutes may be taken to complete this during compressions
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Cardiac motion (fine VF vs true asystole), pericardial effusion, flat IVC, and pleural fluid; requires <10 seconds at the pulse check
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: POCUS can distinguish fine VF from true asystole, and identify a pericardial effusion, a flat IVC (hypovolaemia), and pleural fluid — all within a <10-second pulse-check window.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: When is UNSYNCHRONISED defibrillation used, and why is synchronisation not possible?
options: For an organised tachycardia that still has a pulse; the R waves are too small for the defibrillator to detect and time the shock to
For supraventricular tachycardia, because the ventricular rate is simply too fast for the defibrillator to synchronise a shock to it
For atrial fibrillation only, because the rhythm is far too irregular for the machine to lock onto and synchronise a timed shock to
For asystole, because there is a completely flat trace and no organised electrical rhythm for the device to time the shock delivery to
For VF / pulseless VT; there are no organised R waves to synchronise to, so the shock is delivered immediately on the button press
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: For VF / pulseless VT; there are no organised R waves to synchronise to, so the shock is delivered immediately on the button press
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Unsynchronised defibrillation is used for VF/pVT; with no organised R waves to synchronise to, the device delivers the shock immediately when the button is pressed.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What is the first-shock energy for unsynchronised defibrillation, and how are subsequent shocks managed?
options: A fixed 50 J delivered for the first and all subsequent shocks, with no escalation at any stage
A 200 J first shock, then the energy halved with each successive shock delivered
A fixed 360 J monophasic shock delivered at full energy for the first and every later shock
A fixed 70–120 J biphasic shock repeated at the same energy for every subsequent shock
At least 150 J biphasic first shock, escalating for subsequent shocks up to the device maximum
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: At least 150 J biphasic first shock, escalating for subsequent shocks up to the device maximum
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: The first shock is at least 150 J biphasic, with subsequent shocks escalated up to the device maximum.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: Why does synchronised cardioversion wait for the R wave before delivering the shock?
options: To concentrate and increase the total energy that is delivered to the myocardium during the cardioversion
To avoid delivering the shock during the vulnerable T-wave period (R-on-T), which could induce VF
To give the operator a few extra seconds to confirm the leads and position the paddles safely
To reduce skin burns by spreading the delivered current away from the vulnerable T-wave period
To confirm the underlying rhythm diagnosis on the monitor before finally committing to the shock
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: To avoid delivering the shock during the vulnerable T-wave period (R-on-T), which could induce VF
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Synchronisation times the shock to the R wave, avoiding the vulnerable T-wave period (R-on-T), which could otherwise precipitate VF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: Synchronised cardioversion is used for which type of rhythm?
options: VF and pulseless VT without any output
An organised tachyarrhythmia WITH a pulse
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: An organised tachyarrhythmia WITH a pulse
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Synchronised cardioversion is for an organised tachyarrhythmia with a pulse; pulseless VF/VT requires unsynchronised defibrillation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What are the cardioversion energies for AF versus atrial flutter/SVT?
options: AF at 50 J; atrial flutter and SVT at 70 J
AF at 200 J; atrial flutter and SVT at 150 J
Both AF and flutter/SVT at 120–150 J biphasic
AF at 30 J; flutter and SVT at 360 J
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: AF 120–150 J biphasic; flutter/SVT 70–120 J
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Synchronised cardioversion (RCUK) uses 120–150 J biphasic for AF and 70–120 J for atrial flutter/SVT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What is the correct defibrillation safety drill?
options: 'Charge · Shock · Check pulse' — press charge, deliver the shock and then immediately assess for a central pulse before resuming
'Oxygen on · All clear · Shock' — keep oxygen flowing over the chest, confirm the team is clear, then deliver the shock safely
'Clear · Shock · Resume' — simply call clear once, deliver the shock and immediately resume chest compressions without any pause
Charge during compressions, then 'Stand clear · Oxygen away (≥1 m) · All clear · Shock' — resume compressions immediately
'Pulse check · Charge · Clear' — check for a pulse first, then charge the defibrillator and call clear before delivering the shock
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Charge during compressions, then 'Stand clear · Oxygen away (≥1 m) · All clear · Shock' — resume compressions immediately
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Continue chest compressions while the defibrillator charges, then stand clear, oxygen away (≥1 m from patient), all clear, shock — visually confirming all personnel are clear — and resume compressions immediately. Charging during compressions is what keeps the pre-shock pause under 5 seconds (Resus Council UK).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What is the target oxygen saturation in immediate post-ROSC care, and why?
options: SpO₂ of 100%, using maximal FiO₂ to maximise tissue oxygen delivery
No specific oxygen saturation target is required after ROSC
SpO₂ 88–92% in all post-arrest patients, matching the COPD target
SpO₂ 85–90% deliberately, to limit ongoing reperfusion injury
SpO₂ 94–98%, avoiding hyperoxia (which causes oxidative injury)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: SpO₂ 94–98%, avoiding hyperoxia (which causes oxidative injury)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Post-ROSC, titrate to SpO₂ 94–98% and avoid hyperoxia, which is harmful through oxidative injury.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What is the target PaCO₂ in post-ROSC care?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Normocapnia (PaCO₂ 4.5–6.0 kPa)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Post-ROSC ventilation aims for normocapnia, a PaCO₂ of 4.5–6.0 kPa.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What does targeted temperature management involve post-ROSC?
options: Actively warm the patient to a core temperature of 38°C to support the metabolism
Cool every patient to a core temperature of 28°C for full neuroprotection
Actively prevent fever (keep ≤37.5°C) for at least 72 hours after ROSC
Apply no temperature control at all until 72 hours have elapsed after ROSC
Maintain a core temperature of 40°C to drive and support cerebral metabolism
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Actively prevent fever (keep ≤37.5°C) for at least 72 hours after ROSC
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Targeted temperature management means actively preventing fever (keep ≤37.5°C) for at least 72 hours in comatose survivors. Routine cooling to 33°C is no longer recommended (TTM2).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: When should neurological prognostication be performed after ROSC, and why the delay?
options: Within the first hour after ROSC, before sedation and cooling can confound it
Only after 2 full weeks have passed, once all sedation has completely worn off
At 12 hours post-ROSC, once initial stabilisation on the ICU is complete
Immediately on ICU admission, while the patient is still sedated and cooled
Not before 72 hours — hypothermia (and sedation) delays neurological assessment
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Not before 72 hours — hypothermia (and sedation) delays neurological assessment
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Prognostication should not occur before 72 hours, as hypothermia and sedation delay reliable neurological assessment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: In which situation should CPR NOT be started?
options: A valid DNACPR order, injuries incompatible with life, or rigor mortis / dependent lividity present
A witnessed arrest with a shockable rhythm on the monitor, where defibrillation is likely to succeed
Any cardiac arrest occurring in an elderly patient, where resuscitation is considered futile by age
Any arrest where the underlying cause is unknown, so no reversible factor can be targeted early
A hypothermic cardiac arrest, where the cold core temperature makes any resuscitation pointless
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: A valid DNACPR order, injuries incompatible with life, or rigor mortis / dependent lividity present
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: CPR should not be started if there is a valid DNACPR order, injuries incompatible with life, or signs of death such as rigor mortis or dependent lividity.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: Which set of criteria supports stopping CPR?
options: After exactly 10 minutes of ALS in every case, regardless of rhythm, reversible causes or response to treatment
ROSC achieved; or no ROSC despite prolonged ALS AND all reversible causes excluded or treated, with team-leader consensus
As soon as the very first defibrillation shock fails to restore a perfusing rhythm on the subsequent pulse check
Only when the family present at the bedside specifically requests that all resuscitation efforts now be stopped
When the supply of adrenaline finally runs out, since further ALS cannot continue without the drug being available anymore
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: ROSC achieved; or no ROSC despite prolonged ALS AND all reversible causes excluded or treated, with team-leader consensus
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: CPR stops on ROSC. Otherwise it is a team decision, not a stopwatch: no ROSC despite prolonged ALS (commonly beyond 20–30 min of asystole) AND all reversible causes excluded or treated, with team-leader consensus. No guideline sets a fixed duration, and "reversible causes excluded" is not on its own a reason to stop. Continue longer for hypothermia, PE thrombolysis (60–90 min), toxins, pregnancy or an ECPR candidate (Resus Council UK).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What is described as the most-tested ALS fact regarding adrenaline timing (the 'adrenaline timing trap')?
options: Adrenaline 1 mg IV is given immediately in both the shockable and non-shockable arms as the very first drug
Shockable → adrenaline immediately with the first shock; non-shockable → adrenaline only after the 3rd shock
Non-shockable → adrenaline immediately; shockable → adrenaline only after the 3rd shock (not the 1st)
Adrenaline is withheld until after the 5th shock in both the shockable and non-shockable arms
Adrenaline is never used in modern ALS and has been removed from both arms of the algorithm entirely
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Non-shockable → adrenaline immediately; shockable → adrenaline only after the 3rd shock (not the 1st)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: The classic trap: adrenaline is immediate in non-shockable arrest but only after the 3rd shock (not the 1st) in shockable arrest.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: Which statement about amiodarone in cardiac arrest is correct?
options: It is given in both the shockable and non-shockable arms, alongside adrenaline, as a standard part of every arrest
It is ONLY for the shockable arm; never give it in PEA or asystole — it has no role and no evidence there
It is the first-line antiarrhythmic drug in asystole, given as a 300 mg IV bolus before the first adrenaline
It replaces adrenaline entirely in the non-shockable arm and is given after the first cycle of compressions
It is given immediately at the start of all cardiac arrests, before any rhythm assessment has been made
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: It is ONLY for the shockable arm; never give it in PEA or asystole — it has no role and no evidence there
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Amiodarone is for the shockable arm only; it has no role and no evidence in PEA or asystole.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What is magnesium 2 g IV specifically indicated for in cardiac arrest, and is it routine?
options: It is indicated in all cardiac arrests routinely, given as a standard 2 g IV bolus early in the algorithm
Torsades de pointes (polymorphic VT / long QT) specifically — it is NOT routine in all arrests
It is indicated routinely in asystole, given as a 2 g IV bolus alongside the first dose of adrenaline
It is the first-line treatment for hyperkalaemic arrest, given ahead of calcium to stabilise the heart
It is indicated routinely in pulseless electrical activity, given as a 2 g IV bolus with each cycle
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Torsades de pointes (polymorphic VT / long QT) specifically — it is NOT routine in all arrests
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Magnesium 2 g IV is the specific treatment for torsades de pointes (polymorphic VT / long QT); it is not routine in all cardiac arrests.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What is the most time-critical post-arrest intervention if the post-ROSC 12-lead ECG shows a STEMI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Emergency PCI
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: A STEMI on the post-ROSC 12-lead ECG mandates emergency PCI — the most time-critical post-arrest intervention.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: A patient is in asystole. You have IV access and are asked to give adrenaline. Which preparation and route is correct?
options: 3 mg via the tracheal tube — 3 mL of 1:1000
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: 1 mg IV — 10 mL of 1:10,000
explanation: 1 mg IV — 10 mL of 1:10,000. This is the standard arrest dose and preparation, given immediately in a non-shockable rhythm and repeated every 3–5 minutes, followed by a 20 mL flush.
0.5 mg IM of 1:1000 — the anaphylaxis regimen. Both the dose and the route are wrong for an arrest, and IM absorption is negligible during CPR.
1 mg IM of 1:1000 — the right dose but the wrong route; intramuscular drug will not circulate in a patient with no cardiac output.
0.5 mg IV — half the arrest dose; 1 mg is the standard.
Tracheal administration — no longer recommended; absorption is unreliable and IO access is the alternative when IV fails.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: During a cardiac arrest a colleague draws up 0.5 mL of 1:1000 adrenaline and prepares to give it intramuscularly. What is the correct administration in this situation?
options: 0.5 mg intramuscularly as drawn up — the colleague is correct
1 mg intravenously as 1 mL of 1:1000 given undiluted as a rapid push
Withhold adrenaline until return of spontaneous circulation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: 1 mg intravenously as 10 mL of 1:10,000
explanation: 1 mg intravenously as 10 mL of 1:10,000 — the colleague has drawn up the anaphylaxis regimen. In arrest the dose is double, the route is IV/IO, and the concentration is ten-fold weaker.
0.5 mg IM as drawn up — this is the anaphylaxis dose and route; IM adrenaline will not circulate without cardiac output.
1 mL of 1:1000 IV undiluted — the correct milligram dose but the wrong preparation; the arrest standard is the 1:10,000 pre-filled syringe followed by a 20 mL flush.
0.5 mg IV of 1:1000 — wrong dose and wrong concentration.
Withholding adrenaline — the opposite of correct; in a non-shockable rhythm adrenaline is given as soon as access is obtained.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: You are about to defibrillate a patient in VF who has a permanent pacemaker with the generator visible below the left clavicle. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Place the pads at least 8 cm from the generator, or use anterior-posterior placement
Place a pad directly over the generator to ensure the best possible contact
Reduce the shock energy to 50 J to protect the implanted device
Do not defibrillate at all — the pacemaker will be destroyed
Deactivate the pacemaker with a ring magnet before shocking
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Place the pads at least 8 cm from the generator, or use anterior-posterior placement
explanation: Place the pads at least 8 cm from the generator, or use anterior-posterior placement — this avoids shunting current through the device while still delivering effective energy to the myocardium. The device should be interrogated afterwards.
A pad directly over the generator — shunts current away from the heart and risks damaging the device.
Reducing the energy — would compromise defibrillation; VF needs full energy, and the presence of a device is not a reason to under-treat.
Not defibrillating — VF is fatal without a shock; an implanted device never contraindicates defibrillation.
Applying a magnet — relevant to inhibiting an ICD's own therapies in some settings, but it does not change external defibrillation and would waste time in an arrest.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: How does dry gangrene differ from wet gangrene?
options: Dry gangrene causes florid systemic sepsis and shock; wet gangrene stays localised without any toxaemia
Dry = bacterial infection without ischaemia, warm and pus-filled; wet = pure arterial ischaemia only, cold and dry
Both are clinically identical, spreading at the same rate and treated the same, told apart only by biopsy
Dry = ischaemia without infection, mummified, demarcated; wet = ischaemia + infection, swollen, septic
Dry gangrene always requires urgent same-day amputation, whereas wet gangrene can be safely observed
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Dry = ischaemia without infection, mummified, demarcated; wet = ischaemia + infection, swollen, septic
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Dry gangrene: ischaemic necrosis, mummified, well-demarcated, no systemic upset. Wet gangrene: ischaemia + infection, malodorous, poorly demarcated, systemic sepsis — a surgical emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: Which organism causes gas gangrene and what is its hallmark sign?
options: Clostridium perfringens — crepitus from gas in tissues
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Clostridium perfringens — crepitus from gas in tissues
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Gas gangrene is caused by Clostridium perfringens (Gram-positive anaerobe) — alpha-toxin destroys cell membranes, producing gas (CO₂ + H₂) → crepitus on palpation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What is the treatment of gas gangrene?
options: Oral antibiotics with outpatient wound review in the community clinic
IV broad-spectrum antibiotics alone, without any surgical debridement or amputation
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy alone as the sole definitive treatment, avoiding surgery
Conservative management with regular wound dressings and limb elevation only
Emergency surgical debridement/amputation + IV penicillin G + hyperbaric oxygen
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Emergency surgical debridement/amputation + IV penicillin G + hyperbaric oxygen
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Gas gangrene is a surgical emergency: wide debridement/amputation + high-dose IV penicillin G (± metronidazole) + hyperbaric oxygen as an adjunct.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What is Fournier's gangrene?
options: Wet gangrene of the diabetic foot with infected, malodorous, swollen tissue and surrounding cellulitis
Clostridial gas gangrene of the lower limb muscles, producing crepitus and subcutaneous gas on X-ray after trauma
Dry ischaemic gangrene of the toes and digits caused by chronic atherosclerotic peripheral arterial disease
Necrotising fasciitis of the perineum/scrotum/vulva — polymicrobial, affects diabetics, emergency debridement required
Ischaemic necrosis of the small bowel due to mesenteric arterial occlusion, causing severe abdominal pain
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Necrotising fasciitis of the perineum/scrotum/vulva — polymicrobial, affects diabetics, emergency debridement required
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Fournier's gangrene is polymicrobial necrotising fasciitis of the perineum/genitalia, most common in diabetic/immunocompromised men — emergency debridement + broad-spectrum antibiotics.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What is the hallmark clinical sign of necrotising fasciitis?
options: Pain out of proportion to appearance, with 'dishwater' fluid on incision
A black, mummified, clearly demarcated digit with absent distal pedal pulses
Palpable crepitus, which occurs only in gas gangrene and never in this condition
A well-localised fluctuant abscess with overlying pointing and warmth
Superficial erythema strictly limited to the skin surface, sparing deeper fascia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Pain out of proportion to appearance, with 'dishwater' fluid on incision
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Pain out of proportion + grey/brown dishwater fluid on incision = necrotising fasciitis until proven otherwise. Requires immediate surgical exploration.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: At what ABPI is critical ischaemia with tissue loss/gangrene expected?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: ABPI <0.5 = severe ischaemia; ABPI <0.3 = critical ischaemia with rest pain, non-healing ulcers, and gangrene.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What is the commonest precipitant of lower limb gangrene in clinical practice?
options: Aortic dissection with distal extension occluding the iliac arteries
Acute arterial embolism from atrial fibrillation lodging at a limb artery bifurcation
Buerger's disease (thromboangiitis obliterans) in young male heavy smokers
Diabetic foot — neuropathy + peripheral arterial disease + impaired immunity
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia causing arterial thrombosis and limb ischaemia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Diabetic foot — neuropathy + peripheral arterial disease + impaired immunity
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: The diabetic foot triad — peripheral neuropathy (unnoticed injury), peripheral arterial disease (impaired healing), and impaired immunity (infection) — is the commonest cause of limb gangrene.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What is the definitive management of established limb gangrene?
options: Revascularisation if viable tissue remains; amputation if not — with debridement and antibiotics for wet/gas gangrene
IV broad-spectrum antibiotics alone, continued long-term without any surgical revascularisation or amputation
Conservative wound care only, with regular dressings and bedside debridement of slough without surgery
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy alone as the definitive treatment, avoiding any revascularisation or surgery
Systemic anticoagulation with heparin alone to restore limb perfusion, avoiding surgery or amputation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Revascularisation if viable tissue remains; amputation if not — with debridement and antibiotics for wet/gas gangrene
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Established gangrene: revascularisation (bypass/angioplasty) if viable tissue remains; amputation if not. Wet/gas gangrene require urgent debridement + antibiotics first.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What does the LRINEC score assess?
options: Severity of peripheral arterial disease, stratifying critical limb ischaemia to guide revascularisation
Laboratory risk of necrotising fasciitis — score ≥6 = high risk, prompts urgent surgical exploration
Prognostic scoring tool predicting mortality risk in patients with established septic shock on the ICU
Risk of major amputation in the diabetic foot, combining neuropathy, ischaemia and infection scores
Likelihood of clostridial gas gangrene, based on palpable crepitus and gas seen on plain radiographs
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Laboratory risk of necrotising fasciitis — score ≥6 = high risk, prompts urgent surgical exploration
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: LRINEC (CRP, WCC, Hb, Na, creatinine, glucose) — score ≥6 suggests necrotising fasciitis and prompts urgent surgical exploration, not delay.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: EXAM PEARL: A patient presents with a black mummified fifth toe, clear demarcation, absent pedal pulses, no fever, ABPI 0.25. What is the type of gangrene and management?
options: Dry gangrene from critical ischaemia — urgent vascular review for revascularisation/amputation
Wet gangrene — urgent IV broad-spectrum antibiotics with surgical debridement of infected tissue
Gas gangrene — emergency IV penicillin G with radical surgical debridement of necrotic muscle
Fournier's gangrene — emergency perineal and scrotal surgical debridement with antibiotics
Necrotising fasciitis — urgent LRINEC scoring followed by surgical fascial exploration
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Dry gangrene from critical ischaemia — urgent vascular review for revascularisation/amputation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Dry gangrene: mummified, demarcated, no infection, critical ABPI <0.3 → urgent vascular review for revascularisation; amputation if not feasible.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: EXAM PEARL: A patient has a rapidly spreading wound infection with severe pain, crepitus on palpation, and gas on X-ray. What is the diagnosis and immediate management?
options: Gas gangrene (Clostridium perfringens) — emergency surgical debridement + IV penicillin G + hyperbaric O₂
Dry gangrene — conservative management with dressings, awaiting spontaneous autoamputation of the digit
Wet gangrene — a short course of oral antibiotics with outpatient wound dressing and community review
Fournier's gangrene — localised perineal wound care with dressings and simple oral antibiotics
Necrotising fasciitis Type II — inpatient observation with IV antibiotics and delayed surgery
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Gas gangrene (Clostridium perfringens) — emergency surgical debridement + IV penicillin G + hyperbaric O₂
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Crepitus + gas on XR + rapidly progressive pain = gas gangrene. Emergency: wide surgical debridement/amputation + high-dose IV penicillin G + hyperbaric oxygen.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: A 65-year-old diabetic presents with a 2-day history of severe perineal pain, swelling, and crepitus. He has a fever of 39.5°C and is haemodynamically unstable. What is the diagnosis and priority treatment?
options: Fournier's gangrene — emergency surgical debridement + IV antibiotics
Perianal abscess — theatre incision and drainage of the collection
Perineal cellulitis — IV antibiotics alone without any surgical intervention
Scrotal hydrocele — reassurance and conservative outpatient management
Inguinal hernia — elective outpatient mesh repair on a routine list
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Fournier's gangrene — emergency surgical debridement + IV antibiotics
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Fournier's gangrene is necrotising fasciitis of the perineum — commonest in diabetics. Crepitus, systemic sepsis and rapid progression = emergency debridement. Delay is fatal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: A patient sustained a penetrating wound and now has a wound with a 'sweetish' smell, crepitus, and bronzed discoloration of surrounding skin. He is confused and febrile. What organism is responsible?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Clostridium perfringens
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Gas gangrene is caused by Clostridium perfringens — classically after penetrating wounds or surgery. Crepitus, rapid systemic toxicity, and distinctive smell point to clostridial myonecrosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What is the LRINEC score used for?
options: Predicting in-hospital mortality risk in patients with established septic shock
Risk stratifying suspected necrotising fasciitis using laboratory parameters
Grading the severity and depth of thermal burns to guide fluid resuscitation
Calculating the correct weight-based dose of VTE thromboprophylaxis heparin
Diagnosing and grading the severity of diabetic foot infection and ulceration
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Risk stratifying suspected necrotising fasciitis using laboratory parameters
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: LRINEC uses CRP, WBC, Hb, Na, creatinine, glucose — score ≥6 = high risk for NF. However, high clinical suspicion should still prompt surgical exploration regardless of score.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: A 72-year-old woman with severe peripheral vascular disease has a dry, black, mummified 2nd toe with a clear demarcation line. She has no fever and no systemic sepsis. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Simple wound dressings alone with watchful observation in the community clinic
Emergency wide surgical debridement of the toe with excision of tissue
IV broad-spectrum antibiotics alone without vascular assessment or surgery
Vascular assessment + elective amputation if revascularisation not possible
Long-term warfarin anticoagulation to restore perfusion to the ischaemic toe
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Vascular assessment + elective amputation if revascularisation not possible
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Dry gangrene = ischaemic mummification — stable without systemic sepsis. Assess revascularisation potential (Doppler, ABI, arteriography). If not salvageable, elective digital amputation at appropriate level.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What is the key clinical feature distinguishing necrotising fasciitis from severe cellulitis?
options: Superficial erythema and warmth of the skin only, without deep tissue involvement
Disproportionate severe pain with woody-hard induration and systemic sepsis
Isolated unilateral leg swelling and calf tenderness, as seen in deep vein thrombosis
A markedly elevated serum D-dimer level as the single key diagnostic marker
A positive blood culture being the defining feature that confirms the diagnosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Disproportionate severe pain with woody-hard induration and systemic sepsis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: NF hallmarks: disproportionate pain (nerves involved), woody induration (fascial involvement), rapid spread, skin necrosis/crepitus, systemic sepsis. Cellulitis is softer and more contained.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: Which imaging finding on CT confirms necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Gas tracking along fascial planes
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Gas along fascial planes on CT = necrotising fasciitis until proven otherwise — pathognomonic of gas-forming organisms. Does not exclude NF if absent; surgical exploration is definitive.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What antibiotic combination is used for clostridial gas gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: High-dose IV penicillin + clindamycin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Penicillin G kills Clostridium; clindamycin inhibits toxin production by blocking protein synthesis. This combination is the antibiotic backbone for gas gangrene alongside emergency surgical debridement.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: Why is clindamycin added to penicillin in gas gangrene?
options: It broadens cover against Gram-negative organisms missed by penicillin
It inhibits toxin production by blocking bacterial protein synthesis
It penetrates bone and necrotic muscle much better than penicillin does
It prevents the emergence of clostridial resistance against penicillin
It adds essential anaerobic cover that penicillin lacks in this setting
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: It inhibits toxin production by blocking bacterial protein synthesis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Even after penicillin kills the bacteria, pre-formed alpha-toxin continues to cause tissue destruction. Clindamycin (protein synthesis inhibitor) turns off toxin production — critical in severe clostridial infections.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: A 78-year-old with dry gangrene of the right foot refuses surgery. What complication is most likely to develop without intervention?
options: Wet gangrene with secondary infection and sepsis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Wet gangrene with secondary infection and sepsis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Dry gangrene is initially stable but can become infected (wet gangrene) — especially in diabetics with poor immunity. Secondary bacterial infection leads to systemic sepsis, which is life-threatening.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: A 45-year-old intravenous drug user presents with a tender, erythematous, rapidly spreading arm swelling with skin necrosis and severe pain. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Incision and drainage as for abscess
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Emergency surgical exploration and debridement
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Clinical signs of necrotising fasciitis (IVDU + skin necrosis + rapid progression) = emergency surgical exploration. Do NOT delay for imaging when NF is strongly suspected — every hour increases mortality.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What is the role of hyperbaric oxygen (HBO) in gas gangrene?
options: A definitive standalone cure that reliably avoids the need for surgery
First-line definitive treatment used instead of surgical debridement
Adjunct after surgical debridement — high O₂ inhibits anaerobe growth
Indicated only in wet gangrene and never in clostridial gas gangrene
Absolutely contraindicated in gas gangrene because of oxygen toxicity risk
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Adjunct after surgical debridement — high O₂ inhibits anaerobe growth
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Hyperbaric oxygen inhibits Clostridium (obligate anaerobe) and promotes tissue healing — used as an adjunct after surgical debridement + antibiotics in specialist centres. It does NOT replace surgery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What percentage of necrotising fasciitis cases occur in diabetics?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Diabetes is the strongest risk factor for necrotising fasciitis and Fournier's gangrene — impaired immunity, neuropathy (unnoticed injuries), and vascular disease all contribute. Other risk factors: obesity, IVDU, immunosuppression.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: Which of the following is the key difference between Type 1 and Type 2 necrotising fasciitis?
options: Type 1 = gas-forming clostridial infection; Type 2 = no gas ever produced
Type 1 = mild superficial cellulitis; Type 2 = deep fulminant myonecrosis
Type 1 = polymicrobial; Type 2 = monomicrobial (Group A Streptococcus)
Type 1 = confined to the limbs only; Type 2 = confined to perineum only
Type 1 = managed with antibiotics alone; Type 2 = requires surgery only
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Type 1 = polymicrobial; Type 2 = monomicrobial (Group A Streptococcus)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Type 1 NF is polymicrobial (mixed aerobic/anaerobic), common in diabetics/elderly. Type 2 is monomicrobial, typically Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes), can affect healthy young adults.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the triad of dry gangrene?
options: Palpable gas in tissue + florid systemic toxicity + audible crepitus
Moist swollen tissue + high fever + rapid proximal spread of infection
Black mummified tissue + clear demarcation line + ischaemic cause (PAD)
Perineal scrotal involvement + polymicrobial flora + diabetes mellitus
Warm erythematous swollen limb + deep vein thrombosis + pitting oedema
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Black mummified tissue + clear demarcation line + ischaemic cause (PAD)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Dry gangrene = ischaemic mummification from PAD. Key features: dry, black, shrunken tissue with a clear demarcation line. No systemic sepsis initially (unlike wet gangrene).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What is the classic risk factor combination for developing Fournier's gangrene?
options: Male sex + diabetes + perineal trauma or local infection
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Male sex + diabetes + perineal trauma or local infection
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Fournier's gangrene predominantly affects men (10:1 M:F ratio) — classic risk factors: diabetes, obesity, immunosuppression, perianal/urological procedures, or local infection as a trigger.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What is the gold standard for diagnosing necrotising fasciitis definitively?
options: Surgical exploration (biopsy + direct visualisation of necrotic fascia)
Contrast CT scan showing fascial thickening and subcutaneous gas tracking
MRI demonstrating deep fascial oedema with T2 hyperintense fluid signal
LRINEC score ≥8 combined with raised C-reactive protein and creatinine
Blood cultures growing Group A Streptococcus with positive Gram stain
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Surgical exploration (biopsy + direct visualisation of necrotic fascia)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Only surgical exploration can definitively confirm NF — finger sweep test (fascial planes separate without resistance) and grey necrotic fascia are diagnostic. No imaging has 100% sensitivity.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: A 60-year-old with PAD presents with gangrene of the left big toe. ABI is 0.4. What should be considered before amputation?
options: Revascularisation (angioplasty or bypass) to improve perfusion
Immediate above-knee amputation without any vascular imaging beforehand
IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and serial observation of the toe only
Systemic warfarin anticoagulation targeting an INR of 2 to 3 first
Compression bandaging of the limb to reduce oedema before surgery
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Revascularisation (angioplasty or bypass) to improve perfusion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Before amputation, consider revascularisation to improve distal blood supply — successful bypass may allow a more distal (digit-only) amputation rather than a major limb amputation. ABI 0.4 = severe ischaemia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What skin finding is pathognomonic for gas gangrene?
options: Non-blanching purpuric petechial rash over the dependent limbs
Erythema migrans — an expanding annular rash with central clearing
Target lesion with concentric erythematous rings and dusky centre
Painless indurated ulcer with a rolled raised pearly heaped edge
Crepitus (crackling sensation) + bronze-brown discoloration of skin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Crepitus (crackling sensation) + bronze-brown discoloration of skin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Crepitus = gas in soft tissue from Clostridium fermentation — pathognomonic of gas gangrene when combined with bronze discoloration and systemic toxicity. X-ray may show gas in muscle planes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the most important prognostic factor in necrotising fasciitis?
options: The admission laboratory LRINEC risk score
Choice of first empirical antibiotic combination
Advancing chronological age of the patient
Presence of subcutaneous gas on the CT scan
Speed of surgical debridement (time to theatre)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Speed of surgical debridement (time to theatre)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Every hour of delay increases mortality in NF — early aggressive surgical debridement is the single most important intervention. Antibiotics alone cannot control the infection; surgery achieves source control.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of wet gangrene?
options: Moist, swollen, oedematous discoloured tissue with blistering
Foul-smelling purulent discharge from the necrotic wound margins
Rapid uncontrolled proximal spread along the deep tissue planes
Overwhelming systemic sepsis with hypotension and organ failure
Clear demarcation line with mummified tissue (this is dry gangrene)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Clear demarcation line with mummified tissue (this is dry gangrene)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Wet gangrene has blurred margins, rapid spread, moist tissue, and foul odour. A clear demarcation line and mummified tissue are features of DRY gangrene (ischaemic origin, no infection initially).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: Which intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) indication applies to necrotising fasciitis?
options: Clostridial gas gangrene with myonecrosis and tissue crepitus present
Every case of necrotising fasciitis routinely as first-line therapy
Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome complicating NF (Group A Strep)
Fournier's perineal gangrene only, regardless of causative organism
MRSA-associated necrotising fasciitis confirmed on tissue culture
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome complicating NF (Group A Strep)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: IVIG neutralises superantigen exotoxins from Group A Streptococcus — used as adjunct in streptococcal toxic shock syndrome complicating NF. Not routine for all NF types.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What is the recommended amputation level when a patient has gangrene of toes with a non-reconstructable arterial supply?
options: Above ankle (below-knee or above-knee depending on blood supply)
Always above-knee regardless of the calf and thigh blood supply
Always digital ray amputation confined to the affected toes only
Knee disarticulation performed through the joint in every patient
Amputation exactly at the visible level of demarcated gangrene
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Above ankle (below-knee or above-knee depending on blood supply)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Amputation level depends on adequate blood supply at the stump for healing — typically BKA or AKA. Amputation through ischaemic tissue fails to heal. Doppler pressures and skin perfusion mapping guide level.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: A 58-year-old diabetic has a foot ulcer with surrounding crepitus and gas on X-ray but no systemic sepsis. What is the most appropriate management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Urgent surgical debridement + IV antibiotics
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Gas in soft tissue = gas-forming infection (possibly gas gangrene) even without obvious systemic sepsis — requires urgent surgical debridement and IV antibiotics. Gas in tissue = do not wait.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the mortality of untreated gas gangrene?
options: Zero mortality once hyperbaric oxygen therapy is commenced early
Around 10% mortality when the infection is left entirely untreated
Around 50% mortality even with surgery and intravenous antibiotics
Under 5% mortality when treated with intravenous antibiotics alone
Near 100% without treatment; ~20–30% with surgery + antibiotics
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Near 100% without treatment; ~20–30% with surgery + antibiotics
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Gas gangrene is rapidly lethal without surgical debridement. Even with optimal treatment, mortality is 20–30%. Alpha-toxin from C. perfringens causes massive haemolysis, multi-organ failure, and cardiovascular collapse.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: Which population is at highest risk for non-clostridial gas gangrene (polymicrobial)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Diabetics with foot infections
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Polymicrobial gas-forming infections in diabetic feet (E. coli, Klebsiella, Bacteroides) are more common than clostridial gas gangrene. Poorly controlled diabetics with peripheral neuropathy and vascular disease are highest risk.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What is the 'finger sweep' test in suspected NF?
options: Bedside test assessing capillary refill and perfusion in cold ischaemic toes distal to an occluded artery in peripheral vascular disease
Bedside test assessing the sharpness and clarity of the mummified demarcation line separating dead dry gangrenous tissue from viable skin
Surgical test: finger inserted through small incision — absence of resistance to blunt dissection along fascial planes confirms NF
Palpation test checking for subcutaneous crepitus and gas in the perineum and scrotum of a patient with suspected Fournier's gangrene
Handheld continuous-wave Doppler test assessing arterial flow signals within the digital vessels of the ischaemic gangrenous toes
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Surgical test: finger inserted through small incision — absence of resistance to blunt dissection along fascial planes confirms NF
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: The finger sweep test is intraoperative: a finger passed through a small fascial incision slides easily along necrotic fascial planes without resistance — confirms NF. Normal tissue resists blunt dissection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What organisms are implicated in Fournier's gangrene (perineal necrotising fasciitis)?
options: Staphylococcus aureus alone acting as the sole causative organism spreading through the perineal soft tissues
Polymicrobial synergistic infection — aerobic Gram-negative rods + anaerobes (Bacteroides, Clostridia)
Pseudomonas aeruginosa alone as the single Gram-negative pathogen, without anaerobic or coliform co-infection
Group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus pyogenes only, driving the infection monomicrobially as in type 2 NF
Candida albicans as an invasive monomicrobial fungal pathogen destroying the perineal and scrotal soft tissue
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Polymicrobial synergistic infection — aerobic Gram-negative rods + anaerobes (Bacteroides, Clostridia)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Fournier's gangrene is polymicrobial — synergistic infection by aerobic Gram-negatives (E. coli, Klebsiella) and anaerobes (Bacteroides, Clostridia). The combination drives rapid tissue destruction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: Which imaging is most useful for surgical planning in necrotising fasciitis (showing gas and spread along fascial planes) without delaying surgery?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: CT with IV contrast
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: CT with contrast shows gas tracking along fascial planes, the extent of infection, fluid collections and compartment involvement, and is fast — useful for surgical planning. Necrotising fasciitis is primarily a clinical diagnosis and imaging must NOT delay emergency surgical debridement. (MRI is more sensitive for soft-tissue extent but is slower and rarely appropriate acutely.)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the 'hallmark' clinical finding of necrotising fasciitis that distinguishes it from all other soft tissue infections?
options: Disproportionately severe pain with anaesthesia of the skin (nerve destruction)
High swinging fever alone without any accompanying local skin change
A soft fluctuant swelling indicating a drainable subcutaneous abscess
Copious purulent discharge exuding from the surface of the wound bed
A positive wound swab culture growing the responsible pathogenic organism
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Disproportionately severe pain with anaesthesia of the skin (nerve destruction)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: NF destroys nerve fibres as it spreads — early: disproportionate severe pain; late: paradoxical anaesthesia (nerves dead). This combination of pain then anaesthesia in rapidly progressing soft tissue infection = NF until proven otherwise.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: High probability → skip D-dimer → USS directly.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: Wells score 3 (likely DVT). Next step?

options: DVT probability is low — to rule out DVT
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.answer: DVT probability is low — to rule out DVT
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: High sensitivity, low specificity — only valuable as rule-out in low probability.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: D-dimer is useful when?

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: DOACs cross placenta. Warfarin teratogenic. LMWH safe.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: Pregnant woman with confirmed proximal DVT. Anticoagulation?

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: RCT evidence: DOACs inferior to warfarin in APS.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: Antiphospholipid syndrome requires?

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: Factor V Leiden = most common inherited prothrombotic condition.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: Most common inherited thrombophilia?

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: Unprovoked = high recurrence risk — minimum 6 months, then reassess.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: Duration of anticoagulation for unprovoked proximal DVT?

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: Three pathological mechanisms predisposing to venous thrombosis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: Virchow's triad?

options: No monitoring required + predictable pharmacokinetics + fewer interactions
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.answer: No monitoring required + predictable pharmacokinetics + fewer interactions
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: DOACs: fixed dosing, no INR monitoring, fewer food/drug interactions.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: DOAC is preferred over warfarin in DVT because?

options: Not routinely recommended — no benefit shown
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.answer: Not routinely recommended — no benefit shown
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: Routine compression stockings do not prevent post-thrombotic syndrome.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: Compression stockings for DVT (post-DVT syndrome prevention)?

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: Warfarin/DOACs affect protein C, S, and antithrombin levels — results unreliable during treatment.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: Thrombophilia screen should be done?
A 45-year-old woman returns from a 12-hour flight and develops left calf pain and swelling. Wells score = 3. What is the most appropriate next step?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: Wells ≥2 = high probability → go directly to compression duplex USS. D-dimer is not used in high probability scenarios as it does not change management.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: A 30-year-old man presents with his second unprovoked DVT. Which investigation is most important to guide long-term management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: Recurrent unprovoked DVT at young age warrants thrombophilia screening (Factor V Leiden, prothrombin mutation, protein C/S, antithrombin, antiphospholipid antibodies) to guide duration of anticoagulation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: A 60-year-old woman has a confirmed DVT. She is not pregnant and has no contraindications. What is the NICE first-line treatment?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: NICE recommends DOACs (rivaroxaban or apixaban) as first-line for DVT — simpler dosing, no monitoring, non-inferior efficacy to LMWH/warfarin with similar bleeding risk.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: What is the minimum duration of anticoagulation for a first DVT provoked by a temporary risk factor (e.g. post-surgical)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: Provoked DVT (identifiable temporary trigger) = 3 months anticoagulation. After this, risk of recurrence is low. Unprovoked DVT = 6+ months, recurrent = lifelong.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: D-dimer is elevated in which of the following non-DVT conditions?
options: Only in late pregnancy, normal at all other times
Only in acute DVT and PE, normal in all others
Only in disseminated malignancy, otherwise normal
Never raised in the absence of active thrombosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: D-dimer is highly sensitive but not specific — elevated in any condition causing fibrin turnover (surgery, infection, cancer, pregnancy). A positive result alone does not confirm DVT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: A pregnant woman is diagnosed with DVT at 20 weeks. What is the correct anticoagulant?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: DOACs and warfarin are contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic, foetal bleeding risk). LMWH is safe and used throughout pregnancy, continuing for ≥6 weeks postpartum.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: What is phlegmasia cerulea dolens?
options: An ordinary uncomplicated DVT presenting with only mild calf erythema, warmth and localised tenderness
Superficial thrombophlebitis of the long saphenous vein giving a tender, red, cord-like subcutaneous vein
Massive proximal DVT causing a massively swollen, painful, blue leg with risk of venous gangrene
Acute occlusion of the superficial femoral artery producing a cold, pale, pulseless and painful leg
Chronic post-thrombotic syndrome with venous eczema, brawny oedema and eventual venous ulceration
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.answer: Massive proximal DVT causing a massively swollen, painful, blue leg with risk of venous gangrene
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: Phlegmasia cerulea dolens is a vascular emergency — complete DVT of the iliac and femoral veins causing massive venous obstruction. Risk of compartment syndrome and venous gangrene.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: Which of the following patients does NOT need thrombophilia screening after DVT?
options: Patient with DVT + antiphospholipid syndrome suspected
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: Thrombophilia screening is indicated for unprovoked, recurrent, young patients, or unusual sites. Provoked DVT in an elderly post-surgical patient = low yield; screening rarely changes management.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: Which anticoagulant is preferred for cancer-associated DVT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: DOACs (edoxaban, rivaroxaban) are non-inferior to LMWH for cancer-associated VTE — now preferred over LMWH in most cancer patients without GI malignancy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: A 55-year-old man presents with calf swelling. Wells score = 1. D-dimer = 650 ng/mL (raised). What is the next step?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: Low Wells (≤1) but positive D-dimer = proceed to compression USS. DVT cannot be excluded without imaging when D-dimer is raised, even with a low Wells score.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: What is the mechanism by which DVT causes post-thrombotic syndrome?
options: Organisation of the clot creating an arteriovenous fistula with resulting distal venous hypertension
Arterial embolisation of thrombus to distal tissues causing ischaemic pain and skin ulceration
Lymphatic channel obstruction by the thrombus leading to non-pitting oedema and skin thickening
Direct compressive nerve damage from the thrombus causing chronic pain and sensory loss
Venous valvular damage → venous hypertension → chronic oedema, skin changes, ulceration
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.answer: Venous valvular damage → venous hypertension → chronic oedema, skin changes, ulceration
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: DVT damages venous valves — leading to chronic venous reflux and hypertension. This causes post-thrombotic syndrome affecting 20–50% of DVT patients over 1–2 years.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: In the two-level Wells score for DVT, which single item scores −2 points (making DVT less likely)?
options: An alternative diagnosis at least as likely as DVT
Calf swelling >3 cm vs the other leg
Localised tenderness along the deep veins
Recently bedridden >3 days or major surgery
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.answer: An alternative diagnosis at least as likely as DVT
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: In the Wells DVT score every positive clinical feature (active cancer, immobilisation/paralysis, tenderness, whole-leg or calf swelling, collateral veins, etc.) scores +1. The ONLY item that subtracts is 'an alternative diagnosis at least as likely as DVT', which scores −2. A score of ≥2 makes DVT likely.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: A 58-year-old with known colorectal cancer presents with right leg DVT. Which anticoagulant is relatively contraindicated due to GI bleeding risk?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: In GI malignancy, rivaroxaban and edoxaban are associated with higher GI bleeding. Apixaban and LMWH have more favourable GI safety profiles in this specific setting.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: What is Trousseau's sign in the context of venous thrombosis?
options: A red, warm and tender palpable superficial leg vein
Calf pain on passive foot dorsiflexion in suspected DVT
Carpopedal and facial twitching provoked by hypocalcaemia
Migratory thrombophlebitis associated with occult malignancy
Elicitation of Homans' sign on clinical examination
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.answer: Migratory thrombophlebitis associated with occult malignancy
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: Trousseau's syndrome = recurrent migratory superficial thrombophlebitis as a paraneoplastic phenomenon. Pancreatic cancer is classically associated. (Not to be confused with Trousseau's sign of hypocalcaemia.)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: EXAM PEARL: Which VTE prophylaxis agent is recommended for high-risk surgical patients?
options: Direct oral anticoagulants such as apixaban alone
Warfarin monotherapy titrated to an INR of 2 to 3
Low-dose aspirin combined with early postoperative mobilisation
Unfractionated heparin infusion alone without stockings
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: NICE recommends LMWH + mechanical compression (TED stockings or pneumatic compression) for VTE prophylaxis in high-risk surgical patients. Risk assessed on admission using VTE risk tools.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: A patient with suspected DVT has Wells score ≤1 and a negative D-dimer. What is the correct action?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: Low Wells + negative D-dimer has sufficient NPV to exclude DVT without further imaging. This is the standard diagnostic algorithm recommended by NICE.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: What is the reversal agent for rivaroxaban in life-threatening bleeding?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: Andexanet alfa (recombinant factor Xa decoy protein) specifically reverses factor Xa inhibitors (rivaroxaban, apixaban). Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran. Protamine reverses heparin.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: Which condition is most commonly associated with antiphospholipid syndrome (APS)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: APS is most commonly secondary to SLE (≈30% of SLE patients have antiphospholipid antibodies). It causes arterial/venous thrombosis and recurrent pregnancy loss.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: What are the diagnostic criteria for antiphospholipid syndrome?
options: A purely clinical diagnosis based on recurrent thrombosis and pregnancy loss, with no laboratory antibody confirmation needed at all
A single positive antiphospholipid antibody test taken on one occasion, with no clinical thrombotic or obstetric criterion required
A DVT confirmed on compression ultrasound together with a raised D-dimer, with no antiphospholipid antibody testing required at all
One clinical criterion (thrombosis/pregnancy morbidity) + positive antibody (lupus anticoagulant / anticardiolipin) on two occasions ≥12 weeks apart
Three or more positive antiphospholipid antibody assays taken on a single occasion, with no clinical criterion or repeat testing
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.answer: One clinical criterion (thrombosis/pregnancy morbidity) + positive antibody (lupus anticoagulant / anticardiolipin) on two occasions ≥12 weeks apart
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: Sapporo/Sydney criteria for APS: clinical (arterial/venous thrombosis OR pregnancy morbidity) + laboratory (antibody confirmed twice ≥12 weeks apart) — single positive test insufficient.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the investigation of choice for suspected DVT in a low probability patient with a raised D-dimer?
options: Compression duplex ultrasound of the leg
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.answer: Compression duplex ultrasound of the leg
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: Raised D-dimer (regardless of Wells score) mandates compression USS to exclude DVT. Compression USS is the gold standard for DVT diagnosis — CT is for PE, not DVT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: A patient completes 3 months of anticoagulation for a provoked DVT. How should the recurrence risk be assessed before stopping treatment?
options: Repeat D-dimer testing every month indefinitely to monitor the ongoing recurrence risk
Clinical review — if temporary risk factor has resolved, anticoagulation can stop
Repeat duplex ultrasound of the leg to confirm the clot has fully resolved before stopping
Lifelong anticoagulation is always mandatory regardless of the original provoking factor
Perform a full thrombophilia screen before deciding whether to stop anticoagulation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.answer: Clinical review — if temporary risk factor has resolved, anticoagulation can stop
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: After provoked DVT with a transient reversible cause (surgery, immobility), 3 months is sufficient and anticoagulation can be stopped after clinical review confirming the risk factor has resolved.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: What is the risk of PE in proximal DVT vs distal DVT?
options: Neither proximal nor distal DVT carries any PE risk
Both proximal and distal DVT carry an equal PE risk
Distal calf DVT carries a higher PE risk than proximal
Proximal DVT = higher PE risk (~50%) than distal (<5%)
Distal DVT never embolises or causes pulmonary embolism
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.answer: Proximal DVT = higher PE risk (~50%) than distal (<5%)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: Proximal DVTs (above popliteal fossa) carry significantly higher PE risk than isolated distal calf DVTs. This distinction influences urgency of treatment and follow-up imaging.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: What monitoring is required for rivaroxaban?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: DOACs (rivaroxaban, apixaban, dabigatran) require no routine monitoring — this is a major advantage over warfarin (which requires INR monitoring to maintain 2–3 therapeutic range).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: Which manoeuvre was historically used to assess for DVT but is now known to be unreliable?
options: The Wells clinical probability scoring tool
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: Homan's sign is neither sensitive nor specific for DVT — it should not be used to diagnose or exclude DVT. Wells score + D-dimer + USS is the validated pathway.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: EXAM PEARL: A 50-year-old woman on the OCP presents with a first DVT. What long-term advice should be given?
options: Continue the combined OCP as the DVT is coincidental and unrelated to oestrogen
Stop the combined OCP permanently (switch to progesterone-only or barrier method)
Switch to a lower-dose combined oestrogen pill which is safe after a first DVT
Prescribe anticoagulation and simply continue the combined OCP unchanged
Make no change at all to her current combined hormonal contraception method
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.answer: Stop the combined OCP permanently (switch to progesterone-only or barrier method)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: Combined OCP (oestrogen-containing) significantly increases VTE risk — must be stopped after DVT. Progesterone-only pill or non-hormonal contraception is safer. This also constitutes a provoked DVT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: What is the Wells DVT score for a patient with: swelling of entire leg (+1), tenderness along deep veins (+1), active cancer (+1)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: Wells DVT: score ≥2 = high probability → proceed directly to compression USS. This patient scores 3 (swelling + tenderness + cancer), so D-dimer is not needed — image directly.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: What is the role of an IVC filter in DVT management?
options: First-line treatment for every DVT in place of standard anticoagulation
Prevents PE when anticoagulation is contraindicated (e.g. active bleeding)
Inserted to monitor the response of the clot to anticoagulation therapy
Mandatory in all cancer-associated DVT regardless of bleeding risk
Reliably prevents recurrent DVT in every patient once it is inserted
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.answer: Prevents PE when anticoagulation is contraindicated (e.g. active bleeding)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: IVC filter is a temporary or permanent mechanical barrier placed in the inferior vena cava to prevent pulmonary embolism when anticoagulation is contraindicated — not routine for all DVTs.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: Which clotting factor is deficient in Factor V Leiden thrombophilia?
options: Factor X is congenitally deficient, impairing the common coagulation pathway and raising thrombosis risk
Factor V is completely absent, producing a haemorrhagic bleeding tendency rather than a thrombotic state
Factor V is resistant to inactivation by activated protein C (no deficiency — gain-of-function mutation)
Protein C is deficient, abolishing its normal anticoagulant role and permitting unopposed clot formation
Factor VIII levels are markedly elevated, driving excessive thrombin generation and pathological clotting
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.answer: Factor V is resistant to inactivation by activated protein C (no deficiency — gain-of-function mutation)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: Factor V Leiden = point mutation making Factor V resistant to inactivation by activated protein C — leads to hypercoagulability. It is the most common inherited thrombophilia in Europeans.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: A 68-year-old presents with a first unprovoked DVT. What does current NICE guidance recommend to look for occult cancer?
options: A focused review — history, examination, bloods, CXR and urinalysis (no routine CT)
Routine CT chest/abdomen/pelvis in all patients
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy
A tumour-marker panel (CA-125, CEA, CA19-9) in all patients
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.answer: A focused review — history, examination, bloods, CXR and urinalysis (no routine CT)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: Current NICE does NOT recommend routine extensive cancer screening after unprovoked VTE. Perform a focused assessment — history, examination, baseline bloods, CXR and urinalysis — and investigate further only if this points to a cause. This replaced older advice (routine CT abdomen/pelvis), which was shown to give no benefit.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the most common inherited thrombophilia and what is its inheritance?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: Factor V Leiden is the most common inherited thrombophilia (~5% of Europeans are heterozygous). Autosomal dominant. Homozygous = much higher thrombosis risk. Accounts for ~50% of inherited thrombophilia cases.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: What diameter defines an abdominal aortic aneurysm, and where are most located?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: ≥3 cm; mostly infrarenal
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: An AAA is a permanent localised dilatation of the abdominal aorta ≥3 cm (normal ~2 cm); most are infrarenal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: How do the vast majority of AAAs present?
options: With acute severe back pain radiating to the flank
With acute lower limb ischaemia and absent pulses
Asymptomatic — found on screening or incidentally
With a large upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage
With sudden syncopal collapse and hypotension
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Asymptomatic — found on screening or incidentally
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: The vast majority of AAAs are asymptomatic and found on screening or incidentally — which is why a screening programme exists.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: What is the strongest modifiable risk factor for AAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Smoking
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor for AAA.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: What is the pathological mechanism of AAA formation?
options: Atherosclerotic plaque directly erodes and dilates the aortic wall through progressive luminal narrowing
Acute in-situ thrombosis of the aortic wall occludes flow, causing ischaemic dilatation of the vessel
Chronic inflammation → MMP activation → degradation of elastin and collagen → wall weakening → dilatation
Progressive calcium deposition stiffens the medial layer, which then balloons outward under arterial pressure
Immune complex deposition within the aortic media triggers vasculitic necrosis and aneurysmal outpouching
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Chronic inflammation → MMP activation → degradation of elastin and collagen → wall weakening → dilatation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: Chronic inflammation activates MMPs, which degrade elastin and collagen in the aortic wall, causing progressive weakening and dilatation; atherosclerosis is associated, not directly causative.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: Which major cardiovascular risk factor is protective against AAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Diabetes
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: Diabetes is protective — the only major cardiovascular risk factor that reduces AAA risk; this counterintuitive fact is frequently examined.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: An older man presents with back pain and collapse. What must be assumed until proven otherwise?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Ruptured AAA
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: Back pain + collapse in an older man = ruptured AAA until proven otherwise; renal colic is the key mimic.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: What is found on examination of a symptomatic unruptured AAA?
options: A non-pulsatile mass below the umbilicus
A fixed epigastric mass that does not move
A pulsatile, expansile mass above the umbilicus
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: A pulsatile, expansile mass above the umbilicus
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: Examination reveals a pulsatile, expansile mass above the umbilicus; rarely there are signs of retroperitoneal haemorrhage.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: The National AAA Screening Programme offers screening to which group?
options: All women at age 60 — a one-off abdominal ultrasound
All men at age 65 — a one-off abdominal ultrasound
All adults at age 50 — a one-off abdominal ultrasound
Men and women at age 70 with a screening ultrasound
Only those with a first-degree family history of AAA
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: All men at age 65 — a one-off abdominal ultrasound
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: The programme offers a one-off abdominal ultrasound for all men at age 65; women are not routinely screened (lower risk), with USS considered if >70 with risk factors.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: An AAA measuring 3.0–4.4 cm on screening is classified and managed how?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Small AAA — yearly USS surveillance
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: A 3.0–4.4 cm aorta is a small AAA, managed with yearly USS surveillance.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: An AAA measuring 4.5–5.4 cm warrants what surveillance interval?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: 3-monthly USS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: A 4.5–5.4 cm aorta is a medium AAA, requiring 3-monthly USS surveillance.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: An aorta measuring ≥5.5 cm on screening prompts what action?
options: No further action — reassure and discharge
Repeat a surveillance ultrasound in 5 years
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Refer vascular surgery — consider repair
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: An aorta ≥5.5 cm is a large AAA, prompting referral to vascular surgery to consider repair.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: What are the driving rules for AAA?
options: ≥6 cm → inform DVLA; ≥6.5 cm → disqualified from driving
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: ≥6 cm → inform DVLA; ≥6.5 cm → disqualified from driving
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: AAA ≥6 cm → inform DVLA; AAA ≥6.5 cm → disqualified from driving. Note the thresholds are "or more" — an aorta measuring exactly 6.0 cm must be declared.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: What is the first-line investigation for AAA, and why?
options: MRI aorta — best soft tissue detail
Abdominal USS — cheap, no radiation, repeatable
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Abdominal USS — cheap, no radiation, repeatable
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: Abdominal USS is first-line for diagnosis and surveillance — it is cheap, involves no radiation and is repeatable.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: When is CT angiogram used in AAA?
options: For initial screening of all men aged 65 in place of the standard abdominal ultrasound
Only after open surgical repair to confirm graft position and check for anastomotic leak
Once at threshold (≥5.5 cm) — gives anatomy for EVAR planning; also used in stable rupture
For routine yearly surveillance of small sub-threshold AAAs measuring under 5.5 cm
Never — abdominal ultrasound alone is sufficient for both surveillance and planning
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Once at threshold (≥5.5 cm) — gives anatomy for EVAR planning; also used in stable rupture
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: CT angiogram is used once at threshold (≥5.5 cm) to provide anatomy for EVAR suitability planning, and in stable rupture.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: On ultrasound, how is the AAA distinguished from the IVC?
options: AAA is round, pulsatile, thick-walled; IVC is ovoid, collapsible, thin-walled
