AAA is ovoid, collapsible, thin-walled; IVC is round, pulsatile, thick-walled
AAA lies behind the vertebral body; IVC lies in front
They cannot be distinguished on USS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: AAA is round, pulsatile, thick-walled; IVC is ovoid, collapsible, thin-walled
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: On USS the AAA is round, pulsatile and thick-walled, while the IVC is ovoid, collapsible and thin-walled, with the vertebral body shadow below.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: Which measure has been shown to reduce the growth rate and rupture risk of an AAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Stopping smoking
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: Smoking cessation is the only measure shown to reduce the growth rate and rupture risk of an AAA, and smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor for developing one in the first place. No drug treatment is recommended to slow an aneurysm or prevent rupture — statins, antiplatelets, ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers have all been looked at and the evidence does not support any of them for that purpose (NICE). Most of these patients are nevertheless on a statin, often an antiplatelet, and have their blood pressure controlled, but that is for their overall cardiovascular risk as older vasculopaths, not treatment of the aneurysm.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: Which of the following is an indication for surgical repair of an AAA?
options: Diameter of 4.0 cm on surveillance ultrasound
Slow growth of only 0.3 cm per year on scans
An asymptomatic 3.5 cm AAA found on screening
Growth of >1 cm in one year in an aneurysm already >4.0 cm
Any AAA detected in a patient older than 65
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Growth of >1 cm in one year in an aneurysm already >4.0 cm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: The indications for repair are a diameter of 5.5 cm or more; an aneurysm already larger than 4.0 cm that has grown by more than 1 cm in one year; or a symptomatic aneurysm. The >4.0 cm context matters — an aneurysm below 4.0 cm is not repaired on growth alone. A 4.0 cm aneurysm, growth of only 0.3 cm/year, an asymptomatic 3.5 cm aneurysm and age alone all stay under surveillance.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: Why might repair be deferred in some patients despite a diameter ≥5.5 cm?
options: In unfit patients, due to elective surgical mortality risk
Because aneurysms smaller than 6 cm essentially never rupture
Because EVAR is unavailable at the local vascular centre
To allow further cross-sectional imaging and surgical planning
Because co-existing diabetes is protective against rupture
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: In unfit patients, due to elective surgical mortality risk
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: In unfit or high-risk patients, the mortality of elective repair may outweigh the annual risk of rupture, so surveillance is continued and the decision revisited. The threshold is a starting point for the conversation, not an automatic trigger to operate.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: What is the examinable trade-off between EVAR and open AAA repair?
options: EVAR is more durable long-term; open has lower peri-op mortality
Open repair has a higher reintervention rate
EVAR = better short-term; open = better long-term durability
EVAR is only used for ruptures
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: EVAR = better short-term; open = better long-term durability
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: EVAR offers better short-term outcomes (lower peri-op mortality, shorter stay) while open repair offers better long-term durability with fewer reinterventions. Both are technically valid, but in the UK open repair is offered first-line for unruptured infrarenal AAA, with EVAR reserved for those unsuitable for open surgery (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: Which is a disadvantage of EVAR compared with open repair?
options: Higher 30-day post-operative mortality than open repair
Longer hospital stay and a slower initial recovery
A longer overall recovery period after the procedure
A much larger midline laparotomy incision is required
Higher reintervention rate + endoleak risk + late rupture
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Higher reintervention rate + endoleak risk + late rupture
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: EVAR has lower 30-day mortality and a shorter stay, but a higher reintervention rate, endoleak risk and late rupture.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: What is the overall mortality of a ruptured AAA, and which rupture site is more common?
options: 80% mortality; 80% retroperitoneal (posterior — may be temporarily contained)
50% mortality; rupture is mostly anterior into the free peritoneal cavity
30% mortality; rupture is usually posterior into the inferior vena cava
95% mortality; virtually all ruptures are anterior and intraperitoneal
20% mortality; rupture is mostly retroperitoneal and often contained
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: 80% mortality; 80% retroperitoneal (posterior — may be temporarily contained)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: Ruptured AAA carries 80% overall mortality; 80% of ruptures are retroperitoneal (posterior, may be temporarily contained), 20% into the peritoneal cavity (anterior, very poor prognosis).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: What is the classic triad of a ruptured AAA?
options: Central chest pain + acute dyspnoea + a raised JVP
Flank/back pain + hypotension + pulsatile abdominal mass
High fever + generalised abdominal pain + watery diarrhoea
Severe headache + sudden visual loss + generalised seizures
Frank haematuria + severe loin pain + burning dysuria
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Flank/back pain + hypotension + pulsatile abdominal mass
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: The classic ruptured AAA triad is flank/back pain + hypotension + pulsatile abdominal mass. It is present in only about a quarter to a half of cases, so its absence does not exclude a rupture.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: Why might SpO₂ appear falsely normal in a ruptured AAA, and what is done?
options: The pulse oximeter probe is faulty; replace it and re-measure the saturation
SpO₂ always reads low in rupture, so any normal value reliably excludes it
Hypotension paradoxically raises the measured oxygen saturation reading
The patient is hyperventilating and over-saturated; withhold supplemental O₂
Remaining Hb is fully saturated despite blood loss — still give high-flow O₂
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Remaining Hb is fully saturated despite blood loss — still give high-flow O₂
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: SpO₂ may be falsely normal because the remaining Hb is fully saturated despite blood loss — still give high-flow O₂.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: In a ruptured AAA, what is the permissive hypotension target and its rationale?
options: Aim SBP >120 mmHg to keep vital organs adequately perfused during resuscitation
Aim SBP <100 mmHg — raising BP dislodges the tamponading clot → torrential haemorrhage
Aim MAP >90 mmHg to guarantee full cerebral and renal perfusion until repair
Aim for an SBP of 140 mmHg to maintain flow through the narrowed aortic segment
No blood pressure target is needed; simply transfuse back to normal values
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Aim SBP <100 mmHg — raising BP dislodges the tamponading clot → torrential haemorrhage
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: Permissive hypotension means restrictive fluid resuscitation — accepting a low blood pressure rather than chasing a normal one, because raising it dislodges the tamponading clot and causes torrential haemorrhage. NICE gives the principle rather than a fixed target; the practical endpoint is the conscious level and a palpable radial pulse, and a systolic under about 100 mmHg is the figure usually quoted for teaching.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: A man with a ruptured AAA arrives peri-arrest — unrecordable blood pressure, falling GCS. How is he managed?
options: CT angiogram first to define the anatomy, then proceed to EVAR only if suitable
Arrange yearly ultrasound surveillance and routine outpatient vascular review
Conservative care with permissive hypotension and close observation on the ward only
Immediate transfer to theatre for open repair — no time for imaging, do NOT delay with CT
Discharge home with early outpatient vascular clinic follow-up and analgesia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Immediate transfer to theatre for open repair — no time for imaging, do NOT delay with CT
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: A peri-arrest patient goes straight to theatre for open repair — there is no time for imaging. That is the exception, not the rule: a patient who is shocked but resuscitatable still gets a CT angiogram if it can be done without delaying repair, because it determines whether EVAR is feasible. In rupture EVAR gives more benefit for most people, particularly women of any age and men over 70 (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: How is a stable patient with a ruptured AAA managed?
options: Immediate open surgical repair in theatre without any pre-operative imaging
Permissive hypotension with analgesia, then discharge home once the pain settles
CT angiogram first, assess anatomy + EVAR suitability, EVAR if suitable / open if not
Routine ultrasound surveillance with interval outpatient vascular follow-up
Crossmatch blood only and observe on the ward without any active intervention
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: CT angiogram first, assess anatomy + EVAR suitability, EVAR if suitable / open if not
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: A stable ruptured AAA gets CT angiogram first to assess anatomy and EVAR suitability — EVAR if suitable, open if not.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: What is an endoleak following EVAR?
options: Incomplete seal → blood leaks into the aneurysm sac around the graft → sac re-expands → risk of rupture
Bacterial infection of the endovascular graft causing systemic sepsis and graft breakdown
Migration of the deployed graft down into the iliac arteries, obstructing distal limb flow
Acute thrombosis of the endovascular stent, occluding the graft and causing limb ischaemia
Rupture of the femoral arterial access site, producing a large expanding groin haematoma
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Incomplete seal → blood leaks into the aneurysm sac around the graft → sac re-expands → risk of rupture
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: An endoleak is an incomplete seal around the graft allowing blood into the aneurysm sac, causing the sac to re-expand with a risk of rupture.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: What should prompt investigation for an endoleak after EVAR?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Any post-EVAR sac expansion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: Endoleaks are usually asymptomatic, so any post-EVAR sac expansion should prompt investigation for an endoleak.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: How does the aetiology of AAA differ from thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA)?
options: AAA is predominantly degenerative/inflammatory, whereas TAA has a different aetiology (Marfan's, bicuspid AV, dissection)
AAA is mostly caused by Marfan's syndrome and a bicuspid aortic valve, the same connective-tissue processes seen in TAA
Both AAA and TAA share an identical degenerative aetiology driven by atherosclerosis and connective-tissue disease
TAA is predominantly degenerative/inflammatory, whereas AAA is congenital, arising from Marfan's and a bicuspid valve
AAA is almost always infective (mycotic), seeding the aortic wall from a distant bacterial focus elsewhere
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: AAA is predominantly degenerative/inflammatory, whereas TAA has a different aetiology (Marfan's, bicuspid AV, dissection)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: AAA is predominantly degenerative/inflammatory; TAA has a different aetiology (Marfan's, bicuspid AV, dissection) and is kept separate.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: A 68-year-old man is found to have a 5.8 cm AAA on USS. He is asymptomatic. What is the recommended management?
options: Urgent elective repair (EVAR or open) — threshold 5.5 cm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Urgent elective repair (EVAR or open) — threshold 5.5 cm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: UK practice: elective AAA repair is offered once the diameter reaches 5.5 cm — the same threshold for men and women. At 5.8 cm he is above it, so he is referred for repair. Below 5.5 cm the risk of elective surgery outweighs the risk of rupture; above it, that balance reverses. European guidance differs here — it allows repair to be considered at 5.0 cm in women — but for UK finals the threshold is 5.5 cm for both sexes (NICE). Which repair he is offered is a separate question: in the UK open repair is the default for unruptured infrarenal AAA.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: What is EVAR and when is it preferred over open repair?
options: EVAR can only be performed under general anaesthesia with full laparotomy exposure of the aorta
EVAR is always the first-line option regardless of aortic neck anatomy or iliac access suitability
EVAR avoids the need for any long-term imaging follow-up
Endovascular aortic aneurysm repair — preferred in older/high operative risk patients if anatomy suitable
EVAR cannot be used in a ruptured AAA and is strictly reserved for stable elective cases only
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Endovascular aortic aneurysm repair — preferred in older/high operative risk patients if anatomy suitable
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: EVAR = stent-graft deployed via the femoral arteries. Lower 30-day mortality than open repair, so it is favoured in older or comorbid patients — but only if the aneurysm anatomy will accommodate the graft, which is a specialist assessment. It commits the patient to lifelong imaging surveillance for endoleak.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: Roughly what is the annual rupture risk once an AAA reaches 5.5 cm, and how does that risk change with diameter?
options: Less than 1% per year, essentially unchanged as diameter rises
Around 5–10% per year, rising steeply — not linearly — with diameter
Around 50% per year, rising linearly once it passes 5 cm
It only ruptures once it has grown beyond 7 cm diameter
Rupture risk rises in a linear fashion with diameter
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Around 5–10% per year, rising steeply — not linearly — with diameter
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: Rupture risk rises steeply with diameter rather than in proportion to it. Broadly: below 4 cm the annual risk is very low (well under 1%); 4–5.4 cm carries a low single-figure risk; around 5.5–6 cm it reaches roughly 5–10% per year; and above 6 cm it climbs sharply higher. 5.5 cm is the UK repair threshold precisely because that is the point at which the annual rupture risk starts to exceed the roughly 1–3% mortality of elective repair.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: What investigation is used to plan EVAR in an elective AAA patient?
options: Duplex ultrasound of the aorta and both iliac vessels to assess anatomy
CT angiography of the aorta — shows if the anatomy suits a stent-graft
Conventional invasive catheter angiography of the aorta and iliacs
MRI of the aorta with gadolinium contrast for detailed luminal anatomy
A plain supine abdominal X-ray demonstrating aortic wall calcification
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: CT angiography of the aorta — shows if the anatomy suits a stent-graft
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: CT angiography is required before EVAR: it shows the size and extent of the aneurysm and whether the anatomy will take a stent-graft. Ultrasound is the screening and surveillance tool but does not give the anatomical detail needed to plan the repair.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: Diabetes is consistently associated with a lower risk of AAA. What is the best-supported explanation?
options: Diabetics have consistently higher HDL cholesterol, which protects the aortic wall
Diabetics reliably run lower systemic blood pressures, reducing aortic wall stress
Circulating insulin acts directly on elastin to strengthen the aortic wall matrix
Insulin therapy directly inhibits matrix metalloproteinase activity in the aortic wall
Diabetes promotes collagen crosslinking → stiffer aortic wall resistant to dilation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Diabetes promotes collagen crosslinking → stiffer aortic wall resistant to dilation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: Counter-intuitively, diabetes is associated with a reduced AAA risk. Advanced glycation end-products cause collagen crosslinking → a stiffer, less compliant aortic wall that resists aneurysmal dilation. This is despite diabetes increasing atherosclerosis risk. The mechanism is not settled — some of the effect may come from antidiabetic drugs rather than the disease itself — but glycation-driven crosslinking is the explanation to give.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: How does mortality after a ruptured AAA compare with that of planned elective repair?
options: Elective open surgical repair carries a very high 30-day operative mortality of around 20 to 25%
Ruptured: around 80% survive to discharge; elective repair: only 50% survive the first month
Both ruptured and elective repair carry a broadly similar overall 5-year survival rate of about 60%
Ruptured AAA carries markedly better long-term survival outcomes than planned elective repair
Ruptured: ~50% die before reaching hospital, survival <25%. Elective repair: ~1–3%
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Ruptured: ~50% die before reaching hospital, survival <25%. Elective repair: ~1–3%
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: Ruptured AAA: ~50% die before reaching hospital; of those who reach hospital and have surgery, mortality is ~40%; overall survival <25%. This catastrophic prognosis justifies elective repair when the diameter reaches 5.5 cm, against a UK in-hospital mortality for planned repair of only around 1–3%.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: A 72-year-old man underwent open repair of a 6 cm infrarenal AAA. On the third post-operative day he develops left-sided abdominal pain and passes bloody diarrhoea. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Colonic ischaemia
explanation: Colonic ischaemia — the inferior mesenteric artery is sacrificed during open AAA repair, leaving the left colon dependent on collateral supply. When that is inadequate the colon becomes ischaemic, typically presenting in the first few post-operative days with pain and bloody diarrhoea. Urgent flexible sigmoidoscopy is the investigation.
C. difficile colitis — possible after antibiotics but usually presents later and with watery rather than bloody stool, without this vascular mechanism.
Graft infection — a later complication, presenting with fever and systemic sepsis rather than early bloody diarrhoea.
Aortoenteric fistula — causes major gastrointestinal haemorrhage, characteristically months to years after repair, not on day three.
Small bowel obstruction — causes vomiting and distension with absolute constipation, not bloody diarrhoea.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: A patient is choosing between open repair and EVAR for a 5.8 cm infrarenal AAA. Which statement about EVAR should form part of the consent discussion?
options: It requires lifelong imaging surveillance for endoleak or migration
It is more durable in the long term than open repair
It carries a higher 30-day mortality than open repair
It removes the aneurysm sac entirely
It requires no follow-up once the initial scan is satisfactory
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: It requires lifelong imaging surveillance for endoleak or migration
explanation: It requires lifelong imaging surveillance for endoleak or migration — the stent can leak or migrate at any point, allowing the sac to re-expand and rupture, so imaging continues indefinitely. This is the principal trade-off against its lower peri-operative mortality.
More durable long term — the opposite; open repair has the better long-term durability and a lower reintervention rate.
Higher 30-day mortality — incorrect; EVAR's advantage is precisely a lower peri-operative mortality and shorter stay.
Removes the sac — EVAR lines the aneurysm from within; the sac remains, which is why it can re-pressurise via an endoleak.
No follow-up needed — the reverse, and a patient who defaults loses the protection the procedure provided.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: What is the pathological hallmark of infective endocarditis?
options: A fibrinous pericardial exudate coating the epicardium, a sign of acute pericarditis
The vegetation — a mass of platelets, fibrin, organisms and inflammatory cells
A myocardial abscess of necrotic muscle, the defining lesion of acute viral myocarditis
Concentric ventricular hypertrophy from chronic pressure overload, as in aortic stenosis
A dilated aortic root with cystic medial degeneration, the hallmark of Marfan aortopathy
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: The vegetation — a mass of platelets, fibrin, organisms and inflammatory cells
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: The vegetation — platelets, fibrin, organisms and inflammatory cells on the endocardium/valves — is the pathological hallmark of IE.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: How do acute IE and subacute bacterial endocarditis (SBE) classically differ?
options: Acute: fulminant (hours–days), normal/damaged valves, Staph aureus; subacute: insidious (weeks–months), damaged valves, Strep viridans
Acute: indolent over weeks-months caused by Strep viridans on damaged valves; subacute: fulminant over hours-days caused by Staph aureus on normal valves
Both forms run a fulminant hours-to-days course driven by Staph aureus on previously normal valves, with no insidious subacute variant existing at all
Acute: affects only prosthetic valves early after surgery; subacute: affects only native valves, differing solely by valve type and not by clinical tempo
They are identical in tempo and organism, both progressing over weeks with Strep viridans and showing no clinical or microbiological distinction of note
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Acute: fulminant (hours–days), normal/damaged valves, Staph aureus; subacute: insidious (weeks–months), damaged valves, Strep viridans
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Acute IE is fulminant (hours–days), often Staph aureus on normal or damaged valves; subacute SBE is insidious (weeks–months), classically Strep viridans on damaged valves.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: What is the single strongest risk factor for infective endocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Previous infective endocarditis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Previous IE is the strongest risk factor for developing IE.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: What is the approximate in-hospital mortality of IE, and how often is surgery needed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: 20–30% mortality; surgery in ~50%
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: IE has an in-hospital mortality of 20–30%, with surgery required in roughly half of cases.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: A patient who injects drugs develops IE. Which organism and valve are most likely?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Staph aureus; tricuspid (right-sided)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Staph aureus is the most common organism overall and the classic cause in IVDU, where right-sided (tricuspid) IE predominates.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: IE following poor dental hygiene or a dental procedure is classically caused by which organism?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Strep viridans
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Strep viridans, an oral commensal, classically causes IE after poor dental hygiene or dental procedures.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: Prosthetic valve IE occurring within 2 months of surgery is most likely due to which organism?
options: Strep viridans seeded from oral flora
Strep bovis from a colonic source
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Staph epidermidis (coagulase-negative)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Early prosthetic valve IE (<2 months, perioperative contamination) is classically caused by coagulase-negative Staph epidermidis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: Strep bovis is isolated from blood cultures in a patient with IE. What does this mandate?
options: An urgent dental review to find an oral source of infection
Colonoscopy to exclude colorectal carcinoma ('bovis = bowel')
A bronchoscopy to look for an occult bronchial carcinoma
An immediate valve replacement before any further imaging
A skin biopsy to identify a cutaneous portal of entry
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Colonoscopy to exclude colorectal carcinoma ('bovis = bowel')
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Strep bovis IE is linked to colorectal cancer ('bovis = bowel'), so colonoscopy is mandated to exclude colorectal carcinoma.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: Which set of organisms/causes is associated with culture-negative IE?
options: Staph aureus and Strep viridans, the usual readily culturable causes
HACEK organisms, Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella, Brucella, and prior antibiotics
Enterococcus and Staph epidermidis, both growing easily on standard media
Candida and Aspergillus only, as the sole fungal culture-negative causes
Strep bovis and Strep pneumoniae, both routinely recovered on blood agar
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: HACEK organisms, Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella, Brucella, and prior antibiotics
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Culture-negative IE is caused by fastidious organisms (HACEK, Coxiella/Q fever, Bartonella, Brucella, Tropheryma whipplei) or by prior antibiotic administration. HACEK are the classic group, though modern automated blood cultures usually grow them within about 5 days.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: Which conditions cause non-infective (sterile) vegetations?
options: Prosthetic valves and congenital heart disease
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: SLE (Libman-Sacks) and malignancy (marantic endocarditis)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Sterile vegetations occur in SLE (Libman-Sacks endocarditis) and malignancy (marantic endocarditis).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: What is the correct sequence of events in vegetation formation?
options: Bacteraemia seeds a normal valve, then dystrophic calcification and a mature vegetation form
Systemic embolisation, then valve infarction, then a vegetation growing at the infarcted site
Immune complex deposition on the valve leaflet, then progressive fibrosis, then a vegetation
Endothelial damage → platelet-fibrin thrombus → pathogen seeding during bacteraemia → vegetation
The vegetation forms first on intact endothelium, then causes secondary endothelial damage
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Endothelial damage → platelet-fibrin thrombus → pathogen seeding during bacteraemia → vegetation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Endothelial damage allows a platelet-fibrin thrombus to form, which is then seeded by pathogens during bacteraemia to create a vegetation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: The three consequence streams of IE explain almost every sign. What are they?
options: Inflammation, progressive fibrosis and dystrophic calcification
Local destruction, embolisation, immune complex deposition
Bacteraemia, systemic sepsis and circulatory shock
Tissue ischaemia, infarction and myocardial scarring
Valve stenosis, regurgitation and leaflet prolapse
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Local destruction, embolisation, immune complex deposition
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: The three streams — local destruction, embolisation, and immune complex deposition — account for almost all the signs of IE.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: A patient with aortic-valve IE develops a new AV block on ECG. What does this most likely indicate?
options: A septic pulmonary embolus reaching the conduction system from the right heart
Drug-induced bradycardia from beta-blockers given to control the fever
Immune complex glomerulonephritis causing uraemic slowing of AV conduction
A Janeway lesion embolising to the atrioventricular node and blocking it
An aortic root / annulus abscess from local destruction — a surgical emergency
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: An aortic root / annulus abscess from local destruction — a surgical emergency
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: A new AV block reflects an aortic root/annulus abscess (local destruction extending into the conduction system) and is a surgical emergency until proven otherwise.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: Which finding belongs to the EMBOLISATION stream of IE?
options: Osler's nodes, the painful immune-complex vasculitic lesions of the finger pulps
Roth spots, the immune-mediated retinal haemorrhages with pale centres seen
Glomerulonephritis, an immune-complex deposition phenomenon within the kidney
Janeway lesions (painless infarcts) and septic pulmonary emboli (right-sided)
Splinter haemorrhages, the immune-complex microvascular lesions under the nails
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Janeway lesions (painless infarcts) and septic pulmonary emboli (right-sided)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Embolic phenomena include Janeway lesions (painless infarcts), left-sided emboli (brain, spleen, kidneys, coronary), and right-sided septic pulmonary emboli.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: Which findings belong to the IMMUNE COMPLEX stream of IE?
options: Janeway lesions and embolic stroke, both from vegetation embolisation
Septic pulmonary emboli seeding the lungs from right-sided vegetations
Osler's nodes, Roth spots, splinter haemorrhages and glomerulonephritis
Valve regurgitation and heart failure from local leaflet destruction
Aortic root abscess extending from direct local valvular invasion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Osler's nodes, Roth spots, splinter haemorrhages and glomerulonephritis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Immune complex deposition produces small-vessel vasculitis: Osler's nodes, Roth spots, splinter haemorrhages, and glomerulonephritis (with raised RF).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: What is the most consistent clinical sign of infective endocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Fever
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Fever is the most consistent sign of IE, alongside malaise, night sweats and weight loss.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: Approximately what proportion of patients with infective endocarditis have a murmur?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: A murmur is present in roughly 85% of IE cases. A genuinely NEW or CHANGING murmur is much less common but far more specific — it is the changing murmur, not the murmur itself, that is the classic sign.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: What is the classic exam discrimination between Janeway lesions and Osler's nodes?
options: Both are painful immune-complex phenomena affecting the finger and toe pulps with identical pathophysiology
Both are painless embolic infarcts scattered over the palms and soles with no immune component at all
Janeway = painful vasculitic nodules; Osler's = painless embolic macules on the soles, with features swapped
Janeway = painless embolic infarcts (palms/soles); Osler's = painful immune vasculitis (finger/toe pulps)
Janeway = retinal haemorrhages; Osler's = subungual splinter haemorrhages of the nail beds
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Janeway = painless embolic infarcts (palms/soles); Osler's = painful immune vasculitis (finger/toe pulps)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Janeway lesions are painless embolic infarcts on the palms/soles; Osler's nodes ('Ouch') are painful immune-vasculitic nodules on the finger/toe pulps.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: How should blood cultures be taken in suspected IE?
options: A single set after starting antibiotics
1 set from a central line only
2 sets from the same site after antibiotics
3 sets from different sites before antibiotics
Cultures are not needed if echo is positive
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: 3 sets from different sites before antibiotics
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Three sets from different sites are taken before antibiotics; ≥2 positive with a typical organism is a major Duke criterion, and persistent bacteraemia is characteristic. This applies to the stable or subacute presentation — in severe sepsis or septic shock, 2 sets from different sites are taken within an hour and antibiotics started immediately rather than delayed.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: A patient has a normal transthoracic echo but strong clinical suspicion of IE. What is the correct next step?
options: IE is excluded by the normal echo, so the diagnostic workup can be stopped
Repeat the transthoracic echo in 6 weeks rather than escalating imaging now
Proceed to transoesophageal echo (TOE) — a normal echo does not exclude IE
Start empirical antibiotics and discharge the patient for outpatient review
Perform a CT coronary angiogram to seek the source of the emboli
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Proceed to transoesophageal echo (TOE) — a normal echo does not exclude IE
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: A normal echo does not exclude IE; with strong clinical suspicion, TOE (more sensitive) is indicated, especially for prosthetic valves, poor windows, or complications.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: What is the characteristic echocardiographic finding in IE?
options: A vegetation — a mobile echogenic mass attached to a valve leaflet
A pericardial effusion with diastolic right-atrial collapse
Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with a small cavity
A dilated aortic root measured well above four centimetres
A septal bounce indicating constrictive pericardial physiology
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: A vegetation — a mobile echogenic mass attached to a valve leaflet
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: The characteristic echo finding is a vegetation: a mobile echogenic mass attached to a valve leaflet.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: Under the Modified Duke criteria, which combination establishes 'definite IE'?
options: 1 major criterion alone is sufficient to confirm definite IE
3 minor criteria on their own establish definite disease
2 major, OR 1 major + 3 minor, OR 5 minor, OR pathological proof
1 minor criterion combined with any positive echo finding
Any fever above 38°C accompanied by any audible cardiac murmur
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: 2 major, OR 1 major + 3 minor, OR 5 minor, OR pathological proof
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Definite IE = 2 major, or 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor, or pathological proof.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: Which of the following is a MAJOR Duke criterion?
options: Fever above 38°C, which is only one of the recognised minor supporting criteria rather than a major one
Janeway lesions, a vascular embolic phenomenon that is classified only among the minor Duke criteria
A predisposing cardiac risk factor such as a prosthetic valve or intravenous drug use, counted as a minor criterion
Endocardial involvement (vegetation, abscess, or prosthetic dehiscence on echo; or new valvular regurgitation)
A raised rheumatoid factor, an immunological phenomenon counted merely as a minor Duke criterion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Endocardial involvement (vegetation, abscess, or prosthetic dehiscence on echo; or new valvular regurgitation)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: The two major criteria are positive blood cultures with a typical organism and endocardial involvement on echo (or new valvular regurgitation). Fever, risk factors, Janeway lesions and raised RF are minor criteria.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: Why does IE require prolonged IV bactericidal antibiotics?
options: Oral antibiotics are unavailable for these organisms, so the intravenous route must be used over many weeks
Because essentially all endocarditis organisms are inherently resistant to short oral antibiotic courses
To eradicate the dental focus that seeded the valve and prevent recurrent oral bacteraemia over time
The avascular vegetation has poor vascular penetration, requiring high drug concentrations for weeks
To directly suppress the circulating immune complexes that drive the systemic manifestations of disease
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: The avascular vegetation has poor vascular penetration, requiring high drug concentrations for weeks
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: The vegetation is avascular with poor drug penetration, so prolonged IV bactericidal antibiotics at high concentrations are needed to sterilise it.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: What is the first-line regimen for native-valve MSSA Staph aureus IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Flucloxacillin IV for 4–6 weeks
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Native-valve MSSA endocarditis is treated with IV flucloxacillin for 4–6 weeks; vancomycin + rifampicin is the penicillin-allergic/MRSA alternative.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: What is the empirical (blind) regimen for native-valve IE, and the penicillin-allergy/MRSA alternative?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Amoxicillin (± gentamicin); vancomycin + gentamicin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Empirical native-valve therapy is amoxicillin ± gentamicin; if penicillin-allergic or MRSA, vancomycin + gentamicin.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: What is the regimen for MRSA infective endocarditis?
options: Flucloxacillin given for a full 4 to 6 weeks
Amoxicillin combined with gentamicin for 4 weeks
Rifampicin used as monotherapy across 6 weeks
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Vancomycin + rifampicin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: MRSA endocarditis is treated with vancomycin + rifampicin (at least 4 weeks on a native valve; add gentamicin and extend to ≥6 weeks for a prosthetic valve). Daptomycin is an alternative to vancomycin.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: Which of the following is an indication for surgery in IE?
options: A single positive blood culture growing from just one venepuncture site
An isolated Roth spot seen on fundoscopy without any other systemic feature
Fever settling promptly within 48 hours of starting appropriate antibiotics
Severe heart failure from acute valve regurgitation with haemodynamic compromise
A small vegetation under 5 mm that is shrinking on antibiotic therapy
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Severe heart failure from acute valve regurgitation with haemodynamic compromise
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Surgical indications fall into three groups: heart failure (severe HF from acute regurgitation, valve destruction), uncontrolled infection (root abscess — especially with AV block, resistant organisms, prosthetic dehiscence or persistent bacteraemia), and prevention of embolism (recurrent emboli despite antibiotics, large vegetations).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: An IVDU presents with right-sided IE. Which imaging finding would you expect?
options: Cavitating lung lesions on CXR from septic pulmonary emboli
A globular, flask-shaped cardiac silhouette on the chest film
Bilateral pleural effusions blunting both costophrenic angles
A widened mediastinum suggesting proximal aortic involvement
Pericardial calcification encircling the cardiac border
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Cavitating lung lesions on CXR from septic pulmonary emboli
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Right-sided (tricuspid) IE in IVDU sends septic emboli to the lungs, producing cavitating lung lesions on CXR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: Resistance to which type of organism is itself an indication for surgery in IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Fungi and highly resistant bacteria
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Fungal IE and infection with highly resistant bacteria are difficult to clear with antibiotics alone and are indications for surgery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: What are the Duke criteria used for in infective endocarditis?
options: Diagnosis of IE using major and minor criteria
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Diagnosis of IE using major and minor criteria
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Duke criteria: definite IE = 2 major, or 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor criteria. Major: positive blood cultures + echocardiographic evidence (vegetation/abscess/dehiscence). Widely used in clinical practice.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: What is the most sensitive imaging modality for detecting IE vegetations and perivalvular complications?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Transoesophageal echocardiography (TOE)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: TOE is more sensitive than TTE for vegetations (<5 mm), perivalvular abscesses, prosthetic valve IE. TTE is the first-line investigation; TOE is done if TTE is inconclusive or a prosthetic valve is present — and also when the TTE is positive, to exclude perivalvular complications (ESC).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: Which organism is the most common cause of native valve infective endocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Staphylococcus aureus, a skin commensal
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: In the developed world, Staphylococcus aureus is now the most common cause of infective endocarditis overall, including native-valve IE (acute, often on normal or damaged valves). Streptococcus viridans — from the oral flora, seeded during dental procedures — is the classic cause of SUBACUTE IE and was historically the commonest. Staph aureus also predominates in IVDU (right-sided/tricuspid).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: A 55-year-old with aortic stenosis develops fever, new aortic regurgitation, and embolic stroke. Which complication of IE is most likely responsible?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Vegetation embolising to the brain
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Embolic complications of IE occur in ~30% — cerebral emboli cause ischaemic stroke. Left-sided IE (aortic/mitral) causes systemic emboli; right-sided causes pulmonary emboli. Embolic stroke = IE until proven otherwise in appropriate context.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: A patient with a mechanical aortic valve develops fever and bacteraemia with Staph epidermidis. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: TOE (transoesophageal echocardiography)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Prosthetic valve endocarditis requires TOE — TTE has poor sensitivity for prosthetic valves due to acoustic shadowing. TOE can visualise perivalvular abscesses and dehiscence which are critical for management decisions.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: A 74-year-old with a permanent pacemaker implanted 2 years ago presents with 6 weeks of fever and malaise. Blood cultures grow coagulase-negative staphylococci from 3 sets. Transoesophageal echo shows a mobile vegetation on a pacing lead. He is started on appropriate IV antibiotics. What else is essential?
options: Complete extraction of the generator and leads
Prolonging the antibiotic course to 12 weeks
Replacing the generator but leaving the leads in situ
Adding rifampicin and continuing with the system in place
Repeating blood cultures weekly and observing
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Complete extraction of the generator and leads
explanation: Complete extraction of the generator and leads — the hardware is colonised and biofilm on the leads is not penetrated by antibiotics. Full system removal plus antibiotics is required, exactly as for an infected prosthetic valve.
A longer antibiotic course — will not eradicate biofilm on retained hardware; relapse is the rule.
Replacing the generator but leaving the leads — the leads carry the vegetation, so this leaves the infected material behind.

Adding rifampicin with the system in place — rifampicin has useful activity against staphylococcal biofilm and is used in prosthetic infection, but it is an adjunct, not a substitute for removing the hardware.
Observation — inadequate for established device endocarditis and risks ongoing septic embolisation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: Which organisms are most characteristic of infective endocarditis involving a cardiac pacemaker lead?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Coagulase-negative staphylococci and Staph aureus
explanation: Coagulase-negative staphylococci and Staph aureus — device-related endocarditis behaves like early prosthetic valve infection, because both involve implanted foreign material colonised with skin flora that form biofilm.
Strep viridans — the organism of subacute native-valve endocarditis following dental procedures.
Strep bovis — associated with colorectal carcinoma and prompts colonoscopy, not device infection.
Coxiella and Bartonella — classic causes of culture-negative endocarditis; here the cultures are positive.
Enterococcus faecalis — typically follows genitourinary or gastrointestinal instrumentation rather than device implantation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: How is bradycardia defined, and what is the most clinically important distinction?
options: HR <60 bpm; narrow vs broad QRS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: HR <60 bpm; symptomatic vs incidental
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Bradycardia is HR <60 bpm. The key clinical distinction is symptomatic (haemodynamic compromise → needs treatment) vs incidental (e.g. athlete or sleep → physiologically normal).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: What is the central organising principle for understanding bradycardias and heart block?
options: The patient's age determines the prognosis
The anatomical level of the block determines everything
The P-wave morphology determines the cause
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: The anatomical level of the block determines everything
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: The anatomical level of the block determines the escape rate, QRS width, escape reliability, response to atropine, and whether pacing is needed.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: What are the typical features of a block at the SA node level?
options: Ventricular escape <40 bpm, broad QRS, atropine ineffective
Slow sinus rate (not an escape), narrow QRS, atropine works
Junctional escape 40–60 bpm, broad QRS, pacing mandatory
Escape ~30 bpm, narrow QRS, atropine works
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Slow sinus rate (not an escape), narrow QRS, atropine works
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: SA node-level problems (sinus bradycardia, sick sinus) keep a P wave before every QRS — the sinus rate is simply slow, not a true escape. The QRS is narrow and atropine works.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: An infranodal (His-Purkinje) block produces which set of features?
options: Escape around 60 bpm, narrow QRS, and atropine works well
Junctional escape 40–60 bpm, narrow QRS, usually benign
Ventricular escape <40 bpm, broad QRS, atropine ineffective — must pace
Escape around 50 bpm, narrow QRS, responds well to atropine
No bradycardia at all, simply a conduction delay
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Ventricular escape <40 bpm, broad QRS, atropine ineffective — must pace
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Infranodal blocks (Mobitz II, CHB with broad escape) give a ventricular escape <40 bpm, broad QRS, and atropine is ineffective — the patient must be paced.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Which statement captures the key principle linking the level of block to the escape rhythm?
options: The lower the block, the faster and narrower the escape — and the more stable and reliable it is
The lower the block, the slower and broader the escape — and the less reliable it is
The level of block has no effect at all on the escape rate, width, or its reliability
Higher blocks always need immediate permanent pacing regardless of the escape rhythm present
The escape rate is always fixed at exactly 60 bpm regardless of the level of block
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: The lower the block, the slower and broader the escape — and the less reliable it is
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: The lower the block, the slower, broader and less reliable the escape rhythm becomes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Why is atropine ineffective in an infranodal block?
options: The block sits too high in the conduction system for atropine to physically reach and reverse it
Atropine reliably increases the block ratio in all patients by slowing AV nodal conduction
Atropine only works when the patient is in normal sinus rhythm and never during any block
Infranodal blocks are vagally mediated only at night, so atropine helps during daytime hours
Atropine acts on the AV node, not below it; an infranodal block is below the AV node
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Atropine acts on the AV node, not below it; an infranodal block is below the AV node
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Atropine is an antimuscarinic acting on the vagally-innervated AV node. An infranodal block is below the AV node, so atropine cannot improve conduction there — pacing is required.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: What defines sinus bradycardia on the ECG?
options: Absent P waves with an irregularly irregular baseline
A broad QRS escape rhythm with no P waves
P waves completely dissociated from the QRS complexes
Progressive PR lengthening then a dropped QRS complex
HR <60 bpm with normal-morphology P waves preceding every QRS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: HR <60 bpm with normal-morphology P waves preceding every QRS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: In sinus bradycardia the SA node fires (just slowly): HR <60 bpm with normal P waves preceding every QRS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Which of the following is a DRUG cause of sinus bradycardia?
options: Salbutamol, a beta-2 agonist raising the rate
Dobutamine, a beta-1 agonist raising the rate
Adrenaline, a catecholamine speeding the heart
Atropine, an antimuscarinic speeding the heart
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Rate-limiting CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Drug causes include beta-blockers, digoxin, rate-limiting CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem), and amiodarone/lithium.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: A patient with raised intracranial pressure has bradycardia, hypertension and irregular respirations. What is this triad called?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Cushing's reflex
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Cushing's reflex is the response to raised ICP, producing bradycardia, hypertension and irregular respirations.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Which systemic condition is a recognised cause of sinus bradycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Hypothyroidism (myxoedema)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Systemic causes of sinus bradycardia include hypothyroidism (myxoedema), hypothermia, raised ICP (Cushing's reflex) and cholestasis (bile salts are vagotonic on the SA node).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Why does an inferior MI commonly cause sinus bradycardia?
options: The RCA supplies the SA node in ~60% and inferior MI is vagally mediated
The LAD supplies the SA node in most people, so inferior MI directly infarcts it
Inferior MI always damages the His-Purkinje system, giving a broad escape
It causes acute hyperkalaemia which suppresses the sinus node and slows the rate
The circumflex supplies the AV node exclusively, so any inferior MI blocks it
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: The RCA supplies the SA node in ~60% and inferior MI is vagally mediated
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: The right coronary artery supplies the SA node in ~60% of people, and inferior MI is also vagally mediated, so RCA-territory infarction frequently causes bradycardia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: What is the most common cause of sick sinus syndrome?
options: Acute viral myocarditis inflaming the sinus node tissue
Digoxin toxicity chronically poisoning the sinus node
Idiopathic degenerative fibrosis of the SA node (elderly)
Hyperthyroidism driving degeneration of the sinus node
Congenital heart disease disrupting sinus node development
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Idiopathic degenerative fibrosis of the SA node (elderly)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Sick sinus syndrome is most commonly due to idiopathic degenerative fibrosis of the SA node, typically in elderly patients.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: What characterises brady-tachy syndrome?
options: Fixed complete heart block with a stable junctional escape
AV dissociation with a slow broad ventricular escape rhythm
Persistent inappropriate sinus tachycardia without any pauses
Progressive PR lengthening with intermittently dropped beats
Alternating sinus bradycardia and paroxysmal AF or flutter
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Alternating sinus bradycardia and paroxysmal AF or flutter
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Brady-tachy syndrome (a form of sick sinus syndrome) features alternating sinus bradycardia and paroxysmal AF/flutter; treating the tachy can worsen the brady.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: What is the therapeutic dilemma in brady-tachy syndrome, and how is it resolved?
options: Atropine worsens the tachycardic episodes, so give a beta-blocker first and the bradycardia settles
There is no safe treatment because every option worsens one arm of the syndrome, so only observe closely
Anticoagulation for the AF is what causes the bradycardia, so stop the warfarin first and it is safe
Pacing worsens the paroxysmal AF, so ablate the atrial focus first and a pacemaker becomes unnecessary
Antiarrhythmics for the AF worsen the bradycardia; pace first, then it is safe to use antiarrhythmics
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Antiarrhythmics for the AF worsen the bradycardia; pace first, then it is safe to use antiarrhythmics
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Antiarrhythmics used to control the AF worsen the bradycardia, so the approach is to pace first, after which antiarrhythmics can be used safely. Anticoagulation is given for the AF component.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: How is symptomatic sick sinus syndrome managed when the cause is not reversible?
options: Catheter ablation of the SA node
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: A permanent pacemaker
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Management is to treat any reversible cause (stop offending drugs, replace thyroid hormone) and give atropine for acute episodes; a permanent pacemaker is implanted if symptomatic and the cause is not reversible.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Which ECG morphology is characteristic of RBBB?
options: A deep S (dominant downward deflection) in V1
A delta wave with short PR
An RSR' ('rabbit ears') in V1 and a broad slurred S in V6
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: An RSR' ('rabbit ears') in V1 and a broad slurred S in V6
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: RBBB shows an RSR' ('rabbit ears') in V1 and a broad slurred S wave in V6. LBBB, by contrast, shows a deep S in V1 and a broad/notched R in V6.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: An incidental finding of sinus bradycardia at 52 bpm in a well-trained marathon runner with no symptoms should be managed how?
options: No treatment — it is physiologically normal (enhanced vagal tone)
Atropine immediately to restore a normal resting heart rate
Urgent permanent pacemaker insertion to prevent sudden collapse
Start an isoprenaline infusion to chronotropically drive the rate
Admit for urgent temporary transvenous pacing wire insertion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: No treatment — it is physiologically normal (enhanced vagal tone)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Resting bradycardia is expected in athletes (enhanced vagal tone) and during sleep; incidental, asymptomatic bradycardia needs no treatment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Beyond the degree of block, what is the key discriminator for classifying AV blocks?
options: The patient's absolute resting heart rate measured on the ECG
Where in the conduction system the block sits — nodal vs infranodal
The P-wave axis and its morphology seen across the six limb leads
The presence or absence of associated ischaemic chest pain
The corrected QT interval measured on the surface ECG tracing
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Where in the conduction system the block sits — nodal vs infranodal
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: The nodal-vs-infranodal location determines the escape rhythm, atropine response and need for pacing — not just the degree of block.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: What defines first-degree AV block, and how is it managed?
options: Progressive PR lengthening then a dropped beat; pacemaker
Fixed PR with sudden dropped beats; pacemaker
PR >200 ms, fixed, every P conducts; benign, no treatment
Shortened PR with a delta wave; ablation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: PR >200 ms, fixed, every P conducts; benign, no treatment
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: First-degree AV block is a fixed PR >200 ms with every P wave conducting. It is at the AV node level, benign, and needs no treatment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Which ECG pattern describes Mobitz I (Wenckebach)?
options: Fixed unchanging PR interval with an abrupt, unheralded dropped QRS
Complete dissociation of P waves from the QRS with an escape rhythm
Progressive PR lengthening until a QRS is dropped, then the cycle resets
A prolonged PR over 200 ms but with every single beat still conducting
A short PR interval with a slurred delta-wave upstroke on the QRS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Progressive PR lengthening until a QRS is dropped, then the cycle resets
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Mobitz I (Wenckebach) shows progressive PR lengthening until a beat is dropped, then resets. It is AV nodal, narrow QRS, and usually benign.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: A patient has a fixed PR interval with sudden, unheralded dropped QRS complexes and a broad QRS. What is the diagnosis and key concern?
options: Mobitz I Wenckebach — a benign nodal block; simply monitor with no pacemaker needed at all
Sinus bradycardia — simply identify and treat the underlying reversible cause, no pacing needed
First-degree AV block — entirely benign, needs no treatment and never progresses further
Mobitz II — infranodal, high risk of progression to complete heart block; needs a pacemaker
Complete third-degree heart block — already maximal, so no further progression is possible now
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Mobitz II — infranodal, high risk of progression to complete heart block; needs a pacemaker
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Mobitz II (fixed PR, sudden dropped QRS, broad QRS) is infranodal, carries a high risk of progression to CHB, and requires a pacemaker.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: What is the defining ECG feature of complete (third-degree) heart block?
options: P waves and QRS complexes fully dissociated, ventricles driven by an escape rhythm
Progressive PR lengthening beat by beat until a single QRS complex is finally dropped
A fixed unchanging PR interval with occasional sudden non-conducted dropped beats
A prolonged PR over 200 ms in which every P wave still conducts through to a QRS
A slurred delta wave with an abnormally short PR interval and a wide QRS complex
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: P waves and QRS complexes fully dissociated, ventricles driven by an escape rhythm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: In CHB the atria and ventricles are fully dissociated; ventricular output depends on an escape rhythm. A broad QRS escape indicates an unreliable infranodal origin, and a pacemaker is mandatory.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Which AV block carries NO asystole risk and needs no treatment?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: First-degree block
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: First-degree block has no dropped beats, no asystole risk, and needs no treatment. Mobitz II and complete heart block (broad escape) carry high asystole risk. Mobitz I is usually benign but does drop beats.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: In which AV block is atropine clearly useful?
options: Complete heart block with a broad escape
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Mobitz I
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Atropine works at the AV node, so it is useful in Mobitz I (AV nodal). It is ineffective in Mobitz II and CHB with a broad (infranodal) escape; in CHB it helps only with a narrow escape acutely.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Why may atropine paradoxically worsen the block ratio in an infranodal (e.g. Mobitz II) block?
options: It directly damages and inflames the His-Purkinje fibres, so conduction through the diseased infranodal tissue deteriorates further
It paradoxically slows the sinus node rather than speeding it, so fewer atrial impulses arrive and the block ratio appears worse
It causes an acute rise in serum potassium, and the resulting hyperkalaemia depresses infranodal conduction so more impulses block
It increases the atrial rate, but the diseased infranodal tissue cannot conduct the extra impulses, so more are blocked
It triggers short runs of ventricular fibrillation in the diseased His-Purkinje tissue, disrupting the escape and worsening the block
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: It increases the atrial rate, but the diseased infranodal tissue cannot conduct the extra impulses, so more are blocked
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Atropine raises the atrial (sinus) rate, but infranodal tissue cannot conduct the additional impulses, so a greater proportion are blocked, worsening the block ratio.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: In complete heart block, a NARROW escape (His bundle) has which features?
options: Rate under 40 bpm, broad QRS, unreliable, atropine ineffective, and it demands urgent permanent pacing
Rate around 100 bpm, narrow QRS, entirely stable and reliable, so pacing is never needed under any circumstances
No escape rhythm arises at all, so the ventricles stay in asystole and the patient cannot survive without pacing
Rate 40–60 bpm, narrow QRS, reliable, often inferior MI/reversible, may respond to atropine acutely
Rate under 30 bpm, broad QRS, unreliable, but it responds well to atropine given acutely at the bedside
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Rate 40–60 bpm, narrow QRS, reliable, often inferior MI/reversible, may respond to atropine acutely
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: A His-bundle (narrow) escape is 40–60 bpm with a narrow QRS, more reliable, and often arises from inferior MI or another reversible cause. It may respond to IV atropine acutely and, because the cause is usually reversible, permanent pacing is often not required once that cause is corrected.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: A BROAD escape (His-Purkinje) in complete heart block is characterised by what, and what does it mandate?
options: Rate <40 bpm, broad QRS, unreliable, causes Stokes-Adams attacks; permanent pacemaker mandatory
Rate 50–60 bpm, narrow QRS, reliable and stable, so simple observation on a monitored ward suffices
Rate around 70 bpm, narrow QRS, reliable, and it responds fully to atropine alone with no pacing needed
No significant bradycardia develops, the escape keeps pace, so simple reassurance and discharge suffice
Rate under 40 bpm but with a narrow QRS, which responds promptly to atropine so no pacemaker is needed
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Rate <40 bpm, broad QRS, unreliable, causes Stokes-Adams attacks; permanent pacemaker mandatory
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: A His-Purkinje (broad) escape is <40 bpm, broad QRS, unreliable (may fail without warning), causes Stokes-Adams attacks, is atropine-ineffective, and mandates a permanent pacemaker.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: What is a Stokes-Adams attack?
options: A prolonged epileptic seizure with tonic-clonic movements followed by a long period of post-ictal drowsiness and confusion
A vasovagal faint triggered by prolonged standing, with slow onset, sweating and nausea, and a gradual recovery after
Central crushing ischaemic chest pain radiating to the jaw and left arm, brought on by exertion and relieved by rest
A sudden LOC from CHB due to transient asystole or VT, with rapid complete recovery and no post-ictal confusion
A transient ischaemic attack causing focal neurological deficit and limb weakness that fully resolves within a day
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: A sudden LOC from CHB due to transient asystole or VT, with rapid complete recovery and no post-ictal confusion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: A Stokes-Adams attack is sudden loss of consciousness from CHB (transient asystole or VT) with rapid complete recovery; the patient goes pale then flushes as circulation restores.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Which features help distinguish a Stokes-Adams attack from an epileptic seizure?
options: Prolonged post-ictal drowsiness and confusion for many minutes, with lateral tongue-biting and aching limb muscles
Urinary incontinence during the episode and a slow, prolonged recovery over minutes with lingering drowsiness
An aura of a rising epigastric sensation or déjà vu preceding the collapse, as seen in temporal lobe seizures
Rapid complete recovery, no post-ictal confusion, no tongue-biting, no incontinence, with pallor then flushing
Lateral tongue-biting with rhythmic tonic-clonic limb-jerking and cyanosis during the episode rather than pallor
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Rapid complete recovery, no post-ictal confusion, no tongue-biting, no incontinence, with pallor then flushing
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Stokes-Adams attacks recover rapidly and completely without post-ictal confusion, tongue-biting or incontinence, with characteristic pallor then flushing — distinguishing them from seizures.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Is bundle branch block a bradycardia, and what produces its wide QRS?
options: Yes; the SA node discharges too slowly, producing a sinus bradycardia that widens the QRS as conduction lags
Yes; a slow infranodal ventricular escape rhythm takes over, giving both the bradycardia and the broad QRS
No — it is a conduction delay; the AV node and His bundle conduct normally but the delay is in one bundle branch
No — it results from AV dissociation, with atria and ventricles beating independently and widening the QRS
Yes; it invariably coexists with complete heart block, so the ventricular rate is slow and the QRS is broad
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: No — it is a conduction delay; the AV node and His bundle conduct normally but the delay is in one bundle branch
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: BBB is a conduction delay, not a bradycardia. The AV node and His bundle conduct normally; the delay in one bundle branch produces a wide QRS (>120 ms) with characteristic morphology.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Using the WiLLiaM mnemonic, which morphology indicates LBBB?
options: M in V1, W in V6
W in V1 (deep QS/rS), M in V5/V6
RSR' in V1, slurred S in V6
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: W in V1 (deep QS/rS), M in V5/V6
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: LBBB = WiLLiaM: a W in V1 (deep QS or rS) and an M in V5/V6 (broad notched R), with QRS >120 ms. The axis is usually normal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Which statement about LBBB is correct?
options: It is always pathological (causes include AS, HTN, IHD, cardiomyopathy); LBBB with ongoing ischaemic chest pain is a STEMI equivalent
It is usually a benign normal variant seen in fit young athletes and needs no further cardiac investigation at all
It is best treated with an urgent permanent pacemaker in all cases, to prevent progression to complete heart block
It produces a short PR interval and a slurred delta wave from accessory-pathway pre-excitation of the ventricle
It can be a normal variant in healthy young people and, unlike RBBB, carries no link at all with structural heart disease
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: It is always pathological (causes include AS, HTN, IHD, cardiomyopathy); LBBB with ongoing ischaemic chest pain is a STEMI equivalent
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: LBBB is always pathological. LBBB — new, presumed-new or known — with ongoing ischaemic symptoms is treated as a STEMI equivalent (primary PCI). LBBB alone, without ischaemic symptoms, is not an indication. RBBB, by contrast, can be a normal variant.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Using the MaRRoW mnemonic, which morphology indicates RBBB, and what is its significance?
options: W in V1 and M in V6 (the opposite pattern); always pathological and requiring a pacemaker
Sawtooth flutter waves in V1 indicating underlying atrial flutter with the block
Deep S in V1 with a broad slurred R in V6; always pathological and never a normal variant
A delta wave in V1 indicating ventricular pre-excitation via an accessory pathway
M in V1 (RSR' 'rabbit ears'), W in V5/V6; can be a normal variant in young people
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: M in V1 (RSR' 'rabbit ears'), W in V5/V6; can be a normal variant in young people
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: RBBB = MaRRoW: an M in V1 (RSR') and a W in V5/V6 (broad slurred S). It can be a normal variant in young people; other causes include PE (acute RV strain), RVH and congenital heart disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: A patient presents with ongoing ischaemic chest pain and left bundle branch block on the ECG, which the notes show was present on a previous tracing. How should this be managed?
options: Reassure the patient and discharge home with routine GP follow-up
Insert a permanent pacemaker urgently to restore conduction
Treat as a STEMI equivalent — activate the primary PCI pathway
Give IV atropine 500 mcg to reverse the conduction block
Treat as Mobitz II block and arrange transcutaneous pacing
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Treat as a STEMI equivalent — activate the primary PCI pathway
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: It is the ischaemic symptoms that decide, not whether the LBBB is new — a known LBBB with ongoing ischaemic chest pain still activates the primary PCI (PPCI) pathway.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Which of the following is one of the life-threatening features signifying haemodynamic instability in bradycardia?
options: Palpitations with an intermittent fluttering sensation in the chest
Shock (hypotension, pallor, diaphoresis, cold extremities, confusion)
Mild dizziness only on standing quickly, resolving within seconds
A resting heart rate of 58 bpm noted incidentally on the monitor
An incidental ECG finding in an otherwise well, asymptomatic patient
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Shock (hypotension, pallor, diaphoresis, cold extremities, confusion)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: The life-threatening features are shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia, severe heart failure, and an arrhythmia occurring immediately post-ROSC (Resus Council UK) — any of these means the patient is unstable and needs immediate treatment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Which is one of the four high-risk-of-asystole situations warranting aggressive treatment even if the patient is currently stable?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Mobitz II
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: The four high-risk situations are recent asystole, Mobitz II, complete heart block with a broad QRS, and ventricular pauses >3 seconds.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: What does Step 1 (stabilise) of the peri-arrest bradycardia algorithm involve?
options: Immediate insertion of a permanent transvenous pacemaker before any other assessment or investigation
ABCDE assessment, oxygen, IV access, 12-lead ECG, monitoring, and identifying/treating reversible causes
Give atropine 3 mg IV as a single large bolus dose first, before any assessment or monitoring
Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion at 150 J to restore a normal sinus rhythm and rate
Empirical IV glucagon for all patients regardless of the underlying cause of the bradycardia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: ABCDE assessment, oxygen, IV access, 12-lead ECG, monitoring, and identifying/treating reversible causes
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Step 1 is to stabilise: ABCDE, oxygen, IV access, 12-lead ECG, continuous monitoring, and treating reversible causes (electrolytes, hypoxia, hypothermia, drugs).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: If adverse features are present in bradycardia, what is the first-line drug, dose and maximum?
options: Adrenaline 1 mg IV bolus repeated as needed, with no maximum dose
Atropine 3 mg IV given once as a single large one-off bolus dose
Isoprenaline 5 mcg/min IV infusion, titrated to rate with no maximum
Atropine 500 mcg IV, repeated every 3–5 min to a maximum of 3 mg
Glucagon 10 mg slow IV bolus followed by a maintenance infusion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Atropine 500 mcg IV, repeated every 3–5 min to a maximum of 3 mg
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: First-line is atropine 500 mcg IV, repeated every 3–5 minutes up to a maximum total of 3 mg.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: In which scenarios is atropine ineffective in bradycardia?
options: Sinus bradycardia and Mobitz I, where the block is infranodal and unresponsive to vagal blockade
All bradycardias respond reliably to atropine because it blocks the vagus at the AV node
First-degree AV block, an infranodal delay that atropine cannot overcome once established
Drug-induced bradycardia alone, such as beta-blocker toxicity, which never responds to atropine
Mobitz II, CHB, and a broad escape (all infranodal — below the vagally-innervated AV node)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Mobitz II, CHB, and a broad escape (all infranodal — below the vagally-innervated AV node)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Atropine is an antimuscarinic acting on the AV node, so it is ineffective for infranodal problems (Mobitz II, CHB, broad escape), which sit below the vagally-innervated AV node.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: A patient with refractory bradycardia from a beta-blocker overdose is not responding to atropine and pacing. What is the specific antidote?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Glucagon
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Glucagon is the specific antidote for beta-blocker overdose causing bradycardia when atropine and pacing are insufficient — it bypasses the β-receptor. In calcium-channel-blocker overdose the direct antidote is IV calcium instead, with glucagon only as an adjunct.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: If atropine gives an inadequate response, which is a recognised interim escalation measure?
options: Synchronised DC cardioversion at 150 J under sedation
Rapid IV adenosine 6 mg bolus to restore the rate
Immediate surgical implantation of a permanent ICD device
Transcutaneous pacing (a painful bridge needing sedation)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Transcutaneous pacing (a painful bridge needing sedation)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Interim measures include isoprenaline, adrenaline, aminophylline, transcutaneous pacing (a painful bridge needing sedation), and glucagon for BB/CCB overdose.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: How does transvenous pacing compare with transcutaneous pacing?
options: Transcutaneous pacing is more reliable and definitive, giving consistent capture without needing venous access
Transvenous (pacing wire via subclavian/femoral to the RV) is more reliable; both are bridges to a permanent device
