They are equally reliable, so either can be chosen as the definitive long-term pacing method for the patient
Transvenous pacing is reserved only for cardiac arrest and has no role in peri-arrest bradycardia management
Transcutaneous pacing is painless, well tolerated, and the preferred option for long-term definitive pacing
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Transvenous (pacing wire via subclavian/femoral to the RV) is more reliable; both are bridges to a permanent device
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Transvenous pacing (a wire via the subclavian/femoral/IJV to the RV) is more reliable than transcutaneous pacing; both are temporary bridges to a permanent device.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: In a bradycardic patient with NO adverse features, how is management decided?
options: Always insert a permanent pacemaker urgently, since any bradycardia without adverse features still progresses to arrest
Give IV atropine 500 mcg regardless of the rhythm, as it reliably restores conduction in every type of bradycardia
Assess asystole risk: high (Mobitz II, CHB+broad QRS, pauses >3s, recent asystole) → treat as unstable; low → observe and monitor
Discharge the patient immediately once symptoms settle, as the absence of adverse features excludes any asystole risk
Start an IV glucagon infusion empirically in all such patients to protect against progression to complete heart block
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Assess asystole risk: high (Mobitz II, CHB+broad QRS, pauses >3s, recent asystole) → treat as unstable; low → observe and monitor
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Without adverse features, asystole risk is assessed: high-risk patients are treated as unstable, while low-risk patients are observed and monitored with regular review.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Which is a recognised indication for a permanent pacemaker?
options: Mobitz I in a young patient
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Mobitz II AV block
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Indications include symptomatic sinus bradycardia (reversible causes excluded), sick sinus syndrome, Mobitz II, complete (3rd-degree) HB, symptomatic bifascicular/trifascicular block, and recurrent Stokes-Adams attacks.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: What is the difference between a VVI and a DDD pacemaker?
options: VVI paces both the atrium and ventricle, whereas DDD is a single-lead device that paces only the ventricle
They are functionally identical devices, differing only in the manufacturer's naming convention for the leads
VVI paces/senses the ventricle only; DDD paces both atrium and ventricle, maintaining AV synchrony (atrial kick)
DDD is a temporary external device only, used as a short-term bridge until a VVI system can be implanted
VVI is a dual-chamber system maintaining AV synchrony, whereas DDD paces only the single ventricle
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: VVI paces/senses the ventricle only; DDD paces both atrium and ventricle, maintaining AV synchrony (atrial kick)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: VVI paces and senses the ventricle only; DDD paces both atrium and ventricle, preserving AV synchrony (the atrial kick) — important in impaired LV function.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: How does complete heart block from an ANTERIOR MI compare with that from an INFERIOR MI?
options: Anterior MI = His-Purkinje level, broad QRS, unreliable escape 30–40 bpm → urgent pacing, worse prognosis; inferior = AV nodal, narrow QRS, usually transient, often responds to atropine
Anterior MI produces a narrow, reliable junctional escape near 50 bpm that responds well to atropine, whereas inferior MI causes a broad, unreliable ventricular escape needing urgent pacing
Both produce identical narrow-complex escape rhythms near 50 bpm, are always transient, and reliably respond to atropine without ever requiring temporary or permanent pacing
Inferior MI causes a His-Purkinje block with a broad unreliable escape always needing urgent pacing, whereas anterior MI causes a benign AV nodal block that resolves spontaneously

Neither an anterior nor an inferior MI ever causes heart block, since the coronary arteries supplying both the AV node and the His-Purkinje conduction system remain unaffected by an acute myocardial infarction
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Anterior MI = His-Purkinje level, broad QRS, unreliable escape 30–40 bpm → urgent pacing, worse prognosis; inferior = AV nodal, narrow QRS, usually transient, often responds to atropine
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Anterior MI damages the His-Purkinje system (broad, unreliable escape → urgent pacing, worse prognosis), while inferior MI affects the AV node (narrow, usually transient block that often responds to atropine and resolves with reperfusion).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Why is transcutaneous pacing used only as a bridge rather than a definitive treatment?
options: It is unreliable and ineffective, rarely achieving electrical capture even at maximum output settings
It frequently triggers ventricular fibrillation, so it is abandoned in favour of transvenous pacing
It is fast but painful and needs sedation, so it is used only until a more definitive measure is available
It is a permanent implanted system that cannot easily be removed once the pads are attached
It only captures in narrow-complex escape rhythms and always fails whenever the QRS complex is broad
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: It is fast but painful and needs sedation, so it is used only until a more definitive measure is available
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Transcutaneous pacing (defibrillator pads on the chest) is fast but painful and requires sedation, so it serves as a bridge until transvenous or permanent pacing is established.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: A 72-year-old woman in permanent atrial fibrillation had a single-chamber (VVI) pacemaker implanted 3 months ago for complete heart block. She now reports fatigue, light-headedness and an uncomfortable pulsation in her neck. Device interrogation shows the pacemaker is capturing and sensing normally. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Pacemaker syndrome
explanation: Pacemaker syndrome — VVI pacing gives no AV synchrony, so the atria contract against closed AV valves. That produces cannon A waves (the neck pulsation), fatigue and dizziness, while the device itself functions normally. The fix is an upgrade to a dual-chamber (DDD) system.
Lead displacement — would show loss of capture or sensing on interrogation; here the device is working normally.
Pocket infection — presents with local erythema, swelling, pain or discharge over the generator, often with systemic features, not isolated neck pulsation.
Twiddler's syndrome — the patient rotates the generator and dislodges the leads, so it too would show malfunction on interrogation.
Progressive LV dysfunction — would cause exertional breathlessness and congestion rather than this specific pulsatile neck sensation with a normally functioning device.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: A 68-year-old man becomes breathless a few hours after permanent pacemaker implantation via the left subclavian vein. He is hypoxic, with reduced breath sounds and a hyper-resonant percussion note on the left. What is the most likely complication?
options: Lead displacement into the right atrium
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Pneumothorax
explanation: Pneumothorax — the classic early complication of subclavian venous puncture, which is why a post-procedure chest X-ray is routine. Reduced breath sounds with hyper-resonance on the side of insertion is the giveaway.
Pocket haematoma — causes swelling, bruising and pain over the generator site, not hypoxia or unilateral chest signs.
Pacemaker syndrome — a late complication of VVI pacing from loss of AV synchrony; it does not cause acute hypoxia or focal chest signs.
Lead displacement — presents with loss of capture or sensing on the ECG and device check, not respiratory signs.
Pulmonary embolism — possible after any procedure, but it would not produce hyper-resonance and reduced breath sounds confined to the side of insertion.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: The cardiac conducting system is composed of:
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: The conduction system is made of specialised cardiomyocytes, not nervous tissue; the heartbeat is therefore myogenic, with autonomic nerves only modulating the rate.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: Which structure is the normal pacemaker of the heart?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: The SA node (right atrium near the SVC) has the fastest intrinsic rate (~60–100/min) and sets the pace; it is the dominant pacemaker.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: The physiological delay at the AV node serves to:
options: Allow the atria to finish emptying before the ventricles contract
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: The ~0.1 s AV nodal delay separates atrial from ventricular systole, allowing the ventricles to fill fully before they contract.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: Which part of the conducting system is the only electrical connection between the atria and ventricles?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: The Bundle of His penetrates the fibrous skeleton, which otherwise electrically insulates the atria from the ventricles — so it is their sole normal electrical link.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: On a slide, subendocardial cells that are larger and paler than working cardiomyocytes with peripheral myofibrils are:
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: Purkinje fibres are large, pale (glycogen-rich) subendocardial cells with myofibrils displaced to the periphery — specialised for rapid conduction to the ventricular myocardium.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: If the SA node fails, which is the expected escape rate from the AV node?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: The pacemaker hierarchy is SA (60–100) > AV (40–60) > His–Purkinje (20–40). An AV junctional escape rhythm is typically ~40–60/min.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: Stimulation of the vagus nerve on the conduction system will:
options: Increase SA firing and speed AV conduction
Slow SA firing and slow AV conduction (lower heart rate)
Block the Bundle of His permanently
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: Parasympathetic (vagal) activity slows SA node firing and AV nodal conduction, lowering the heart rate; sympathetic activity does the opposite.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: Which stain best demonstrates the abundant glycogen of Purkinje fibres?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: PAS stains glycogen magenta, highlighting the glycogen-rich cytoplasm of Purkinje fibres (which appears clear on routine H&E because the glycogen is dissolved).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: An abnormal accessory pathway (Bundle of Kent) that bypasses the AV node causes:
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: The Bundle of Kent directly connects atrium to ventricle, bypassing the AV nodal delay — producing pre-excitation (delta wave) and a substrate for AV re-entrant tachycardia (WPW).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: Complete (third-degree) heart block results from disease of which structures?
options: The AV node / Bundle of His conduction
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: Third-degree AV block reflects failure of conduction through the AV node/His bundle, so atria and ventricles beat independently; the ventricles are driven by a slow escape pacemaker.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: Spontaneous pacemaker depolarisation in the SA node is generated by the:
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: The funny current (If) is a slow inward cation current that drives the gradual diastolic depolarisation giving nodal cells their automaticity.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: The AV node lies within which anatomical landmark?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: The AV node sits in the floor of the right atrium within the triangle of Koch — a key landmark to identify (and avoid) during catheter ablation.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: Which cells are small, pale and ovoid with very few myofibrils, specialised for impulse generation?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: Nodal (P) cells are small, pale, spindle-shaped cells with sparse myofibrils, specialised for impulse generation rather than contraction. Purkinje fibres are large and pale.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: The SA and AV nodes are most commonly supplied by which artery, explaining nodal block in inferior MI?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: In most individuals the right coronary artery gives the SA and AV nodal branches, so inferior (RCA-territory) MIs can produce sinus or AV nodal dysfunction/block.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: Ventricular contraction begins at the apex and moves toward the base because:
options: The AV node is at the apex
Purkinje fibres deliver the impulse to the apex first
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: The His–Purkinje system carries the impulse rapidly to the ventricular apex, so contraction starts there and sweeps toward the outflow, ejecting blood efficiently.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: Unlike a ventricular myocyte, the upstroke of the SA-node action potential is generated mainly by:
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: Nodal cells lack functional fast Na+ channels; their slow upstroke is carried by L-type Ca2+ channels, which is why they conduct slowly and are sensitive to calcium-channel blockers. Phase-4 automaticity is driven by the funny current (If, HCN channels).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: The PR interval on the ECG corresponds chiefly to conduction delay in the:
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: The PR segment reflects the slow conduction (delay) through the AV node; the P wave is atrial depolarisation and the QRS is His-Purkinje/ventricular activation.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: Mobitz type II second-degree AV block usually reflects disease in the:
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: Mobitz II block is infranodal (His-Purkinje), often with a broad QRS and a high risk of progression to complete heart block — a pacemaker indication; Mobitz I (Wenckebach) is AV-nodal and usually benign.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.question: A 74-year-old man has a mass above the umbilicus that pushes your fingers apart as it pulsates. What does this finding indicate?
options: A mass transmitting the aortic pulse
Normal aortic pulsation in a thin patient
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.explanation: A mass that pushes the fingers apart (expansile) is a true abdominal aortic aneurysm. A mass merely transmitting the pulse pushes the fingers up only; the other options are non-aortic and would not be expansile.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.question: A 78-year-old arteriopath presents with sudden abdominal and back pain, a pulsatile abdominal mass and a systolic BP of 80 mmHg. What is the immediate priority?
options: Immediate vascular surgery and major-haemorrhage protocol
CT angiogram to confirm the rupture before intervention
Analgesia and observe on the ward
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.explanation: This is a ruptured AAA (pain + pulsatile mass + shock). An unstable patient goes straight to theatre with major-haemorrhage activation — do not delay for CT. CT is only appropriate if the patient is haemodynamically stable.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.question: An asymptomatic 68-year-old is found to have a 4.2 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm. What is the appropriate management?
options: Reassure and discharge with no follow-up
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.explanation: A 4.2 cm asymptomatic AAA is below the 5.5 cm threshold, so it enters ultrasound surveillance. Elective repair is offered at ≥5.5 cm, if symptomatic, or if expanding >1 cm/year; discharging with no follow-up would miss dangerous growth.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.question: At which of the following should an asymptomatic infrarenal AAA generally be offered elective repair?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.explanation: Elective repair is generally offered at a diameter of ≥5.5 cm (or if symptomatic / expanding >1 cm per year). Smaller aneurysms are kept under ultrasound surveillance because the rupture risk is outweighed by operative risk.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.question: The UK abdominal aortic aneurysm screening programme offers what, to whom?
options: Annual ultrasound to all adults over 50
A one-off CT angiogram to women at 70
Aortic MRI to anyone with hypertension
A one-off abdominal ultrasound to men at 65
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.explanation: The NHS AAA screening programme offers a single abdominal ultrasound to men in the year they turn 65, the group with the highest prevalence. Detected aneurysms then enter size-based surveillance.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.question: A 70-year-old has a central abdominal mass that pushes your fingers upward but not apart, with weight loss and painless jaundice. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Pancreatic carcinoma transmitting the aortic pulse
Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm with shock
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.explanation: A non-expansile (transmitted) epigastric mass with painless jaundice and weight loss is a pancreatic head carcinoma overlying the aorta. It is not expansile, so it is not an AAA; a CT abdomen confirms it.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.question: A patient with a 6 cm AAA develops sudden blue, painful toes with palpable femoral and popliteal pulses. What has happened?
options: Acute compartment syndrome of the leg
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.explanation: Blue, painful toes with preserved proximal pulses is distal embolisation of mural thrombus from the aneurysm (‘trash foot’). It signals an unstable aneurysm and warrants urgent vascular assessment; rupture would cause pain and shock, not isolated digital ischaemia.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.question: A 72-year-old with a previous open AAA graft repair presents with a large haematemesis and melaena. What complication must be excluded?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.explanation: Massive GI bleeding in a patient with a previous aortic graft (or known AAA) is an aortoenteric fistula until proven otherwise — a communication between the aorta / graft and the duodenum. A herald bleed may precede catastrophic haemorrhage.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.question: A 55-year-old has a ballotable left flank mass, visible haematuria and weight loss. Which diagnosis best fits?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.explanation: A ballotable flank mass with haematuria and loin/flank pain is the classic triad of renal cell carcinoma (weight loss is a common constitutional feature but not part of the classic triad). It is bimanually ballotable in the flank and moves with respiration, unlike a midline expansile AAA.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.question: Which additional peripheral examination is most important in a patient found to have an abdominal aortic aneurysm?
options: Checking for radio-femoral and radial delay
Palpating the popliteal and femoral pulses
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.explanation: AAAs frequently coexist with popliteal and femoral artery aneurysms, so those pulses must be palpated (a widened, prominent popliteal pulse suggests an aneurysm). The other examinations do not address the aneurysmal disease.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.question: What is the first-line investigation to confirm and measure a suspected abdominal aortic aneurysm in a stable patient?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.explanation: Abdominal ultrasound is first-line — fast, non-invasive and accurate for diameter, and usable at the bedside. A CT angiogram then characterises morphology for operative planning in the stable patient.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.question: A slim, well 30-year-old is worried after feeling their own abdominal pulsation. Examination shows a midline pulsation that does not push the fingers apart, and ultrasound shows a 1.9 cm aorta. What is the explanation?
options: Normal aortic pulsation in a thin person
A transmitted pulse from an overlying tumour
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pulsatile Abdomin.explanation: A non-expansile midline pulsation with a normal-calibre (<3 cm) aorta in a thin person is simply the normal aorta being easily palpable. An AAA requires a diameter ≥3 cm and is expansile; reassurance is appropriate.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Why does the location of a thoracic aortic aneurysm matter so much?
options: It precisely reveals the patient's chronological age and predicts life expectancy
It drives both the symptoms (compression syndromes) and the repair thresholds
It reliably alters the full blood count and clotting profile in a diagnostic way
It solely dictates the ultrasound surveillance interval and nothing else clinically
It carries no clinical relevance and never influences symptoms or management at all
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: It drives both the symptoms (compression syndromes) and the repair thresholds
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Location matters because it drives both the symptoms (compression syndromes) and the repair thresholds.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: What proportion of TAAs occur at the ascending aorta/root, and what are the most common causes?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: 60% — Marfan's, bicuspid AV, syphilis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: 60% of TAAs are at the ascending aorta/root, most commonly caused by Marfan's, bicuspid AV and syphilis, with a repair threshold ≥5.5 cm (lower in CT disease).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Which TAA location has the highest repair threshold and a preference for TEVAR?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Descending aorta — ≥5.5–6 cm, TEVAR
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: The descending aorta (~35–40% of TAAs) has the highest threshold — ≥5.5 cm where TEVAR is feasible, ≥6 cm where open repair would be needed — and TEVAR is preferred. It is associated with posterior thoracic pain and atherosclerosis/dissection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: How does TAA differ from AAA in aetiology and screening?
options: Both arise chiefly from atherosclerosis and both have national screening programmes
TAA: CT disease/bicuspid/syphilis, no national screening; AAA: atherosclerosis
TAA is caused by atherosclerosis, whereas AAA arises from Marfan's connective disease
Both share an identical atherosclerotic aetiology and identical screening pathways
TAA has a national ultrasound screening programme, whereas AAA has no screening at all
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: TAA: CT disease/bicuspid/syphilis, no national screening; AAA: atherosclerosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: TAA and AAA share definition and Laplace physics, but TAA has different aetiology (CT disease/bicuspid/syphilis vs atherosclerosis) and no national screening programme, unlike AAA.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: A false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm) is best described as what?
options: Intima + media rupture, blood contained only by adventitia
Blood entering between the intima and media
Dilatation of all layers from atherosclerosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Intima + media rupture, blood contained only by adventitia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: A false aneurysm involves rupture of intima and media with blood contained only by adventitia, caused by trauma, surgery or infection; a true aneurysm has all 3 layers intact but dilated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: What is the mechanism of TAA formation?
options: Tunica media degeneration → loss of tensile strength → dilatation → increased wall tension (Laplace) → further dilatation
Acute thrombosis of the aortic lumen occludes flow, and the trapped high-pressure clot balloons the wall outward into an aneurysm
Progressive calcification of the intima stiffens the inner wall, which then bulges outward under arterial pressure to form the aneurysm
Immune complex deposition in the aortic wall drives inflammation that weakens the media and lets the vessel dilate into an aneurysm
Spasm of the vasa vasorum chokes the wall's blood supply, causing ischaemic injury that weakens the media and dilates the aorta
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Tunica media degeneration → loss of tensile strength → dilatation → increased wall tension (Laplace) → further dilatation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: TAA forms by tunica media degeneration causing loss of tensile strength and dilatation, which increases wall tension (Laplace) and drives further dilatation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Approximately what proportion of people with a bicuspid aortic valve develop aortopathy (ascending aortic dilatation)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Around 50–70% of people with a bicuspid aortic valve develop some degree of aortopathy (ascending aortic dilatation) over time, from the shared connective-tissue/haemodynamic abnormality — hence the need for lifelong aortic surveillance. (Conversely, BAV underlies roughly 20–30% of ascending TAAs.)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Which cause is described as the classic ascending aneurysm and an exam favourite?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Tertiary syphilis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Tertiary syphilis is the classic ascending aneurysm and an exam favourite.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: What is 'the discriminator' between TAA and AAA aetiology?
options: TAA → atherosclerosis; AAA → Marfan's and connective tissue disease
TAA → chronic infection such as syphilis; AAA → blunt traumatic injury
Both TAA and AAA → atherosclerosis as the shared underlying cause
There is no reliable discriminator between TAA and AAA aetiology
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: TAA → Marfan's/EDS/bicuspid AV/syphilis; AAA → atherosclerosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: The discriminator: TAA points to Marfan's/EDS/bicuspid AV/syphilis, while AAA points to atherosclerosis — a frequently tested contrast.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: How do most TAAs present?
options: With severe tearing chest pain radiating through to the back at onset
With haemoptysis from erosion of the aneurysm into the adjacent lung
Asymptomatic — found incidentally on CXR or cross-sectional imaging
With sudden collapse and syncope from a transient fall in cardiac output
With progressive dysphagia from oesophageal compression by the aneurysm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Asymptomatic — found incidentally on CXR or cross-sectional imaging
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Most TAAs are asymptomatic and found incidentally on CXR or cross-sectional imaging; there is no national screening programme.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Which pain location corresponds to a descending aorta TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Posterior thoracic/back pain
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Descending aorta TAA causes posterior thoracic/back pain; ascending → anterior chest pain; arch → neck pain.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Distended neck veins and facial oedema in a TAA indicate compression of what?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: SVC
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: SVC compression causes distended neck veins, facial oedema and SVC obstruction syndrome.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Which compression effect produces dysphagia in TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Oesophagus
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Oesophageal compression causes dysphagia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Aortic valve involvement in TAA leads to what?
options: A hoarse voice from recurrent laryngeal palsy
Interscapular back pain from local expansion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Aortic regurgitation → heart failure signs
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Aortic valve involvement causes aortic regurgitation, leading to heart failure signs.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Which of the following is a listed key differential for TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Pneumothorax
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Key differentials for TAA are PE, ACS, pneumothorax and aortic dissection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: What is the role of ECG in the work-up of TAA?
options: Excludes ACS; may show LVH from chronic HTN
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Excludes ACS; may show LVH from chronic HTN
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: ECG is used to exclude ACS and may show LVH from chronic hypertension.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Which CXR findings are characteristic of a TAA?
options: A boot-shaped cardiac silhouette with an upturned, uplifted cardiac apex
Inferior rib notching from enlarged, tortuous intercostal collateral vessels
Kerley B lines with upper-lobe pulmonary venous diversion and interstitial oedema
Widened mediastinal silhouette, enlarged aortic knob, tracheal deviation
An isolated large left-sided pleural effusion with no other mediastinal changes
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Widened mediastinal silhouette, enlarged aortic knob, tracheal deviation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: CXR shows a widened mediastinal silhouette, enlarged aortic knob and tracheal deviation — often the incidental finding.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Which is the preferred/definitive imaging modality in TAA, and what does it provide?
options: CXR — incidental detection of a widened mediastinum
ECG — exclude acute coronary syndrome as the pain cause
CT angiogram — anatomy, size, extent, TEVAR suitability
TOE — valve assessment and proximal root imaging only
Routine bloods — baseline renal function and crossmatch
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: CT angiogram — anatomy, size, extent, TEVAR suitability
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: CT angiogram is the preferred/definitive modality, giving anatomy, size, extent and TEVAR suitability for surgical planning.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Serial TTE surveillance is done in all of which patient group with TAA, and what does it assess?
options: All elderly patients — assesses aortic wall atherosclerotic plaque burden
All Marfan's patients — assesses root size, valve involvement and AR
All hypertensive patients — assesses left ventricular hypertrophy severity
All smokers — assesses aneurysmal involvement of the adjacent lung tissue
All diabetics — assesses resting cardiac output and ejection fraction
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: All Marfan's patients — assesses root size, valve involvement and AR
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: TTE is first-line surveillance in all Marfan's patients, assessing aortic root size, valve involvement and AR. TOE is reserved for peri-operative use and suspected dissection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Which medical measure is the key modifiable factor for all TAA patients?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: BP control
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: BP control is the key modifiable factor; medical management also includes a statin, smoking cessation and optimising diabetes, hyperlipidaemia and weight. Antiplatelet therapy is given only where there is a separate atherosclerotic indication, not for the aneurysm itself.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: What is the surgical threshold and procedure for an ascending/root TAA?
options: ≥6 cm; TEVAR stent graft deployed across the ascending aorta
≥5.5 cm; Dacron graft replacement, Bentall if root involved
≥4 cm; multi-limbed branched graft with valve sparing
≥5.5 cm; open repair only, never with a Bentall root graft
≥7 cm; continued observation with interval CT surveillance
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: ≥5.5 cm; Dacron graft replacement, Bentall if root involved
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Ascending/root TAA: threshold ≥5.5 cm for degenerative disease with a tricuspid valve; Dacron graft replacement, with a Bentall procedure if the root is involved. The threshold falls to ≥5 cm in Marfan (≥4.5 cm with risk factors) and ≥4.5 cm in Loeys-Dietz — but bicuspid AV is usually still ≥5.5 cm (ESC).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: What is the procedure and key risk for an aortic arch TAA repair?
options: TEVAR stent graft across the arch; main risk is a type I endoleak with continued sac filling
Open repair via thoracotomy; main risk is spinal cord ischaemia causing paraplegia
Dacron tube graft replacement of the arch; carries no specific procedure-related risk
Bentall procedure with composite valved conduit; main risk is prosthetic valve failure
Multi-limbed graft (allows great vessel branching); high cerebral ischaemia/embolism risk
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Multi-limbed graft (allows great vessel branching); high cerebral ischaemia/embolism risk
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Aortic arch TAA (threshold ≥5.5 cm) is repaired with open graft replacement of the arch. Because the great vessels must be interrupted, the key risk is stroke from cerebral ischaemia or embolism.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Why is the repair threshold lower in Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndrome?
options: Because the aorta is inherently smaller in these patients
Because the wall is structurally weaker — operate earlier
Because these patients are younger with a longer life expectancy
Because TEVAR is absolutely contraindicated in these disorders
Because these connective tissue disorders cause atherosclerosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Because the wall is structurally weaker — operate earlier
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: The media is structurally weaker, so dissection occurs at smaller diameters — Marfan ≥5 cm, or ≥4.5 cm with risk factors, and Loeys-Dietz ≥4.5 cm, versus ≥5.5 cm for degenerative disease. Bicuspid AV is not equivalent — it usually stays at ≥5.5 cm (ESC).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: What is the Bentall procedure?
options: Endovascular stent across the descending aorta
Dacron tube graft of the descending aorta
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Aortic root replacement + prosthetic valve
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: The Bentall procedure is aortic root replacement plus a prosthetic valve — a key eponym.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: How is TEVAR performed?
options: Open chest on cardiopulmonary bypass, with the diseased descending segment excised and replaced by a sewn-in Dacron tube graft
A covered femoral stent graft advanced up into the abdominal aorta to line and exclude the diseased infrarenal segment from flow
Replacement of the aortic root with a mechanical valve and coronary reimplantation to restore flow through the ascending aorta
A multi-limbed branched graft sewn into the arch, allowing each great vessel to be reattached to a separate limb of the prosthesis
A stent graft delivered via catheter and deployed across the descending TAA, excluding the aneurysm from circulation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: A stent graft delivered via catheter and deployed across the descending TAA, excluding the aneurysm from circulation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: TEVAR delivers a stent graft via catheter, deploying it across the descending TAA to exclude the aneurysm from circulation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: When a TAA ruptures, where does it bleed and what determines the clinical picture?
options: Into the peritoneal cavity; the clinical picture is determined by the patient's age
Into the retroperitoneum; the picture is determined solely by the blood pressure
Into the pleural space only; the clinical picture is always exactly the same
Into the pericardium only; the presentation never varies between patients
Into the mediastinum; the site of bleeding determines the clinical picture
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Into the mediastinum; the site of bleeding determines the clinical picture
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Rupture causes bleeding into the mediastinum with high mortality; the site of bleeding determines the clinical picture.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: A ruptured TAA bleeding into the pericardial cavity produces what?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Cardiac tamponade
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Rupture into the pericardial cavity causes cardiac tamponade; into the oesophagus causes haematemesis, and into the airway/lungs causes haemoptysis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Which signs accompany a ruptured TAA?
options: Reflex bradycardia with sustained hypertension, plus a bounding pulse and warm peripheries from raised cardiac output
Haemodynamic instability (tachycardia + hypotension), signs of tamponade (raised JVP, muffled sounds, hypotension)
A malar flush with a loud first heart sound and an opening snap, pointing to coexisting rheumatic mitral stenosis
Bilateral papilloedema with cotton-wool spots and flame haemorrhages on fundoscopy from malignant hypertension
A pulsatile enlarged liver with giant V waves in the JVP, indicating severe tricuspid regurgitation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Haemodynamic instability (tachycardia + hypotension), signs of tamponade (raised JVP, muffled sounds, hypotension)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Signs of a ruptured TAA include haemodynamic instability (tachycardia + hypotension) and tamponade signs (raised JVP, muffled sounds, hypotension).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: What is the management of a ruptured TAA?
options: Emergency repair — open graft for ascending/arch, TEVAR for descending
TEVAR stent grafting alone in every case, regardless of the rupture site or the patient's stability
Permissive hypotension with fluid restriction and watchful observation, avoiding any surgery
Conservative management with tight blood pressure control and beta-blockade, deferring operation
A Bentall procedure with valved root conduit regardless of the rupture site
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Emergency repair — open graft for ascending/arch, TEVAR for descending
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: A ruptured TAA needs emergency repair: open graft replacement for ascending/arch rupture, while emergency TEVAR is usually preferred for a ruptured descending aneurysm where the anatomy allows. Mortality is high either way.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: A 45-year-old with Marfan syndrome has an ascending aortic aneurysm of 4.6 cm on CT. At what diameter should prophylactic surgery be offered?
options: Only once the aneurysm becomes symptomatic, irrespective of its measured diameter on imaging
≥6.0 cm, using the same fixed threshold for everyone regardless of Marfan's or connective disease
≥5.5 cm for all patients regardless of any underlying genetic or connective tissue disorder present
≥4.5–5.0 cm (or at smaller diameters if rapid expansion or genetic connective tissue disorder)
Only if the aneurysm extends to involve the arch vessels, irrespective of its diameter
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: ≥4.5–5.0 cm (or at smaller diameters if rapid expansion or genetic connective tissue disorder)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: In Marfan the ascending aorta/root is replaced at ≥5 cm, falling to ≥4.5 cm where there are risk factors — family history of dissection, growth ≥3 mm/year, severe aortic regurgitation, planned pregnancy — versus ≥5.5 cm for degenerative disease with a tricuspid valve. Bicuspid AV is usually still ≥5.5 cm, and Loeys-Dietz is ≥4.5 cm (ESC). At 4.6 cm he sits in the range where risk factors decide.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: What is the most common genetic condition associated with thoracic aortic aneurysm?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Marfan syndrome (FBN1 mutation)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Marfan syndrome (fibrillin-1 mutation) causes cystic medial necrosis of the aortic wall — predisposing to ascending aortic aneurysm and dissection. Also associated: bicuspid aortic valve, Loeys-Dietz syndrome, Turner syndrome.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: What is the surgical repair of ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm called?
options: Bentall procedure (if aortic root involved) or tube graft replacement
EVAR — an endovascular stent graft deployed within the ascending aorta
TEVAR (thoracic EVAR) — a stent graft placed across the ascending aorta
Insertion of an intra-aortic balloon pump to support the ascending aorta
Carotid endarterectomy to relieve pressure on the ascending aorta
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Bentall procedure (if aortic root involved) or tube graft replacement
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Ascending aortic aneurysm repair: tube graft replacement (aortic body only) or Bentall procedure (root + ascending aorta + valve composite graft). TEVAR is for DESCENDING thoracic aorta; ascending repairs require open sternotomy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Which drug class is used for medical management of aortic aneurysm in Marfan syndrome?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Beta-blockers (and losartan — ARB)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Beta-blockade is first-line, reducing aortic wall stress by lowering dP/dt (the rate of pressure rise). An ARB such as losartan roughly halves the rate of aortic root growth in Marfan, and does so whether or not the patient is already on a beta-blocker — so it is used when beta-blockers are not tolerated and increasingly in combination, not merely for blood-pressure control.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: What complication is specific to TEVAR for descending thoracic aortic aneurysm (not EVAR)?
options: Acute renal failure from contrast use
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Spinal cord ischaemia (paraplegia)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: TEVAR covers intercostal arteries including the artery of Adamkiewicz (major anterior spinal artery) — risk of spinal cord ischaemia/paraplegia. CSF drainage lowers CSF pressure and so RAISES spinal cord perfusion pressure (SCPP = MAP − CSF pressure), used both prophylactically and to treat established paraplegia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: A 55-year-old presents with a hoarse voice. CT shows a 5.5 cm left-sided thoracic aortic aneurysm. What is the cause of hoarseness?
options: Compression of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve by the aneurysm
Direct involvement of the left common carotid artery by the aneurysm
External compression of the trachea and larynx by the expanding aneurysm
Compression of the left phrenic nerve as it runs beside the aneurysm
Extension of an aortic dissection flap up into the left carotid artery
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Compression of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve by the aneurysm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops around the aortic arch — compression by a thoracic aneurysm or mass causes hoarse voice (left vocal cord palsy). This is an indication for urgent CT and surgical referral.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: What is the combined annual risk of rupture, dissection or death for a thoracic aortic aneurysm >6 cm?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: ~10–14% per year
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Above 6 cm the combined annual rate of rupture, dissection or death is roughly 10–15% — rupture or dissection alone accounts for about 7% of that, and rupture alone under 4%. The steep rise at 6 cm is why the degenerative threshold sits at 5.5 cm, and lower again (≥5 cm, or ≥4.5 cm with risk factors) in Marfan and other heritable aortopathy. Ruptured TAA carries >50% mortality.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Which imaging modality is definitive for measuring size and extent and for planning repair in TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: CT aortography (CTA)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: CT aortography is the gold standard for measuring size and extent and for planning intervention — 3D reconstruction allows precise diameter measurement. MR angiography is the radiation-free alternative, and TTE is used for serial aortic root surveillance in Marfan. CXR may show a widened mediastinum but is not diagnostic.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: A 34-year-old man is diagnosed with a 4.8 cm ascending aortic aneurysm and found to have Marfan syndrome. Besides planning his own surgery, what should be arranged?
options: Imaging of first-degree relatives and referral for genetic counselling
Enrolment of his relatives in the national aortic screening programme
No family action unless a relative develops symptoms
Screening of his relatives with abdominal ultrasound at age 65
Annual chest X-ray for all household contacts
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Imaging of first-degree relatives and referral for genetic counselling
explanation: Imaging of first-degree relatives and referral for genetic counselling — Marfan syndrome is autosomal dominant, so each first-degree relative has a substantial risk of carrying it and of harbouring an undetected aneurysm. They need aortic imaging and formal genetic assessment.
The national programme — there is no national screening programme for thoracic aortic aneurysm; the NHS programme is a one-off abdominal ultrasound for men at 65 and would not detect this.
Waiting for symptoms — thoracic aneurysms are typically silent until dissection or rupture, which is precisely why relatives are screened before symptoms appear.
Abdominal ultrasound at 65 — wrong territory and wrong age; the aneurysm risk here is thoracic and presents decades earlier.
Chest X-ray of household contacts — the condition is inherited, not transmissible, and plain films are insensitive for aortic root dilatation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Why is hypertension described as the 'silent killer'?
options: It always presents with a severe pounding morning headache
It causes sudden painless bilateral loss of vision
It only affects elderly patients over eighty years of age
It is rapidly fatal within a few days without treatment
It is usually asymptomatic until end-organ damage occurs
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: It is usually asymptomatic until end-organ damage occurs
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Hypertension is a sustained elevation of BP that is usually asymptomatic until end-organ damage occurs — hence the 'silent killer'.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Why must a raised clinic BP be confirmed with ABPM or HBPM before diagnosing hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: To exclude the white-coat effect
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Clinic measurement is confirmed with ABPM or HBPM to exclude the white-coat effect; white-coat hypertension is common and ABPM prevents over-treatment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: What are the Stage 1 hypertension thresholds for clinic and ABPM/HBPM?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Clinic ≥140/90, ABPM/HBPM ≥135/85
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Stage 1 is clinic BP ≥140/90 and ABPM/HBPM ≥135/85.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: When should Stage 1 hypertension be treated?
options: Always, regardless of age, cardiovascular risk, diabetes or evidence of target organ damage
If aged under 80 with target organ damage, established CVD, renal disease, diabetes, or CV risk ≥10%
Only if the patient is over 80 with target organ damage or established cardiovascular disease
Only in pregnancy, or in women of childbearing age who are planning a pregnancy
Never — Stage 1 hypertension is observed with annual review whatever the risk score
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: If aged under 80 with target organ damage, established CVD, renal disease, diabetes, or CV risk ≥10%
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Stage 1 is treated if the patient is under 80 with target organ damage, established CVD, renal disease, diabetes (type 1 or 2), or a 10-year CV risk ≥10% (NICE) — five criteria, not three. Also consider treatment under 60 even if risk is below 10%. Stage 2 is treated regardless of other factors.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: A patient has a clinic BP of ≥180/120. What is the appropriate action?
options: Routine review in 4 weeks, with no urgent bloods or examination needed today
Offer antihypertensive treatment immediately regardless of any other risk factor
Assess for target organ damage as soon as possible; the action then depends on what is found
Repeat ABPM at home and review the averaged readings again in 3 months
No action needed, as this reading sits within acceptable clinic limits
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Assess for target organ damage as soon as possible; the action then depends on what is found
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Stage 3/severe (≥180/120) warrants assessment for target organ damage as soon as possible — "same-day" is reserved for the referral branch — then three branches: retinal haemorrhage/papilloedema or life-threatening symptoms → same-day referral (emergency); target organ damage such as LVH or albuminuria → start oral treatment immediately without waiting for ABPM; neither → repeat clinic BP or ABPM/HBPM with review within 7 days.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Approximately what proportion of hypertension is primary/essential, and what characterises it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: ~90% — no identifiable cause, polygenic
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Primary/essential hypertension accounts for ~90%, has no identifiable cause and is polygenic (multiple genes plus lifestyle).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: What is the commonest category of secondary hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Renal (~80% of secondary)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Renal causes are traditionally quoted as the commonest category of secondary hypertension (~80%), including CKD, renovascular disease and polycystic kidney disease. Note that primary aldosteronism is increasingly recognised as the commonest single secondary cause.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Which of the following is listed as an endocrine cause of secondary hypertension?
options: Coarctation of the aorta (a vascular cause)
Chronic NSAID use retaining salt and water
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Conn's syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Endocrine causes include Conn's syndrome, phaeochromocytoma, Cushing's, acromegaly and thyroid disease (hyper- or hypothyroidism).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Which of these drugs is listed as a cause of secondary hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Liquorice
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Listed drug causes are NSAIDs, oestrogen (OCP), alcohol, liquorice, cocaine and ciclosporin.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: When should you 'think secondary' hypertension?
options: Young, resistant (≥3 drugs), or sudden onset
Only if the patient is pregnant
Only if BP is below target
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Young, resistant (≥3 drugs), or sudden onset
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Think secondary if Young, Resistant (≥3 drugs) or Sudden onset — especially under 40, refractory HTN, or with a clinical clue (e.g. hypokalaemia → Conn's).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: A patient with hypertension has muscle weakness, polyuria and cramps, with hypokalaemia. Which secondary cause does this suggest, and what is the clue?
options: Phaeochromocytoma — paroxysmal BP spikes with sweating, palpitations and episodic headache
Cushing's — moon face with central obesity, striae and proximal muscle weakness
Conn's syndrome — hypokalaemia + HTN → primary hyperaldosteronism until proven otherwise
Coarctation — radiofemoral delay with weaker, delayed pulses felt in both legs
Renal/RAS — an audible renal bruit heard on auscultation of the flank or abdomen
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Conn's syndrome — hypokalaemia + HTN → primary hyperaldosteronism until proven otherwise
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Muscle weakness, polyuria, cramps with hypokalaemia point to Conn's; hypokalaemia + HTN means primary hyperaldosteronism until proven otherwise.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Episodic headache, sweating, palpitations and pallor with paroxysmal BP spikes suggest which secondary cause, and what is the investigation clue?
options: Conn's — a raised aldosterone:renin ratio on screening bloods
Phaeochromocytoma — plasma free or 24h urinary fractionated metanephrines
Cushing's — failure of overnight dexamethasone suppression
Pre-eclampsia — screen for HELLP with proteinuria after 20 weeks
Coarctation — inferior rib notching seen on the chest X-ray
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Phaeochromocytoma — plasma free or 24h urinary fractionated metanephrines
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Episodic headache, sweating, palpitations and pallor with paroxysmal BP spikes suggest phaeochromocytoma; the test is plasma free metanephrines, or 24h urinary fractionated metanephrines — explicitly not catecholamines, which are secreted episodically and have short half-lives.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: A young patient has radiofemoral delay and weak femoral pulses. Which secondary cause is this, and what confirms it?
options: Renal/RAS — asymmetric kidney sizes seen on ultrasound scanning
Cushing's — central obesity with moon face and purple striae
Conn's — hypokalaemia with a raised aldosterone:renin ratio
Coarctation — BP differential arms vs legs; chest X-ray rib notching
Pre-eclampsia — new proteinuria and oedema after 20 weeks gestation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Coarctation — BP differential arms vs legs; chest X-ray rib notching
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Radiofemoral delay and weak femoral pulses in a young patient suggest coarctation; clue is a BP differential between arms and legs, with rib notching on chest X-ray.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Which fundoscopy finding confirms grade IV Keith-Wagener retinopathy in a hypertensive emergency?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Papilloedema — a blurred disc margin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Papilloedema (blurred disc margin) is grade IV Keith-Wagener retinopathy and confirms accelerated/malignant hypertension. Here it reflects ischaemia at the optic nerve head — it is NOT primarily a raised-ICP sign. A normal disc has a sharp margin.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: On fundoscopy, cotton-wool spots (soft exudates) represent what, and which retinopathy grade do they mark?
options: Retinal micro-infarcts from arteriolar occlusion — hallmark of grade III–IV
Lipid deposits — hard yellow exudates marking grade I retinopathy
Normal healthy vessels — grade 0 with no hypertensive changes seen
Drusen deposits beneath the retina — marking grade II retinopathy
Retinal pigment changes — an early feature marking grade I disease
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Retinal micro-infarcts from arteriolar occlusion — hallmark of grade III–IV
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Cotton-wool spots (soft exudates) are retinal micro-infarcts due to arteriolar occlusion and are a hallmark of grade III–IV hypertensive retinopathy in a hypertensive emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: How is the clinic measurement performed in Step 1 of diagnosis?
options: A single clinic reading is taken and needs no device validation or repeat
Average of 5 readings taken over 1 week and reviewed before any diagnosis
Validated device; record the lower of the last two readings
Home readings only, taken twice daily over a week, with no clinic reading
Confirm the diagnosis on a second visit only if the reading is ≥140/90
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Validated device; record the lower of the last two readings
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Step 1: clinic ≥140/90 on a validated device. Check both arms (use the higher if they differ by >15 mmHg), take a second reading and record the LOWER of the last two — NICE does not average. If clinic BP is 140/90–180/120, ABPM (or HBPM if ABPM is declined or not tolerated) is the confirmation — NICE has no repeat-clinic-visit step.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Which ECG finding is assessed as part of end-organ damage in hypertension, and by which criteria?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: LVH — Sokolow-Lyon criteria
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: The ECG is checked for LVH (Sokolow-Lyon criteria) and AF as part of assessing end-organ damage.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Which test screens for Conn's syndrome when there is low K+ or resistant hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Aldosterone:renin ratio
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: The aldosterone:renin ratio screens for Conn's if there is low K+ or resistant HTN.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: How is QRISK3 used in hypertension management?
options: Calculate 10-year CV risk; if ≥10% offer atorvastatin 20 mg; statin regardless if established CVD
Confirm the diagnosis of secondary hypertension and identify the underlying cause of raised BP
Grade the severity of hypertensive retinopathy from the fundoscopic examination findings
Set the individual patient's target blood pressure according to their calculated risk score
Decide between an ACE inhibitor and a calcium-channel blocker as first-line therapy
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Calculate 10-year CV risk; if ≥10% offer atorvastatin 20 mg; statin regardless if established CVD
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: QRISK3 calculates 10-year CV risk; if ≥10% offer atorvastatin 20 mg (primary prevention), and give a statin regardless of score if CVD is established — atorvastatin 80 mg for secondary prevention (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Why is antihypertensive drug choice driven by age and ethnicity?
options: Because a patient's age and ethnicity together reliably determine their ideal body weight
Because age and ethnicity directly determine the measured creatinine clearance and renal dose
Because they predict renin status — the mechanism that determines which drug class works best
Because age and ethnicity reliably predict a patient's long-term adherence to daily therapy
Because a patient's age and ethnicity together set the individual target blood pressure
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Because they predict renin status — the mechanism that determines which drug class works best
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Age and ethnicity predict renin status, which determines which drug class works best (the basis of the ACD algorithm).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: According to the renin logic, which patient group is high-renin and responds best to ACEi/ARB?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Younger/Caucasian
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Younger/Caucasian patients are high-renin (RAAS-dependent), so ACEi/ARB works best; older/Black African/Caribbean are low-renin, favouring CCB or diuretic.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: A 48-year-old Caucasian (not Black African/Caribbean) needs monotherapy. What is first-line?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: A — ACEi or ARB
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: For patients <55 yrs and not Black African/Caribbean, step 1 is A (ACEi or ARB) — a high-renin state where RAAS blockade is most effective.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: A patient with T2DM of any age/ethnicity needs first-line monotherapy. What is chosen?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: A — ACEi or ARB (renoprotective)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: T2DM at any age/ethnicity → A (ACEi or ARB), which is renoprotective. In people of black African or African–Caribbean family origin, choose an ARB in preference to an ACEi (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: What is the Step 2 two-drug combination in hypertension?
options: A + D in every patient, as a diuretic is always the best second agent
C + D only, combining a calcium-channel blocker with a thiazide diuretic
A + C or A + D — NICE offers a choice of CCB or thiazide-like diuretic
A + spironolactone, adding an aldosterone antagonist as the second drug
C + beta-blocker, combining a calcium-channel blocker with bisoprolol
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: A + C or A + D — NICE offers a choice of CCB or thiazide-like diuretic
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: At step 2 NICE offers a choice rather than a preference: add either a CCB or a thiazide-like diuretic to the ACEi/ARB (NICE). A thiazide-like diuretic suits fluid overload or CCB intolerance. In people of black African or African–Caribbean family origin, choose an ARB in preference to an ACEi.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: In Step 4 resistant hypertension with K+ ≤4.5 mmol/L, what is added and what must be monitored?
options: Add an alpha-blocker such as doxazosin; monitor fasting blood glucose regularly
Spironolactone 25 mg; check U&E before and 1 month after (hyperkalaemia risk)
Add a beta-blocker such as bisoprolol; monitor the resting heart rate closely
Add a second calcium-channel blocker; monitor for worsening ankle oedema
Add a thiazide-like diuretic; monitor serum urate for a rising gout risk
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Spironolactone 25 mg; check U&E before and 1 month after (hyperkalaemia risk)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: If K+ ≤4.5, add spironolactone 25 mg (aldosterone antagonist); check U&E before and 1 month after because of hyperkalaemia risk — especially effective if a Conn's component is suspected.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: In Step 4 resistant hypertension with K+ >4.5 mmol/L, what is added?
options: Add spironolactone 25 mg, since a low potassium always favours an aldosterone antagonist
Add a second ACE inhibitor to intensify blockade of the renin-angiotensin system further
An alpha-blocker (doxazosin) or beta-blocker (bisoprolol); beta-blockers less preferred
Add a thiazide-like diuretic such as indapamide to enhance sodium and water excretion
Nothing further — stop escalation as maximal medical therapy has already been reached
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: An alpha-blocker (doxazosin) or beta-blocker (bisoprolol); beta-blockers less preferred
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: If K+ >4.5, add an alpha-blocker (doxazosin) or beta-blocker (bisoprolol); beta-blockers are less preferred due to metabolic side effects, and specialist advice is sought.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Which is a recognised non-pharmacological measure for hypertension at all stages?
options: A high-salt diet with liberal added table salt to maintain circulating volume
Increase alcohol intake modestly each day to promote peripheral vasodilation
Salt restriction <6g/day, DASH diet, aerobic exercise ≥150 min/week
Strict bed rest with avoidance of exertion until the blood pressure settles
Daily high-protein supplements to support the endothelium and lower the BP
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Salt restriction <6g/day, DASH diet, aerobic exercise ≥150 min/week
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Non-pharmacological measures at all stages: salt restriction (<6g/day), DASH diet, aerobic exercise ≥150 min/week, weight loss, limit alcohol, stop smoking.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Why are ACEi (and ARBs) contraindicated in bilateral renal artery stenosis?
options: They raise the serum potassium far too much, causing dangerous life-threatening hyperkalaemia
They precipitate acute gout attacks by markedly raising the serum urate concentration
They cause a persistent dry irritating cough through accumulation of bradykinin in the lungs
They are strongly teratogenic, causing fetal renal and skull defects in early pregnancy
They reduce GFR by removing the efferent arteriolar tone that maintains filtration pressure
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: They reduce GFR by removing the efferent arteriolar tone that maintains filtration pressure
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: In bilateral RAS, ACEi reduce GFR by removing the efferent arteriolar tone that maintains filtration pressure, so they are contraindicated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Which is the most common side effect of dihydropyridine CCBs such as amlodipine?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Ankle oedema
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Ankle oedema is the most common side effect of dihydropyridine CCBs, along with flushing, headache and reflex tachycardia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Which antihypertensive class is a relative contraindication in gout, and why?
options: ACEi — causes hyperkalaemia by reducing aldosterone
CCB — causes dose-dependent ankle oedema and flushing
Beta-blocker — masks the warning signs of hypoglycaemia
ARB — raises serum creatinine and reduces filtration
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Thiazide-like diuretic — raises urate (gout attacks)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Thiazide-like diuretics raise urate and can precipitate gout attacks, making gout a relative contraindication; caution also applies in T2DM.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Which side effects are associated with spironolactone, the Step 4 aldosterone antagonist?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Hyperkalaemia, gynaecomastia (men), menstrual irregularity
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Spironolactone causes hyperkalaemia, gynaecomastia in men and menstrual irregularity; check K+ before starting and use caution if eGFR <45.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Which antihypertensives are recommended in pregnancy, and which classes are absolutely contraindicated?
options: Use an ACE inhibitor throughout pregnancy; avoid labetalol because of the risk of fetal bradycardia and growth restriction
Use spironolactone to control the pressure; avoid all calcium-channel blockers as they are unsafe in pregnancy
Use labetalol, then modified-release nifedipine, then methyldopa; ACEi and ARBs are absolutely contraindicated (teratogenic)
Use thiazide diuretics as first-line control; avoid methyldopa because of its sedating and depressive effects
Use ARBs safely in all three trimesters; avoid all beta-blockers as they reliably restrict fetal growth
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Use labetalol, then modified-release nifedipine, then methyldopa; ACEi and ARBs are absolutely contraindicated (teratogenic)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: NICE orders them: labetalol first-line, modified-release nifedipine if labetalol is unsuitable, methyldopa if both are unsuitable. Target BP in pregnancy is 135/85. ACEi and ARBs are teratogenic and absolutely contraindicated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: What is the clinic BP target for a patient under 80 years?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: For patients <80 years the clinic target is <140/90 (ABPM/HBPM <135/85).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: What is the tighter clinic BP target reserved for CKD with an ACR of 70 mg/mmol or more?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: The clinic target is <140/90 for most people (<150/90 if aged 80 or over). It tightens to <130/80 only in CKD with an ACR of 70 mg/mmol or more (NICE). Type 2 diabetes takes the same target as everyone else — <140/90 — and established CVD on its own does not lower the target either.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Why is the BP target less aggressive in patients over 80 years?
options: Their kidneys are always structurally and functionally normal
Aggressive lowering risks falls, syncope and hypoperfusion
They cannot tolerate any antihypertensive medication at all
Their blood pressure is never genuinely high at this age
They have no established end-organ damage to protect against
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Aggressive lowering risks falls, syncope and hypoperfusion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: In the elderly (>80), aggressive lowering risks falls, syncope and hypoperfusion, so the clinic target is 150/90 unless significant CVD/CKD warrants tighter control.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: How is a malignant / accelerated hypertensive emergency defined?
options: BP ≥180/120 plus evidence of end-organ damage; severity is defined by the damage, not the number alone
A clinic reading of ≥140/90 alone, which on its own is sufficient to define the emergency
Any raised blood pressure accompanied by a headache, regardless of any organ involvement seen
A BP of ≥160/100 in a young patient, as youth alone makes the reading an emergency by definition
A BP of >130/80 in a patient with diabetes, as this threshold on its own defines the emergency
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: BP ≥180/120 plus evidence of end-organ damage; severity is defined by the damage, not the number alone
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Malignant/accelerated HTN is BP ≥180/120 with evidence of end-organ damage; severity is defined by the damage, not the number alone.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: In a hypertensive emergency with chest pain, what is done if aortic dissection is identified?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: IV labetalol urgently
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: For the ACS/aortic dissection presentation, work-up is ECG, troponin and CXR; if dissection is present, give IV labetalol urgently.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Why must BP be lowered slowly in a hypertensive emergency, and what is the target rate?
options: Rapid reduction causes cerebral and renal hypoperfusion; reduce MAP by ≤25% in the first hour, then to 160/100 over 2–6 hours
To save on medication costs; the BP should simply be dropped by 50% immediately with a single large IV bolus
To allow an early switch to oral dosing; the BP should be brought fully down to a normal level within 30 minutes
Because the automated BP machine reads inaccurately at high pressures, so it must be rechecked before acting on it
There is no real need to lower it slowly; rapid normalisation is perfectly safe and the pressure can be dropped fast
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Rapid reduction causes cerebral and renal hypoperfusion; reduce MAP by ≤25% in the first hour, then to 160/100 over 2–6 hours
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Rapid reduction causes cerebral and renal hypoperfusion, so reduce MAP by no more than 25% in the first hour, then cautiously towards 160/100 over 2–6 hours. The exception is acute aortic dissection, where systolic BP must be brought to 100–120 mmHg within about 20 minutes. Uncomplicated malignant hypertension — retinopathy without another acute emergency — is managed with oral therapy in the UK (BIHS).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Which IV agent is preferred when a hypertensive emergency has an ACS or acute LVF component?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: GTN infusion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: A GTN infusion is preferred where the emergency has an ACS or acute LVF component, because nitrate-driven venodilatation reduces preload and relieves pulmonary congestion. IV labetalol remains first-line for most other emergencies, including aortic dissection and pregnancy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Which IV agent is first-line for most hypertensive emergencies in the UK, including aortic dissection and pregnancy?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Labetalol IV
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: IV labetalol is first-line for most hypertensive emergencies in the UK, including aortic dissection and pregnancy, because it lowers BP and heart rate together. GTN is used where there is an ACS or acute LVF component.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Which set of complications represents the cardiac end-organ damage of untreated hypertension?
options: Stroke, TIA and vascular dementia from small-vessel disease
Hypertensive retinopathy graded from 1 to 4 on fundoscopy
CKD with nephrosclerosis and proteinuria from chronic renal damage
PAD, aortic aneurysm and dissection from large-vessel disease
LVH → heart failure (HFpEF), IHD, AF, sudden cardiac death
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: LVH → heart failure (HFpEF), IHD, AF, sudden cardiac death
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Cardiac complications are LVH leading to heart failure (HFpEF), IHD, AF and sudden cardiac death.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Hypertension is the second commonest cause of which end-stage condition?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: End-stage renal disease (ESRD)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Among renal complications (CKD, nephrosclerosis, proteinuria), hypertension is a major cause of end-stage kidney disease. In UK Renal Registry data diabetes is the commonest cause; the "second commonest" ranking comes from US data.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: In the retinal complications of hypertension, which retinopathy grade signifies malignant HTN?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Grade 3/4
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Hypertensive retinopathy is graded 1–4; grade 3/4 signifies malignant HTN.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Exam pearl: a patient on an ACEi develops a persistent dry cough. What is the appropriate switch, and why does it work?
options: Switch to an ARB — same mechanism, no bradykinin accumulation → no cough
Switch to a CCB — a different mechanism with no direct effect on renal function
Switch to a thiazide — a diuretic acting on an entirely different drug target
Switch to spironolactone — a potassium-sparing diuretic that avoids the cough
Stop all antihypertensive drugs and simply monitor the BP off treatment
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Switch to an ARB — same mechanism, no bradykinin accumulation → no cough
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: ACEi dry cough occurs in 10–15%; switch to an ARB, which has the same mechanism but no bradykinin accumulation, so no cough.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: A 52-year-old has a clinic BP of 192/124 at a routine check. He is asymptomatic. Fundoscopy is normal, ECG shows no LVH, urine ACR is normal and U&Es are normal. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Repeat the clinic blood pressure within 7 days
Admit for IV labetalol to lower the blood pressure
Start treatment immediately without any further measurement
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Repeat the clinic blood pressure within 7 days
explanation: Repeat the clinic blood pressure within 7 days — severe hypertension with no target organ damage and no symptoms is not an emergency. NICE advises repeating clinic BP within 7 days, or arranging ABPM/HBPM with clinical review in the same timeframe.
IV labetalol — reserved for a hypertensive emergency, which requires end-organ damage. Rapid reduction here risks cerebral and renal hypoperfusion.
Immediate treatment without further measurement — appropriate only when target organ damage is present; here the workup is clean.
Same-day referral — indicated for retinal haemorrhage or papilloedema, or life-threatening symptoms such as confusion, chest pain, heart failure or AKI, none of which are present.
Review in 3 months — far too slow for a BP of this level, which needs re-assessment within a week.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: A 60-year-old has a clinic BP of 188/122. She is asymptomatic, but ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy and urine ACR is elevated. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Start antihypertensive treatment immediately without waiting for ABPM
Arrange ABPM and start treatment only once it confirms hypertension
Repeat the clinic blood pressure in 7 days before deciding
Start treatment only if she becomes symptomatic
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Start antihypertensive treatment immediately without waiting for ABPM
