explanation: Start antihypertensive treatment immediately without waiting for ABPM — target organ damage is present (LVH and albuminuria), which is the specific exception to the usual rule of confirming with ambulatory or home monitoring first.
Waiting for ABPM — would delay treatment in a patient already sustaining end-organ damage.
Repeat in 7 days — the correct pathway only when no target organ damage is found.
IV therapy — reserved for a hypertensive emergency with acute life-threatening features; she is asymptomatic and this is chronic damage.
Waiting for symptoms — hypertension is usually asymptomatic until damage is advanced, which is precisely why the damage itself triggers treatment.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.question: A tall 19-year-old with long fingers, a high-arched palate and an upwardly dislocated lens is found to have a dilated aortic root. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.explanation: A marfanoid habitus with upward ectopia lentis and aortic root dilatation is Marfan syndrome. Downward lens dislocation with thrombosis and learning difficulty would suggest homocystinuria instead.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.question: A marfanoid patient has downward lens dislocation, a history of venous thrombosis and learning difficulty. Which diagnosis is most likely?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.explanation: Downward lens dislocation with thromboembolism and intellectual disability points to homocystinuria (autosomal recessive). Marfan causes upward lens dislocation without these thrombotic and cognitive features.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.question: What is the leading cause of death in Marfan syndrome?
options: Aortic root dilatation leading to dissection or rupture
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.explanation: Aortic root dilatation progressing to dissection or rupture is the leading cause of death, which is why aortic surveillance and prophylactic treatment are central to management.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.question: Which medication is used to slow the rate of aortic root dilatation in Marfan syndrome?
options: A calcium-channel blocker such as amlodipine
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.explanation: A beta-blocker (or an ARB) reduces aortic wall stress and slows root dilatation. Diuretics, digoxin and aspirin do not address the aortopathy.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.question: Which bedside sign specifically demonstrates arachnodactyly?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.explanation: The thumb (Steinberg) sign — the thumb projecting beyond the ulnar border of the clenched fist — demonstrates arachnodactyly, as does the wrist (Walker-Murdoch) sign. The other signs relate to tetany, DVT or nerve lesions.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.question: A 25-year-old man with Marfan syndrome presents with sudden severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back. What is the immediate concern?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.explanation: Sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back in a Marfan patient is aortic dissection until proven otherwise, and needs urgent imaging (CT aortogram). The dilated aortic root is the substrate.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.question: A marfanoid habitus combined with mucosal neuromas on the lips and tongue should prompt screening for which malignancy?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.explanation: A marfanoid habitus with mucosal neuromas is MEN 2B, which carries a high risk of medullary thyroid carcinoma (and phaeochromocytoma). This is distinct from Marfan syndrome.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.question: Which investigation confirms homocystinuria in a marfanoid patient with downward lens dislocation?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.explanation: Urinary (and plasma) homocysteine confirms homocystinuria. Echo and FBN1 testing address Marfan; the slit-lamp shows the lens direction but does not establish the metabolic diagnosis.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.question: Which valvular lesion is most commonly associated with Marfan syndrome besides aortic regurgitation?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.explanation: Mitral valve prolapse (a mid-systolic click) is commonly associated with Marfan syndrome. Aortic regurgitation may develop as the dilated root stretches the aortic valve.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.question: The Ghent criteria used to diagnose Marfan syndrome place greatest weight on which two features?
options: Aortic root dilatation and ectopia lentis
High-arched palate and skin striae atrophicae
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.explanation: The Ghent criteria weight aortic root dilatation and ectopia lentis most heavily (with family history and FBN1), because these are the most specific and clinically important features. The others contribute to the systemic score.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.question: A tall, thin 20-year-old with Marfan syndrome develops sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. Besides dissection, what is the likely complication?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.explanation: Marfan patients are predisposed to spontaneous pneumothorax from apical blebs, presenting with sudden pleuritic pain and breathlessness. Aortic dissection must also be excluded given the tearing-pain overlap.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.question: Why should the first-degree relatives of a patient with Marfan syndrome be offered assessment?
options: Autosomal dominant: each has a 50% risk of inheriting it
It is autosomal recessive with a 25% risk
Relatives are never affected once the index case is treated
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.explanation: Marfan syndrome is autosomal dominant, so each first-degree relative has a 50% chance of inheriting it and may harbour silent, life-threatening aortic disease — hence clinical, echo and genetic assessment.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.question: A man with Marfan syndrome has a progressively dilating aortic root. At approximately which diameter is elective aortic root replacement usually recommended?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Marfanoid Habitus.explanation: Elective aortic root replacement is generally advised at around 5.0 cm in Marfan syndrome (with a lower ~4.5 cm threshold for a family history of dissection, rapid growth, pregnancy or Loeys-Dietz). Waiting until 6.5–7.0 cm carries an unacceptable dissection / rupture risk.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.question: A 68-year-old is hypotensive with a raised JVP, muffled heart sounds and pulsus paradoxus after a recent MI. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.explanation: Beck’s triad (hypotension + raised JVP + muffled sounds) with pulsus paradoxus after MI indicates cardiac tamponade (e.g. free-wall rupture/effusion). Massive PE gives a clear chest and pleuritic features; acute MR gives a pansystolic murmur and pulmonary oedema; tension pneumothorax gives a hyper-resonant silent hemithorax with tracheal deviation; constriction gives a preserved y descent and pericardial knock, not muffled sounds.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.question: A 72-year-old with syncope has a pulse of 36, and irregular large pulsations are visible in the neck. What do these neck pulsations represent?
options: Giant v waves from tricuspid regurgitation
Cannon ‘a’ waves from complete heart block
Large a waves from pulmonary hypertension
Carotid pulsations transmitted to the neck veins
Absent a waves from atrial fibrillation
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.explanation: Irregular cannon a waves — the atrium contracting against a closed tricuspid valve in complete heart block (AV dissociation). Giant v waves are systolic and accompany a pulsatile liver in TR; large a waves are regular; AF abolishes a waves; the carotid is palpable and single.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.question: A patient has a raised JVP with prominent systolic waves and a pulsatile, enlarged liver, plus a pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge that is louder on inspiration. Which lesion is most likely?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.explanation: Giant v waves + a pulsatile liver + a pansystolic murmur at the LLSE that increases on inspiration (Carvallo’s sign) indicate tricuspid regurgitation. MR radiates to the axilla and does not give giant v waves; AS is an ejection murmur to the carotids; PS and VSD do not cause a pulsatile liver.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.question: A patient has a raised JVP that rises on inspiration, a preserved sharp y descent and an early diastolic pericardial knock. What is the diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.explanation: Kussmaul’s sign, a preserved/prominent y descent and a pericardial knock indicate constrictive pericarditis. Tamponade blunts the y descent (prominent x, absent y); TR gives giant v waves; restrictive cardiomyopathy can mimic constriction but lacks the knock and is distinguished on imaging/haemodynamics; isolated RV failure does not give a knock.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.question: A 60-year-old with an inferior STEMI becomes hypotensive after GTN. He has a raised JVP but clear lung fields. What complication is most likely?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.explanation: A raised JVP with clear lungs and nitrate-induced hypotension after an inferior MI indicates right ventricular infarction — the RV is preload-dependent, so nitrates drop output. Confirm with right-sided lead V4R; treat with fluids. Pulmonary oedema would give crepitations; VSD/rupture give a new murmur or tamponade physiology.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.question: A 63-year-old smoker has facial and arm swelling, distended non-pulsatile neck and chest wall veins, and a positive Pemberton’s sign. What explains the raised JVP?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.explanation: A fixed, non-pulsatile raised JVP with facial/arm swelling and Pemberton’s sign is SVC obstruction (usually lung cancer/mediastinal mass). The others give a pulsatile JVP with a readable waveform: tamponade adds muffled sounds and pulsus paradoxus; right heart failure and tricuspid regurgitation give a pulsatile column (giant v waves in TR); constriction shows a preserved y descent and pericardial knock.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.question: Which feature confirms that a neck pulsation is the JVP rather than the carotid?
options: It is occludable by light pressure
It has a palpable single upstroke
It increases with carotid sinus massage
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.explanation: The JVP is occludable by light pressure (and impalpable, biphasic, fills from above, falls on sitting up, positive HJR). The carotid has a palpable single upstroke and is not occludable; the JVP falls (not rises) on standing and does vary with respiration; carotid sinus massage slows the heart rather than raising the venous pulse.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.question: A 66-year-old with COPD has a raised JVP with large ‘a’ waves, a loud pulmonary second sound and a left parasternal heave. What does this indicate?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.explanation: Large a waves (forceful atrial contraction against a high-pressure RV), a loud P2 and an RV heave indicate pulmonary hypertension / cor pulmonale. LV failure and AS affect the left heart; MS gives a tapping apex; tamponade gives muffled sounds with an impalpable apex, not an RV heave.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.question: A patient has a raised JVP with completely absent ‘a’ waves. What is the most likely explanation?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.explanation: Absent a waves reflect the loss of coordinated atrial contraction in atrial fibrillation. Complete heart block gives intermittent cannon a waves; tricuspid stenosis and pulmonary hypertension give large a waves; TR gives giant v waves.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.question: A patient has a raised JVP of uncertain cause. Which investigation is most useful to establish the diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.explanation: Echocardiography characterises RV function, tamponade physiology, constriction, tricuspid regurgitation and pericardial effusion, establishing the cause. CXR and ECG give supportive clues; BNP indicates strain but not the mechanism; CTPA is targeted only if PE is suspected.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.question: During examination you apply firm pressure over the right upper quadrant for 10 seconds and the JVP rises by 5 cm and stays up. What does this indicate?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.explanation: A sustained rise = a positive hepatojugular reflux, indicating raised right heart filling pressure (e.g. right heart failure). A transient rise that falls again is normal; SVC obstruction gives a fixed non-pulsatile JVP unaffected in this way.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.question: A 30-year-old woman is acutely breathless and shocked with a raised JVP, tachycardia and clear lung fields; ECG shows S1Q3T3. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.explanation: A raised JVP with shock and a clear chest plus S1Q3T3 indicates massive PE (acute right heart strain/obstructive shock). Tamponade gives muffled sounds and pulsus paradoxus; LV failure gives crepitations and an S3; asthma gives wheeze; constriction is chronic with a pericardial knock.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.question: Which feature favours constrictive pericarditis over cardiac tamponade?
options: A globular heart on chest X-ray
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.explanation: Constriction gives a prominent/preserved y descent (rapid early filling) with Kussmaul’s sign. Tamponade blunts the y descent (prominent x, absent y), and pulsus paradoxus, muffled sounds and a globular heart favour a tamponading effusion.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.question: In which condition is Kussmaul’s sign classically ABSENT?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.explanation: Kussmaul’s sign (inspiratory rise in JVP) is classically absent in uncomplicated tamponade but present in constriction, RV infarction and restrictive cardiomyopathy — a useful discriminator.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.question: What is the upper limit of normal for the JVP height above the sternal angle?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.explanation: Normal JVP is ≤3 cm above the sternal angle (≈≤8 cmH₂O once ~5 cm is added for the right atrium). Values above this indicate raised right atrial pressure.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.question: Echocardiography is performed for a raised JVP with hypotension and muffled heart sounds. Which finding confirms cardiac tamponade?
options: Diastolic right atrial / right ventricular collapse
Dilated left ventricle with low ejection fraction
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Raised JVP & Wave.explanation: Tamponade is confirmed by a pericardial effusion with diastolic collapse of the right atrium/ventricle, a plethoric non-collapsing IVC and exaggerated respiratory inflow variation. A dilated poor-EF LV indicates heart failure; LA enlargement and LVH are chronic pressure/volume changes; valve vegetations indicate endocarditis — none is tamponade.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: A 58-year-old presents with crushing chest pain. ECG shows 2 mm ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF. Which artery is most likely occluded?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: II, III and aVF are the inferior leads, supplied by the RCA in most people. The RCA also supplies the AV node, which is why inferior MIs are associated with heart block.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: A patient with an inferior STEMI becomes profoundly hypotensive after a single dose of GTN spray. What is the most likely explanation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Inferior MIs can extend to the RV, which is preload-dependent. Nitrates reduce preload and can precipitate severe hypotension. This is why right-sided leads (V4R) are recorded in inferior STEMIs before giving nitrates.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Which finding most reliably distinguishes NSTEMI from unstable angina?
options: The presence of chest pain at rest
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Both can present identically with partial occlusion and ST depression/T inversion. Only NSTEMI causes myocyte necrosis, so troponin rises in NSTEMI but remains normal in unstable angina.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: A 70-year-old diabetic presents with sudden dyspnoea, sweating and nausea but no chest pain. Troponin is markedly raised. What does this illustrate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Diabetics and the elderly may infarct without classic chest pain (often due to autonomic neuropathy), presenting instead with dyspnoea, sweating or collapse. A normal pain history does not exclude MI in these groups.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Place the early atherosclerosis steps in the correct order: (1) fibrous cap formation, (2) endothelial dysfunction, (3) foam cell formation, (4) plaque rupture.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Endothelial dysfunction comes first, then LDL-laden macrophages form foam cells (fatty streak), then smooth muscle migrates to form a fibrous cap, and finally the cap ruptures, triggering thrombosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Which of the following is a NON-modifiable risk factor for acute coronary syndrome?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Non-modifiable risk factors are increasing age, male sex and a positive family history. The other options listed are all modifiable.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: A positive family history of premature coronary disease is defined by a first-degree relative affected before which age (male/female)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: A 1st-degree relative with cardiac disease before age 55 (male) or 65 (female) counts as a positive family history.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: A patient with chest pain has a 12-lead ECG showing a new left bundle branch block. What is the correct management approach?
options: Treat as unstable angina with medical therapy only
Treat as STEMI and activate the primary PCI pathway
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: Treat as STEMI and activate the primary PCI pathway
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: New LBBB with ischaemic chest pain is treated as a STEMI-equivalent, warranting the primary PCI (PPCI) pathway, because LBBB masks the usual ST-segment changes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: A troponin taken 1 hour after the onset of chest pain is normal. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: MI is excluded, since a single normal troponin at 1 hour rules it out
A negative early troponin does not rule out ACS; repeat sampling is needed
MI is confirmed, as any troponin drawn within 1 hour is diagnostic of infarction
The patient has unstable angina by definition once the 1-hour troponin is normal
The chest pain is non-cardiac, proven by the normal troponin on early sampling
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: A negative early troponin does not rule out ACS; repeat sampling is needed
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Troponin rises ~3–6 hours after symptom onset, so a single early sample can be falsely reassuring. Serial troponins (e.g. 0h and 1h, or 0h and 3h) showing a rise/fall pattern are needed.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Which feature on serial troponin testing best supports an acute myocardial infarction rather than a chronic cause?
options: A dynamic rise and/or fall between samples
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: A dynamic rise and/or fall between samples
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Acute MI produces a dynamic rise and/or fall pattern. A static raised troponin is more suggestive of a chronic cause such as CKD or chronic heart failure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: What is the single most common cause of death within the first hour following a myocardial infarction?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Malignant ventricular arrhythmias (VF/VT) are the commonest cause of death in the first hour. The other complications listed tend to occur later.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: A patient develops fever, pleuritic chest pain and a pericardial rub 3 weeks after an MI, with raised CRP and ESR. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Dressler's syndrome is an autoimmune pericarditis occurring 2–6 weeks post-MI, with fever, pleuritic pain, a pericardial rub and raised inflammatory markers. Treat with aspirin or an NSAID plus colchicine, reserving steroids for refractory cases (ESC). The earlier peri-infarction pericarditis at 24–72h is treated with high-dose aspirin, avoiding other NSAIDs and steroids which impair infarct healing.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Three days after an anterior MI, a patient suddenly develops a loud pansystolic murmur, a raised JVP and signs of right heart failure, with a step-up in oxygen saturation between the right atrium and right ventricle. Which complication is most likely?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Septal rupture (VSD) and papillary muscle rupture both occur ~3–5 days post-MI. A VSD classically produces a new pansystolic murmur with acute decompensation; papillary muscle rupture causes acute mitral regurgitation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Persistent ST elevation several weeks after an MI, with no ongoing pain, most suggests which complication?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: A LV aneurysm causes persistent ST elevation weeks after the acute event and carries a risk of mural thrombus formation and embolism.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Which post-MI complication classically presents with sudden tamponade and pulseless electrical activity (electromechanical dissociation)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Free wall rupture causes haemopericardium, tamponade and electromechanical dissociation, and is usually rapidly fatal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) after ACS most commonly consists of which combination?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: DAPT = aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor (e.g. clopidogrel or ticagrelor), usually continued for 12 months post-ACS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Which scoring system is used to risk-stratify patients with NSTEMI to guide management decisions?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: The GRACE score predicts mortality after an NSTEMI and is used to decide how urgently the patient needs angiography. CHA₂DS₂-VASc is for stroke risk in AF, Wells for VTE, CURB-65 for pneumonia and QRISK3 for primary cardiovascular prevention.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Which investigation finding would most specifically prompt consideration of aortic dissection as an alternative to ACS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: A widened mediastinum on chest X-ray is a classic clue to aortic dissection, an important differential of acute chest pain that a CXR can help flag.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: What is the preferred vascular access route for coronary angiography in ACS, and its main dual purpose?
options: Radial; diagnostic and therapeutic (PCI at the same sitting)
Femoral; purely diagnostic, reserved only for imaging the coronaries
Brachial; therapeutic only, used solely to deliver coronary stents
Femoral; therapeutic only, used to perform PCI but never for imaging
Radial; purely diagnostic, with no option to intervene at all
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: Radial; diagnostic and therapeutic (PCI at the same sitting)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Radial access is preferred (lower bleeding risk). Angiography both defines the coronary anatomy and allows therapeutic PCI during the same procedure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: What is the earliest ECG change in an evolving STEMI, appearing within minutes to hours?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Hyperacute tall, peaked T waves are the first change, preceding ST elevation. Q waves and T inversion appear later in the evolution.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Which ECG feature persists permanently as a marker of a previous full-thickness MI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: By weeks–months, the ST segment returns to baseline and T waves normalise, but pathological Q waves remain permanently as evidence of myocardial scar.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Which of the following correctly defines a pathological Q wave?
options: >0.5 mm wide or >10% of R-wave height
>1 mm wide (>40 ms) or >25% of the R-wave height
>2 mm tall in two contiguous leads
>3 mm wide in any single lead
Any Q wave in lead III
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: >1 mm wide (>40 ms) or >25% of the R-wave height
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: A pathological Q wave is >1 mm wide (>40 ms) or exceeds 25% of the height of the following R wave, indicating established necrosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: A STEMI shows ST elevation in V1–V4. Which artery is the likely culprit?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: V1–V4 are the anterior leads, supplied by the LAD. Inferior (II, III, aVF) maps to the RCA and lateral (I, aVL, V5–V6) to the circumflex.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: ST elevation in leads I, aVL, V5 and V6 indicates infarction of which territory?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: I, aVL, V5 and V6 are the lateral leads, supplied by the left circumflex artery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: A patient has a dominant R wave in V1 with ST depression in V1–V3. What does this most likely represent?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: These anterior-lead changes are the mirror image of true posterior ST elevation, indicating a posterior STEMI (RCA or circumflex territory).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: What does the 'MONA' mnemonic represent in the immediate management of ACS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: MONA = Morphine, Oxygen, Nitrates, Aspirin — the immediate measures applied across all ACS presentations.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Why should supplemental oxygen be withheld unless SpO₂ falls below 94% in ACS?
options: It is expensive to administer and depletes scarce ward oxygen supplies
Hyperoxia causes coronary vasoconstriction and worsens infarct size
It masks chest pain, delaying recognition of ongoing myocardial ischaemia
It interferes with troponin assays, producing falsely elevated readings
It increases the risk of arrhythmia directly by raising cardiac excitability
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: Hyperoxia causes coronary vasoconstriction and worsens infarct size
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Routine high-flow oxygen in non-hypoxic patients causes coronary vasoconstriction and can enlarge the infarct, so it is reserved for SpO₂ <94% — targeting 94–98%, or 88–92% in those at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (BTS).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: In which scenario should nitrates be given with particular caution during ACS?
options: Inferior MI with right ventricular involvement
Stable patient with normal blood pressure
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: Inferior MI with right ventricular involvement
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: RV infarction is preload-dependent; nitrates reduce preload and can cause profound hypotension. They should also be avoided if the patient is already hypotensive.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: How should the 300 mg loading dose of aspirin be administered in acute ACS for fastest effect?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Aspirin 300 mg is chewed or crushed to speed absorption and achieve rapid antiplatelet action.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Besides sedation and respiratory depression, what is a key pharmacological drawback of morphine in ACS?
options: It delays absorption of P2Y12 inhibitors
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: It delays absorption of P2Y12 inhibitors
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Morphine slows gastric emptying and delays P2Y12 inhibitor absorption, blunting antiplatelet onset. It's reserved for severe pain and given with an anti-emetic.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: A STEMI is confirmed within 12 hours of symptom onset and primary PCI can be delivered within 120 minutes of the time fibrinolysis could have been given. What is the correct reperfusion strategy?
options: Wait and repeat ECG in 90 minutes
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: NICE: offer primary PCI when the patient presents within 12 hours of symptom onset and PCI can be delivered within 120 minutes of the time fibrinolysis could have been given. Otherwise, fibrinolysis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: A STEMI is confirmed but the nearest PCI centre cannot treat the patient within 120 minutes. What is the appropriate next step?
options: Discharge home on aspirin with outpatient follow-up
Give an intravenous beta-blocker as sole therapy
Await the troponin result before any intervention
Repeat the troponin at 12 hours before deciding
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: If primary PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes of the time fibrinolysis could have been given, fibrinolysis is given instead — in the UK usually tenecteplase, a single weight-based bolus that ambulance crews can give pre-hospital. It goes alongside an antithrombin (fondaparinux or enoxaparin) and a second antiplatelet (clopidogrel). Screen for bleeding risk first, and repeat the ECG at 60–90 minutes to check for reperfusion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: After fibrinolysis for STEMI, the ECG is repeated at 60–90 minutes and still shows persistent ST elevation. What does this indicate?
options: Failed lysis — proceed to rescue PCI
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: Failed lysis — proceed to rescue PCI
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Persistent ST elevation at 60–90 minutes signals failed fibrinolysis, and the patient should undergo rescue PCI.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: A patient with STEMI is on a long-term oral anticoagulant and is going for primary PCI. Which second antiplatelet is preferred?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Clopidogrel is preferred over prasugrel/ticagrelor as the second antiplatelet when a patient is already on an oral anticoagulant, to reduce bleeding risk.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Which of the following is a component of the '6 A's' of secondary prevention after ACS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: The 6 A's are Aspirin, Another antiplatelet, Atorvastatin, ACE inhibitor, Atenolol/beta-blocker, and Aldosterone antagonist (if HF post-MI).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: What is the principal benefit of a beta-blocker in the months following a myocardial infarction?
options: It raises the heart rate to improve output
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Beta-blockers (e.g. bisoprolol) are titrated up post-MI to limit adverse ventricular remodelling and improve prognosis. Continue indefinitely if LVEF is reduced; at least 12 months if LVEF is preserved (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: An aldosterone antagonist such as eplerenone is added post-MI. Which is the most important parameter to monitor?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Eplerenone causes hyperkalaemia, so potassium must be monitored — especially when combined with an ACE inhibitor, which also raises potassium.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Why does combining an ACE inhibitor with an aldosterone antagonist after MI require careful monitoring?
options: Both cause hyperkalaemia and can impair renal function
Both lower blood pressure to dangerous levels only when combined
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: Both cause hyperkalaemia and can impair renal function
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: ACE inhibitors and aldosterone antagonists each raise potassium and can worsen renal function, so U&Es must be monitored when used together.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Which of the following is part of the duration recommendation for dual antiplatelet therapy in secondary prevention?
options: Aspirin alone for 12 months and then stopping all therapy
No antiplatelet therapy at all once the patient is discharged
Both antiplatelet agents continued indefinitely for life
Aspirin for just 1 month, then no further antiplatelet cover
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: In secondary prevention, aspirin continues indefinitely while the second antiplatelet (ticagrelor 90 mg BD or clopidogrel 75 mg OD) is given for 12 months — this combination is DAPT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Why does an NSTEMI characteristically cause subendocardial rather than transmural ischaemia?
options: The occlusion is total but selectively spares the epicardium, injuring only the inner wall
Troponin is released only from the epicardium, so subendocardial injury dominates the picture
The subendocardium has the richest collateral supply, so it resists ischaemia longest of the layers
Partial occlusion affects the subendocardium first, as it is the watershed region of perfusion
The outer epicardial wall is perfused directly by the coronary sinus, protecting it from ischaemia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: Partial occlusion affects the subendocardium first, as it is the watershed region of perfusion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: NSTEMI involves partial occlusion. The subendocardium is the most distal, watershed zone of coronary perfusion, so it becomes ischaemic first while the outer wall is relatively spared.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Which ECG pattern is consistent with an NSTEMI?
options: Tombstoning ST elevation in inferior leads
ST depression, T-wave inversion, or a normal ECG
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: ST depression, T-wave inversion, or a normal ECG
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: By definition NSTEMI shows no ST elevation and no new LBBB; the ECG may show ST depression, T-wave inversion, or be normal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: A patient has chest pain and ST depression on ECG; the troponin is raised, so this is an NSTEMI. With an identical presentation but a normal troponin, what would the diagnosis be instead?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: NSTEMI and unstable angina present identically; the raised troponin (myocyte necrosis) defines NSTEMI, whereas a normal troponin would make it unstable angina.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: On GRACE risk stratification, a predicted 6-month mortality above which threshold warrants early angiography, and within what timeframe?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: A GRACE-predicted 6-month mortality above 3% indicates intermediate or higher risk, prompting angiography within 72 hours. GRACE itself returns a points score, e.g. 141 — it is the mortality it predicts that carries the 3% threshold (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: What does the 'BATMAN' mnemonic represent in the management of NSTEMI / unstable angina?
options: Base on GRACE, Aspirin, Ticagrelor, Morphine, Antithrombin, Nitrate
Beta-blocker, Aspirin, Thrombolysis, Morphine, ACEi, Nitrate
Bisoprolol, Atorvastatin, Ticagrelor, Metoclopramide, ACEi, Naloxone
Base on GRACE, Atropine, Thrombolysis, Magnesium, Antithrombin, Nitrate
Beta-blocker, Adenosine, Ticagrelor, Morphine, Aspirin, Naloxone
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: Base on GRACE, Aspirin, Ticagrelor, Morphine, Antithrombin, Nitrate
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: BATMAN = Base on GRACE score, Aspirin 300 mg, Ticagrelor 180 mg, Morphine (if severe pain), Antithrombin (fondaparinux/enoxaparin), Nitrate (for ongoing pain).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: In the BATMAN protocol, what does the letter 'B' direct the clinician to do?
options: Begin intravenous beta-blockade immediately in every patient
Book an urgent bedside echocardiogram before anything else
Bolus intravenous unfractionated heparin as the first step
Base management on the GRACE score to guide angiography timing
Begin fibrinolytic therapy without delay in all cases
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: Base management on the GRACE score to guide angiography timing
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: The 'B' stands for Base on GRACE score, which risk-stratifies the patient and determines the timing of angiography/PCI.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: What is the standard second antiplatelet and dose in the BATMAN approach to NSTEMI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Ticagrelor 180 mg stat is the standard second antiplatelet; clopidogrel 300 mg is used if high bleeding risk, and prasugrel if proceeding to angiography.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Which second antiplatelet is preferred in NSTEMI/UA when the patient has a high bleeding risk?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Clopidogrel 300 mg replaces ticagrelor when bleeding risk is high, as it carries a lower bleeding risk.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Which antithrombin agent is the preferred choice in the BATMAN management of NSTEMI/UA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Fondaparinux is the preferred antithrombin in NSTEMI/UA unless there is high bleeding risk or immediate angiography is planned. Unfractionated heparin is the alternative where renal function is significantly impaired, and everyone going to the cath lab receives systemic UFH there as well (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: What is the defining feature of unstable angina compared with the other acute coronary syndromes?
options: Total coronary occlusion with transmural necrosis
A raised troponin with normal ECG
ST elevation in two contiguous leads
Partial occlusion causing ischaemia without infarction
Complete resolution of pain at rest
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: Partial occlusion causing ischaemia without infarction
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Unstable angina is partial occlusion producing ischaemia but no myocyte necrosis, which is why troponin stays normal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: A patient has rest chest pain, ST depression on ECG, and a normal troponin on serial testing. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Ischaemic symptoms and ECG changes with a normal troponin define unstable angina; a raised troponin would make it an NSTEMI.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Which of the following is NOT a typical presentation of unstable angina?
options: Predictable exertional pain relieved by rest, stable for years
Pain at rest with normal troponin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: Predictable exertional pain relieved by rest, stable for years
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Stable, predictable exertional angina is stable angina. Unstable angina is defined by new-onset pain, rest pain, or crescendo (rapidly worsening) angina.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: A patient with longstanding stable angina reports that over the past week attacks are far more frequent and triggered by minimal effort. What is this called?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Rapidly progressive angina on minimal exertion is crescendo angina, a form of unstable angina reflecting an unstable plaque and requiring ACS assessment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: What is the appropriate initial management approach for unstable angina?
options: Primary PCI within 120 minutes regardless of the patient's risk stratification
The same as NSTEMI — the BATMAN protocol with GRACE risk stratification
Immediate fibrinolysis with alteplase to dissolve the occluding thrombus
Discharge home with a GTN spray and no further investigation or workup
Immediate coronary artery bypass grafting as the first-line approach
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: The same as NSTEMI — the BATMAN protocol with GRACE risk stratification
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Unstable angina shares its initial management with NSTEMI: the BATMAN approach, using the GRACE score to guide angiography timing.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Which ECG finding would make a diagnosis of unstable angina LESS likely and point instead to STEMI?
options: ST elevation ≥1 mm in two contiguous leads
ST depression in the inferolateral leads
Sinus tachycardia with a rapid ventricular rate
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: ST elevation ≥1 mm in two contiguous leads
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Unstable angina shows ST depression, T-wave inversion, or a normal ECG. ST elevation indicates a STEMI, not unstable angina.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: What is the fundamental mechanism underlying pain in stable angina?
options: Plaque rupture with superimposed thrombus causing total coronary occlusion
Embolic occlusion of a small distal coronary branch during exertion
Transient coronary artery vasospasm occurring spontaneously at rest
Inflammation of the pericardial sac irritating the underlying myocardium
A fixed flow-limiting stenosis where demand exceeds supply on exertion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: A fixed flow-limiting stenosis where demand exceeds supply on exertion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Stable angina arises from a fixed, intact atheromatous plaque causing flow-limiting stenosis. Ischaemia occurs only when oxygen demand outstrips supply during exertion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Using the 3-feature typicality ladder, chest pain meeting only 2 of the 3 angina characteristics is classified as what?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: All 3 features = typical; 2 of 3 = atypical; ≤1 of 3 = non-anginal. The three features are constricting central pain, exertional onset, and relief by rest/GTN within ~5 minutes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Which of the following is one of the three defining features of typical angina?
options: Pleuritic chest pain worse on inspiration
Pain reproduced by chest wall palpation
Relief by rest or GTN within ~5 minutes
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: Relief by rest or GTN within ~5 minutes
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: The three features are constricting central/retrosternal pain ± radiation, exertional onset, and relief by rest or GTN within ~5 minutes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: According to NICE, what is the first-line investigation for stable chest pain of suspected cardiac origin in a patient with no known coronary artery disease?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: NICE recommends CTCA first-line; it is non-invasive, identifies plaque burden and stenosis, and has an excellent negative predictive value for ruling out significant CAD.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Which property of CTCA makes it especially useful as a first-line test in stable angina?
options: Its ability to deliver simultaneous PCI
Its measurement of fractional flow reserve
Its assessment of wall motion under stress
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: CTCA's strength is its excellent negative predictive value, allowing it to effectively rule out significant coronary disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: When is troponin appropriately measured in the assessment of suspected angina?
options: Routinely in all stable angina patients
Only if there is an unstable or acute presentation
As the first-line test before CTCA
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: Only if there is an unstable or acute presentation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Troponin is reserved for unstable/acute presentations; it is not part of the routine stable angina workup.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: How does antiplatelet therapy for stable angina differ from that following ACS?
options: Stable angina uses a single antiplatelet (aspirin); ACS uses DAPT
Stable angina uses DAPT; ACS uses a single antiplatelet
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: Stable angina uses a single antiplatelet (aspirin); ACS uses DAPT
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Stable angina is managed with a single antiplatelet (aspirin 75 mg, or clopidogrel if intolerant), whereas ACS requires dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + a P2Y12 inhibitor).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: A patient with stable angina also has type 2 diabetes and hypertension. Which additional drug class is specifically indicated?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: An ACE inhibitor is indicated where there is co-existing diabetes, hypertension, CKD or heart failure — it is cardioprotective and reduces afterload.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: A patient using GTN spray for an angina attack gets no relief after the first dose and a repeat 5 minutes later. What should they be advised to do?
options: Take a third dose and wait another 10 minutes
Lie flat and rest until it passes
Call 999, as this may represent ACS
Take aspirin and review with the GP next week
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: Call 999, as this may represent ACS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: The GTN protocol is: dose → wait 5 min → repeat dose → wait 5 min → call 999 if still no relief, as ongoing pain may indicate an acute coronary syndrome.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: What is the mechanism by which sublingual GTN relieves anginal pain?
options: Beta-blockade reducing heart rate and thereby lowering myocardial oxygen demand
Calcium channel blockade reducing contractility and afterload on the heart
Nitric oxide donation causing venodilation, reducing preload and oxygen demand
Inhibition of the funny (If) current in the sinoatrial node to slow the rate
Late sodium-channel inhibition reducing calcium overload in ischaemic myocytes
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: Nitric oxide donation causing venodilation, reducing preload and oxygen demand
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: GTN is a nitric oxide donor; venodilation reduces preload and therefore myocardial oxygen demand, and it also dilates the coronary arteries.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Which of the following is a first-line agent for prophylactic symptom control in stable angina?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: First-line prophylaxis is a beta-blocker OR a rate-limiting CCB (if the beta-blocker is contraindicated). Statins, aspirin and ACEi are secondary prevention, not symptom control.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Why must a beta-blocker NOT be combined with verapamil or diltiazem in stable angina?
options: It risks bradycardia, heart block or sinus arrest
It causes a dangerous rise in blood pressure
It provokes a marked compensatory reflex tachycardia
It substantially increases the risk of bleeding
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: It risks bradycardia, heart block or sinus arrest
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Beta-blockers and rate-limiting CCBs both suppress AV conduction and heart rate; together they risk profound bradycardia, complete heart block or sinus arrest. Beta-blocker + amlodipine is the safe combination.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: A patient with stable angina and HFrEF needs a calcium channel blocker added. Which is the safest choice?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Rate-limiting CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem) are negative inotropes and can decompensate HFrEF. Amlodipine, a dihydropyridine, is the safer choice when a CCB is required in heart failure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: A beta-blocker-intolerant patient in sinus rhythm needs additional rate-lowering anti-anginal therapy. Which add-on agent works via the funny (If) current?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Ivabradine is an If-channel inhibitor that lowers heart rate, useful if a beta-blocker is not tolerated, but it only works in sinus rhythm.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: When is CABG generally favoured over PCI for revascularisation?
options: Single discrete vessel disease in an otherwise low-risk patient with preserved LV function
Mild non-obstructive coronary disease found incidentally on angiography imaging
When a shorter recovery time and avoidance of sternotomy are the main priorities
When the patient is unable to tolerate even a brief course of dual antiplatelet therapy
Left main stem or severe multivessel disease, especially with diabetes or poor LV function
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: Left main stem or severe multivessel disease, especially with diabetes or poor LV function
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: CABG is favoured for left main stem disease, severe/multivessel disease, diabetes, and poor LV function (EF <30%), giving better long-term outcomes in complex disease. PCI suits single/discrete vessel disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Which bypass graft is considered the gold standard, and to which vessel is it anastomosed?
options: Saphenous vein graft, to the right coronary artery
Radial artery graft, to the circumflex
Saphenous vein graft, to the LAD
Radial artery graft, to the LAD
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: The left internal mammary artery is grafted to the LAD. It is the gold standard because an arterial graft stays patent far longer than a vein graft, and the LAD is the vessel where that durability matters most.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: What antiplatelet regimen is required after PCI with a stent for stable angina?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: After elective PCI with a stent for stable angina, dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + clopidogrel) is given for 6 months to prevent stent thrombosis, shortened to 1–3 months if bleeding risk is high. Aspirin then continues indefinitely. The 12-month DAPT duration is the figure for ACS, not for elective PCI — that is the discrimination being tested.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Which statement about plaque behaviour correctly contrasts stable angina with ACS?
options: Both stable angina and ACS involve plaque rupture with overlying thrombus and vessel occlusion
Stable angina involves complete total occlusion, while ACS involves only partial vessel narrowing
Stable angina causes ischaemia at rest, whereas ACS produces symptoms only on physical exertion
Both stable angina and ACS produce equally unpredictable, unprovoked symptoms at any time of day
Stable angina involves an intact plaque with fixed stenosis; ACS involves plaque rupture and thrombus
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: Stable angina involves an intact plaque with fixed stenosis; ACS involves plaque rupture and thrombus
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: In stable angina the plaque is intact, causing predictable exertional ischaemia. In ACS the plaque ruptures, forming thrombus with partial or complete occlusion and ischaemia at rest.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: A 26-year-old man is brought in with severe central chest pain 2 hours after a party. He is agitated and diaphoretic. HR 128, BP 182/104. ECG shows 2 mm ST elevation in V2–V4. He admits to using cocaine. Alongside aspirin, GTN and activation of the primary PCI pathway, which drug is most appropriate?
explanation: IV diazepam — a benzodiazepine is first-line in cocaine-associated ACS. It damps the sympathetic surge causing the agitation, tachycardia and hypertension, which lowers myocardial oxygen demand and relieves coronary vasoconstriction at the same time.
IV metoprolol — a pure beta-blocker is the classic wrong answer: blocking β leaves α-mediated coronary vasoconstriction unopposed, worsening ischaemia and raising BP.
Oral bisoprolol — same objection, and oral dosing is far too slow for an evolving STEMI.
IV labetalol — has α-blocking activity, but its β effect predominates, so it is still conventionally avoided; a benzodiazepine is the first move.
IV adenosine — a diagnostic/therapeutic agent for SVT with a several-second half-life; it has no role here.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: Why are beta-blockers conventionally avoided in the acute management of cocaine-associated acute coronary syndrome?
options: They leave α-adrenergic coronary vasoconstriction unopposed
They prevent troponin from rising, masking the infarct
They interact with aspirin to increase bleeding risk
They cause reflex tachycardia that shortens diastole
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: They leave α-adrenergic coronary vasoconstriction unopposed
explanation: They leave α-adrenergic coronary vasoconstriction unopposed — cocaine stimulates both α and β receptors; blocking only β allows unchecked α-mediated coronary vasoconstriction and a rise in blood pressure, worsening ischaemia.
Hyperkalaemia — not a recognised mechanism of cocaine toxicity in this context.
Masking troponin — beta-blockers do not alter troponin release from infarcting myocardium.
Aspirin interaction — there is no such clinically important bleeding interaction.
Reflex tachycardia — beta-blockers slow the heart; this describes the opposite of their effect.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: An 82-year-old woman is admitted with urosepsis and fast atrial fibrillation at 165 bpm. She reports chest discomfort; ECG shows lateral ST depression and troponin is raised and rising. Coronary angiography is not immediately available. What is the most likely diagnosis and the priority of management?
options: Type 2 MI — treat the sepsis and control the ventricular rate
Type 1 MI — activate the primary PCI pathway immediately
Type 1 MI — give fibrinolysis as PCI is unavailable
Unstable angina — start ticagrelor and fondaparinux
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: Type 2 MI — treat the sepsis and control the ventricular rate
explanation: Type 2 MI — treat the sepsis and control the ventricular rate. There is no acute plaque event: a rate of 165 shortens diastole (reducing coronary filling) while sepsis raises demand and lowers SVR, so supply falls below demand. Management targets the underlying cause.
Type 1 MI with primary PCI — reserved for an acute atherothrombotic occlusion; there is no ST elevation and the clinical picture points to demand ischaemia.
Fibrinolysis — indicated only for a genuine STEMI when PCI is not deliverable in time; here it adds bleeding risk with no thrombus to lyse.
Unstable angina — excluded by the raised troponin, which by definition indicates infarction rather than unstable angina.
Dressler's syndrome — an autoimmune pericarditis 2–6 weeks after a previous MI, with pleuritic pain and a rub, not this presentation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: A 54-year-old man had an NSTEMI treated with successful PCI to all diseased vessels. His LVEF is 55% and no further revascularisation is planned. He holds an ordinary car licence and asks about driving. What is the correct advice?
options: Stop driving for 1 week; the DVLA does not need to be notified
Stop driving for 4 weeks; the DVLA does not need to be notified
Stop driving for 6 weeks and notify the DVLA
He may drive immediately with no restriction
He must surrender his licence permanently
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: Stop driving for 1 week; the DVLA does not need to be notified
explanation: Stop driving for 1 week; the DVLA does not need to be notified — for a Group 1 licence after successful PCI, 1 week suffices provided all diseased vessels were treated, LVEF is ≥40%, and no further revascularisation is planned.
4 weeks — this is the Group 1 rule when the ACS was not successfully treated by PCI, or the LVEF/revascularisation criteria are not met.
6 weeks and notify — these are the Group 2 (HGV/PSV) rules, which also require a functional test before re-licensing.
No restriction — incorrect; every ACS carries a minimum off-road period for Group 1.
Permanent surrender — a successfully treated ACS with preserved LV function carries no permanent Group 1 bar.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: A 58-year-old has an inferior STEMI at a rural hospital 3 hours from the nearest PCI centre. He had a haemorrhagic stroke two years ago. What is the most appropriate reperfusion strategy?
options: Fibrinolysis with alteplase, since PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes
Fibrinolysis at half dose to reduce the bleeding risk
Transfer for primary PCI - previous haemorrhagic stroke makes fibrinolysis unsafe
Aspirin and ticagrelor alone, with no reperfusion attempted
Await a troponin result before deciding on reperfusion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: Transfer for primary PCI - previous haemorrhagic stroke makes fibrinolysis unsafe
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: A previous haemorrhagic stroke is one of the situations in which fibrinolysis should not be given at all - the drug dissolves clot indiscriminately and the risk of intracranial bleeding is unacceptable. Dose reduction does not make it safe. The other bars to lysis are active bleeding or a known bleeding disorder, recent major surgery, serious trauma or head injury, suspected aortic dissection, and severe uncontrolled hypertension. Where lysis is contraindicated the answer is transfer for primary PCI even if that takes longer, and a STEMI is diagnosed and treated on the ECG, so waiting for a troponin would only cause delay.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.question: A 41-year-old smoker has recurrent severe chest pain at 3 am. An ECG captured during an episode shows transient ST elevation that resolves completely as the pain settles; troponin is normal and angiography shows only minor irregularities. What is the diagnosis and the appropriate treatment?
options: NSTEMI - start dual antiplatelet therapy and a beta-blocker
Vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina - a calcium channel blocker, avoiding beta-blockers
Stable angina - a beta-blocker and referral for CT coronary angiography
Pericarditis - colchicine and a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory
Musculoskeletal chest pain - reassurance and simple analgesia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.answer: Vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina - a calcium channel blocker, avoiding beta-blockers
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.explanation: Rest pain, often nocturnal, with transient ST elevation that resolves as the pain settles, a normal troponin and near-normal coronaries is vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina - spasm rather than plaque. Catching the ECG during the episode is effectively the diagnosis. Treatment is a calcium channel blocker with nitrates and smoking cessation. Beta-blockers should be avoided because they leave alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed and can worsen the spasm - the same reasoning as in cocaine-associated chest pain. There is no infarction, so this is not an NSTEMI, and pericarditis gives widespread saddle-shaped elevation that does not resolve within minutes.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.question: A 19-year-old faints after standing in a hot assembly; beforehand she felt hot, nauseated and her vision tunnelled, and she recovered within a minute. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.explanation: A clear prodrome (warmth, nausea, tunnel vision) with a typical trigger (prolonged standing in heat) and rapid full recovery is vasovagal syncope. Arrhythmia gives sudden collapse without warning; orthostatic syncope occurs on standing with a BP drop; seizure has a post-ictal phase; aortic stenosis causes exertional syncope.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.question: A 68-year-old man collapses without warning while sitting watching television; there was no prodrome and he recovered rapidly. His ECG shows complete heart block. What is the mechanism of his syncope?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.explanation: Sudden syncope with no prodrome at rest and complete heart block indicates arrhythmic (cardiac) syncope (Stokes-Adams). The lack of trigger/prodrome and the abnormal ECG exclude reflex and orthostatic causes; it is not situational or psychogenic.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.question: A 75-year-old on ramipril, doxazosin and furosemide feels dizzy and blacks out on standing from bed. Lying BP is 140/80, standing BP 112/66. What is the diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.explanation: A postural systolic drop of ≥20 mmHg reproducing symptoms, on multiple hypotensive agents, is orthostatic hypotension. It is provoked by standing (not a vagal trigger or head-turning), and the mechanism is failure to defend BP on standing rather than an arrhythmia or valve lesion.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.question: A 70-year-old man with an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids and a slow-rising pulse blacks out while climbing stairs. What is the most likely cause of his syncope?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.explanation: Exertional syncope with an ejection systolic murmur to the carotids and a slow-rising pulse is aortic stenosis — a fixed outflow obstruction that cannot meet exercise demand. The other causes do not classically produce exertional syncope with these signs.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.question: A 22-year-old collapses; a witness reports an aura, 90 seconds of rhythmic limb jerking, lateral tongue biting and 20 minutes of confusion afterwards. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.explanation: An aura, sustained rhythmic convulsions, lateral tongue biting and a prolonged post-ictal phase indicate an epileptic seizure. Syncope (including convulsive syncope with brief jerks) has rapid recovery without a true post-ictal phase; lateral tongue biting is fairly specific for seizure.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.question: A 35-year-old faints immediately after a bout of coughing. Examination and ECG are normal. What type of syncope is this?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.explanation: Syncope triggered by a specific act such as coughing (or micturition, swallowing, defecation) is situational reflex syncope, mediated by a vagal surge. It is distinguished by the specific precipitant and a normal ECG.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.question: Which two investigations are mandatory in the initial assessment of every patient presenting with syncope?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.explanation: A 12-lead ECG and a lying and standing BP are mandatory in everyone — cheap, fast, and they identify the dangerous arrhythmic substrates and orthostatic hypotension. Echo, tilt-table, EEG, CT and D-dimer are targeted second-line tests.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.question: A 60-year-old has recurrent syncope; the resting ECG shows a coved ST elevation in V1–V2. What diagnosis does this ECG pattern suggest?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.explanation: A coved ST elevation in V1–V2 is the Brugada pattern, a sodium-channelopathy predisposing to VF and sudden death. WPW shows a delta wave; long QT shows QT prolongation; complete heart block shows AV dissociation; pericarditis shows widespread saddle ST elevation.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.question: A 78-year-old repeatedly faints when turning his head or wearing a tight collar. Examination is otherwise normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.explanation: Syncope reproducibly triggered by head-turning or a tight collar in an older patient is carotid sinus hypersensitivity; carotid sinus massage (with monitoring, no bruit) can confirm it. The trigger is not postural change (orthostatic) or a classic vagal stressor (vasovagal).

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.question: A previously well 45-year-old reports his syncope was preceded by a few seconds of a rapid, forceful heartbeat before he blacked out suddenly. What does this history most suggest?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.explanation: Syncope preceded by palpitations with a sudden collapse points to a tachyarrhythmia (e.g. VT/SVT) — investigate with an ECG and ambulatory monitoring. The reflex and orthostatic causes have prodromes or postural/situational triggers, not a fast forceful heartbeat before collapse.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.question: A 30-year-old has recurrent unexplained faints; history is equivocal, examination normal and ECG normal. Which investigation is most appropriate to support a reflex/orthostatic cause?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.explanation: When the history is unclear and cardiac tests are normal, a tilt-table test supports a diagnosis of recurrent reflex (vasovagal) or orthostatic syncope. Angiography, EP study, CTPA and MRI target specific structural/ischaemic/arrhythmic hypotheses, not reflex syncope.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.question: A 25-year-old woman has exertional syncope, a jerky pulse and an ejection systolic murmur that gets louder on standing and Valsalva; there is a family history of sudden death. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.explanation: Exertional syncope with a murmur that increases on Valsalva/standing, a jerky pulse and a family history of sudden death indicates HOCM. Aortic stenosis softens with reduced preload and gives a slow-rising pulse; the others do not fit this high-risk picture.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.question: A 55-year-old faints and is found to have long QT on his ECG after starting a new medication. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Start a beta-blocker empirically without review
Stop the culprit drug; correct electrolytes
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.explanation: Drug-induced long QT risks torsades de pointes; stop the offending drug and correct electrolytes (K⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺). Discharge or a tilt-table test would miss the danger; fludrocortisone treats orthostatic hypotension, not long QT.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.question: A lorry driver (Group 2 licence) has an episode of unexplained syncope. What is the most appropriate advice regarding driving?
options: Stop driving and notify the DVLA
Stop driving for 4 weeks only, no notification
Continue driving once symptom-free for 24 hours
No restriction as for a simple faint
Stop driving for 1 week then resume
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.explanation: Unexplained syncope requires the driver to stop and notify the DVLA; for a Group 2 (HGV/PCV) licence the disqualification is long (typically 12 months if unexplained/cardiac, vs 4 weeks–6 months for Group 1). The short fixed periods and ‘simple faint’ options understate a Group 2 unexplained event.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.question: A 40-year-old collapses with sudden breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain and hypoxia; ECG shows sinus tachycardia with S1Q3T3. What is the most likely cause of the syncope?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.explanation: Syncope with acute dyspnoea, pleuritic pain, hypoxia and S1Q3T3 indicates massive pulmonary embolism causing obstructive shock. The other options do not produce hypoxia with this ECG pattern.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.question: A 72-year-old with syncope has a resting ECG showing right bundle branch block with left axis deviation and a prolonged PR interval. Why is this concerning?
options: It is diagnostic of aortic stenosis
It confirms a previous myocardial infarction
It is a normal variant in the elderly
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.explanation: RBBB + left anterior hemiblock (left axis) is bifascicular block; with a long PR it signals advanced conduction disease that may progress to complete heart block and arrhythmic syncope, warranting monitoring/pacing assessment.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.question: A diabetic on insulin becomes progressively light-headed, sweaty and tremulous before nearly passing out; symptoms resolve promptly after a sugary drink. What is the diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.explanation: Gradual light-headedness with autonomic features (sweating, tremor, hunger) in an insulin-treated diabetic, relieved by glucose, is hypoglycaemia — a syncope mimic. Always check a capillary glucose in a collapse.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.question: Which single feature most strongly suggests a syncopal episode was actually an epileptic seizure rather than a faint?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.explanation: Lateral tongue biting is relatively specific for a generalised seizure. Incontinence and brief jerks occur in syncope too; pallor and rapid recovery of orientation actually favour syncope.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.question: A 65-year-old has recurrent syncope with a normal ECG and echocardiogram; episodes are roughly monthly and never captured. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.explanation: For infrequent, unexplained, potentially arrhythmic syncope with normal initial tests, an implantable loop recorder provides prolonged monitoring to capture a rare event. A 24-hour Holter will likely miss monthly episodes; a repeat ECG adds little; exercise and tilt testing target other mechanisms.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.question: A 50-year-old has an uncomplicated single vasovagal faint with a clear trigger and full recovery, a normal ECG and examination. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Ambulatory Holter monitor and cardiology referral
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Syncope & Pre-syn.explanation: A single typical vasovagal faint with a normal ECG and examination needs only reassurance and conservative advice (recognise the prodrome, counter-pressure manoeuvres, hydration/salt, review drugs). A Holter, tilt-table, echo or fludrocortisone are unnecessary investigations/treatment for an uncomplicated first faint.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.question: A vessel on a histology slide has a large, flattened lumen full of red cells, a very thin wall in which the outermost collagenous layer is clearly the thickest, and no distinct elastic laminae. It is most likely a:
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.explanation: A large collapsed lumen, thin wall with a dominant (thickest) adventitia and absent elastic laminae are classic for a vein. Arteries have a thick media and defined elastic laminae.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.question: Which statement correctly contrasts the layers of arteries and veins?
options: The media is thickest in both
The adventitia is thickest in both
The media is thickest in arteries; the adventitia is thickest in veins
The intima is thickest in veins
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.explanation: The defining contrast: arteries have the thickest tunica media, veins have the thickest tunica adventitia.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.question: Venous valves are formed by folds of which layer?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.explanation: Valves are paired semilunar folds of the tunica intima (endothelium over a thin CT core), with cusps directed toward the heart.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.question: In which vessel do leukocyte rolling, adhesion and diapedesis predominantly occur during acute inflammation?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.explanation: The postcapillary venule is the principal site of leukocyte emigration and of histamine-mediated increased permeability.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.question: Venous valves are normally ABSENT from which of the following?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.explanation: The venae cavae (like the portal, dural and most visceral veins) lack valves; limb veins such as the saphenous, femoral, popliteal and cephalic are richly valved.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.question: A large vein near the heart shows prominent longitudinally arranged smooth-muscle bundles in its outer coat. This vessel is most likely the:
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.explanation: Large veins such as the venae cavae characteristically have longitudinal smooth-muscle bundles in the tunica adventitia.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.question: Why is venous return highly dependent on the skeletal-muscle and respiratory pumps?
options: Veins have thick muscular walls that need assistance
Venous pressure is high and pulsatile
Venous pressure is low and the wall is thin/compliant, so blood needs external propulsion
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.explanation: Because venous pressure is low and the wall is thin and compliant, blood is moved mainly by external compression (muscle and respiratory pumps) and venous tone rather than by the wall itself.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.question: Which best describes the elastic-stain appearance of a vein compared with an artery?
options: A vein has a thicker internal elastic lamina
A vein has crisp internal and external elastic laminae
A vein has no elastic tissue at all
A vein has more elastic than an elastic artery
A vein has sparse, scattered elastic with no distinct laminae
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.explanation: Veins contain only sparse, scattered elastic fibres and lack the discrete internal/external elastic laminae that arteries display on elastic stains.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.question: A patient develops a DVT after a long flight. Which component of Virchow's triad is most directly related to prolonged immobility?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.explanation: Immobility causes venous stasis (loss of the muscle-pump effect), one of the three arms of Virchow's triad predisposing to venous thrombosis.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.question: High endothelial venules (HEVs) are distinguished by tall cuboidal endothelium and are the site where lymphocytes enter lymphoid tissue. They are found in:
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.explanation: HEVs are specialised postcapillary venules in lymph nodes and Peyer's patches that permit lymphocyte recirculation into lymphoid tissue.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.question: Chronic venous hypertension in the lower limb classically produces which skin change?
options: Pallor and hair loss with cold toes
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.explanation: Chronic venous insufficiency causes oedema, brown haemosiderin staining, lipodermatosclerosis and venous ulcers in the gaiter area. Pallor/hair loss/cold toes suggest arterial disease.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.question: Veins are described as 'capacitance vessels' primarily because:
options: Their thin compliant walls and large lumens store a large blood volume
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.explanation: Their high compliance and large capacity let veins hold ~65–70% of blood volume; venoconstriction can mobilise this reservoir to raise preload.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.question: Histamine released during an allergic reaction increases vascular permeability mainly by acting on the endothelium of the:
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.explanation: Histamine acts chiefly on postcapillary venule endothelium, causing inter-endothelial gaps and a protein-rich exudate (oedema).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.question: Oesophageal varices arise because portal hypertension is transmitted directly to gut veins. Which feature of these veins permits that unimpeded pressure transmission?
options: The absence of valves (valveless portal drainage)
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.explanation: The portal and gut venous drainage is valveless, so raised portal pressure passes directly to thin submucosal veins at porto-systemic anastomoses, which dilate and can rupture.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.question: Which vessel type has endothelium and pericytes but essentially no tunica media?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.explanation: The postcapillary venule consists of endothelium supported by pericytes and lacks a true muscular media; smooth muscle appears only in the collecting (muscular) venule.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.question: A varicose vein results most directly from:
options: Incompetent venous valves causing venous hypertension
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.explanation: Valvular incompetence leads to reflux and sustained venous hypertension, dilating and tortuosing superficial veins (varicose veins).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.question: Which pair of immunohistochemical markers would confirm that irregular channels in a tumour are of vascular (endothelial) origin?
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.explanation: CD31 and CD34 are endothelial markers used to identify vascular channels. SMA/desmin mark smooth muscle; the others are glial/epithelial/neuronal markers.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.question: Compared with the companion artery, a normal vein at the same site typically shows all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Frequent presence of blood in the lumen
A thicker tunica media than the artery
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.explanation: A vein's tunica media is thinner (not thicker) than the accompanying artery's; the vein's larger irregular lumen, relatively thin wall and dominant adventitia are all expected.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.question: Recurrent superficial thrombophlebitis appearing at different sites (Trousseau sign) is a paraneoplastic marker classically of:
