BNP — diagnostic of MR and quantifies the regurgitant volume and vena contracta width precisely
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Echo — quantifies severity (regurgitant fraction, vena contracta, ERO area) and LV dimensions/function
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Echo is the key investigation: it quantifies severity (regurgitant fraction, vena contracta, ERO area) and assesses LV dimensions and function, which trigger surgery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Which ECG finding reflects LA enlargement from volume overload in chronic MR?
options: P mitrale — broad notched (bifid) P wave
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: P mitrale — broad notched (bifid) P wave
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: P mitrale (a broad notched/bifid P wave if in sinus rhythm) reflects LA enlargement from volume overload; AF is also common in chronic MR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Which CXR findings are described in mitral regurgitation?
options: Boot-shaped heart with an upturned apex and a heavily calcified aortic valve
LA enlargement (double heart border, widened carina), pulmonary oedema, cardiomegaly
Kerley B lines with dense mitral valve calcification as the only abnormality seen
Rib notching from dilated intercostal collateral vessels eroding the rib margins
Entirely normal cardiac silhouette with clear lung fields and no chamber enlargement
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: LA enlargement (double heart border, widened carina), pulmonary oedema, cardiomegaly
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: MR on CXR shows LA enlargement (double heart border, widened carina), pulmonary oedema and cardiomegaly.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: What is the role of cardiac MRI in mitral regurgitation?
options: First-line screening test performed routinely before echo
Assesses coronary artery anatomy before valve surgery
Diagnoses atrial fibrillation and quantifies its burden
Directly measures the plasma BNP concentration in blood
Quantifies regurgitant volume if echo is inadequate
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Quantifies regurgitant volume if echo is inadequate
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Cardiac MRI quantifies regurgitant volume when echo is inadequate; BNP is a separate marker of LV stress.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: In the medical management of chronic MR, why are ACEi/ARB used?
options: To slow progressive calcification of the mitral valve
To prevent infective endocarditis of the mitral valve
To increase preload and augment ventricular filling
To reduce afterload and lower the regurgitant fraction
To raise the resting heart rate and cardiac output
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: To reduce afterload and lower the regurgitant fraction
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: ACEi/ARB reduce afterload, which lowers the regurgitant fraction; diuretics and beta-blockers are also used, with rate control/anticoagulation if AF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Which is a recognised surgical indication in mitral regurgitation?
options: Asymptomatic mild MR with a normal ejection fraction and no left ventricular dilatation
MR only once irreversible LV dysfunction and end-stage heart failure have developed
Any degree of MR regardless of severity, symptoms, or ventricular dimensions on echo
Asymptomatic severe MR with LV dilatation (LVESD ≥40 mm), EF ≤60%, AF or pulmonary HTN
Chronic MR with a preserved EF above 70% and no symptoms on any exertion at all
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Asymptomatic severe MR with LV dilatation (LVESD ≥40 mm), EF ≤60%, AF or pulmonary HTN
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Surgical indications include symptomatic severe MR with preserved EF, and asymptomatic severe MR with LVESD ≥40 mm (or indexed LVESD ≥20 mm/m²), EF ≤60%, AF or pulmonary HTN; acute severe MR needs emergency surgery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Why is valve repair preferred over replacement in MR when anatomically feasible, and what is MitraClip?
options: Repair carries higher operative mortality than replacement; MitraClip is a surgically implanted mechanical prosthesis requiring lifelong anticoagulation
Repair requires lifelong warfarin like a mechanical valve; MitraClip is an open surgical procedure reserved for young low-risk patients with mild MR
Repair gives lower mortality and avoids anticoagulation; MitraClip is percutaneous leaflet repair for very high surgical risk patients
Repair is used only in acute MR; MitraClip completely replaces the whole valve with a bioprosthesis via a percutaneous transcatheter approach here
There is no outcome difference between repair and replacement; MitraClip is a diagnostic catheter test used to grade regurgitation severity only
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Repair gives lower mortality and avoids anticoagulation; MitraClip is percutaneous leaflet repair for very high surgical risk patients
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: When feasible, repair is preferred (lower mortality, no anticoagulation). MitraClip is a percutaneous leaflet repair option for very high surgical risk patients with severe symptomatic MR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: What is the overwhelming cause of mitral stenosis, and what is the typical time lag from the initial illness?
options: Senile calcific degeneration — present from birth, slowly progressive
Congenital mitral stenosis — apparent in early infancy from birth
Rheumatic origin — often 10–20 years after the initial illness
Infective endocarditis — developing acutely within days of infection
Carcinoid syndrome — evolving over just a few weeks from serotonin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Rheumatic origin — often 10–20 years after the initial illness
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Almost all MS is rheumatic in origin, typically presenting 10–20 years after the initial illness.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: How does post-streptococcal pharyngitis lead to mitral stenosis at the valve level?
options: Immune-mediated cardiac inflammation → valve fibrosis + commissural fusion + chordal shortening
Direct bacterial invasion of the valve leaflets seeding vegetations and destroying the cusps
Passive calcium deposition on an otherwise structurally normal valve slowly narrowing the orifice
Annular dilatation driven by progressive left ventricular enlargement stretching the valve ring
Myxomatous degeneration of the leaflets with redundant tissue causing prolapse and leaflet fusion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Immune-mediated cardiac inflammation → valve fibrosis + commissural fusion + chordal shortening
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Group A strep pharyngitis triggers immune-mediated cardiac inflammation producing valve fibrosis, commissural fusion and chordal shortening.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Which of the following is a recognised rare non-rheumatic cause (or mimic) of mitral stenosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Large LA myxoma (mimics)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Rare non-rheumatic causes include congenital MS, a large LA myxoma (which mimics MS), and systemic lupus (Libman-Sacks).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: In the pathophysiology of mitral stenosis, what is the state of the left ventricle?
options: Underfilled and often normal or small
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Underfilled and often normal or small
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: The stenotic valve limits filling, so in MS the LV is actually underfilled and often normal or small.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Trace the pathway by which mitral stenosis leads to right heart failure.
options: LV outflow obstruction → concentric pressure hypertrophy → back-pressure → RHF
Raised LA pressure → pulmonary venous HTN → pulmonary arterial HTN → RHF
Mitral volume overload → eccentric LV dilatation → forward failure → RHF
Aortic root dilatation → chronic aortic regurgitation → LV volume load → RHF
Coronary ischaemia → left ventricular systolic failure → congestion → RHF
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Raised LA pressure → pulmonary venous HTN → pulmonary arterial HTN → RHF
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Raised LA pressure causes pulmonary venous hypertension → pulmonary arterial hypertension → right heart failure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Why might pregnancy, tachycardia or infection precipitate pulmonary oedema in mitral stenosis?
options: They directly accelerate calcification and fibrosis of the stenotic mitral valve leaflets over time
They provoke aortic regurgitation by acutely dilating the aortic root and separating the valve cusps
They cause acute mechanical rupture of the thickened valve leaflets producing torrential regurgitation
They slow the heart rate excessively, prolonging diastole and worsening filling across the narrow valve
They are listed precipitants that raise LA pressure and tip the patient into pulmonary oedema
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: They are listed precipitants that raise LA pressure and tip the patient into pulmonary oedema
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Tachycardia, pregnancy and infection are noted as precipitants of pulmonary oedema in MS, as they raise LA pressure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Fully describe the mitral stenosis murmur and how it is best heard.
options: Mid-diastolic, low-pitched rumble at the apex in left lateral decubitus, using the bell, on expiration
Pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, loudest using the diaphragm on held expiration
Early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal edge, heard sitting forward in end-expiration
Ejection systolic murmur at the right second intercostal space radiating loudly to both carotid arteries
Continuous machinery murmur at the upper left sternal edge, present through systole and diastole alike
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Mid-diastolic, low-pitched rumble at the apex in left lateral decubitus, using the bell, on expiration
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: The MS murmur is a mid-diastolic, low-pitched rumble, best heard at the apex in left lateral decubitus using the bell on expiration, with presystolic accentuation if in sinus rhythm.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: What does an opening snap occurring earlier after S2 indicate in mitral stenosis?
options: Lower LA pressure and milder stenosis
Higher LA pressure and more severe stenosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Higher LA pressure and more severe stenosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: An earlier snap after S2 reflects higher LA pressure and more severe stenosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Why is S1 loud in mitral stenosis?
options: Forceful closure of the stiff (but still mobile) mitral leaflets
The valve fails to close completely, allowing systolic regurgitation
Rapid early ventricular filling striking a stiffened chamber wall
Atrial contraction forced against a stiff, non-compliant left ventricle
Heavily calcified, immobile leaflets that can barely move at all
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Forceful closure of the stiff (but still mobile) mitral leaflets
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: S1 is loud in MS because of forceful closure of the stiff but still mobile mitral leaflets.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: What is the mechanism of the malar flush (mitral facies) in mitral stenosis?
options: Wide pulse pressure with a hyperdynamic, high-output circulation flushing the cheeks
Chronic low CO plus pulmonary HTN → peripheral vasoconstriction + venous congestion
Hepatic venous congestion backing up and dilating the facial venous plexus visibly
Chronic subendocardial ischaemia driving reflex facial vasodilation and flushing
Systolic regurgitation of blood back into the right atrium raising facial pressure
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Chronic low CO plus pulmonary HTN → peripheral vasoconstriction + venous congestion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Malar flush in MS results from chronic low cardiac output and pulmonary hypertension, causing peripheral VASOCONSTRICTION with cutaneous cyanosis, plus venous congestion of the cheeks.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Why is the apex beat tapping and non-displaced in mitral stenosis?
options: LV volume overload from regurgitation displacing the apex down and out
It is a palpable loud S1; non-displaced because the LV is normal
Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy giving a sustained heaving apex
Right ventricular pressure overload displacing the apex laterally outward
A large pericardial effusion damping the impulse and making it impalpable
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: It is a palpable loud S1; non-displaced because the LV is normal
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: The tapping apex beat is a palpable loud S1; it is non-displaced because the LV is normal in MS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Which echo values define severe mitral stenosis?
options: AVA <1.5 cm² and mean gradient >20 mmHg
AVA <1 cm² and mean gradient >40 mmHg
MVA <2 cm² and mean gradient >5 mmHg
MVA <1.5 cm² and peak gradient >64 mmHg
MVA <1 cm² and mean gradient >10 mmHg
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: MVA <1 cm² and mean gradient >10 mmHg
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: On echo, MS is severe if the mitral valve area is <1 cm² and the mean gradient across the valve is >10 mmHg.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Which ECG findings are characteristic of mitral stenosis?
options: Left ventricular hypertrophy with a lateral strain pattern and deep S waves in the right precordial leads
Delta wave with a short PR interval indicating ventricular pre-excitation via an accessory pathway
P mitrale (bifid P in II >120 ms, broad P in V1), AF, right axis deviation (RVH from pulmonary HTN)
Widespread ST-segment elevation across the lateral leads with reciprocal inferior ST depression seen
Tall, peaked, symmetrical P waves in lead II reflecting isolated right atrial enlargement only here
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: P mitrale (bifid P in II >120 ms, broad P in V1), AF, right axis deviation (RVH from pulmonary HTN)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: MS shows P mitrale (bifid notched P in lead II >120 ms, broad P in V1), AF, and right axis deviation from RVH due to pulmonary HTN.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Why does rate control benefit a patient with mitral stenosis?
options: It mechanically enlarges the effective mitral valve orifice area, easing transvalvular flow
It lowers the regurgitant fraction by reducing systolic backflow across the mitral valve
It reverses commissural fusion of the leaflets, restoring the valve to its normal structure
Slowing the heart rate allows more time for diastolic filling across the stenotic valve
It increases afterload, which paradoxically improves left ventricular emptying and filling
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Slowing the heart rate allows more time for diastolic filling across the stenotic valve
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Rate control (beta-blocker, digoxin, rate-limiting CCB) slows the heart rate, giving more time for diastolic filling across the stenotic valve.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: What is notable about anticoagulation thresholds in mitral stenosis with AF?
options: Only anticoagulate when the CHA₂DS₂-VASc score is 2 or more, as in non-valvular AF patients
All patients with MS + AF are anticoagulated — high embolic risk even with CHA₂DS₂-VASc = 0
Anticoagulation is absolutely contraindicated in mitral stenosis due to valvular bleeding risk
Use aspirin monotherapy alone, which gives adequate stroke protection in mitral stenosis
Anticoagulate only after mitral valve replacement has been performed, never before any intervention
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: All patients with MS + AF are anticoagulated — high embolic risk even with CHA₂DS₂-VASc = 0
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: All patients with MS + AF are anticoagulated (warfarin); the embolic risk is high even when the CHA₂DS₂-VASc score is 0. A DOAC must not be used — DOACs are contraindicated in moderate-to-severe rheumatic MS and in mechanical valves, and those two situations are what "valvular AF" means. AF with any other valve lesion is treated as ordinary AF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Which additional medical measure is indicated if there is a history of rheumatic fever in MS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Penicillin prophylaxis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Penicillin prophylaxis is indicated if there is a history of rheumatic fever.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: What is the first-line interventional treatment for suitable mitral stenosis, and which anatomy makes it appropriate?
options: Surgical mitral valve replacement — indicated first-line for all patients irrespective of leaflet anatomy
Surgical commissurotomy — specifically indicated when left atrial appendage thrombus is present on imaging
Balloon valvotomy — appropriate only when severe coexisting mitral regurgitation is also present on echo
MitraClip — the interventional treatment of choice for heavily calcified, rigid, immobile stenotic valves
Percutaneous balloon mitral valvotomy — pliable non-calcified leaflets, no significant MR, no LA thrombus
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Percutaneous balloon mitral valvotomy — pliable non-calcified leaflets, no significant MR, no LA thrombus
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Percutaneous balloon mitral valvotomy is first-line if anatomy is suitable (pliable non-calcified leaflets, no significant MR, no LA thrombus), giving immediate haemodynamic improvement.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: When is surgical mitral commissurotomy or valve replacement preferred over balloon valvotomy?
options: When the leaflets are pliable and non-calcified
In all asymptomatic patients regardless of valve anatomy
If anatomy is unsuitable for balloon, or if severe MR coexists
When there is no left atrial thrombus on imaging
Only during pregnancy, whatever the valve anatomy
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: If anatomy is unsuitable for balloon, or if severe MR coexists
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Surgical commissurotomy/valve replacement is used when anatomy is unsuitable for balloon valvotomy or when severe MR coexists.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: What are the indications for intervention in mitral stenosis?
options: Asymptomatic mild mitral stenosis with a valve area above 2 cm²
Symptomatic significant MS, or asymptomatic with pulmonary HTN or new AF
Any mitral stenosis regardless of symptoms or measured valve severity
Only once right heart failure and tricuspid regurgitation have developed
Valve area above 2 cm² with mild exertional symptoms and no pulmonary HTN
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Symptomatic significant MS, or asymptomatic with pulmonary HTN or new AF
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Intervention in MS requires haemodynamically significant stenosis (MVA ≤1.5 cm²) that is symptomatic; in an asymptomatic patient with significant MS the triggers are pulmonary hypertension, new-onset AF, previous embolism, or a desire for pregnancy — intervene before conceiving, because pregnancy reliably decompensates significant MS. Pulmonary HTN or AF alone, without significant stenosis, is not an indication.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Why does cardiac catheterisation have a role in mitral stenosis?
options: To directly measure the aortic valve area and the transaortic gradient
To quantify the mitral regurgitant fraction and regurgitant volume precisely
Used if echo is insufficient; measures pulmonary capillary wedge pressure
To diagnose atrial fibrillation and characterise the underlying atrial rhythm
To assess coronary artery anatomy routinely in all patients with MS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Used if echo is insufficient; measures pulmonary capillary wedge pressure
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Cardiac catheterisation is used if echo is insufficient and measures the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: What single haemodynamic fact underlies the eponymous peripheral signs of aortic regurgitation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Wide pulse pressure
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: A wide pulse pressure underlies all the eponymous AR signs; regurgitation lowers diastolic BP while compensatory increased stroke volume raises systolic BP.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Which of these is an aortic root (dilatation) cause of aortic regurgitation rather than a valve/leaflet cause?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Marfan syndrome
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Marfan syndrome causes cystic medial necrosis → aortic root dilatation. Rheumatic fever, bicuspid valve, IE and collagen vascular disease are valve/leaflet causes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Which two emergencies cause acute AR with haemodynamic collapse?
options: Rheumatic fever and chronic long-standing systemic hypertension
Marfan syndrome and tertiary syphilitic aortitis of the aortic root
IE (leaflet destruction) and aortic dissection (root involvement)
Ankylosing spondylitis and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
Congenital bicuspid aortic valve and reactive Reiter's syndrome
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: IE (leaflet destruction) and aortic dissection (root involvement)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Acute AR emergencies are IE (leaflet destruction) and aortic dissection (root involvement) — both cause acute haemodynamic collapse needing emergency surgery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Which classic cause of AR involves obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Syphilitic aortitis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Syphilitic aortitis is the classic cause involving obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: In chronic AR, what compensatory LV change maintains forward output for years?
options: Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy from chronic pressure overload maintaining output
Reduced preload lowering wall stress and preserving forward cardiac output for years
Atrial fibrillation restoring an effective atrial kick to sustain forward stroke volume
Eccentric LV dilatation (volume overload) with compensatory increased stroke volume
Subendocardial infarction remodelling the ventricle to maintain forward output long-term
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Eccentric LV dilatation (volume overload) with compensatory increased stroke volume
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Diastolic regurgitation raises LV end-diastolic volume, driving eccentric LV dilatation; compensatory increased stroke volume maintains forward output for years until the LV dilates and fails.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Why does the murmur in acute AR tend to be short or soft?
options: The valve is rigidly calcified, blunting the regurgitant jet velocity
The regurgitant fraction across the valve is trivial and minimal
Coexisting AF lowers the diastolic gradient, shortening the murmur
There is coexisting mitral stenosis limiting the regurgitant flow
Pressures equalise rapidly because the LV has no time to dilate
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Pressures equalise rapidly because the LV has no time to dilate
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: In acute AR the LV has no time to dilate, so LVEDP and LA pressure rise rapidly and pressures equalise quickly, making the murmur short/soft.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Why does aortic regurgitation cause angina even with normal coronaries?
options: Increased O₂ demand plus reduced diastolic coronary filling pressure
Coronary artery spasm from catecholamine surge reducing myocardial flow
Coronary embolism from small vegetations shed off the aortic valve leaflets
Pulmonary hypertension raising right-sided pressures and cardiac workload
Atrial fibrillation causing rapid rates that shorten diastolic filling
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Increased O₂ demand plus reduced diastolic coronary filling pressure
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: In AR, increased myocardial O₂ demand combines with reduced diastolic coronary filling pressure (from the low diastolic BP) to cause angina.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Fully describe the aortic regurgitation murmur and its optimal listening position.
options: Pansystolic, blowing murmur heard best at the apex and radiating to the axilla, loudest in the left lateral decubitus position on expiration
Continuous machinery murmur heard at the upper left sternal edge throughout systole and diastole, best appreciated with the patient lying flat
Low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble heard at the apex with the bell, in the left lateral decubitus position with presystolic accentuation
Harsh ejection systolic murmur at the right 2nd intercostal space radiating to the carotids, loudest on expiration
Early diastolic, blowing, high-pitched, decrescendo at the left sternal edge, sitting forward with breath held in expiration
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Early diastolic, blowing, high-pitched, decrescendo at the left sternal edge, sitting forward with breath held in expiration
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: The AR murmur is early diastolic, blowing, high-pitched and decrescendo at the left sternal edge, best heard sitting forward with breath held in expiration; there is also a systolic ejection murmur from the large stroke volume.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: What is the Austin Flint murmur, and how is it distinguished from true mitral stenosis?
options: A systolic ejection murmur at the aortic area; distinguished from mitral stenosis by its radiation to the carotids and an accompanying thrill
An early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge accompanied by an opening snap and a loud S1, distinguishing it from true mitral stenosis
A mid-diastolic apical rumble from the regurgitant jet hitting the anterior mitral leaflet — no opening snap, unlike true MS
A continuous machinery murmur heard throughout the cardiac cycle; distinguished from mitral stenosis by its timing and location
A pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla; distinguished from mitral stenosis by its systolic timing and blowing quality
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: A mid-diastolic apical rumble from the regurgitant jet hitting the anterior mitral leaflet — no opening snap, unlike true MS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: The Austin Flint murmur is a mid-diastolic apical rumble caused by the regurgitant jet impinging on the anterior mitral leaflet (functional MS); there is no opening snap, unlike true MS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: A patient's head nods with each heartbeat. Which eponymous sign of AR is this?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: de Musset's sign
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: de Musset's sign is head nodding with each heartbeat from carotid hyperdynamic pulsation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Capillary pulsation visible at the nail-bed on light pressure describes which sign?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Quincke's sign
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Quincke's sign is capillary pulsation at the nail-bed — systolic flushing and diastolic blanching from the wide pulse pressure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: A 'pistol-shot' sound heard over the femoral artery in AR is which sign?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Traube's sign
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Traube's sign is a 'pistol-shot' sound over the femoral artery from hyperdynamic systolic pulsation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Which AR sign is defined by leg BP exceeding arm BP by more than 20 mmHg and is significant in severe AR?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Hill's sign
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Hill's sign: popliteal systolic BP exceeds brachial systolic — the wider the difference, the more severe the AR. Like the other AR eponyms it is explained by the wide pulse pressure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Duroziez's sign in aortic regurgitation refers to what?
options: Visible nail-bed capillary pulsation seen on gently pressing the fingertip, reflecting the wide pulse pressure
Rhythmic head nodding occurring with each heartbeat, produced by the forceful pulsation transmitted to the carotids
A systolic and diastolic murmur over the femoral artery on partial compression — from retrograde diastolic flow
A sharp pistol-shot sound heard over the femoral artery on auscultation, caused by the abrupt distension of the vessel
Leg systolic BP exceeding arm systolic BP by more than 60 mmHg, measured with a thigh cuff, reflecting a widened pulse pressure
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: A systolic and diastolic murmur over the femoral artery on partial compression — from retrograde diastolic flow
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Duroziez's sign is a systolic and diastolic murmur heard over the femoral artery on partial compression with the stethoscope, due to retrograde diastolic flow.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Which echo finding triggers surgery in asymptomatic aortic regurgitation?
options: An aortic root diameter of less than 30 mm on serial imaging
A mitral valve area below 1 cm² on serial echocardiography
An end-systolic diameter above 45 mm and nothing else
Progressive LV dilatation or EF <50% on serial echo
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Progressive LV dilatation or EF <50% on serial echo
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: The trigger is to operate BEFORE irreversible LV dysfunction: progressive LV dilatation on serial echo, or a falling EF (<50%). The dimension criteria are LVESD >50 mm, or indexed LVESD >24 mm/m² in a smaller patient (NICE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Which investigation is the most accurate for quantifying regurgitant volume in AR?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Cardiac MRI
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Cardiac MRI is the most accurate investigation for quantifying regurgitant volume; CT aorta is used if dissection is suspected or root dilatation >45 mm.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: In the medical management of AR, why are vasodilators/ACEi used and when are they indicated?
options: To increase afterload and boost forward stroke volume; indicated in all patients regardless of LV size or blood pressure to protect the valve
To reduce afterload and lower the regurgitant fraction; indicated if LV dilatation/hypertension and not a surgical candidate
To slow progression of valve calcification and leaflet fibrosis; indicated pre-operatively in every patient awaiting aortic valve replacement
To raise diastolic BP and improve coronary perfusion; indicated in acute AR to buy time before emergency surgery can be arranged
To control the ventricular heart rate and prolong diastole; indicated only if there is coexisting atrial fibrillation with a rapid response
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: To reduce afterload and lower the regurgitant fraction; indicated if LV dilatation/hypertension and not a surgical candidate
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Vasodilators/ACEi reduce afterload and lower the regurgitant fraction; they are indicated if there is LV dilatation/hypertension and the patient is not a surgical candidate.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Why are beta-blockers generally avoided in aortic regurgitation?
options: They reduce afterload too much and worsen forward flow
They raise the regurgitant fraction by increasing heart rate
They precipitate atrial fibrillation in a dilated ventricle
They worsen the systolic ejection murmur heard at the base
They lengthen diastole, prolonging the time for regurgitation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: They lengthen diastole, prolonging the time for regurgitation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: By slowing the heart and lengthening diastole, beta-blockers increase the duration of regurgitation, so they are avoided in AR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Which is a recognised indication for surgical AVR in aortic regurgitation?
options: Asymptomatic severe AR with EF >60%, LVESD <40 mm and no LV dilatation
Chronic moderate AR with no symptoms and a completely normal echocardiogram
Any mild AR detected incidentally on echocardiography in an asymptomatic patient
Severe AR only once irreversible LV dysfunction and end-stage heart failure are established
Asymptomatic severe AR with EF <50%, LVESD >50 mm, or indexed LVESD >24 mm/m²
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Asymptomatic severe AR with EF <50%, LVESD >50 mm, or indexed LVESD >24 mm/m²
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Surgical AVR is indicated for symptomatic severe AR, and for asymptomatic severe AR with EF <50%, LVESD >50 mm, or indexed LVESD >24 mm/m² (NICE); acute severe AR from IE or dissection needs emergency surgery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Why should AVR in AR be performed before irreversible LV dysfunction develops?
options: Because surgery becomes technically impossible once the EF falls below normal
Because once EF falls, surgery is still beneficial but the risk increases
Because the diastolic murmur disappears once the ventricle fails, hiding the lesion
Because lifelong anticoagulation then becomes mandatory once the ventricle dilates
Because the dilated aortic root inevitably ruptures once LV function declines
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Because once EF falls, surgery is still beneficial but the risk increases
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: AVR should be done before irreversible LV dysfunction: once EF falls, surgery is still beneficial but the operative risk increases.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: What is the most common cause of tricuspid regurgitation, and why are the leaflets normal?
options: Rheumatic fever causing leaflet fibrosis, thickening and retraction of the tricuspid cusps
Ebstein's anomaly with congenital apical displacement of the septal tricuspid leaflet
Carcinoid syndrome causing fibrous plaque deposition that stiffens the tricuspid leaflets
Functional — RV dilatation from any cause → annular dilatation; leaflets normal
Infective endocarditis with vegetations directly destroying the tricuspid valve leaflets
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Functional — RV dilatation from any cause → annular dilatation; leaflets normal
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Functional TR is most common: RV dilatation (e.g. pulmonary HTN, RV failure) causes annular dilatation while the leaflets remain normal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Right-sided infective endocarditis causing tricuspid regurgitation is especially associated with which group?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Intravenous drug users (IVDU)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: IE causing TR is especially associated with IVDU (right-sided IE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Which congenital condition causes tricuspid regurgitation by displacing the tricuspid valve into the RV?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Ebstein's anomaly
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Ebstein's anomaly is a congenital cause of TR in which the tricuspid valve is displaced into the RV.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Which set of features is characteristic of tricuspid regurgitation?
options: Slow-rising pulse of small volume, narrow pulse pressure, soft or absent S2, and an apical thrusting sustained impulse
Low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble at the apex, a loud S1 and opening snap, malar flush, and a tapping non-displaced apex
Pansystolic murmur at lower left sternal edge louder on inspiration, giant V waves in JVP, pulsatile liver
Collapsing water-hammer pulse, wide pulse pressure, de Musset's head-nodding sign, and a displaced hyperdynamic apex beat
Ejection systolic murmur at the upper left sternal edge with an ejection click, louder on inspiration, and a left parasternal heave
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Pansystolic murmur at lower left sternal edge louder on inspiration, giant V waves in JVP, pulsatile liver
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: TR features: a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge louder on inspiration, giant V waves in the JVP, a pulsatile/enlarged liver, peripheral oedema/ascites and a raised JVP.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: How is tricuspid regurgitation managed?
options: Lifelong warfarin anticoagulation in all patients to prevent thromboembolism
Immediate mechanical valve replacement in all cases irrespective of symptoms
Percutaneous balloon valvuloplasty as the first-line treatment for all patients
High-dose vasodilators to reduce afterload and lower the regurgitant fraction
Treat the underlying cause; diuretics; surgery if severe and refractory
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Treat the underlying cause; diuretics; surgery if severe and refractory
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: TR management: treat the underlying cause, use diuretics, and consider surgery if severe and refractory.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: What is the cause and key JVP finding in tricuspid stenosis?
options: Functional right ventricular dilatation from pulmonary hypertension; giant V waves seen in the JVP
Congenital malformation of the valve; irregular cannon a waves from atrioventricular dissociation
Carcinoid fibrous plaques stiffening the valve; absent a waves with a slow y descent in the JVP
Almost always rheumatic (with MS); giant a waves from atrial contraction against obstruction
Infective endocarditis from IV drug use; a rapid y descent with prominent V waves in the JVP
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Almost always rheumatic (with MS); giant a waves from atrial contraction against obstruction
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: TS is rare and almost always rheumatic (with MS); fixed obstruction raises RA pressure, giving giant a waves in the JVP from prominent atrial contraction against the obstruction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Why does tricuspid stenosis cause hepatomegaly, ascites and oedema without pulmonary congestion?
options: Because it raises left atrial pressure and drives blood backward into the pulmonary veins
Because it causes acute pulmonary oedema by flooding the alveoli with fluid from the left heart
Because it causes pulmonary arterial hypertension that backs up and congests the lungs
Because it reduces systemic venous return to the heart, relieving pressure in the venous system
Because the obstruction is upstream of the lungs (blocked before blood reaches them)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Because the obstruction is upstream of the lungs (blocked before blood reaches them)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: In TS the obstruction is upstream of the lungs, so congestion is systemic (hepatomegaly, ascites, oedema) without pulmonary congestion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: How is tricuspid stenosis treated?
options: ACE inhibitors and loop diuretics used alone
Rate-limiting beta-blockers to slow the heart rate
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Balloon valvuloplasty or surgical commissurotomy
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: TS is treated with balloon valvuloplasty or surgical commissurotomy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: What is the Graham Steell murmur, and what is its most common cause?
options: A pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge arising from tricuspid regurgitation, louder on inspiration with giant V waves
An early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge from pulmonary regurgitation secondary to pulmonary hypertension
An ejection systolic murmur at the upper left sternal edge from pulmonary stenosis, preceded by an ejection click
A low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble at the lower left sternal edge from tricuspid stenosis, becoming louder during inspiration
A continuous machinery murmur heard throughout systole and diastole at the upper left sternal edge arising from a patent ductus
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: An early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge from pulmonary regurgitation secondary to pulmonary hypertension
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: The Graham Steell murmur is an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge due to pulmonary regurgitation, most commonly secondary to pulmonary hypertension.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: How does pulmonary stenosis usually arise, and what is its prognosis by severity?
options: Usually rheumatic in origin following childhood rheumatic fever; even severe cases carry an excellent prognosis and rarely need any intervention
Usually functional, arising secondary to right ventricular dilatation; no treatment is needed as it resolves once the underlying cause is corrected
Usually calcific and degenerative in the elderly; treated effectively with vasodilators and diuretics rather than any valve procedure
Usually congenital (isolated or part of Fallot's/Noonan's); mild-moderate excellent prognosis, severe needs balloon valvuloplasty
Usually infective, arising from endocarditis in IV drug users; treated with a prolonged course of intravenous antibiotics alone without surgery
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Usually congenital (isolated or part of Fallot's/Noonan's); mild-moderate excellent prognosis, severe needs balloon valvuloplasty
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Pulmonary stenosis is usually congenital (isolated or part of Fallot's tetralogy or Noonan's); mild-moderate has an excellent prognosis, while severe disease is treated with balloon valvuloplasty.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Exam pearl: which two murmurs have signature radiation, and what should it prompt you to examine?
options: AR radiates to the carotids and MS to the axilla; always examine the back for basal crackles
MR radiates to the carotids and AS to the axilla; always examine the apex beat for displacement
MS radiates to the carotids and TR to the axilla; always examine the abdomen for organomegaly
PDA radiates to the carotids and AR to the axilla; always examine the legs for oedema
AS → carotids; MR → axilla; always examine the neck and axilla when you hear a murmur
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: AS → carotids; MR → axilla; always examine the neck and axilla when you hear a murmur
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: AS radiates to the carotids and MR to the axilla; always examine the neck and axilla when you hear a murmur.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Exam pearl: the AS triad on examination consists of which findings?
options: Slow-rising pulse + narrow pulse pressure + soft S2, with S4 from a stiff hypertrophied LV
Collapsing water-hammer pulse + wide pulse pressure + soft S2, with a displaced hyperdynamic apex
Loud S1 + opening snap + malar flush, with a tapping non-displaced apex and a mid-diastolic rumble
Giant V waves + pulsatile liver + raised JVP, with a pansystolic murmur louder on inspiration
Tapping non-displaced apex + low-volume pulse + loud S1, with an opening snap and malar flush
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Slow-rising pulse + narrow pulse pressure + soft S2, with S4 from a stiff hypertrophied LV
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: The AS triad is a slow-rising pulse, narrow pulse pressure and soft S2, with an S4 arising from the stiff hypertrophied LV.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Exam pearl: how is P mitrale distinguished from the Austin Flint murmur?
options: P mitrale indicates AR; the Austin Flint murmur indicates true MS and is accompanied by a loud opening snap
Both P mitrale and the Austin Flint murmur reliably indicate underlying mitral stenosis on examination
P mitrale = MS (bifid P in lead II, >120 ms); Austin Flint = AR mimicking MS (no opening snap)
P mitrale indicates TR while the Austin Flint murmur indicates tricuspid stenosis on the ECG
P mitrale is an added heart sound, while the Austin Flint is a peripheral pulse finding felt at the wrist
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: P mitrale = MS (bifid P in lead II, >120 ms); Austin Flint = AR mimicking MS (no opening snap)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: P mitrale (bifid P in lead II, >120 ms) reflects MS, whereas the Austin Flint murmur is AR mimicking MS, distinguished by the absence of an opening snap.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Exam pearl: a bicuspid aortic valve can cause which lesions, and what must be screened for?
options: AS developing only in the elderly through calcification; screen these patients for atrial fibrillation
AS in middle age (calcification) AND AR (leaflet dysfunction); screen for aortic root dilatation
It causes MR and MS from leaflet dysfunction; screen the left atrium for thrombus with echocardiography
It causes TR and TS from annular involvement; screen for hepatomegaly and a pulsatile enlarged liver
It causes PR and PS from congenital malformation; screen for Fallot's tetralogy and associated defects
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: AS in middle age (calcification) AND AR (leaflet dysfunction); screen for aortic root dilatation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: A bicuspid aortic valve causes AS in middle age (calcification) and AR (leaflet dysfunction); screen for aortic root dilatation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Exam pearl: which acute valve lesions are emergencies, and what are their listed causes?
options: Acute severe MS or TS are the emergencies; causes: rheumatic fever with rapid leaflet fusion and sudden valve obstruction
Acute severe AS is the emergency; cause: rapid calcification of the leaflets causing sudden critical outflow obstruction
Acute severe MR or AR; causes: IE (leaflet destruction), aortic dissection (AR), papillary muscle rupture (MR)
Acute severe TR is the emergency; cause: IV drug use leading to tricuspid endocarditis and rapid leaflet destruction
Acute severe PS is the emergency; cause: congenital valve malformation presenting suddenly with right ventricular failure
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Acute severe MR or AR; causes: IE (leaflet destruction), aortic dissection (AR), papillary muscle rupture (MR)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Acute severe MR or AR is an emergency (pulmonary oedema); causes include IE (leaflet destruction), aortic dissection (AR) and papillary muscle rupture (MR).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Exam pearl: what is the rheumatic fever valve thread, and what prophylaxis is given?
options: AS → AR → MS → TR is the rheumatic sequence; lifelong aspirin prophylaxis is given
AR → AS → MR → MS is the rheumatic sequence; lifelong warfarin prophylaxis is used
TR → TS → PR → PS is the rheumatic thread; no antibiotic prophylaxis is required
MR → AS → PS → TS is the rheumatic order; long-term statin prophylaxis is advised
MS → MR → AR → TS/TR; almost all MS is rheumatic; penicillin prophylaxis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: MS → MR → AR → TS/TR; almost all MS is rheumatic; penicillin prophylaxis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: The rheumatic fever thread runs MS → MR → AR → TS/TR; almost all MS is rheumatic, and penicillin prophylaxis is given.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Exam pearl: in mitral stenosis, what does the timing of the opening snap tell you, and what does its absence imply?
options: Earlier snap = higher LA pressure = more severe stenosis; no opening snap = heavily calcified immobile leaflets
A later opening snap indicates more severe stenosis; its absence indicates only mild, early disease with a mobile valve
The timing of the opening snap is irrelevant to severity; its absence simply indicates a normal, healthy mitral valve
An earlier opening snap indicates milder stenosis with lower LA pressure; its absence indicates coexisting aortic regurgitation
A later opening snap indicates a heavily calcified valve; its absence indicates coexisting severe mitral regurgitation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Earlier snap = higher LA pressure = more severe stenosis; no opening snap = heavily calcified immobile leaflets
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: An earlier opening snap means higher LA pressure and more severe stenosis; absence of an opening snap implies heavily calcified, immobile leaflets.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Exam pearl: which signs accompany pulmonary stenosis, and what is its murmur?
options: Pansystolic murmur heard best at the apex and radiating to the axilla, louder on expiration, with giant V waves in the JVP and a pulsatile enlarged liver
Early diastolic, blowing, high-pitched decrescendo murmur at the left sternal edge, best heard sitting forward in expiration, with a collapsing water-hammer pulse
Ejection systolic murmur at upper left sternal edge + ejection click, louder on inspiration, with signs of RV pressure overload (heave, raised JVP)
Low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble at the apex with presystolic accentuation, preceded by a loud S1 and an opening snap, heard best in the left lateral position
Continuous machinery murmur heard throughout systole and diastole at the upper left sternal edge, with a bounding collapsing pulse and wide pulse pressure
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Ejection systolic murmur at upper left sternal edge + ejection click, louder on inspiration, with signs of RV pressure overload (heave, raised JVP)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Pulmonary stenosis gives an ejection systolic murmur at the upper left sternal edge with an ejection click, louder on inspiration, plus signs of RV pressure overload (heave, raised JVP).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: A 42-year-old woman with severe aortic stenosis is being counselled before valve replacement. She hopes to become pregnant in the next few years. Which consideration most directly affects the choice of prosthesis?
options: Warfarin required for a mechanical valve is teratogenic
Bioprosthetic valves are contraindicated in women of childbearing age
Mechanical valves cannot be implanted below the age of 50
Pregnancy accelerates thrombosis of bioprosthetic valves specifically
A mechanical valve would prevent vaginal delivery
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Warfarin required for a mechanical valve is teratogenic
explanation: Warfarin required for a mechanical valve is teratogenic — a mechanical valve commits her to lifelong warfarin, which carries fetal risk, so the durability advantage has to be weighed against that. It is a central part of the counselling.
Bioprosthetic valves contraindicated in childbearing age — the opposite; avoiding anticoagulation is often why a tissue valve is chosen, accepting that it will degenerate and need replacing.
Mechanical valves below age 50 — no such rule; younger patients are in fact the group in whom durability most favours a mechanical valve.
Pregnancy accelerating bioprosthetic thrombosis — thrombosis is the mechanical valve's problem; tissue valves fail by structural degeneration.
Preventing vaginal delivery — a prosthesis does not itself dictate mode of delivery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: A patient with a mechanical mitral valve replacement attends for review. He has been started on apixaban by another clinician. What is the correct action?
options: Stop the apixaban and anticoagulate with warfarin to a target INR
Continue apixaban, as DOACs and warfarin are equivalent for mechanical valves
Continue apixaban but add low-dose aspirin
Stop all anticoagulation as the valve has endothelialised
Switch to a treatment-dose low molecular weight heparin indefinitely
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Stop the apixaban and anticoagulate with warfarin to a target INR
explanation: Stop the apixaban and anticoagulate with warfarin to a target INR — DOACs are contraindicated in mechanical valves, having performed worse than warfarin in trials with both more valve thrombosis and more bleeding. Warfarin with an INR target set by valve type and position is the standard.
DOACs equivalent to warfarin — incorrect, and the reason for the contraindication.
Apixaban plus aspirin — adds bleeding risk without addressing the inadequate protection against valve thrombosis.
Stopping anticoagulation — a mechanical valve requires lifelong anticoagulation; stopping risks valve thrombosis and systemic embolism.
Indefinite LMWH — used only as a bridge in specific situations, not as long-term therapy for a mechanical valve.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.question: A 55-year-old with fever and a new murmur has tender, purplish nodules on the pulps of several fingers. What do these lesions represent?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.explanation: Tender purplish nodules on the finger pulps are Osler’s nodes (“Osler = Ouch”), an immune-complex sign of endocarditis. Janeway lesions are painless palm/sole macules; splinters are subungual; Roth spots are retinal; tophi are chalky and chronic.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.question: A 68-year-old with subacute endocarditis, iron-deficiency anaemia and a change in bowel habit grows Streptococcus gallolyticus (bovis) on blood cultures. What further investigation is essential?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.explanation: Strep gallolyticus (bovis) endocarditis is strongly linked to colorectal cancer — “bovis in the blood, cancer in the bowel” — so a colonoscopy is mandatory. The iron-deficiency anaemia and altered bowel habit reinforce this; the other biopsies do not address the association.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.question: A stable febrile patient has peripheral stigmata of infective endocarditis. What should be done first?
options: Take three blood cultures before antibiotics
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.explanation: In a stable patient, take three sets of blood cultures before antibiotics — they identify the organism (a major Duke criterion) and guide weeks of therapy. Empirical antibiotics come first only in sepsis/instability; echo follows; anticoagulation is not routine.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.question: Infective endocarditis is strongly suspected but the transthoracic echo is normal in a high-risk patient. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat the same TTE in a month
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.explanation: Transoesophageal echocardiography is far more sensitive than TTE for vegetations, abscess and prosthetic valves, so a normal TTE in a high-risk patient warrants TOE. Discharge or delay would miss endocarditis.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.question: A patient with infective endocarditis develops a newly prolonged PR interval. What does this most likely indicate?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.explanation: New PR prolongation / AV block signals peri-valvular extension — an aortic root abscess — and is an indication for urgent surgery. The other options do not cause new conduction delay.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.question: A patient has tender finger-pulp nodules from endocarditis. What is their underlying mechanism?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.explanation: Osler’s nodes arise from immune-complex vasculitis in the digital pulps (hence tender). Septic microemboli explain Janeway lesions; the others describe splinters, cholesterol emboli and gout.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.question: A young woman has tender acral nodules, a malar rash and arthralgia, with a new murmur but persistently negative blood cultures. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.explanation: Tender acral nodules with a malar rash and arthralgia and negative cultures point to SLE (which can also cause Libman-Sacks non-infective endocarditis). Bacterial endocarditis usually yields positive cultures; rheumatic fever is post-streptococcal; gonococcal and Buerger’s differ.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.question: Which single finding is a major criterion in the modified Duke criteria?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.explanation: Echocardiographic endocardial involvement (and typical positive blood cultures) are the two major Duke criteria. Osler’s nodes, fever, haematuria (immune phenomena) and IVDU (predisposition) are minor criteria.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.question: A febrile IV drug user has Osler's nodes and a pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge that is louder on inspiration. Which valve is most likely affected?
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.explanation: In IVDU endocarditis the tricuspid valve (right-sided) is typical, giving a pansystolic murmur louder on inspiration (Carvallo’s sign) and septic pulmonary emboli; S. aureus is usual.

signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.question: A patient with peripheral stigmata of endocarditis is profoundly septic and haemodynamically unstable. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Give antibiotics and skip blood cultures entirely
Wait 48 hours for three separate cultures before any antibiotics
Take cultures then start empirical antibiotics without delay
Arrange an outpatient echo before treating
signs__CARDIOVASCULAR__Osler's Nodes.explanation: In an unstable/septic patient, take cultures quickly and start empirical antibiotics without delay — the “cultures strictly before antibiotics” rule is for the stable patient. Skipping cultures loses the organism; delaying treatment or anticoagulating first is unsafe.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: What is the central mechanism producing pulmonary oedema in acute heart failure?
options: Right ventricular failure backing up into the systemic veins, raising jugular venous pressure
Increased capillary permeability from inflammatory cytokine-mediated endothelial damage
LV unable to pump forward → backlog into the left atrium, pulmonary veins and lungs
Lymphatic obstruction in the thorax impairing drainage of interstitial fluid from the lungs
Reduced plasma oncotic pressure from hypoalbuminaemia allowing fluid to leak into the alveoli
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: LV unable to pump forward → backlog into the left atrium, pulmonary veins and lungs
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: In AHF the LV cannot pump blood forward efficiently, so blood backs up into the LA, pulmonary veins and lungs, filling the alveoli with interstitial fluid (pulmonary oedema).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: A patient with no prior cardiac history presents with acute heart failure following a new MI. How is this best classified?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: De novo acute heart failure
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: De novo AHF is a first-ever presentation with no prior HF diagnosis, often caused by a new MI, hypertensive emergency or acute valve rupture, and requires a full diagnostic workup.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: Which is the more common form of acute heart failure, and what is the key management priority?
options: De novo AHF; complete a full diagnostic workup before initiating any empirical treatment
Decompensated chronic HF; abruptly stop all chronic heart failure medications to reduce load
High-output failure; correct the underlying cause such as anaemia, sepsis or thyrotoxicosis
De novo AHF; arrange immediate cardiac transplant referral without further medical management
Decompensated chronic HF; identify and treat the trigger while optimising chronic therapy
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Decompensated chronic HF; identify and treat the trigger while optimising chronic therapy
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: Decompensated chronic HF is the more common form; management focuses on identifying and treating the precipitating trigger while optimising chronic therapy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: Which of the following is a recognised trigger for decompensation of chronic heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: New AF or arrhythmia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: Triggers include MI/ACS, new AF/arrhythmia, hypertensive emergency, sepsis/infection, iatrogenic IV fluids, medication non-compliance, anaemia/PE and valvular rupture.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: Which symptom is characteristic of acute heart failure?
options: Sharp central chest pain relieved by sitting forward and worsened by lying flat
Localised chest wall pain that is reproduced by palpation over costochondral joints
Gradual painless ankle and leg swelling developing slowly over several months
Acute shortness of breath that is worse lying flat and improves sitting up
Productive green sputum with fever, malaise and pleuritic pain but no breathlessness
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Acute shortness of breath that is worse lying flat and improves sitting up
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: Acute SOB worse when flat and relieved by sitting up is characteristic, often with cough productive of frothy white/pink sputum, raised RR, low sats and extreme anxiety.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: Hypotension in a patient with acute heart failure most concerningly indicates what?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Cardiogenic shock
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: Hypotension occurs in severe AHF and signals cardiogenic shock.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: What is the main purpose of performing an arterial blood gas in acute heart failure?
options: To measure serum troponin and confirm an acute myocardial infarction
To exclude a pulmonary embolism by assessing oxygenation and alveolar gradient
To diagnose anaemia and correct the reduced oxygen-carrying capacity
To assess hypoxia and hypercapnia, guiding the need for NIV/intubation
To classify the ejection fraction and grade the severity of systolic dysfunction
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: To assess hypoxia and hypercapnia, guiding the need for NIV/intubation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: The ABG assesses the degree of hypoxia and hypercapnia, which guides whether NIV or intubation is required.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: What is the primary role of a 12-lead ECG in the acute heart failure workup?
options: To measure the ejection fraction and quantify the degree of ventricular impairment
To quantify the severity of pulmonary oedema seen on the chest radiograph
To identify the trigger — arrhythmia (AF), ischaemia (STEMI/NSTEMI), LBBB
To assess renal function and detect any electrolyte abnormalities present
To measure the BNP level and confirm myocardial wall stretch and volume overload
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: To identify the trigger — arrhythmia (AF), ischaemia (STEMI/NSTEMI), LBBB
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: The ECG looks for arrhythmias, ischaemia and LBBB, helping to identify the precipitating trigger of AHF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: Which level of care is warranted for a patient with severe pulmonary oedema or cardiogenic shock?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: HDU or ITU
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: AHF requires hospital admission; severe pulmonary oedema or cardiogenic shock warrants HDU or ITU level care.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: What does the SODIUM mnemonic for first-line acute heart failure management stand for?
options: Sit up, Oxygen, Diuretic IV, IV fluids stop, Underlying cause, Monitor
Statin, Oxygen, Digoxin, IV fluids, Ultrasound, Morphine
Sit up, Oxygen, Dobutamine, Inotrope, Underlying cause, Morphine
Sodium restrict, Oxygen, Diuretic, IV fluids, Underlying cause, MRA
Sit up, Opioids, Diuretic, Inotrope, Ultrasound, Monitor
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Sit up, Oxygen, Diuretic IV, IV fluids stop, Underlying cause, Monitor
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: SODIUM = Sit up, Oxygen, IV Diuretic, IV fluids stop, Underlying cause (treat trigger), Monitor.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: Why is sitting the patient upright beneficial in acute heart failure?
options: It increases venous return to the heart, boosting preload and stroke volume output
It prevents aspiration of gastric contents only, protecting the airway during treatment
It raises systemic blood pressure by increasing peripheral vascular resistance and afterload
It reduces the heart's cardiac output demand to almost zero by resting the myocardium
It reduces venous return (preload) and improves diaphragmatic mechanics, easing the work of breathing
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: It reduces venous return (preload) and improves diaphragmatic mechanics, easing the work of breathing
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: Sitting up reduces venous return (preload) and lets the diaphragm move more freely, improving respiratory mechanics and gas exchange.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: What is the oxygen saturation target in acute heart failure, and what is added if it is not met on oxygen alone?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: SpO₂ ≥94%; add CPAP/NIV
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: Target SpO₂ 94–98%, or 88–92% in a patient at risk of CO₂ retention (BTS) — which is why the 88–92% option is the right target for the wrong patient. Oxygen is for hypoxia only. CPAP/NIV is added if the target is not achieved on oxygen alone.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: What IV diuretic regimen is used first-line in a diuretic-naive patient with acute heart failure, and what is its effect?
options: IV bumetanide 1 mg — a loop diuretic that increases venous preload and filling pressure
IV furosemide 40 mg — increases urine output and reduces circulating volume
IV spironolactone 50 mg — a potassium-sparing diuretic that blocks aldosterone receptors
IV mannitol — an osmotic diuretic that draws fluid into the tubules for rapid diuresis
Oral furosemide 20 mg — a slower enteral route to gently offload fluid over hours
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: IV furosemide 40 mg — increases urine output and reduces circulating volume
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: First-line is IV furosemide 40 mg in a diuretic-naive patient (BNF: 20–50 mg by slow IV injection, increasing in 20 mg steps; by infusion above 50 mg), increasing urine output and reducing circulating volume. Someone already taking a loop diuretic needs at least their usual total daily oral dose given intravenously.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: A fluid-overloaded patient in acute heart failure is on maintenance IV fluids. What should be done?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Stop all IV fluid infusions
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: The 'I' in SODIUM is IV fluids stop — all IV fluid infusions should be stopped in the fluid-overloaded AHF patient.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: In the BP-stratified approach, a patient with AHF and SBP >100 mmHg should be managed with which strategy?
options: An inotrope or vasopressor, with specialist mechanical support if needed
Immediate intravenous beta-blockade to slow the heart
IV loop diuretic, adding GTN only if hypertensive, ischaemic or severely congested
Watchful waiting with observation and no treatment
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: IV loop diuretic, adding GTN only if hypertensive, ischaemic or severely congested
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: With SBP >100 mmHg the cornerstone is the IV loop diuretic. A vasodilator (IV GTN) is added only where there is hypertension, ischaemia or severe congestion — not routinely — and with close BP monitoring, plus CPAP/NIV for respiratory failure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: A patient with AHF has an SBP of 90 mmHg. According to the BP-stratified approach, what is the appropriate strategy?
options: High-dose IV vasodilator alone to aggressively reduce afterload despite the low pressure
Cautious diuretic; inotrope only if hypoperfused, with continuous BP monitoring
A 250 mg IV furosemide bolus alone, without inotropic support
A rapid IV crystalloid fluid bolus to raise the filling pressure and cardiac output
Stop all pharmacological therapy and simply observe the patient on cardiac monitoring
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Cautious diuretic; inotrope only if hypoperfused, with continuous BP monitoring
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: For SBP 90–100 mmHg, treat cautiously with a diuretic and reserve inotropes for hypoperfusion — cool peripheries, mottling, oliguria, confusion, rising lactate (NICE). A well-perfused patient sitting at SBP 95 should not get dobutamine: perfusion is a separate question from blood pressure. Low-dose GTN only under continuous BP monitoring.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: A patient in cardiogenic shock has an SBP of 78 mmHg. Which approach is appropriate?
options: A vasodilator-led strategy with high-dose IV GTN to reduce afterload and relieve the pulmonary congestion rapidly
Inotrope/vasopressor ± mechanical support (dobutamine, noradrenaline, consider specialist mechanical circulatory support)
Repeated large IV crystalloid fluid boluses to restore preload and improve the low blood pressure
An IV beta-blocker to slow the heart rate and reduce myocardial oxygen demand in shock
Oral furosemide with early discharge home and outpatient cardiology follow-up arranged
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Inotrope/vasopressor ± mechanical support (dobutamine, noradrenaline, consider specialist mechanical circulatory support)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: For SBP <90 mmHg with hypoperfusion (cardiogenic shock): inotrope/vasopressor ± mechanical support — dobutamine (↑contractility/CO), noradrenaline (↑SVR), and specialist mechanical circulatory support if no response.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: Why is IV morphine no longer routinely recommended in acute heart failure?
options: Evidence shows harm — increased ventilation rates and mortality in registries
It is too expensive and not cost-effective compared with standard diuretic therapy
It causes dangerous hyperkalaemia by impairing renal potassium and acid excretion
It raises the systemic blood pressure dangerously and worsens myocardial oxygen demand
It interferes with furosemide absorption and blunts the diuretic response to treatment
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Evidence shows harm — increased ventilation rates and mortality in registries
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: Although historically used for anxiolysis and preload reduction, morphine is associated with increased ventilation rates and mortality, so it is avoided unless in a palliative context.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: In which situations is IV GTN specifically indicated in acute heart failure?
options: Cardiogenic shock with a systolic blood pressure below 90 mmHg
Isolated right heart failure only, with a raised JVP and peripheral oedema
All cases of acute heart failure, regardless of the blood pressure or cause
Septic acute heart failure only, driven by systemic vasodilation
Concomitant ischaemia, severe hypertension, or regurgitant aortic/mitral valve disease
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Concomitant ischaemia, severe hypertension, or regurgitant aortic/mitral valve disease
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: An IV nitrate is not routine in acute heart failure. NICE names three circumstances: concomitant myocardial ischaemia, severe hypertension, or regurgitant aortic or mitral valve disease — the last a classic exam point (acute MR from papillary muscle rupture). Give it only with close BP monitoring in a setting providing at least level 2 care. SBP >100 is the safety floor for giving it, not a definition of hypertensive AHF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: How does fluid management in cardiogenic shock differ from that in septic shock?
options: Both require aggressive fluid resuscitation with crystalloid boluses to restore preload and cardiac output
Cardiogenic shock is treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics first to cover the infective trigger
Cardiogenic shock needs far more fluids than septic shock to raise its low filling pressures
Neither is given any treatment acutely; both are simply observed until they settle on their own
In cardiogenic shock do not fluid-load a congested patient — give inotropes and arrange urgent revascularisation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: In cardiogenic shock do not fluid-load a congested patient — give inotropes and arrange urgent revascularisation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: Unlike septic shock, a congested patient in cardiogenic shock should not be fluid-loaded; management is inotropes plus urgent revascularisation. A cautious fluid challenge is appropriate where there are no signs of fluid overload (ESC), and is specifically indicated in right ventricular infarction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: What is the role of NIV/CPAP in acute heart failure?
options: It replaces diuretics entirely, so no IV furosemide is needed once CPAP is started to clear the pulmonary oedema
It is only used in cardiogenic shock, once systolic BP has fallen and inotropes such as dobutamine have been started
Used early if oxygen alone is insufficient — reduces work of breathing, decreases preload, improves oxygenation
It increases preload to support the circulation, raising venous return and left ventricular filling to boost output
It is reserved for palliative cases, offered only for comfort once active treatment of the heart failure is stopped
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Used early if oxygen alone is insufficient — reduces work of breathing, decreases preload, improves oxygenation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: NICE does not recommend non-invasive ventilation routinely for every patient with cardiogenic pulmonary oedema — the trigger is severe dyspnoea with acidaemia, or failure to respond to oxygen and medical therapy. Used at that point, it reduces work of breathing, decreases preload and afterload, and improves oxygenation. In cardiogenic pulmonary oedema CPAP is the usual first modality, with BiPAP (NIV proper) added mainly if the patient is hypercapnic or tiring. It is given alongside the IV diuretic, not instead of it, and is not restricted to shock or to palliative care. Invasive ventilation is for refractory cases.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: In cardiogenic shock, what are the respective roles of dobutamine and noradrenaline?
options: Dobutamine is an inotrope (↑contractility/CO); noradrenaline is a vasopressor (↑SVR)
Both are pure vasopressors that raise vascular resistance without affecting contractility
Dobutamine raises SVR by vasoconstriction; noradrenaline raises contractility and stroke volume
Both are vasodilators reducing systemic vascular resistance and afterload to improve flow
Dobutamine is a loop diuretic promoting fluid loss; noradrenaline is an inotrope agent
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Dobutamine is an inotrope (↑contractility/CO); noradrenaline is a vasopressor (↑SVR)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: Dobutamine increases contractility and cardiac output (inotrope); noradrenaline increases systemic vascular resistance (vasopressor). Specialist mechanical circulatory support is considered if there is no response.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: A 72-year-old man with known ischaemic cardiomyopathy presents with acute breathlessness, SpO₂ 84% on air, widespread crepitations, and pink frothy sputum. BP 90/60 mmHg, HR 120 bpm, peripheries cool and mottled, no urine output for 4 hours, lactate 4.1 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Sublingual GTN spray plus oral bisoprolol then reassess
Oral furosemide with early discharge home and GP follow-up
IV furosemide alone and observe on the ward overnight
IV fluids 500 mL bolus to support blood pressure and perfusion
IV furosemide + IV dobutamine + non-invasive ventilation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: IV furosemide + IV dobutamine + non-invasive ventilation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: This is cardiogenic shock — hypotension with hypoperfusion, not a low number alone. It needs IV loop diuretic for the congestion, non-invasive ventilation for the respiratory failure, and inotropic support; inotropes are reserved for potentially reversible cardiogenic shock and given where level 2 or 3 care is available (NICE). Oral furosemide is insufficient in this emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: What is the CXR finding most specific for cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (as opposed to ARDS)?
options: Bilateral diffuse infiltrates with normal heart size
Cardiomegaly + upper lobe blood diversion + Kerley B lines
